144::COMO;;# %%
145::COMO;;# All is well. We are now ready to do some predictive modeling!
146::COMO;;#
147::COMO;;# Gradient Boosting
148::COMO;;# -----------------
149::COMO;;#
150::COMO;;# Gradient Boosting Regression with decision trees is often flexible enough to
151::COMO;;# efficiently handle heterogeneous tabular data with a mix of categorical and
152::COMO;;# numerical features as long as the number of samples is large enough.
153::COMO;;#
154::COMO;;# Here, we use the modern
155::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` with native support
156::COMO;;# for categorical features. Therefore, we only need to set
157::COMO;;# `categorical_features="from_dtype"` such that features with categorical dtype
158::COMO;;# are considered categorical features. For reference, we extract the categorical
159::COMO;;# features from the dataframe based on the dtype. The internal trees use a dedicated
160::COMO;;# tree splitting rule for these features.
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# The numerical variables need no preprocessing and, for the sake of simplicity,
163::COMO;;# we only try the default hyper-parameters for this model:
171::COMO;;# %%
172::COMO;;#
173::COMO;;# Let's evaluate our gradient boosting model with the mean absolute error of the
174::COMO;;# relative demand averaged across our 5 time-based cross-validation splits:
200::COMO;;# %%
201::COMO;;# We see that we set `max_iter` large enough such that early stopping took place.
202::COMO;;#
203::COMO;;# This model has an average error around 4 to 5% of the maximum demand. This is
204::COMO;;# quite good for a first trial without any hyper-parameter tuning! We just had
205::COMO;;# to make the categorical variables explicit. Note that the time related
206::COMO;;# features are passed as is, i.e. without processing them. But this is not much
207::COMO;;# of a problem for tree-based models as they can learn a non-monotonic
208::COMO;;# relationship between ordinal input features and the target.
209::COMO;;#
210::COMO;;# This is not the case for linear regression models as we will see in the
211::COMO;;# following.
212::COMO;;#
213::COMO;;# Naive linear regression
214::COMO;;# -----------------------
215::COMO;;#
216::COMO;;# As usual for linear models, categorical variables need to be one-hot encoded.
217::COMO;;# For consistency, we scale the numerical features to the same 0-1 range using
218::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler`, although in this case it does not
219::COMO;;# impact the results much because they are already on comparable scales:
236::COMO;;# %%
237::COMO;;# It is affirmative to see that the selected `alpha_` is in our specified
238::COMO;;# range.
239::COMO;;#
240::COMO;;# The performance is not good: the average error is around 14% of the maximum
241::COMO;;# demand. This is more than three times higher than the average error of the
242::COMO;;# gradient boosting model. We can suspect that the naive original encoding
243::COMO;;# (merely min-max scaled) of the periodic time-related features might prevent
244::COMO;;# the linear regression model to properly leverage the time information: linear
245::COMO;;# regression does not automatically model non-monotonic relationships between
246::COMO;;# the input features and the target. Non-linear terms have to be engineered in
247::COMO;;# the input.
248::COMO;;#
249::COMO;;# For example, the raw numerical encoding of the `"hour"` feature prevents the
250::COMO;;# linear model from recognizing that an increase of hour in the morning from 6
251::COMO;;# to 8 should have a strong positive impact on the number of bike rentals while
252::COMO;;# an increase of similar magnitude in the evening from 18 to 20 should have a
253::COMO;;# strong negative impact on the predicted number of bike rentals.
254::COMO;;#
255::COMO;;# Time-steps as categories
256::COMO;;# ------------------------
257::COMO;;#
258::COMO;;# Since the time features are encoded in a discrete manner using integers (24
259::COMO;;# unique values in the "hours" feature), we could decide to treat those as
260::COMO;;# categorical variables using a one-hot encoding and thereby ignore any
261::COMO;;# assumption implied by the ordering of the hour values.
262::COMO;;#
263::COMO;;# Using one-hot encoding for the time features gives the linear model a lot
264::COMO;;# more flexibility as we introduce one additional feature per discrete time
265::COMO;;# level.
277::COMO;;# %%
278::COMO;;# The average error rate of this model is 10% which is much better than using
279::COMO;;# the original (ordinal) encoding of the time feature, confirming our intuition
280::COMO;;# that the linear regression model benefits from the added flexibility to not
281::COMO;;# treat time progression in a monotonic manner.
282::COMO;;#
283::COMO;;# However, this introduces a very large number of new features. If the time of
284::COMO;;# the day was represented in minutes since the start of the day instead of
285::COMO;;# hours, one-hot encoding would have introduced 1440 features instead of 24.
286::COMO;;# This could cause some significant overfitting. To avoid this we could use
287::COMO;;# :func:`sklearn.preprocessing.KBinsDiscretizer` instead to re-bin the number
288::COMO;;# of levels of fine-grained ordinal or numerical variables while still
289::COMO;;# benefitting from the non-monotonic expressivity advantages of one-hot
290::COMO;;# encoding.
291::COMO;;#
292::COMO;;# Finally, we also observe that one-hot encoding completely ignores the
293::COMO;;# ordering of the hour levels while this could be an interesting inductive bias
294::COMO;;# to preserve to some level. In the following we try to explore smooth,
295::COMO;;# non-monotonic encoding that locally preserves the relative ordering of time
296::COMO;;# features.
297::COMO;;#
298::COMO;;# Trigonometric features
299::COMO;;# ----------------------
300::COMO;;#
301::COMO;;# As a first attempt, we can try to encode each of those periodic features
302::COMO;;# using a sine and cosine transformation with the matching period.
303::COMO;;#
304::COMO;;# Each ordinal time feature is transformed into 2 features that together encode
305::COMO;;# equivalent information in a non-monotonic way, and more importantly without
306::COMO;;# any jump between the first and the last value of the periodic range.
312::COMO;;# %%
313::COMO;;#
314::COMO;;# Let us visualize the effect of this feature expansion on some synthetic hour
315::COMO;;# data with a bit of extrapolation beyond hour=23:
325::COMO;;# %%
326::COMO;;#
327::COMO;;# Let's use a 2D scatter plot with the hours encoded as colors to better see
328::COMO;;# how this representation maps the 24 hours of the day to a 2D space, akin to
329::COMO;;# some sort of a 24 hour version of an analog clock. Note that the "25th" hour
330::COMO;;# is mapped back to the 1st hour because of the periodic nature of the
331::COMO;;# sine/cosine representation.
339::COMO;;# %%
340::COMO;;#
341::COMO;;# We can now build a feature extraction pipeline using this strategy:
359::COMO;;# %%
360::COMO;;#
361::COMO;;# The performance of our linear regression model with this simple feature
362::COMO;;# engineering is a bit better than using the original ordinal time features but
363::COMO;;# worse than using the one-hot encoded time features. We will further analyze
364::COMO;;# possible reasons for this disappointing outcome at the end of this notebook.
365::COMO;;#
366::COMO;;# Periodic spline features
367::COMO;;# ------------------------
368::COMO;;#
369::COMO;;# We can try an alternative encoding of the periodic time-related features
370::COMO;;# using spline transformations with a large enough number of splines, and as a
371::COMO;;# result a larger number of expanded features compared to the sine/cosine
372::COMO;;# transformation:
377::COMC;;n_knots = n_splines + 1 # periodic and include_bias is True
385::COMO;;# %%
386::COMO;;#
387::COMO;;# Again, let us visualize the effect of this feature expansion on some
388::COMO;;# synthetic hour data with a bit of extrapolation beyond hour=23:
400::COMO;;# %%
401::COMO;;# Thanks to the use of the `extrapolation="periodic"` parameter, we observe
402::COMO;;# that the feature encoding stays smooth when extrapolating beyond midnight.
403::COMO;;#
404::COMO;;# We can now build a predictive pipeline using this alternative periodic
405::COMO;;# feature engineering strategy.
406::COMO;;#
407::COMO;;# It is possible to use fewer splines than discrete levels for those ordinal
408::COMO;;# values. This makes spline-based encoding more efficient than one-hot encoding
409::COMO;;# while preserving most of the expressivity:
424::COMO;;# %%
425::COMO;;# Spline features make it possible for the linear model to successfully
426::COMO;;# leverage the periodic time-related features and reduce the error from ~14% to
427::COMO;;# ~10% of the maximum demand, which is similar to what we observed with the
428::COMO;;# one-hot encoded features.
429::COMO;;#
430::COMO;;# Qualitative analysis of the impact of features on linear model predictions
431::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
432::COMO;;#
433::COMO;;# Here, we want to visualize the impact of the feature engineering choices on
434::COMO;;# the time related shape of the predictions.
435::COMO;;#
436::COMO;;# To do so we consider an arbitrary time-based split to compare the predictions
437::COMO;;# on a range of held out data points.
446::COMO;;# %%
447::COMO;;# We visualize those predictions by zooming on the last 96 hours (4 days) of
448::COMO;;# the test set to get some qualitative insights:
476::COMO;;# %%
477::COMO;;# We can draw the following conclusions from the above plot:
478::COMO;;#
479::COMO;;# - The **raw ordinal time-related features** are problematic because they do
480::COMO;;# not capture the natural periodicity: we observe a big jump in the
481::COMO;;# predictions at the end of each day when the hour features goes from 23 back
482::COMO;;# to 0. We can expect similar artifacts at the end of each week or each year.
483::COMO;;#
484::COMO;;# - As expected, the **trigonometric features** (sine and cosine) do not have
485::COMO;;# these discontinuities at midnight, but the linear regression model fails to
486::COMO;;# leverage those features to properly model intra-day variations.
487::COMO;;# Using trigonometric features for higher harmonics or additional
488::COMO;;# trigonometric features for the natural period with different phases could
489::COMO;;# potentially fix this problem.
490::COMO;;#
491::COMO;;# - the **periodic spline-based features** fix those two problems at once: they
492::COMO;;# give more expressivity to the linear model by making it possible to focus
493::COMO;;# on specific hours thanks to the use of 12 splines. Furthermore the
494::COMO;;# `extrapolation="periodic"` option enforces a smooth representation between
495::COMO;;# `hour=23` and `hour=0`.
496::COMO;;#
497::COMO;;# - The **one-hot encoded features** behave similarly to the periodic
498::COMO;;# spline-based features but are more spiky: for instance they can better
499::COMO;;# model the morning peak during the week days since this peak lasts shorter
500::COMO;;# than an hour. However, we will see in the following that what can be an
501::COMO;;# advantage for linear models is not necessarily one for more expressive
502::COMO;;# models.
503::COMO;;# %%
504::COMO;;# We can also compare the number of features extracted by each feature
505::COMO;;# engineering pipeline:
507::COMO;;# %%
509::COMO;;# %%
511::COMO;;# %%
513::COMO;;# %%
514::COMO;;# This confirms that the one-hot encoding and the spline encoding strategies
515::COMO;;# create a lot more features for the time representation than the alternatives,
516::COMO;;# which in turn gives the downstream linear model more flexibility (degrees of
517::COMO;;# freedom) to avoid underfitting.
518::COMO;;#
519::COMO;;# Finally, we observe that none of the linear models can approximate the true
520::COMO;;# bike rentals demand, especially for the peaks that can be very sharp at rush
521::COMO;;# hours during the working days but much flatter during the week-ends: the most
522::COMO;;# accurate linear models based on splines or one-hot encoding tend to forecast
523::COMO;;# peaks of commuting-related bike rentals even on the week-ends and
524::COMO;;# under-estimate the commuting-related events during the working days.
525::COMO;;#
526::COMO;;# These systematic prediction errors reveal a form of under-fitting and can be
527::COMO;;# explained by the lack of interactions terms between features, e.g.
528::COMO;;# "workingday" and features derived from "hours". This issue will be addressed
529::COMO;;# in the following section.
530::COMO;;# %%
531::COMO;;# Modeling pairwise interactions with splines and polynomial features
532::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------------
533::COMO;;#
534::COMO;;# Linear models do not automatically capture interaction effects between input
535::COMO;;# features. It does not help that some features are marginally non-linear as is
536::COMO;;# the case with features constructed by `SplineTransformer` (or one-hot
537::COMO;;# encoding or binning).
538::COMO;;#
539::COMO;;# However, it is possible to use the `PolynomialFeatures` class on coarse
540::COMO;;# grained spline encoded hours to model the "workingday"/"hours" interaction
541::COMO;;# explicitly without introducing too many new variables:
553::COMO;;# %%
554::COMO;;# Those features are then combined with the ones already computed in the
555::COMO;;# previous spline-base pipeline. We can observe a nice performance improvement
556::COMO;;# by modeling this pairwise interaction explicitly:
567::COMO;;# %%
568::COMO;;# Modeling non-linear feature interactions with kernels
569::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------
570::COMO;;#
571::COMO;;# The previous analysis highlighted the need to model the interactions between
572::COMO;;# `"workingday"` and `"hours"`. Another example of a such a non-linear
573::COMO;;# interaction that we would like to model could be the impact of the rain that
574::COMO;;# might not be the same during the working days and the week-ends and holidays
575::COMO;;# for instance.
576::COMO;;#
577::COMO;;# To model all such interactions, we could either use a polynomial expansion on
578::COMO;;# all marginal features at once, after their spline-based expansion. However,
579::COMO;;# this would create a quadratic number of features which can cause overfitting
580::COMO;;# and computational tractability issues.
581::COMO;;#
582::COMO;;# Alternatively, we can use the Nyström method to compute an approximate
583::COMO;;# polynomial kernel expansion. Let us try the latter:
591::COMO;;# %%
592::COMO;;#
593::COMO;;# We observe that this model can almost rival the performance of the gradient
594::COMO;;# boosted trees with an average error around 5% of the maximum demand.
595::COMO;;#
596::COMO;;# Note that while the final step of this pipeline is a linear regression model,
597::COMO;;# the intermediate steps such as the spline feature extraction and the Nyström
598::COMO;;# kernel approximation are highly non-linear. As a result the compound pipeline
599::COMO;;# is much more expressive than a simple linear regression model with raw features.
600::COMO;;#
601::COMO;;# For the sake of completeness, we also evaluate the combination of one-hot
602::COMO;;# encoding and kernel approximation:
615::COMO;;# %%
616::COMO;;# While one-hot encoded features were competitive with spline-based features
617::COMO;;# when using linear models, this is no longer the case when using a low-rank
618::COMO;;# approximation of a non-linear kernel: this can be explained by the fact that
619::COMO;;# spline features are smoother and allow the kernel approximation to find a
620::COMO;;# more expressive decision function.
621::COMO;;#
622::COMO;;# Let us now have a qualitative look at the predictions of the kernel models
623::COMO;;# and of the gradient boosted trees that should be able to better model
624::COMO;;# non-linear interactions between features:
631::COMO;;# %%
632::COMO;;# Again we zoom on the last 4 days of the test set:
659::COMO;;# %%
660::COMO;;# First, note that trees can naturally model non-linear feature interactions
661::COMO;;# since, by default, decision trees are allowed to grow beyond a depth of 2
662::COMO;;# levels.
663::COMO;;#
664::COMO;;# Here, we can observe that the combinations of spline features and non-linear
665::COMO;;# kernels works quite well and can almost rival the accuracy of the gradient
666::COMO;;# boosting regression trees.
667::COMO;;#
668::COMO;;# On the contrary, one-hot encoded time features do not perform that well with
669::COMO;;# the low rank kernel model. In particular, they significantly over-estimate
670::COMO;;# the low demand hours more than the competing models.
671::COMO;;#
672::COMO;;# We also observe that none of the models can successfully predict some of the
673::COMO;;# peak rentals at the rush hours during the working days. It is possible that
674::COMO;;# access to additional features would be required to further improve the
675::COMO;;# accuracy of the predictions. For instance, it could be useful to have access
676::COMO;;# to the geographical repartition of the fleet at any point in time or the
677::COMO;;# fraction of bikes that are immobilized because they need servicing.
678::COMO;;#
679::COMO;;# Let us finally get a more quantitative look at the prediction errors of those
680::COMO;;# three models using the true vs predicted demand scatter plots:
715::COMO;;# %%
716::COMO;;# This visualization confirms the conclusions we draw on the previous plot.
717::COMO;;#
718::COMO;;# All models under-estimate the high demand events (working day rush hours),
719::COMO;;# but gradient boosting a bit less so. The low demand events are well predicted
720::COMO;;# on average by gradient boosting while the one-hot polynomial regression
721::COMO;;# pipeline seems to systematically over-estimate demand in that regime. Overall
722::COMO;;# the predictions of the gradient boosted trees are closer to the diagonal than
723::COMO;;# for the kernel models.
724::COMO;;#
725::COMO;;# Concluding remarks
726::COMO;;# ------------------
727::COMO;;#
728::COMO;;# We note that we could have obtained slightly better results for kernel models
729::COMO;;# by using more components (higher rank kernel approximation) at the cost of
730::COMO;;# longer fit and prediction durations. For large values of `n_components`, the
731::COMO;;# performance of the one-hot encoded features would even match the spline
732::COMO;;# features.
733::COMO;;#
734::COMO;;# The `Nystroem` + `RidgeCV` regressor could also have been replaced by
735::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor` with one or two hidden layers
736::COMO;;# and we would have obtained quite similar results.
737::COMO;;#
738::COMO;;# The dataset we used in this case study is sampled on an hourly basis. However
739::COMO;;# cyclic spline-based features could model time-within-day or time-within-week
740::COMO;;# very efficiently with finer-grained time resolutions (for instance with
741::COMO;;# measurements taken every minute instead of every hour) without introducing
742::COMO;;# more features. One-hot encoding time representations would not offer this
743::COMO;;# flexibility.
744::COMO;;#
745::COMO;;# Finally, in this notebook we used `RidgeCV` because it is very efficient from
746::COMO;;# a computational point of view. However, it models the target variable as a
747::COMO;;# Gaussian random variable with constant variance. For positive regression
748::COMO;;# problems, it is likely that using a Poisson or Gamma distribution would make
749::COMO;;# more sense. This could be achieved by using
750::COMO;;# `GridSearchCV(TweedieRegressor(power=2), param_grid({"alpha": alphas}))`
751::COMO;;# instead of `RidgeCV`.
2::COMM;;================================
3::COMM;;Image denoising using kernel PCA
4::COMM;;================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how to use :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA` to
6::COMM;;denoise images. In short, we take advantage of the approximation function
7::COMM;;learned during `fit` to reconstruct the original image.
8::COMM;;We will compare the results with an exact reconstruction using
9::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`.
10::COMM;;We will use USPS digits dataset to reproduce presented in Sect. 4 of [1]_.
11::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
12::COMM;;.. [1] `Bakır, Gökhan H., Jason Weston, and Bernhard Schölkopf.
13::COMM;;"Learning to find pre-images."
14::COMM;;Advances in neural information processing systems 16 (2004): 449-456.
15::COMM;;<https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2003/file/ac1ad983e08ad3304a97e147f522747e-Paper.pdf>`_
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
19::COMO;;# %%
20::COMO;;# Load the dataset via OpenML
21::COMO;;# ---------------------------
22::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# The USPS digits datasets is available in OpenML. We use
24::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml` to get this dataset. In addition, we
25::COMO;;# normalize the dataset such that all pixel values are in the range (0, 1).
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# The idea will be to learn a PCA basis (with and without a kernel) on
34::COMO;;# noisy images and then use these models to reconstruct and denoise these
35::COMO;;# images.
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# Thus, we split our dataset into a training and testing set composed of 1,000
38::COMO;;# samples for the training and 100 samples for testing. These images are
39::COMO;;# noise-free and we will use them to evaluate the efficiency of the denoising
40::COMO;;# approaches. In addition, we create a copy of the original dataset and add a
41::COMO;;# Gaussian noise.
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# The idea of this application, is to show that we can denoise corrupted images
44::COMO;;# by learning a PCA basis on some uncorrupted images. We will use both a PCA
45::COMO;;# and a kernel-based PCA to solve this problem.
54::COMO;;# %%
55::COMO;;# In addition, we will create a helper function to qualitatively assess the
56::COMO;;# image reconstruction by plotting the test images.
60::COMM;;fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=10, ncols=10, figsize=(8, 8))
61::COMM;;for img, ax in zip(X, axs.ravel()):
62::COMM;;ax.imshow(img.reshape((16, 16)), cmap="Greys")
63::COMM;;ax.axis("off")
64::COMM;;fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=24)
65::COMM;;# %%
66::COMM;;# In addition, we will use the mean squared error (MSE) to quantitatively
67::COMM;;# assess the image reconstruction.
68::COMM;;#
69::COMM;;# Let's first have a look to see the difference between noise-free and noisy
70::COMM;;# images. We will check the test set in this regard.
71::COMM;;plot_digits(X_test, "Uncorrupted test images")
72::COMM;;plot_digits(
73::COMM;;X_test_noisy, f"Noisy test images\nMSE: {np.mean((X_test - X_test_noisy) ** 2):.2f}"
74::COMM;;)
75::COMM;;# %%
76::COMM;;# Learn the `PCA` basis
77::COMM;;# ---------------------
78::COMM;;#
79::COMM;;# We can now learn our PCA basis using both a linear PCA and a kernel PCA that
80::COMM;;# uses a radial basis function (RBF) kernel.
81::COMM;;from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, KernelPCA
82::COMM;;pca = PCA(n_components=32, random_state=42)
83::COMM;;kernel_pca = KernelPCA(
84::COMM;;n_components=400,
85::COMM;;kernel="rbf",
86::COMM;;gamma=1e-3,
87::COMM;;fit_inverse_transform=True,
88::COMM;;alpha=5e-3,
89::COMM;;random_state=42,
90::COMM;;)
91::COMM;;pca.fit(X_train_noisy)
92::COMM;;_ = kernel_pca.fit(X_train_noisy)
93::COMM;;# %%
94::COMM;;# Reconstruct and denoise test images
95::COMM;;# -----------------------------------
96::COMM;;#
97::COMM;;# Now, we can transform and reconstruct the noisy test set. Since we used less
98::COMM;;# components than the number of original features, we will get an approximation
99::COMM;;# of the original set. Indeed, by dropping the components explaining variance
100::COMM;;# in PCA the least, we hope to remove noise. Similar thinking happens in kernel
101::COMM;;# PCA; however, we expect a better reconstruction because we use a non-linear
102::COMM;;# kernel to learn the PCA basis and a kernel ridge to learn the mapping
103::COMM;;# function.
104::COMM;;X_reconstructed_kernel_pca = kernel_pca.inverse_transform(
105::COMM;;kernel_pca.transform(X_test_noisy)
106::COMM;;)
107::COMM;;X_reconstructed_pca = pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(X_test_noisy))
108::COMM;;# %%
109::COMM;;plot_digits(X_test, "Uncorrupted test images")
110::COMM;;plot_digits(
111::COMM;;X_reconstructed_pca,
112::COMM;;f"PCA reconstruction\nMSE: {np.mean((X_test - X_reconstructed_pca) ** 2):.2f}",
113::COMM;;)
114::COMM;;plot_digits(
115::COMM;;X_reconstructed_kernel_pca,
116::COMM;;(
117::COMM;;"Kernel PCA reconstruction\n"
118::COMM;;f"MSE: {np.mean((X_test - X_reconstructed_kernel_pca) ** 2):.2f}"
119::COMM;;),
120::COMM;;)
121::COMM;;# %%
122::COMM;;# PCA has a lower MSE than kernel PCA. However, the qualitative analysis might
123::COMM;;# not favor PCA instead of kernel PCA. We observe that kernel PCA is able to
124::COMM;;# remove background noise and provide a smoother image.
125::COMM;;#
126::COMM;;# However, it should be noted that the results of the denoising with kernel PCA
127::COMM;;# will depend of the parameters `n_components`, `gamma`, and `alpha`.

2::COMM;;==========================
3::COMM;;Model Complexity Influence
4::COMM;;==========================
5::COMM;;Demonstrate how model complexity influences both prediction accuracy and
6::COMM;;computational performance.
7::COMM;;We will be using two datasets:
8::COMM;;- :ref:`diabetes_dataset` for regression.
9::COMM;;This dataset consists of 10 measurements taken from diabetes patients.
10::COMM;;The task is to predict disease progression;
11::COMM;;- :ref:`20newsgroups_dataset` for classification. This dataset consists of
12::COMM;;newsgroup posts. The task is to predict on which topic (out of 20 topics)
13::COMM;;the post is written about.
14::COMM;;We will model the complexity influence on three different estimators:
15::COMM;;- :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.SGDClassifier` (for classification data)
16::COMM;;which implements stochastic gradient descent learning;
17::COMM;;- :class:`~sklearn.svm.NuSVR` (for regression data) which implements
18::COMM;;Nu support vector regression;
19::COMM;;- :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` builds an additive
20::COMM;;model in a forward stage-wise fashion. Notice that
21::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` is much faster
22::COMM;;than :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` starting with
23::COMM;;intermediate datasets (`n_samples >= 10_000`), which is not the case for
24::COMM;;this example.
25::COMM;;We make the model complexity vary through the choice of relevant model
26::COMM;;parameters in each of our selected models. Next, we will measure the influence
27::COMM;;on both computational performance (latency) and predictive power (MSE or
28::COMM;;Hamming Loss).
30::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
31::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
41::COMO;;# Initialize random generator
43::COMO;;##############################################################################
44::COMO;;# Load the data
45::COMO;;# -------------
46::COMO;;#
47::COMO;;# First we load both datasets.
48::COMO;;#
49::COMO;;# .. note:: We are using
50::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.fetch_20newsgroups_vectorized` to download 20
51::COMO;;# newsgroups dataset. It returns ready-to-use features.
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# .. note:: ``X`` of the 20 newsgroups dataset is a sparse matrix while ``X``
54::COMO;;# of diabetes dataset is a numpy array.
55::COMO;;#
58::COMM;;if case == "regression":
59::COMM;;X, y = datasets.load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)
60::COMM;;train_size = 0.8
61::COMM;;elif case == "classification":
62::COMM;;X, y = datasets.fetch_20newsgroups_vectorized(subset="all", return_X_y=True)
63::COMM;;train_size = 0.4 # to make the example run faster
64::COMM;;X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
65::COMM;;X, y, train_size=train_size, random_state=0
66::COMM;;)
67::COMM;;data = {"X_train": X_train, "X_test": X_test, "y_train": y_train, "y_test": y_test}
68::COMM;;return data
69::COMM;;regression_data = generate_data("regression")
70::COMM;;classification_data = generate_data("classification")
71::COMM;;##############################################################################
72::COMM;;# Benchmark influence
73::COMM;;# -------------------
74::COMM;;# Next, we can calculate the influence of the parameters on the given
75::COMM;;# estimator. In each round, we will set the estimator with the new value of
76::COMM;;# ``changing_param`` and we will be collecting the prediction times, prediction
77::COMM;;# performance and complexities to see how those changes affect the estimator.
78::COMM;;# We will calculate the complexity using ``complexity_computer`` passed as a
79::COMM;;# parameter.
80::COMM;;#
81::COMM;;def benchmark_influence(conf):
85::COMM;;prediction_times = []
86::COMM;;prediction_powers = []
87::COMM;;complexities = []
88::COMM;;for param_value in conf["changing_param_values"]:
89::COMM;;conf["tuned_params"][conf["changing_param"]] = param_value
90::COMM;;estimator = conf["estimator"](**conf["tuned_params"])
91::COMM;;print("Benchmarking %s" % estimator)
92::COMM;;estimator.fit(conf["data"]["X_train"], conf["data"]["y_train"])
93::COMM;;conf["postfit_hook"](estimator)
94::COMM;;complexity = conf["complexity_computer"](estimator)
95::COMM;;complexities.append(complexity)
96::COMM;;start_time = time.time()
97::COMM;;for _ in range(conf["n_samples"]):
98::COMM;;y_pred = estimator.predict(conf["data"]["X_test"])
99::COMM;;elapsed_time = (time.time() - start_time) / float(conf["n_samples"])
100::COMM;;prediction_times.append(elapsed_time)
101::COMM;;pred_score = conf["prediction_performance_computer"](
102::COMM;;conf["data"]["y_test"], y_pred
103::COMM;;)
104::COMM;;prediction_powers.append(pred_score)
105::COMM;;print(
106::COMM;;"Complexity: %d | %s: %.4f | Pred. Time: %fs\n"
107::COMM;;% (
108::COMM;;complexity,
109::COMM;;conf["prediction_performance_label"],
110::COMM;;pred_score,
111::COMM;;elapsed_time,
112::COMM;;)
113::COMM;;)
114::COMM;;return prediction_powers, prediction_times, complexities
115::COMM;;##############################################################################
116::COMM;;# Choose parameters
117::COMM;;# -----------------
118::COMM;;#
119::COMM;;# We choose the parameters for each of our estimators by making
120::COMM;;# a dictionary with all the necessary values.
121::COMM;;# ``changing_param`` is the name of the parameter which will vary in each
122::COMM;;# estimator.
123::COMM;;# Complexity will be defined by the ``complexity_label`` and calculated using
124::COMM;;# `complexity_computer`.
125::COMM;;# Also note that depending on the estimator type we are passing
126::COMM;;# different data.
127::COMM;;#
128::COMM;;def _count_nonzero_coefficients(estimator):
129::COMM;;a = estimator.coef_.toarray()
130::COMM;;return np.count_nonzero(a)
131::COMM;;configurations = [
132::COMM;;{
133::COMM;;"estimator": SGDClassifier,
134::COMM;;"tuned_params": {
135::COMM;;"penalty": "elasticnet",
136::COMM;;"alpha": 0.001,
137::COMM;;"loss": "modified_huber",
138::COMM;;"fit_intercept": True,
139::COMM;;"tol": 1e-1,
140::COMM;;"n_iter_no_change": 2,
141::COMM;;},
142::COMM;;"changing_param": "l1_ratio",
143::COMM;;"changing_param_values": [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9],
144::COMM;;"complexity_label": "non_zero coefficients",
145::COMM;;"complexity_computer": _count_nonzero_coefficients,
146::COMM;;"prediction_performance_computer": hamming_loss,
147::COMM;;"prediction_performance_label": "Hamming Loss (Misclassification Ratio)",
148::COMM;;"postfit_hook": lambda x: x.sparsify(),
149::COMM;;"data": classification_data,
150::COMM;;"n_samples": 5,
151::COMM;;},
152::COMM;;{
153::COMM;;"estimator": NuSVR,
154::COMM;;"tuned_params": {"C": 1e3, "gamma": 2**-15},
155::COMM;;"changing_param": "nu",
156::COMM;;"changing_param_values": [0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5],
157::COMM;;"complexity_label": "n_support_vectors",
158::COMM;;"complexity_computer": lambda x: len(x.support_vectors_),
159::COMM;;"data": regression_data,
160::COMM;;"postfit_hook": lambda x: x,
161::COMM;;"prediction_performance_computer": mean_squared_error,
162::COMM;;"prediction_performance_label": "MSE",
163::COMM;;"n_samples": 15,
164::COMM;;},
165::COMM;;{
166::COMM;;"estimator": GradientBoostingRegressor,
167::COMM;;"tuned_params": {
168::COMM;;"loss": "squared_error",
169::COMM;;"learning_rate": 0.05,
170::COMM;;"max_depth": 2,
171::COMM;;},
172::COMM;;"changing_param": "n_estimators",
173::COMM;;"changing_param_values": [10, 25, 50, 75, 100],
174::COMM;;"complexity_label": "n_trees",
175::COMM;;"complexity_computer": lambda x: x.n_estimators,
176::COMM;;"data": regression_data,
177::COMM;;"postfit_hook": lambda x: x,
178::COMM;;"prediction_performance_computer": mean_squared_error,
179::COMM;;"prediction_performance_label": "MSE",
180::COMM;;"n_samples": 15,
181::COMM;;},
182::COMM;;]
183::COMM;;##############################################################################
184::COMM;;# Run the code and plot the results
185::COMM;;# ---------------------------------
186::COMM;;#
187::COMM;;# We defined all the functions required to run our benchmark. Now, we will loop
188::COMM;;# over the different configurations that we defined previously. Subsequently,
189::COMM;;# we can analyze the plots obtained from the benchmark:
190::COMM;;# Relaxing the `L1` penalty in the SGD classifier reduces the prediction error
191::COMM;;# but leads to an increase in the training time.
192::COMM;;# We can draw a similar analysis regarding the training time which increases
193::COMM;;# with the number of support vectors with a Nu-SVR. However, we observed that
194::COMM;;# there is an optimal number of support vectors which reduces the prediction
195::COMM;;# error. Indeed, too few support vectors lead to an under-fitted model while
196::COMM;;# too many support vectors lead to an over-fitted model.
197::COMM;;# The exact same conclusion can be drawn for the gradient-boosting model. The
198::COMM;;# only the difference with the Nu-SVR is that having too many trees in the
199::COMM;;# ensemble is not as detrimental.
200::COMM;;#
201::COMM;;def plot_influence(conf, mse_values, prediction_times, complexities):
205::COMM;;fig = plt.figure()
206::COMM;;fig.subplots_adjust(right=0.75)
207::COMM;;# first axes (prediction error)
208::COMM;;ax1 = fig.add_subplot(111)
209::COMM;;line1 = ax1.plot(complexities, mse_values, c="tab:blue", ls="-")[0]
210::COMM;;ax1.set_xlabel("Model Complexity (%s)" % conf["complexity_label"])
211::COMM;;y1_label = conf["prediction_performance_label"]
212::COMM;;ax1.set_ylabel(y1_label)
213::COMM;;ax1.spines["left"].set_color(line1.get_color())
214::COMM;;ax1.yaxis.label.set_color(line1.get_color())
215::COMM;;ax1.tick_params(axis="y", colors=line1.get_color())
216::COMM;;# second axes (latency)
217::COMM;;ax2 = fig.add_subplot(111, sharex=ax1, frameon=False)
218::COMM;;line2 = ax2.plot(complexities, prediction_times, c="tab:orange", ls="-")[0]
219::COMM;;ax2.yaxis.tick_right()
220::COMM;;ax2.yaxis.set_label_position("right")
221::COMM;;y2_label = "Time (s)"
222::COMM;;ax2.set_ylabel(y2_label)
223::COMM;;ax1.spines["right"].set_color(line2.get_color())
224::COMM;;ax2.yaxis.label.set_color(line2.get_color())
225::COMM;;ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors=line2.get_color())
226::COMM;;plt.legend(
227::COMM;;(line1, line2), ("prediction error", "prediction latency"), loc="upper center"
228::COMM;;)
229::COMM;;plt.title(
230::COMM;;"Influence of varying '%s' on %s"
231::COMM;;% (conf["changing_param"], conf["estimator"].__name__)
232::COMM;;)
233::COMM;;for conf in configurations:
234::COMM;;prediction_performances, prediction_times, complexities = benchmark_influence(conf)
235::COMM;;plot_influence(conf, prediction_performances, prediction_times, complexities)
236::COMM;;plt.show()
237::COMM;;##############################################################################
238::COMM;;# Conclusion
239::COMM;;# ----------
240::COMM;;#
241::COMM;;# As a conclusion, we can deduce the following insights:
242::COMM;;#
243::COMM;;# * a model which is more complex (or expressive) will require a larger
244::COMM;;# training time;
245::COMM;;# * a more complex model does not guarantee to reduce the prediction error.
246::COMM;;#
247::COMM;;# These aspects are related to model generalization and avoiding model
248::COMM;;# under-fitting or over-fitting.
2::COMM;;======================================================
3::COMM;;Out-of-core classification of text documents
4::COMM;;======================================================
5::COMM;;This is an example showing how scikit-learn can be used for classification
6::COMM;;using an out-of-core approach: learning from data that doesn't fit into main
7::COMM;;memory. We make use of an online classifier, i.e., one that supports the
8::COMM;;partial_fit method, that will be fed with batches of examples. To guarantee
9::COMM;;that the features space remains the same over time we leverage a
10::COMM;;HashingVectorizer that will project each example into the same feature space.
11::COMM;;This is especially useful in the case of text classification where new
12::COMM;;features (words) may appear in each batch.

2::COMM;;====================================
3::COMM;;Outlier detection on a real data set
4::COMM;;====================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates the need for robust covariance estimation
6::COMM;;on a real data set. It is useful both for outlier detection and for
7::COMM;;a better understanding of the data structure.
8::COMM;;We selected two sets of two variables from the Wine data set
9::COMM;;as an illustration of what kind of analysis can be done with several
10::COMM;;outlier detection tools. For the purpose of visualization, we are working
11::COMM;;with two-dimensional examples, but one should be aware that things are
12::COMM;;not so trivial in high-dimension, as it will be pointed out.
13::COMM;;In both examples below, the main result is that the empirical covariance
14::COMM;;estimate, as a non-robust one, is highly influenced by the heterogeneous
15::COMM;;structure of the observations. Although the robust covariance estimate is
16::COMM;;able to focus on the main mode of the data distribution, it sticks to the
17::COMM;;assumption that the data should be Gaussian distributed, yielding some biased
18::COMM;;estimation of the data structure, but yet accurate to some extent.
19::COMM;;The One-Class SVM does not assume any parametric form of the data distribution
20::COMM;;and can therefore model the complex shape of the data much better.
22::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
23::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
24::COMO;;# %%
25::COMO;;# First example
26::COMO;;# -------------
27::COMO;;#
28::COMO;;# The first example illustrates how the Minimum Covariance Determinant
29::COMO;;# robust estimator can help concentrate on a relevant cluster when outlying
30::COMO;;# points exist. Here the empirical covariance estimation is skewed by points
31::COMO;;# outside of the main cluster. Of course, some screening tools would have pointed
32::COMO;;# out the presence of two clusters (Support Vector Machines, Gaussian Mixture
33::COMO;;# Models, univariate outlier detection, ...). But had it been a high-dimensional
34::COMO;;# example, none of these could be applied that easily.
45::COMO;;# %%
49::COMC;;X = load_wine()["data"][:, [1, 2]] # two clusters
52::COMO;;# Learn a frontier for outlier detection with several classifiers
84::COMO;;# %%
85::COMO;;# Second example
86::COMO;;# --------------
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# The second example shows the ability of the Minimum Covariance Determinant
89::COMO;;# robust estimator of covariance to concentrate on the main mode of the data
90::COMO;;# distribution: the location seems to be well estimated, although the
91::COMO;;# covariance is hard to estimate due to the banana-shaped distribution. Anyway,
92::COMO;;# we can get rid of some outlying observations. The One-Class SVM is able to
93::COMO;;# capture the real data structure, but the difficulty is to adjust its kernel
94::COMO;;# bandwidth parameter so as to obtain a good compromise between the shape of
95::COMO;;# the data scatter matrix and the risk of over-fitting the data.
96::COMC;;X = load_wine()["data"][:, [6, 9]] # "banana"-shaped
99::COMO;;# Learn a frontier for outlier detection with several classifiers

3::COMM;;Species distribution modeling

5::COMM;;Modeling species' geographic distributions is an important

10::COMM;;no unsuccessful observations), we cast this problem as a

12::COMM;;as our modeling tool. The dataset is provided by Phillips et. al. (2006).
13::COMM;;If available, the example uses

15::COMM;;to plot the coast lines and national boundaries of South America.

23::COMM;;Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela.

2::COMM;;=======================================
3::COMM;;Visualizing the stock market structure
4::COMM;;=======================================
5::COMM;;This example employs several unsupervised learning techniques to extract
6::COMM;;the stock market structure from variations in historical quotes.
7::COMM;;The quantity that we use is the daily variation in quote price: quotes
8::COMM;;that are linked tend to fluctuate in relation to each other during a day.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# Retrieve the data from Internet
14::COMO;;# -------------------------------
15::COMO;;#
16::COMO;;# The data is from 2003 - 2008. This is reasonably calm: not too long ago so
17::COMO;;# that we get high-tech firms, and before the 2008 crash. This kind of
18::COMO;;# historical data can be obtained from APIs like the
19::COMO;;# `data.nasdaq.com <https://data.nasdaq.com/>`_ and
20::COMO;;# `alphavantage.co <https://www.alphavantage.co/>`_.
93::COMO;;# The daily variations of the quotes are what carry the most information
95::COMO;;# %%
96::COMO;;# .. _stock_market:
97::COMO;;#
98::COMO;;# Learning a graph structure
99::COMO;;# --------------------------
100::COMO;;#
101::COMO;;# We use sparse inverse covariance estimation to find which quotes are
102::COMO;;# correlated conditionally on the others. Specifically, sparse inverse
103::COMO;;# covariance gives us a graph, that is a list of connections. For each
104::COMO;;# symbol, the symbols that it is connected to are those useful to explain
105::COMO;;# its fluctuations.
109::COMO;;# standardize the time series: using correlations rather than covariance
110::COMO;;# former is more efficient for structure recovery
114::COMO;;# %%
115::COMO;;# Clustering using affinity propagation
116::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# We use clustering to group together quotes that behave similarly. Here,
119::COMO;;# amongst the :ref:`various clustering techniques <clustering>` available
120::COMO;;# in the scikit-learn, we use :ref:`affinity_propagation` as it does
121::COMO;;# not enforce equal-size clusters, and it can choose automatically the
122::COMO;;# number of clusters from the data.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# Note that this gives us a different indication than the graph, as the
125::COMO;;# graph reflects conditional relations between variables, while the
126::COMO;;# clustering reflects marginal properties: variables clustered together can
127::COMO;;# be considered as having a similar impact at the level of the full stock
128::COMO;;# market.
134::COMO;;# %%
135::COMO;;# Embedding in 2D space
136::COMO;;# ---------------------
137::COMO;;#
138::COMO;;# For visualization purposes, we need to lay out the different symbols on a
139::COMO;;# 2D canvas. For this, we use :ref:`manifold` techniques to retrieve 2D
140::COMO;;# embedding.
141::COMO;;# We use a dense ``eigen_solver`` to achieve reproducibility (arpack is initiated
142::COMO;;# with the random vectors that we do not control). In addition, we use a large
143::COMO;;# number of neighbors to capture the large-scale structure.
144::COMO;;# Finding a low-dimension embedding for visualization: find the best position of
145::COMO;;# the nodes (the stocks) on a 2D plane
151::COMO;;# %%
152::COMO;;# Visualization
153::COMO;;# -------------
154::COMO;;#
155::COMO;;# The output of the 3 models are combined in a 2D graph where nodes
156::COMO;;# represent the stocks and edges the connections (partial correlations):
157::COMO;;#
158::COMO;;# - cluster labels are used to define the color of the nodes
159::COMO;;# - the sparse covariance model is used to display the strength of the edges
160::COMO;;# - the 2D embedding is used to position the nodes in the plan
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# This example has a fair amount of visualization-related code, as
163::COMO;;# visualization is crucial here to display the graph. One of the challenges
164::COMO;;# is to position the labels minimizing overlap. For this, we use an
165::COMO;;# heuristic based on the direction of the nearest neighbor along each
166::COMO;;# axis.
173::COMO;;# Plot the graph of partial correlations
179::COMO;;# Plot the nodes using the coordinates of our embedding
183::COMO;;# Plot the edges
185::COMO;;# a sequence of (*line0*, *line1*, *line2*), where::
186::COMO;;# linen = (x0, y0), (x1, y1), ... (xm, ym)
197::COMO;;# Add a label to each node. The challenge here is that we want to
198::COMO;;# position the labels to avoid overlap with other labels
2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;Lagged features for time series forecasting
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates how Polars-engineered lagged features can be used
6::COMM;;for time series forecasting with
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` on the Bike Sharing
8::COMM;;Demand dataset.
9::COMM;;See the example on
10::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_applications_plot_cyclical_feature_engineering.py`
11::COMM;;for some data exploration on this dataset and a demo on periodic feature
12::COMM;;engineering.
14::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
15::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# Analyzing the Bike Sharing Demand dataset
18::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# We start by loading the data from the OpenML repository as a raw parquet file
21::COMO;;# to illustrate how to work with an arbitrary parquet file instead of hiding this
22::COMO;;# step in a convenience tool such as `sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml`.
23::COMO;;#
24::COMO;;# The URL of the parquet file can be found in the JSON description of the
25::COMO;;# Bike Sharing Demand dataset with id 44063 on openml.org
26::COMO;;# (https://openml.org/search?type=data&status=active&id=44063).
27::COMO;;#
28::COMO;;# The `sha256` hash of the file is also provided to ensure the integrity of the
29::COMO;;# downloaded file.
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# We load the parquet file with Polars for feature engineering. Polars
41::COMO;;# automatically caches common subexpressions which are reused in multiple
42::COMO;;# expressions (like `pl.col("count").shift(1)` below). See
43::COMO;;# https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/lazy/optimizations/ for more information.
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# Next, we take a look at the statistical summary of the dataset
47::COMO;;# so that we can better understand the data that we are working with.
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# Let us look at the count of the seasons `"fall"`, `"spring"`, `"summer"`
53::COMO;;# and `"winter"` present in the dataset to confirm they are balanced.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Generating Polars-engineered lagged features
58::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------
59::COMO;;# Let's consider the problem of predicting the demand at the
60::COMO;;# next hour given past demands. Since the demand is a continuous
61::COMO;;# variable, one could intuitively use any regression model. However, we do
62::COMO;;# not have the usual `(X_train, y_train)` dataset. Instead, we just have
63::COMO;;# the `y_train` demand data sequentially organized by time.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# Watch out however, the first lines have undefined values because their own
81::COMO;;# past is unknown. This depends on how much lag we used:
83::COMO;;# %%
84::COMO;;# We can now separate the lagged features in a matrix `X` and the target variable
85::COMO;;# (the counts to predict) in an array of the same first dimension `y`.
90::COMO;;# %%
91::COMO;;# Naive evaluation of the next hour bike demand regression
92::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------
93::COMO;;# Let's randomly split our tabularized dataset to train a gradient
94::COMO;;# boosting regression tree (GBRT) model and evaluate it using Mean
95::COMO;;# Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). If our model is aimed at forecasting
96::COMO;;# (i.e., predicting future data from past data), we should not use training
97::COMO;;# data that are ulterior to the testing data. In time series machine learning
98::COMO;;# the "i.i.d" (independent and identically distributed) assumption does not
99::COMO;;# hold true as the data points are not independent and have a temporal
100::COMO;;# relationship.
107::COMO;;# %%
108::COMO;;# Taking a look at the performance of the model.
112::COMO;;# %%
113::COMO;;# Proper next hour forecasting evaluation
114::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------
115::COMO;;# Let's use a proper evaluation splitting strategies that takes into account
116::COMO;;# the temporal structure of the dataset to evaluate our model's ability to
117::COMO;;# predict data points in the future (to avoid cheating by reading values from
118::COMO;;# the lagged features in the training set).
121::COMC;;n_splits=3, # to keep the notebook fast enough on common laptops
122::COMC;;gap=48, # 2 days data gap between train and test
123::COMC;;max_train_size=10000, # keep train sets of comparable sizes
124::COMC;;test_size=3000, # for 2 or 3 digits of precision in scores
127::COMO;;# %%
128::COMO;;# Training the model and evaluating its performance based on MAPE.
135::COMO;;# %%
136::COMO;;# The generalization error measured via a shuffled trained test split
137::COMO;;# is too optimistic. The generalization via a time-based split is likely to
138::COMO;;# be more representative of the true performance of the regression model.
139::COMO;;# Let's assess this variability of our error evaluation with proper
140::COMO;;# cross-validation:
146::COMO;;# %%
147::COMO;;# The variability across splits is quite large! In a real life setting
148::COMO;;# it would be advised to use more splits to better assess the variability.
149::COMO;;# Let's report the mean CV scores and their standard deviation from now on.
151::COMO;;# %%
152::COMO;;# We can compute several combinations of evaluation metrics and loss functions,
153::COMO;;# which are reported a bit below.
195::COMO;;# %%
196::COMO;;# Modeling predictive uncertainty via quantile regression
197::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------
198::COMO;;# Instead of modeling the expected value of the distribution of
199::COMO;;# :math:`Y|X` like the least squares and Poisson losses do, one could try to
200::COMO;;# estimate quantiles of the conditional distribution.
201::COMO;;#
202::COMO;;# :math:`Y|X=x_i` is expected to be a random variable for a given data point
203::COMO;;# :math:`x_i` because we expect that the number of rentals cannot be 100%
204::COMO;;# accurately predicted from the features. It can be influenced by other
205::COMO;;# variables not properly captured by the existing lagged features. For
206::COMO;;# instance whether or not it will rain in the next hour cannot be fully
207::COMO;;# anticipated from the past hours bike rental data. This is what we
208::COMO;;# call aleatoric uncertainty.
209::COMO;;#
210::COMO;;# Quantile regression makes it possible to give a finer description of that
211::COMO;;# distribution without making strong assumptions on its shape.
232::COMO;;# %%
233::COMO;;# Let us take a look at the losses that minimise each metric.
245::COMO;;# %%
246::COMO;;# Even if the score distributions overlap due to the variance in the dataset,
247::COMO;;# it is true that the average RMSE is lower when `loss="squared_error"`, whereas
248::COMO;;# the average MAPE is lower when `loss="absolute_error"` as expected. That is
249::COMO;;# also the case for the Mean Pinball Loss with the quantiles 5 and 95. The score
250::COMO;;# corresponding to the 50 quantile loss is overlapping with the score obtained
251::COMO;;# by minimizing other loss functions, which is also the case for the MAE.
252::COMO;;#
253::COMO;;# A qualitative look at the predictions
254::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
255::COMO;;# We can now visualize the performance of the model with regards
256::COMO;;# to the 5th percentile, median and the 95th percentile:
280::COMO;;# %%
281::COMO;;# We can now take a look at the predictions made by the regression models:
310::COMO;;# %%
311::COMO;;# Here it's interesting to notice that the blue area between the 5% and 95%
312::COMO;;# percentile estimators has a width that varies with the time of the day:
313::COMO;;#
314::COMO;;# - At night, the blue band is much narrower: the pair of models is quite
315::COMO;;# certain that there will be a small number of bike rentals. And furthermore
316::COMO;;# these seem correct in the sense that the actual demand stays in that blue
317::COMO;;# band.
318::COMO;;# - During the day, the blue band is much wider: the uncertainty grows, probably
319::COMO;;# because of the variability of the weather that can have a very large impact,
320::COMO;;# especially on week-ends.
321::COMO;;# - We can also see that during week-days, the commute pattern is still visible in
322::COMO;;# the 5% and 95% estimations.
323::COMO;;# - Finally, it is expected that 10% of the time, the actual demand does not lie
324::COMO;;# between the 5% and 95% percentile estimates. On this test span, the actual
325::COMO;;# demand seems to be higher, especially during the rush hours. It might reveal that
326::COMO;;# our 95% percentile estimator underestimates the demand peaks. This could be be
327::COMO;;# quantitatively confirmed by computing empirical coverage numbers as done in
328::COMO;;# the :ref:`calibration of confidence intervals <calibration-section>`.
329::COMO;;#
330::COMO;;# Looking at the performance of non-linear regression models vs
331::COMO;;# the best models:
356::COMO;;# %%
357::COMO;;# Conclusion
358::COMO;;# ----------
359::COMO;;# Through this example we explored time series forecasting using lagged
360::COMO;;# features. We compared a naive regression (using the standardized
361::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split`) with a proper time
362::COMO;;# series evaluation strategy using
363::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit`. We observed that the
364::COMO;;# model trained using :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split`,
365::COMO;;# having a default value of `shuffle` set to `True` produced an overly
366::COMO;;# optimistic Mean Average Percentage Error (MAPE). The results
367::COMO;;# produced from the time-based split better represent the performance
368::COMO;;# of our time-series regression model. We also analyzed the predictive uncertainty
369::COMO;;# of our model via Quantile Regression. Predictions based on the 5th and
370::COMO;;# 95th percentile using `loss="quantile"` provide us with a quantitative estimate
371::COMO;;# of the uncertainty of the forecasts made by our time series regression model.
372::COMO;;# Uncertainty estimation can also be performed
373::COMO;;# using `MAPIE <https://mapie.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html>`_,
374::COMO;;# that provides an implementation based on recent work on conformal prediction
375::COMO;;# methods and estimates both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty at the same time.
376::COMO;;# Furthermore, functionalities provided
377::COMO;;# by `sktime <https://www.sktime.net/en/latest/users.html>`_
378::COMO;;# can be used to extend scikit-learn estimators by making use of recursive time
379::COMO;;# series forecasting, that enables dynamic predictions of future values.
2::COMM;;======================================================================
3::COMM;;Compressive sensing: tomography reconstruction with L1 prior (Lasso)
4::COMM;;======================================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows the reconstruction of an image from a set of parallel
6::COMM;;projections, acquired along different angles. Such a dataset is acquired in
7::COMM;;**computed tomography** (CT).
8::COMM;;Without any prior information on the sample, the number of projections
9::COMM;;required to reconstruct the image is of the order of the linear size
10::COMM;;``l`` of the image (in pixels). For simplicity we consider here a sparse
11::COMM;;image, where only pixels on the boundary of objects have a non-zero
12::COMM;;value. Such data could correspond for example to a cellular material.
13::COMM;;Note however that most images are sparse in a different basis, such as
14::COMM;;the Haar wavelets. Only ``l/7`` projections are acquired, therefore it is
15::COMM;;necessary to use prior information available on the sample (its
16::COMM;;sparsity): this is an example of **compressive sensing**.
17::COMM;;The tomography projection operation is a linear transformation. In
18::COMM;;addition to the data-fidelity term corresponding to a linear regression,
19::COMM;;we penalize the L1 norm of the image to account for its sparsity. The
20::COMM;;resulting optimization problem is called the :ref:`lasso`. We use the
21::COMM;;class :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso`, that uses the coordinate descent
22::COMM;;algorithm. Importantly, this implementation is more computationally efficient
23::COMM;;on a sparse matrix, than the projection operator used here.
24::COMM;;The reconstruction with L1 penalization gives a result with zero error
25::COMM;;(all pixels are successfully labeled with 0 or 1), even if noise was
26::COMM;;added to the projections. In comparison, an L2 penalization
27::COMM;;(:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`) produces a large number of labeling
28::COMM;;errors for the pixels. Important artifacts are observed on the
29::COMM;;reconstructed image, contrary to the L1 penalization. Note in particular
30::COMM;;the circular artifact separating the pixels in the corners, that have
31::COMM;;contributed to fewer projections than the central disk.
33::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
34::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
52::COMM;;Parameters
53::COMM;;----------
54::COMM;;l_x : int
55::COMM;;linear size of image array
56::COMM;;n_dir : int
57::COMM;;number of angles at which projections are acquired.
58::COMM;;Returns
59::COMM;;-------
60::COMM;;p : sparse matrix of shape (n_dir l_x, l_x**2)
78::COMM;;rs = np.random.RandomState(0)
79::COMM;;n_pts = 36
80::COMM;;x, y = np.ogrid[0:l, 0:l]
81::COMM;;mask_outer = (x - l / 2.0) ** 2 + (y - l / 2.0) ** 2 < (l / 2.0) ** 2
82::COMM;;mask = np.zeros((l, l))
83::COMM;;points = l * rs.rand(2, n_pts)
84::COMM;;mask[(points[0]).astype(int), (points[1]).astype(int)] = 1
85::COMM;;mask = ndimage.gaussian_filter(mask, sigma=l / n_pts)
86::COMM;;res = np.logical_and(mask > mask.mean(), mask_outer)
87::COMM;;return np.logical_xor(res, ndimage.binary_erosion(res))
88::COMM;;# Generate synthetic images, and projections
89::COMM;;l = 128
90::COMM;;proj_operator = build_projection_operator(l, l // 7)
91::COMM;;data = generate_synthetic_data()
92::COMM;;proj = proj_operator @ data.ravel()[:, np.newaxis]
93::COMM;;proj += 0.15 * np.random.randn(*proj.shape)
94::COMM;;# Reconstruction with L2 (Ridge) penalization
95::COMM;;rgr_ridge = Ridge(alpha=0.2)
96::COMM;;rgr_ridge.fit(proj_operator, proj.ravel())
97::COMM;;rec_l2 = rgr_ridge.coef_.reshape(l, l)
98::COMM;;# Reconstruction with L1 (Lasso) penalization
99::COMM;;# the best value of alpha was determined using cross validation
100::COMM;;# with LassoCV
101::COMM;;rgr_lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.001)
102::COMM;;rgr_lasso.fit(proj_operator, proj.ravel())
103::COMM;;rec_l1 = rgr_lasso.coef_.reshape(l, l)
104::COMM;;plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3.3))
105::COMM;;plt.subplot(131)

107::COMM;;plt.axis("off")
108::COMM;;plt.title("original image")

111::COMM;;plt.title("L2 penalization")

2::COMM;;===============================
3::COMM;;Wikipedia principal eigenvector
4::COMM;;===============================
5::COMM;;A classical way to assert the relative importance of vertices in a
6::COMM;;graph is to compute the principal eigenvector of the adjacency matrix
7::COMM;;so as to assign to each vertex the values of the components of the first
8::COMM;;eigenvector as a centrality score: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvector_centrality.
9::COMM;;On the graph of webpages and links those values are called the PageRank
10::COMM;;scores by Google.
11::COMM;;The goal of this example is to analyze the graph of links inside
12::COMM;;wikipedia articles to rank articles by relative importance according to
13::COMM;;this eigenvector centrality.
14::COMM;;The traditional way to compute the principal eigenvector is to use the
15::COMM;;`power iteration method <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_iteration>`_.
16::COMM;;Here the computation is achieved thanks to Martinsson's Randomized SVD
17::COMM;;algorithm implemented in scikit-learn.
18::COMM;;The graph data is fetched from the DBpedia dumps. DBpedia is an extraction
19::COMM;;of the latent structured data of the Wikipedia content.
21::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
22::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

33::COMO;;# Download data, if not already on disk
34::COMO;;# -------------------------------------

52::COMO;;# --------------------------

56::COMM;;return index_map.setdefault(k, len(index_map))

74::COMM;;# compute the transitive closure

76::COMM;;for l, source in enumerate(redirects.keys()):

87::COMM;;if l % 1000000 == 0:
88::COMM;;print("[%s] line: %08d" % (datetime.now().isoformat(), l))
89::COMM;;return redirects

145::COMM;;# ---------------------------
146::COMM;;def centrality_scores(X, alpha=0.85, max_iter=100, tol=1e-10):
155::COMM;;n = X.shape[0]
156::COMM;;X = X.copy()
157::COMM;;incoming_counts = np.asarray(X.sum(axis=1)).ravel()
158::COMM;;print("Normalizing the graph")
159::COMM;;for i in incoming_counts.nonzero()[0]:
160::COMM;;X.data[X.indptr[i] : X.indptr[i + 1]] *= 1.0 / incoming_counts[i]
161::COMM;;dangle = np.asarray(np.where(np.isclose(X.sum(axis=1), 0), 1.0 / n, 0)).ravel()
162::COMM;;scores = np.full(n, 1.0 / n, dtype=np.float32) # initial guess
163::COMM;;for i in range(max_iter):
164::COMM;;print("power iteration #%d" % i)
165::COMM;;prev_scores = scores
166::COMM;;scores = (
167::COMM;;alpha * (scores * X + np.dot(dangle, prev_scores))
168::COMM;;+ (1 - alpha) * prev_scores.sum() / n
169::COMM;;)
170::COMM;;# check convergence: normalized l_inf norm
171::COMM;;scores_max = np.abs(scores).max()
172::COMM;;if scores_max == 0.0:
173::COMM;;scores_max = 1.0
174::COMM;;err = np.abs(scores - prev_scores).max() / scores_max
175::COMM;;print("error: %0.6f" % err)
176::COMM;;if err < n * tol:
177::COMM;;return scores
178::COMM;;return scores
179::COMM;;print("Computing principal eigenvector score using a power iteration method")
180::COMM;;t0 = time()
181::COMM;;scores = centrality_scores(X, max_iter=100)
182::COMM;;print("done in %0.3fs" % (time() - t0))
183::COMM;;pprint([names[i] for i in np.abs(scores).argsort()[-10:]])

2::COMM;;=============================================
3::COMM;;A demo of the Spectral Biclustering algorithm
4::COMM;;=============================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates how to generate a checkerboard dataset and bicluster
6::COMM;;it using the :class:`~sklearn.cluster.SpectralBiclustering` algorithm. The
7::COMM;;spectral biclustering algorithm is specifically designed to cluster data by
8::COMM;;simultaneously considering both the rows (samples) and columns (features) of a
9::COMM;;matrix. It aims to identify patterns not only between samples but also within
10::COMM;;subsets of samples, allowing for the detection of localized structure within the
11::COMM;;data. This makes spectral biclustering particularly well-suited for datasets
12::COMM;;where the order or arrangement of features is fixed, such as in images, time
13::COMM;;series, or genomes.
14::COMM;;The data is generated, then shuffled and passed to the spectral biclustering
15::COMM;;algorithm. The rows and columns of the shuffled matrix are then rearranged to
16::COMM;;plot the biclusters found.
18::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
19::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
20::COMO;;# %%
21::COMO;;# Generate sample data
22::COMO;;# --------------------
23::COMO;;# We generate the sample data using the
24::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.make_checkerboard` function. Each pixel within
25::COMO;;# `shape=(300, 300)` represents with its color a value from a uniform
26::COMO;;# distribution. The noise is added from a normal distribution, where the value
27::COMO;;# chosen for `noise` is the standard deviation.
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# As you can see, the data is distributed over 12 cluster cells and is
30::COMO;;# relatively well distinguishable.
40::COMO;;# %%
41::COMO;;# We shuffle the data and the goal is to reconstruct it afterwards using
42::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.SpectralBiclustering`.
44::COMO;;# Creating lists of shuffled row and column indices
48::COMO;;# %%
49::COMO;;# We redefine the shuffled data and plot it. We observe that we lost the
50::COMO;;# structure of original data matrix.
55::COMO;;# %%
56::COMO;;# Fitting `SpectralBiclustering`
57::COMO;;# ------------------------------
58::COMO;;# We fit the model and compare the obtained clusters with the ground truth. Note
59::COMO;;# that when creating the model we specify the same number of clusters that we
60::COMO;;# used to create the dataset (`n_clusters = (4, 3)`), which will contribute to
61::COMO;;# obtain a good result.
66::COMO;;# Compute the similarity of two sets of biclusters
71::COMO;;# %%
72::COMO;;# The score is between 0 and 1, where 1 corresponds to a perfect matching. It
73::COMO;;# shows the quality of the biclustering.
74::COMO;;# %%
75::COMO;;# Plotting results
76::COMO;;# ----------------
77::COMO;;# Now, we rearrange the data based on the row and column labels assigned by the
78::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.SpectralBiclustering` model in ascending order and
79::COMO;;# plot again. The `row_labels_` range from 0 to 3, while the `column_labels_`
80::COMO;;# range from 0 to 2, representing a total of 4 clusters per row and 3 clusters
81::COMO;;# per column.
82::COMO;;# Reordering first the rows and then the columns.
88::COMO;;# %%
89::COMO;;# As a last step, we want to demonstrate the relationships between the row
90::COMO;;# and column labels assigned by the model. Therefore, we create a grid with
91::COMO;;# :func:`numpy.outer`, which takes the sorted `row_labels_` and `column_labels_`
92::COMO;;# and adds 1 to each to ensure that the labels start from 1 instead of 0 for
93::COMO;;# better visualization.
100::COMO;;# %%
101::COMO;;# The outer product of the row and column label vectors shows a representation
102::COMO;;# of the checkerboard structure, where different combinations of row and column
103::COMO;;# labels are represented by different shades of blue.

2::COMM;;======================================
3::COMM;;Probability calibration of classifiers
4::COMM;;======================================
5::COMM;;When performing classification you often want to predict not only
6::COMM;;the class label, but also the associated probability. This probability
7::COMM;;gives you some kind of confidence on the prediction. However, not all
8::COMM;;classifiers provide well-calibrated probabilities, some being over-confident
9::COMM;;while others being under-confident. Thus, a separate calibration of predicted
10::COMM;;probabilities is often desirable as a postprocessing. This example illustrates
11::COMM;;two different methods for this calibration and evaluates the quality of the
12::COMM;;returned probabilities using Brier's score
13::COMM;;(see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brier_score).
14::COMM;;Compared are the estimated probability using a Gaussian naive Bayes classifier
15::COMM;;without calibration, with a sigmoid calibration, and with a non-parametric
16::COMM;;isotonic calibration. One can observe that only the non-parametric model is
17::COMM;;able to provide a probability calibration that returns probabilities close
18::COMM;;to the expected 0.5 for most of the samples belonging to the middle
19::COMM;;cluster with heterogeneous labels. This results in a significantly improved
20::COMM;;Brier score.

23::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

33::COMO;;# blob is therefore 0.5.
