16::COMO;;# -------
17::COMO;;#
18::COMO;;# We will use a synthetic binary classification dataset with 100,000 samples
19::COMO;;# and 20 features. Of the 20 features, only 2 are informative, 10 are
20::COMO;;# redundant (random combinations of the informative features) and the
21::COMO;;# remaining 8 are uninformative (random numbers). Of the 100,000 samples, 1,000
22::COMO;;# will be used for model fitting and the rest for testing.
31::COMO;;# %%
32::COMO;;# Calibration curves
33::COMO;;# ------------------
34::COMO;;#
35::COMO;;# Gaussian Naive Bayes
36::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# First, we will compare:
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` (used as baseline
41::COMO;;# since very often, properly regularized logistic regression is well
42::COMO;;# calibrated by default thanks to the use of the log-loss)
43::COMO;;# * Uncalibrated :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB`
44::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB` with isotonic and sigmoid
45::COMO;;# calibration (see :ref:`User Guide <calibration>`)
46::COMO;;#
47::COMO;;# Calibration curves for all 4 conditions are plotted below, with the average
48::COMO;;# predicted probability for each bin on the x-axis and the fraction of positive
49::COMO;;# classes in each bin on the y-axis.
65::COMO;;# %%
85::COMO;;# Add histogram
100::COMO;;# %%
101::COMO;;# Uncalibrated :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB` is poorly calibrated
102::COMO;;# because of
103::COMO;;# the redundant features which violate the assumption of feature-independence
104::COMO;;# and result in an overly confident classifier, which is indicated by the
105::COMO;;# typical transposed-sigmoid curve. Calibration of the probabilities of
106::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB` with :ref:`isotonic` can fix
107::COMO;;# this issue as can be seen from the nearly diagonal calibration curve.
108::COMO;;# :ref:`Sigmoid regression <sigmoid_regressor>` also improves calibration
109::COMO;;# slightly,
110::COMO;;# albeit not as strongly as the non-parametric isotonic regression. This can be
111::COMO;;# attributed to the fact that we have plenty of calibration data such that the
112::COMO;;# greater flexibility of the non-parametric model can be exploited.
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# Below we will make a quantitative analysis considering several classification
115::COMO;;# metrics: :ref:`brier_score_loss`, :ref:`log_loss`,
116::COMO;;# :ref:`precision, recall, F1 score <precision_recall_f_measure_metrics>` and
117::COMO;;# :ref:`ROC AUC <roc_metrics>`.
143::COMO;;# %%
144::COMO;;# Notice that although calibration improves the :ref:`brier_score_loss` (a
145::COMO;;# metric composed
146::COMO;;# of calibration term and refinement term) and :ref:`log_loss`, it does not
147::COMO;;# significantly alter the prediction accuracy measures (precision, recall and
148::COMO;;# F1 score).
149::COMO;;# This is because calibration should not significantly change prediction
150::COMO;;# probabilities at the location of the decision threshold (at x = 0.5 on the
151::COMO;;# graph). Calibration should however, make the predicted probabilities more
152::COMO;;# accurate and thus more useful for making allocation decisions under
153::COMO;;# uncertainty.
154::COMO;;# Further, ROC AUC, should not change at all because calibration is a
155::COMO;;# monotonic transformation. Indeed, no rank metrics are affected by
156::COMO;;# calibration.
157::COMO;;#
158::COMO;;# Linear support vector classifier
159::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
160::COMO;;# Next, we will compare:
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` (baseline)
163::COMO;;# * Uncalibrated :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`. Since SVC does not output
164::COMO;;# probabilities by default, we naively scale the output of the
165::COMO;;# :term:`decision_function` into [0, 1] by applying min-max scaling.
166::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC` with isotonic and sigmoid
167::COMO;;# calibration (see :ref:`User Guide <calibration>`)
180::COMM;;df = self.decision_function(X)
181::COMM;;calibrated_df = (df - self.df_min_) / (self.df_max_ - self.df_min_)
182::COMM;;proba_pos_class = np.clip(calibrated_df, 0, 1)
183::COMM;;proba_neg_class = 1 - proba_pos_class
184::COMM;;proba = np.c_[proba_neg_class, proba_pos_class]
185::COMM;;return proba
186::COMM;;# %%
187::COMM;;lr = LogisticRegression(C=1.0)
188::COMM;;svc = NaivelyCalibratedLinearSVC(max_iter=10_000)
189::COMM;;svc_isotonic = CalibratedClassifierCV(svc, cv=2, method="isotonic")
190::COMM;;svc_sigmoid = CalibratedClassifierCV(svc, cv=2, method="sigmoid")
191::COMM;;clf_list = [
192::COMM;;(lr, "Logistic"),
193::COMM;;(svc, "SVC"),
194::COMM;;(svc_isotonic, "SVC + Isotonic"),
195::COMM;;(svc_sigmoid, "SVC + Sigmoid"),
196::COMM;;]
197::COMM;;# %%
198::COMM;;fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
199::COMM;;gs = GridSpec(4, 2)
200::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve = fig.add_subplot(gs[:2, :2])
201::COMM;;calibration_displays = {}
202::COMM;;for i, (clf, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
203::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
204::COMM;;display = CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator(
205::COMM;;clf,
206::COMM;;X_test,
207::COMM;;y_test,
208::COMM;;n_bins=10,
209::COMM;;name=name,
210::COMM;;ax=ax_calibration_curve,
211::COMM;;color=colors(i),
212::COMM;;)
213::COMM;;calibration_displays[name] = display
214::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve.grid()
215::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve.set_title("Calibration plots (SVC)")
216::COMM;;# Add histogram
217::COMM;;grid_positions = [(2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1)]
218::COMM;;for i, (_, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
219::COMM;;row, col = grid_positions[i]
220::COMM;;ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])
221::COMM;;ax.hist(
222::COMM;;calibration_displays[name].y_prob,
223::COMM;;range=(0, 1),
224::COMM;;bins=10,
225::COMM;;label=name,
226::COMM;;color=colors(i),
227::COMM;;)
228::COMM;;ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Mean predicted probability", ylabel="Count")
229::COMM;;plt.tight_layout()
230::COMM;;plt.show()
231::COMM;;# %%
232::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC` shows the opposite
233::COMM;;# behavior to :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB`; the calibration
234::COMM;;# curve has a sigmoid shape, which is typical for an under-confident
235::COMM;;# classifier. In the case of :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`, this is caused
236::COMM;;# by the margin property of the hinge loss, which focuses on samples that are
237::COMM;;# close to the decision boundary (support vectors). Samples that are far
238::COMM;;# away from the decision boundary do not impact the hinge loss. It thus makes
239::COMM;;# sense that :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC` does not try to separate samples
240::COMM;;# in the high confidence region regions. This leads to flatter calibration
241::COMM;;# curves near 0 and 1 and is empirically shown with a variety of datasets
242::COMM;;# in Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana [1]_.
243::COMM;;#
244::COMM;;# Both kinds of calibration (sigmoid and isotonic) can fix this issue and
245::COMM;;# yield similar results.
246::COMM;;#
247::COMM;;# As before, we show the :ref:`brier_score_loss`, :ref:`log_loss`,
248::COMM;;# :ref:`precision, recall, F1 score <precision_recall_f_measure_metrics>` and
249::COMM;;# :ref:`ROC AUC <roc_metrics>`.
250::COMM;;scores = defaultdict(list)
251::COMM;;for i, (clf, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
252::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
253::COMM;;y_prob = clf.predict_proba(X_test)
254::COMM;;y_pred = clf.predict(X_test)
255::COMM;;scores["Classifier"].append(name)
256::COMM;;for metric in [brier_score_loss, log_loss, roc_auc_score]:
257::COMM;;score_name = metric.__name__.replace("_", " ").replace("score", "").capitalize()
258::COMM;;scores[score_name].append(metric(y_test, y_prob[:, 1]))
259::COMM;;for metric in [precision_score, recall_score, f1_score]:
260::COMM;;score_name = metric.__name__.replace("_", " ").replace("score", "").capitalize()
261::COMM;;scores[score_name].append(metric(y_test, y_pred))
262::COMM;;score_df = pd.DataFrame(scores).set_index("Classifier")
263::COMM;;score_df.round(decimals=3)
264::COMM;;score_df
265::COMM;;# %%
266::COMM;;# As with :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB` above, calibration improves
267::COMM;;# both :ref:`brier_score_loss` and :ref:`log_loss` but does not alter the
268::COMM;;# prediction accuracy measures (precision, recall and F1 score) much.
269::COMM;;#
270::COMM;;# Summary
271::COMM;;# -------
272::COMM;;#
273::COMM;;# Parametric sigmoid calibration can deal with situations where the calibration
274::COMM;;# curve of the base classifier is sigmoid (e.g., for
275::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`) but not where it is transposed-sigmoid
276::COMM;;# (e.g., :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB`). Non-parametric
277::COMM;;# isotonic calibration can deal with both situations but may require more
278::COMM;;# data to produce good results.
279::COMM;;#
280::COMM;;# References
281::COMM;;# ----------
282::COMM;;#
283::COMM;;# .. [1] `Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning
284::COMM;;# <https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/1102351.1102430>`_,
285::COMM;;# A. Niculescu-Mizil & R. Caruana, ICML 2005
2::COMM;;==================================================
3::COMM;;Probability Calibration for 3-class classification
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates how sigmoid :ref:`calibration <calibration>` changes
6::COMM;;predicted probabilities for a 3-class classification problem. Illustrated is
7::COMM;;the standard 2-simplex, where the three corners correspond to the three
8::COMM;;classes. Arrows point from the probability vectors predicted by an uncalibrated
9::COMM;;classifier to the probability vectors predicted by the same classifier after
10::COMM;;sigmoid calibration on a hold-out validation set. Colors indicate the true
11::COMM;;class of an instance (red: class 1, green: class 2, blue: class 3).
13::COMO;;# %%
14::COMO;;# Data
15::COMO;;# ----
16::COMO;;# Below, we generate a classification dataset with 2000 samples, 2 features
17::COMO;;# and 3 target classes. We then split the data as follows:
18::COMO;;#
19::COMO;;# * train: 600 samples (for training the classifier)
20::COMO;;# * valid: 400 samples (for calibrating predicted probabilities)
21::COMO;;# * test: 1000 samples
22::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# Note that we also create `X_train_valid` and `y_train_valid`, which consists
24::COMO;;# of both the train and valid subsets. This is used when we only want to train
25::COMO;;# the classifier but not calibrate the predicted probabilities.
26::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
27::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
38::COMO;;# %%
39::COMO;;# Fitting and calibration
40::COMO;;# -----------------------
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# First, we will train a :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier`
43::COMO;;# with 25 base estimators (trees) on the concatenated train and validation
44::COMO;;# data (1000 samples). This is the uncalibrated classifier.
48::COMO;;# %%
49::COMO;;# To train the calibrated classifier, we start with the same
50::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` but train it using only
51::COMO;;# the train data subset (600 samples) then calibrate, with `method='sigmoid'`,
52::COMO;;# using the valid data subset (400 samples) in a 2-stage process.
59::COMO;;# %%
60::COMO;;# Compare probabilities
61::COMO;;# ---------------------
62::COMO;;# Below we plot a 2-simplex with arrows showing the change in predicted
63::COMO;;# probabilities of the test samples.
69::COMO;;# Plot arrows
79::COMO;;# Plot perfect predictions, at each vertex
83::COMO;;# Plot boundaries of unit simplex
85::COMO;;# Annotate points 6 points around the simplex, and mid point inside simplex
150::COMO;;# Add grid
162::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# In the figure above, each vertex of the simplex represents
164::COMO;;# a perfectly predicted class (e.g., 1, 0, 0). The mid point
165::COMO;;# inside the simplex represents predicting the three classes with equal
166::COMO;;# probability (i.e., 1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Each arrow starts at the
167::COMO;;# uncalibrated probabilities and end with the arrow head at the calibrated
168::COMO;;# probability. The color of the arrow represents the true class of that test
169::COMO;;# sample.
170::COMO;;#
171::COMO;;# The uncalibrated classifier is overly confident in its predictions and
172::COMO;;# incurs a large :ref:`log loss <log_loss>`. The calibrated classifier incurs
173::COMO;;# a lower :ref:`log loss <log_loss>` due to two factors. First, notice in the
174::COMO;;# figure above that the arrows generally point away from the edges of the
175::COMO;;# simplex, where the probability of one class is 0. Second, a large proportion
176::COMO;;# of the arrows point towards the true class, e.g., green arrows (samples where
177::COMO;;# the true class is 'green') generally point towards the green vertex. This
178::COMO;;# results in fewer over-confident, 0 predicted probabilities and at the same
179::COMO;;# time an increase in the predicted probabilities of the correct class.
180::COMO;;# Thus, the calibrated classifier produces more accurate predicted probabilities
181::COMO;;# that incur a lower :ref:`log loss <log_loss>`
182::COMO;;#
183::COMO;;# We can show this objectively by comparing the :ref:`log loss <log_loss>` of
184::COMO;;# the uncalibrated and calibrated classifiers on the predictions of the 1000
185::COMO;;# test samples. Note that an alternative would have been to increase the number
186::COMO;;# of base estimators (trees) of the
187::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` which would have resulted
188::COMO;;# in a similar decrease in :ref:`log loss <log_loss>`.
195::COMO;;# %%
196::COMO;;# We can also assess calibration with the Brier score for probabilistics predictions
197::COMO;;# (lower is better, possible range is [0, 2]):
204::COMO;;# %%
205::COMO;;# According to the Brier score, the calibrated classifier is not better than
206::COMO;;# the original model.
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# Finally we generate a grid of possible uncalibrated probabilities over
209::COMO;;# the 2-simplex, compute the corresponding calibrated probabilities and
210::COMO;;# plot arrows for each. The arrows are colored according the highest
211::COMO;;# uncalibrated probability. This illustrates the learned calibration map:
213::COMO;;# Generate grid of probability values
219::COMO;;# Use the three class-wise calibrators to compute calibrated probabilities
227::COMO;;# Re-normalize the calibrated predictions to make sure they stay inside the
228::COMO;;# simplex. This same renormalization step is performed internally by the
229::COMO;;# predict method of CalibratedClassifierCV on multiclass problems.
231::COMO;;# Plot changes in predicted probabilities induced by the calibrators
241::COMO;;# Plot the boundaries of the unit simplex
254::COMO;;# %%
255::COMO;;# One can observe that, on average, the calibrator is pushing highly confident
256::COMO;;# predictions away from the boundaries of the simplex while simultaneously
257::COMO;;# moving uncertain predictions towards one of three modes, one for each class.
258::COMO;;# We can also observe that the mapping is not symmetric. Furthermore some
259::COMO;;# arrows seem to cross class assignment boundaries which is not necessarily
260::COMO;;# what one would expect from a calibration map as it means that some predicted
261::COMO;;# classes will change after calibration.
262::COMO;;#
263::COMO;;# All in all, the One-vs-Rest multiclass-calibration strategy implemented in
264::COMO;;# `CalibratedClassifierCV` should not be trusted blindly.
2::COMM;;========================================
3::COMM;;Comparison of Calibration of Classifiers
4::COMM;;========================================
5::COMM;;Well calibrated classifiers are probabilistic classifiers for which the output
6::COMM;;of :term:`predict_proba` can be directly interpreted as a confidence level.
7::COMM;;For instance, a well calibrated (binary) classifier should classify the samples
8::COMM;;such that for the samples to which it gave a :term:`predict_proba` value close
9::COMM;;to 0.8, approximately 80% actually belong to the positive class.
10::COMM;;In this example we will compare the calibration of four different
11::COMM;;models: :ref:`Logistic_regression`, :ref:`gaussian_naive_bayes`,
12::COMM;;:ref:`Random Forest Classifier <forest>` and :ref:`Linear SVM
13::COMM;;<svm_classification>`.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMO;;# %%
18::COMO;;# Dataset
19::COMO;;# -------
20::COMO;;#
21::COMO;;# We will use a synthetic binary classification dataset with 100,000 samples
22::COMO;;# and 20 features. Of the 20 features, only 2 are informative, 2 are
23::COMO;;# redundant (random combinations of the informative features) and the
24::COMO;;# remaining 16 are uninformative (random numbers).
25::COMO;;#
26::COMO;;# Of the 100,000 samples, 100 will be used for model fitting and the remaining
27::COMO;;# for testing. Note that this split is quite unusual: the goal is to obtain
28::COMO;;# stable calibration curve estimates for models that are potentially prone to
29::COMO;;# overfitting. In practice, one should rather use cross-validation with more
30::COMO;;# balanced splits but this would make the code of this example more complicated
31::COMO;;# to follow.
37::COMC;;train_samples = 100 # Samples used for training the models
44::COMO;;# %%
45::COMO;;# Calibration curves
46::COMO;;# ------------------
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# Below, we train each of the four models with the small training dataset, then
49::COMO;;# plot calibration curves (also known as reliability diagrams) using
50::COMO;;# predicted probabilities of the test dataset. Calibration curves are created
51::COMO;;# by binning predicted probabilities, then plotting the mean predicted
52::COMO;;# probability in each bin against the observed frequency ('fraction of
53::COMO;;# positives'). Below the calibration curve, we plot a histogram showing
54::COMO;;# the distribution of the predicted probabilities or more specifically,
55::COMO;;# the number of samples in each predicted probability bin.
68::COMM;;df = self.decision_function(X)
69::COMM;;calibrated_df = (df - self.df_min_) / (self.df_max_ - self.df_min_)
70::COMM;;proba_pos_class = np.clip(calibrated_df, 0, 1)
71::COMM;;proba_neg_class = 1 - proba_pos_class
72::COMM;;proba = np.c_[proba_neg_class, proba_pos_class]
73::COMM;;return proba
74::COMM;;# %%
75::COMM;;from sklearn.calibration import CalibrationDisplay
76::COMM;;from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
77::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV
78::COMM;;from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
79::COMM;;# Define the classifiers to be compared in the study.
80::COMM;;#
81::COMM;;# Note that we use a variant of the logistic regression model that can
82::COMM;;# automatically tune its regularization parameter.
83::COMM;;#
84::COMM;;# For a fair comparison, we should run a hyper-parameter search for all the
85::COMM;;# classifiers but we don't do it here for the sake of keeping the example code
86::COMM;;# concise and fast to execute.
87::COMM;;lr = LogisticRegressionCV(
88::COMM;;Cs=np.logspace(-6, 6, 101),
89::COMM;;cv=10,
90::COMM;;scoring="neg_log_loss",
91::COMM;;max_iter=1_000,
92::COMM;;use_legacy_attributes=False,
93::COMM;;)
94::COMM;;gnb = GaussianNB()
95::COMM;;svc = NaivelyCalibratedLinearSVC(C=1.0)
96::COMM;;rfc = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
97::COMM;;clf_list = [
98::COMM;;(lr, "Logistic Regression"),
99::COMM;;(gnb, "Naive Bayes"),
100::COMM;;(svc, "SVC"),
101::COMM;;(rfc, "Random forest"),
102::COMM;;]
103::COMM;;# %%
104::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
105::COMM;;from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec
106::COMM;;fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
107::COMM;;gs = GridSpec(4, 2)
108::COMM;;colors = plt.get_cmap("Dark2")
109::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve = fig.add_subplot(gs[:2, :2])
110::COMM;;calibration_displays = {}
111::COMM;;markers = ["^", "v", "s", "o"]
112::COMM;;for i, (clf, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
113::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
114::COMM;;display = CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator(
115::COMM;;clf,
116::COMM;;X_test,
117::COMM;;y_test,

121::COMM;;color=colors(i),

123::COMM;;)
124::COMM;;calibration_displays[name] = display
125::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve.grid()
126::COMM;;ax_calibration_curve.set_title("Calibration plots")
127::COMM;;# Add histogram
128::COMM;;grid_positions = [(2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1)]
129::COMM;;for i, (_, name) in enumerate(clf_list):
130::COMM;;row, col = grid_positions[i]
131::COMM;;ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[row, col])
132::COMM;;ax.hist(
133::COMM;;calibration_displays[name].y_prob,
134::COMM;;range=(0, 1),
135::COMM;;bins=10,
136::COMM;;label=name,
137::COMM;;color=colors(i),
138::COMM;;)
139::COMM;;ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Mean predicted probability", ylabel="Count")
140::COMM;;plt.tight_layout()
141::COMM;;plt.show()
142::COMM;;# %%
143::COMM;;#
144::COMM;;# Analysis of the results
145::COMM;;# -----------------------
146::COMM;;#
147::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegressionCV` returns reasonably well
148::COMM;;# calibrated predictions despite the small training set size: its reliability
149::COMM;;# curve is the closest to the diagonal among the four models.
150::COMM;;#
151::COMM;;# Logistic regression is trained by minimizing the log-loss which is a strictly
152::COMM;;# proper scoring rule: in the limit of infinite training data, strictly proper
153::COMM;;# scoring rules are minimized by the model that predicts the true conditional
154::COMM;;# probabilities. That (hypothetical) model would therefore be perfectly
155::COMM;;# calibrated. However, using a proper scoring rule as training objective is not
156::COMM;;# sufficient to guarantee a well-calibrated model by itself: even with a very
157::COMM;;# large training set, logistic regression could still be poorly calibrated, if
158::COMM;;# it was too strongly regularized or if the choice and preprocessing of input
159::COMM;;# features made this model mis-specified (e.g. if the true decision boundary of
160::COMM;;# the dataset is a highly non-linear function of the input features).
161::COMM;;#
162::COMM;;# In this example the training set was intentionally kept very small. In this
163::COMM;;# setting, optimizing the log-loss can still lead to poorly calibrated models
164::COMM;;# because of overfitting. To mitigate this, the
165::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegressionCV` class was configured to
166::COMM;;# tune the `C` regularization parameter to also minimize the log-loss via inner
167::COMM;;# cross-validation so as to find the best compromise for this model in the
168::COMM;;# small training set setting.
169::COMM;;#
170::COMM;;# Because of the finite training set size and the lack of guarantee for
171::COMM;;# well-specification, we observe that the calibration curve of the logistic
172::COMM;;# regression model is close but not perfectly on the diagonal. The shape of the
173::COMM;;# calibration curve of this model can be interpreted as slightly
174::COMM;;# under-confident: the predicted probabilities are a bit too close to 0.5
175::COMM;;# compared to the true fraction of positive samples.
176::COMM;;#
177::COMM;;# The other methods all output less well calibrated probabilities:
178::COMM;;#
179::COMM;;# * :class:`~sklearn.naive_bayes.GaussianNB` tends to push probabilities to 0
180::COMM;;# or 1 (see histogram) on this particular dataset (over-confidence). This is
181::COMM;;# mainly because the naive Bayes equation only provides correct estimate of
182::COMM;;# probabilities when the assumption that features are conditionally
183::COMM;;# independent holds [2]_. However, features can be correlated and this is the case
184::COMM;;# with this dataset, which contains 2 features generated as random linear
185::COMM;;# combinations of the informative features. These correlated features are
186::COMM;;# effectively being 'counted twice', resulting in pushing the predicted
187::COMM;;# probabilities towards 0 and 1 [3]_. Note, however, that changing the seed
188::COMM;;# used to generate the dataset can lead to widely varying results for the
189::COMM;;# naive Bayes estimator.
190::COMM;;#
191::COMM;;# * :class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC` is not a natural probabilistic classifier.
192::COMM;;# In order to interpret its prediction as such, we naively scaled the output
193::COMM;;# of the :term:`decision_function` into [0, 1] by applying min-max scaling in
194::COMM;;# the `NaivelyCalibratedLinearSVC` wrapper class defined above. This
195::COMM;;# estimator shows a typical sigmoid-shaped calibration curve on this data:
196::COMM;;# predictions larger than 0.5 correspond to samples with an even larger
197::COMM;;# effective positive class fraction (above the diagonal), while predictions
198::COMM;;# below 0.5 corresponds to even lower positive class fractions (below the
199::COMM;;# diagonal). This under-confident predictions are typical for maximum-margin
200::COMM;;# methods [1]_.
201::COMM;;#
202::COMM;;# * :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier`'s prediction histogram
203::COMM;;# shows peaks at approx. 0.2 and 0.9 probability, while probabilities close to
204::COMM;;# 0 or 1 are very rare. An explanation for this is given by [1]_:
205::COMM;;# "Methods such as bagging and random forests that average
206::COMM;;# predictions from a base set of models can have difficulty making
207::COMM;;# predictions near 0 and 1 because variance in the underlying base models
208::COMM;;# will bias predictions that should be near zero or one away from these
209::COMM;;# values. Because predictions are restricted to the interval [0, 1], errors
210::COMM;;# caused by variance tend to be one-sided near zero and one. For example, if
211::COMM;;# a model should predict p = 0 for a case, the only way bagging can achieve
212::COMM;;# this is if all bagged trees predict zero. If we add noise to the trees that
213::COMM;;# bagging is averaging over, this noise will cause some trees to predict
214::COMM;;# values larger than 0 for this case, thus moving the average prediction of
215::COMM;;# the bagged ensemble away from 0. We observe this effect most strongly with
216::COMM;;# random forests because the base-level trees trained with random forests
217::COMM;;# have relatively high variance due to feature subsetting." This effect can
218::COMM;;# make random forests under-confident. Despite this possible bias, note that
219::COMM;;# the trees themselves are fit by minimizing either the Gini or Entropy
220::COMM;;# criterion, both of which lead to splits that minimize proper scoring rules:
221::COMM;;# the Brier score or the log-loss respectively. See :ref:`the user guide
222::COMM;;# <tree_mathematical_formulation>` for more details. This can explain why
223::COMM;;# this model shows a good enough calibration curve on this particular example
224::COMM;;# dataset. Indeed the Random Forest model is not significantly more
225::COMM;;# under-confident than the Logistic Regression model.
226::COMM;;#
227::COMM;;# Feel free to re-run this example with different random seeds and other
228::COMM;;# dataset generation parameters to see how different the calibration plots can
229::COMM;;# look. In general, Logistic Regression and Random Forest will tend to be the
230::COMM;;# best calibrated classifiers, while SVC will often display the typical
231::COMM;;# under-confident miscalibration. The naive Bayes model is also often poorly
232::COMM;;# calibrated but the general shape of its calibration curve can vary widely
233::COMM;;# depending on the dataset.
234::COMM;;#
235::COMM;;# Finally, note that for some dataset seeds, all models are poorly calibrated,
236::COMM;;# even when tuning the regularization parameter as above. This is bound to
237::COMM;;# happen when the training size is too small or when the model is severely
238::COMM;;# misspecified.
239::COMM;;#
240::COMM;;# References
241::COMM;;# ----------
242::COMM;;#
243::COMM;;# .. [1] `Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning
244::COMM;;# <https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/1102351.1102430>`_, A.
245::COMM;;# Niculescu-Mizil & R. Caruana, ICML 2005
246::COMM;;#
247::COMM;;# .. [2] `Beyond independence: Conditions for the optimality of the simple
248::COMM;;# Bayesian classifier
249::COMM;;# <https://www.ics.uci.edu/~pazzani/Publications/mlc96-pedro.pdf>`_
250::COMM;;# Domingos, P., & Pazzani, M., Proc. 13th Intl. Conf. Machine Learning.
251::COMM;;# 1996.
252::COMM;;#
253::COMM;;# .. [3] `Obtaining calibrated probability estimates from decision trees and
254::COMM;;# naive Bayesian classifiers
255::COMM;;# <https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~elkan/calibrated.pdf>`_
256::COMM;;# Zadrozny, Bianca, and Charles Elkan. Icml. Vol. 1. 2001.

175::COMO;;# Quantitative evaluation
176::COMO;;# -----------------------
178::COMO;;# %%
179::COMO;;# Analysis
180::COMO;;# --------
181::COMO;;#
182::COMO;;# The two logistic regression models fitted on the original features display
183::COMO;;# linear decision boundaries as expected. For this particular problem, this
184::COMO;;# does not seem to be detrimental as both models are competitive with the
185::COMO;;# non-linear models when quantitatively evaluated on the test set. We can
186::COMO;;# observe that the amount of regularization influences the model confidence:
187::COMO;;# lighter colors for the strongly regularized model with a lower value of `C`.
188::COMO;;# Regularization also impacts the orientation of decision boundary leading to
189::COMO;;# slightly different ROC AUC.
190::COMO;;#
191::COMO;;# The log-loss on the other hand evaluates both sharpness and calibration and
192::COMO;;# as a result strongly favors the weakly regularized logistic-regression model,
193::COMO;;# probably because the strongly regularized model is under-confident. This
194::COMO;;# could be confirmed by looking at the calibration curve using
195::COMO;;# :class:`sklearn.calibration.CalibrationDisplay`.
196::COMO;;#
197::COMO;;# The logistic regression model with RBF features has a "blobby" decision
198::COMO;;# boundary that is non-linear in the original feature space and is quite
199::COMO;;# similar to the decision boundary of the Gaussian process classifier which is
200::COMO;;# configured to use an RBF kernel.
201::COMO;;#
202::COMO;;# The logistic regression model fitted on binned features with interactions has
203::COMO;;# a decision boundary that is non-linear in the original feature space and is
204::COMO;;# quite similar to the decision boundary of the gradient boosting classifier:
205::COMO;;# both models favor axis-aligned decisions when extrapolating to unseen region
206::COMO;;# of the feature space.
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# The logistic regression model fitted on spline features with interactions
209::COMO;;# has a similar axis-aligned extrapolation behavior but a smoother decision
210::COMO;;# boundary in the dense region of the feature space than the two previous
211::COMO;;# models.
212::COMO;;#
213::COMO;;# To conclude, it is interesting to observe that feature engineering for
214::COMO;;# logistic regression models can be used to mimic some of the inductive bias of
215::COMO;;# various non-linear models. However, for this particular dataset, using the
216::COMO;;# raw features is enough to train a competitive model. This would not
217::COMO;;# necessarily the case for other datasets.

2::COMM;;====================================================================
3::COMM;;Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis with covariance ellipsoid
4::COMM;;====================================================================
5::COMM;;This example plots the covariance ellipsoids of each class and the decision boundary
6::COMM;;learned by :class:`~sklearn.discriminant_analysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` (LDA) and
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.discriminant_analysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis` (QDA). The
8::COMM;;ellipsoids display the double standard deviation for each class. With LDA, the standard
9::COMM;;deviation is the same for all the classes, while each class has its own standard
10::COMM;;deviation with QDA.
12::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
13::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
14::COMO;;# %%
15::COMO;;# Data generation
16::COMO;;# ---------------
17::COMO;;#
18::COMO;;# First, we define a function to generate synthetic data. It creates two blobs centered
19::COMO;;# at `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)`. Each blob is assigned a specific class. The dispersion of
20::COMO;;# the blob is controlled by the parameters `cov_class_1` and `cov_class_2`, that are the
21::COMO;;# covariance matrices used when generating the samples from the Gaussian distributions.
33::COMO;;# %%
34::COMO;;# We generate three datasets. In the first dataset, the two classes share the same
35::COMO;;# covariance matrix, and this covariance matrix has the specificity of being spherical
36::COMO;;# (isotropic). The second dataset is similar to the first one but does not enforce the
37::COMO;;# covariance to be spherical. Finally, the third dataset has a non-spherical covariance
38::COMO;;# matrix for each class.
64::COMO;;# %%
65::COMO;;# Plotting Functions
66::COMO;;# ------------------
67::COMO;;#
68::COMO;;# The code below is used to plot several pieces of information from the estimators used,
69::COMO;;# i.e., :class:`~sklearn.discriminant_analysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` (LDA) and
70::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.discriminant_analysis.QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis` (QDA). The
71::COMO;;# displayed information includes:
72::COMO;;#
73::COMO;;# - the decision boundary based on the probability estimate of the estimator;
74::COMO;;# - a scatter plot with circles representing the well-classified samples;
75::COMO;;# - a scatter plot with crosses representing the misclassified samples;
76::COMO;;# - the mean of each class, estimated by the estimator, marked with a star;
77::COMO;;# - the estimated covariance represented by an ellipse at 2 standard deviations from the
78::COMO;;# mean.
86::COMC;;angle = 180 * angle / np.pi # convert to degrees
87::COMO;;# filled Gaussian at 2 standard deviation
153::COMO;;# %%
154::COMO;;# Comparison of LDA and QDA
155::COMO;;# -------------------------
156::COMO;;#
157::COMO;;# We compare the two estimators LDA and QDA on all three datasets.
186::COMO;;# %%
187::COMO;;# The first important thing to notice is that LDA and QDA are equivalent for the
188::COMO;;# first and second datasets. Indeed, the major difference is that LDA assumes
189::COMO;;# that the covariance matrix of each class is equal, while QDA estimates a
190::COMO;;# covariance matrix per class. Since in these cases the data generative process
191::COMO;;# has the same covariance matrix for both classes, QDA estimates two covariance
192::COMO;;# matrices that are (almost) equal and therefore equivalent to the covariance
193::COMO;;# matrix estimated by LDA.
194::COMO;;#
195::COMO;;# In the first dataset the covariance matrix used to generate the dataset is
196::COMO;;# spherical, which results in a discriminant boundary that aligns with the
197::COMO;;# perpendicular bisector between the two means. This is no longer the case for
198::COMO;;# the second dataset. The discriminant boundary only passes through the middle
199::COMO;;# of the two means.
200::COMO;;#
201::COMO;;# Finally, in the third dataset, we observe the real difference between LDA and
202::COMO;;# QDA. QDA fits two covariance matrices and provides a non-linear discriminant
203::COMO;;# boundary, whereas LDA underfits since it assumes that both classes share a
204::COMO;;# single covariance matrix.
2::COMM;;==========================================================
3::COMM;;Adjustment for chance in clustering performance evaluation
4::COMM;;==========================================================
5::COMM;;This notebook explores the impact of uniformly-distributed random labeling on
6::COMM;;the behavior of some clustering evaluation metrics. For such purpose, the
7::COMM;;metrics are computed with a fixed number of samples and as a function of the number
8::COMM;;of clusters assigned by the estimator. The example is divided into two
9::COMM;;experiments:
10::COMM;;- a first experiment with fixed "ground truth labels" (and therefore fixed
11::COMM;;number of classes) and randomly "predicted labels";
12::COMM;;- a second experiment with varying "ground truth labels", randomly "predicted
13::COMM;;labels". The "predicted labels" have the same number of classes and clusters
14::COMM;;as the "ground truth labels".
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMO;;# %%
19::COMO;;# Defining the list of metrics to evaluate
20::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
21::COMO;;#
22::COMO;;# Clustering algorithms are fundamentally unsupervised learning methods.
23::COMO;;# However, since we assign class labels for the synthetic clusters in this
24::COMO;;# example, it is possible to use evaluation metrics that leverage this
25::COMO;;# "supervised" ground truth information to quantify the quality of the resulting
26::COMO;;# clusters. Examples of such metrics are the following:
27::COMO;;#
28::COMO;;# - V-measure, the harmonic mean of completeness and homogeneity;
29::COMO;;#
30::COMO;;# - Rand index, which measures how frequently pairs of data points are grouped
31::COMO;;# consistently according to the result of the clustering algorithm and the
32::COMO;;# ground truth class assignment;
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# - Adjusted Rand index (ARI), a chance-adjusted Rand index such that a random
35::COMO;;# cluster assignment has an ARI of 0.0 in expectation;
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# - Mutual Information (MI) is an information theoretic measure that quantifies
38::COMO;;# how dependent are the two labelings. Note that the maximum value of MI for
39::COMO;;# perfect labelings depends on the number of clusters and samples;
40::COMO;;#
41::COMO;;# - Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), a Mutual Information defined between 0
42::COMO;;# (no mutual information) in the limit of large number of data points and 1
43::COMO;;# (perfectly matching label assignments, up to a permutation of the labels).
44::COMO;;# It is not adjusted for chance: then the number of clustered data points is
45::COMO;;# not large enough, the expected values of MI or NMI for random labelings can
46::COMO;;# be significantly non-zero;
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# - Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI), a chance-adjusted Mutual Information.
49::COMO;;# Similarly to ARI, random cluster assignment has an AMI of 0.0 in
50::COMO;;# expectation.
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# For more information, see the :ref:`clustering_evaluation` module.
62::COMO;;# %%
63::COMO;;# First experiment: fixed ground truth labels and growing number of clusters
64::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
65::COMO;;#
66::COMO;;# We first define a function that creates uniformly-distributed random labeling.
71::COMO;;# %%
72::COMO;;# Another function will use the `random_labels` function to create a fixed set
73::COMO;;# of ground truth labels (`labels_a`) distributed in `n_classes` and then score
74::COMO;;# several sets of randomly "predicted" labels (`labels_b`) to assess the
75::COMO;;# variability of a given metric at a given `n_clusters`.
86::COMO;;# %%
87::COMO;;# In this first example we set the number of classes (true number of clusters) to
88::COMO;;# `n_classes=10`. The number of clusters varies over the values provided by
89::COMO;;# `n_clusters_range`.
123::COMO;;# %%
124::COMO;;# The Rand index saturates for `n_clusters` > `n_classes`. Other non-adjusted
125::COMO;;# measures such as the V-Measure show a linear dependency between the number of
126::COMO;;# clusters and the number of samples.
127::COMO;;#
128::COMO;;# Adjusted for chance measure, such as ARI and AMI, display some random
129::COMO;;# variations centered around a mean score of 0.0, independently of the number of
130::COMO;;# samples and clusters.
131::COMO;;#
132::COMO;;# Second experiment: varying number of classes and clusters
133::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
134::COMO;;#
135::COMO;;# In this section we define a similar function that uses several metrics to
136::COMO;;# score 2 uniformly-distributed random labelings. In this case, the number of
137::COMO;;# classes and assigned number of clusters are matched for each possible value in
138::COMO;;# `n_clusters_range`.
147::COMO;;# %%
148::COMO;;# In this case, we use `n_samples=100` to show the effect of having a number of
149::COMO;;# clusters similar or equal to the number of samples.
176::COMO;;# %%
177::COMO;;# We observe similar results as for the first experiment: adjusted for chance
178::COMO;;# metrics stay constantly near zero while other metrics tend to get larger with
179::COMO;;# finer-grained labelings. The mean V-measure of random labeling increases
180::COMO;;# significantly as the number of clusters is closer to the total number of
181::COMO;;# samples used to compute the measure. Furthermore, raw Mutual Information is
182::COMO;;# unbounded from above and its scale depends on the dimensions of the clustering
183::COMO;;# problem and the cardinality of the ground truth classes. This is why the
184::COMO;;# curve goes off the chart.
185::COMO;;#
186::COMO;;# Only adjusted measures can hence be safely used as a consensus index to
187::COMO;;# evaluate the average stability of clustering algorithms for a given value of k
188::COMO;;# on various overlapping sub-samples of the dataset.
189::COMO;;#
190::COMO;;# Non-adjusted clustering evaluation metric can therefore be misleading as they
191::COMO;;# output large values for fine-grained labelings, one could be lead to think
192::COMO;;# that the labeling has captured meaningful groups while they can be totally
193::COMO;;# random. In particular, such non-adjusted metrics should not be used to compare
194::COMO;;# the results of different clustering algorithms that output a different number
195::COMO;;# of clusters.

2::COMM;;Agglomerative clustering with different metrics
3::COMM;;===============================================
4::COMM;;Demonstrates the effect of different metrics on the hierarchical clustering.
5::COMM;;The example is engineered to show the effect of the choice of different
6::COMM;;metrics. It is applied to waveforms, which can be seen as
7::COMM;;high-dimensional vector. Indeed, the difference between metrics is
8::COMM;;usually more pronounced in high dimension (in particular for euclidean
9::COMM;;and cityblock).
10::COMM;;We generate data from three groups of waveforms. Two of the waveforms
11::COMM;;(waveform 1 and waveform 2) are proportional one to the other. The cosine
12::COMM;;distance is invariant to a scaling of the data, as a result, it cannot
13::COMM;;distinguish these two waveforms. Thus even with no noise, clustering
14::COMM;;using this distance will not separate out waveform 1 and 2.
15::COMM;;We add observation noise to these waveforms. We generate very sparse
16::COMM;;noise: only 6% of the time points contain noise. As a result, the
17::COMM;;l1 norm of this noise (ie "cityblock" distance) is much smaller than its
18::COMM;;l2 norm ("euclidean" distance). This can be seen on the inter-class
19::COMM;;distance matrices: the values on the diagonal, that characterize the
20::COMM;;spread of the class, are much bigger for the Euclidean distance than for
21::COMM;;the cityblock distance.
22::COMM;;When we apply clustering to the data, we find that the clustering
23::COMM;;reflects what was in the distance matrices. Indeed, for the Euclidean
24::COMM;;distance, the classes are ill-separated because of the noise, and thus
25::COMM;;the clustering does not separate the waveforms. For the cityblock
26::COMM;;distance, the separation is good and the waveform classes are recovered.
27::COMM;;Finally, the cosine distance does not separate at all waveform 1 and 2,
28::COMM;;thus the clustering puts them in the same cluster.
30::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
31::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

50::COMO;;# Make the noise sparse
64::COMC;;colors = ["#f7bd01", "#377eb8", "#f781bf"]
65::COMO;;# Plot the ground-truth labelling
75::COMO;;# Plot the distances

3::COMM;;Compare BIRCH and MiniBatchKMeans
4::COMM;;=================================
5::COMM;;This example compares the timing of BIRCH (with and without the global
6::COMM;;clustering step) and MiniBatchKMeans on a synthetic dataset having
7::COMM;;25,000 samples and 2 features generated using make_blobs.

3::COMM;;Segmenting the picture of greek coins in regions

5::COMM;;This example uses :ref:`spectral_clustering` on a graph created from
6::COMM;;voxel-to-voxel difference on an image to break this image into multiple
7::COMM;;partly-homogeneous regions.
8::COMM;;This procedure (spectral clustering on an image) is an efficient
9::COMM;;approximate solution for finding normalized graph cuts.
10::COMM;;There are three options to assign labels:
11::COMM;;* 'kmeans' spectral clustering clusters samples in the embedding space
12::COMM;;using a kmeans algorithm
13::COMM;;* 'discrete' iteratively searches for the closest partition
14::COMM;;space to the embedding space of spectral clustering.
15::COMM;;* 'cluster_qr' assigns labels using the QR factorization with pivoting
16::COMM;;that directly determines the partition in the embedding space.

32::COMO;;# reduces aliasing artifacts.

36::COMO;;# edges.
38::COMO;;# Take a decreasing function of the gradient: an exponential
39::COMO;;# The smaller beta is, the more independent the segmentation is of the
40::COMO;;# actual image. For beta=1, the segmentation is close to a voronoi
44::COMO;;# The number of segmented regions to display needs to be chosen manually.
45::COMO;;# The current version of 'spectral_clustering' does not support determining
46::COMO;;# the number of good quality clusters automatically.

50::COMO;;# Computing a few extra eigenvectors may speed up the eigen_solver.

52::COMO;;# extra regions for segmentation.
54::COMO;;# Apply spectral clustering using the default eigen_solver='arpack'.
55::COMO;;# Any implemented solver can be used: eigen_solver='arpack', 'lobpcg', or 'amg'.
56::COMO;;# Choosing eigen_solver='amg' requires an extra package called 'pyamg'.
57::COMO;;# The quality of segmentation and the speed of calculations is mostly determined
58::COMO;;# by the choice of the solver and the value of the tolerance 'eigen_tol'.

2::COMM;;=============================================================================
3::COMM;;Various Agglomerative Clustering on a 2D embedding of digits
4::COMM;;=============================================================================
5::COMM;;An illustration of various linkage option for agglomerative clustering on
6::COMM;;a 2D embedding of the digits dataset.
7::COMM;;The goal of this example is to show intuitively how the metrics behave, and
8::COMM;;not to find good clusters for the digits. This is why the example works on a
9::COMM;;2D embedding.
10::COMM;;What this example shows us is the behavior "rich getting richer" of
11::COMM;;agglomerative clustering that tends to create uneven cluster sizes.
12::COMM;;This behavior is pronounced for the average linkage strategy,
13::COMM;;that ends up with a couple of clusters with few datapoints.
14::COMM;;The case of single linkage is even more pathologic with a very
15::COMM;;large cluster covering most digits, an intermediate size (clean)
16::COMM;;cluster with most zero digits and all other clusters being drawn
17::COMM;;from noise points around the fringes.
18::COMM;;The other linkage strategies lead to more evenly distributed
19::COMM;;clusters that are therefore likely to be less sensible to a
20::COMM;;random resampling of the dataset.

2::COMM;;===========================
3::COMM;;Vector Quantization Example
4::COMM;;===========================
5::COMM;;This example shows how one can use :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.KBinsDiscretizer`
6::COMM;;to perform vector quantization on a set of toy image, the raccoon face.
8::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
9::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
10::COMO;;# %%
11::COMO;;# Original image
12::COMO;;# --------------
13::COMO;;#
14::COMO;;# We start by loading the raccoon face image from SciPy. We will additionally check
15::COMO;;# a couple of information regarding the image, such as the shape and data type used
16::COMO;;# to store the image.
17::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# %%
24::COMO;;# Thus the image is a 2D array of 768 pixels in height and 1024 pixels in width. Each
25::COMO;;# value is a 8-bit unsigned integer, which means that the image is encoded using 8
26::COMO;;# bits per pixel. The total memory usage of the image is 786 kilobytes (1 byte equals
27::COMO;;# 8 bits).
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# Using 8-bit unsigned integer means that the image is encoded using 256 different
30::COMO;;# shades of gray, at most. We can check the distribution of these values.
41::COMO;;# %%
42::COMO;;# Compression via vector quantization
43::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# The idea behind compression via vector quantization is to reduce the number of
46::COMO;;# gray levels to represent an image. For instance, we can use 8 values instead
47::COMO;;# of 256 values. Therefore, it means that we could efficiently use 3 bits instead
48::COMO;;# of 8 bits to encode a single pixel and therefore reduce the memory usage by a
49::COMO;;# factor of approximately 2.5. We will later discuss about this memory usage.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Encoding strategy
53::COMM;;#
54::COMM;;# The compression can be done using a
55::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.KBinsDiscretizer`. We need to choose a strategy
56::COMM;;# to define the 8 gray values to sub-sample. The simplest strategy is to define
57::COMM;;# them equally spaced, which correspond to setting `strategy="uniform"`. From
58::COMM;;# the previous histogram, we know that this strategy is certainly not optimal.
59::COMM;;from sklearn.preprocessing import KBinsDiscretizer
60::COMM;;n_bins = 8
61::COMM;;encoder = KBinsDiscretizer(
62::COMM;;n_bins=n_bins,
63::COMM;;encode="ordinal",
64::COMM;;strategy="uniform",
65::COMM;;random_state=0,
66::COMM;;)
67::COMM;;compressed_raccoon_uniform = encoder.fit_transform(raccoon_face.reshape(-1, 1)).reshape(
68::COMM;;raccoon_face.shape
69::COMM;;)
70::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(12, 4))
71::COMM;;ax[0].imshow(compressed_raccoon_uniform, cmap=plt.cm.gray)
72::COMM;;ax[0].axis("off")
73::COMM;;ax[0].set_title("Rendering of the image")
74::COMM;;ax[1].hist(compressed_raccoon_uniform.ravel(), bins=256)
75::COMM;;ax[1].set_xlabel("Pixel value")
76::COMM;;ax[1].set_ylabel("Count of pixels")
77::COMM;;ax[1].set_title("Sub-sampled distribution of the pixel values")
78::COMM;;_ = fig.suptitle("Raccoon face compressed using 3 bits and a uniform strategy")
79::COMM;;# %%
80::COMM;;# Qualitatively, we can spot some small regions where we see the effect of the
81::COMM;;# compression (e.g. leaves on the bottom right corner). But after all, the resulting
82::COMM;;# image is still looking good.
83::COMM;;#
84::COMM;;# We observe that the distribution of pixels values have been mapped to 8
85::COMM;;# different values. We can check the correspondence between such values and the
86::COMM;;# original pixel values.
87::COMM;;bin_edges = encoder.bin_edges_[0]
88::COMM;;bin_center = bin_edges[:-1] + (bin_edges[1:] - bin_edges[:-1]) / 2
89::COMM;;bin_center
90::COMM;;# %%
91::COMM;;_, ax = plt.subplots()
92::COMM;;ax.hist(raccoon_face.ravel(), bins=256)
93::COMM;;color = "tab:orange"
94::COMM;;for center in bin_center:
95::COMM;;ax.axvline(center, color=color)
96::COMM;;ax.text(center - 10, ax.get_ybound()[1] + 100, f"{center:.1f}", color=color)
97::COMM;;# %%
98::COMM;;# As previously stated, the uniform sampling strategy is not optimal. Notice for
99::COMM;;# instance that the pixels mapped to the value 7 will encode a rather small
100::COMM;;# amount of information, whereas the mapped value 3 will represent a large
101::COMM;;# amount of counts. We can instead use a clustering strategy such as k-means to
102::COMM;;# find a more optimal mapping.
103::COMM;;encoder = KBinsDiscretizer(
104::COMM;;n_bins=n_bins,
105::COMM;;encode="ordinal",
106::COMM;;strategy="kmeans",
107::COMM;;random_state=0,
108::COMM;;)
109::COMM;;compressed_raccoon_kmeans = encoder.fit_transform(raccoon_face.reshape(-1, 1)).reshape(
110::COMM;;raccoon_face.shape
111::COMM;;)
112::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(12, 4))
113::COMM;;ax[0].imshow(compressed_raccoon_kmeans, cmap=plt.cm.gray)
114::COMM;;ax[0].axis("off")
115::COMM;;ax[0].set_title("Rendering of the image")
116::COMM;;ax[1].hist(compressed_raccoon_kmeans.ravel(), bins=256)
117::COMM;;ax[1].set_xlabel("Pixel value")
118::COMM;;ax[1].set_ylabel("Number of pixels")
119::COMM;;ax[1].set_title("Distribution of the pixel values")
120::COMM;;_ = fig.suptitle("Raccoon face compressed using 3 bits and a K-means strategy")
121::COMM;;# %%
122::COMM;;bin_edges = encoder.bin_edges_[0]
123::COMM;;bin_center = bin_edges[:-1] + (bin_edges[1:] - bin_edges[:-1]) / 2
124::COMM;;bin_center
125::COMM;;# %%
126::COMM;;_, ax = plt.subplots()
127::COMM;;ax.hist(raccoon_face.ravel(), bins=256)
128::COMM;;color = "tab:orange"
129::COMM;;for center in bin_center:
130::COMM;;ax.axvline(center, color=color)
131::COMM;;ax.text(center - 10, ax.get_ybound()[1] + 100, f"{center:.1f}", color=color)
132::COMM;;# %%
133::COMM;;# The counts in the bins are now more balanced and their centers are no longer
134::COMM;;# equally spaced. Note that we could enforce the same number of pixels per bin
135::COMM;;# by using the `strategy="quantile"` instead of `strategy="kmeans"`.
136::COMM;;#
137::COMM;;# Memory footprint
139::COMO;;#
140::COMO;;# We previously stated that we should save 8 times less memory. Let's verify it.
143::COMO;;# %%
144::COMO;;# It is quite surprising to see that our compressed image is taking x8 more
145::COMO;;# memory than the original image. This is indeed the opposite of what we
146::COMO;;# expected. The reason is mainly due to the type of data used to encode the
147::COMO;;# image.
149::COMO;;# %%
150::COMO;;# Indeed, the output of the :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.KBinsDiscretizer` is
151::COMO;;# an array of 64-bit float. It means that it takes x8 more memory. However, we
152::COMO;;# use this 64-bit float representation to encode 8 values. Indeed, we will save
153::COMO;;# memory only if we cast the compressed image into an array of 3-bits integers. We
154::COMO;;# could use the method `numpy.ndarray.astype`. However, a 3-bits integer
155::COMO;;# representation does not exist and to encode the 8 values, we would need to use
156::COMO;;# the 8-bit unsigned integer representation as well.
157::COMO;;#
158::COMO;;# In practice, observing a memory gain would require the original image to be in
159::COMO;;# a 64-bit float representation.

3::COMM;;====================================
4::COMM;;Demo of HDBSCAN clustering algorithm
5::COMM;;====================================
6::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
7::COMM;;In this demo we will take a look at :class:`cluster.HDBSCAN` from the
8::COMM;;perspective of generalizing the :class:`cluster.DBSCAN` algorithm.
9::COMM;;We'll compare both algorithms on specific datasets. Finally we'll evaluate
10::COMM;;HDBSCAN's sensitivity to certain hyperparameters.
11::COMM;;We first define a couple utility functions for convenience.
13::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
14::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
15::COMO;;# %%
25::COMO;;# Black removed and is used for noise instead.
28::COMO;;# The probability of a point belonging to its labeled cluster determines
29::COMO;;# the size of its marker
33::COMO;;# Black used for noise.
53::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# Generate sample data
55::COMO;;# --------------------
56::COMO;;# One of the greatest advantages of HDBSCAN over DBSCAN is its out-of-the-box
57::COMO;;# robustness. It's especially remarkable on heterogeneous mixtures of data.
58::COMO;;# Like DBSCAN, it can model arbitrary shapes and distributions, however unlike
59::COMO;;# DBSCAN it does not require specification of an arbitrary and sensitive
60::COMO;;# `eps` hyperparameter.
61::COMO;;#
62::COMO;;# For example, below we generate a dataset from a mixture of three bi-dimensional
63::COMO;;# and isotropic Gaussian distributions.
69::COMO;;# %%
70::COMO;;# Scale Invariance
71::COMO;;# -----------------
72::COMO;;# It's worth remembering that, while DBSCAN provides a default value for `eps`
73::COMO;;# parameter, it hardly has a proper default value and must be tuned for the
74::COMO;;# specific dataset at use.
75::COMO;;#
76::COMO;;# As a simple demonstration, consider the clustering for a `eps` value tuned
77::COMO;;# for one dataset, and clustering obtained with the same value but applied to
78::COMO;;# rescaled versions of the dataset.
84::COMO;;# %%
85::COMO;;# Indeed, in order to maintain the same results we would have to scale `eps` by
86::COMO;;# the same factor.
90::COMO;;# %%
91::COMO;;# While standardizing data (e.g. using
92::COMO;;# :class:`sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler`) helps mitigate this problem,
93::COMO;;# great care must be taken to select the appropriate value for `eps`.
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# HDBSCAN is much more robust in this sense: HDBSCAN can be seen as
96::COMO;;# clustering over all possible values of `eps` and extracting the best
97::COMO;;# clusters from all possible clusters (see :ref:`User Guide <HDBSCAN>`).
98::COMO;;# One immediate advantage is that HDBSCAN is scale-invariant.
110::COMO;;# %%
111::COMO;;# Multi-Scale Clustering
112::COMO;;# ----------------------
113::COMO;;# HDBSCAN is much more than scale invariant though -- it is capable of
114::COMO;;# multi-scale clustering, which accounts for clusters with varying density.
115::COMO;;# Traditional DBSCAN assumes that any potential clusters are homogeneous in
116::COMO;;# density. HDBSCAN is free from such constraints. To demonstrate this we
117::COMO;;# consider the following dataset
123::COMO;;# %%
124::COMO;;# This dataset is more difficult for DBSCAN due to the varying densities and
125::COMO;;# spatial separation:
126::COMO;;#
127::COMO;;# - If `eps` is too large then we risk falsely clustering the two dense
128::COMO;;# clusters as one since their mutual reachability will extend
129::COMO;;# clusters.
130::COMO;;# - If `eps` is too small, then we risk fragmenting the sparser clusters
131::COMO;;# into many false clusters.
132::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# Not to mention this requires manually tuning choices of `eps` until we
134::COMO;;# find a tradeoff that we are comfortable with.
142::COMO;;# %%
143::COMO;;# To properly cluster the two dense clusters, we would need a smaller value of
144::COMO;;# epsilon, however at `eps=0.3` we are already fragmenting the sparse clusters,
145::COMO;;# which would only become more severe as we decrease epsilon. Indeed it seems
146::COMO;;# that DBSCAN is incapable of simultaneously separating the two dense clusters
147::COMO;;# while preventing the sparse clusters from fragmenting. Let's compare with
148::COMO;;# HDBSCAN.
151::COMO;;# %%
152::COMO;;# HDBSCAN is able to adapt to the multi-scale structure of the dataset without
153::COMO;;# requiring parameter tuning. While any sufficiently interesting dataset will
154::COMO;;# require tuning, this case demonstrates that HDBSCAN can yield qualitatively
155::COMO;;# better classes of clusterings without users' intervention which are
156::COMO;;# inaccessible via DBSCAN.
157::COMO;;# %%
158::COMO;;# Hyperparameter Robustness
159::COMO;;# -------------------------
160::COMO;;# Ultimately tuning will be an important step in any real world application, so
161::COMO;;# let's take a look at some of the most important hyperparameters for HDBSCAN.
162::COMO;;# While HDBSCAN is free from the `eps` parameter of DBSCAN, it does still have
163::COMO;;# some hyperparameters like `min_cluster_size` and `min_samples` which tune its
164::COMO;;# results regarding density. We will however see that HDBSCAN is relatively robust
165::COMO;;# to various real world examples thanks to those parameters whose clear meaning
166::COMO;;# helps tuning them.
167::COMO;;#
168::COMO;;# `min_cluster_size`
169::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
170::COMO;;# `min_cluster_size` is the minimum number of samples in a group for that
171::COMO;;# group to be considered a cluster.
172::COMO;;#
173::COMO;;# Clusters smaller than the ones of this size will be left as noise.
174::COMO;;# The default value is 5. This parameter is generally tuned to
175::COMO;;# larger values as needed. Smaller values will likely to lead to results with
176::COMO;;# fewer points labeled as noise. However values which too small will lead to
177::COMO;;# false sub-clusters being picked up and preferred. Larger values tend to be
178::COMO;;# more robust with respect to noisy datasets, e.g. high-variance clusters with
179::COMO;;# significant overlap.
186::COMO;;# %%
187::COMO;;# `min_samples`
188::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
189::COMO;;# `min_samples` is the number of samples in a neighborhood for a point to
190::COMO;;# be considered as a core point, including the point itself.
191::COMO;;# `min_samples` defaults to `min_cluster_size`.
192::COMO;;# Similarly to `min_cluster_size`, larger values for `min_samples` increase
193::COMO;;# the model's robustness to noise, but risks ignoring or discarding
194::COMO;;# potentially valid but small clusters.
195::COMO;;# `min_samples` better be tuned after finding a good value for `min_cluster_size`.
206::COMO;;# %%
207::COMO;;# `dbscan_clustering`
208::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
209::COMO;;# During `fit`, `HDBSCAN` builds a single-linkage tree which encodes the
210::COMO;;# clustering of all points across all values of :class:`~cluster.DBSCAN`'s
211::COMO;;# `eps` parameter.
212::COMO;;# We can thus plot and evaluate these clusterings efficiently without fully
213::COMO;;# recomputing intermediate values such as core-distances, mutual-reachability,
214::COMO;;# and the minimum spanning tree. All we need to do is specify the `cut_distance`
215::COMO;;# (equivalent to `eps`) we want to cluster with.
2::COMM;;====================
3::COMM;;Inductive Clustering
4::COMM;;====================
5::COMM;;Clustering can be expensive, especially when our dataset contains millions
6::COMM;;of datapoints. Many clustering algorithms are not :term:`inductive` and so
7::COMM;;cannot be directly applied to new data samples without recomputing the
8::COMM;;clustering, which may be intractable. Instead, we can use clustering to then
9::COMM;;learn an inductive model with a classifier, which has several benefits:
10::COMM;;- it allows the clusters to scale and apply to new data
11::COMM;;- unlike re-fitting the clusters to new samples, it makes sure the labelling
12::COMM;;procedure is consistent over time
13::COMM;;- it allows us to use the inferential capabilities of the classifier to
14::COMM;;describe or explain the clusters
15::COMM;;This example illustrates a generic implementation of a meta-estimator which
16::COMM;;extends clustering by inducing a classifier from the cluster labels.
18::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
19::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMM;;First, we check the first fitted classifier if available, otherwise we
33::COMM;;check the unfitted classifier.

67::COMO;;# Train a clustering algorithm on the training data and get the cluster labels

83::COMO;;# predict cluster membership for unknown instances

2::COMM;;====================================
3::COMM;;Demonstration of k-means assumptions
4::COMM;;====================================
5::COMM;;This example is meant to illustrate situations where k-means produces
6::COMM;;unintuitive and possibly undesirable clusters.
8::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
9::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
10::COMO;;# %%
11::COMO;;# Data generation
12::COMO;;# ---------------
13::COMO;;#
14::COMO;;# The function :func:`~sklearn.datasets.make_blobs` generates isotropic
15::COMO;;# (spherical) gaussian blobs. To obtain anisotropic (elliptical) gaussian blobs
16::COMO;;# one has to define a linear `transformation`.
23::COMC;;X_aniso = np.dot(X, transformation) # Anisotropic blobs
26::COMC;;) # Unequal variance
29::COMC;;) # Unevenly sized blobs
31::COMO;;# %%
32::COMO;;# We can visualize the resulting data:
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# Fit models and plot results
47::COMO;;# ---------------------------
48::COMO;;#
49::COMO;;# The previously generated data is now used to show how
50::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` behaves in the following scenarios:
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# - Non-optimal number of clusters: in a real setting there is no uniquely
53::COMO;;# defined **true** number of clusters. An appropriate number of clusters has
54::COMO;;# to be decided from data-based criteria and knowledge of the intended goal.
55::COMO;;# - Anisotropically distributed blobs: k-means consists of minimizing sample's
56::COMO;;# euclidean distances to the centroid of the cluster they are assigned to. As
57::COMO;;# a consequence, k-means is more appropriate for clusters that are isotropic
58::COMO;;# and normally distributed (i.e. spherical gaussians).
59::COMO;;# - Unequal variance: k-means is equivalent to taking the maximum likelihood
60::COMO;;# estimator for a "mixture" of k gaussian distributions with the same
61::COMO;;# variances but with possibly different means.
62::COMO;;# - Unevenly sized blobs: there is no theoretical result about k-means that
63::COMO;;# states that it requires similar cluster sizes to perform well, yet
64::COMO;;# minimizing euclidean distances does mean that the more sparse and
65::COMO;;# high-dimensional the problem is, the higher is the need to run the algorithm
66::COMO;;# with different centroid seeds to ensure a global minimal inertia.
87::COMO;;# %%
88::COMO;;# Possible solutions
89::COMO;;# ------------------
90::COMO;;#
91::COMO;;# For an example on how to find a correct number of blobs, see
92::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_kmeans_silhouette_analysis.py`.
93::COMO;;# In this case it suffices to set `n_clusters=3`.
98::COMO;;# %%
99::COMO;;# To deal with unevenly sized blobs one can increase the number of random
100::COMO;;# initializations. In this case we set `n_init=10` to avoid finding a
101::COMO;;# sub-optimal local minimum. For more details see :ref:`kmeans_sparse_high_dim`.
108::COMO;;# %%
109::COMO;;# As anisotropic and unequal variances are real limitations of the k-means
110::COMO;;# algorithm, here we propose instead the use of
111::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture`, which also assumes gaussian
112::COMO;;# clusters but does not impose any constraints on their variances. Notice that
113::COMO;;# one still has to find the correct number of blobs (see
114::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_mixture_plot_gmm_selection.py`).
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# For an example on how other clustering methods deal with anisotropic or
117::COMO;;# unequal variance blobs, see the example
118::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_cluster_comparison.py`.
129::COMO;;# %%
130::COMO;;# Final remarks
131::COMO;;# -------------
132::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# In high-dimensional spaces, Euclidean distances tend to become inflated
134::COMO;;# (not shown in this example). Running a dimensionality reduction algorithm
135::COMO;;# prior to k-means clustering can alleviate this problem and speed up the
136::COMO;;# computations (see the example
137::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_clustering.py`).
138::COMO;;#
139::COMO;;# In the case where clusters are known to be isotropic, have similar variance
140::COMO;;# and are not too sparse, the k-means algorithm is quite effective and is one of
141::COMO;;# the fastest clustering algorithms available. This advantage is lost if one has
142::COMO;;# to restart it several times to avoid convergence to a local minimum.

2::COMM;;===============================================================================
3::COMM;;Selecting the number of clusters with silhouette analysis on KMeans clustering
4::COMM;;===============================================================================
5::COMM;;Silhouette analysis can be used to study the separation distance between the
6::COMM;;resulting clusters. The silhouette plot displays a measure of how close each
7::COMM;;point in one cluster is to points in the neighboring clusters and thus provides
8::COMM;;a way to assess parameters like number of clusters visually. This measure has a
9::COMM;;range of [-1, 1].
10::COMM;;Silhouette coefficients (as these values are referred to as) near +1 indicate
11::COMM;;that the sample is far away from the neighboring clusters. A value of 0
12::COMM;;indicates that the sample is on or very close to the decision boundary between
13::COMM;;two neighboring clusters and negative values indicate that those samples might
14::COMM;;have been assigned to the wrong cluster.
15::COMM;;In this example the silhouette analysis is used to choose an optimal value for
16::COMM;;``n_clusters``. The silhouette plot shows that the ``n_clusters`` value of 3, 5
17::COMM;;and 6 are a bad pick for the given data due to the presence of clusters with
18::COMM;;below average silhouette scores and also due to wide fluctuations in the size
19::COMM;;of the silhouette plots. Silhouette analysis is more ambivalent in deciding
20::COMM;;between 2 and 4.
21::COMM;;Also from the thickness of the silhouette plot the cluster size can be
22::COMM;;visualized. The silhouette plot for cluster 0 when ``n_clusters`` is equal to
23::COMM;;2, is bigger in size owing to the grouping of the 3 sub clusters into one big
24::COMM;;cluster. However when the ``n_clusters`` is equal to 4, all the plots are more
25::COMM;;or less of similar thickness and hence are of similar sizes as can be also
26::COMM;;verified from the labelled scatter plot on the right.

2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;Spectral clustering for image segmentation
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;In this example, an image with connected circles is generated and
6::COMM;;spectral clustering is used to separate the circles.
7::COMM;;In these settings, the :ref:`spectral_clustering` approach solves the problem
8::COMM;;know as 'normalized graph cuts': the image is seen as a graph of
9::COMM;;connected voxels, and the spectral clustering algorithm amounts to
10::COMM;;choosing graph cuts defining regions while minimizing the ratio of the
11::COMM;;gradient along the cut, and the volume of the region.
12::COMM;;As the algorithm tries to balance the volume (ie balance the region
13::COMM;;sizes), if we take circles with different sizes, the segmentation fails.
14::COMM;;In addition, as there is no useful information in the intensity of the image,

2::COMM;;===================================================
3::COMM;;Hierarchical clustering with and without structure
4::COMM;;===================================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates hierarchical clustering with and without
6::COMM;;connectivity constraints. It shows the effect of imposing a connectivity
7::COMM;;graph to capture local structure in the data. Without connectivity constraints,
8::COMM;;the clustering is based purely on distance, while with constraints, the
9::COMM;;clustering respects local structure.
10::COMM;;For more information, see :ref:`hierarchical_clustering`.
11::COMM;;There are two advantages of imposing connectivity. First, clustering
12::COMM;;with sparse connectivity matrices is faster in general.
13::COMM;;Second, when using a connectivity matrix, single, average and complete
14::COMM;;linkage are unstable and tend to create a few clusters that grow very
15::COMM;;quickly. Indeed, average and complete linkage fight this percolation behavior
16::COMM;;by considering all the distances between two clusters when merging them
17::COMM;;(while single linkage exaggerates the behaviour by considering only the
18::COMM;;shortest distance between clusters). The connectivity graph breaks this
19::COMM;;mechanism for average and complete linkage, making them resemble the more
20::COMM;;brittle single linkage. This effect is more pronounced for very sparse graphs
21::COMM;;(try decreasing the number of neighbors in `kneighbors_graph`) and with
22::COMM;;complete linkage. In particular, having a very small number of neighbors in
23::COMM;;the graph, imposes a geometry that is close to that of single linkage,
24::COMM;;which is well known to have this percolation instability.
25::COMM;;The effect of imposing connectivity is illustrated on two different but
26::COMM;;similar datasets which show a spiral structure. In the first example we
27::COMM;;build a Swiss roll dataset and run hierarchical clustering on the position
28::COMM;;of the data. Here, we compare unstructured Ward clustering with a
29::COMM;;structured variant that enforces k-Nearest Neighbors connectivity. In the
30::COMM;;second example we include the effects of applying a such a connectivity graph
31::COMM;;to single, average and complete linkage.
33::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
34::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

37::COMO;;# --------------------------------

76::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------------

89::COMO;;# Plot structured clustering result
