2::COMM;;=======================================================================
3::COMM;;Shrinkage covariance estimation: LedoitWolf vs OAS and max-likelihood
4::COMM;;=======================================================================
5::COMM;;When working with covariance estimation, the usual approach is to use
6::COMM;;a maximum likelihood estimator, such as the
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.covariance.EmpiricalCovariance`. It is unbiased, i.e. it
8::COMM;;converges to the true (population) covariance when given many
9::COMM;;observations. However, it can also be beneficial to regularize it, in
10::COMM;;order to reduce its variance; this, in turn, introduces some bias. This
11::COMM;;example illustrates the simple regularization used in
12::COMM;;:ref:`shrunk_covariance` estimators. In particular, it focuses on how to
13::COMM;;set the amount of regularization, i.e. how to choose the bias-variance
14::COMM;;trade-off.
15::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
16::COMM;;.. [1] "Shrinkage Algorithms for MMSE Covariance Estimation"
17::COMM;;Chen et al., IEEE Trans. on Sign. Proc., Volume 58, Issue 10, October 2010.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# Generate sample data
23::COMO;;# --------------------
29::COMO;;# Color samples
33::COMO;;# %%
34::COMO;;# Compute the likelihood on test data
35::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
38::COMO;;# spanning a range of possible shrinkage coefficient values
43::COMO;;# under the ground-truth model, which we would not have access to in real
44::COMO;;# settings
48::COMO;;# %%
49::COMO;;# Compare different approaches to setting the regularization parameter
50::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# Here we compare 3 approaches:
53::COMO;;#
54::COMO;;# * Setting the parameter by cross-validating the likelihood on three folds
55::COMO;;# according to a grid of potential shrinkage parameters.
56::COMO;;#
57::COMO;;# * A close formula proposed by Ledoit and Wolf to compute
58::COMO;;# the asymptotically optimal regularization parameter (minimizing a MSE
59::COMO;;# criterion), yielding the :class:`~sklearn.covariance.LedoitWolf`
60::COMO;;# covariance estimate.
61::COMO;;#
62::COMO;;# * An improvement of the Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage, the
63::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.covariance.OAS`, proposed by Chen et al. [1]_. Its
64::COMO;;# convergence is significantly better under the assumption that the data
65::COMO;;# are Gaussian, in particular for small samples.
68::COMO;;# GridSearch for an optimal shrinkage coefficient
72::COMO;;# Ledoit-Wolf optimal shrinkage coefficient estimate
75::COMO;;# OAS coefficient estimate
78::COMO;;# %%
79::COMO;;# Plot results
80::COMO;;# ------------
81::COMO;;#
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# To quantify estimation error, we plot the likelihood of unseen data for
84::COMO;;# different values of the shrinkage parameter. We also show the choices by
85::COMO;;# cross-validation, or with the LedoitWolf and OAS estimates.
91::COMO;;# range shrinkage curve
94::COMO;;# adjust view
101::COMO;;# LW likelihood
110::COMO;;# OAS likelihood
114::COMO;;# best CV estimator likelihood
127::COMO;;# %%
128::COMO;;# .. note::
129::COMO;;#
130::COMO;;# The maximum likelihood estimate corresponds to no shrinkage,
131::COMO;;# and thus performs poorly. The Ledoit-Wolf estimate performs really well,
132::COMO;;# as it is close to the optimal and is not computationally costly. In this
133::COMO;;# example, the OAS estimate is a bit further away. Interestingly, both
134::COMO;;# approaches outperform cross-validation, which is significantly most
135::COMO;;# computationally costly.
2::COMM;;=============================
3::COMM;;Ledoit-Wolf vs OAS estimation
4::COMM;;=============================
5::COMM;;The usual covariance maximum likelihood estimate can be regularized
6::COMM;;using shrinkage. Ledoit and Wolf proposed a close formula to compute
7::COMM;;the asymptotically optimal shrinkage parameter (minimizing a MSE
8::COMM;;criterion), yielding the Ledoit-Wolf covariance estimate.
9::COMM;;Chen et al. [1]_ proposed an improvement of the Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage
10::COMM;;parameter, the OAS coefficient, whose convergence is significantly
11::COMM;;better under the assumption that the data are Gaussian.
12::COMM;;This example, inspired from Chen's publication [1]_, shows a comparison
13::COMM;;of the estimated MSE of the LW and OAS methods, using Gaussian
14::COMM;;distributed data.
15::COMM;;.. rubric :: References
16::COMM;;.. [1] "Shrinkage Algorithms for MMSE Covariance Estimation"
17::COMM;;Chen et al., IEEE Trans. on Sign. Proc., Volume 58, Issue 10, October 2010.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
26::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# simulation covariance matrix (AR(1) process)
49::COMO;;# plot MSE

2::COMM;;================================================================
3::COMM;;Robust covariance estimation and Mahalanobis distances relevance
4::COMM;;================================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows covariance estimation with Mahalanobis
6::COMM;;distances on Gaussian distributed data.
7::COMM;;For Gaussian distributed data, the distance of an observation
8::COMM;;:math:`x_i` to the mode of the distribution can be computed using its
9::COMM;;Mahalanobis distance:
10::COMM;;.. math::
11::COMM;;d_{(\mu,\Sigma)}(x_i)^2 = (x_i - \mu)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x_i - \mu)
12::COMM;;where :math:`\mu` and :math:`\Sigma` are the location and the covariance of
13::COMM;;the underlying Gaussian distributions.
14::COMM;;In practice, :math:`\mu` and :math:`\Sigma` are replaced by some
15::COMM;;estimates. The standard covariance maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is very
16::COMM;;sensitive to the presence of outliers in the data set and therefore,
17::COMM;;the downstream Mahalanobis distances also are. It would be better to
18::COMM;;use a robust estimator of covariance to guarantee that the estimation is
19::COMM;;resistant to "erroneous" observations in the dataset and that the
20::COMM;;calculated Mahalanobis distances accurately reflect the true
21::COMM;;organization of the observations.
22::COMM;;The Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator (MCD) is a robust,
23::COMM;;high-breakdown point (i.e. it can be used to estimate the covariance
24::COMM;;matrix of highly contaminated datasets, up to
25::COMM;;:math:`\frac{n_\text{samples}-n_\text{features}-1}{2}` outliers)
26::COMM;;estimator of covariance. The idea behind the MCD is to find
27::COMM;;:math:`\frac{n_\text{samples}+n_\text{features}+1}{2}`
28::COMM;;observations whose empirical covariance has the smallest determinant,
29::COMM;;yielding a "pure" subset of observations from which to compute
30::COMM;;standards estimates of location and covariance. The MCD was introduced by
31::COMM;;P.J.Rousseuw in [1]_.
32::COMM;;This example illustrates how the Mahalanobis distances are affected by
33::COMM;;outlying data. Observations drawn from a contaminating distribution
34::COMM;;are not distinguishable from the observations coming from the real,
35::COMM;;Gaussian distribution when using standard covariance MLE based Mahalanobis
36::COMM;;distances. Using MCD-based
37::COMM;;Mahalanobis distances, the two populations become
38::COMM;;distinguishable. Associated applications include outlier detection,
39::COMM;;observation ranking and clustering.
40::COMM;;.. note::
41::COMM;;See also :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_covariance_plot_robust_vs_empirical_covariance.py`
42::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
43::COMM;;.. [1] P. J. Rousseeuw. `Least median of squares regression
44::COMM;;<http://web.ipac.caltech.edu/staff/fmasci/home/astro_refs/LeastMedianOfSquares.pdf>`_. J. Am
45::COMM;;Stat Ass, 79:871, 1984.
46::COMM;;.. [2] Wilson, E. B., & Hilferty, M. M. (1931). `The distribution of chi-square.
47::COMM;;<https://water.usgs.gov/osw/bulletin17b/Wilson_Hilferty_1931.pdf>`_
48::COMM;;Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States
49::COMM;;of America, 17, 684-688.
51::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
52::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
53::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# Generate data
55::COMO;;# --------------
56::COMO;;#
57::COMO;;# First, we generate a dataset of 125 samples and 2 features. Both features
58::COMO;;# are Gaussian distributed with mean of 0 but feature 1 has a standard
59::COMO;;# deviation equal to 2 and feature 2 has a standard deviation equal to 1. Next,
60::COMO;;# 25 samples are replaced with Gaussian outlier samples where feature 1 has
61::COMO;;# a standard deviation equal to 1 and feature 2 has a standard deviation equal
62::COMO;;# to 7.
64::COMO;;# for consistent results
69::COMO;;# generate Gaussian data of shape (125, 2)

85::COMO;;# robust estimator is much more resistant to the outlier samples, which were
86::COMO;;# designed to have a much larger variance in feature 2.

102::COMO;;# whereas the MLE based distances are more influenced by the outlier
103::COMO;;# red points.

2::COMM;;=======================================
3::COMM;;Robust vs Empirical covariance estimate
4::COMM;;=======================================
5::COMM;;The usual covariance maximum likelihood estimate is very sensitive to the
6::COMM;;presence of outliers in the data set. In such a case, it would be better to
7::COMM;;use a robust estimator of covariance to guarantee that the estimation is
8::COMM;;resistant to "erroneous" observations in the data set. [1]_, [2]_
9::COMM;;Minimum Covariance Determinant Estimator
10::COMM;;----------------------------------------
11::COMM;;The Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator is a robust, high-breakdown point
12::COMM;;(i.e. it can be used to estimate the covariance matrix of highly contaminated
13::COMM;;datasets, up to
14::COMM;;:math:`\frac{n_\text{samples} - n_\text{features}-1}{2}` outliers) estimator of
15::COMM;;covariance. The idea is to find
16::COMM;;:math:`\frac{n_\text{samples} + n_\text{features}+1}{2}`
17::COMM;;observations whose empirical covariance has the smallest determinant, yielding
18::COMM;;a "pure" subset of observations from which to compute standards estimates of
19::COMM;;location and covariance. After a correction step aiming at compensating the
20::COMM;;fact that the estimates were learned from only a portion of the initial data,
21::COMM;;we end up with robust estimates of the data set location and covariance.
22::COMM;;The Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator (MCD) has been introduced by
23::COMM;;P.J.Rousseuw in [3]_.
24::COMM;;Evaluation
25::COMM;;----------
26::COMM;;In this example, we compare the estimation errors that are made when using
27::COMM;;various types of location and covariance estimates on contaminated Gaussian
28::COMM;;distributed data sets:
29::COMM;;- The mean and the empirical covariance of the full dataset, which break
30::COMM;;down as soon as there are outliers in the data set
31::COMM;;- The robust MCD, that has a low error provided
32::COMM;;:math:`n_\text{samples} > 5n_\text{features}`
33::COMM;;- The mean and the empirical covariance of the observations that are known
34::COMM;;to be good ones. This can be considered as a "perfect" MCD estimation,
35::COMM;;so one can trust our implementation by comparing to this case.
36::COMM;;References
37::COMM;;----------
38::COMM;;.. [1] Johanna Hardin, David M Rocke. The distribution of robust distances.
39::COMM;;Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics. December 1, 2005,
40::COMM;;14(4): 928-946.
41::COMM;;.. [2] Zoubir A., Koivunen V., Chakhchoukh Y. and Muma M. (2012). Robust
42::COMM;;estimation in signal processing: A tutorial-style treatment of
43::COMM;;fundamental concepts. IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 29(4), 61-80.
44::COMM;;.. [3] P. J. Rousseeuw. Least median of squares regression. Journal of American
45::COMM;;Statistical Ass., 79:871, 1984.
47::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
48::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;======================================
3::COMM;;Sparse inverse covariance estimation
4::COMM;;======================================
5::COMM;;Using the GraphicalLasso estimator to learn a covariance and sparse precision
6::COMM;;from a small number of samples.
7::COMM;;To estimate a probabilistic model (e.g. a Gaussian model), estimating the
8::COMM;;precision matrix, that is the inverse covariance matrix, is as important
9::COMM;;as estimating the covariance matrix. Indeed a Gaussian model is
10::COMM;;parametrized by the precision matrix.
11::COMM;;To be in favorable recovery conditions, we sample the data from a model
12::COMM;;with a sparse inverse covariance matrix. In addition, we ensure that the
13::COMM;;data is not too much correlated (limiting the largest coefficient of the
14::COMM;;precision matrix) and that there a no small coefficients in the
15::COMM;;precision matrix that cannot be recovered. In addition, with a small
16::COMM;;number of observations, it is easier to recover a correlation matrix
17::COMM;;rather than a covariance, thus we scale the time series.
18::COMM;;Here, the number of samples is slightly larger than the number of
19::COMM;;dimensions, thus the empirical covariance is still invertible. However,
20::COMM;;as the observations are strongly correlated, the empirical covariance
21::COMM;;matrix is ill-conditioned and as a result its inverse --the empirical
22::COMM;;precision matrix-- is very far from the ground truth.
23::COMM;;If we use l2 shrinkage, as with the Ledoit-Wolf estimator, as the number
24::COMM;;of samples is small, we need to shrink a lot. As a result, the
25::COMM;;Ledoit-Wolf precision is fairly close to the ground truth precision, that
26::COMM;;is not far from being diagonal, but the off-diagonal structure is lost.
27::COMM;;The l1-penalized estimator can recover part of this off-diagonal
28::COMM;;structure. It learns a sparse precision. It is not able to
29::COMM;;recover the exact sparsity pattern: it detects too many non-zero
30::COMM;;coefficients. However, the highest non-zero coefficients of the l1
31::COMM;;estimated correspond to the non-zero coefficients in the ground truth.
32::COMM;;Finally, the coefficients of the l1 precision estimate are biased toward
33::COMM;;zero: because of the penalty, they are all smaller than the corresponding
34::COMM;;ground truth value, as can be seen on the figure.
35::COMM;;Note that, the color range of the precision matrices is tweaked to
36::COMM;;improve readability of the figure. The full range of values of the
37::COMM;;empirical precision is not displayed.
38::COMM;;The alpha parameter of the GraphicalLasso setting the sparsity of the model is
39::COMM;;set by internal cross-validation in the GraphicalLassoCV. As can be
40::COMM;;seen on figure 2, the grid to compute the cross-validation score is
41::COMM;;iteratively refined in the neighborhood of the maximum.
43::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
44::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

10::COMM;;Given 2 multivariate covarying two-dimensional datasets, X, and Y,
11::COMM;;PLS extracts the 'directions of covariance', i.e. the components of each
12::COMM;;datasets that explain the most shared variance between both datasets.
13::COMM;;This is apparent on the **scatterplot matrix** display: components 1 in
14::COMM;;dataset X and dataset Y are maximally correlated (points lie around the
15::COMM;;first diagonal). This is also true for components 2 in both dataset,
16::COMM;;however, the correlation across datasets for different components is
17::COMM;;weak: the point cloud is very spherical.

2::COMM;;==================================================================
3::COMM;;Principal Component Regression vs Partial Least Squares Regression
4::COMM;;==================================================================
5::COMM;;This example compares `Principal Component Regression
6::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_component_regression>`_ (PCR) and
7::COMM;;`Partial Least Squares Regression
8::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_least_squares_regression>`_ (PLS) on a
9::COMM;;toy dataset. Our goal is to illustrate how PLS can outperform PCR when the
10::COMM;;target is strongly correlated with some directions in the data that have a
11::COMM;;low variance.
12::COMM;;PCR is a regressor composed of two steps: first,
13::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` is applied to the training data, possibly
14::COMM;;performing dimensionality reduction; then, a regressor (e.g. a linear
15::COMM;;regressor) is trained on the transformed samples. In
16::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, the transformation is purely
17::COMM;;unsupervised, meaning that no information about the targets is used. As a
18::COMM;;result, PCR may perform poorly in some datasets where the target is strongly
19::COMM;;correlated with *directions* that have low variance. Indeed, the
20::COMM;;dimensionality reduction of PCA projects the data into a lower dimensional
21::COMM;;space where the variance of the projected data is greedily maximized along
22::COMM;;each axis. Despite them having the most predictive power on the target, the
23::COMM;;directions with a lower variance will be dropped, and the final regressor
24::COMM;;will not be able to leverage them.
25::COMM;;PLS is both a transformer and a regressor, and it is quite similar to PCR: it
26::COMM;;also applies a dimensionality reduction to the samples before applying a
27::COMM;;linear regressor to the transformed data. The main difference with PCR is
28::COMM;;that the PLS transformation is supervised. Therefore, as we will see in this
29::COMM;;example, it does not suffer from the issue we just mentioned.
31::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
32::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
33::COMO;;# %%
34::COMO;;# The data
35::COMO;;# --------
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# We start by creating a simple dataset with two features. Before we even dive
38::COMO;;# into PCR and PLS, we fit a PCA estimator to display the two principal
39::COMO;;# components of this dataset, i.e. the two directions that explain the most
40::COMO;;# variance in the data.
51::COMC;;comp = comp * var # scale component by its variance explanation power
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# For the purpose of this example, we now define the target `y` such that it is
69::COMO;;# strongly correlated with a direction that has a small variance. To this end,
70::COMO;;# we will project `X` onto the second component, and add some noise to it.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# Projection on one component and predictive power
81::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------------
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# We now create two regressors: PCR and PLS, and for our illustration purposes
84::COMO;;# we set the number of components to 1. Before feeding the data to the PCA step
85::COMO;;# of PCR, we first standardize it, as recommended by good practice. The PLS
86::COMO;;# estimator has built-in scaling capabilities.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# For both models, we plot the projected data onto the first component against
89::COMO;;# the target. In both cases, this projected data is what the regressors will
90::COMO;;# use as training data.
100::COMC;;pca = pcr.named_steps["pca"] # retrieve the PCA step of the pipeline
120::COMO;;# %%
121::COMO;;# As expected, the unsupervised PCA transformation of PCR has dropped the
122::COMO;;# second component, i.e. the direction with the lowest variance, despite
123::COMO;;# it being the most predictive direction. This is because PCA is a completely
124::COMO;;# unsupervised transformation, and results in the projected data having a low
125::COMO;;# predictive power on the target.
126::COMO;;#
127::COMO;;# On the other hand, the PLS regressor manages to capture the effect of the
128::COMO;;# direction with the lowest variance, thanks to its use of target information
129::COMO;;# during the transformation: it can recognize that this direction is actually
130::COMO;;# the most predictive. We note that the first PLS component is negatively
131::COMO;;# correlated with the target, which comes from the fact that the signs of
132::COMO;;# eigenvectors are arbitrary.
133::COMO;;#
134::COMO;;# We also print the R-squared scores of both estimators, which further confirms
135::COMO;;# that PLS is a better alternative than PCR in this case. A negative R-squared
136::COMO;;# indicates that PCR performs worse than a regressor that would simply predict
137::COMO;;# the mean of the target.
140::COMO;;# %%
141::COMO;;# As a final remark, we note that PCR with 2 components performs as well as
142::COMO;;# PLS: this is because in this case, PCR was able to leverage the second
143::COMO;;# component which has the most preditive power on the target.

195::COMO;;# %%
196::COMO;;# Decomposition: Dictionary learning
197::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
198::COMO;;#
199::COMO;;# In the further section, let's consider :ref:`DictionaryLearning` more precisely.
200::COMO;;# Dictionary learning is a problem that amounts to finding a sparse representation
201::COMO;;# of the input data as a combination of simple elements. These simple elements form
202::COMO;;# a dictionary. It is possible to constrain the dictionary and/or coding coefficients
203::COMO;;# to be positive to match constraints that may be present in the data.
204::COMO;;#
205::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.MiniBatchDictionaryLearning` implements a

2::COMM;;==========================
3::COMM;;FastICA on 2D point clouds
4::COMM;;==========================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates visually in the feature space a comparison by
6::COMM;;results using two different component analysis techniques.
7::COMM;;:ref:`ICA` vs :ref:`PCA`.
8::COMM;;Representing ICA in the feature space gives the view of 'geometric ICA':
9::COMM;;ICA is an algorithm that finds directions in the feature space
10::COMM;;corresponding to projections with high non-Gaussianity. These directions
11::COMM;;need not be orthogonal in the original feature space, but they are
12::COMM;;orthogonal in the whitened feature space, in which all directions
13::COMM;;correspond to the same variance.
14::COMM;;PCA, on the other hand, finds orthogonal directions in the raw feature
15::COMM;;space that correspond to directions accounting for maximum variance.
16::COMM;;Here we simulate independent sources using a highly non-Gaussian
17::COMM;;process, 2 student T with a low number of degrees of freedom (top left
18::COMM;;figure). We mix them to create observations (top right figure).
19::COMM;;In this raw observation space, directions identified by PCA are
20::COMM;;represented by orange vectors. We represent the signal in the PCA space,
21::COMM;;after whitening by the variance corresponding to the PCA vectors (lower
22::COMM;;left). Running ICA corresponds to finding a rotation in this space to
23::COMM;;identify the directions of largest non-Gaussianity (lower right).
25::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
26::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
27::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# Generate sample data
29::COMO;;# --------------------
35::COMO;;# Mix data
36::COMC;;A = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 2]]) # Mixing matrix
37::COMC;;X = np.dot(S, A.T) # Generate observations
41::COMC;;S_ica_ = ica.fit(X).transform(X) # Estimate the sources

3::COMM;;Image denoising using dictionary learning
4::COMM;;=========================================
5::COMM;;An example comparing the effect of reconstructing noisy fragments
6::COMM;;of a raccoon face image using firstly online :ref:`DictionaryLearning` and
7::COMM;;various transform methods.
8::COMM;;The dictionary is fitted on the distorted left half of the image, and
9::COMM;;subsequently used to reconstruct the right half. Note that even better
10::COMM;;performance could be achieved by fitting to an undistorted (i.e.
11::COMM;;noiseless) image, but here we start from the assumption that it is not
12::COMM;;available.
13::COMM;;A common practice for evaluating the results of image denoising is by looking
14::COMM;;at the difference between the reconstruction and the original image. If the
15::COMM;;reconstruction is perfect this will look like Gaussian noise.
16::COMM;;It can be seen from the plots that the results of :ref:`omp` with two
17::COMM;;non-zero coefficients is a bit less biased than when keeping only one
18::COMM;;(the edges look less prominent). It is in addition closer from the ground
19::COMM;;truth in Frobenius norm.
20::COMM;;The result of :ref:`least_angle_regression` is much more strongly biased: the
21::COMM;;difference is reminiscent of the local intensity value of the original image.
22::COMM;;Thresholding is clearly not useful for denoising, but it is here to show that
23::COMM;;it can produce a suggestive output with very high speed, and thus be useful
24::COMM;;for other tasks such as object classification, where performance is not
25::COMM;;necessarily related to visualisation.

2::COMM;;===============
3::COMM;;Incremental PCA
4::COMM;;===============
5::COMM;;Incremental principal component analysis (IPCA) is typically used as a
6::COMM;;replacement for principal component analysis (PCA) when the dataset to be
7::COMM;;decomposed is too large to fit in memory. IPCA builds a low-rank approximation
8::COMM;;for the input data using an amount of memory which is independent of the
9::COMM;;number of input data samples. It is still dependent on the input data features,
10::COMM;;but changing the batch size allows for control of memory usage.
11::COMM;;This example serves as a visual check that IPCA is able to find a similar
12::COMM;;projection of the data to PCA (to a sign flip), while only processing a
13::COMM;;few samples at a time. This can be considered a "toy example", as IPCA is
14::COMM;;intended for large datasets which do not fit in main memory, requiring
15::COMM;;incremental approaches.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
2::COMM;;==========
3::COMM;;Kernel PCA
4::COMM;;==========
5::COMM;;This example shows the difference between the Principal Components Analysis
6::COMM;;(:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`) and its kernelized version
7::COMM;;(:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA`).
8::COMM;;On the one hand, we show that :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA` is able
9::COMM;;to find a projection of the data which linearly separates them while it is not the case
10::COMM;;with :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`.
11::COMM;;Finally, we show that inverting this projection is an approximation with
12::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA`, while it is exact with
13::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMO;;# %%
18::COMO;;# Projecting data: `PCA` vs. `KernelPCA`
19::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
20::COMO;;#
21::COMO;;# In this section, we show the advantages of using a kernel when
22::COMO;;# projecting data using a Principal Component Analysis (PCA). We create a
23::COMO;;# dataset made of two nested circles.
28::COMO;;# %%
29::COMO;;# Let's have a quick first look at the generated dataset.
33::COMC;;train_ax.set_ylabel("Feature #1")
34::COMC;;train_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
37::COMC;;test_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# The samples from each class cannot be linearly separated: there is no
41::COMO;;# straight line that can split the samples of the inner set from the outer
42::COMO;;# set.
43::COMO;;#
44::COMO;;# Now, we will use PCA with and without a kernel to see what is the effect of
45::COMO;;# using such a kernel. The kernel used here is a radial basis function (RBF)
46::COMO;;# kernel.
54::COMO;;# %%
59::COMC;;orig_data_ax.set_ylabel("Feature #1")
60::COMC;;orig_data_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
63::COMC;;pca_proj_ax.set_ylabel("Principal component #1")
64::COMC;;pca_proj_ax.set_xlabel("Principal component #0")
67::COMC;;kernel_pca_proj_ax.set_ylabel("Principal component #1")
68::COMC;;kernel_pca_proj_ax.set_xlabel("Principal component #0")
70::COMO;;# %%
71::COMO;;# We recall that PCA transforms the data linearly. Intuitively, it means that
72::COMO;;# the coordinate system will be centered, rescaled on each component
73::COMO;;# with respected to its variance and finally be rotated.
74::COMO;;# The obtained data from this transformation is isotropic and can now be
75::COMO;;# projected on its *principal components*.
76::COMO;;#
77::COMO;;# Thus, looking at the projection made using PCA (i.e. the middle figure), we
78::COMO;;# see that there is no change regarding the scaling; indeed the data being two
79::COMO;;# concentric circles centered in zero, the original data is already isotropic.
80::COMO;;# However, we can see that the data have been rotated. As a
81::COMO;;# conclusion, we see that such a projection would not help if define a linear
82::COMO;;# classifier to distinguish samples from both classes.
83::COMO;;#
84::COMO;;# Using a kernel allows to make a non-linear projection. Here, by using an RBF
85::COMO;;# kernel, we expect that the projection will unfold the dataset while keeping
86::COMO;;# approximately preserving the relative distances of pairs of data points that
87::COMO;;# are close to one another in the original space.
88::COMO;;#
89::COMO;;# We observe such behaviour in the figure on the right: the samples of a given
90::COMO;;# class are closer to each other than the samples from the opposite class,
91::COMO;;# untangling both sample sets. Now, we can use a linear classifier to separate
92::COMO;;# the samples from the two classes.
93::COMO;;#
94::COMO;;# Projecting into the original feature space
95::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------
96::COMO;;#
97::COMO;;# One particularity to have in mind when using
98::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA` is related to the reconstruction
99::COMO;;# (i.e. the back projection in the original feature space). With
100::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, the reconstruction will be exact if
101::COMO;;# `n_components` is the same than the number of original features.
102::COMO;;# This is the case in this example.
103::COMO;;#
104::COMO;;# We can investigate if we get the original dataset when back projecting with
105::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA`.
108::COMO;;# %%
113::COMC;;orig_data_ax.set_ylabel("Feature #1")
114::COMC;;orig_data_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
117::COMC;;pca_back_proj_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
122::COMC;;kernel_pca_back_proj_ax.set_xlabel("Feature #0")
124::COMO;;# %%
125::COMO;;# While we see a perfect reconstruction with
126::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` we observe a different result for
127::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA`.
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# Indeed, :meth:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA.inverse_transform` cannot
130::COMO;;# rely on an analytical back-projection and thus an exact reconstruction.
131::COMO;;# Instead, a :class:`~sklearn.kernel_ridge.KernelRidge` is internally trained
132::COMO;;# to learn a mapping from the kernalized PCA basis to the original feature
133::COMO;;# space. This method therefore comes with an approximation introducing small
134::COMO;;# differences when back projecting in the original feature space.
135::COMO;;#
136::COMO;;# To improve the reconstruction using
137::COMO;;# :meth:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA.inverse_transform`, one can tune
138::COMO;;# `alpha` in :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.KernelPCA`, the regularization term
139::COMO;;# which controls the reliance on the training data during the training of
140::COMO;;# the mapping.

2::COMM;;===============================================================
3::COMM;;Model selection with Probabilistic PCA and Factor Analysis (FA)
4::COMM;;===============================================================
5::COMM;;Probabilistic PCA and Factor Analysis are probabilistic models.
6::COMM;;The consequence is that the likelihood of new data can be used
7::COMM;;for model selection and covariance estimation.
8::COMM;;Here we compare PCA and FA with cross-validation on low rank data corrupted
9::COMM;;with homoscedastic noise (noise variance
10::COMM;;is the same for each feature) or heteroscedastic noise (noise variance
11::COMM;;is the different for each feature). In a second step we compare the model
12::COMM;;likelihood to the likelihoods obtained from shrinkage covariance estimators.
13::COMM;;One can observe that with homoscedastic noise both FA and PCA succeed
14::COMM;;in recovering the size of the low rank subspace. The likelihood with PCA
15::COMM;;is higher than FA in this case. However PCA fails and overestimates
16::COMM;;the rank when heteroscedastic noise is present. Under appropriate
17::COMM;;circumstances (choice of the number of components), the held-out
18::COMM;;data is more likely for low rank models than for shrinkage models.
19::COMM;;The automatic estimation from
20::COMM;;Automatic Choice of Dimensionality for PCA. NIPS 2000: 598-604
21::COMM;;by Thomas P. Minka is also compared.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Create the data
27::COMO;;# ---------------
35::COMO;;# Adding homoscedastic noise
37::COMO;;# Adding heteroscedastic noise

42::COMO;;# --------------

2::COMM;;=======================================================
3::COMM;;Comparison of LDA and PCA 2D projection of Iris dataset
4::COMM;;=======================================================
5::COMM;;The Iris dataset represents 3 kind of Iris flowers (Setosa, Versicolour
6::COMM;;and Virginica) with 4 attributes: sepal length, sepal width, petal length
7::COMM;;and petal width.
8::COMM;;Principal Component Analysis (PCA) applied to this data identifies the
9::COMM;;combination of attributes (principal components, or directions in the
10::COMM;;feature space) that account for the most variance in the data. Here we
11::COMM;;plot the different samples on the 2 first principal components.
12::COMM;;Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) tries to identify attributes that
13::COMM;;account for the most variance *between classes*. In particular,
14::COMM;;LDA, in contrast to PCA, is a supervised method, using known class labels.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;Sparse coding with a precomputed dictionary
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;Transform a signal as a sparse combination of Ricker wavelets. This example
6::COMM;;visually compares different sparse coding methods using the
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.SparseCoder` estimator. The Ricker (also known
8::COMM;;as Mexican hat or the second derivative of a Gaussian) is not a particularly
9::COMM;;good kernel to represent piecewise constant signals like this one. It can
10::COMM;;therefore be seen how much adding different widths of atoms matters and it
11::COMM;;therefore motivates learning the dictionary to best fit your type of signals.
12::COMM;;The richer dictionary on the right is not larger in size, heavier subsampling
13::COMM;;is performed in order to stay on the same order of magnitude.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
22::COMM;;x = np.linspace(0, resolution - 1, resolution)

2::COMM;;=====================================
3::COMM;;Multi-class AdaBoosted Decision Trees
4::COMM;;=====================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how boosting can improve the prediction accuracy on a
6::COMM;;multi-label classification problem. It reproduces a similar experiment as
7::COMM;;depicted by Figure 1 in Zhu et al [1]_.
8::COMM;;The core principle of AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting) is to fit a sequence of weak
9::COMM;;learners (e.g. Decision Trees) on repeatedly re-sampled versions of the data.
10::COMM;;Each sample carries a weight that is adjusted after each training step, such
11::COMM;;that misclassified samples will be assigned higher weights. The re-sampling
12::COMM;;process with replacement takes into account the weights assigned to each sample.
13::COMM;;Samples with higher weights have a greater chance of being selected multiple
14::COMM;;times in the new data set, while samples with lower weights are less likely to
15::COMM;;be selected. This ensures that subsequent iterations of the algorithm focus on
16::COMM;;the difficult-to-classify samples.
17::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
18::COMM;;.. [1] :doi:`J. Zhu, H. Zou, S. Rosset, T. Hastie, "Multi-class adaboost."
19::COMM;;Statistics and its Interface 2.3 (2009): 349-360.
20::COMM;;<10.4310/SII.2009.v2.n3.a8>`
22::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
23::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
24::COMO;;# %%
25::COMO;;# Creating the dataset
26::COMO;;# --------------------
27::COMO;;# The classification dataset is constructed by taking a ten-dimensional standard
28::COMO;;# normal distribution (:math:`x` in :math:`R^{10}`) and defining three classes
29::COMO;;# separated by nested concentric ten-dimensional spheres such that roughly equal
30::COMO;;# numbers of samples are in each class (quantiles of the :math:`\chi^2`
31::COMO;;# distribution).
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# We split the dataset into 2 sets: 70 percent of the samples are used for
38::COMO;;# training and the remaining 30 percent for testing.
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# Training the `AdaBoostClassifier`
45::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
46::COMO;;# We train the :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier`. The estimator
47::COMO;;# utilizes boosting to improve the classification accuracy. Boosting is a method
48::COMO;;# designed to train weak learners (i.e. `estimator`) that learn from their
49::COMO;;# predecessor's mistakes.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Here, we define the weak learner as a
52::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` and set the maximum number of
53::COMO;;# leaves to 8. In a real setting, this parameter should be tuned. We set it to a
54::COMO;;# rather low value to limit the runtime of the example.
55::COMO;;#
56::COMO;;# The `SAMME` algorithm build into the
57::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier` then uses the correct or
58::COMO;;# incorrect predictions made be the current weak learner to update the sample
59::COMO;;# weights used for training the consecutive weak learners. Also, the weight of
60::COMO;;# the weak learner itself is calculated based on its accuracy in classifying the
61::COMO;;# training examples. The weight of the weak learner determines its influence on
62::COMO;;# the final ensemble prediction.
72::COMO;;# %%
73::COMO;;# Analysis
74::COMO;;# --------
75::COMO;;# Convergence of the `AdaBoostClassifier`
76::COMO;;# ***************************************
77::COMO;;# To demonstrate the effectiveness of boosting in improving accuracy, we
78::COMO;;# evaluate the misclassification error of the boosted trees in comparison to two
79::COMO;;# baseline scores. The first baseline score is the `misclassification_error`
80::COMO;;# obtained from a single weak-learner (i.e.
81::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier`), which serves as a reference
82::COMO;;# point. The second baseline score is obtained from the
83::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.dummy.DummyClassifier`, which predicts the most prevalent
84::COMO;;# class in a dataset.
104::COMO;;# %%
105::COMO;;# After training the :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` model, the
106::COMO;;# achieved error surpasses the expected value that would have been obtained by
107::COMO;;# guessing the most frequent class label, as the
108::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.dummy.DummyClassifier` does.
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# Now, we calculate the `misclassification_error`, i.e. `1 - accuracy`, of the
111::COMO;;# additive model (:class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier`) at each
112::COMO;;# boosting iteration on the test set to assess its performance.
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# We use :meth:`~sklearn.ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier.staged_predict` that makes
115::COMO;;# as many iterations as the number of fitted estimator (i.e. corresponding to
116::COMO;;# `n_estimators`). At iteration `n`, the predictions of AdaBoost only use the
117::COMO;;# `n` first weak learners. We compare these predictions with the true
118::COMO;;# predictions `y_test` and we, therefore, conclude on the benefit (or not) of adding a
119::COMO;;# new weak learner into the chain.
120::COMO;;#
121::COMO;;# We plot the misclassification error for the different stages:
153::COMO;;# %%
154::COMO;;# The plot shows the missclassification error on the test set after each
155::COMO;;# boosting iteration. We see that the error of the boosted trees converges to an
156::COMO;;# error of around 0.3 after 50 iterations, indicating a significantly higher
157::COMO;;# accuracy compared to a single tree, as illustrated by the dashed line in the
158::COMO;;# plot.
159::COMO;;#
160::COMO;;# The misclassification error jitters because the `SAMME` algorithm uses the
161::COMO;;# discrete outputs of the weak learners to train the boosted model.
162::COMO;;#
163::COMO;;# The convergence of :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier` is mainly
164::COMO;;# influenced by the learning rate (i.e. `learning_rate`), the number of weak
165::COMO;;# learners used (`n_estimators`), and the expressivity of the weak learners
166::COMO;;# (e.g. `max_leaf_nodes`).
167::COMO;;# %%
168::COMO;;# Errors and weights of the Weak Learners
169::COMO;;# ***************************************
170::COMO;;# As previously mentioned, AdaBoost is a forward stagewise additive model. We
171::COMO;;# now focus on understanding the relationship between the attributed weights of
172::COMO;;# the weak learners and their statistical performance.
173::COMO;;#
174::COMO;;# We use the fitted :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.AdaBoostClassifier`'s attributes
175::COMO;;# `estimator_errors_` and `estimator_weights_` to investigate this link.
193::COMO;;# %%
194::COMO;;# On the left plot, we show the weighted error of each weak learner on the
195::COMO;;# reweighted training set at each boosting iteration. On the right plot, we show
196::COMO;;# the weights associated with each weak learner later used to make the
197::COMO;;# predictions of the final additive model.
198::COMO;;#
199::COMO;;# We see that the error of the weak learner is the inverse of the weights. It
200::COMO;;# means that our additive model will trust more a weak learner that makes
201::COMO;;# smaller errors (on the training set) by increasing its impact on the final
202::COMO;;# decision. Indeed, this exactly is the formulation of updating the base
203::COMO;;# estimators' weights after each iteration in AdaBoost.
204::COMO;;#
205::COMO;;# .. dropdown:: Mathematical details
206::COMO;;#
207::COMO;;# The weight associated with a weak learner trained at the stage :math:`m` is
208::COMO;;# inversely associated with its misclassification error such that:
209::COMO;;#
210::COMO;;# .. math:: \alpha^{(m)} = \log \frac{1 - err^{(m)}}{err^{(m)}} + \log (K - 1),
211::COMO;;#
212::COMO;;# where :math:`\alpha^{(m)}` and :math:`err^{(m)}` are the weight and the error
213::COMO;;# of the :math:`m` th weak learner, respectively, and :math:`K` is the number of
214::COMO;;# classes in our classification problem.
215::COMO;;#
216::COMO;;# Another interesting observation boils down to the fact that the first weak
217::COMO;;# learners of the model make fewer errors than later weak learners of the
218::COMO;;# boosting chain.
219::COMO;;#
220::COMO;;# The intuition behind this observation is the following: due to the sample
221::COMO;;# reweighting, later classifiers are forced to try to classify more difficult or
222::COMO;;# noisy samples and to ignore already well classified samples. Therefore, the
223::COMO;;# overall error on the training set will increase. That's why the weak learner's
224::COMO;;# weights are built to counter-balance the worse performing weak learners.

2::COMM;;============================================================
3::COMM;;Single estimator versus bagging: bias-variance decomposition
4::COMM;;============================================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates and compares the bias-variance decomposition of the
6::COMM;;expected mean squared error of a single estimator against a bagging ensemble.
7::COMM;;In regression, the expected mean squared error of an estimator can be
8::COMM;;decomposed in terms of bias, variance and noise. On average over datasets of
9::COMM;;the regression problem, the bias term measures the average amount by which the
10::COMM;;predictions of the estimator differ from the predictions of the best possible
11::COMM;;estimator for the problem (i.e., the Bayes model). The variance term measures
12::COMM;;the variability of the predictions of the estimator when fit over different
13::COMM;;random instances of the same problem. Each problem instance is noted "LS", for
14::COMM;;"Learning Sample", in the following. Finally, the noise measures the irreducible part
15::COMM;;of the error which is due the variability in the data.
16::COMM;;The upper left figure illustrates the predictions (in dark red) of a single
17::COMM;;decision tree trained over a random dataset LS (the blue dots) of a toy 1d
18::COMM;;regression problem. It also illustrates the predictions (in light red) of other
19::COMM;;single decision trees trained over other (and different) randomly drawn
20::COMM;;instances LS of the problem. Intuitively, the variance term here corresponds to
21::COMM;;the width of the beam of predictions (in light red) of the individual
22::COMM;;estimators. The larger the variance, the more sensitive are the predictions for
23::COMM;;`x` to small changes in the training set. The bias term corresponds to the
24::COMM;;difference between the average prediction of the estimator (in cyan) and the
25::COMM;;best possible model (in dark blue). On this problem, we can thus observe that
26::COMM;;the bias is quite low (both the cyan and the blue curves are close to each
27::COMM;;other) while the variance is large (the red beam is rather wide).
28::COMM;;The lower left figure plots the pointwise decomposition of the expected mean
29::COMM;;squared error of a single decision tree. It confirms that the bias term (in
30::COMM;;blue) is low while the variance is large (in green). It also illustrates the
31::COMM;;noise part of the error which, as expected, appears to be constant and around
32::COMM;;`0.01`.
33::COMM;;The right figures correspond to the same plots but using instead a bagging
34::COMM;;ensemble of decision trees. In both figures, we can observe that the bias term
35::COMM;;is larger than in the previous case. In the upper right figure, the difference
36::COMM;;between the average prediction (in cyan) and the best possible model is larger
37::COMM;;(e.g., notice the offset around `x=2`). In the lower right figure, the bias
38::COMM;;curve is also slightly higher than in the lower left figure. In terms of
39::COMM;;variance however, the beam of predictions is narrower, which suggests that the
40::COMM;;variance is lower. Indeed, as the lower right figure confirms, the variance
41::COMM;;term (in green) is lower than for single decision trees. Overall, the bias-variance
42::COMM;;decomposition is therefore no longer the same. The tradeoff is better
43::COMM;;for bagging: averaging several decision trees fit on bootstrap copies of the
44::COMM;;dataset slightly increases the bias term but allows for a larger reduction of
45::COMM;;the variance, which results in a lower overall mean squared error (compare the
46::COMM;;red curves int the lower figures). The script output also confirms this
47::COMM;;intuition. The total error of the bagging ensemble is lower than the total
48::COMM;;error of a single decision tree, and this difference indeed mainly stems from a
49::COMM;;reduced variance.
50::COMM;;For further details on bias-variance decomposition, see section 7.3 of [1]_.
51::COMM;;References
52::COMM;;----------
53::COMM;;.. [1] T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman,
54::COMM;;"Elements of Statistical Learning", Springer, 2009.
56::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
57::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

71::COMO;;# linear models).

2::COMM;;=============================
3::COMM;;OOB Errors for Random Forests
4::COMM;;=============================
5::COMM;;The ``RandomForestClassifier`` is trained using *bootstrap aggregation*, where
6::COMM;;each new tree is fit from a bootstrap sample of the training observations
7::COMM;;:math:`z_i = (x_i, y_i)`. The *out-of-bag* (OOB) error is the average error for
8::COMM;;each :math:`z_i` calculated using predictions from the trees that do not
9::COMM;;contain :math:`z_i` in their respective bootstrap sample. This allows the
10::COMM;;``RandomForestClassifier`` to be fit and validated whilst being trained [1]_.
11::COMM;;The example below demonstrates how the OOB error can be measured at the
12::COMM;;addition of each new tree during training. The resulting plot allows a
13::COMM;;practitioner to approximate a suitable value of ``n_estimators`` at which the
14::COMM;;error stabilizes.
15::COMM;;.. [1] T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, "Elements of Statistical
16::COMM;;Learning Ed. 2", p592-593, Springer, 2009.
18::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
19::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

33::COMO;;# NOTE: Setting the `warm_start` construction parameter to `True` disables
34::COMO;;# support for parallelized ensembles but is necessary for tracking the OOB
35::COMO;;# error trajectory during training.

2::COMM;;===============================================
3::COMM;;Feature transformations with ensembles of trees
4::COMM;;===============================================
5::COMM;;Transform your features into a higher dimensional, sparse space. Then train a
6::COMM;;linear model on these features.
7::COMM;;First fit an ensemble of trees (totally random trees, a random forest, or
8::COMM;;gradient boosted trees) on the training set. Then each leaf of each tree in the
9::COMM;;ensemble is assigned a fixed arbitrary feature index in a new feature space.
10::COMM;;These leaf indices are then encoded in a one-hot fashion.
11::COMM;;Each sample goes through the decisions of each tree of the ensemble and ends up
12::COMM;;in one leaf per tree. The sample is encoded by setting feature values for these
13::COMM;;leaves to 1 and the other feature values to 0.
14::COMM;;The resulting transformer has then learned a supervised, sparse,
15::COMM;;high-dimensional categorical embedding of the data.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
19::COMO;;# %%
20::COMO;;# First, we will create a large dataset and split it into three sets:
21::COMO;;#
22::COMO;;# - a set to train the ensemble methods which are later used to as a feature
23::COMO;;# engineering transformer;
24::COMO;;# - a set to train the linear model;
25::COMO;;# - a set to test the linear model.
26::COMO;;#
27::COMO;;# It is important to split the data in such way to avoid overfitting by leaking
28::COMO;;# data.
38::COMO;;# %%
39::COMO;;# For each of the ensemble methods, we will use 10 estimators and a maximum
40::COMO;;# depth of 3 levels.
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# First, we will start by training the random forest and gradient boosting on
45::COMO;;# the separated training set
55::COMO;;# %%
56::COMO;;# Notice that :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier` is much
57::COMO;;# faster than :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier` starting
58::COMO;;# with intermediate datasets (`n_samples >= 10_000`), which is not the case of
59::COMO;;# the present example.
60::COMO;;#
61::COMO;;# The :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomTreesEmbedding` is an unsupervised method
62::COMO;;# and thus does not required to be trained independently.
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# Now, we will create three pipelines that will use the above embedding as
69::COMO;;# a preprocessing stage.
70::COMO;;#
71::COMO;;# The random trees embedding can be directly pipelined with the logistic
72::COMO;;# regression because it is a standard scikit-learn transformer.
77::COMO;;# %%
78::COMO;;# Then, we can pipeline random forest or gradient boosting with a logistic
79::COMO;;# regression. However, the feature transformation will happen by calling the
80::COMO;;# method `apply`. The pipeline in scikit-learn expects a call to `transform`.
81::COMO;;# Therefore, we wrapped the call to `apply` within a `FunctionTransformer`.

2::COMM;;===============================================================
3::COMM;;Comparing Random Forests and Histogram Gradient Boosting models
4::COMM;;===============================================================
5::COMM;;In this example we compare the performance of Random Forest (RF) and Histogram
6::COMM;;Gradient Boosting (HGBT) models in terms of score and computation time for a
7::COMM;;regression dataset, though **all the concepts here presented apply to
8::COMM;;classification as well**.
9::COMM;;The comparison is made by varying the parameters that control the number of
10::COMM;;trees according to each estimator:
11::COMM;;- `n_estimators` controls the number of trees in the forest. It's a fixed number.
12::COMM;;- `max_iter` is the maximum number of iterations in a gradient boosting
13::COMM;;based model. The number of iterations corresponds to the number of trees for
14::COMM;;regression and binary classification problems. Furthermore, the actual number
15::COMM;;of trees required by the model depends on the stopping criteria.
16::COMM;;HGBT uses gradient boosting to iteratively improve the model's performance by
17::COMM;;fitting each tree to the negative gradient of the loss function with respect to
18::COMM;;the predicted value. RFs, on the other hand, are based on bagging and use a
19::COMM;;majority vote to predict the outcome.
20::COMM;;See the :ref:`User Guide <ensemble>` for more information on ensemble models or
21::COMM;;see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_hgbt_regression.py` for an
22::COMM;;example showcasing some other features of HGBT models.
24::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
25::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# Load dataset
28::COMO;;# ------------
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# HGBT uses a histogram-based algorithm on binned feature values that can
34::COMO;;# efficiently handle large datasets (tens of thousands of samples or more) with
35::COMO;;# a high number of features (see :ref:`Why_it's_faster`). The scikit-learn
36::COMO;;# implementation of RF does not use binning and relies on exact splitting, which
37::COMO;;# can be computationally expensive.
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# Compute score and computation times
41::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# Notice that many parts of the implementation of
44::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier` and
45::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` are parallelized by
46::COMO;;# default.
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# The implementation of :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor` and
49::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` can also be run on multiple
50::COMO;;# cores by using the `n_jobs` parameter, here set to match the number of
51::COMO;;# physical cores on the host machine. See :ref:`parallelism` for more
52::COMO;;# information.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Unlike RF, HGBT models offer an early-stopping option (see
58::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_early_stopping.py`)
59::COMO;;# to avoid adding new unnecessary trees. Internally, the algorithm uses an
60::COMO;;# out-of-sample set to compute the generalization performance of the model at
61::COMO;;# each addition of a tree. Thus, if the generalization performance is not
62::COMO;;# improving for more than `n_iter_no_change` iterations, it stops adding trees.
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# The other parameters of both models were tuned but the procedure is not shown
65::COMO;;# here to keep the example simple.
92::COMO;;# %%
93::COMO;;# .. Note::
94::COMO;;# Tuning the `n_estimators` for RF generally results in a waste of computer
95::COMO;;# power. In practice one just needs to ensure that it is large enough so that
96::COMO;;# doubling its value does not lead to a significant improvement of the testing
97::COMO;;# score.
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# Plot results
100::COMO;;# ------------
101::COMO;;# We can use a `plotly.express.scatter
102::COMO;;# <https://plotly.com/python-api-reference/generated/plotly.express.scatter.html>`_
103::COMO;;# to visualize the trade-off between elapsed computing time and mean test score.
104::COMO;;# Passing the cursor over a given point displays the corresponding parameters.
105::COMO;;# Error bars correspond to one standard deviation as computed in the different
106::COMO;;# folds of the cross-validation.
172::COMO;;# %%
173::COMO;;# Both HGBT and RF models improve when increasing the number of trees in the
174::COMO;;# ensemble. However, the scores reach a plateau where adding new trees just
175::COMO;;# makes fitting and scoring slower. The RF model reaches such plateau earlier
176::COMO;;# and can never reach the test score of the largest HGBDT model.
177::COMO;;#
178::COMO;;# Note that the results shown on the above plot can change slightly across runs
179::COMO;;# and even more significantly when running on other machines: try to run this
180::COMO;;# example on your own local machine.
181::COMO;;#
182::COMO;;# Overall, one should often observe that the Histogram-based gradient boosting
183::COMO;;# models uniformly dominate the Random Forest models in the "test score vs
184::COMO;;# training speed trade-off" (the HGBDT curve should be on the top left of the RF
185::COMO;;# curve, without ever crossing). The "test score vs prediction speed" trade-off
186::COMO;;# can also be more disputed, but it's most often favorable to HGBDT. It's always
187::COMO;;# a good idea to check both kinds of model (with hyper-parameter tuning) and
188::COMO;;# compare their performance on your specific problem to determine which model is
189::COMO;;# the best fit but **HGBT almost always offers a more favorable speed-accuracy
190::COMO;;# trade-off than RF**, either with the default hyper-parameters or including the
191::COMO;;# hyper-parameter tuning cost.
192::COMO;;#
193::COMO;;# There is one exception to this rule of thumb though: when training a
194::COMO;;# multiclass classification model with a large number of possible classes, HGBDT
195::COMO;;# fits internally one-tree per class at each boosting iteration while the trees
196::COMO;;# used by the RF models are naturally multiclass which should improve the speed
197::COMO;;# accuracy trade-off of the RF models in this case.
