2::COMM;;================================================
3::COMM;;Categorical Feature Support in Gradient Boosting
4::COMM;;================================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
6::COMM;;In this example, we compare the training times and prediction performances of
7::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` with different encoding
8::COMM;;strategies for categorical features. In particular, we evaluate:
9::COMM;;- "Dropped": dropping the categorical features;
10::COMM;;- "One Hot": using a :class:`~preprocessing.OneHotEncoder`;
11::COMM;;- "Ordinal": using an :class:`~preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder` and treat
12::COMM;;categories as ordered, equidistant quantities;
13::COMM;;- "Target": using a :class:`~preprocessing.TargetEncoder`;
14::COMM;;- "Native": relying on the :ref:`native category support
15::COMM;;<categorical_support_gbdt>` of the
16::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` estimator.
17::COMM;;For such purpose we use the Ames Iowa Housing dataset, which consists of
18::COMM;;numerical and categorical features, where the target is the house sale price.
19::COMM;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_hgbt_regression.py` for an
20::COMM;;example showcasing some other features of
21::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
22::COMM;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_preprocessing_plot_target_encoder.py` for a
23::COMM;;comparison of encoding strategies in the presence of high cardinality
24::COMM;;categorical features.
26::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
27::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
28::COMO;;# %%
29::COMO;;# Load Ames Housing dataset
30::COMO;;# -------------------------
31::COMO;;# First, we load the Ames Housing data as a pandas dataframe. The features
32::COMO;;# are either categorical or numerical:
35::COMO;;# Select only a subset of features of X to make the example faster to run
69::COMO;;# %%
70::COMO;;# Gradient boosting estimator with dropped categorical features
71::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------
72::COMO;;# As a baseline, we create an estimator where the categorical features are
73::COMO;;# dropped:
82::COMO;;# %%
83::COMO;;# Gradient boosting estimator with one-hot encoding
84::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------
85::COMO;;# Next, we create a pipeline to one-hot encode the categorical features,
86::COMO;;# while letting the remaining features `"passthrough"` unchanged:
99::COMO;;# %%
100::COMO;;# Gradient boosting estimator with ordinal encoding
101::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------
102::COMO;;# Next, we create a pipeline that treats categorical features as ordered
103::COMO;;# quantities, i.e. the categories are encoded as 0, 1, 2, etc., and treated as
104::COMO;;# continuous features.
118::COMO;;# %%
119::COMO;;# Gradient boosting estimator with target encoding
120::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------------
121::COMO;;# Another possibility is to use the :class:`~preprocessing.TargetEncoder`, which
122::COMO;;# encodes the categories computed from the mean of the (training) target
123::COMO;;# variable, as computed using a smoothed `np.mean(y, axis=0)` i.e.:
124::COMO;;#
125::COMO;;# - in regression it uses the mean of `y`;
126::COMO;;# - in binary classification, the positive-class rate;
127::COMO;;# - in multiclass, a vector of class rates (one per class).
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# For each category, it computes these target averages using :term:`cross
130::COMO;;# fitting`, meaning that the training data are split into folds: in each fold
131::COMO;;# the averages are calculated only on a subset of data and then applied to the
132::COMO;;# held-out part. This way, each sample is encoded using statistics from data it
133::COMO;;# was not part of, preventing information leakage from the target.
146::COMO;;# %%
147::COMO;;# Gradient boosting estimator with native categorical support
148::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------------
149::COMO;;# We now create a :class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` estimator
150::COMO;;# that can natively handle categorical features without explicit encoding. Such
151::COMO;;# functionality can be enabled by setting `categorical_features="from_dtype"`,
152::COMO;;# which automatically detects features with categorical dtypes, or more explicitly
153::COMO;;# by `categorical_features=categorical_columns_subset`.
154::COMO;;#
155::COMO;;# Unlike previous encoding approaches, the estimator natively deals with the
156::COMO;;# categorical features. At each split, it partitions the categories of such a
157::COMO;;# feature into disjoint sets using a heuristic that sorts them by their effect
158::COMO;;# on the target variable, see `Split finding with categorical features
159::COMO;;# <https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html#split-finding-with-categorical-features>`_
160::COMO;;# for details.
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# While ordinal encoding may work well for low-cardinality features even if
163::COMO;;# categories have no natural order, reaching meaningful splits requires deeper
164::COMO;;# trees as the cardinality increases. The native categorical support avoids this
165::COMO;;# by directly working with unordered categories. The advantage over one-hot
166::COMO;;# encoding is the omitted preprocessing and faster fit and predict time.
171::COMO;;# %%
172::COMO;;# Model comparison
173::COMO;;# ----------------
174::COMO;;# Here we use :term:`cross validation` to compare the models performance in
175::COMO;;# terms of :func:`~metrics.mean_absolute_percentage_error` and fit times. In the
176::COMO;;# upcoming plots, error bars represent 1 standard deviation as computed across
177::COMO;;# cross-validation splits.
192::COMO;;# %%
251::COMO;;# %%
252::COMO;;# In the plot above, the "best models" are those that are closer to the
253::COMO;;# down-left corner, as indicated by the arrow. Those models would indeed
254::COMO;;# correspond to faster fitting and lower error.
255::COMO;;#
256::COMO;;# The model using one-hot encoded data is the slowest. This is to be expected,
257::COMO;;# as one-hot encoding creates an additional feature for each category value of
258::COMO;;# every categorical feature, greatly increasing the number of split candidates
259::COMO;;# during training. In theory, we expect the native handling of categorical
260::COMO;;# features to be slightly slower than treating categories as ordered quantities
261::COMO;;# ('Ordinal'), since native handling requires :ref:`sorting categories
262::COMO;;# <categorical_support_gbdt>`. Fitting times should however be close when the
263::COMO;;# number of categories is small, and this may not always be reflected in
264::COMO;;# practice.
265::COMO;;#
266::COMO;;# The time required to fit when using the `TargetEncoder` depends on the
267::COMO;;# cross fitting parameter `cv`, as adding splits come at a computational cost.
268::COMO;;#
269::COMO;;# In terms of prediction performance, dropping the categorical features leads to
270::COMO;;# the worst performance. The four models that make use of the categorical
271::COMO;;# features have comparable error rates, with a slight edge for the native
272::COMO;;# handling.
273::COMO;;# %%
274::COMO;;# Limiting the number of splits
275::COMO;;# -----------------------------
276::COMO;;# In general, one can expect poorer predictions from one-hot-encoded data,
277::COMO;;# especially when the tree depths or the number of nodes are limited: with
278::COMO;;# one-hot-encoded data, one needs more split points, i.e. more depth, in order
279::COMO;;# to recover an equivalent split that could be obtained in one single split
280::COMO;;# point with native handling.
281::COMO;;#
282::COMO;;# This is also true when categories are treated as ordinal quantities: if
283::COMO;;# categories are `A..F` and the best split is `ACF - BDE` the one-hot-encoder
284::COMO;;# model would need 3 split points (one per category in the left node), and the
285::COMO;;# ordinal non-native model would need 4 splits: 1 split to isolate `A`, 1 split
286::COMO;;# to isolate `F`, and 2 splits to isolate `C` from `BCDE`.
287::COMO;;#
288::COMO;;# How strongly the models' performances differ in practice depends on the
289::COMO;;# dataset and on the flexibility of the trees.
290::COMO;;#
291::COMO;;# To see this, let us re-run the same analysis with under-fitting models where
292::COMO;;# we artificially limit the total number of splits by both limiting the number
293::COMO;;# of trees and the depth of each tree.
296::COMO;;# The native model does not use a pipeline so, we can set the parameters
297::COMO;;# directly.
316::COMO;;# %%
320::COMO;;# %%
321::COMO;;# The results for these underfitting models confirm our previous intuition: the
322::COMO;;# native category handling strategy performs the best when the splitting budget
323::COMO;;# is constrained. The three explicit encoding strategies (one-hot, ordinal and
324::COMO;;# target encoding) lead to slightly larger errors than the estimator's native
325::COMO;;# handling, but still perform better than the baseline model that just dropped
326::COMO;;# the categorical features altogether.
2::COMM;;===================================
3::COMM;;Early stopping in Gradient Boosting
4::COMM;;===================================
5::COMM;;Gradient Boosting is an ensemble technique that combines multiple weak
6::COMM;;learners, typically decision trees, to create a robust and powerful
7::COMM;;predictive model. It does so in an iterative fashion, where each new stage
8::COMM;;(tree) corrects the errors of the previous ones.
9::COMM;;Early stopping is a technique in Gradient Boosting that allows us to find
10::COMM;;the optimal number of iterations required to build a model that generalizes
11::COMM;;well to unseen data and avoids overfitting. The concept is simple: we set
12::COMM;;aside a portion of our dataset as a validation set (specified using
13::COMM;;`validation_fraction`) to assess the model's performance during training.
14::COMM;;As the model is iteratively built with additional stages (trees), its
15::COMM;;performance on the validation set is monitored as a function of the
16::COMM;;number of steps.
17::COMM;;Early stopping becomes effective when the model's performance on the
18::COMM;;validation set plateaus or worsens (within deviations specified by `tol`)
19::COMM;;over a certain number of consecutive stages (specified by `n_iter_no_change`).
20::COMM;;This signals that the model has reached a point where further iterations may
21::COMM;;lead to overfitting, and it's time to stop training.
22::COMM;;The number of estimators (trees) in the final model, when early stopping is
23::COMM;;applied, can be accessed using the `n_estimators_` attribute. Overall, early
24::COMM;;stopping is a valuable tool to strike a balance between model performance and
25::COMM;;efficiency in gradient boosting.
27::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
28::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
29::COMO;;# %%
30::COMO;;# Data Preparation
31::COMO;;# ----------------
32::COMO;;# First we load and prepares the California Housing Prices dataset for
33::COMO;;# training and evaluation. It subsets the dataset, splits it into training
34::COMO;;# and validation sets.
44::COMO;;# %%
45::COMO;;# Model Training and Comparison
46::COMO;;# -----------------------------
47::COMO;;# Two :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` models are trained:
48::COMO;;# one with and another without early stopping. The purpose is to compare their
49::COMO;;# performance. It also calculates the training time and the `n_estimators_`
50::COMO;;# used by both models.
66::COMO;;# %%
67::COMO;;# Error Calculation
68::COMO;;# -----------------
69::COMO;;# The code calculates the :func:`~sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error` for both
70::COMO;;# training and validation datasets for the models trained in the previous
71::COMO;;# section. It computes the errors for each boosting iteration. The purpose is
72::COMO;;# to assess the performance and convergence of the models.
93::COMO;;# %%
94::COMO;;# Visualize Comparison
95::COMO;;# --------------------
96::COMO;;# It includes three subplots:
97::COMO;;#
98::COMO;;# 1. Plotting training errors of both models over boosting iterations.
99::COMO;;# 2. Plotting validation errors of both models over boosting iterations.
100::COMO;;# 3. Creating a bar chart to compare the training times and the estimator used
101::COMO;;# of the models with and without early stopping.
102::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# %%
134::COMO;;# The difference in training error between the `gbm_full` and the
135::COMO;;# `gbm_early_stopping` stems from the fact that `gbm_early_stopping` sets
136::COMO;;# aside `validation_fraction` of the training data as internal validation set.
137::COMO;;# Early stopping is decided based on this internal validation score.
138::COMO;;# %%
139::COMO;;# Summary
140::COMO;;# -------
141::COMO;;# In our example with the :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`
142::COMO;;# model on the California Housing Prices dataset, we have demonstrated the
143::COMO;;# practical benefits of early stopping:
144::COMO;;#
145::COMO;;# - **Preventing Overfitting:** We showed how the validation error stabilizes
146::COMO;;# or starts to increase after a certain point, indicating that the model
147::COMO;;# generalizes better to unseen data. This is achieved by stopping the training
148::COMO;;# process before overfitting occurs.
149::COMO;;# - **Improving Training Efficiency:** We compared training times between
150::COMO;;# models with and without early stopping. The model with early stopping
151::COMO;;# achieved comparable accuracy while requiring significantly fewer
152::COMO;;# estimators, resulting in faster training.
2::COMM;;======================================
3::COMM;;Gradient Boosting Out-of-Bag estimates
4::COMM;;======================================
5::COMM;;Out-of-bag (OOB) estimates can be a useful heuristic to estimate
6::COMM;;the "optimal" number of boosting iterations.
7::COMM;;OOB estimates are almost identical to cross-validation estimates but
8::COMM;;they can be computed on-the-fly without the need for repeated model
9::COMM;;fitting.
10::COMM;;OOB estimates are only available for Stochastic Gradient Boosting
11::COMM;;(i.e. ``subsample < 1.0``), the estimates are derived from the improvement
12::COMM;;in loss based on the examples not included in the bootstrap sample
13::COMM;;(the so-called out-of-bag examples).
14::COMM;;The OOB estimator is a pessimistic estimator of the true
15::COMM;;test loss, but remains a fairly good approximation for a small number of trees.
16::COMM;;The figure shows the cumulative sum of the negative OOB improvements
17::COMM;;as a function of the boosting iteration. As you can see, it tracks the test
18::COMM;;loss for the first hundred iterations but then diverges in a
19::COMM;;pessimistic way.
20::COMM;;The figure also shows the performance of 3-fold cross validation which
21::COMM;;usually gives a better estimate of the test loss
22::COMM;;but is computationally more demanding.
24::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
25::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMO;;# Generate data (adapted from G. Ridgeway's gbm example)
43::COMO;;# Fit classifier with out-of-bag estimates
60::COMM;;score = np.zeros((n_estimators,), dtype=np.float64)
61::COMM;;for i, y_proba in enumerate(clf.staged_predict_proba(X_test)):
62::COMM;;score[i] = 2 * log_loss(y_test, y_proba[:, 1])
63::COMM;;return score
64::COMM;;def cv_estimate(n_splits=None):
65::COMM;;cv = KFold(n_splits=n_splits)
66::COMM;;cv_clf = ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier(**params)
67::COMM;;val_scores = np.zeros((n_estimators,), dtype=np.float64)
68::COMM;;for train, test in cv.split(X_train, y_train):
69::COMM;;cv_clf.fit(X_train[train], y_train[train])
70::COMM;;val_scores += heldout_score(cv_clf, X_train[test], y_train[test])
71::COMM;;val_scores /= n_splits
72::COMM;;return val_scores
73::COMM;;# Estimate best n_estimator using cross-validation
74::COMM;;cv_score = cv_estimate(3)
75::COMM;;# Compute best n_estimator for test data
76::COMM;;test_score = heldout_score(clf, X_test, y_test)
77::COMM;;# negative cumulative sum of oob improvements
78::COMM;;cumsum = -np.cumsum(clf.oob_improvement_)
79::COMM;;# min loss according to OOB
80::COMM;;oob_best_iter = x[np.argmin(cumsum)]
81::COMM;;# min loss according to test (normalize such that first loss is 0)
82::COMM;;test_score -= test_score[0]
83::COMM;;test_best_iter = x[np.argmin(test_score)]
84::COMM;;# min loss according to cv (normalize such that first loss is 0)
85::COMM;;cv_score -= cv_score[0]
86::COMM;;cv_best_iter = x[np.argmin(cv_score)]
87::COMM;;# color brew for the three curves
88::COMM;;oob_color = list(map(lambda x: x / 256.0, (190, 174, 212)))
89::COMM;;test_color = list(map(lambda x: x / 256.0, (127, 201, 127)))
90::COMM;;cv_color = list(map(lambda x: x / 256.0, (253, 192, 134)))
91::COMM;;# line type for the three curves
92::COMM;;oob_line = "dashed"
93::COMM;;test_line = "solid"
94::COMM;;cv_line = "dashdot"
95::COMM;;# plot curves and vertical lines for best iterations
96::COMM;;plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.8))
97::COMM;;plt.plot(x, cumsum, label="OOB loss", color=oob_color, linestyle=oob_line)
98::COMM;;plt.plot(x, test_score, label="Test loss", color=test_color, linestyle=test_line)
99::COMM;;plt.plot(x, cv_score, label="CV loss", color=cv_color, linestyle=cv_line)
100::COMM;;plt.axvline(x=oob_best_iter, color=oob_color, linestyle=oob_line)
101::COMM;;plt.axvline(x=test_best_iter, color=test_color, linestyle=test_line)
102::COMM;;plt.axvline(x=cv_best_iter, color=cv_color, linestyle=cv_line)
103::COMM;;# add three vertical lines to xticks
104::COMM;;xticks = plt.xticks()
105::COMM;;xticks_pos = np.array(
106::COMM;;xticks[0].tolist() + [oob_best_iter, cv_best_iter, test_best_iter]
107::COMM;;)
108::COMM;;xticks_label = np.array(list(map(lambda t: int(t), xticks[0])) + ["OOB", "CV", "Test"])
109::COMM;;ind = np.argsort(xticks_pos)
110::COMM;;xticks_pos = xticks_pos[ind]
111::COMM;;xticks_label = xticks_label[ind]
112::COMM;;plt.xticks(xticks_pos, xticks_label, rotation=90)
113::COMM;;plt.legend(loc="upper center")
114::COMM;;plt.ylabel("normalized loss")
115::COMM;;plt.xlabel("number of iterations")
116::COMM;;plt.show()
2::COMM;;=====================================================
3::COMM;;Prediction Intervals for Gradient Boosting Regression
4::COMM;;=====================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how quantile regression can be used to create prediction
6::COMM;;intervals. See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_hgbt_regression.py`
7::COMM;;for an example showcasing some other features of
8::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# Generate some data for a synthetic regression problem by applying the
14::COMO;;# function f to uniformly sampled random inputs.
19::COMM;;return x * np.sin(x)
20::COMM;;rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
21::COMM;;X = np.atleast_2d(rng.uniform(0, 10.0, size=1000)).T
22::COMM;;expected_y = f(X).ravel()
23::COMM;;# %%
24::COMM;;# To make the problem interesting, we generate observations of the target y as
25::COMM;;# the sum of a deterministic term computed by the function f and a random noise
26::COMM;;# term that follows a centered `log-normal
27::COMM;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution>`_. To make this even
28::COMM;;# more interesting we consider the case where the amplitude of the noise
29::COMM;;# depends on the input variable x (heteroscedastic noise).
30::COMM;;#
31::COMM;;# The lognormal distribution is non-symmetric and long tailed: observing large
32::COMM;;# outliers is likely but it is impossible to observe small outliers.
33::COMM;;sigma = 0.5 + X.ravel() / 10
34::COMM;;noise = rng.lognormal(sigma=sigma) - np.exp(sigma**2 / 2)
35::COMM;;y = expected_y + noise
36::COMM;;# %%
37::COMM;;# Split into train, test datasets:
38::COMM;;X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)
39::COMM;;# %%
40::COMM;;# Fitting non-linear quantile and least squares regressors
41::COMM;;# --------------------------------------------------------
42::COMM;;#
43::COMM;;# Fit gradient boosting models trained with the quantile loss and
44::COMM;;# alpha=0.05, 0.5, 0.95.
45::COMM;;#
46::COMM;;# The models obtained for alpha=0.05 and alpha=0.95 produce a 90% confidence
47::COMM;;# interval (95% - 5% = 90%).
48::COMM;;#
49::COMM;;# The model trained with alpha=0.5 produces a regression of the median: on
50::COMM;;# average, there should be the same number of target observations above and
51::COMM;;# below the predicted values.
52::COMM;;from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
53::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import mean_pinball_loss, mean_squared_error
54::COMM;;all_models = {}
55::COMM;;common_params = dict(
56::COMM;;learning_rate=0.05,
57::COMM;;n_estimators=200,
58::COMM;;max_depth=2,
59::COMM;;min_samples_leaf=9,
60::COMM;;min_samples_split=9,
61::COMM;;)
62::COMM;;for alpha in [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]:
63::COMM;;gbr = GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", alpha=alpha, **common_params)
64::COMM;;all_models["q %1.2f" % alpha] = gbr.fit(X_train, y_train)
65::COMM;;# %%
66::COMM;;# Notice that :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` is much
67::COMM;;# faster than :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` starting with
68::COMM;;# intermediate datasets (`n_samples >= 10_000`), which is not the case of the
69::COMM;;# present example.
70::COMM;;#
71::COMM;;# For the sake of comparison, we also fit a baseline model trained with the
72::COMM;;# usual (mean) squared error (MSE).
73::COMM;;gbr_ls = GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="squared_error", **common_params)
74::COMM;;all_models["mse"] = gbr_ls.fit(X_train, y_train)
75::COMM;;# %%
76::COMM;;# Create an evenly spaced evaluation set of input values spanning the [0, 10]
77::COMM;;# range.
78::COMM;;xx = np.atleast_2d(np.linspace(0, 10, 1000)).T
79::COMM;;# %%
80::COMM;;# Plot the true conditional mean function f, the predictions of the conditional
81::COMM;;# mean (loss equals squared error), the conditional median and the conditional
82::COMM;;# 90% interval (from 5th to 95th conditional percentiles).
83::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
84::COMM;;y_pred = all_models["mse"].predict(xx)
85::COMM;;y_lower = all_models["q 0.05"].predict(xx)
86::COMM;;y_upper = all_models["q 0.95"].predict(xx)
87::COMM;;y_med = all_models["q 0.50"].predict(xx)
88::COMM;;fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
89::COMM;;plt.plot(xx, f(xx), "black", linewidth=3, label=r"$f(x) = x\,\sin(x)$")
90::COMM;;plt.plot(X_test, y_test, "b.", markersize=10, label="Test observations")
91::COMM;;plt.plot(xx, y_med, "tab:orange", linewidth=3, label="Predicted median")
92::COMM;;plt.plot(xx, y_pred, "tab:green", linewidth=3, label="Predicted mean")
93::COMM;;plt.fill_between(
94::COMM;;xx.ravel(), y_lower, y_upper, alpha=0.4, label="Predicted 90% interval"
95::COMM;;)
96::COMM;;plt.xlabel("$x$")
97::COMM;;plt.ylabel("$f(x)$")
98::COMM;;plt.ylim(-10, 25)
99::COMM;;plt.legend(loc="upper left")
100::COMM;;plt.show()
101::COMM;;# %%
102::COMM;;# Comparing the predicted median with the predicted mean, we note that the
103::COMM;;# median is on average below the mean as the noise is skewed towards high
104::COMM;;# values (large outliers). The median estimate also seems to be smoother
105::COMM;;# because of its natural robustness to outliers.
106::COMM;;#
107::COMM;;# Also observe that the inductive bias of gradient boosting trees is
108::COMM;;# unfortunately preventing our 0.05 quantile to fully capture the sinoisoidal
109::COMM;;# shape of the signal, in particular around x=8. Tuning hyper-parameters can
110::COMM;;# reduce this effect as shown in the last part of this notebook.
111::COMM;;#
112::COMM;;# Analysis of the error metrics
113::COMM;;# -----------------------------
114::COMM;;#
115::COMM;;# Measure the models with :func:`~sklearn.metrics.mean_squared_error` and
116::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.mean_pinball_loss` metrics on the training dataset.
117::COMM;;import pandas as pd
118::COMM;;def highlight_min(x):
119::COMM;;x_min = x.min()
120::COMM;;return ["font-weight: bold" if v == x_min else "" for v in x]
121::COMM;;results = []
122::COMM;;for name, gbr in sorted(all_models.items()):
123::COMM;;metrics = {"model": name}
124::COMM;;y_pred = gbr.predict(X_train)
125::COMM;;for alpha in [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]:
126::COMM;;metrics["pbl=%1.2f" % alpha] = mean_pinball_loss(y_train, y_pred, alpha=alpha)
127::COMM;;metrics["MSE"] = mean_squared_error(y_train, y_pred)
128::COMM;;results.append(metrics)
129::COMM;;pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("model").style.apply(highlight_min)
130::COMM;;# %%
131::COMM;;# One column shows all models evaluated by the same metric. The minimum number
132::COMM;;# on a column should be obtained when the model is trained and measured with
133::COMM;;# the same metric. This should be always the case on the training set if the
134::COMM;;# training converged.
135::COMM;;#
136::COMM;;# Note that because the target distribution is asymmetric, the expected
137::COMM;;# conditional mean and conditional median are significantly different and
138::COMM;;# therefore one could not use the squared error model get a good estimation of
139::COMM;;# the conditional median nor the converse.
140::COMM;;#
141::COMM;;# If the target distribution were symmetric and had no outliers (e.g. with a
142::COMM;;# Gaussian noise), then median estimator and the least squares estimator would
143::COMM;;# have yielded similar predictions.
144::COMM;;#
145::COMM;;# We then do the same on the test set.
146::COMM;;results = []
147::COMM;;for name, gbr in sorted(all_models.items()):
148::COMM;;metrics = {"model": name}
149::COMM;;y_pred = gbr.predict(X_test)
150::COMM;;for alpha in [0.05, 0.5, 0.95]:
151::COMM;;metrics["pbl=%1.2f" % alpha] = mean_pinball_loss(y_test, y_pred, alpha=alpha)
152::COMM;;metrics["MSE"] = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred)
153::COMM;;results.append(metrics)
154::COMM;;pd.DataFrame(results).set_index("model").style.apply(highlight_min)
155::COMM;;# %%
156::COMM;;# Errors are higher meaning the models slightly overfitted the data. It still
157::COMM;;# shows that the best test metric is obtained when the model is trained by
158::COMM;;# minimizing this same metric.
159::COMM;;#
160::COMM;;# Note that the conditional median estimator is competitive with the squared
161::COMM;;# error estimator in terms of MSE on the test set: this can be explained by
162::COMM;;# the fact the squared error estimator is very sensitive to large outliers
163::COMM;;# which can cause significant overfitting. This can be seen on the right hand
164::COMM;;# side of the previous plot. The conditional median estimator is biased
165::COMM;;# (underestimation for this asymmetric noise) but is also naturally robust to
166::COMM;;# outliers and overfits less.
167::COMM;;#
168::COMM;;# .. _calibration-section:
169::COMM;;#
170::COMM;;# Calibration of the confidence interval
171::COMM;;# --------------------------------------
172::COMM;;#
173::COMM;;# We can also evaluate the ability of the two extreme quantile estimators at
174::COMM;;# producing a well-calibrated conditional 90%-confidence interval.
175::COMM;;#
176::COMM;;# To do this we can compute the fraction of observations that fall between the
177::COMM;;# predictions:
178::COMM;;def coverage_fraction(y, y_low, y_high):
179::COMM;;return np.mean(np.logical_and(y >= y_low, y <= y_high))
180::COMM;;coverage_fraction(
181::COMM;;y_train,
182::COMM;;all_models["q 0.05"].predict(X_train),
183::COMM;;all_models["q 0.95"].predict(X_train),
184::COMM;;)
185::COMM;;# %%
186::COMM;;# On the training set the calibration is very close to the expected coverage
187::COMM;;# value for a 90% confidence interval.
188::COMM;;coverage_fraction(
189::COMM;;y_test, all_models["q 0.05"].predict(X_test), all_models["q 0.95"].predict(X_test)
190::COMM;;)
191::COMM;;# %%
192::COMM;;# On the test set, the estimated confidence interval is slightly too narrow.
193::COMM;;# Note, however, that we would need to wrap those metrics in a cross-validation
194::COMM;;# loop to assess their variability under data resampling.
195::COMM;;#
196::COMM;;# Tuning the hyper-parameters of the quantile regressors
197::COMM;;# ------------------------------------------------------
198::COMM;;#
199::COMM;;# In the plot above, we observed that the 5th percentile regressor seems to
200::COMM;;# underfit and could not adapt to sinusoidal shape of the signal.
201::COMM;;#
202::COMM;;# The hyper-parameters of the model were approximately hand-tuned for the
203::COMM;;# median regressor and there is no reason that the same hyper-parameters are
204::COMM;;# suitable for the 5th percentile regressor.
205::COMM;;#
206::COMM;;# To confirm this hypothesis, we tune the hyper-parameters of a new regressor
207::COMM;;# of the 5th percentile by selecting the best model parameters by
208::COMM;;# cross-validation on the pinball loss with alpha=0.05:
209::COMM;;# %%
210::COMM;;from pprint import pprint
211::COMM;;from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv # noqa: F401
212::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import make_scorer
213::COMM;;from sklearn.model_selection import HalvingRandomSearchCV
214::COMM;;param_grid = dict(
215::COMM;;learning_rate=[0.05, 0.1, 0.2],
216::COMM;;max_depth=[2, 5, 10],
217::COMM;;min_samples_leaf=[1, 5, 10, 20],
218::COMM;;min_samples_split=[5, 10, 20, 30, 50],
219::COMM;;)
220::COMM;;alpha = 0.05
221::COMM;;neg_mean_pinball_loss_05p_scorer = make_scorer(
222::COMM;;mean_pinball_loss,
223::COMM;;alpha=alpha,
224::COMM;;greater_is_better=False, # maximize the negative loss
225::COMM;;)
226::COMM;;gbr = GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", alpha=alpha, random_state=0)
227::COMM;;search_05p = HalvingRandomSearchCV(
228::COMM;;gbr,
229::COMM;;param_grid,
230::COMM;;resource="n_estimators",
231::COMM;;max_resources=250,
232::COMM;;min_resources=50,
233::COMM;;scoring=neg_mean_pinball_loss_05p_scorer,
234::COMM;;n_jobs=2,
235::COMM;;random_state=0,
236::COMM;;).fit(X_train, y_train)
237::COMM;;pprint(search_05p.best_params_)
238::COMM;;# %%
239::COMM;;# We observe that the hyper-parameters that were hand-tuned for the median
240::COMM;;# regressor are in the same range as the hyper-parameters suitable for the 5th
241::COMM;;# percentile regressor.
242::COMM;;#
243::COMM;;# Let's now tune the hyper-parameters for the 95th percentile regressor. We
244::COMM;;# need to redefine the `scoring` metric used to select the best model, along
245::COMM;;# with adjusting the alpha parameter of the inner gradient boosting estimator
246::COMM;;# itself:
247::COMM;;from sklearn.base import clone
248::COMM;;alpha = 0.95
249::COMM;;neg_mean_pinball_loss_95p_scorer = make_scorer(
250::COMM;;mean_pinball_loss,
251::COMM;;alpha=alpha,
252::COMM;;greater_is_better=False, # maximize the negative loss
253::COMM;;)
254::COMM;;search_95p = clone(search_05p).set_params(
255::COMM;;estimator__alpha=alpha,
256::COMM;;scoring=neg_mean_pinball_loss_95p_scorer,
257::COMM;;)
258::COMM;;search_95p.fit(X_train, y_train)
259::COMM;;pprint(search_95p.best_params_)
260::COMM;;# %%
261::COMM;;# The result shows that the hyper-parameters for the 95th percentile regressor
262::COMM;;# identified by the search procedure are roughly in the same range as the hand-tuned
263::COMM;;# hyper-parameters for the median regressor and the hyper-parameters
264::COMM;;# identified by the search procedure for the 5th percentile regressor. However,
265::COMM;;# the hyper-parameter searches did lead to an improved 90% confidence interval
266::COMM;;# that is comprised by the predictions of those two tuned quantile regressors.
267::COMM;;# Note that the prediction of the upper 95th percentile has a much coarser shape
268::COMM;;# than the prediction of the lower 5th percentile because of the outliers:
269::COMM;;y_lower = search_05p.predict(xx)
270::COMM;;y_upper = search_95p.predict(xx)
271::COMM;;fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))
272::COMM;;plt.plot(xx, f(xx), "black", linewidth=3, label=r"$f(x) = x\,\sin(x)$")
273::COMM;;plt.plot(X_test, y_test, "b.", markersize=10, label="Test observations")
274::COMM;;plt.fill_between(
275::COMM;;xx.ravel(), y_lower, y_upper, alpha=0.4, label="Predicted 90% interval"
276::COMM;;)
277::COMM;;plt.xlabel("$x$")
278::COMM;;plt.ylabel("$f(x)$")
279::COMM;;plt.ylim(-10, 25)
280::COMM;;plt.legend(loc="upper left")
281::COMM;;plt.title("Prediction with tuned hyper-parameters")
282::COMM;;plt.show()
283::COMM;;# %%
284::COMM;;# The plot looks qualitatively better than for the untuned models, especially
285::COMM;;# for the shape of the of lower quantile.
286::COMM;;#
287::COMM;;# We now quantitatively evaluate the joint-calibration of the pair of
288::COMM;;# estimators:
289::COMM;;coverage_fraction(y_train, search_05p.predict(X_train), search_95p.predict(X_train))
290::COMM;;# %%
291::COMM;;coverage_fraction(y_test, search_05p.predict(X_test), search_95p.predict(X_test))
292::COMM;;# %%
293::COMM;;# The calibration of the tuned pair is sadly not better on the test set: the
294::COMM;;# width of the estimated confidence interval is still too narrow.
295::COMM;;#
296::COMM;;# Again, we would need to wrap this study in a cross-validation loop to
297::COMM;;# better assess the variability of those estimates.
2::COMM;;============================
3::COMM;;Gradient Boosting regression
4::COMM;;============================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates Gradient Boosting to produce a predictive
6::COMM;;model from an ensemble of weak predictive models. Gradient boosting can be used
7::COMM;;for regression and classification problems. Here, we will train a model to
8::COMM;;tackle a diabetes regression task. We will obtain the results from
9::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` with least squares loss
10::COMM;;and 500 regression trees of depth 4.
11::COMM;;Note: For larger datasets (n_samples >= 10000), please refer to
12::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`. See
13::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_hgbt_regression.py` for an example
14::COMM;;showcasing some other advantages of
15::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
27::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# Load the data
29::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# First we need to load the data.
34::COMO;;# %%
35::COMO;;# Data preprocessing
36::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# Next, we will split our dataset to use 90% for training and leave the rest
39::COMO;;# for testing. We will also set the regression model parameters. You can play
40::COMO;;# with these parameters to see how the results change.
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# `n_estimators` : the number of boosting stages that will be performed.
43::COMO;;# Later, we will plot deviance against boosting iterations.
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# `max_depth` : limits the number of nodes in the tree.
46::COMO;;# The best value depends on the interaction of the input variables.
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# `min_samples_split` : the minimum number of samples required to split an
49::COMO;;# internal node.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# `learning_rate` : how much the contribution of each tree will shrink.
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# `loss` : loss function to optimize. The least squares function is used in
54::COMO;;# this case however, there are many other options (see
55::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor` ).
66::COMO;;# %%
67::COMO;;# Fit regression model
68::COMO;;# --------------------
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# Now we will initiate the gradient boosting regressors and fit it with our
71::COMO;;# training data. Let's also look and the mean squared error on the test data.
76::COMO;;# %%
77::COMO;;# Plot training deviance
78::COMO;;# ----------------------
79::COMO;;#
80::COMO;;# Finally, we will visualize the results. To do that we will first compute the
81::COMO;;# test set deviance and then plot it against boosting iterations.
102::COMO;;# %%
103::COMO;;# Plot feature importance
104::COMO;;# -----------------------
105::COMO;;#
106::COMO;;# .. warning::
107::COMO;;# Careful, impurity-based feature importances can be misleading for
108::COMO;;# **high cardinality** features (many unique values). As an alternative,
109::COMO;;# the permutation importances of ``reg`` can be computed on a
110::COMO;;# held out test set. See :ref:`permutation_importance` for more details.
111::COMO;;#
112::COMO;;# For this example, the impurity-based and permutation methods identify the
113::COMO;;# same 2 strongly predictive features but not in the same order. The third most
114::COMO;;# predictive feature, "bp", is also the same for the 2 methods. The remaining
115::COMO;;# features are less predictive and the error bars of the permutation plot
116::COMO;;# show that they overlap with 0.
130::COMO;;# `labels` argument in boxplot is deprecated in matplotlib 3.9 and has been
131::COMO;;# renamed to `tick_labels`. The following code handles this, but as a
132::COMO;;# scikit-learn user you probably can write simpler code by using `labels=...`
133::COMO;;# (matplotlib < 3.9) or `tick_labels=...` (matplotlib >= 3.9).
2::COMM;;================================
3::COMM;;Gradient Boosting regularization
4::COMM;;================================
5::COMM;;Illustration of the effect of different regularization strategies
6::COMM;;for Gradient Boosting. The example is taken from Hastie et al 2009 [1]_.
7::COMM;;The loss function used is binomial deviance. Regularization via
8::COMM;;shrinkage (``learning_rate < 1.0``) improves performance considerably.
9::COMM;;In combination with shrinkage, stochastic gradient boosting
10::COMM;;(``subsample < 1.0``) can produce more accurate models by reducing the
11::COMM;;variance via bagging.
12::COMM;;Subsampling without shrinkage usually does poorly.
13::COMM;;Another strategy to reduce the variance is by subsampling the features
14::COMM;;analogous to the random splits in Random Forests
15::COMM;;(via the ``max_features`` parameter).
16::COMM;;.. [1] T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, "Elements of Statistical
17::COMM;;Learning Ed. 2", Springer, 2009.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
27::COMO;;# map labels from {-1, 1} to {0, 1}
57::COMO;;# compute test set deviance
2::COMM;;==============================================
3::COMM;;Features in Histogram Gradient Boosting Trees
4::COMM;;==============================================
5::COMM;;:ref:`histogram_based_gradient_boosting` (HGBT) models may be one of the most
6::COMM;;useful supervised learning models in scikit-learn. They are based on a modern
7::COMM;;gradient boosting implementation comparable to LightGBM and XGBoost. As such,
8::COMM;;HGBT models are more feature rich than and often outperform alternative models
9::COMM;;like random forests, especially when the number of samples is larger than some
10::COMM;;ten thousands (see
11::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_forest_hist_grad_boosting_comparison.py`).
12::COMM;;The top usability features of HGBT models are:
13::COMM;;1. Several available loss functions for mean and quantile regression tasks, see
14::COMM;;:ref:`Quantile loss <quantile_support_hgbdt>`.
15::COMM;;2. :ref:`categorical_support_gbdt`, see
16::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_categorical.py`.
17::COMM;;3. Early stopping.
18::COMM;;4. :ref:`nan_support_hgbt`, which avoids the need for an imputer.
19::COMM;;5. :ref:`monotonic_cst_gbdt`.
20::COMM;;6. :ref:`interaction_cst_hgbt`.
21::COMM;;This example aims at showcasing all points except 2 and 6 in a real life
22::COMM;;setting.
24::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
25::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# Preparing the data
28::COMO;;# ==================
29::COMO;;# The `electricity dataset <http://www.openml.org/d/151>`_ consists of data
30::COMO;;# collected from the Australian New South Wales Electricity Market. In this
31::COMO;;# market, prices are not fixed and are affected by supply and demand. They are
32::COMO;;# set every five minutes. Electricity transfers to/from the neighboring state of
33::COMO;;# Victoria were done to alleviate fluctuations.
34::COMO;;#
35::COMO;;# The dataset, originally named ELEC2, contains 45,312 instances dated from 7
36::COMO;;# May 1996 to 5 December 1998. Each sample of the dataset refers to a period of
37::COMO;;# 30 minutes, i.e. there are 48 instances for each time period of one day. Each
38::COMO;;# sample on the dataset has 7 columns:
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# - date: between 7 May 1996 to 5 December 1998. Normalized between 0 and 1;
41::COMO;;# - day: day of week (1-7);
42::COMO;;# - period: half hour intervals over 24 hours. Normalized between 0 and 1;
43::COMO;;# - nswprice/nswdemand: electricity price/demand of New South Wales;
44::COMO;;# - vicprice/vicdemand: electricity price/demand of Victoria.

47::COMO;;# task to predict the scheduled electricity transfer between states.

77::COMO;;# Effect of number of trees and early stopping
78::COMO;;# ============================================
79::COMO;;# For the sake of illustrating the effect of the (maximum) number of trees, we
80::COMO;;# train a :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` over the
81::COMO;;# daily electricity transfer using the whole dataset. Then we visualize its
82::COMO;;# predictions depending on the `max_iter` parameter. Here we don't try to
83::COMO;;# evaluate the performance of the model and its capacity to generalize but
84::COMO;;# rather its capability to learn from the training data.
91::COMO;;# %%
121::COMO;;# %%
122::COMO;;# With just a few iterations, HGBT models can achieve convergence (see
123::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_forest_hist_grad_boosting_comparison.py`),
124::COMO;;# meaning that adding more trees does not improve the model anymore. In the
125::COMO;;# figure above, 5 iterations are not enough to get good predictions. With 50
126::COMO;;# iterations, we are already able to do a good job.
127::COMO;;#
128::COMO;;# Setting `max_iter` too high might degrade the prediction quality and cost a lot of
129::COMO;;# avoidable computing resources. Therefore, the HGBT implementation in scikit-learn
130::COMO;;# provides an automatic **early stopping** strategy. With it, the model
131::COMO;;# uses a fraction of the training data as internal validation set
132::COMO;;# (`validation_fraction`) and stops training if the validation score does not
133::COMO;;# improve (or degrades) after `n_iter_no_change` iterations up to a certain
134::COMO;;# tolerance (`tol`).
135::COMO;;#
136::COMO;;# Notice that there is a trade-off between `learning_rate` and `max_iter`:
137::COMO;;# Generally, smaller learning rates are preferable but require more iterations
138::COMO;;# to converge to the minimum loss, while larger learning rates converge faster
139::COMO;;# (less iterations/trees needed) but at the cost of a larger minimum loss.
140::COMO;;#
141::COMO;;# Because of this high correlation between the learning rate the number of iterations,
142::COMO;;# a good practice is to tune the learning rate along with all (important) other
143::COMO;;# hyperparameters, fit the HBGT on the training set with a large enough value
144::COMO;;# for `max_iter` and determine the best `max_iter` via early stopping and some
145::COMO;;# explicit `validation_fraction`.
163::COMO;;# %%
164::COMO;;# We can then overwrite the value for `max_iter` to a reasonable value and avoid
165::COMO;;# the extra computational cost of the inner validation. Rounding up the number
166::COMO;;# of iterations may account for variability of the training set:
171::COMO;;# %%
172::COMO;;# .. note:: The inner validation done during early stopping is not optimal for
173::COMO;;# time series.
174::COMO;;#
175::COMO;;# Support for missing values
176::COMO;;# ==========================
177::COMO;;# HGBT models have native support of missing values. During training, the tree
178::COMO;;# grower decides where samples with missing values should go (left or right
179::COMO;;# child) at each split, based on the potential gain. When predicting, these
180::COMO;;# samples are sent to the learnt child accordingly. If a feature had no missing
181::COMO;;# values during training, then for prediction, samples with missing values for that
182::COMO;;# feature are sent to the child with the most samples (as seen during fit).
183::COMO;;#
184::COMO;;# The present example shows how HGBT regressions deal with values missing
185::COMO;;# completely at random (MCAR), i.e. the missingness does not depend on the
186::COMO;;# observed data or the unobserved data. We can simulate such scenario by
187::COMO;;# randomly replacing values from randomly selected features with `nan` values.
191::COMC;;first_week = slice(0, 336) # first week in the test set as 7 * 48 = 336
222::COMO;;# %%
223::COMO;;# As expected, the model degrades as the proportion of missing values increases.
224::COMO;;#
225::COMO;;# Support for quantile loss
226::COMO;;# =========================
227::COMO;;#
228::COMO;;# The quantile loss in regression enables a view of the variability or
229::COMO;;# uncertainty of the target variable. For instance, predicting the 5th and 95th
230::COMO;;# percentiles can provide a 90% prediction interval, i.e. the range within which
231::COMO;;# we expect a new observed value to fall with 90% probability.
265::COMO;;# %%
266::COMO;;# We observe a tendence to over-estimate the energy transfer. This could be be
267::COMO;;# quantitatively confirmed by computing empirical coverage numbers as done in
268::COMO;;# the :ref:`calibration of confidence intervals section <calibration-section>`.
269::COMO;;# Keep in mind that those predicted percentiles are just estimations from a
270::COMO;;# model. One can still improve the quality of such estimations by:
271::COMO;;#
272::COMO;;# - collecting more data-points;
273::COMO;;# - better tuning of the model hyperparameters, see
274::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_ensemble_plot_gradient_boosting_quantile.py`;
275::COMO;;# - engineering more predictive features from the same data, see
276::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_applications_plot_cyclical_feature_engineering.py`.
277::COMO;;#
278::COMO;;# Monotonic constraints
279::COMO;;# =====================
280::COMO;;#
281::COMO;;# Given specific domain knowledge that requires the relationship between a
282::COMO;;# feature and the target to be monotonically increasing or decreasing, one can
283::COMO;;# enforce such behaviour in the predictions of a HGBT model using monotonic
284::COMO;;# constraints. This makes the model more interpretable and can reduce its
285::COMO;;# variance (and potentially mitigate overfitting) at the risk of increasing
286::COMO;;# bias. Monotonic constraints can also be used to enforce specific regulatory
287::COMO;;# requirements, ensure compliance and align with ethical considerations.
288::COMO;;#
289::COMO;;# In the present example, the policy of transferring energy from Victoria to New
290::COMO;;# South Wales is meant to alleviate price fluctuations, meaning that the model
291::COMO;;# predictions have to enforce such goal, i.e. transfer should increase with
292::COMO;;# price and demand in New South Wales, but also decrease with price and demand
293::COMO;;# in Victoria, in order to benefit both populations.
294::COMO;;#
295::COMO;;# If the training data has feature names, it’s possible to specify the monotonic
296::COMO;;# constraints by passing a dictionary with the convention:
297::COMO;;#
298::COMO;;# - 1: monotonic increase
299::COMO;;# - 0: no constraint
300::COMO;;# - -1: monotonic decrease
301::COMO;;#
302::COMO;;# Alternatively, one can pass an array-like object encoding the above convention by
303::COMO;;# position.
350::COMO;;# %%
351::COMO;;# Observe that `nswdemand` and `vicdemand` seem already monotonic without constraint.
352::COMO;;# This is a good example to show that the model with monotonicity constraints is
353::COMO;;# "overconstraining".
354::COMO;;#
355::COMO;;# Additionally, we can verify that the predictive quality of the model is not
356::COMO;;# significantly degraded by introducing the monotonic constraints. For such
357::COMO;;# purpose we use :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit`
358::COMO;;# cross-validation to estimate the variance of the test score. By doing so we
359::COMO;;# guarantee that the training data does not succeed the testing data, which is
360::COMO;;# crucial when dealing with data that have a temporal relationship.
363::COMC;;ts_cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=48, test_size=336) # a week has 336 samples
371::COMO;;# %%
372::COMO;;# That being said, notice the comparison is between two different models that
373::COMO;;# may be optimized by a different combination of hyperparameters. That is the
374::COMO;;# reason why we do no use the `common_params` in this section as done before.
2::COMM;;=======================
3::COMM;;IsolationForest example
4::COMM;;=======================
5::COMM;;An example using :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest` for anomaly
6::COMM;;detection.
7::COMM;;The :ref:`isolation_forest` is an ensemble of "Isolation Trees" that "isolate"
8::COMM;;observations by recursive random partitioning, which can be represented by a
9::COMM;;tree structure. The number of splittings required to isolate a sample is lower
10::COMM;;for outliers and higher for inliers.
11::COMM;;In the present example we demo two ways to visualize the decision boundary of an
12::COMM;;Isolation Forest trained on a toy dataset.
14::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
15::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# Data generation
18::COMO;;# ---------------
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# We generate two clusters (each one containing `n_samples`) by randomly
21::COMO;;# sampling the standard normal distribution as returned by
22::COMO;;# :func:`numpy.random.randn`. One of them is spherical and the other one is
23::COMO;;# slightly deformed.
24::COMO;;#
25::COMO;;# For consistency with the :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest` notation,
26::COMO;;# the inliers (i.e. the gaussian clusters) are assigned a ground truth label `1`
27::COMO;;# whereas the outliers (created with :func:`numpy.random.uniform`) are assigned
28::COMO;;# the label `-1`.
34::COMC;;cluster_1 = 0.4 * rng.randn(n_samples, 2) @ covariance + np.array([2, 2]) # general
35::COMC;;cluster_2 = 0.3 * rng.randn(n_samples, 2) + np.array([-2, -2]) # spherical

43::COMO;;# We can visualize the resulting clusters:
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# Training of the model
53::COMO;;# ---------------------
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# Plot discrete decision boundary
59::COMO;;# -------------------------------
60::COMO;;#
61::COMO;;# We use the class :class:`~sklearn.inspection.DecisionBoundaryDisplay` to
62::COMO;;# visualize a discrete decision boundary. The background color represents
63::COMO;;# whether a sample in that given area is predicted to be an outlier
64::COMO;;# or not. The scatter plot displays the true labels.
78::COMO;;# %%
79::COMO;;# Plot path length decision boundary
80::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
81::COMO;;#
82::COMO;;# By setting the `response_method="decision_function"`, the background of the
83::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.inspection.DecisionBoundaryDisplay` represents the measure of
84::COMO;;# normality of an observation. Such score is given by the path length averaged
85::COMO;;# over a forest of random trees, which itself is given by the depth of the leaf
86::COMO;;# (or equivalently the number of splits) required to isolate a given sample.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# When a forest of random trees collectively produce short path lengths for
89::COMO;;# isolating some particular samples, they are highly likely to be anomalies and
90::COMO;;# the measure of normality is close to `0`. Similarly, large paths correspond to
91::COMO;;# values close to `1` and are more likely to be inliers.

6::COMM;;boosting estimator.

3::COMM;;Combine predictors using stacking
4::COMM;;=================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
6::COMM;;Stacking refers to a method to blend estimators. In this strategy, some
7::COMM;;estimators are individually fitted on some training data while a final
8::COMM;;estimator is trained using the stacked predictions of these base estimators.
9::COMM;;In this example, we illustrate the use case in which different regressors are
10::COMM;;stacked together and a final linear penalized regressor is used to output the
11::COMM;;prediction. We compare the performance of each individual regressor with the
12::COMM;;stacking strategy. Stacking slightly improves the overall performance.

62::COMO;;# prediction made by :class:`~ensemble.VotingRegressor`.
2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;Comparison of F-test and mutual information
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates the differences between univariate F-test statistics
6::COMM;;and mutual information.
7::COMM;;We consider 3 features x_1, x_2, x_3 distributed uniformly over [0, 1], the
8::COMM;;target depends on them as follows:
9::COMM;;y = x_1 + sin(6 * pi * x_2) + 0.1 * N(0, 1), that is the third feature is
10::COMM;;completely irrelevant.
11::COMM;;The code below plots the dependency of y against individual x_i and normalized
12::COMM;;values of univariate F-tests statistics and mutual information.
13::COMM;;As F-test captures only linear dependency, it rates x_1 as the most
14::COMM;;discriminative feature. On the other hand, mutual information can capture any
15::COMM;;kind of dependency between variables and it rates x_2 as the most
16::COMM;;discriminative feature, which probably agrees better with our intuitive
17::COMM;;perception for this example. Both methods correctly mark x_3 as irrelevant.

20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;==================
3::COMM;;Pipeline ANOVA SVM
4::COMM;;==================
5::COMM;;This example shows how a feature selection can be easily integrated within
6::COMM;;a machine learning pipeline.
7::COMM;;We also show that you can easily inspect part of the pipeline.
9::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
10::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
11::COMO;;# %%
12::COMO;;# We will start by generating a binary classification dataset. Subsequently, we
13::COMO;;# will divide the dataset into two subsets.
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# A common mistake done with feature selection is to search a subset of
27::COMO;;# discriminative features on the full dataset, instead of only using the
28::COMO;;# training set. The usage of scikit-learn :func:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`
29::COMO;;# prevents to make such mistake.
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# Here, we will demonstrate how to build a pipeline where the first step will
32::COMO;;# be the feature selection.
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# When calling `fit` on the training data, a subset of feature will be selected
35::COMO;;# and the index of these selected features will be stored. The feature selector
36::COMO;;# will subsequently reduce the number of features, and pass this subset to the
37::COMO;;# classifier which will be trained.
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# Once the training is complete, we can predict on new unseen samples. In this
47::COMO;;# case, the feature selector will only select the most discriminative features
48::COMO;;# based on the information stored during training. Then, the data will be
49::COMO;;# passed to the classifier which will make the prediction.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Here, we show the final metrics via a classification report.
55::COMO;;# %%
56::COMO;;# Be aware that you can inspect a step in the pipeline. For instance, we might
57::COMO;;# be interested about the parameters of the classifier. Since we selected
58::COMO;;# three features, we expect to have three coefficients.
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# However, we do not know which features were selected from the original
62::COMO;;# dataset. We could proceed by several manners. Here, we will invert the
63::COMO;;# transformation of these coefficients to get information about the original
64::COMO;;# space.
66::COMO;;# %%
67::COMO;;# We can see that the features with non-zero coefficients are the selected
68::COMO;;# features by the first step.

4::COMM;;===================================================

17::COMO;;# features are non-informative as they are drawn at random.

37::COMO;;# strategy "accuracy" optimizes the proportion of correctly classified samples.

56::COMO;;# generative model) is found to be the most optimal.
57::COMO;;#
58::COMO;;# Plot number of features VS. cross-validation scores
59::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
78::COMO;;# %%
79::COMO;;# From the plot above one can further notice a plateau of equivalent scores
80::COMO;;# (similar mean value and overlapping errorbars) for 3 to 5 selected features.
81::COMO;;# This is the result of introducing correlated features. Indeed, the optimal
82::COMO;;# model selected by the RFE can lie within this range, depending on the
83::COMO;;# cross-validation technique. The test accuracy decreases above 5 selected
84::COMO;;# features, this is, keeping non-informative features leads to over-fitting and

96::COMO;;# it means that the selection is stable across folds, and it confirms that

2::COMM;;============================================
3::COMM;;Model-based and sequential feature selection
4::COMM;;============================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates and compares two approaches for feature selection:
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel` which is based on feature
7::COMM;;importance, and
8::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector` which relies
9::COMM;;on a greedy approach.
10::COMM;;We use the Diabetes dataset, which consists of 10 features collected from 442
11::COMM;;diabetes patients.
13::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
14::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
15::COMO;;# %%
16::COMO;;# Loading the data
17::COMO;;# ----------------
18::COMO;;#
19::COMO;;# We first load the diabetes dataset which is available from within
20::COMO;;# scikit-learn, and print its description:
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Feature importance from coefficients
27::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# To get an idea of the importance of the features, we are going to use the
30::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.RidgeCV` estimator. The features with the
31::COMO;;# highest absolute `coef_` value are considered the most important.
32::COMO;;# We can observe the coefficients directly without needing to scale them (or
33::COMO;;# scale the data) because from the description above, we know that the features
34::COMO;;# were already standardized.
35::COMO;;# For a more complete example on the interpretations of the coefficients of
36::COMO;;# linear models, you may refer to
37::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_inspection_plot_linear_model_coefficient_interpretation.py`. # noqa: E501
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# Selecting features based on importance
49::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Now we want to select the two features which are the most important according
52::COMO;;# to the coefficients. The :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel`
53::COMO;;# is meant just for that. :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel`
54::COMO;;# accepts a `threshold` parameter and will select the features whose importance
55::COMO;;# (defined by the coefficients) are above this threshold.
56::COMO;;#
57::COMO;;# Since we want to select only 2 features, we will set this threshold slightly
58::COMO;;# above the coefficient of third most important feature.
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# Selecting features with Sequential Feature Selection
69::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------------
70::COMO;;#
71::COMO;;# Another way of selecting features is to use
72::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector`
73::COMO;;# (SFS). SFS is a greedy procedure where, at each iteration, we choose the best
74::COMO;;# new feature to add to our selected features based a cross-validation score.
75::COMO;;# That is, we start with 0 features and choose the best single feature with the
76::COMO;;# highest score. The procedure is repeated until we reach the desired number of
77::COMO;;# selected features.
78::COMO;;#
79::COMO;;# We can also go in the reverse direction (backward SFS), *i.e.* start with all
80::COMO;;# the features and greedily choose features to remove one by one. We illustrate
81::COMO;;# both approaches here.
103::COMO;;# %%
104::COMO;;# Interestingly, forward and backward selection have selected the same set of
105::COMO;;# features. In general, this isn't the case and the two methods would lead to
106::COMO;;# different results.
107::COMO;;#
108::COMO;;# We also note that the features selected by SFS differ from those selected by
109::COMO;;# feature importance: SFS selects `bmi` instead of `s1`. This does sound
110::COMO;;# reasonable though, since `bmi` corresponds to the third most important
111::COMO;;# feature according to the coefficients. It is quite remarkable considering
112::COMO;;# that SFS makes no use of the coefficients at all.
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# To finish with, we should note that
115::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel` is significantly faster
116::COMO;;# than SFS. Indeed, :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel` only
117::COMO;;# needs to fit a model once, while SFS needs to cross-validate many different
118::COMO;;# models for each of the iterations. SFS however works with any model, while
119::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SelectFromModel` requires the underlying
120::COMO;;# estimator to expose a `coef_` attribute or a `feature_importances_`
121::COMO;;# attribute. The forward SFS is faster than the backward SFS because it only
122::COMO;;# needs to perform `n_features_to_select = 2` iterations, while the backward
123::COMO;;# SFS needs to perform `n_features - n_features_to_select = 8` iterations.
124::COMO;;#
125::COMO;;# Using negative tolerance values
126::COMO;;# -------------------------------
127::COMO;;#
128::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector` can be used
129::COMO;;# to remove features present in the dataset and return a
130::COMO;;# smaller subset of the original features with `direction="backward"`
131::COMO;;# and a negative value of `tol`.
132::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# We begin by loading the Breast Cancer dataset, consisting of 30 different
134::COMO;;# features and 569 samples.
141::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# We will make use of the :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression`
143::COMO;;# estimator with :class:`~sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector`
144::COMO;;# to perform the feature selection.
166::COMO;;# %%
167::COMO;;# We can see that the number of features selected tend to increase as negative
168::COMO;;# values of `tol` approach to zero. The time taken for feature selection also
169::COMO;;# decreases as the values of `tol` come closer to zero.

3::COMM;;Examples of Using `FrozenEstimator`
4::COMM;;===================================
5::COMM;;This example showcases some use cases of :class:`~sklearn.frozen.FrozenEstimator`.
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.frozen.FrozenEstimator` is a utility class that allows to freeze a
7::COMM;;fitted estimator. This is useful, for instance, when we want to pass a fitted estimator

14::COMO;;# Setting a decision threshold for a pre-fitted classifier
15::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------
16::COMO;;# Fitted classifiers in scikit-learn use an arbitrary decision threshold to decide
17::COMO;;# which class the given sample belongs to. The decision threshold is either `0.0` on the
18::COMO;;# value returned by :term:`decision_function`, or `0.5` on the probability returned by
19::COMO;;# :term:`predict_proba`.
20::COMO;;#
21::COMO;;# However, one might want to set a custom decision threshold. We can do this by

23::COMO;;# classifier with :class:`~sklearn.frozen.FrozenEstimator`.

41::COMO;;# estimates. We can do this by wrapping the classifier with

43::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.FixedThresholdClassifier`.
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# Note that in the above piece of code, calling `fit` on
49::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.FixedThresholdClassifier` does not refit the
50::COMO;;# underlying classifier.
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# Now, let's see how the predictions changed with respect to the probability
53::COMO;;# threshold.

63::COMO;;# We see that the probability estimates stay the same, but since a different decision
64::COMO;;# threshold is used, the predicted classes are different.
65::COMO;;#
66::COMO;;# Please refer to
67::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_cost_sensitive_learning.py`
68::COMO;;# to learn about cost-sensitive learning and decision threshold tuning.
69::COMO;;# %%
70::COMO;;# Calibration of a pre-fitted classifier
71::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
72::COMO;;# You can use :class:`~sklearn.frozen.FrozenEstimator` to calibrate a pre-fitted
73::COMO;;# classifier using :class:`~sklearn.calibration.CalibratedClassifierCV`.
2::COMM;;==========================================================
3::COMM;;Comparison of kernel ridge and Gaussian process regression
4::COMM;;==========================================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates differences between a kernel ridge regression and a
6::COMM;;Gaussian process regression.
7::COMM;;Both kernel ridge regression and Gaussian process regression are using a
8::COMM;;so-called "kernel trick" to make their models expressive enough to fit
9::COMM;;the training data. However, the machine learning problems solved by the two
10::COMM;;methods are drastically different.
11::COMM;;Kernel ridge regression will find the target function that minimizes a loss
12::COMM;;function (the mean squared error).
13::COMM;;Instead of finding a single target function, the Gaussian process regression
14::COMM;;employs a probabilistic approach : a Gaussian posterior distribution over
15::COMM;;target functions is defined based on the Bayes' theorem, Thus prior
16::COMM;;probabilities on target functions are being combined with a likelihood function
17::COMM;;defined by the observed training data to provide estimates of the posterior
18::COMM;;distributions.
19::COMM;;We will illustrate these differences with an example and we will also focus on
20::COMM;;tuning the kernel hyperparameters.
22::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
23::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
24::COMO;;# %%
25::COMO;;# Generating a dataset
26::COMO;;# --------------------
27::COMO;;#
28::COMO;;# We create a synthetic dataset. The true generative process will take a 1-D
29::COMO;;# vector and compute its sine. Note that the period of this sine is thus
30::COMO;;# :math:`2 \pi`. We will reuse this information later in this example.
35::COMO;;# %%
36::COMO;;# Now, we can imagine a scenario where we get observations from this true
37::COMO;;# process. However, we will add some challenges:
38::COMO;;#
39::COMO;;# - the measurements will be noisy;
40::COMO;;# - only samples from the beginning of the signal will be available.
46::COMO;;# %%
47::COMO;;# Let's plot the true signal and the noisy measurements available for training.
63::COMO;;# %%
64::COMO;;# Limitations of a simple linear model
65::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
66::COMO;;#
67::COMO;;# First, we would like to highlight the limitations of a linear model given
68::COMO;;# our dataset. We fit a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge` and check the
69::COMO;;# predictions of this model on our dataset.
84::COMO;;# %%
85::COMO;;# Such a ridge regressor underfits data since it is not expressive enough.
86::COMO;;#
87::COMO;;# Kernel methods: kernel ridge and Gaussian process
88::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------
89::COMO;;#
90::COMO;;# Kernel ridge
91::COMO;;# ............
92::COMO;;#
93::COMO;;# We can make the previous linear model more expressive by using a so-called
94::COMO;;# kernel. A kernel is an embedding from the original feature space to another
95::COMO;;# one. Simply put, it is used to map our original data into a newer and more
96::COMO;;# complex feature space. This new space is explicitly defined by the choice of
97::COMO;;# kernel.
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# In our case, we know that the true generative process is a periodic function.
100::COMO;;# We can use a :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.ExpSineSquared` kernel
101::COMO;;# which allows recovering the periodicity. The class
102::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.kernel_ridge.KernelRidge` will accept such a kernel.
103::COMO;;#
104::COMO;;# Using this model together with a kernel is equivalent to embed the data
105::COMO;;# using the mapping function of the kernel and then apply a ridge regression.
106::COMO;;# In practice, the data are not mapped explicitly; instead the dot product
107::COMO;;# between samples in the higher dimensional feature space is computed using the
108::COMO;;# "kernel trick".
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# Thus, let's use such a :class:`~sklearn.kernel_ridge.KernelRidge`.
120::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# %%
143::COMO;;# This fitted model is not accurate. Indeed, we did not set the parameters of
144::COMO;;# the kernel and instead used the default ones. We can inspect them.
146::COMO;;# %%
147::COMO;;# Our kernel has two parameters: the length-scale and the periodicity. For our
148::COMO;;# dataset, we use `sin` as the generative process, implying a
149::COMO;;# :math:`2 \pi`-periodicity for the signal. The default value of the parameter
150::COMO;;# being :math:`1`, it explains the high frequency observed in the predictions of
151::COMO;;# our model.
152::COMO;;# Similar conclusions could be drawn with the length-scale parameter. Thus, it
153::COMO;;# tells us that the kernel parameters need to be tuned. We will use a randomized
154::COMO;;# search to tune the different parameters the kernel ridge model: the `alpha`
155::COMO;;# parameter and the kernel parameters.
156::COMO;;# %%
173::COMO;;# %%
174::COMO;;# Fitting the model is now more computationally expensive since we have to try
175::COMO;;# several combinations of hyperparameters. We can have a look at the
176::COMO;;# hyperparameters found to get some intuitions.
178::COMO;;# %%
179::COMO;;# Looking at the best parameters, we see that they are different from the
180::COMO;;# defaults. We also see that the periodicity is closer to the expected value:
181::COMO;;# :math:`2 \pi`. We can now inspect the predictions of our tuned kernel ridge.
185::COMO;;# %%
207::COMO;;# %%
208::COMO;;# We get a much more accurate model. We still observe some errors mainly due to
209::COMO;;# the noise added to the dataset.
210::COMO;;#
211::COMO;;# Gaussian process regression
212::COMO;;# ...........................
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# Now, we will use a
215::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor` to fit the same
216::COMO;;# dataset. When training a Gaussian process, the hyperparameters of the kernel
217::COMO;;# are optimized during the fitting process. There is no need for an external
218::COMO;;# hyperparameter search. Here, we create a slightly more complex kernel than
219::COMO;;# for the kernel ridge regressor: we add a
220::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.WhiteKernel` that is used to
221::COMO;;# estimate the noise in the dataset.
233::COMO;;# %%
234::COMO;;# The computation cost of training a Gaussian process is much less than the
235::COMO;;# kernel ridge that uses a randomized search. We can check the parameters of
236::COMO;;# the kernels that we computed.
238::COMO;;# %%
239::COMO;;# Indeed, we see that the parameters have been optimized. Looking at the
240::COMO;;# `periodicity` parameter, we see that we found a period close to the
241::COMO;;# theoretical value :math:`2 \pi`. We can have a look now at the predictions of
242::COMO;;# our model.
251::COMO;;# %%
259::COMO;;# Plot the predictions of the kernel ridge
267::COMO;;# Plot the predictions of the gaussian process regressor
286::COMO;;# %%
287::COMO;;# We observe that the results of the kernel ridge and the Gaussian process
288::COMO;;# regressor are close. However, the Gaussian process regressor also provide
289::COMO;;# an uncertainty information that is not available with a kernel ridge.
290::COMO;;# Due to the probabilistic formulation of the target functions, the
291::COMO;;# Gaussian process can output the standard deviation (or the covariance)
292::COMO;;# together with the mean predictions of the target functions.
293::COMO;;#
294::COMO;;# However, it comes at a cost: the time to compute the predictions is higher
295::COMO;;# with a Gaussian process.
296::COMO;;#
297::COMO;;# Final conclusion
298::COMO;;# ----------------
299::COMO;;#
300::COMO;;# We can give a final word regarding the possibility of the two models to
301::COMO;;# extrapolate. Indeed, we only provided the beginning of the signal as a
302::COMO;;# training set. Using a periodic kernel forces our model to repeat the pattern
303::COMO;;# found on the training set. Using this kernel information together with the
304::COMO;;# capacity of the both models to extrapolate, we observe that the models will
305::COMO;;# continue to predict the sine pattern.
306::COMO;;#
307::COMO;;# Gaussian process allows to combine kernels together. Thus, we could associate
308::COMO;;# the exponential sine squared kernel together with a radial basis function
309::COMO;;# kernel.
320::COMO;;# %%
328::COMO;;# Plot the predictions of the kernel ridge
336::COMO;;# Plot the predictions of the gaussian process regressor
355::COMO;;# %%
356::COMO;;# The effect of using a radial basis function kernel will attenuate the
357::COMO;;# periodicity effect once that no sample are available in the training.
358::COMO;;# As testing samples get further away from the training ones, predictions
359::COMO;;# are converging towards their mean and their standard deviation
360::COMO;;# also increases.
2::COMM;;====================================================================
3::COMM;;Probabilistic predictions with Gaussian process classification (GPC)
4::COMM;;====================================================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates the predicted probability of GPC for an RBF kernel
6::COMM;;with different choices of the hyperparameters. The first figure shows the
7::COMM;;predicted probability of GPC with arbitrarily chosen hyperparameters and with
8::COMM;;the hyperparameters corresponding to the maximum log-marginal-likelihood (LML).
9::COMM;;While the hyperparameters chosen by optimizing LML have a considerable larger
10::COMM;;LML, they perform slightly worse according to the log-loss on test data. The
11::COMM;;figure shows that this is because they exhibit a steep change of the class
12::COMM;;probabilities at the class boundaries (which is good) but have predicted
13::COMM;;probabilities close to 0.5 far away from the class boundaries (which is bad)
14::COMM;;This undesirable effect is caused by the Laplace approximation used
15::COMM;;internally by GPC.
