2::COMM;;====================================================================================
3::COMM;;Forecasting of CO2 level on Mona Loa dataset using Gaussian process regression (GPR)
4::COMM;;====================================================================================
5::COMM;;This example is based on Section 5.4.3 of "Gaussian Processes for Machine
6::COMM;;Learning" [1]_. It illustrates an example of complex kernel engineering
7::COMM;;and hyperparameter optimization using gradient ascent on the
8::COMM;;log-marginal-likelihood. The data consists of the monthly average atmospheric
9::COMM;;CO2 concentrations (in parts per million by volume (ppm)) collected at the
10::COMM;;Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii, between 1958 and 2001. The objective is to
11::COMM;;model the CO2 concentration as a function of the time :math:`t` and extrapolate
12::COMM;;for years after 2001.
13::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
14::COMM;;.. [1] `Rasmussen, Carl Edward. "Gaussian processes in machine learning."
15::COMM;;Summer school on machine learning. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 2003
16::COMM;;<http://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf>`_.
18::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
19::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
20::COMO;;# %%
21::COMO;;# Build the dataset
22::COMO;;# -----------------
23::COMO;;#
24::COMO;;# We will derive a dataset from the Mauna Loa Observatory that collected air
25::COMO;;# samples. We are interested in estimating the concentration of CO2 and
26::COMO;;# extrapolate it for further years. First, we load the original dataset available
27::COMO;;# in OpenML as a pandas dataframe. This will be replaced with Polars
28::COMO;;# once `fetch_openml` adds a native support for it.
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# First, we process the original dataframe to create a date column and select
34::COMO;;# it along with the CO2 column.
40::COMO;;# %%
42::COMO;;# %%
43::COMO;;# We see that we get CO2 concentration for some days from March, 1958 to
44::COMO;;# December, 2001. We can plot the raw information to have a better
45::COMO;;# understanding.
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# We will preprocess the dataset by taking a monthly average and drop months
53::COMO;;# for which no measurements were collected. Such a processing will have a
54::COMO;;# smoothing effect on the data.
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# The idea in this example will be to predict the CO2 concentration in function
69::COMO;;# of the date. We are as well interested in extrapolating for upcoming year
70::COMO;;# after 2001.
71::COMO;;#
72::COMO;;# As a first step, we will divide the data and the target to estimate. The data
73::COMO;;# being a date, we will convert it into a numeric.
78::COMO;;# %%
79::COMO;;# Design the proper kernel
80::COMO;;# ------------------------
81::COMO;;#
82::COMO;;# To design the kernel to use with our Gaussian process, we can make some
83::COMO;;# assumption regarding the data at hand. We observe that they have several
84::COMO;;# characteristics: we see a long term rising trend, a pronounced seasonal
85::COMO;;# variation and some smaller irregularities. We can use different appropriate
86::COMO;;# kernel that would capture these features.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# First, the long term rising trend could be fitted using a radial basis
89::COMO;;# function (RBF) kernel with a large length-scale parameter. The RBF kernel
90::COMO;;# with a large length-scale enforces this component to be smooth. A trending
91::COMO;;# increase is not enforced as to give a degree of freedom to our model. The
92::COMO;;# specific length-scale and the amplitude are free hyperparameters.
95::COMO;;# %%
96::COMO;;# The seasonal variation is explained by the periodic exponential sine squared
97::COMO;;# kernel with a fixed periodicity of 1 year. The length-scale of this periodic
98::COMO;;# component, controlling its smoothness, is a free parameter. In order to allow
99::COMO;;# decaying away from exact periodicity, the product with an RBF kernel is
100::COMO;;# taken. The length-scale of this RBF component controls the decay time and is
101::COMO;;# a further free parameter. This type of kernel is also known as locally
102::COMO;;# periodic kernel.
109::COMO;;# %%
110::COMO;;# The small irregularities are to be explained by a rational quadratic kernel
111::COMO;;# component, whose length-scale and alpha parameter, which quantifies the
112::COMO;;# diffuseness of the length-scales, are to be determined. A rational quadratic
113::COMO;;# kernel is equivalent to an RBF kernel with several length-scale and will
114::COMO;;# better accommodate the different irregularities.
117::COMO;;# %%
118::COMO;;# Finally, the noise in the dataset can be accounted with a kernel consisting
119::COMO;;# of an RBF kernel contribution, which shall explain the correlated noise
120::COMO;;# components such as local weather phenomena, and a white kernel contribution
121::COMO;;# for the white noise. The relative amplitudes and the RBF's length scale are
122::COMO;;# further free parameters.
127::COMO;;# %%
128::COMO;;# Thus, our final kernel is an addition of all previous kernel.
133::COMO;;# %%
134::COMO;;# Model fitting and extrapolation
135::COMO;;# -------------------------------
136::COMO;;#
137::COMO;;# Now, we are ready to use a Gaussian process regressor and fit the available
138::COMO;;# data. To follow the example from the literature, we will subtract the mean
139::COMO;;# from the target. We could have used `normalize_y=True`. However, doing so
140::COMO;;# would have also scaled the target (dividing `y` by its standard deviation).
141::COMO;;# Thus, the hyperparameters of the different kernel would have had different
142::COMO;;# meaning since they would not have been expressed in ppm.
147::COMO;;# %%
148::COMO;;# Now, we will use the Gaussian process to predict on:
149::COMO;;#
150::COMO;;# - training data to inspect the goodness of fit;
151::COMO;;# - future data to see the extrapolation done by the model.
152::COMO;;#
153::COMO;;# Thus, we create synthetic data from 1958 to the current month. In addition,
154::COMO;;# we need to add the subtracted mean computed during training.
162::COMO;;# %%
178::COMO;;# %%
179::COMO;;# Our fitted model is capable to fit previous data properly and extrapolate to
180::COMO;;# future year with confidence.
181::COMO;;#
182::COMO;;# Interpretation of kernel hyperparameters
183::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
184::COMO;;#
185::COMO;;# Now, we can have a look at the hyperparameters of the kernel.
187::COMO;;# %%
188::COMO;;# Thus, most of the target signal, with the mean subtracted, is explained by a
189::COMO;;# long-term rising trend for ~45 ppm and a length-scale of ~52 years. The
190::COMO;;# periodic component has an amplitude of ~2.6ppm, a decay time of ~90 years and
191::COMO;;# a length-scale of ~1.5. The long decay time indicates that we have a
192::COMO;;# component very close to a seasonal periodicity. The correlated noise has an
193::COMO;;# amplitude of ~0.2 ppm with a length scale of ~0.12 years and a white-noise
194::COMO;;# contribution of ~0.04 ppm. Thus, the overall noise level is very small,
195::COMO;;# indicating that the data can be very well explained by the model.
2::COMM;;=========================================================================
3::COMM;;Ability of Gaussian process regression (GPR) to estimate data noise-level
4::COMM;;=========================================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows the ability of the
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.WhiteKernel` to estimate the noise
7::COMM;;level in the data. Moreover, we show the importance of kernel hyperparameters
8::COMM;;initialization.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# Data generation
14::COMO;;# ---------------
15::COMO;;#
16::COMO;;# We will work in a setting where `X` will contain a single feature. We create a
17::COMO;;# function that will generate the target to be predicted. We will add an
18::COMO;;# option to add some noise to the generated target.
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# Let's have a look to the target generator where we will not add any noise to
28::COMO;;# observe the signal that we would like to predict.
31::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# %%
38::COMO;;# The target is transforming the input `X` using a sine function. Now, we will
39::COMO;;# generate few noisy training samples. To illustrate the noise level, we will
40::COMO;;# plot the true signal together with the noisy training samples.
44::COMO;;# %%
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Optimisation of kernel hyperparameters in GPR
58::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------
59::COMO;;#
60::COMO;;# Now, we will create a
61::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor`
62::COMO;;# using an additive kernel adding a
63::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.RBF` and
64::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.WhiteKernel` kernels.
65::COMO;;# The :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.WhiteKernel` is a kernel that
66::COMO;;# will able to estimate the amount of noise present in the data while the
67::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.RBF` will serve at fitting the
68::COMO;;# non-linearity between the data and the target.
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# However, we will show that the hyperparameter space contains several local
71::COMO;;# minima. It will highlights the importance of initial hyperparameter values.
72::COMO;;#
73::COMO;;# We will create a model using a kernel with a high noise level and a large
74::COMO;;# length scale, which will explain all variations in the data by noise.
83::COMO;;# %%
97::COMO;;# %%
98::COMO;;# We see that the optimum kernel found still has a high noise level and an even
99::COMO;;# larger length scale. The length scale reaches the maximum bound that we
100::COMO;;# allowed for this parameter and we got a warning as a result.
101::COMO;;#
102::COMO;;# More importantly, we observe that the model does not provide useful
103::COMO;;# predictions: the mean prediction seems to be constant: it does not follow the
104::COMO;;# expected noise-free signal.
105::COMO;;#
106::COMO;;# Now, we will initialize the :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.RBF`
107::COMO;;# with a larger `length_scale` initial value and the
108::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels.WhiteKernel` with a smaller initial
109::COMO;;# noise level lower while keeping the parameter bounds unchanged.
116::COMO;;# %%
130::COMO;;# %%
131::COMO;;# First, we see that the model's predictions are more precise than the
132::COMO;;# previous model's: this new model is able to estimate the noise-free
133::COMO;;# functional relationship.
134::COMO;;#
135::COMO;;# Looking at the kernel hyperparameters, we see that the best combination found
136::COMO;;# has a smaller noise level and shorter length scale than the first model.
137::COMO;;#
138::COMO;;# We can inspect the negative Log-Marginal-Likelihood (LML) of
139::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor`
140::COMO;;# for different hyperparameters to get a sense of the local minima.
150::COMO;;# %%
167::COMO;;# %%
168::COMO;;#
169::COMO;;# We see that there are two local minima that correspond to the combination of
170::COMO;;# hyperparameters previously found. Depending on the initial values for the
171::COMO;;# hyperparameters, the gradient-based optimization might or might not
172::COMO;;# converge to the best model. It is thus important to repeat the optimization
173::COMO;;# several times for different initializations. This can be done by setting the
174::COMO;;# `n_restarts_optimizer` parameter of the
175::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor` class.
176::COMO;;#
177::COMO;;# Let's try again to fit our model with the bad initial values but this time
178::COMO;;# with 10 random restarts.
187::COMO;;# %%
201::COMO;;# %%
202::COMO;;#
203::COMO;;# As we hoped, random restarts allow the optimization to find the best set
204::COMO;;# of hyperparameters despite the bad initial values.

3::COMM;;Gaussian Processes regression: basic introductory example
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;A simple one-dimensional regression example computed in two different ways:
6::COMM;;1. A noise-free case
7::COMM;;2. A noisy case with known noise-level per datapoint
8::COMM;;In both cases, the kernel's parameters are estimated using the maximum
9::COMM;;likelihood principle.
10::COMM;;The figures illustrate the interpolating property of the Gaussian Process model
11::COMM;;as well as its probabilistic nature in the form of a pointwise 95% confidence
12::COMM;;interval.
13::COMM;;Note that `alpha` is a parameter to control the strength of the Tikhonov
14::COMM;;regularization on the assumed training points' covariance matrix.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMO;;# %%
19::COMO;;# Dataset generation
20::COMO;;# ------------------
21::COMO;;#
22::COMO;;# We will start by generating a synthetic dataset. The true generative process
23::COMO;;# is defined as :math:`f(x) = x \sin(x)`.
27::COMO;;# %%
34::COMO;;# %%
35::COMO;;# We will use this dataset in the next experiment to illustrate how Gaussian
36::COMO;;# Process regression is working.
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# Example with noise-free target
39::COMO;;# ------------------------------
40::COMO;;#
41::COMO;;# In this first example, we will use the true generative process without
42::COMO;;# adding any noise. For training the Gaussian Process regression, we will only
43::COMO;;# select few samples.
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# Now, we fit a Gaussian process on these few training data samples. We will
49::COMO;;# use a radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a constant parameter to fit the
50::COMO;;# amplitude.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# After fitting our model, we see that the hyperparameters of the kernel have
59::COMO;;# been optimized. Now, we will use our kernel to compute the mean prediction
60::COMO;;# of the full dataset and plot the 95% confidence interval.
76::COMO;;# %%
77::COMO;;# We see that for a prediction made on a data point close to the one from the
78::COMO;;# training set, the 95% confidence has a small amplitude. Whenever a sample
79::COMO;;# falls far from training data, our model's prediction is less accurate and the
80::COMO;;# model prediction is less precise (higher uncertainty).
81::COMO;;#
82::COMO;;# Example with noisy targets
83::COMO;;# --------------------------
84::COMO;;#
85::COMO;;# We can repeat a similar experiment adding an additional noise to the target
86::COMO;;# this time. It will allow seeing the effect of the noise on the fitted model.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# We add some random Gaussian noise to the target with an arbitrary
89::COMO;;# standard deviation.
92::COMO;;# %%
93::COMO;;# We create a similar Gaussian process model. In addition to the kernel, this
94::COMO;;# time, we specify the parameter `alpha` which can be interpreted as the
95::COMO;;# variance of a Gaussian noise.
101::COMO;;# %%
102::COMO;;# Let's plot the mean prediction and the uncertainty region as before.
127::COMO;;# %%
128::COMO;;# The noise affects the predictions close to the training samples: the
129::COMO;;# predictive uncertainty near to the training samples is larger because we
130::COMO;;# explicitly model a given level target noise independent of the input
131::COMO;;# variable.

22::COMM;;to make predictions on the 3rd and 6th sequences.

24::COMM;;sequences and make predictions on another 5 sequences. The ground truth here is

2::COMM;;=========================================================
3::COMM;;Imputing missing values with variants of IterativeImputer
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
6::COMM;;The :class:`~impute.IterativeImputer` class is very flexible - it can be
7::COMM;;used with a variety of estimators to do round-robin regression, treating every
8::COMM;;variable as an output in turn.
9::COMM;;In this example we compare some estimators for the purpose of missing feature
10::COMM;;imputation with :class:`~impute.IterativeImputer`:
11::COMM;;* :class:`~linear_model.BayesianRidge`: regularized linear regression
12::COMM;;* :class:`~ensemble.RandomForestRegressor`: forests of randomized trees regression
13::COMM;;* :func:`~pipeline.make_pipeline` (:class:`~kernel_approximation.Nystroem`,
14::COMM;;:class:`~linear_model.Ridge`): a pipeline with the expansion of a degree 2
15::COMM;;polynomial kernel and regularized linear regression
16::COMM;;* :class:`~neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor`: comparable to other KNN
17::COMM;;imputation approaches
18::COMM;;Of particular interest is the ability of
19::COMM;;:class:`~impute.IterativeImputer` to mimic the behavior of missForest, a
20::COMM;;popular imputation package for R.
21::COMM;;Note that :class:`~neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor` is different from KNN
22::COMM;;imputation, which learns from samples with missing values by using a distance
23::COMM;;metric that accounts for missing values, rather than imputing them.
24::COMM;;The goal is to compare different estimators to see which one is best for the
25::COMM;;:class:`~impute.IterativeImputer` when using a
26::COMM;;:class:`~linear_model.BayesianRidge` estimator on the California housing
27::COMM;;dataset with a single value randomly removed from each row.
28::COMM;;For this particular pattern of missing values we see that
29::COMM;;:class:`~linear_model.BayesianRidge` and
30::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.RandomForestRegressor` give the best results.
31::COMM;;It should be noted that some estimators such as
32::COMM;;:class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` can natively deal with
33::COMM;;missing features and are often recommended over building pipelines with
34::COMM;;complex and costly missing values imputation strategies.
36::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
37::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
43::COMO;;# To use this experimental feature, we need to explicitly ask for it:
44::COMC;;from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer # noqa: F401
54::COMO;;# ~2k samples is enough for the purpose of the example.
55::COMO;;# Remove the following two lines for a slower run with different error bars.
60::COMO;;# We scale data before imputation and training a target estimator,
61::COMO;;# because our target estimator and some of the imputers assume
62::COMO;;# that the features have similar scales.
70::COMO;;# Estimate the score on the entire dataset, with no missing values
75::COMO;;# Add a single missing value to each row
82::COMO;;# Estimate the score after imputation (mean and median strategies)
88::COMO;;# Estimate the score after iterative imputation of the missing values
89::COMO;;# with different estimators
95::COMO;;# We tuned the hyperparameters of the RandomForestRegressor to get a good
96::COMO;;# enough predictive performance for a restricted execution time.
117::COMO;;# Iterative imputer is sensitive to the tolerance and
118::COMO;;# dependent on the estimator used internally.
119::COMO;;# We tuned the tolerance to keep this example run with limited computational
120::COMO;;# resources while not changing the results too much compared to keeping the
121::COMO;;# stricter default value for the tolerance parameter.
136::COMO;;# plot california housing results
2::COMM;;====================================================
3::COMM;;Imputing missing values before building an estimator
4::COMM;;====================================================
5::COMM;;Missing values can be replaced by the mean, the median or the most frequent
6::COMM;;value using the basic :class:`~sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer`.
7::COMM;;In this example we will investigate different imputation techniques:
8::COMM;;- imputation by the constant value 0
9::COMM;;- imputation by the mean value of each feature
10::COMM;;- k nearest neighbor imputation
11::COMM;;- iterative imputation
12::COMM;;In all the cases, for each feature, we add a new feature indicating the missingness.
13::COMM;;We will use two datasets: Diabetes dataset which consists of 10 feature
14::COMM;;variables collected from diabetes patients with an aim to predict disease
15::COMM;;progression and California housing dataset for which the target is the median
16::COMM;;house value for California districts.
17::COMM;;As neither of these datasets have missing values, we will remove some
18::COMM;;values to create new versions with artificially missing data. The performance
19::COMM;;of
20::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor` on the full original dataset
21::COMM;;is then compared the performance on the altered datasets with the artificially
22::COMM;;missing values imputed using different techniques.

25::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

32::COMO;;# dataset is much larger with 20640 entries and 8 features. It needs to be
33::COMO;;# downloaded. We will only use the first 300 entries for the sake of speeding
34::COMO;;# up the calculations but feel free to use the whole dataset.

2::COMM;;===================================================
3::COMM;;Failure of Machine Learning to infer causal effects
4::COMM;;===================================================
5::COMM;;Machine Learning models are great for measuring statistical associations.
6::COMM;;Unfortunately, unless we're willing to make strong assumptions about the data,
7::COMM;;those models are unable to infer causal effects.
8::COMM;;To illustrate this, we will simulate a situation in which we try to answer one
9::COMM;;of the most important questions in economics of education: **what is the causal
10::COMM;;effect of earning a college degree on hourly wages?** Although the answer to
11::COMM;;this question is crucial to policy makers, `Omitted-Variable Biases
12::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omitted-variable_bias>`_ (OVB) prevent us from
13::COMM;;identifying that causal effect.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMO;;# %%
18::COMO;;# The dataset: simulated hourly wages
19::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
20::COMO;;#
21::COMO;;# The data generating process is laid out in the code below. Work experience in
22::COMO;;# years and a measure of ability are drawn from Normal distributions; the
23::COMO;;# hourly wage of one of the parents is drawn from Beta distribution. We then
24::COMO;;# create an indicator of college degree which is positively impacted by ability
25::COMO;;# and parental hourly wage. Finally, we model hourly wages as a linear function
26::COMO;;# of all the previous variables and a random component. Note that all variables
27::COMO;;# have a positive effect on hourly wages.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Description of the simulated data
58::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
59::COMO;;#
60::COMO;;# The following plot shows the distribution of each variable, and pairwise
61::COMO;;# scatter plots. Key to our OVB story is the positive relationship between
62::COMO;;# ability and college degree.
74::COMO;;# %%
75::COMO;;# In the next section, we train predictive models and we therefore split the
76::COMO;;# target column from over features and we split the data into a training and a
77::COMO;;# testing set.
82::COMO;;# %%
83::COMO;;# Income prediction with fully observed variables
84::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------
85::COMO;;#
86::COMO;;# First, we train a predictive model, a
87::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` model. In this experiment,
88::COMO;;# we assume that all variables used by the true generative model are available.
97::COMO;;# %%
98::COMO;;# This model predicts well the hourly wages as shown by the high R2 score. We
99::COMO;;# plot the model coefficients to show that we exactly recover the values of
100::COMO;;# the true generative model.
112::COMO;;# %%
113::COMO;;# Income prediction with partial observations
114::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# In practice, intellectual abilities are not observed or are only estimated
117::COMO;;# from proxies that inadvertently measure education as well (e.g. by IQ tests).
118::COMO;;# But omitting the "ability" feature from a linear model inflates the estimate
119::COMO;;# via a positive OVB.
126::COMO;;# %%
127::COMO;;# The predictive power of our model is similar when we omit the ability feature
128::COMO;;# in terms of R2 score. We now check if the coefficient of the model are
129::COMO;;# different from the true generative model.
141::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# To compensate for the omitted variable, the model inflates the coefficient of
143::COMO;;# the college degree feature. Therefore, interpreting this coefficient value
144::COMO;;# as a causal effect of the true generative model is incorrect.
145::COMO;;#
146::COMO;;# Lessons learned
147::COMO;;# ---------------
148::COMO;;#
149::COMO;;# Machine learning models are not designed for the estimation of causal
150::COMO;;# effects. While we showed this with a linear model, OVB can affect any type of
151::COMO;;# model.
152::COMO;;#
153::COMO;;# Whenever interpreting a coefficient or a change in predictions brought about
154::COMO;;# by a change in one of the features, it is important to keep in mind
155::COMO;;# potentially unobserved variables that could be correlated with both the
156::COMO;;# feature in question and the target variable. Such variables are called
157::COMO;;# `Confounding Variables <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confounding>`_. In
158::COMO;;# order to still estimate causal effect in the presence of confounding,
159::COMO;;# researchers usually conduct experiments in which the treatment variable (e.g.
160::COMO;;# college degree) is randomized. When an experiment is prohibitively expensive
161::COMO;;# or unethical, researchers can sometimes use other causal inference techniques
162::COMO;;# such as `Instrumental Variables
163::COMO;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental_variables_estimation>`_ (IV)
164::COMO;;# estimations.
2::COMM;;======================================================================
3::COMM;;Common pitfalls in the interpretation of coefficients of linear models
4::COMM;;======================================================================
5::COMM;;In linear models, the target value is modeled as a linear combination of the
6::COMM;;features (see the :ref:`linear_model` User Guide section for a description of a
7::COMM;;set of linear models available in scikit-learn). Coefficients in multiple linear
8::COMM;;models represent the relationship between the given feature, :math:`X_i` and the
9::COMM;;target, :math:`y`, assuming that all the other features remain constant
10::COMM;;(`conditional dependence
11::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_dependence>`_). This is different
12::COMM;;from plotting :math:`X_i` versus :math:`y` and fitting a linear relationship: in
13::COMM;;that case all possible values of the other features are taken into account in
14::COMM;;the estimation (marginal dependence).
15::COMM;;This example will provide some hints in interpreting coefficient in linear
16::COMM;;models, pointing at problems that arise when either the linear model is not
17::COMM;;appropriate to describe the dataset, or when features are correlated.
18::COMM;;.. note::
19::COMM;;Keep in mind that the features :math:`X` and the outcome :math:`y` are in
20::COMM;;general the result of a data generating process that is unknown to us.
21::COMM;;Machine learning models are trained to approximate the unobserved
22::COMM;;mathematical function that links :math:`X` to :math:`y` from sample data. As
23::COMM;;a result, any interpretation made about a model may not necessarily
24::COMM;;generalize to the true data generating process. This is especially true when
25::COMM;;the model is of bad quality or when the sample data is not representative of
26::COMM;;the population.
27::COMM;;We will use data from the `"Current Population Survey"
28::COMM;;<https://www.openml.org/d/534>`_ from 1985 to predict wage as a function of
29::COMM;;various features such as experience, age, or education.
31::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
32::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
33::COMO;;# %%
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# The dataset: wages
41::COMO;;# ------------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# We fetch the data from `OpenML <http://openml.org/>`_.
44::COMO;;# Note that setting the parameter `as_frame` to True will retrieve the data
45::COMO;;# as a pandas dataframe.
48::COMO;;# %%
49::COMO;;# Then, we identify features `X` and target `y`: the column WAGE is our
50::COMO;;# target variable (i.e. the variable which we want to predict).
53::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# Note that the dataset contains categorical and numerical variables.
55::COMO;;# We will need to take this into account when preprocessing the dataset
56::COMO;;# thereafter.
58::COMO;;# %%
59::COMO;;# Our target for prediction: the wage.
60::COMO;;# Wages are described as floating-point number in dollars per hour.
61::COMO;;# %%
64::COMO;;# %%
65::COMO;;# We split the sample into a train and a test dataset.
66::COMO;;# Only the train dataset will be used in the following exploratory analysis.
67::COMO;;# This is a way to emulate a real situation where predictions are performed on
68::COMO;;# an unknown target, and we don't want our analysis and decisions to be biased
69::COMO;;# by our knowledge of the test data.
72::COMO;;# %%
73::COMO;;# First, let's get some insights by looking at the variables' distributions and
74::COMO;;# at the pairwise relationships between them. Only numerical
75::COMO;;# variables will be used. In the following plot, each dot represents a sample.
76::COMO;;#
77::COMO;;# .. _marginal_dependencies:
81::COMO;;# %%
82::COMO;;# Looking closely at the WAGE distribution reveals that it has a
83::COMO;;# long tail. For this reason, we should take its logarithm
84::COMO;;# to turn it approximately into a normal distribution (linear models such
85::COMO;;# as ridge or lasso work best for a normal distribution of error).
86::COMO;;#
87::COMO;;# The WAGE is increasing when EDUCATION is increasing.
88::COMO;;# Note that the dependence between WAGE and EDUCATION
89::COMO;;# represented here is a marginal dependence, i.e. it describes the behavior
90::COMO;;# of a specific variable without keeping the others fixed.
91::COMO;;#
92::COMO;;# Also, the EXPERIENCE and AGE are strongly linearly correlated.
93::COMO;;#
94::COMO;;# .. _the-pipeline:
95::COMO;;#
96::COMO;;# The machine-learning pipeline
97::COMO;;# -----------------------------
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# To design our machine-learning pipeline, we first manually
100::COMO;;# check the type of data that we are dealing with:
102::COMO;;# %%
103::COMO;;# As seen previously, the dataset contains columns with different data types
104::COMO;;# and we need to apply a specific preprocessing for each data types.
105::COMO;;# In particular categorical variables cannot be included in linear model if not
106::COMO;;# coded as integers first. In addition, to avoid categorical features to be
107::COMO;;# treated as ordered values, we need to one-hot-encode them.
108::COMO;;# Our pre-processor will:
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# - one-hot encode (i.e., generate a column by category) the categorical
111::COMO;;# columns, only for non-binary categorical variables;
112::COMO;;# - as a first approach (we will see after how the normalisation of numerical
113::COMO;;# values will affect our discussion), keep numerical values as they are.
121::COMC;;verbose_feature_names_out=False, # avoid to prepend the preprocessor names
123::COMO;;# %%
124::COMO;;# We use a ridge regressor
125::COMO;;# with a very small regularization to model the logarithm of the WAGE.
135::COMO;;# %%
136::COMO;;# Processing the dataset
137::COMO;;# ----------------------
138::COMO;;#
139::COMO;;# First, we fit the model.
141::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# Then we check the performance of the computed model by plotting its predictions
143::COMO;;# against the actual values on the test set, and by computing
144::COMO;;# the median absolute error.
153::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# %%
164::COMO;;# The model learnt is far from being a good model making accurate predictions:
165::COMO;;# this is obvious when looking at the plot above, where good predictions
166::COMO;;# should lie on the black dashed line.
167::COMO;;#
168::COMO;;# In the following section, we will interpret the coefficients of the model.
169::COMO;;# While we do so, we should keep in mind that any conclusion we draw is
170::COMO;;# about the model that we build, rather than about the true (real-world)
171::COMO;;# generative process of the data.
172::COMO;;#
173::COMO;;# Interpreting coefficients: scale matters
174::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
175::COMO;;#
176::COMO;;# First of all, we can take a look to the values of the coefficients of the
177::COMO;;# regressor we have fitted.
185::COMO;;# %%
186::COMO;;# The AGE coefficient is expressed in "dollars/hour per living years" while the
187::COMO;;# EDUCATION one is expressed in "dollars/hour per years of education". This
188::COMO;;# representation of the coefficients has the benefit of making clear the
189::COMO;;# practical predictions of the model: an increase of :math:`1` year in AGE
190::COMO;;# means a decrease of :math:`0.030867` dollars/hour, while an increase of
191::COMO;;# :math:`1` year in EDUCATION means an increase of :math:`0.054699`
192::COMO;;# dollars/hour. On the other hand, categorical variables (as UNION or SEX) are
193::COMO;;# adimensional numbers taking either the value 0 or 1. Their coefficients
194::COMO;;# are expressed in dollars/hour. Then, we cannot compare the magnitude of
195::COMO;;# different coefficients since the features have different natural scales, and
196::COMO;;# hence value ranges, because of their different unit of measure. This is more
197::COMO;;# visible if we plot the coefficients.
203::COMO;;# %%
204::COMO;;# Indeed, from the plot above the most important factor in determining WAGE
205::COMO;;# appears to be the
206::COMO;;# variable UNION, even if our intuition might tell us that variables
207::COMO;;# like EXPERIENCE should have more impact.
208::COMO;;#
209::COMO;;# Looking at the coefficient plot to gauge feature importance can be
210::COMO;;# misleading as some of them vary on a small scale, while others, like AGE,
211::COMO;;# varies a lot more, several decades.
212::COMO;;#
213::COMO;;# This is visible if we compare the standard deviations of different
214::COMO;;# features.
222::COMO;;# %%
223::COMO;;# Multiplying the coefficients by the standard deviation of the related
224::COMO;;# feature would reduce all the coefficients to the same unit of measure.
225::COMO;;# As we will see :ref:`after<scaling_num>` this is equivalent to normalize
226::COMO;;# numerical variables to their standard deviation,
227::COMO;;# as :math:`y = \sum{coef_i \times X_i} =
228::COMO;;# \sum{(coef_i \times std_i) \times (X_i / std_i)}`.
229::COMO;;#
230::COMO;;# In that way, we emphasize that the
231::COMO;;# greater the variance of a feature, the larger the weight of the corresponding
232::COMO;;# coefficient on the output, all else being equal.
243::COMO;;# %%
244::COMO;;# Now that the coefficients have been scaled, we can safely compare them.
245::COMO;;#
246::COMO;;# .. note::
247::COMO;;#
248::COMO;;# Why does the plot above suggest that an increase in age leads to a
249::COMO;;# decrease in wage? Why is the :ref:`initial pairplot
250::COMO;;# <marginal_dependencies>` telling the opposite?
251::COMO;;# This difference is the difference between marginal and conditional dependence.
252::COMO;;#
253::COMO;;# The plot above tells us about dependencies between a specific feature and
254::COMO;;# the target when all other features remain constant, i.e., **conditional
255::COMO;;# dependencies**. An increase of the AGE will induce a decrease
256::COMO;;# of the WAGE when all other features remain constant. On the contrary, an
257::COMO;;# increase of the EXPERIENCE will induce an increase of the WAGE when all
258::COMO;;# other features remain constant.
259::COMO;;# Also, AGE, EXPERIENCE and EDUCATION are the three variables that most
260::COMO;;# influence the model.
261::COMO;;#
262::COMO;;# Interpreting coefficients: being cautious about causality
263::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
264::COMO;;#
265::COMO;;# Linear models are a great tool for measuring statistical association, but we
266::COMO;;# should be cautious when making statements about causality, after all
267::COMO;;# correlation doesn't always imply causation. This is particularly difficult in
268::COMO;;# the social sciences because the variables we observe only function as proxies
269::COMO;;# for the underlying causal process.
270::COMO;;#
271::COMO;;# In our particular case we can think of the EDUCATION of an individual as a
272::COMO;;# proxy for their professional aptitude, the real variable we're interested in
273::COMO;;# but can't observe. We'd certainly like to think that staying in school for
274::COMO;;# longer would increase technical competency, but it's also quite possible that
275::COMO;;# causality goes the other way too. That is, those who are technically
276::COMO;;# competent tend to stay in school for longer.
277::COMO;;#
278::COMO;;# An employer is unlikely to care which case it is (or if it's a mix of both),
279::COMO;;# as long as they remain convinced that a person with more EDUCATION is better
280::COMO;;# suited for the job, they will be happy to pay out a higher WAGE.
281::COMO;;#
282::COMO;;# This confounding of effects becomes problematic when thinking about some
283::COMO;;# form of intervention e.g. government subsidies of university degrees or
284::COMO;;# promotional material encouraging individuals to take up higher education.
285::COMO;;# The usefulness of these measures could end up being overstated, especially if
286::COMO;;# the degree of confounding is strong. Our model predicts a :math:`0.054699`
287::COMO;;# increase in hourly wage for each year of education. The actual causal effect
288::COMO;;# might be lower because of this confounding.
289::COMO;;#
290::COMO;;# Checking the variability of the coefficients
291::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------
292::COMO;;#
293::COMO;;# We can check the coefficient variability through cross-validation:
294::COMO;;# it is a form of data perturbation (related to
295::COMO;;# `resampling <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resampling_(statistics)>`_).
296::COMO;;#
297::COMO;;# If coefficients vary significantly when changing the input dataset
298::COMO;;# their robustness is not guaranteed, and they should probably be interpreted
299::COMO;;# with caution.
317::COMO;;# %%
326::COMO;;# %%
327::COMO;;# The problem of correlated variables
328::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
329::COMO;;#
330::COMO;;# The AGE and EXPERIENCE coefficients are affected by strong variability which
331::COMO;;# might be due to the collinearity between the 2 features: as AGE and
332::COMO;;# EXPERIENCE vary together in the data, their effect is difficult to tease
333::COMO;;# apart.
334::COMO;;#
335::COMO;;# To verify this interpretation we plot the variability of the AGE and
336::COMO;;# EXPERIENCE coefficient.
337::COMO;;#
338::COMO;;# .. _covariation:
346::COMO;;# %%
347::COMO;;# Two regions are populated: when the EXPERIENCE coefficient is
348::COMO;;# positive the AGE one is negative and vice-versa.
349::COMO;;#
350::COMO;;# To go further we remove one of the two features, AGE, and check what is the impact
351::COMO;;# on the model stability.
369::COMO;;# %%
378::COMO;;# %%
379::COMO;;# The estimation of the EXPERIENCE coefficient now shows a much reduced
380::COMO;;# variability. EXPERIENCE remains important for all models trained during
381::COMO;;# cross-validation.
382::COMO;;#
383::COMO;;# .. _scaling_num:
384::COMO;;#
385::COMO;;# Preprocessing numerical variables
386::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
387::COMO;;#
388::COMO;;# As said above (see ":ref:`the-pipeline`"), we could also choose to scale
389::COMO;;# numerical values before training the model.
390::COMO;;# This can be useful when we apply a similar amount of regularization to all of them
391::COMO;;# in the ridge.
392::COMO;;# The preprocessor is redefined in order to subtract the mean and scale
393::COMO;;# variables to unit variance.
399::COMO;;# %%
400::COMO;;# The model will stay unchanged.
408::COMO;;# %%
409::COMO;;# Again, we check the performance of the computed
410::COMO;;# model using the median absolute error.
427::COMO;;# %%
428::COMO;;# For the coefficient analysis, scaling is not needed this time because it
429::COMO;;# was performed during the preprocessing step.
440::COMO;;# %%
441::COMO;;# We now inspect the coefficients across several cross-validation folds.
453::COMO;;# %%
460::COMO;;# %%
461::COMO;;# The result is quite similar to the non-normalized case.
462::COMO;;#
463::COMO;;# Linear models with regularization
464::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
465::COMO;;#
466::COMO;;# In machine-learning practice, ridge regression is more often used with
467::COMO;;# non-negligible regularization.
468::COMO;;#
469::COMO;;# Above, we limited this regularization to a very little amount. Regularization
470::COMO;;# improves the conditioning of the problem and reduces the variance of the
471::COMO;;# estimates. :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.RidgeCV` applies cross validation
472::COMO;;# in order to determine which value of the regularization parameter (`alpha`)
473::COMO;;# is best suited for prediction.
475::COMC;;alphas = np.logspace(-10, 10, 21) # alpha values to be chosen from by cross-validation
485::COMO;;# %%
486::COMO;;# First we check which value of :math:`\alpha` has been selected.
488::COMO;;# %%
489::COMO;;# Then we check the quality of the predictions.
506::COMO;;# %%
507::COMO;;# The ability to reproduce the data of the regularized model is similar to
508::COMO;;# the one of the non-regularized model.
519::COMO;;# %%
520::COMO;;# The coefficients are significantly different.
521::COMO;;# AGE and EXPERIENCE coefficients are both positive but they now have less
522::COMO;;# influence on the prediction.
523::COMO;;#
524::COMO;;# The regularization reduces the influence of correlated
525::COMO;;# variables on the model because the weight is shared between the two
526::COMO;;# predictive variables, so neither alone would have strong weights.
527::COMO;;#
528::COMO;;# On the other hand, the weights obtained with regularization are more
529::COMO;;# stable (see the :ref:`ridge_regression` User Guide section). This
530::COMO;;# increased stability is visible from the plot, obtained from data
531::COMO;;# perturbations, in a cross-validation. This plot can be compared with
532::COMO;;# the :ref:`previous one<covariation>`.
544::COMO;;# %%
552::COMO;;# %%
553::COMO;;# Linear models with sparse coefficients
554::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
555::COMO;;#
556::COMO;;# Another possibility to take into account correlated variables in the dataset,
557::COMO;;# is to estimate sparse coefficients. In some way we already did it manually
558::COMO;;# when we dropped the AGE column in a previous ridge estimation.
559::COMO;;#
560::COMO;;# Lasso models (see the :ref:`lasso` User Guide section) estimates sparse
561::COMO;;# coefficients. :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoCV` applies cross
562::COMO;;# validation in order to determine which value of the regularization parameter
563::COMO;;# (`alpha`) is best suited for the model estimation.
565::COMC;;alphas = np.logspace(-10, 10, 21) # alpha values to be chosen from by cross-validation
575::COMO;;# %%
576::COMO;;# First we verify which value of :math:`\alpha` has been selected.
578::COMO;;# %%
579::COMO;;# Then we check the quality of the predictions.
596::COMO;;# %%
597::COMO;;# For our dataset, again the model is not very predictive.
607::COMO;;# %%
608::COMO;;# A Lasso model identifies the correlation between
609::COMO;;# AGE and EXPERIENCE and suppresses one of them for the sake of the prediction.
610::COMO;;#
611::COMO;;# It is important to keep in mind that the coefficients that have been
612::COMO;;# dropped may still be related to the outcome by themselves: the model
613::COMO;;# chose to suppress them because they bring little or no additional
614::COMO;;# information on top of the other features. Additionally, this selection
615::COMO;;# is unstable for correlated features, and should be interpreted with
616::COMO;;# caution.
617::COMO;;#
618::COMO;;# Indeed, we can check the variability of the coefficients across folds.
630::COMO;;# %%
637::COMO;;# %%
638::COMO;;# We observe that the AGE and EXPERIENCE coefficients are varying a lot
639::COMO;;# depending of the fold.
640::COMO;;#
641::COMO;;# Wrong causal interpretation
642::COMO;;# ---------------------------
643::COMO;;#
644::COMO;;# Policy makers might want to know the effect of education on wage to assess
645::COMO;;# whether or not a certain policy designed to entice people to pursue more
646::COMO;;# education would make economic sense. While Machine Learning models are great
647::COMO;;# for measuring statistical associations, they are generally unable to infer
648::COMO;;# causal effects.
649::COMO;;#
650::COMO;;# It might be tempting to look at the coefficient of education on wage from our
651::COMO;;# last model (or any model for that matter) and conclude that it captures the
652::COMO;;# true effect of a change in the standardized education variable on wages.
653::COMO;;#
654::COMO;;# Unfortunately there are likely unobserved confounding variables that either
655::COMO;;# inflate or deflate that coefficient. A confounding variable is a variable that
656::COMO;;# causes both EDUCATION and WAGE. One example of such variable is ability.
657::COMO;;# Presumably, more able people are more likely to pursue education while at the
658::COMO;;# same time being more likely to earn a higher hourly wage at any level of
659::COMO;;# education. In this case, ability induces a positive `Omitted Variable Bias
660::COMO;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omitted-variable_bias>`_ (OVB) on the EDUCATION
661::COMO;;# coefficient, thereby exaggerating the effect of education on wages.
662::COMO;;#
663::COMO;;# See the :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_inspection_plot_causal_interpretation.py`
664::COMO;;# for a simulated case of ability OVB.
665::COMO;;#
666::COMO;;# Lessons learned
667::COMO;;# ---------------
668::COMO;;#
669::COMO;;# * Coefficients must be scaled to the same unit of measure to retrieve
670::COMO;;# feature importance. Scaling them with the standard-deviation of the
671::COMO;;# feature is a useful proxy.
672::COMO;;# * Coefficients in multivariate linear models represent the dependency
673::COMO;;# between a given feature and the target, **conditional** on the other
674::COMO;;# features.
675::COMO;;# * Correlated features induce instabilities in the coefficients of linear
676::COMO;;# models and their effects cannot be well teased apart.
677::COMO;;# * Different linear models respond differently to feature correlation and
678::COMO;;# coefficients could significantly vary from one another.
679::COMO;;# * Inspecting coefficients across the folds of a cross-validation loop
680::COMO;;# gives an idea of their stability.
681::COMO;;# * Interpreting causality is difficult when there are confounding effects. If
682::COMO;;# the relationship between two variables is also affected by something
683::COMO;;# unobserved, we should be careful when making conclusions about causality.
2::COMM;;===============================================================
3::COMM;;Partial Dependence and Individual Conditional Expectation Plots
4::COMM;;===============================================================
5::COMM;;Partial dependence plots show the dependence between the target function [2]_
6::COMM;;and a set of features of interest, marginalizing over the values of all other
7::COMM;;features (the complement features). Due to the limits of human perception, the
8::COMM;;size of the set of features of interest must be small (usually, one or two)
9::COMM;;thus they are usually chosen among the most important features.
10::COMM;;Similarly, an individual conditional expectation (ICE) plot [3]_
11::COMM;;shows the dependence between the target function and a feature of interest.
12::COMM;;However, unlike partial dependence plots, which show the average effect of the
13::COMM;;features of interest, ICE plots visualize the dependence of the prediction on a
14::COMM;;feature for each :term:`sample` separately, with one line per sample.
15::COMM;;Only one feature of interest is supported for ICE plots.
16::COMM;;This example shows how to obtain partial dependence and ICE plots from a
17::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor` and a
18::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` trained on the
19::COMM;;bike sharing dataset. The example is inspired by [1]_.
20::COMM;;.. [1] `Molnar, Christoph. "Interpretable machine learning.
21::COMM;;A Guide for Making Black Box Models Explainable",
22::COMM;;2019. <https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/>`_
23::COMM;;.. [2] For classification you can think of it as the regression score before
24::COMM;;the link function.
25::COMM;;.. [3] :arxiv:`Goldstein, A., Kapelner, A., Bleich, J., and Pitkin, E. (2015).
26::COMM;;"Peeking Inside the Black Box: Visualizing Statistical Learning With Plots of
27::COMM;;Individual Conditional Expectation". Journal of Computational and
28::COMM;;Graphical Statistics, 24(1): 44-65 <1309.6392>`
30::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
31::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# Bike sharing dataset preprocessing
34::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
35::COMO;;#
36::COMO;;# We will use the bike sharing dataset. The goal is to predict the number of bike
37::COMO;;# rentals using weather and season data as well as the datetime information.
40::COMO;;# Make an explicit copy to avoid "SettingWithCopyWarning" from pandas
42::COMO;;# We use only a subset of the data to speed up the example.
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# The feature `"weather"` has a particularity: the category `"heavy_rain"` is a rare
47::COMO;;# category.
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# Because of this rare category, we collapse it into `"rain"`.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# We now have a closer look at the `"year"` feature:
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# We see that we have data from two years. We use the first year to train the
62::COMO;;# model and the second year to test the model.
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# We can check the dataset information to see that we have heterogeneous data types. We
69::COMO;;# have to preprocess the different columns accordingly.
71::COMO;;# %%
72::COMO;;# From the previous information, we will consider the `category` columns as nominal
73::COMO;;# categorical features. In addition, we will consider the date and time information as
74::COMO;;# categorical features as well.
75::COMO;;#
76::COMO;;# We manually define the columns containing numerical and categorical
77::COMO;;# features.
85::COMO;;# %%
86::COMO;;# Before we go into the details regarding the preprocessing of the different machine
87::COMO;;# learning pipelines, we will try to get some additional intuition regarding the dataset
88::COMO;;# that will be helpful to understand the model's statistical performance and results of
89::COMO;;# the partial dependence analysis.
90::COMO;;#
91::COMO;;# We plot the average number of bike rentals by grouping the data by season and
92::COMO;;# by year.
106::COMO;;# decorate the plot
123::COMO;;# %%
124::COMO;;# The first striking difference between the train and test set is that the number of
125::COMO;;# bike rentals is higher in the test set. For this reason, it will not be surprising to
126::COMO;;# get a machine learning model that underestimates the number of bike rentals. We
127::COMO;;# also observe that the number of bike rentals is lower during the spring season. In
128::COMO;;# addition, we see that during working days, there is a specific pattern around 6-7
129::COMO;;# am and 5-6 pm with some peaks of bike rentals. We can keep in mind these different
130::COMO;;# insights and use them to understand the partial dependence plot.
131::COMO;;#
132::COMO;;# Preprocessor for machine-learning models
133::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
134::COMO;;#
135::COMO;;# Since we later use two different models, a
136::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor` and a
137::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`, we create two different
138::COMO;;# preprocessors, specific for each model.
139::COMO;;#
140::COMO;;# Preprocessor for the neural network model
141::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
142::COMO;;#
143::COMO;;# We will use a :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer` to scale the
144::COMO;;# numerical features and encode the categorical features with a
145::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder`.
155::COMO;;# %%
156::COMO;;# Preprocessor for the gradient boosting model
157::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
158::COMO;;#
159::COMO;;# For the gradient boosting model, we leave the numerical features as-is and only
160::COMO;;# encode the categorical features using a
161::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder`.
172::COMO;;# %%
173::COMO;;# 1-way partial dependence with different models
174::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------
175::COMO;;#
176::COMO;;# In this section, we will compute 1-way partial dependence with two different
177::COMO;;# machine-learning models: (i) a multi-layer perceptron and (ii) a
178::COMO;;# gradient-boosting model. With these two models, we illustrate how to compute and
179::COMO;;# interpret both partial dependence plot (PDP) for both numerical and categorical
180::COMO;;# features and individual conditional expectation (ICE).
181::COMO;;#
182::COMO;;# Multi-layer perceptron
183::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
184::COMO;;#
185::COMO;;# Let's fit a :class:`~sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor` and compute
186::COMO;;# single-variable partial dependence plots.
204::COMO;;# %%
205::COMO;;# We configured a pipeline using the preprocessor that we created specifically for the
206::COMO;;# neural network and tuned the neural network size and learning rate to get a reasonable
207::COMO;;# compromise between training time and predictive performance on a test set.
208::COMO;;#
209::COMO;;# Importantly, this tabular dataset has very different dynamic ranges for its
210::COMO;;# features. Neural networks tend to be very sensitive to features with varying
211::COMO;;# scales and forgetting to preprocess the numeric feature would lead to a very
212::COMO;;# poor model.
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# It would be possible to get even higher predictive performance with a larger
215::COMO;;# neural network but the training would also be significantly more expensive.
216::COMO;;#
217::COMO;;# Note that it is important to check that the model is accurate enough on a
218::COMO;;# test set before plotting the partial dependence since there would be little
219::COMO;;# use in explaining the impact of a given feature on the prediction function of
220::COMO;;# a model with poor predictive performance. In this regard, our MLP model works
221::COMO;;# reasonably well.
222::COMO;;#
223::COMO;;# We will plot the averaged partial dependence.
234::COMO;;# features of interest
236::COMO;;# type of partial dependence plot
238::COMO;;# information regarding categorical features
258::COMO;;# %%
259::COMO;;# Gradient boosting
260::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
261::COMO;;#
262::COMO;;# Let's now fit a :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and
263::COMO;;# compute the partial dependence on the same features. We also use the
264::COMO;;# specific preprocessor we created for this model.
279::COMO;;# %%
280::COMO;;# Here, we used the default hyperparameters for the gradient boosting model
281::COMO;;# without any preprocessing as tree-based models are naturally robust to
282::COMO;;# monotonic transformations of numerical features.
283::COMO;;#
284::COMO;;# Note that on this tabular dataset, Gradient Boosting Machines are both
285::COMO;;# significantly faster to train and more accurate than neural networks. It is
286::COMO;;# also significantly cheaper to tune their hyperparameters (the defaults tend
287::COMO;;# to work well while this is not often the case for neural networks).
288::COMO;;#
289::COMO;;# We will plot the partial dependence for some of the numerical and categorical
290::COMO;;# features.
309::COMO;;# %%
310::COMO;;# Analysis of the plots
311::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
312::COMO;;#
313::COMO;;# We will first look at the PDPs for the numerical features. For both models, the
314::COMO;;# general trend of the PDP of the temperature is that the number of bike rentals is
315::COMO;;# increasing with temperature. We can make a similar analysis but with the opposite
316::COMO;;# trend for the humidity features. The number of bike rentals is decreasing when the
317::COMO;;# humidity increases. Finally, we see the same trend for the wind speed feature. The
318::COMO;;# number of bike rentals is decreasing when the wind speed is increasing for both
319::COMO;;# models. We also observe that :class:`~sklearn.neural_network.MLPRegressor` has much
320::COMO;;# smoother predictions than :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
321::COMO;;#
322::COMO;;# Now, we will look at the partial dependence plots for the categorical features.
323::COMO;;#
324::COMO;;# We observe that the spring season is the lowest bar for the season feature. With the
325::COMO;;# weather feature, the rain category is the lowest bar. Regarding the hour feature,
326::COMO;;# we see two peaks around the 7 am and 6 pm. These findings are in line with the
327::COMO;;# the observations we made earlier on the dataset.
328::COMO;;#
329::COMO;;# However, it is worth noting that we are creating potential meaningless
330::COMO;;# synthetic samples if features are correlated.
331::COMO;;#
332::COMO;;# .. _ice-vs-pdp:
333::COMO;;#
334::COMO;;# ICE vs. PDP
335::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~
336::COMO;;#
337::COMO;;# PDP is an average of the marginal effects of the features. We are averaging the
338::COMO;;# response of all samples of the provided set. Thus, some effects could be hidden. In
339::COMO;;# this regard, it is possible to plot each individual response. This representation is
340::COMO;;# called the Individual Effect Plot (ICE). In the plot below, we plot 50 randomly
341::COMO;;# selected ICEs for the temperature and humidity features.
359::COMO;;# %%
360::COMO;;# We see that the ICE for the temperature feature gives us some additional information:
361::COMO;;# Some of the ICE lines are flat while some others show a decrease of the dependence
362::COMO;;# for temperature above 35 degrees Celsius. We observe a similar pattern for the
363::COMO;;# humidity feature: some of the ICEs lines show a sharp decrease when the humidity is
364::COMO;;# above 80%.
365::COMO;;#
366::COMO;;# Not all ICE lines are parallel, this indicates that the model finds
367::COMO;;# interactions between features. We can repeat the experiment by constraining the
368::COMO;;# gradient boosting model to not use any interactions between features using the
369::COMO;;# parameter `interaction_cst`:
378::COMO;;# %%
389::COMO;;# %%
390::COMO;;# 2D interaction plots
391::COMO;;# --------------------
392::COMO;;#
393::COMO;;# PDPs with two features of interest enable us to visualize interactions among them.
394::COMO;;# However, ICEs cannot be plotted in an easy manner and thus interpreted. We will show
395::COMO;;# the representation of available in
396::COMO;;# :meth:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator` that is a 2D
397::COMO;;# heatmap.
416::COMO;;# %%
417::COMO;;# The two-way partial dependence plot shows the dependence of the number of bike rentals
418::COMO;;# on joint values of temperature and humidity.
419::COMO;;# We clearly see an interaction between the two features. For a temperature higher than
420::COMO;;# 20 degrees Celsius, the humidity has an impact on the number of bike rentals
421::COMO;;# that seems independent on the temperature.
422::COMO;;#
423::COMO;;# On the other hand, for temperatures lower than 20 degrees Celsius, both the
424::COMO;;# temperature and humidity continuously impact the number of bike rentals.
425::COMO;;#
426::COMO;;# Furthermore, the slope of the of the impact ridge of the 20 degrees Celsius
427::COMO;;# threshold is very dependent on the humidity level: the ridge is steep under
428::COMO;;# dry conditions but much smoother under wetter conditions above 70% of humidity.
429::COMO;;#
430::COMO;;# We now contrast those results with the same plots computed for the model
431::COMO;;# constrained to learn a prediction function that does not depend on such
432::COMO;;# non-linear feature interactions.
451::COMO;;# %%
452::COMO;;# The 1D partial dependence plots for the model constrained to not model feature
453::COMO;;# interactions show local spikes for each features individually, in particular for
454::COMO;;# for the "humidity" feature. Those spikes might be reflecting a degraded behavior
455::COMO;;# of the model that attempts to somehow compensate for the forbidden interactions
456::COMO;;# by overfitting particular training points. Note that the predictive performance
457::COMO;;# of this model as measured on the test set is significantly worse than that of
458::COMO;;# the original, unconstrained model.
459::COMO;;#
460::COMO;;# Also note that the number of local spikes visible on those plots is depends on
461::COMO;;# the grid resolution parameter of the PD plot itself.
462::COMO;;#
463::COMO;;# Those local spikes result in a noisily gridded 2D PD plot. It is quite
464::COMO;;# challenging to tell whether or not there are no interaction between those
465::COMO;;# features because of the high frequency oscillations in the humidity feature.
466::COMO;;# However it can clearly be seen that the simple interaction effect observed when
467::COMO;;# the temperature crosses the 20 degrees boundary is no longer visible for this
468::COMO;;# model.
469::COMO;;#
470::COMO;;# The partial dependence between categorical features will provide a discrete
471::COMO;;# representation that can be shown as a heatmap. For instance the interaction between
472::COMO;;# the season, the weather, and the target would be as follow:
492::COMO;;# %%
493::COMO;;# 3D representation
494::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
495::COMO;;#
496::COMO;;# Let's make the same partial dependence plot for the 2 features interaction,
497::COMO;;# this time in 3 dimensions.
498::COMO;;# unused but required import for doing 3d projections with matplotlib < 3.2
499::COMC;;import mpl_toolkits.mplot3d # noqa: F401
