524::COMO;;# .. _plt_partial_dependence_custom_values:
525::COMO;;#
526::COMO;;# Custom Inspection Points
527::COMO;;# ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
528::COMO;;#
529::COMO;;# None of the examples so far specify _which_ points are evaluated to create the
530::COMO;;# partial dependence plots. By default we use percentiles defined by the input dataset.
531::COMO;;# In some cases it can be helpful to specify the exact points where you would like the
532::COMO;;# model evaluated. For instance, if a user wants to test the model behavior on
533::COMO;;# out-of-distribution data or compare two models that were fit on slightly different
534::COMO;;# data. The `custom_values` parameter allows the user to pass in the values that they
535::COMO;;# want the model to be evaluated on. This overrides the `grid_resolution` and
536::COMO;;# `percentiles` parameters. Let's return to our gradient boosting example above
537::COMO;;# but with custom values
551::COMO;;# we set custom values for temp feature -
552::COMO;;# all other features are evaluated based on the data
2::COMM;;================================================================
3::COMM;;Permutation Importance vs Random Forest Feature Importance (MDI)
4::COMM;;================================================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we will compare the impurity-based feature importance of
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` with the
7::COMM;;permutation importance on the titanic dataset using
8::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`. We will show that the
9::COMM;;impurity-based feature importance can inflate the importance of numerical
10::COMM;;features.
11::COMM;;Furthermore, the impurity-based feature importance of random forests suffers
12::COMM;;from being computed on statistics derived from the training dataset: the
13::COMM;;importances can be high even for features that are not predictive of the target
14::COMM;;variable, as long as the model has the capacity to use them to overfit.
15::COMM;;This example shows how to use Permutation Importances as an alternative that
16::COMM;;can mitigate those limitations.
17::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
18::COMM;;* :doi:`L. Breiman, "Random Forests", Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32,
19::COMM;;2001. <10.1023/A:1010933404324>`
21::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
22::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
23::COMO;;# %%
24::COMO;;# Data Loading and Feature Engineering
25::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
26::COMO;;# Let's use pandas to load a copy of the titanic dataset. The following shows
27::COMO;;# how to apply separate preprocessing on numerical and categorical features.
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# We further include two random variables that are not correlated in any way
30::COMO;;# with the target variable (``survived``):
31::COMO;;#
32::COMO;;# - ``random_num`` is a high cardinality numerical variable (as many unique
33::COMO;;# values as records).
34::COMO;;# - ``random_cat`` is a low cardinality categorical variable (3 possible
35::COMO;;# values).
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# We define a predictive model based on a random forest. Therefore, we will make
49::COMO;;# the following preprocessing steps:
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# - use :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder` to encode the
52::COMO;;# categorical features;
53::COMO;;# - use :class:`~sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer` to fill missing values for
54::COMO;;# numerical features using a mean strategy.
78::COMO;;# %%
79::COMO;;# Accuracy of the Model
80::COMO;;# ---------------------
81::COMO;;# Before inspecting the feature importances, it is important to check that
82::COMO;;# the model predictive performance is high enough. Indeed, there would be little
83::COMO;;# interest in inspecting the important features of a non-predictive model.
86::COMO;;# %%
87::COMO;;# Here, one can observe that the train accuracy is very high (the forest model
88::COMO;;# has enough capacity to completely memorize the training set) but it can still
89::COMO;;# generalize well enough to the test set thanks to the built-in bagging of
90::COMO;;# random forests.
91::COMO;;#
92::COMO;;# It might be possible to trade some accuracy on the training set for a
93::COMO;;# slightly better accuracy on the test set by limiting the capacity of the
94::COMO;;# trees (for instance by setting ``min_samples_leaf=5`` or
95::COMO;;# ``min_samples_leaf=10``) so as to limit overfitting while not introducing too
96::COMO;;# much underfitting.
97::COMO;;#
98::COMO;;# However, let us keep our high capacity random forest model for now so that we can
99::COMO;;# illustrate some pitfalls about feature importance on variables with many
100::COMO;;# unique values.
101::COMO;;# %%
102::COMO;;# Tree's Feature Importance from Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI)
103::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------
104::COMO;;# The impurity-based feature importance ranks the numerical features to be the
105::COMO;;# most important features. As a result, the non-predictive ``random_num``
106::COMO;;# variable is ranked as one of the most important features!
107::COMO;;#
108::COMO;;# This problem stems from two limitations of impurity-based feature
109::COMO;;# importances:
110::COMO;;#
111::COMO;;# - impurity-based importances are biased towards high cardinality features;
112::COMO;;# - impurity-based importances are computed on training set statistics and
113::COMO;;# therefore do not reflect the ability of feature to be useful to make
114::COMO;;# predictions that generalize to the test set (when the model has enough
115::COMO;;# capacity).
116::COMO;;#
117::COMO;;# The bias towards high cardinality features explains why the `random_num` has
118::COMO;;# a really large importance in comparison with `random_cat` while we would
119::COMO;;# expect that both random features have a null importance.
120::COMO;;#
121::COMO;;# The fact that we use training set statistics explains why both the
122::COMO;;# `random_num` and `random_cat` features have a non-null importance.
128::COMO;;# %%
132::COMO;;# %%
133::COMO;;# As an alternative, the permutation importances of ``rf`` are computed on a
134::COMO;;# held out test set. This shows that the low cardinality categorical feature,
135::COMO;;# `sex` and `pclass` are the most important features. Indeed, permuting the
136::COMO;;# values of these features will lead to the most decrease in accuracy score of the
137::COMO;;# model on the test set.
138::COMO;;#
139::COMO;;# Also, note that both random features have very low importances (close to 0) as
140::COMO;;# expected.
155::COMO;;# %%
156::COMO;;# It is also possible to compute the permutation importances on the training
157::COMO;;# set. This reveals that `random_num` and `random_cat` get a significantly
158::COMO;;# higher importance ranking than when computed on the test set. The difference
159::COMO;;# between those two plots is a confirmation that the RF model has enough
160::COMO;;# capacity to use that random numerical and categorical features to overfit.
174::COMO;;# %%
175::COMO;;# We can further retry the experiment by limiting the capacity of the trees
176::COMO;;# to overfit by setting `min_samples_leaf` at 20 data points.
178::COMO;;# %%
179::COMO;;# Observing the accuracy score on the training and testing set, we observe that
180::COMO;;# the two metrics are very similar now. Therefore, our model is not overfitting
181::COMO;;# anymore. We can then check the permutation importances with this new model.
184::COMO;;# %%
192::COMO;;# %%
201::COMO;;# %%
208::COMO;;# %%
209::COMO;;# Now, we can observe that on both sets, the `random_num` and `random_cat`
210::COMO;;# features have a lower importance compared to the overfitting random forest.
211::COMO;;# However, the conclusions regarding the importance of the other features are
212::COMO;;# still valid.
2::COMM;;=================================================================
3::COMM;;Permutation Importance with Multicollinear or Correlated Features
4::COMM;;=================================================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we compute the
6::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance` of the features to a trained
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` using the
8::COMM;;:ref:`breast_cancer_dataset`. The model can easily get about 97% accuracy on a
9::COMM;;test dataset. Because this dataset contains multicollinear features, the
10::COMM;;permutation importance shows that none of the features are important, in
11::COMM;;contradiction with the high test accuracy.
12::COMM;;We demo a possible approach to handling multicollinearity, which consists of
13::COMM;;hierarchical clustering on the features' Spearman rank-order correlations,
14::COMM;;picking a threshold, and keeping a single feature from each cluster.
15::COMM;;.. note::
16::COMM;;See also
17::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_inspection_plot_permutation_importance.py`
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# Random Forest Feature Importance on Breast Cancer Data
23::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------------------
24::COMO;;#
25::COMO;;# First, we define a function to ease the plotting:
32::COMO;;# `labels` argument in boxplot is deprecated in matplotlib 3.9 and has been
33::COMO;;# renamed to `tick_labels`. The following code handles this, but as a
34::COMO;;# scikit-learn user you probably can write simpler code by using `labels=...`
35::COMO;;# (matplotlib < 3.9) or `tick_labels=...` (matplotlib >= 3.9).
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# We then train a :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` on the
47::COMO;;# :ref:`breast_cancer_dataset` and evaluate its accuracy on a test set:
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Next, we plot the tree based feature importance and the permutation
58::COMO;;# importance. The permutation importance is calculated on the training set to
59::COMO;;# show how much the model relies on each feature during training.
74::COMO;;# %%
75::COMO;;# The plot on the left shows the Gini importance of the model. As the
76::COMO;;# scikit-learn implementation of
77::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier` uses a random subsets of
78::COMO;;# :math:`\sqrt{n_\text{features}}` features at each split, it is able to dilute
79::COMO;;# the dominance of any single correlated feature. As a result, the individual
80::COMO;;# feature importance may be distributed more evenly among the correlated
81::COMO;;# features. Since the features have large cardinality and the classifier is
82::COMO;;# non-overfitted, we can relatively trust those values.
83::COMO;;#
84::COMO;;# The permutation importance on the right plot shows that permuting a feature
85::COMO;;# drops the accuracy by at most `0.012`, which would suggest that none of the
86::COMO;;# features are important. This is in contradiction with the high test accuracy
87::COMO;;# computed as baseline: some feature must be important.
88::COMO;;#
89::COMO;;# Similarly, the change in accuracy score computed on the test set appears to be
90::COMO;;# driven by chance:
96::COMO;;# %%
97::COMO;;# Nevertheless, one can still compute a meaningful permutation importance in the
98::COMO;;# presence of correlated features, as demonstrated in the following section.
99::COMO;;#
100::COMO;;# Handling Multicollinear Features
101::COMO;;# --------------------------------
102::COMO;;# When features are collinear, permuting one feature has little effect on the
103::COMO;;# models performance because it can get the same information from a correlated
104::COMO;;# feature. Note that this is not the case for all predictive models and depends
105::COMO;;# on their underlying implementation.
106::COMO;;#
107::COMO;;# One way to handle multicollinear features is by performing hierarchical
108::COMO;;# clustering on the Spearman rank-order correlations, picking a threshold, and
109::COMO;;# keeping a single feature from each cluster. First, we plot a heatmap of the
110::COMO;;# correlated features:
116::COMO;;# Ensure the correlation matrix is symmetric
119::COMO;;# We convert the correlation matrix to a distance matrix before performing
120::COMO;;# hierarchical clustering using Ward's linkage.
133::COMO;;# %%
134::COMO;;# Next, we manually pick a threshold by visual inspection of the dendrogram to
135::COMO;;# group our features into clusters and choose a feature from each cluster to
136::COMO;;# keep, select those features from our dataset, and train a new random forest.
137::COMO;;# The test accuracy of the new random forest did not change much compared to the
138::COMO;;# random forest trained on the complete dataset.
154::COMO;;# %%
155::COMO;;# We can finally explore the permutation importance of the selected subset of
156::COMO;;# features:
2::COMM;;======================================================
3::COMM;;Scalable learning with polynomial kernel approximation
4::COMM;;======================================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.kernel_approximation
6::COMM;;This example illustrates the use of :class:`PolynomialCountSketch` to
7::COMM;;efficiently generate polynomial kernel feature-space approximations.
8::COMM;;This is used to train linear classifiers that approximate the accuracy
9::COMM;;of kernelized ones.
10::COMM;;We use the Covtype dataset [2]_, trying to reproduce the experiments on the
11::COMM;;original paper of Tensor Sketch [1]_, i.e. the algorithm implemented by
12::COMM;;:class:`PolynomialCountSketch`.
13::COMM;;First, we compute the accuracy of a linear classifier on the original
14::COMM;;features. Then, we train linear classifiers on different numbers of
15::COMM;;features (`n_components`) generated by :class:`PolynomialCountSketch`,
16::COMM;;approximating the accuracy of a kernelized classifier in a scalable manner.
18::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
19::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
20::COMO;;# %%
21::COMO;;# Preparing the data
22::COMO;;# ------------------
23::COMO;;#
24::COMO;;# Load the Covtype dataset, which contains 581,012 samples
25::COMO;;# with 54 features each, distributed among 6 classes. The goal of this dataset
26::COMO;;# is to predict forest cover type from cartographic variables only
27::COMO;;# (no remotely sensed data). After loading, we transform it into a binary
28::COMO;;# classification problem to match the version of the dataset in the
29::COMO;;# LIBSVM webpage [2]_, which was the one used in [1]_.
33::COMC;;y[y == 2] = 1 # We will try to separate class 2 from the other 6 classes.
34::COMO;;# %%
35::COMO;;# Partitioning the data
36::COMO;;# ---------------------
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# Here we select 5,000 samples for training and 10,000 for testing.
39::COMO;;# To actually reproduce the results in the original Tensor Sketch paper,
40::COMO;;# select 100,000 for training.
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# Feature normalization
47::COMO;;# ---------------------
48::COMO;;#
49::COMO;;# Now scale features to the range [0, 1] to match the format of the dataset in
50::COMO;;# the LIBSVM webpage, and then normalize to unit length as done in the
51::COMO;;# original Tensor Sketch paper [1]_.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# Establishing a baseline model
59::COMO;;# -----------------------------
60::COMO;;#
61::COMO;;# As a baseline, train a linear SVM on the original features and print the
62::COMO;;# accuracy. We also measure and store accuracies and training times to
63::COMO;;# plot them later.
74::COMO;;# %%
75::COMO;;# Establishing the kernel approximation model
76::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;# Then we train linear SVMs on the features generated by
79::COMO;;# :class:`PolynomialCountSketch` with different values for `n_components`,
80::COMO;;# showing that these kernel feature approximations improve the accuracy
81::COMO;;# of linear classification. In typical application scenarios, `n_components`
82::COMO;;# should be larger than the number of features in the input representation
83::COMO;;# in order to achieve an improvement with respect to linear classification.
84::COMO;;# As a rule of thumb, the optimum of evaluation score / run time cost is
85::COMO;;# typically achieved at around `n_components` = 10 * `n_features`, though this
86::COMO;;# might depend on the specific dataset being handled. Note that, since the
87::COMO;;# original samples have 54 features, the explicit feature map of the
88::COMO;;# polynomial kernel of degree four would have approximately 8.5 million
89::COMO;;# features (precisely, 54^4). Thanks to :class:`PolynomialCountSketch`, we can
90::COMO;;# condense most of the discriminative information of that feature space into a
91::COMO;;# much more compact representation. While we run the experiment only a single time
92::COMO;;# (`n_runs` = 1) in this example, in practice one should repeat the experiment several
93::COMO;;# times to compensate for the stochastic nature of :class:`PolynomialCountSketch`.
119::COMO;;# %%
120::COMO;;# Establishing the kernelized SVM model
121::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# Train a kernelized SVM to see how well :class:`PolynomialCountSketch`
124::COMO;;# is approximating the performance of the kernel. This, of course, may take
125::COMO;;# some time, as the SVC class has a relatively poor scalability. This is the
126::COMO;;# reason why kernel approximators are so useful:
135::COMO;;# %%
136::COMO;;# Comparing the results
137::COMO;;# ---------------------
138::COMO;;#
139::COMO;;# Finally, plot the results of the different methods against their training
140::COMO;;# times. As we can see, the kernelized SVM achieves a higher accuracy,
141::COMO;;# but its training time is much larger and, most importantly, will grow
142::COMO;;# much faster if the number of training samples increases.
200::COMO;;# %%
201::COMO;;# References
202::COMO;;# ==========
203::COMO;;#
204::COMO;;# .. [1] Pham, Ninh and Rasmus Pagh. "Fast and scalable polynomial kernels via
205::COMO;;# explicit feature maps." KDD '13 (2013).
206::COMO;;# https://doi.org/10.1145/2487575.2487591
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# .. [2] LIBSVM binary datasets repository
209::COMO;;# https://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvmtools/datasets/binary.html
2::COMM;;====================================
3::COMM;;Comparing Linear Bayesian Regressors
4::COMM;;====================================
5::COMM;;This example compares two different bayesian regressors:
6::COMM;;- an :ref:`automatic_relevance_determination`
7::COMM;;- a :ref:`bayesian_ridge_regression`
8::COMM;;In the first part, we use an :ref:`ordinary_least_squares` (OLS) model as a
9::COMM;;baseline for comparing the models' coefficients with respect to the true
10::COMM;;coefficients. Thereafter, we show that the estimation of such models is done by
11::COMM;;iteratively maximizing the marginal log-likelihood of the observations.
12::COMM;;In the last section we plot predictions and uncertainties for the ARD and the
13::COMM;;Bayesian Ridge regressions using a polynomial feature expansion to fit a
14::COMM;;non-linear relationship between `X` and `y`.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMO;;# %%
19::COMO;;# Models robustness to recover the ground truth weights
20::COMO;;# =====================================================
21::COMO;;#
22::COMO;;# Generate synthetic dataset
23::COMO;;# --------------------------
24::COMO;;#
25::COMO;;# We generate a dataset where `X` and `y` are linearly linked: 10 of the
26::COMO;;# features of `X` will be used to generate `y`. The other features are not
27::COMO;;# useful at predicting `y`. In addition, we generate a dataset where `n_samples
28::COMO;;# == n_features`. Such a setting is challenging for an OLS model and leads
29::COMO;;# potentially to arbitrary large weights. Having a prior on the weights and a
30::COMO;;# penalty alleviates the problem. Finally, gaussian noise is added.
40::COMO;;# %%
41::COMO;;# Fit the regressors
42::COMO;;# ------------------
43::COMO;;#
44::COMO;;# We now fit both Bayesian models and the OLS to later compare the models'
45::COMO;;# coefficients.
59::COMO;;# %%
60::COMO;;# Plot the true and estimated coefficients
61::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
62::COMO;;#
63::COMO;;# Now we compare the coefficients of each model with the weights of
64::COMO;;# the true generative model.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# Due to the added noise, none of the models recover the true weights. Indeed,
81::COMO;;# all models always have more than 10 non-zero coefficients. Compared to the OLS
82::COMO;;# estimator, the coefficients using a Bayesian Ridge regression are slightly
83::COMO;;# shifted toward zero, which stabilises them. The ARD regression provides a
84::COMO;;# sparser solution: some of the non-informative coefficients are set exactly to
85::COMO;;# zero, while shifting others closer to zero. Some non-informative coefficients
86::COMO;;# are still present and retain large values.
87::COMO;;# %%
88::COMO;;# Plot the marginal log-likelihood
89::COMO;;# --------------------------------
100::COMO;;# %%
101::COMO;;# Indeed, both models minimize the log-likelihood up to an arbitrary cutoff
102::COMO;;# defined by the `max_iter` parameter.
103::COMO;;#
104::COMO;;# Bayesian regressions with polynomial feature expansion
105::COMO;;# ======================================================
106::COMO;;# Generate synthetic dataset
107::COMO;;# --------------------------
108::COMO;;# We create a target that is a non-linear function of the input feature.
109::COMO;;# Noise following a standard uniform distribution is added.
114::COMO;;# sort the data to make plotting easier later
120::COMO;;# extrapolation
125::COMO;;# %%
126::COMO;;# Fit the regressors
127::COMO;;# ------------------
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# Here we try a degree 10 polynomial to potentially overfit, though the bayesian
130::COMO;;# linear models regularize the size of the polynomial coefficients. As
131::COMO;;# `fit_intercept=True` by default for
132::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ARDRegression` and
133::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.BayesianRidge`, then
134::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures` should not introduce an
135::COMO;;# additional bias feature. By setting `return_std=True`, the bayesian regressors
136::COMO;;# return the standard deviation of the posterior distribution for the model
137::COMO;;# parameters.
150::COMO;;# %%
151::COMO;;# Plotting polynomial regressions with std errors of the scores
152::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------
175::COMO;;# %%
176::COMO;;# The error bars represent one standard deviation of the predicted gaussian
177::COMO;;# distribution of the query points. Notice that the ARD regression captures the
178::COMO;;# ground truth the best when using the default parameters in both models, but
179::COMO;;# further reducing the `lambda_init` hyperparameter of the Bayesian Ridge can
180::COMO;;# reduce its bias (see example
181::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_bayesian_ridge_curvefit.py`).
182::COMO;;# Finally, due to the intrinsic limitations of a polynomial regression, both
183::COMO;;# models fail when extrapolating.
2::COMM;;============================================
3::COMM;;Curve Fitting with Bayesian Ridge Regression
4::COMM;;============================================
5::COMM;;Computes a Bayesian Ridge Regression of Sinusoids.
6::COMM;;See :ref:`bayesian_ridge_regression` for more information on the regressor.
7::COMM;;In general, when fitting a curve with a polynomial by Bayesian ridge
8::COMM;;regression, the selection of initial values of
9::COMM;;the regularization parameters (alpha, lambda) may be important.
10::COMM;;This is because the regularization parameters are determined by an iterative
11::COMM;;procedure that depends on initial values.
12::COMM;;In this example, the sinusoid is approximated by a polynomial using different
13::COMM;;pairs of initial values.
14::COMM;;When starting from the default values (alpha_init = 1.90, lambda_init = 1.),
15::COMM;;the bias of the resulting curve is large, and the variance is small.
16::COMM;;So, lambda_init should be relatively small (1.e-3) so as to reduce the bias.
17::COMM;;Also, by evaluating log marginal likelihood (L) of
18::COMM;;these models, we can determine which one is better.
19::COMM;;It can be concluded that the model with larger L is more likely.

3::COMM;;Fitting an Elastic Net with a precomputed Gram Matrix and Weighted Samples
4::COMM;;==========================================================================
5::COMM;;The following example shows how to precompute the gram matrix
6::COMM;;while using weighted samples with an :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet`.
7::COMM;;If weighted samples are used, the design matrix must be centered and then
8::COMM;;rescaled by the square root of the weight vector before the gram matrix
9::COMM;;is computed.
10::COMM;;.. note::
11::COMM;;`sample_weight` vector is also rescaled to sum to `n_samples`, see the
12::COMM;;documentation for the `sample_weight` parameter to
13::COMM;;:meth:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet.fit`.

16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

25::COMO;;# normalize the sample weights
27::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# To fit the elastic net using the `precompute` option together with the sample
29::COMO;;# weights, we must first center the design matrix, and rescale it by the
30::COMO;;# normalized weights prior to computing the gram matrix.
35::COMO;;# %%
36::COMO;;# We can now proceed with fitting. We must passed the centered design matrix to
37::COMO;;# `fit` otherwise the elastic net estimator will detect that it is uncentered
38::COMO;;# and discard the gram matrix we passed. However, if we pass the scaled design
39::COMO;;# matrix, the preprocessing code will incorrectly rescale it a second time.

2::COMM;;==================================
3::COMM;;L1-based models for Sparse Signals
4::COMM;;==================================
5::COMM;;The present example compares three l1-based regression models on a synthetic
6::COMM;;signal obtained from sparse and correlated features that are further corrupted
7::COMM;;with additive Gaussian noise:
8::COMM;;- a :ref:`lasso`;
9::COMM;;- an :ref:`automatic_relevance_determination`;
10::COMM;;- an :ref:`elastic_net`.
11::COMM;;It is known that the Lasso estimates turn to be close to the model selection
12::COMM;;estimates when the data dimensions grow, given that the irrelevant variables are
13::COMM;;not too correlated with the relevant ones. In the presence of correlated
14::COMM;;features, Lasso itself cannot select the correct sparsity pattern [1]_.
15::COMM;;Here we compare the performance of the three models in terms of the :math:`R^2`
16::COMM;;score, the fitting time and the sparsity of the estimated coefficients when
17::COMM;;compared with the ground-truth.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# Generate synthetic dataset
23::COMO;;# --------------------------
24::COMO;;#
25::COMO;;# We generate a dataset where the number of samples is lower than the total
26::COMO;;# number of features. This leads to an underdetermined system, i.e. the solution
27::COMO;;# is not unique, and thus we cannot apply an :ref:`ordinary_least_squares` by
28::COMO;;# itself. Regularization introduces a penalty term to the objective function,
29::COMO;;# which modifies the optimization problem and can help alleviate the
30::COMO;;# underdetermined nature of the system.
31::COMO;;#
32::COMO;;# The target `y` is a linear combination with alternating signs of sinusoidal
33::COMO;;# signals. Only the 10 lowest out of the 100 frequencies in `X` are used to
34::COMO;;# generate `y`, while the rest of the features are not informative. This results
35::COMO;;# in a high dimensional sparse feature space, where some degree of
36::COMO;;# l1-penalization is necessary.
47::COMC;;true_coef[n_informative:] = 0 # sparsify coef
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# Some of the informative features have close frequencies to induce
51::COMO;;# (anti-)correlations.
53::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# A random phase is introduced using :func:`numpy.random.random_sample`
55::COMO;;# and some Gaussian noise (implemented by :func:`numpy.random.normal`)
56::COMO;;# is added to both the features and the target.
61::COMO;;# %%
62::COMO;;# Such sparse, noisy and correlated features can be obtained, for instance, from
63::COMO;;# sensor nodes monitoring some environmental variables, as they typically register
64::COMO;;# similar values depending on their positions (spatial correlations).
65::COMO;;# We can visualize the target.
71::COMO;;# %%
72::COMO;;# We split the data into train and test sets for simplicity. In practice one
73::COMO;;# should use a :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit`
74::COMO;;# cross-validation to estimate the variance of the test score. Here we set
75::COMO;;# `shuffle="False"` as we must not use training data that succeed the testing
76::COMO;;# data when dealing with data that have a temporal relationship.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# In the following, we compute the performance of three l1-based models in terms
81::COMO;;# of the goodness of fit :math:`R^2` score and the fitting time. Then we make a
82::COMO;;# plot to compare the sparsity of the estimated coefficients with respect to the
83::COMO;;# ground-truth coefficients and finally we analyze the previous results.
84::COMO;;#
85::COMO;;# Lasso
86::COMO;;# -----
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# In this example, we demo a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` with a fixed
89::COMO;;# value of the regularization parameter `alpha`. In practice, the optimal
90::COMO;;# parameter `alpha` should be selected by passing a
91::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit` cross-validation strategy to a
92::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoCV`. To keep the example simple and fast to
93::COMO;;# execute, we directly set the optimal value for alpha here.
103::COMO;;# %%
104::COMO;;# Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD)
105::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------
106::COMO;;#
107::COMO;;# An ARD regression is the Bayesian version of the Lasso. It can produce
108::COMO;;# interval estimates for all of the parameters, including the error variance, if
109::COMO;;# required. It is a suitable option when the signals have Gaussian noise. See
110::COMO;;# the example :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_ard.py` for a
111::COMO;;# comparison of :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ARDRegression` and
112::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.BayesianRidge` regressors.
120::COMO;;# %%
121::COMO;;# ElasticNet
122::COMO;;# ----------
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet` is a middle ground between
125::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` and :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`,
126::COMO;;# as it combines a L1 and a L2-penalty. The amount of regularization is
127::COMO;;# controlled by the two hyperparameters `l1_ratio` and `alpha`. For `l1_ratio =
128::COMO;;# 0` the penalty is pure L2 and the model is equivalent to a
129::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`. Similarly, `l1_ratio = 1` is a pure L1
130::COMO;;# penalty and the model is equivalent to a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso`.
131::COMO;;# For `0 < l1_ratio < 1`, the penalty is a combination of L1 and L2.
132::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# As done before, we train the model with fix values for `alpha` and `l1_ratio`.
134::COMO;;# To select their optimal value we used an
135::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNetCV`, not shown here to keep the
136::COMO;;# example simple.
144::COMO;;# %%
145::COMO;;# Plot and analysis of the results
146::COMO;;# --------------------------------
147::COMO;;#
148::COMO;;# In this section, we use a heatmap to visualize the sparsity of the true
149::COMO;;# and estimated coefficients of the respective linear models.
177::COMO;;# %%
178::COMO;;# In the present example :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet` yields the
179::COMO;;# best score and captures the most of the predictive features, yet still fails
180::COMO;;# at finding all the true components. Notice that both
181::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet` and
182::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ARDRegression` result in a less sparse model
183::COMO;;# than a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso`.
184::COMO;;#
185::COMO;;# Conclusions
186::COMO;;# -----------
187::COMO;;#
188::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` is known to recover sparse data
189::COMO;;# effectively but does not perform well with highly correlated features. Indeed,
190::COMO;;# if several correlated features contribute to the target,
191::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` would end up selecting a single one of
192::COMO;;# them. In the case of sparse yet non-correlated features, a
193::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` model would be more suitable.
194::COMO;;#
195::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet` introduces some sparsity on the
196::COMO;;# coefficients and shrinks their values to zero. Thus, in the presence of
197::COMO;;# correlated features that contribute to the target, the model is still able to
198::COMO;;# reduce their weights without setting them exactly to zero. This results in a
199::COMO;;# less sparse model than a pure :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` and may
200::COMO;;# capture non-predictive features as well.
201::COMO;;#
202::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ARDRegression` is better when handling Gaussian
203::COMO;;# noise, but is still unable to handle correlated features and requires a larger
204::COMO;;# amount of time due to fitting a prior.
205::COMO;;#
206::COMO;;# References
207::COMO;;# ----------
208::COMO;;#
209::COMO;;# .. [1] :doi:`"Lasso-type recovery of sparse representations for
210::COMO;;# high-dimensional data" N. Meinshausen, B. Yu - The Annals of Statistics

2::COMM;;==============================================
3::COMM;;Lasso model selection via information criteria
4::COMM;;==============================================
5::COMM;;This example reproduces the example of Fig. 2 of [ZHT2007]_. A
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsIC` estimator is fit on a
7::COMM;;diabetes dataset and the AIC and the BIC criteria are used to select
8::COMM;;the best model.
9::COMM;;.. note::
10::COMM;;It is important to note that the optimization to find `alpha` with
11::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsIC` relies on the AIC or BIC
12::COMM;;criteria that are computed in-sample, thus on the training set directly.
13::COMM;;This approach differs from the cross-validation procedure. For a comparison
14::COMM;;of the two approaches, you can refer to the following example:
15::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_lasso_model_selection.py`.
16::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
17::COMM;;.. [ZHT2007] :arxiv:`Zou, Hui, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani.
18::COMM;;"On the degrees of freedom of the lasso."
19::COMM;;The Annals of Statistics 35.5 (2007): 2173-2192.
20::COMM;;<0712.0881>`
22::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
23::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
24::COMO;;# %%
25::COMO;;# We will use the diabetes dataset.
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# Scikit-learn provides an estimator called
32::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsIC` that uses either Akaike's
33::COMO;;# information criterion (AIC) or the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) to
34::COMO;;# select the best model. Before fitting
35::COMO;;# this model, we will scale the dataset.
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# In the following, we are going to fit two models to compare the values
38::COMO;;# reported by AIC and BIC.
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# To be in line with the definition in [ZHT2007]_, we need to rescale the
45::COMO;;# AIC and the BIC. Indeed, Zou et al. are ignoring some constant terms
46::COMO;;# compared to the original definition of AIC derived from the maximum
47::COMO;;# log-likelihood of a linear model. You can refer to
48::COMO;;# :ref:`mathematical detail section for the User Guide <lasso_lars_ic>`.
51::COMM;;return criterion - n_samples * np.log(2 * np.pi * noise_variance) - n_samples
52::COMM;;# %%
53::COMM;;import numpy as np
54::COMM;;aic_criterion = zou_et_al_criterion_rescaling(
55::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].criterion_,
56::COMM;;n_samples,
57::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].noise_variance_,
58::COMM;;)
59::COMM;;index_alpha_path_aic = np.flatnonzero(
60::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].alphas_ == lasso_lars_ic[-1].alpha_
61::COMM;;)[0]
62::COMM;;# %%
63::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic.set_params(lassolarsic__criterion="bic").fit(X, y)
64::COMM;;bic_criterion = zou_et_al_criterion_rescaling(
65::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].criterion_,
66::COMM;;n_samples,
67::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].noise_variance_,
68::COMM;;)
69::COMM;;index_alpha_path_bic = np.flatnonzero(
70::COMM;;lasso_lars_ic[-1].alphas_ == lasso_lars_ic[-1].alpha_
71::COMM;;)[0]
72::COMM;;# %%
73::COMM;;# Now that we collected the AIC and BIC, we can as well check that the minima
74::COMM;;# of both criteria happen at the same alpha. Then, we can simplify the
75::COMM;;# following plot.
76::COMM;;index_alpha_path_aic == index_alpha_path_bic
77::COMM;;# %%
78::COMM;;# Finally, we can plot the AIC and BIC criterion and the subsequent selected
79::COMM;;# regularization parameter.
80::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
81::COMM;;plt.plot(aic_criterion, color="tab:blue", marker="o", label="AIC criterion")
82::COMM;;plt.plot(bic_criterion, color="tab:orange", marker="o", label="BIC criterion")
83::COMM;;plt.vlines(
84::COMM;;index_alpha_path_bic,
85::COMM;;aic_criterion.min(),
86::COMM;;aic_criterion.max(),

2::COMM;;========================================
3::COMM;;Lasso, Lasso-LARS, and Elastic Net paths
4::COMM;;========================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how to compute the "paths" of coefficients along the Lasso,
6::COMM;;Lasso-LARS, and Elastic Net regularization paths. In other words, it shows the
7::COMM;;relationship between the regularization parameter (alpha) and the coefficients.
8::COMM;;Lasso and Lasso-LARS impose a sparsity constraint on the coefficients,
9::COMM;;encouraging some of them to be zero. Elastic Net is a generalization of
10::COMM;;Lasso that adds an L2 penalty term to the L1 penalty term. This allows for
11::COMM;;some coefficients to be non-zero while still encouraging sparsity.
12::COMM;;Lasso and Elastic Net use a coordinate descent method to compute the paths, while
13::COMM;;Lasso-LARS uses the LARS algorithm to compute the paths.
14::COMM;;The paths are computed using :func:`~sklearn.linear_model.lasso_path`,
15::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.linear_model.lars_path`, and :func:`~sklearn.linear_model.enet_path`.
16::COMM;;The results show different comparison plots:
17::COMM;;- Compare Lasso and Lasso-LARS
18::COMM;;- Compare Lasso and Elastic Net
19::COMM;;- Compare Lasso with positive Lasso
20::COMM;;- Compare LARS and Positive LARS
21::COMM;;- Compare Elastic Net and positive Elastic Net
22::COMM;;Each plot shows how the model coefficients vary as the regularization strength changes,
23::COMM;;offering insight into the behavior of these models
24::COMM;;under different constraints.
26::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
27::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;=================================================
3::COMM;;Lasso model selection: AIC-BIC / cross-validation
4::COMM;;=================================================
5::COMM;;This example focuses on model selection for Lasso models that are
6::COMM;;linear models with an L1 penalty for regression problems.
7::COMM;;Indeed, several strategies can be used to select the value of the
8::COMM;;regularization parameter: via cross-validation or using an information
9::COMM;;criterion, namely AIC or BIC.
10::COMM;;In what follows, we will discuss in details the different strategies.
12::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
13::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
14::COMO;;# %%
15::COMO;;# Dataset
16::COMO;;# -------
17::COMO;;# In this example, we will use the diabetes dataset.
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# In addition, we add some random features to the original data to
23::COMO;;# better illustrate the feature selection performed by the Lasso model.
33::COMO;;# Show only a subset of the columns
35::COMO;;# %%
36::COMO;;# Selecting Lasso via an information criterion
37::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------
38::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsIC` provides a Lasso estimator that
39::COMO;;# uses the Akaike information criterion (AIC) or the Bayes information
40::COMO;;# criterion (BIC) to select the optimal value of the regularization
41::COMO;;# parameter alpha.
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# Before fitting the model, we will standardize the data with a
44::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler`. In addition, we will
45::COMO;;# measure the time to fit and tune the hyperparameter alpha in order to
46::COMO;;# compare with the cross-validation strategy.
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# We will first fit a Lasso model with the AIC criterion.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# We store the AIC metric for each value of alpha used during `fit`.
65::COMO;;# %%
66::COMO;;# Now, we perform the same analysis using the BIC criterion.
70::COMO;;# %%
71::COMO;;# We can check which value of `alpha` leads to the minimum AIC and BIC.
76::COMO;;# %%
77::COMO;;# Finally, we can plot the AIC and BIC values for the different alpha values.
78::COMO;;# The vertical lines in the plot correspond to the alpha chosen for each
79::COMO;;# criterion. The selected alpha corresponds to the minimum of the AIC or BIC
80::COMO;;# criterion.
105::COMO;;# %%
106::COMO;;# Model selection with an information-criterion is very fast. It relies on
107::COMO;;# computing the criterion on the in-sample set provided to `fit`. Both criteria
108::COMO;;# estimate the model generalization error based on the training set error and
109::COMO;;# penalize this overly optimistic error. However, this penalty relies on a
110::COMO;;# proper estimation of the degrees of freedom and the noise variance. Both are
111::COMO;;# derived for large samples (asymptotic results) and assume the model is
112::COMO;;# correct, i.e. that the data are actually generated by this model.
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# These models also tend to break when the problem is badly conditioned (more
115::COMO;;# features than samples). It is then required to provide an estimate of the
116::COMO;;# noise variance.
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# Selecting Lasso via cross-validation
119::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
120::COMO;;# The Lasso estimator can be implemented with different solvers: coordinate
121::COMO;;# descent and least angle regression. They differ with regards to their
122::COMO;;# execution speed and sources of numerical errors.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# In scikit-learn, two different estimators are available with integrated
125::COMO;;# cross-validation: :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoCV` and
126::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsCV` that respectively solve the
127::COMO;;# problem with coordinate descent and least angle regression.
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# In the remainder of this section, we will present both approaches. For both
130::COMO;;# algorithms, we will use a 20-fold cross-validation strategy.
131::COMO;;#
132::COMO;;# Lasso via coordinate descent
133::COMO;;# ............................
134::COMO;;# Let's start by making the hyperparameter tuning using
135::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoCV`.
140::COMO;;# %%
160::COMO;;# %%
161::COMO;;# Lasso via least angle regression
162::COMO;;# ................................
163::COMO;;# Let's start by making the hyperparameter tuning using
164::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LassoLarsCV`.
169::COMO;;# %%
185::COMO;;# %%
186::COMO;;# Summary of cross-validation approach
187::COMO;;# ....................................
188::COMO;;# Both algorithms give roughly the same results.
189::COMO;;#
190::COMO;;# Lars computes a solution path only for each kink in the path. As a result, it
191::COMO;;# is very efficient when there are only of few kinks, which is the case if
192::COMO;;# there are few features or samples. Also, it is able to compute the full path
193::COMO;;# without setting any hyperparameter. On the opposite, coordinate descent
194::COMO;;# computes the path points on a pre-specified grid (here we use the default).
195::COMO;;# Thus it is more efficient if the number of grid points is smaller than the
196::COMO;;# number of kinks in the path. Such a strategy can be interesting if the number
197::COMO;;# of features is really large and there are enough samples to be selected in
198::COMO;;# each of the cross-validation fold. In terms of numerical errors, for heavily
199::COMO;;# correlated variables, Lars will accumulate more errors, while the coordinate
200::COMO;;# descent algorithm will only sample the path on a grid.
201::COMO;;#
202::COMO;;# Note how the optimal value of alpha varies for each fold. This illustrates
203::COMO;;# why nested-cross validation is a good strategy when trying to evaluate the
204::COMO;;# performance of a method for which a parameter is chosen by cross-validation:
205::COMO;;# this choice of parameter may not be optimal for a final evaluation on
206::COMO;;# unseen test set only.
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# Conclusion
209::COMO;;# ----------
210::COMO;;# In this tutorial, we presented two approaches for selecting the best
211::COMO;;# hyperparameter `alpha`: one strategy finds the optimal value of `alpha`
212::COMO;;# by only using the training set and some information criterion, and another
213::COMO;;# strategy is based on cross-validation.
214::COMO;;#
215::COMO;;# In this example, both approaches are working similarly. The in-sample
216::COMO;;# hyperparameter selection even shows its efficacy in terms of computational
217::COMO;;# performance. However, it can only be used when the number of samples is large
218::COMO;;# enough compared to the number of features.
219::COMO;;#
220::COMO;;# That's why hyperparameter optimization via cross-validation is a safe
221::COMO;;# strategy: it works in different settings.

2::COMM;;======================================================================
3::COMM;;Decision Boundaries of Multinomial and One-vs-Rest Logistic Regression
4::COMM;;======================================================================
5::COMM;;This example compares decision boundaries of multinomial and one-vs-rest
6::COMM;;logistic regression on a 2D dataset with three classes.
7::COMM;;We make a comparison of the decision boundaries of both methods that is equivalent
8::COMM;;to call the method `predict`. In addition, we plot the hyperplanes that correspond to
9::COMM;;the line when the probability estimate for a class is of 0.5.
11::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
12::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
13::COMO;;# %%
14::COMO;;# Dataset Generation
15::COMO;;# ------------------
16::COMO;;#
17::COMO;;# We generate a synthetic dataset using :func:`~sklearn.datasets.make_blobs` function.
18::COMO;;# The dataset consists of 1,000 samples from three different classes,
19::COMO;;# centered around [-5, 0], [0, 1.5], and [5, -1]. After generation, we apply a linear
20::COMO;;# transformation to introduce some correlation between features and make the problem
21::COMO;;# more challenging. This results in a 2D dataset with three overlapping classes,
22::COMO;;# suitable for demonstrating the differences between multinomial and one-vs-rest
23::COMO;;# logistic regression.
35::COMO;;# %%
36::COMO;;# Classifier Training
37::COMO;;# -------------------
38::COMO;;#
39::COMO;;# We train two different logistic regression classifiers: multinomial and one-vs-rest.
40::COMO;;# The multinomial classifier handles all classes simultaneously, while the one-vs-rest
41::COMO;;# approach trains a binary classifier for each class against all others.
48::COMO;;# %%
49::COMO;;# Decision Boundaries Visualization
50::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# Let's visualize the decision boundaries of both models that is provided by the
53::COMO;;# method `predict` of the classifiers.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# We see that the decision boundaries are different. This difference stems from their
81::COMO;;# approaches:
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# - Multinomial logistic regression considers all classes simultaneously during
84::COMO;;# optimization.
85::COMO;;# - One-vs-rest logistic regression fits each class independently against all others.
86::COMO;;#
87::COMO;;# These distinct strategies can lead to varying decision boundaries, especially in
88::COMO;;# complex multi-class problems.
89::COMO;;#
90::COMO;;# Hyperplanes Visualization
91::COMO;;# --------------------------
92::COMO;;#
93::COMO;;# We also visualize the hyperplanes that correspond to the line when the probability
94::COMO;;# estimate for a class is of 0.5.
112::COMO;;# %%
130::COMO;;# %%
131::COMO;;# While the hyperplanes for classes 0 and 2 are quite similar between the two methods,
132::COMO;;# we observe that the hyperplane for class 1 is notably different. This difference stems
133::COMO;;# from the fundamental approaches of one-vs-rest and multinomial logistic regression:
134::COMO;;#
135::COMO;;# For one-vs-rest logistic regression:
136::COMO;;#
137::COMO;;# - Each hyperplane is determined independently by considering one class against all
138::COMO;;# others.
139::COMO;;# - For class 1, the hyperplane represents the decision boundary that best separates
140::COMO;;# class 1 from the combined classes 0 and 2.
141::COMO;;# - This binary approach can lead to simpler decision boundaries but may not capture
142::COMO;;# complex relationships between all classes simultaneously.
143::COMO;;# - There is no possible interpretation of the conditional class probabilities.
144::COMO;;#
145::COMO;;# For multinomial logistic regression:
146::COMO;;#
147::COMO;;# - All hyperplanes are determined simultaneously, considering the relationships between
148::COMO;;# all classes at once.
149::COMO;;# - The loss minimized by the model is a proper scoring rule, which means that the model
150::COMO;;# is optimized to estimate the conditional class probabilities that are, therefore,
151::COMO;;# meaningful.
152::COMO;;# - Each hyperplane represents the decision boundary where the probability of one class
153::COMO;;# becomes higher than the others, based on the overall probability distribution.
154::COMO;;# - This approach can capture more nuanced relationships between classes, potentially
155::COMO;;# leading to more accurate classification in multi-class problems.
156::COMO;;#
157::COMO;;# The difference in hyperplanes, especially for class 1, highlights how these methods
158::COMO;;# can produce different decision boundaries despite similar overall accuracy.
159::COMO;;#
160::COMO;;# In practice, using multinomial logistic regression is recommended since it minimizes a
161::COMO;;# well-formulated loss function, leading to better-calibrated class probabilities and
162::COMO;;# thus more interpretable results. When it comes to decision boundaries, one should
163::COMO;;# formulate a utility function to transform the class probabilities into a meaningful
164::COMO;;# quantity for the problem at hand. One-vs-rest allows for different decision boundaries
165::COMO;;# but does not allow for fine-grained control over the trade-off between the classes as
166::COMO;;# a utility function would.

15::COMM;;has converged before collecting the coefficients.

17::COMM;;reused to initialize the next model fit to speed-up the computation of the
18::COMM;;full-path.

2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;Ordinary Least Squares and Ridge Regression
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;1. Ordinary Least Squares:
6::COMM;;We illustrate how to use the ordinary least squares (OLS) model,
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression`, on a single feature of
8::COMM;;the diabetes dataset. We train on a subset of the data, evaluate on a
9::COMM;;test set, and visualize the predictions.
10::COMM;;2. Ordinary Least Squares and Ridge Regression Variance:
11::COMM;;We then show how OLS can have high variance when the data is sparse or
12::COMM;;noisy, by fitting on a very small synthetic sample repeatedly. Ridge
13::COMM;;regression, :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`, reduces this variance
14::COMM;;by penalizing (shrinking) the coefficients, leading to more stable
15::COMM;;predictions.

32::COMO;;# -----------------------
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# We create a linear regression model and fit it on the training data. Note that by
35::COMO;;# default, an intercept is added to the model. We can control this behavior by setting
36::COMO;;# the `fit_intercept` parameter.
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# Model evaluation
41::COMO;;# ----------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# We evaluate the model's performance on the test set using the mean squared error
44::COMO;;# and the coefficient of determination.
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# Plotting the results
51::COMO;;# --------------------
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# Finally, we visualize the results on the train and test data.
72::COMO;;# %%
73::COMO;;#
74::COMO;;# OLS on this single-feature subset learns a linear function that minimizes
75::COMO;;# the mean squared error on the training data. We can see how well (or poorly)
76::COMO;;# it generalizes by looking at the R^2 score and mean squared error on the
77::COMO;;# test set. In higher dimensions, pure OLS often overfits, especially if the
78::COMO;;# data is noisy. Regularization techniques (like Ridge or Lasso) can help
79::COMO;;# reduce that.
80::COMO;;# %%
81::COMO;;# Ordinary Least Squares and Ridge Regression Variance
82::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------------------
83::COMO;;#
84::COMO;;# Next, we illustrate the problem of high variance more clearly by using
85::COMO;;# a tiny synthetic dataset. We sample only two data points, then repeatedly
86::COMO;;# add small Gaussian noise to them and refit both OLS and Ridge. We plot
87::COMO;;# each new line to see how much OLS can jump around, whereas Ridge remains
88::COMO;;# more stable thanks to its penalty term.
116::COMO;;# %%
117::COMO;;# Conclusion
118::COMO;;# ----------
119::COMO;;#
120::COMO;;# - In the first example, we applied OLS to a real dataset, showing
121::COMO;;# how a plain linear model can fit the data by minimizing the squared error
122::COMO;;# on the training set.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# - In the second example, OLS lines varied drastically each time noise
125::COMO;;# was added, reflecting its high variance when data is sparse or noisy. By
126::COMO;;# contrast, **Ridge** regression introduces a regularization term that shrinks
127::COMO;;# the coefficients, stabilizing predictions.
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# Techniques like :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge` or
130::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Lasso` (which applies an L1 penalty) are both
131::COMO;;# common ways to improve generalization and reduce overfitting. A well-tuned
132::COMO;;# Ridge or Lasso often outperforms pure OLS when features are correlated, data
133::COMO;;# is noisy, or sample size is small.

3::COMM;;Orthogonal Matching Pursuit
4::COMM;;===========================

6::COMM;;measurement encoded with a dictionary

28::COMO;;# distort the clean signal
