36::COMO;;# plot the noise-free reconstruction
45::COMO;;# plot the noisy reconstruction
53::COMO;;# plot the noisy reconstruction with number of non-zeros set by CV
1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
4::COMM;;======================================
5::COMM;;Poisson regression and non-normal loss
6::COMM;;======================================
7::COMM;;This example illustrates the use of log-linear Poisson regression on the
8::COMM;;`French Motor Third-Party Liability Claims dataset
9::COMM;;<https://www.openml.org/d/41214>`_ from [1]_ and compares it with a linear
10::COMM;;model fitted with the usual least squared error and a non-linear GBRT model
11::COMM;;fitted with the Poisson loss (and a log-link).
12::COMM;;A few definitions:
13::COMM;;- A **policy** is a contract between an insurance company and an individual:
14::COMM;;the **policyholder**, that is, the vehicle driver in this case.
15::COMM;;- A **claim** is the request made by a policyholder to the insurer to
16::COMM;;compensate for a loss covered by the insurance.
17::COMM;;- The **exposure** is the duration of the insurance coverage of a given policy,
18::COMM;;in years.
19::COMM;;- The claim **frequency** is the number of claims divided by the exposure,
20::COMM;;typically measured in number of claims per year.
21::COMM;;In this dataset, each sample corresponds to an insurance policy. Available
22::COMM;;features include driver age, vehicle age, vehicle power, etc.
23::COMM;;Our goal is to predict the expected frequency of claims following car accidents
24::COMM;;for a new policyholder given the historical data over a population of
25::COMM;;policyholders.
26::COMM;;.. [1] A. Noll, R. Salzmann and M.V. Wuthrich, Case Study: French Motor
27::COMM;;Third-Party Liability Claims (November 8, 2018). `doi:10.2139/ssrn.3164764
28::COMM;;<https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3164764>`_
33::COMO;;##############################################################################
34::COMO;;# The French Motor Third-Party Liability Claims dataset
35::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# Let's load the motor claim dataset from OpenML:
38::COMO;;# https://www.openml.org/d/41214
42::COMO;;# %%
43::COMO;;# The number of claims (``ClaimNb``) is a positive integer that can be modeled
44::COMO;;# as a Poisson distribution. It is then assumed to be the number of discrete
45::COMO;;# events occurring with a constant rate in a given time interval (``Exposure``,
46::COMO;;# in units of years).
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# Here we want to model the frequency ``y = ClaimNb / Exposure`` conditionally
49::COMO;;# on ``X`` via a (scaled) Poisson distribution, and use ``Exposure`` as
50::COMO;;# ``sample_weight``.
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# The remaining columns can be used to predict the frequency of claim events.
69::COMO;;# Those columns are very heterogeneous with a mix of categorical and numeric
70::COMO;;# variables with different scales, possibly very unevenly distributed.
71::COMO;;#
72::COMO;;# In order to fit linear models with those predictors it is therefore
73::COMO;;# necessary to perform standard feature transformations as follows:
104::COMO;;# %%
105::COMO;;# A constant prediction baseline
106::COMO;;# ------------------------------
107::COMO;;#
108::COMO;;# It is worth noting that more than 93% of policyholders have zero claims. If
109::COMO;;# we were to convert this problem into a binary classification task, it would
110::COMO;;# be significantly imbalanced, and even a simplistic model that would only
111::COMO;;# predict mean can achieve an accuracy of 93%.
112::COMO;;#
113::COMO;;# To evaluate the pertinence of the used metrics, we will consider as a
114::COMO;;# baseline a "dummy" estimator that constantly predicts the mean frequency of
115::COMO;;# the training sample.
126::COMO;;##############################################################################
127::COMO;;# Let's compute the performance of this constant prediction baseline with 3
128::COMO;;# different regression metrics:
136::COMM;;y_pred = estimator.predict(df_test)
137::COMM;;print(
138::COMM;;"MSE: %.3f"
139::COMM;;% mean_squared_error(
140::COMM;;df_test["Frequency"], y_pred, sample_weight=df_test["Exposure"]
141::COMM;;)
142::COMM;;)
143::COMM;;print(
144::COMM;;"MAE: %.3f"
145::COMM;;% mean_absolute_error(
146::COMM;;df_test["Frequency"], y_pred, sample_weight=df_test["Exposure"]
147::COMM;;)
148::COMM;;)
149::COMM;;# Ignore non-positive predictions, as they are invalid for
150::COMM;;# the Poisson deviance.
151::COMM;;mask = y_pred > 0
152::COMM;;if (~mask).any():
153::COMM;;n_masked, n_samples = (~mask).sum(), mask.shape[0]
154::COMM;;print(
155::COMM;;"WARNING: Estimator yields invalid, non-positive predictions "
156::COMM;;f" for {n_masked} samples out of {n_samples}. These predictions "
157::COMM;;"are ignored when computing the Poisson deviance."
158::COMM;;)
159::COMM;;print(
160::COMM;;"mean Poisson deviance: %.3f"
161::COMM;;% mean_poisson_deviance(
162::COMM;;df_test["Frequency"][mask],
163::COMM;;y_pred[mask],
164::COMM;;sample_weight=df_test["Exposure"][mask],
165::COMM;;)
166::COMM;;)
167::COMM;;print("Constant mean frequency evaluation:")
168::COMM;;score_estimator(dummy, df_test)
169::COMM;;# %%
170::COMM;;# (Generalized) linear models
171::COMM;;# ---------------------------
172::COMM;;#
173::COMM;;# We start by modeling the target variable with the (l2 penalized) least
174::COMM;;# squares linear regression model, more commonly known as Ridge regression. We
175::COMM;;# use a low penalization `alpha`, as we expect such a linear model to under-fit
176::COMM;;# on such a large dataset.
177::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
178::COMM;;ridge_glm = Pipeline(
179::COMM;;[
180::COMM;;("preprocessor", linear_model_preprocessor),
181::COMM;;("regressor", Ridge(alpha=1e-6)),
182::COMM;;]
183::COMM;;).fit(df_train, df_train["Frequency"], regressor__sample_weight=df_train["Exposure"])
184::COMM;;# %%
185::COMM;;# The Poisson deviance cannot be computed on non-positive values predicted by
186::COMM;;# the model. For models that do return a few non-positive predictions (e.g.
187::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`) we ignore the corresponding samples,
188::COMM;;# meaning that the obtained Poisson deviance is approximate. An alternative
189::COMM;;# approach could be to use :class:`~sklearn.compose.TransformedTargetRegressor`
190::COMM;;# meta-estimator to map ``y_pred`` to a strictly positive domain.
191::COMM;;print("Ridge evaluation:")
192::COMM;;score_estimator(ridge_glm, df_test)
193::COMM;;# %%
194::COMM;;# Next we fit the Poisson regressor on the target variable. We set the
195::COMM;;# regularization strength ``alpha`` to approximately 1e-6 over number of
196::COMM;;# samples (i.e. `1e-12`) in order to mimic the Ridge regressor whose L2 penalty
197::COMM;;# term scales differently with the number of samples.
198::COMM;;#
199::COMM;;# Since the Poisson regressor internally models the log of the expected target
200::COMM;;# value instead of the expected value directly (log vs identity link function),
201::COMM;;# the relationship between X and y is not exactly linear anymore. Therefore the
202::COMM;;# Poisson regressor is called a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) rather than a
203::COMM;;# vanilla linear model as is the case for Ridge regression.
204::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
205::COMM;;n_samples = df_train.shape[0]
206::COMM;;poisson_glm = Pipeline(
207::COMM;;[
208::COMM;;("preprocessor", linear_model_preprocessor),
209::COMM;;("regressor", PoissonRegressor(alpha=1e-12, solver="newton-cholesky")),
210::COMM;;]
211::COMM;;)
212::COMM;;poisson_glm.fit(
213::COMM;;df_train, df_train["Frequency"], regressor__sample_weight=df_train["Exposure"]
214::COMM;;)
215::COMM;;print("PoissonRegressor evaluation:")
216::COMM;;score_estimator(poisson_glm, df_test)
217::COMM;;# %%
218::COMM;;# Gradient Boosting Regression Trees for Poisson regression
219::COMM;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
220::COMM;;#
221::COMM;;# Finally, we will consider a non-linear model, namely Gradient Boosting
222::COMM;;# Regression Trees. Tree-based models do not require the categorical data to be
223::COMM;;# one-hot encoded: instead, we can encode each category label with an arbitrary
224::COMM;;# integer using :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder`. With this
225::COMM;;# encoding, the trees will treat the categorical features as ordered features,
226::COMM;;# which might not be always a desired behavior. However this effect is limited
227::COMM;;# for deep enough trees which are able to recover the categorical nature of the
228::COMM;;# features. The main advantage of the
229::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder` over the
230::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder` is that it will make training
231::COMM;;# faster.
232::COMM;;#
233::COMM;;# Gradient Boosting also gives the possibility to fit the trees with a Poisson
234::COMM;;# loss (with an implicit log-link function) instead of the default
235::COMM;;# least-squares loss. Here we only fit trees with the Poisson loss to keep this
236::COMM;;# example concise.
237::COMM;;from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
238::COMM;;from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder
239::COMM;;tree_preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
240::COMM;;[
241::COMM;;(
242::COMM;;"categorical",
243::COMM;;OrdinalEncoder(),
244::COMM;;["VehBrand", "VehPower", "VehGas", "Region", "Area"],
245::COMM;;),
246::COMM;;("numeric", "passthrough", ["VehAge", "DrivAge", "BonusMalus", "Density"]),
247::COMM;;],
248::COMM;;remainder="drop",
249::COMM;;)
250::COMM;;poisson_gbrt = Pipeline(
251::COMM;;[
252::COMM;;("preprocessor", tree_preprocessor),
253::COMM;;(
254::COMM;;"regressor",
255::COMM;;HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss="poisson", max_leaf_nodes=128),
256::COMM;;),
257::COMM;;]
258::COMM;;)
259::COMM;;poisson_gbrt.fit(
260::COMM;;df_train, df_train["Frequency"], regressor__sample_weight=df_train["Exposure"]
261::COMM;;)
262::COMM;;print("Poisson Gradient Boosted Trees evaluation:")
263::COMM;;score_estimator(poisson_gbrt, df_test)
264::COMM;;# %%
265::COMM;;# Like the Poisson GLM above, the gradient boosted trees model minimizes
266::COMM;;# the Poisson deviance. However, because of a higher predictive power,
267::COMM;;# it reaches lower values of Poisson deviance.
268::COMM;;#
269::COMM;;# Evaluating models with a single train / test split is prone to random
270::COMM;;# fluctuations. If computing resources allow, it should be verified that
271::COMM;;# cross-validated performance metrics would lead to similar conclusions.
272::COMM;;#
273::COMM;;# The qualitative difference between these models can also be visualized by
274::COMM;;# comparing the histogram of observed target values with that of predicted
275::COMM;;# values:
276::COMM;;fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=2, ncols=4, figsize=(16, 6), sharey=True)
277::COMM;;fig.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.2)
278::COMM;;n_bins = 20
279::COMM;;for row_idx, label, df in zip(range(2), ["train", "test"], [df_train, df_test]):
280::COMM;;df["Frequency"].hist(bins=np.linspace(-1, 30, n_bins), ax=axes[row_idx, 0])
281::COMM;;axes[row_idx, 0].set_title("Data")
282::COMM;;axes[row_idx, 0].set_yscale("log")
283::COMM;;axes[row_idx, 0].set_xlabel("y (observed Frequency)")
284::COMM;;axes[row_idx, 0].set_ylim([1e1, 5e5])
285::COMM;;axes[row_idx, 0].set_ylabel(label + " samples")
286::COMM;;for idx, model in enumerate([ridge_glm, poisson_glm, poisson_gbrt]):
287::COMM;;y_pred = model.predict(df)
288::COMM;;pd.Series(y_pred).hist(
289::COMM;;bins=np.linspace(-1, 4, n_bins), ax=axes[row_idx, idx + 1]
290::COMM;;)
291::COMM;;axes[row_idx, idx + 1].set(
292::COMM;;title=model[-1].__class__.__name__,
293::COMM;;yscale="log",
294::COMM;;xlabel="y_pred (predicted expected Frequency)",
295::COMM;;)
296::COMM;;plt.tight_layout()
297::COMM;;# %%
298::COMM;;# The experimental data presents a long tail distribution for ``y``. In all
299::COMM;;# models, we predict the expected frequency of a random variable, so we will
300::COMM;;# have necessarily fewer extreme values than for the observed realizations of
301::COMM;;# that random variable. This explains that the mode of the histograms of model
302::COMM;;# predictions doesn't necessarily correspond to the smallest value.
303::COMM;;# Additionally, the normal distribution used in ``Ridge`` has a constant
304::COMM;;# variance, while for the Poisson distribution used in ``PoissonRegressor`` and
305::COMM;;# ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor``, the variance is proportional to the
306::COMM;;# predicted expected value.
307::COMM;;#
308::COMM;;# Thus, among the considered estimators, ``PoissonRegressor`` and
309::COMM;;# ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor`` are a-priori better suited for modeling the
310::COMM;;# long tail distribution of the non-negative data as compared to the ``Ridge``
311::COMM;;# model which makes a wrong assumption on the distribution of the target
312::COMM;;# variable.
313::COMM;;#
314::COMM;;# The ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor`` estimator has the most flexibility and
315::COMM;;# is able to predict higher expected values.
316::COMM;;#
317::COMM;;# Note that we could have used the least squares loss for the
318::COMM;;# ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor`` model. This would wrongly assume a normal
319::COMM;;# distributed response variable as does the `Ridge` model, and possibly
320::COMM;;# also lead to slightly negative predictions. However the gradient boosted
321::COMM;;# trees would still perform relatively well and in particular better than
322::COMM;;# ``PoissonRegressor`` thanks to the flexibility of the trees combined with the
323::COMM;;# large number of training samples.
324::COMM;;#
325::COMM;;# Evaluation of the calibration of predictions
326::COMM;;# --------------------------------------------
327::COMM;;#
328::COMM;;# To ensure that estimators yield reasonable predictions for different
329::COMM;;# policyholder types, we can bin test samples according to ``y_pred`` returned
330::COMM;;# by each model. Then for each bin, we compare the mean predicted ``y_pred``,
331::COMM;;# with the mean observed target:
332::COMM;;from sklearn.utils import gen_even_slices
333::COMM;;def _mean_frequency_by_risk_group(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None, n_bins=100):
356::COMM;;idx_sort = np.argsort(y_pred)
357::COMM;;bin_centers = np.arange(0, 1, 1 / n_bins) + 0.5 / n_bins
358::COMM;;y_pred_bin = np.zeros(n_bins)
359::COMM;;y_true_bin = np.zeros(n_bins)
360::COMM;;for n, sl in enumerate(gen_even_slices(len(y_true), n_bins)):
361::COMM;;weights = sample_weight[idx_sort][sl]
362::COMM;;y_pred_bin[n] = np.average(y_pred[idx_sort][sl], weights=weights)
363::COMM;;y_true_bin[n] = np.average(y_true[idx_sort][sl], weights=weights)
364::COMM;;return bin_centers, y_true_bin, y_pred_bin
365::COMM;;print(f"Actual number of claims: {df_test['ClaimNb'].sum()}")
366::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(nrows=2, ncols=2, figsize=(12, 8))
367::COMM;;plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.3)
368::COMM;;for axi, model in zip(ax.ravel(), [ridge_glm, poisson_glm, poisson_gbrt, dummy]):
369::COMM;;y_pred = model.predict(df_test)
370::COMM;;y_true = df_test["Frequency"].values
371::COMM;;exposure = df_test["Exposure"].values
372::COMM;;q, y_true_seg, y_pred_seg = _mean_frequency_by_risk_group(
373::COMM;;y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=exposure, n_bins=10
374::COMM;;)
375::COMM;;# Name of the model after the estimator used in the last step of the
376::COMM;;# pipeline.
377::COMM;;print(f"Predicted number of claims by {model[-1]}: {np.sum(y_pred * exposure):.1f}")
378::COMM;;axi.plot(q, y_pred_seg, marker="x", linestyle="--", label="predictions")
379::COMM;;axi.plot(q, y_true_seg, marker="o", linestyle="--", label="observations")
380::COMM;;axi.set_xlim(0, 1.0)
381::COMM;;axi.set_ylim(0, 0.5)
382::COMM;;axi.set(
383::COMM;;title=model[-1],
384::COMM;;xlabel="Fraction of samples sorted by y_pred",
385::COMM;;ylabel="Mean Frequency (y_pred)",
386::COMM;;)
387::COMM;;axi.legend()
388::COMM;;plt.tight_layout()
389::COMM;;# %%
390::COMM;;# The dummy regression model predicts a constant frequency. This model does not
391::COMM;;# attribute the same tied rank to all samples but is none-the-less globally
392::COMM;;# well calibrated (to estimate the mean frequency of the entire population).
393::COMM;;#
394::COMM;;# The ``Ridge`` regression model can predict very low expected frequencies that
395::COMM;;# do not match the data. It can therefore severely under-estimate the risk for
396::COMM;;# some policyholders.
397::COMM;;#
398::COMM;;# ``PoissonRegressor`` and ``HistGradientBoostingRegressor`` show better
399::COMM;;# consistency between predicted and observed targets, especially for low
400::COMM;;# predicted target values.
401::COMM;;#
402::COMM;;# The sum of all predictions also confirms the calibration issue of the
403::COMM;;# ``Ridge`` model: it under-estimates by more than 3% the total number of
404::COMM;;# claims in the test set while the other three models can approximately recover
405::COMM;;# the total number of claims of the test portfolio.
406::COMM;;#
407::COMM;;# Evaluation of the ranking power
408::COMM;;# -------------------------------
409::COMM;;#
410::COMM;;# For some business applications, we are interested in the ability of the model
411::COMM;;# to rank the riskiest from the safest policyholders, irrespective of the
412::COMM;;# absolute value of the prediction. In this case, the model evaluation would
413::COMM;;# cast the problem as a ranking problem rather than a regression problem.
414::COMM;;#
415::COMM;;# To compare the 3 models from this perspective, one can plot the cumulative
416::COMM;;# proportion of claims vs the cumulative proportion of exposure for the test
417::COMM;;# samples order by the model predictions, from safest to riskiest according to
418::COMM;;# each model.
419::COMM;;#
420::COMM;;# This plot is called a Lorenz curve and can be summarized by the Gini index:
421::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import auc
422::COMM;;def lorenz_curve(y_true, y_pred, exposure):
423::COMM;;y_true, y_pred = np.asarray(y_true), np.asarray(y_pred)
424::COMM;;exposure = np.asarray(exposure)
425::COMM;;# order samples by increasing predicted risk:
426::COMM;;ranking = np.argsort(y_pred)
427::COMM;;ranked_frequencies = y_true[ranking]
428::COMM;;ranked_exposure = exposure[ranking]
429::COMM;;cumulated_claims = np.cumsum(ranked_frequencies * ranked_exposure)
430::COMM;;cumulated_claims /= cumulated_claims[-1]
431::COMM;;cumulated_exposure = np.cumsum(ranked_exposure)
432::COMM;;cumulated_exposure /= cumulated_exposure[-1]
433::COMM;;return cumulated_exposure, cumulated_claims
434::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
435::COMM;;for model in [dummy, ridge_glm, poisson_glm, poisson_gbrt]:
436::COMM;;y_pred = model.predict(df_test)
437::COMM;;cum_exposure, cum_claims = lorenz_curve(
438::COMM;;df_test["Frequency"], y_pred, df_test["Exposure"]
439::COMM;;)
440::COMM;;gini = 1 - 2 * auc(cum_exposure, cum_claims)
441::COMM;;label = "{} (Gini: {:.2f})".format(model[-1], gini)
442::COMM;;ax.plot(cum_exposure, cum_claims, linestyle="-", label=label)
443::COMM;;# Oracle model: y_pred == y_test
444::COMM;;cum_exposure, cum_claims = lorenz_curve(
445::COMM;;df_test["Frequency"], df_test["Frequency"], df_test["Exposure"]
446::COMM;;)
447::COMM;;gini = 1 - 2 * auc(cum_exposure, cum_claims)
448::COMM;;label = "Oracle (Gini: {:.2f})".format(gini)
449::COMM;;ax.plot(cum_exposure, cum_claims, linestyle="-.", color="gray", label=label)
450::COMM;;# Random Baseline
451::COMM;;ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="black", label="Random baseline")
452::COMM;;ax.set(
453::COMM;;title="Lorenz curves by model",
454::COMM;;xlabel="Cumulative proportion of exposure (from safest to riskiest)",
455::COMM;;ylabel="Cumulative proportion of claims",
456::COMM;;)
457::COMM;;ax.legend(loc="upper left")
458::COMM;;# %%
459::COMM;;# As expected, the dummy regressor is unable to correctly rank the samples and
460::COMM;;# therefore performs the worst on this plot.
461::COMM;;#
462::COMM;;# The tree-based model is significantly better at ranking policyholders by risk
463::COMM;;# while the two linear models perform similarly.
464::COMM;;#
465::COMM;;# All three models are significantly better than chance but also very far from
466::COMM;;# making perfect predictions.
467::COMM;;#
468::COMM;;# This last point is expected due to the nature of the problem: the occurrence
469::COMM;;# of accidents is mostly dominated by circumstantial causes that are not
470::COMM;;# captured in the columns of the dataset and can indeed be considered as purely
471::COMM;;# random.
472::COMM;;#
473::COMM;;# The linear models assume no interactions between the input variables which
474::COMM;;# likely causes under-fitting. Inserting a polynomial feature extractor
475::COMM;;# (:func:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures`) indeed increases their
476::COMM;;# discrimative power by 2 points of Gini index. In particular it improves the
477::COMM;;# ability of the models to identify the top 5% riskiest profiles.
478::COMM;;#
479::COMM;;# Main takeaways
480::COMM;;# --------------
481::COMM;;#
482::COMM;;# - The performance of the models can be evaluated by their ability to yield
483::COMM;;# well-calibrated predictions and a good ranking.
484::COMM;;#
485::COMM;;# - The calibration of the model can be assessed by plotting the mean observed
486::COMM;;# value vs the mean predicted value on groups of test samples binned by
487::COMM;;# predicted risk.
488::COMM;;#
489::COMM;;# - The least squares loss (along with the implicit use of the identity link
490::COMM;;# function) of the Ridge regression model seems to cause this model to be
491::COMM;;# badly calibrated. In particular, it tends to underestimate the risk and can
492::COMM;;# even predict invalid negative frequencies.
493::COMM;;#
494::COMM;;# - Using the Poisson loss with a log-link can correct these problems and lead
495::COMM;;# to a well-calibrated linear model.
496::COMM;;#
497::COMM;;# - The Gini index reflects the ability of a model to rank predictions
498::COMM;;# irrespective of their absolute values, and therefore only assess their
499::COMM;;# ranking power.
500::COMM;;#
501::COMM;;# - Despite the improvement in calibration, the ranking power of both linear
502::COMM;;# models are comparable and well below the ranking power of the Gradient
503::COMM;;# Boosting Regression Trees.
504::COMM;;#
505::COMM;;# - The Poisson deviance computed as an evaluation metric reflects both the
506::COMM;;# calibration and the ranking power of the model. It also makes a linear
507::COMM;;# assumption on the ideal relationship between the expected value and the
508::COMM;;# variance of the response variable. For the sake of conciseness we did not
509::COMM;;# check whether this assumption holds.
510::COMM;;#
511::COMM;;# - Traditional regression metrics such as Mean Squared Error and Mean Absolute
512::COMM;;# Error are hard to meaningfully interpret on count values with many zeros.
513::COMM;;plt.show()
2::COMM;;===================================
3::COMM;;Polynomial and Spline interpolation
4::COMM;;===================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates how to approximate a function with polynomials up to
6::COMM;;degree ``degree`` by using ridge regression. We show two different ways given
7::COMM;;``n_samples`` of 1d points ``x_i``:
8::COMM;;- :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures` generates all monomials
9::COMM;;up to ``degree``. This gives us the so called Vandermonde matrix with
10::COMM;;``n_samples`` rows and ``degree + 1`` columns::
11::COMM;;[[1, x_0, x_0 ** 2, x_0 ** 3, ..., x_0 ** degree],
12::COMM;;[1, x_1, x_1 ** 2, x_1 ** 3, ..., x_1 ** degree],
13::COMM;;...]
14::COMM;;Intuitively, this matrix can be interpreted as a matrix of pseudo features
15::COMM;;(the points raised to some power). The matrix is akin to (but different from)
16::COMM;;the matrix induced by a polynomial kernel.
17::COMM;;- :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.SplineTransformer` generates B-spline basis
18::COMM;;functions. A basis function of a B-spline is a piece-wise polynomial function
19::COMM;;of degree ``degree`` that is non-zero only between ``degree+1`` consecutive
20::COMM;;knots. Given ``n_knots`` number of knots, this results in matrix of
21::COMM;;``n_samples`` rows and ``n_knots + degree - 1`` columns::
22::COMM;;[[basis_1(x_0), basis_2(x_0), ...],
23::COMM;;[basis_1(x_1), basis_2(x_1), ...],
24::COMM;;...]
25::COMM;;This example shows that these two transformers are well suited to model
26::COMM;;non-linear effects with a linear model, using a pipeline to add non-linear
27::COMM;;features. Kernel methods extend this idea and can induce very high (even
28::COMM;;infinite) dimensional feature spaces.
30::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
31::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
37::COMO;;# %%
38::COMO;;# We start by defining a function that we intend to approximate and prepare
39::COMO;;# plotting it.
42::COMM;;return x * np.sin(x)
43::COMM;;# whole range we want to plot
44::COMM;;x_plot = np.linspace(-1, 11, 100)
45::COMM;;# %%
46::COMM;;# To make it interesting, we only give a small subset of points to train on.
47::COMM;;x_train = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
48::COMM;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
49::COMM;;x_train = np.sort(rng.choice(x_train, size=20, replace=False))
50::COMM;;y_train = f(x_train)
51::COMM;;# create 2D-array versions of these arrays to feed to transformers
52::COMM;;X_train = x_train[:, np.newaxis]
53::COMM;;X_plot = x_plot[:, np.newaxis]
54::COMM;;# %%
55::COMM;;# Now we are ready to create polynomial features and splines, fit on the
56::COMM;;# training points and show how well they interpolate.
57::COMM;;# plot function
58::COMM;;lw = 2
59::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots()
60::COMM;;ax.set_prop_cycle(
61::COMM;;color=["black", "teal", "yellowgreen", "gold", "darkorange", "tomato"]
62::COMM;;)
63::COMM;;ax.plot(x_plot, f(x_plot), linewidth=lw, label="ground truth")
64::COMM;;# plot training points
65::COMM;;ax.scatter(x_train, y_train, label="training points")
66::COMM;;# polynomial features
67::COMM;;for degree in [3, 4, 5]:
68::COMM;;model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), Ridge(alpha=1e-3))
69::COMM;;model.fit(X_train, y_train)
70::COMM;;y_plot = model.predict(X_plot)
71::COMM;;ax.plot(x_plot, y_plot, label=f"degree {degree}")
72::COMM;;# B-spline with 4 + 3 - 1 = 6 basis functions
73::COMM;;model = make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(n_knots=4, degree=3), Ridge(alpha=1e-3))
74::COMM;;model.fit(X_train, y_train)
75::COMM;;y_plot = model.predict(X_plot)
76::COMM;;ax.plot(x_plot, y_plot, label="B-spline")
77::COMM;;ax.legend(loc="lower center")
78::COMM;;ax.set_ylim(-20, 10)
79::COMM;;plt.show()
80::COMM;;# %%
81::COMM;;# This shows nicely that higher degree polynomials can fit the data better. But
82::COMM;;# at the same time, too high powers can show unwanted oscillatory behaviour
83::COMM;;# and are particularly dangerous for extrapolation beyond the range of fitted
84::COMM;;# data. This is an advantage of B-splines. They usually fit the data as well as
85::COMM;;# polynomials and show very nice and smooth behaviour. They have also good
86::COMM;;# options to control the extrapolation, which defaults to continue with a
87::COMM;;# constant. Note that most often, you would rather increase the number of knots
88::COMM;;# but keep ``degree=3``.
89::COMM;;#
90::COMM;;# In order to give more insights into the generated feature bases, we plot all
91::COMM;;# columns of both transformers separately.
92::COMM;;fig, axes = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(16, 5))
93::COMM;;pft = PolynomialFeatures(degree=3).fit(X_train)
94::COMM;;axes[0].plot(x_plot, pft.transform(X_plot))
95::COMM;;axes[0].legend(axes[0].lines, [f"degree {n}" for n in range(4)])
96::COMM;;axes[0].set_title("PolynomialFeatures")
97::COMM;;splt = SplineTransformer(n_knots=4, degree=3).fit(X_train)
98::COMM;;axes[1].plot(x_plot, splt.transform(X_plot))
99::COMM;;axes[1].legend(axes[1].lines, [f"spline {n}" for n in range(6)])
100::COMM;;axes[1].set_title("SplineTransformer")
101::COMM;;# plot knots of spline
102::COMM;;knots = splt.bsplines_[0].t
103::COMM;;axes[1].vlines(knots[3:-3], ymin=0, ymax=0.8, linestyles="dashed")
104::COMM;;plt.show()
105::COMM;;# %%
106::COMM;;# In the left plot, we recognize the lines corresponding to simple monomials
107::COMM;;# from ``x**0`` to ``x**3``. In the right figure, we see the six B-spline
108::COMM;;# basis functions of ``degree=3`` and also the four knot positions that were
109::COMM;;# chosen during ``fit``. Note that there are ``degree`` number of additional
110::COMM;;# knots each to the left and to the right of the fitted interval. These are
111::COMM;;# there for technical reasons, so we refrain from showing them. Every basis
112::COMM;;# function has local support and is continued as a constant beyond the fitted
113::COMM;;# range. This extrapolating behaviour could be changed by the argument
114::COMM;;# ``extrapolation``.

116::COMM;;# Periodic Splines
117::COMM;;# ----------------
118::COMM;;# In the previous example we saw the limitations of polynomials and splines for
119::COMM;;# extrapolation beyond the range of the training observations. In some
120::COMM;;# settings, e.g. with seasonal effects, we expect a periodic continuation of
121::COMM;;# the underlying signal. Such effects can be modelled using periodic splines,
122::COMM;;# which have equal function value and equal derivatives at the first and last
123::COMM;;# knot. In the following case we show how periodic splines provide a better fit
124::COMM;;# both within and outside of the range of training data given the additional
125::COMM;;# information of periodicity. The splines period is the distance between
126::COMM;;# the first and last knot, which we specify manually.
127::COMM;;#
128::COMM;;# Periodic splines can also be useful for naturally periodic features (such as
129::COMM;;# day of the year), as the smoothness at the boundary knots prevents a jump in
130::COMM;;# the transformed values (e.g. from Dec 31st to Jan 1st). For such naturally
131::COMM;;# periodic features or more generally features where the period is known, it is
132::COMM;;# advised to explicitly pass this information to the `SplineTransformer` by
133::COMM;;# setting the knots manually.

2::COMM;;===================
3::COMM;;Quantile regression
4::COMM;;===================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates how quantile regression can predict non-trivial
6::COMM;;conditional quantiles.
7::COMM;;The left figure shows the case when the error distribution is normal,
8::COMM;;but has non-constant variance, i.e. with heteroscedasticity.
9::COMM;;The right figure shows an example of an asymmetric error distribution,
10::COMM;;namely the Pareto distribution.
12::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
13::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
14::COMO;;# %%
15::COMO;;# Dataset generation
16::COMO;;# ------------------
17::COMO;;#
18::COMO;;# To illustrate the behaviour of quantile regression, we will generate two
19::COMO;;# synthetic datasets. The true generative random processes for both datasets
20::COMO;;# will be composed by the same expected value with a linear relationship with a
21::COMO;;# single feature `x`.
27::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# We will create two subsequent problems by changing the distribution of the
29::COMO;;# target `y` while keeping the same expected value:
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# - in the first case, a heteroscedastic Normal noise is added;
32::COMO;;# - in the second case, an asymmetric Pareto noise is added.
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# Let's first visualize the datasets as well as the distribution of the
38::COMO;;# residuals `y - mean(y)`.
61::COMO;;# %%
62::COMO;;# With the heteroscedastic Normal distributed target, we observe that the
63::COMO;;# variance of the noise is increasing when the value of the feature `x` is
64::COMO;;# increasing.
65::COMO;;#
66::COMO;;# With the asymmetric Pareto distributed target, we observe that the positive
67::COMO;;# residuals are bounded.
68::COMO;;#
69::COMO;;# These types of noisy targets make the estimation via
70::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` less efficient, i.e. we need
71::COMO;;# more data to get stable results and, in addition, large outliers can have a
72::COMO;;# huge impact on the fitted coefficients. (Stated otherwise: in a setting with
73::COMO;;# constant variance, ordinary least squares estimators converge much faster to
74::COMO;;# the *true* coefficients with increasing sample size.)
75::COMO;;#
76::COMO;;# In this asymmetric setting, the median or different quantiles give additional
77::COMO;;# insights. On top of that, median estimation is much more robust to outliers
78::COMO;;# and heavy tailed distributions. But note that extreme quantiles are estimated
79::COMO;;# by very few data points. 95% quantile are more or less estimated by the 5%
80::COMO;;# largest values and thus also a bit sensitive outliers.
81::COMO;;#
82::COMO;;# In the remainder of this tutorial, we will show how
83::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor` can be used in practice and
84::COMO;;# give the intuition into the properties of the fitted models. Finally,
85::COMO;;# we will compare the both :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor`
86::COMO;;# and :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression`.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# Fitting a `QuantileRegressor`
89::COMO;;# -----------------------------
90::COMO;;#
91::COMO;;# In this section, we want to estimate the conditional median as well as
92::COMO;;# a low and high quantile fixed at 5% and 95%, respectively. Thus, we will get
93::COMO;;# three linear models, one for each quantile.
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# We will use the quantiles at 5% and 95% to find the outliers in the training
96::COMO;;# sample beyond the central 90% interval.
97::COMO;;# %%
114::COMO;;# %%
115::COMO;;# Now, we can plot the three linear models and the distinguished samples that
116::COMO;;# are within the central 90% interval from samples that are outside this
117::COMO;;# interval.
140::COMO;;# %%
141::COMO;;# Since the noise is still Normally distributed, in particular is symmetric,
142::COMO;;# the true conditional mean and the true conditional median coincide. Indeed,
143::COMO;;# we see that the estimated median almost hits the true mean. We observe the
144::COMO;;# effect of having an increasing noise variance on the 5% and 95% quantiles:
145::COMO;;# the slopes of those quantiles are very different and the interval between
146::COMO;;# them becomes wider with increasing `x`.
147::COMO;;#
148::COMO;;# To get an additional intuition regarding the meaning of the 5% and 95%
149::COMO;;# quantiles estimators, one can count the number of samples above and below the
150::COMO;;# predicted quantiles (represented by a cross on the above plot), considering
151::COMO;;# that we have a total of 100 samples.
152::COMO;;#
153::COMO;;# We can repeat the same experiment using the asymmetric Pareto distributed
154::COMO;;# target.
170::COMO;;# %%
193::COMO;;# %%
194::COMO;;# Due to the asymmetry of the distribution of the noise, we observe that the
195::COMO;;# true mean and estimated conditional median are different. We also observe
196::COMO;;# that each quantile model has different parameters to better fit the desired
197::COMO;;# quantile. Note that ideally, all quantiles would be parallel in this case,
198::COMO;;# which would become more visible with more data points or less extreme
199::COMO;;# quantiles, e.g. 10% and 90%.
200::COMO;;#
201::COMO;;# Comparing `QuantileRegressor` and `LinearRegression`
202::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------------
203::COMO;;#
204::COMO;;# In this section, we will linger on the difference regarding the loss functions that
205::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor` and
206::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` are minimizing.
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# Indeed, :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` is a least squares
209::COMO;;# approach minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the training and
210::COMO;;# predicted targets. In contrast,
211::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor` with `quantile=0.5`
212::COMO;;# minimizes the mean absolute error (MAE) instead.
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# Why does it matter? The loss functions specify what exactly the model is aiming
215::COMO;;# to predict, see
216::COMO;;# :ref:`user guide on the choice of scoring function<which_scoring_function>`.
217::COMO;;# In short, a model minimizing MSE predicts the mean (expectation) and a model
218::COMO;;# minimizing MAE predicts the median.
219::COMO;;#
220::COMO;;# Let's compute the training errors of such models in terms of mean
221::COMO;;# squared error and mean absolute error. We will use the asymmetric Pareto
222::COMO;;# distributed target to make it more interesting as mean and median are not
223::COMO;;# equal.
240::COMO;;# %%
241::COMO;;# On the training set, we see that MAE is lower for
242::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor` than
243::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression`. In contrast to that, MSE is
244::COMO;;# lower for :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` than
245::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor`. These results confirms that
246::COMO;;# MAE is the loss minimized by :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.QuantileRegressor`
247::COMO;;# while MSE is the loss minimized
248::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression`.
249::COMO;;#
250::COMO;;# We can make a similar evaluation by looking at the test error obtained by
251::COMO;;# cross-validation.
277::COMO;;# %%
278::COMO;;# We reach similar conclusions on the out-of-sample evaluation.

2::COMM;;=========================================================
3::COMM;;Ridge coefficients as a function of the L2 Regularization
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;A model that overfits learns the training data too well, capturing both the
6::COMM;;underlying patterns and the noise in the data. However, when applied to unseen
7::COMM;;data, the learned associations may not hold. We normally detect this when we
8::COMM;;apply our trained predictions to the test data and see the statistical
9::COMM;;performance drop significantly compared to the training data.
10::COMM;;One way to overcome overfitting is through regularization, which can be done by
11::COMM;;penalizing large weights (coefficients) in linear models, forcing the model to
12::COMM;;shrink all coefficients. Regularization reduces a model's reliance on specific
13::COMM;;information obtained from the training samples.
14::COMM;;This example illustrates how L2 regularization in a
15::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge` regression affects a model's performance by
16::COMM;;adding a penalty term to the loss that increases with the coefficients
17::COMM;;:math:`\\beta`.
18::COMM;;The regularized loss function is given by: :math:`\\mathcal{L}(X, y, \\beta) =
19::COMM;;\\| y - X \\beta \\|^{2}_{2} + \\alpha \\| \\beta \\|^{2}_{2}`
20::COMM;;where :math:`X` is the input data, :math:`y` is the target variable,
21::COMM;;:math:`\\beta` is the vector of coefficients associated with the features, and
22::COMM;;:math:`\\alpha` is the regularization strength.
23::COMM;;The regularized loss function aims to balance the trade-off between accurately
24::COMM;;predicting the training set and to prevent overfitting.
25::COMM;;In this regularized loss, the left-hand side (e.g. :math:`\\|y -
26::COMM;;X\\beta\\|^{2}_{2}`) measures the squared difference between the actual target
27::COMM;;variable, :math:`y`, and the predicted values. Minimizing this term alone could
28::COMM;;lead to overfitting, as the model may become too complex and sensitive to noise
29::COMM;;in the training data.
30::COMM;;To address overfitting, Ridge regularization adds a constraint, called a penalty
31::COMM;;term, (:math:`\\alpha \\| \\beta\\|^{2}_{2}`) to the loss function. This penalty
32::COMM;;term is the sum of the squares of the model's coefficients, multiplied by the
33::COMM;;regularization strength :math:`\\alpha`. By introducing this constraint, Ridge
34::COMM;;regularization discourages any single coefficient :math:`\\beta_{i}` from taking
35::COMM;;an excessively large value and encourages smaller and more evenly distributed
36::COMM;;coefficients. Higher values of :math:`\\alpha` force the coefficients towards
37::COMM;;zero. However, an excessively high :math:`\\alpha` can result in an underfit
38::COMM;;model that fails to capture important patterns in the data.
39::COMM;;Therefore, the regularized loss function combines the prediction accuracy term
40::COMM;;and the penalty term. By adjusting the regularization strength, practitioners
41::COMM;;can fine-tune the degree of constraint imposed on the weights, training a model
42::COMM;;capable of generalizing well to unseen data while avoiding overfitting.
44::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
45::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
46::COMO;;# %%
47::COMO;;# Purpose of this example
48::COMO;;# -----------------------
49::COMO;;# For the purpose of showing how Ridge regularization works, we will create a
50::COMO;;# non-noisy data set. Then we will train a regularized model on a range of
51::COMO;;# regularization strengths (:math:`\alpha`) and plot how the trained
52::COMO;;# coefficients and the mean squared error between those and the original values
53::COMO;;# behave as functions of the regularization strength.
54::COMO;;#
55::COMO;;# Creating a non-noisy data set
56::COMO;;# *****************************
57::COMO;;# We make a toy data set with 100 samples and 10 features, that's suitable to
58::COMO;;# detect regression. Out of the 10 features, 8 are informative and contribute to
59::COMO;;# the regression, while the remaining 2 features do not have any effect on the
60::COMO;;# target variable (their true coefficients are 0). Please note that in this
61::COMO;;# example the data is non-noisy, hence we can expect our regression model to
62::COMO;;# recover exactly the true coefficients w.
67::COMO;;# Obtain the true coefficients
69::COMO;;# %%
70::COMO;;# Training the Ridge Regressor
71::COMO;;# ****************************
72::COMO;;# We use :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge`, a linear model with L2
73::COMO;;# regularization. We train several models, each with a different value for the
74::COMO;;# model parameter `alpha`, which is a positive constant that multiplies the
75::COMO;;# penalty term, controlling the regularization strength. For each trained model
76::COMO;;# we then compute the error between the true coefficients `w` and the
77::COMO;;# coefficients found by the model `clf`. We store the identified coefficients
78::COMO;;# and the calculated errors for the corresponding coefficients in lists, which
79::COMO;;# makes it convenient for us to plot them.
84::COMO;;# Generate values for `alpha` that are evenly distributed on a logarithmic scale
88::COMO;;# Train the model with different regularisation strengths
93::COMO;;# %%
94::COMO;;# Plotting trained Coefficients and Mean Squared Errors
95::COMO;;# *****************************************************
96::COMO;;# We now plot the 10 different regularized coefficients as a function of the
97::COMO;;# regularization parameter `alpha` where each color represents a different
98::COMO;;# coefficient.
99::COMO;;#
100::COMO;;# On the right-hand-side, we plot how the errors of the coefficients from the
101::COMO;;# estimator change as a function of regularization.
120::COMO;;# %%
121::COMO;;# Interpreting the plots
122::COMO;;# **********************
123::COMO;;# The plot on the left-hand side shows how the regularization strength (`alpha`)
124::COMO;;# affects the Ridge regression coefficients. Smaller values of `alpha` (weak
125::COMO;;# regularization), allow the coefficients to closely resemble the true
126::COMO;;# coefficients (`w`) used to generate the data set. This is because no
127::COMO;;# additional noise was added to our artificial data set. As `alpha` increases,
128::COMO;;# the coefficients shrink towards zero, gradually reducing the impact of the
129::COMO;;# features that were formerly more significant.
130::COMO;;#
131::COMO;;# The right-hand side plot shows the mean squared error (MSE) between the
132::COMO;;# coefficients found by the model and the true coefficients (`w`). It provides a
133::COMO;;# measure that relates to how exact our ridge model is in comparison to the true
134::COMO;;# generative model. A low error means that it found coefficients closer to the
135::COMO;;# ones of the true generative model. In this case, since our toy data set was
136::COMO;;# non-noisy, we can see that the least regularized model retrieves coefficients
137::COMO;;# closest to the true coefficients (`w`) (error is close to 0).
138::COMO;;#
139::COMO;;# When `alpha` is small, the model captures the intricate details of the
140::COMO;;# training data, whether those were caused by noise or by actual information. As
141::COMO;;# `alpha` increases, the highest coefficients shrink more rapidly, rendering
142::COMO;;# their corresponding features less influential in the training process. This
143::COMO;;# can enhance a model's ability to generalize to unseen data (if there was a lot
144::COMO;;# of noise to capture), but it also poses the risk of losing performance if the
145::COMO;;# regularization becomes too strong compared to the amount of noise the data
146::COMO;;# contained (as in this example).
147::COMO;;#
148::COMO;;# In real-world scenarios where data typically includes noise, selecting an
149::COMO;;# appropriate `alpha` value becomes crucial in striking a balance between an
150::COMO;;# overfitting and an underfitting model.
151::COMO;;#
152::COMO;;# Here, we saw that :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.Ridge` adds a penalty to the
153::COMO;;# coefficients to fight overfitting. Another problem that occurs is linked to
154::COMO;;# the presence of outliers in the training dataset. An outlier is a data point
155::COMO;;# that differs significantly from other observations. Concretely, these outliers
156::COMO;;# impact the left-hand side term of the loss function that we showed earlier.
157::COMO;;# Some other linear models are formulated to be robust to outliers such as the
158::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.HuberRegressor`. You can learn more about it in
159::COMO;;# the :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_huber_vs_ridge.py` example.
2::COMM;;===========================================================
3::COMM;;Plot Ridge coefficients as a function of the regularization
4::COMM;;===========================================================
5::COMM;;Shows the effect of collinearity in the coefficients of an estimator.
6::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.linear_model
7::COMM;;:class:`Ridge` Regression is the estimator used in this example.
8::COMM;;Each color represents a different feature of the
9::COMM;;coefficient vector, and this is displayed as a function of the
10::COMM;;regularization parameter.
11::COMM;;This example also shows the usefulness of applying Ridge regression
12::COMM;;to highly ill-conditioned matrices. For such matrices, a slight
13::COMM;;change in the target variable can cause huge variances in the
14::COMM;;calculated weights. In such cases, it is useful to set a certain
15::COMM;;regularization (alpha) to reduce this variation (noise).
16::COMM;;When alpha is very large, the regularization effect dominates the
17::COMM;;squared loss function and the coefficients tend to zero.
18::COMM;;At the end of the path, as alpha tends toward zero
19::COMM;;and the solution tends towards the ordinary least squares, coefficients
20::COMM;;exhibit big oscillations. In practice it is necessary to tune alpha
21::COMM;;in such a way that a balance is maintained between both.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
28::COMO;;# X is the 10x10 Hilbert matrix

32::COMO;;# Compute paths

2::COMM;;Robust linear estimator fitting
3::COMM;;===============================
4::COMM;;Here a sine function is fit with a polynomial of order 3, for values
5::COMM;;close to zero.
6::COMM;;Robust fitting is demonstrated in different situations:
7::COMM;;- No measurement errors, only modelling errors (fitting a sine with a
8::COMM;;polynomial)
9::COMM;;- Measurement errors in X
10::COMM;;- Measurement errors in y
11::COMM;;The median absolute deviation to non corrupt new data is used to judge
12::COMM;;the quality of the prediction.
13::COMM;;What we can see that:
14::COMM;;- RANSAC is good for strong outliers in the y direction
15::COMM;;- TheilSen is good for small outliers, both in direction X and y, but has
16::COMM;;a break point above which it performs worse than OLS.
17::COMM;;- The scores of HuberRegressor may not be compared directly to both TheilSen
18::COMM;;and RANSAC because it does not attempt to completely filter the outliers
19::COMM;;but lessen their effect.
21::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
22::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
37::COMO;;# Make sure that it X is 2D
2::COMM;;=============================================
3::COMM;;Early stopping of Stochastic Gradient Descent
4::COMM;;=============================================
5::COMM;;Stochastic Gradient Descent is an optimization technique which minimizes a loss
6::COMM;;function in a stochastic fashion, performing a gradient descent step sample by
7::COMM;;sample. In particular, it is a very efficient method to fit linear models.
8::COMM;;As a stochastic method, the loss function is not necessarily decreasing at each
9::COMM;;iteration, and convergence is only guaranteed in expectation. For this reason,
10::COMM;;monitoring the convergence on the loss function can be difficult.
11::COMM;;Another approach is to monitor convergence on a validation score. In this case,
12::COMM;;the input data is split into a training set and a validation set. The model is
13::COMM;;then fitted on the training set and the stopping criterion is based on the
14::COMM;;prediction score computed on the validation set. This enables us to find the
15::COMM;;least number of iterations which is sufficient to build a model that
16::COMM;;generalizes well to unseen data and reduces the chance of over-fitting the
17::COMM;;training data.
18::COMM;;This early stopping strategy is activated if ``early_stopping=True``; otherwise
19::COMM;;the stopping criterion only uses the training loss on the entire input data. To
20::COMM;;better control the early stopping strategy, we can specify a parameter
21::COMM;;``validation_fraction`` which set the fraction of the input dataset that we
22::COMM;;keep aside to compute the validation score. The optimization will continue
23::COMM;;until the validation score did not improve by at least ``tol`` during the last
24::COMM;;``n_iter_no_change`` iterations. The actual number of iterations is available
25::COMM;;at the attribute ``n_iter_``.
26::COMM;;This example illustrates how the early stopping can used in the
27::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.SGDClassifier` model to achieve almost the same
28::COMM;;accuracy as compared to a model built without early stopping. This can
29::COMM;;significantly reduce training time. Note that scores differ between the
30::COMM;;stopping criteria even from early iterations because some of the training data
31::COMM;;is held out with the validation stopping criterion.
33::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
34::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
48::COMM;;# Load data from http://openml.org/d/554
49::COMM;;mnist = fetch_openml("mnist_784", version=1, as_frame=False)
50::COMM;;# take only two classes for binary classification
51::COMM;;mask = np.logical_or(mnist.target == class_0, mnist.target == class_1)
52::COMM;;X, y = shuffle(mnist.data[mask], mnist.target[mask], random_state=42)
53::COMM;;if n_samples is not None:
54::COMM;;X, y = X[:n_samples], y[:n_samples]
55::COMM;;return X, y

2::COMM;;====================================================
3::COMM;;Multiclass sparse logistic regression on 20newgroups
4::COMM;;====================================================
5::COMM;;Comparison of multinomial logistic L1 vs one-versus-rest L1 logistic regression
6::COMM;;to classify documents from the newgroups20 dataset. Multinomial logistic
7::COMM;;regression yields more accurate results and is faster to train on the larger
8::COMM;;scale dataset.
9::COMM;;Here we use the l1 sparsity that trims the weights of not informative
10::COMM;;features to zero. This is good if the goal is to extract the strongly
11::COMM;;discriminative vocabulary of each class. If the goal is to get the best
12::COMM;;predictive accuracy, it is better to use the non sparsity-inducing l2 penalty
13::COMM;;instead.
14::COMM;;A more traditional (and possibly better) way to predict on a sparse subset of
15::COMM;;input features would be to use univariate feature selection followed by a
16::COMM;;traditional (l2-penalised) logistic regression model.

2::COMM;;=====================================================
3::COMM;;MNIST classification using multinomial logistic + L1
4::COMM;;=====================================================
5::COMM;;Here we fit a multinomial logistic regression with L1 penalty on a subset of
6::COMM;;the MNIST digits classification task. We use the SAGA algorithm for this
7::COMM;;purpose: this a solver that is fast when the number of samples is significantly
8::COMM;;larger than the number of features and is able to finely optimize non-smooth
9::COMM;;objective functions which is the case with the l1-penalty. Test accuracy
10::COMM;;reaches > 0.8, while weight vectors remains *sparse* and therefore more easily
11::COMM;;*interpretable*.
12::COMM;;Note that this accuracy of this l1-penalized linear model is significantly
13::COMM;;below what can be reached by an l2-penalized linear model or a non-linear
14::COMM;;multi-layer perceptron model on this dataset.

2::COMM;;====================
3::COMM;;Theil-Sen Regression
4::COMM;;====================
5::COMM;;Computes a Theil-Sen Regression on a synthetic dataset.
6::COMM;;See :ref:`theil_sen_regression` for more information on the regressor.
7::COMM;;Compared to the OLS (ordinary least squares) estimator, the Theil-Sen
8::COMM;;estimator is robust against outliers. It has a breakdown point of about 29.3%
9::COMM;;in case of a simple linear regression which means that it can tolerate
10::COMM;;arbitrary corrupted data (outliers) of up to 29.3% in the two-dimensional
11::COMM;;case.
12::COMM;;The estimation of the model is done by calculating the slopes and intercepts
13::COMM;;of a subpopulation of all possible combinations of p subsample points. If an
14::COMM;;intercept is fitted, p must be greater than or equal to n_features + 1. The
15::COMM;;final slope and intercept is then defined as the spatial median of these
16::COMM;;slopes and intercepts.
17::COMM;;In certain cases Theil-Sen performs better than :ref:`RANSAC
18::COMM;;<ransac_regression>` which is also a robust method. This is illustrated in the
19::COMM;;second example below where outliers with respect to the x-axis perturb RANSAC.
20::COMM;;Tuning the ``residual_threshold`` parameter of RANSAC remedies this but in
21::COMM;;general a priori knowledge about the data and the nature of the outliers is
22::COMM;;needed.
23::COMM;;Due to the computational complexity of Theil-Sen it is recommended to use it
24::COMM;;only for small problems in terms of number of samples and features. For larger
25::COMM;;problems the ``max_subpopulation`` parameter restricts the magnitude of all
26::COMM;;possible combinations of p subsample points to a randomly chosen subset and
27::COMM;;therefore also limits the runtime. Therefore, Theil-Sen is applicable to larger
28::COMM;;problems with the drawback of losing some of its mathematical properties since
29::COMM;;it then works on a random subset.
31::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
32::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
44::COMO;;# %%
45::COMO;;# Outliers only in the y direction
46::COMO;;# --------------------------------
49::COMO;;# Linear model y = 3*x + N(2, 0.1**2)
55::COMO;;# 10% outliers
75::COMO;;# %%
76::COMO;;# Outliers in the X direction
77::COMO;;# ---------------------------
79::COMO;;# Linear model y = 3*x + N(2, 0.1**2)
83::COMO;;# 10% outliers
1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
4::COMM;;======================================
5::COMM;;Tweedie regression on insurance claims
6::COMM;;======================================
7::COMM;;This example illustrates the use of Poisson, Gamma and Tweedie regression on
8::COMM;;the `French Motor Third-Party Liability Claims dataset
9::COMM;;<https://www.openml.org/d/41214>`_, and is inspired by an R tutorial [1]_.
10::COMM;;In this dataset, each sample corresponds to an insurance policy, i.e. a
11::COMM;;contract within an insurance company and an individual (policyholder).
12::COMM;;Available features include driver age, vehicle age, vehicle power, etc.
13::COMM;;A few definitions: a *claim* is the request made by a policyholder to the
14::COMM;;insurer to compensate for a loss covered by the insurance. The *claim amount*
15::COMM;;is the amount of money that the insurer must pay. The *exposure* is the
16::COMM;;duration of the insurance coverage of a given policy, in years.
17::COMM;;Here our goal is to predict the expected
18::COMM;;value, i.e. the mean, of the total claim amount per exposure unit also
19::COMM;;referred to as the pure premium.
20::COMM;;There are several possibilities to do that, two of which are:
21::COMM;;1. Model the number of claims with a Poisson distribution, and the average
22::COMM;;claim amount per claim, also known as severity, as a Gamma distribution
23::COMM;;and multiply the predictions of both in order to get the total claim
24::COMM;;amount.
25::COMM;;2. Model the total claim amount per exposure directly, typically with a Tweedie
26::COMM;;distribution of Tweedie power :math:`p \\in (1, 2)`.
27::COMM;;In this example we will illustrate both approaches. We start by defining a few
28::COMM;;helper functions for loading the data and visualizing results.
29::COMM;;.. [1] A. Noll, R. Salzmann and M.V. Wuthrich, Case Study: French Motor
30::COMM;;Third-Party Liability Claims (November 8, 2018). `doi:10.2139/ssrn.3164764
31::COMM;;<https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3164764>`_
33::COMO;;# %%
46::COMM;;Parameters
47::COMM;;----------
48::COMM;;n_samples: int, default=None
49::COMM;;number of samples to select (for faster run time). Full dataset has
50::COMM;;678013 samples.
52::COMO;;# freMTPL2freq dataset from https://www.openml.org/d/41214
56::COMO;;# freMTPL2sev dataset from https://www.openml.org/d/41215
58::COMO;;# sum ClaimAmount over identical IDs
62::COMO;;# unquote string fields
78::COMM;;Parameters
79::COMM;;----------
80::COMM;;df : DataFrame
81::COMM;;input data
82::COMM;;feature: str
83::COMM;;a column name of df for the feature to be plotted
84::COMM;;weight : str
85::COMM;;column name of df with the values of weights or exposure
86::COMM;;observed : str
87::COMM;;a column name of df with the observed target
88::COMM;;predicted : DataFrame
89::COMM;;a dataframe, with the same index as df, with the predicted target
90::COMM;;fill_legend : bool, default=False
91::COMM;;whether to show fill_between legend
93::COMO;;# aggregate observed and predicted variables by feature level
129::COMM;;metrics = [
130::COMM;;("D² explained", None), # Use default scorer if it exists
131::COMM;;("mean abs. error", mean_absolute_error),
132::COMM;;("mean squared error", mean_squared_error),
133::COMM;;]
134::COMM;;if tweedie_powers:
135::COMM;;metrics += [
136::COMM;;(
137::COMM;;"mean Tweedie dev p={:.4f}".format(power),
138::COMM;;partial(mean_tweedie_deviance, power=power),
139::COMM;;)
140::COMM;;for power in tweedie_powers
141::COMM;;]
142::COMM;;res = []
143::COMM;;for subset_label, X, df in [
144::COMM;;("train", X_train, df_train),
145::COMM;;("test", X_test, df_test),
146::COMM;;]:
147::COMM;;y, _weights = df[target], df[weights]
148::COMM;;for score_label, metric in metrics:
149::COMM;;if isinstance(estimator, tuple) and len(estimator) == 2:
150::COMM;;# Score the model consisting of the product of frequency and
151::COMM;;# severity models.

154::COMM;;else:

158::COMM;;continue

160::COMM;;else:
161::COMM;;score = metric(y, y_pred, sample_weight=_weights)
162::COMM;;res.append({"subset": subset_label, "metric": score_label, "score": score})
163::COMM;;res = (
164::COMM;;pd.DataFrame(res)
165::COMM;;.set_index(["metric", "subset"])
166::COMM;;.score.unstack(-1)
167::COMM;;.round(4)
168::COMM;;.loc[:, ["train", "test"]]
169::COMM;;)
170::COMM;;return res

232::COMM;;# Frequency model -- Poisson distribution
233::COMM;;# ---------------------------------------
234::COMM;;#
235::COMM;;# The number of claims (``ClaimNb``) is a positive integer (0 included).
236::COMM;;# Thus, this target can be modelled by a Poisson distribution.
237::COMM;;# It is then assumed to be the number of discrete events occurring with a
238::COMM;;# constant rate in a given time interval (``Exposure``, in units of years).
239::COMM;;# Here we model the frequency ``y = ClaimNb / Exposure``, which is still a
240::COMM;;# (scaled) Poisson distribution, and use ``Exposure`` as `sample_weight`.
241::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
242::COMM;;from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

247::COMM;;# this dataset, the number of evaluation points where the claim amount is
248::COMM;;# non-zero is quite small:
249::COMM;;len(df_test)

255::COMM;;# evaluation upon random resampling of the train test split.

258::COMM;;# on the training set via a Newton solver. Some of the features are collinear
259::COMM;;# (e.g. because we did not drop any categorical level in the `OneHotEncoder`),
260::COMM;;# we use a weak L2 penalization to avoid numerical issues.
261::COMM;;glm_freq = PoissonRegressor(alpha=1e-4, solver="newton-cholesky")

329::COMM;;# %%
330::COMM;;# According to the observed data, the frequency of accidents is higher for
331::COMM;;# drivers younger than 30 years old, and is positively correlated with the
332::COMM;;# `BonusMalus` variable. Our model is able to mostly correctly model this
333::COMM;;# behaviour.
334::COMM;;#
335::COMM;;# Severity Model - Gamma distribution
336::COMM;;# ------------------------------------
337::COMM;;# The mean claim amount or severity (`AvgClaimAmount`) can be empirically
338::COMM;;# shown to follow approximately a Gamma distribution. We fit a GLM model for
339::COMM;;# the severity with the same features as the frequency model.
340::COMM;;#
341::COMM;;# Note:
342::COMM;;#
343::COMM;;# - We filter out ``ClaimAmount == 0`` as the Gamma distribution has support
344::COMM;;# on :math:`(0, \infty)`, not :math:`[0, \infty)`.
345::COMM;;# - We use ``ClaimNb`` as `sample_weight` to account for policies that contain
346::COMM;;# more than one claim.
347::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import GammaRegressor
348::COMM;;mask_train = df_train["ClaimAmount"] > 0
349::COMM;;mask_test = df_test["ClaimAmount"] > 0
350::COMM;;glm_sev = GammaRegressor(alpha=10.0, solver="newton-cholesky")
351::COMM;;glm_sev.fit(
352::COMM;;X_train[mask_train.values],

445::COMM;;# Overall, the drivers age (``DrivAge``) has a weak impact on the claim
446::COMM;;# severity, both in observed and predicted data.
447::COMM;;#
448::COMM;;# Pure Premium Modeling via a Product Model vs single TweedieRegressor
449::COMM;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------
450::COMM;;# As mentioned in the introduction, the total claim amount per unit of
451::COMM;;# exposure can be modeled as the product of the prediction of the
452::COMM;;# frequency model by the prediction of the severity model.
453::COMM;;#
454::COMM;;# Alternatively, one can directly model the total loss with a unique
455::COMM;;# Compound Poisson Gamma generalized linear model (with a log link function).
456::COMM;;# This model is a special case of the Tweedie GLM with a "power" parameter
457::COMM;;# :math:`p \in (1, 2)`. Here, we fix apriori the `power` parameter of the
458::COMM;;# Tweedie model to some arbitrary value (1.9) in the valid range. Ideally one
459::COMM;;# would select this value via grid-search by minimizing the negative
460::COMM;;# log-likelihood of the Tweedie model, but unfortunately the current
461::COMM;;# implementation does not allow for this (yet).
462::COMM;;#
463::COMM;;# We will compare the performance of both approaches.
464::COMM;;# To quantify the performance of both models, one can compute
465::COMM;;# the mean deviance of the train and test data assuming a Compound
466::COMM;;# Poisson-Gamma distribution of the total claim amount. This is equivalent to
467::COMM;;# a Tweedie distribution with a `power` parameter between 1 and 2.
468::COMM;;#
469::COMM;;# The :func:`sklearn.metrics.mean_tweedie_deviance` depends on a `power`
470::COMM;;# parameter. As we do not know the true value of the `power` parameter, we here
471::COMM;;# compute the mean deviances for a grid of possible values, and compare the
472::COMM;;# models side by side, i.e. we compare them at identical values of `power`.
473::COMM;;# Ideally, we hope that one model will be consistently better than the other,
474::COMM;;# regardless of `power`.
475::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import TweedieRegressor
476::COMM;;glm_pure_premium = TweedieRegressor(power=1.9, alpha=0.1, solver="newton-cholesky")
477::COMM;;glm_pure_premium.fit(
478::COMM;;X_train, df_train["PurePremium"], sample_weight=df_train["Exposure"]
479::COMM;;)
480::COMM;;tweedie_powers = [1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 1.99, 1.999, 1.9999]
481::COMM;;scores_product_model = score_estimator(
482::COMM;;(glm_freq, glm_sev),
483::COMM;;X_train,
484::COMM;;X_test,
485::COMM;;df_train,
486::COMM;;df_test,
487::COMM;;target="PurePremium",
488::COMM;;weights="Exposure",
489::COMM;;tweedie_powers=tweedie_powers,
490::COMM;;)
491::COMM;;scores_glm_pure_premium = score_estimator(
492::COMM;;glm_pure_premium,
493::COMM;;X_train,
494::COMM;;X_test,
495::COMM;;df_train,
496::COMM;;df_test,
497::COMM;;target="PurePremium",
498::COMM;;weights="Exposure",
499::COMM;;tweedie_powers=tweedie_powers,
500::COMM;;)
501::COMM;;scores = pd.concat(
502::COMM;;[scores_product_model, scores_glm_pure_premium],
503::COMM;;axis=1,
504::COMM;;sort=True,
505::COMM;;keys=("Product Model", "TweedieRegressor"),
506::COMM;;)
507::COMM;;print("Evaluation of the Product Model and the Tweedie Regressor on target PurePremium")
508::COMM;;with pd.option_context("display.expand_frame_repr", False):
509::COMM;;print(scores)
510::COMM;;# %%
511::COMM;;# In this example, both modeling approaches yield comparable performance
512::COMM;;# metrics. For implementation reasons, the percentage of explained variance
513::COMM;;# :math:`D^2` is not available for the product model.
514::COMM;;#
515::COMM;;# We can additionally validate these models by comparing observed and
516::COMM;;# predicted total claim amount over the test and train subsets. We see that,
517::COMM;;# on average, both model tend to underestimate the total claim (but this
518::COMM;;# behavior depends on the amount of regularization).
519::COMM;;res = []
520::COMM;;for subset_label, X, df in [
521::COMM;;("train", X_train, df_train),
522::COMM;;("test", X_test, df_test),
523::COMM;;]:
524::COMM;;exposure = df["Exposure"].values
525::COMM;;res.append(
526::COMM;;{
527::COMM;;"subset": subset_label,
528::COMM;;"observed": df["ClaimAmount"].values.sum(),
529::COMM;;"predicted, frequency*severity model": np.sum(
530::COMM;;exposure * glm_freq.predict(X) * glm_sev.predict(X)
531::COMM;;),
532::COMM;;"predicted, tweedie, power=%.2f" % glm_pure_premium.power: np.sum(
533::COMM;;exposure * glm_pure_premium.predict(X)
534::COMM;;),
535::COMM;;}
536::COMM;;)
537::COMM;;print(pd.DataFrame(res).set_index("subset").T)
538::COMM;;# %%
539::COMM;;#
540::COMM;;# Finally, we can compare the two models using a plot of cumulative claims: for
541::COMM;;# each model, the policyholders are ranked from safest to riskiest based on the
542::COMM;;# model predictions and the cumulative proportion of claim amounts is plotted
543::COMM;;# against the cumulative proportion of exposure. This plot is often called
544::COMM;;# the ordered Lorenz curve of the model.
545::COMM;;#
546::COMM;;# The Gini coefficient (based on the area between the curve and the diagonal)
547::COMM;;# can be used as a model selection metric to quantify the ability of the model
548::COMM;;# to rank policyholders. Note that this metric does not reflect the ability of
549::COMM;;# the models to make accurate predictions in terms of absolute value of total
550::COMM;;# claim amounts but only in terms of relative amounts as a ranking metric. The
551::COMM;;# Gini coefficient is upper bounded by 1.0 but even an oracle model that ranks
552::COMM;;# the policyholders by the observed claim amounts cannot reach a score of 1.0.
553::COMM;;#
554::COMM;;# We observe that both models are able to rank policyholders by riskiness
555::COMM;;# significantly better than chance although they are also both far from the
556::COMM;;# oracle model due to the natural difficulty of the prediction problem from a
557::COMM;;# few features: most accidents are not predictable and can be caused by
558::COMM;;# environmental circumstances that are not described at all by the input
559::COMM;;# features of the models.
560::COMM;;#
561::COMM;;# Note that the Gini index only characterizes the ranking performance of the
562::COMM;;# model but not its calibration: any monotonic transformation of the predictions
563::COMM;;# leaves the Gini index of the model unchanged.
564::COMM;;#
565::COMM;;# Finally one should highlight that the Compound Poisson Gamma model that is
566::COMM;;# directly fit on the pure premium is operationally simpler to develop and
567::COMM;;# maintain as it consists of a single scikit-learn estimator instead of a pair
568::COMM;;# of models, each with its own set of hyperparameters.
569::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import auc
570::COMM;;def lorenz_curve(y_true, y_pred, exposure):
571::COMM;;y_true, y_pred = np.asarray(y_true), np.asarray(y_pred)
572::COMM;;exposure = np.asarray(exposure)
573::COMM;;# order samples by increasing predicted risk:
574::COMM;;ranking = np.argsort(y_pred)
575::COMM;;ranked_exposure = exposure[ranking]
576::COMM;;ranked_pure_premium = y_true[ranking]
577::COMM;;cumulative_claim_amount = np.cumsum(ranked_pure_premium * ranked_exposure)
578::COMM;;cumulative_claim_amount /= cumulative_claim_amount[-1]
579::COMM;;cumulative_exposure = np.cumsum(ranked_exposure)
580::COMM;;cumulative_exposure /= cumulative_exposure[-1]
581::COMM;;return cumulative_exposure, cumulative_claim_amount
582::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
583::COMM;;y_pred_product = glm_freq.predict(X_test) * glm_sev.predict(X_test)
584::COMM;;y_pred_total = glm_pure_premium.predict(X_test)
585::COMM;;for label, y_pred in [
586::COMM;;("Frequency * Severity model", y_pred_product),
587::COMM;;("Compound Poisson Gamma", y_pred_total),
588::COMM;;]:
589::COMM;;cum_exposure, cum_claims = lorenz_curve(
590::COMM;;df_test["PurePremium"], y_pred, df_test["Exposure"]
591::COMM;;)
592::COMM;;gini = 1 - 2 * auc(cum_exposure, cum_claims)
593::COMM;;label += " (Gini index: {:.3f})".format(gini)
594::COMM;;ax.plot(cum_exposure, cum_claims, linestyle="-", label=label)
595::COMM;;# Oracle model: y_pred == y_test
596::COMM;;cum_exposure, cum_claims = lorenz_curve(
597::COMM;;df_test["PurePremium"], df_test["PurePremium"], df_test["Exposure"]
598::COMM;;)
599::COMM;;gini = 1 - 2 * auc(cum_exposure, cum_claims)
600::COMM;;label = "Oracle (Gini index: {:.3f})".format(gini)
601::COMM;;ax.plot(cum_exposure, cum_claims, linestyle="-.", color="gray", label=label)
602::COMM;;# Random baseline
603::COMM;;ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="black", label="Random baseline")
604::COMM;;ax.set(
605::COMM;;title="Lorenz Curves",
606::COMM;;xlabel=(
607::COMM;;"Cumulative proportion of exposure\n(ordered by model from safest to riskiest)"
608::COMM;;),
609::COMM;;ylabel="Cumulative proportion of claim amounts",
610::COMM;;)
611::COMM;;ax.legend(loc="upper left")
612::COMM;;plt.plot()

3::COMM;;Comparison of Manifold Learning methods
4::COMM;;=========================================
5::COMM;;An illustration of dimensionality reduction on the S-curve dataset
6::COMM;;with various manifold learning methods.
7::COMM;;For a discussion and comparison of these algorithms, see the
8::COMM;;:ref:`manifold module page <manifold>`
9::COMM;;For a similar example, where the methods are applied to a
10::COMM;;sphere dataset, see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_manifold_plot_manifold_sphere.py`
11::COMM;;Note that the purpose of the MDS is to find a low-dimensional
12::COMM;;representation of the data (here 2D) in which the distances respect well
13::COMM;;the distances in the original high-dimensional space, unlike other
14::COMM;;manifold-learning algorithms, it does not seeks an isotropic
15::COMM;;representation of the data in the low-dimensional space.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
19::COMO;;# %%
20::COMO;;# Dataset preparation
21::COMO;;# -------------------
22::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# We start by generating the S-curve dataset.
25::COMO;;# unused but required import for doing 3d projections with matplotlib < 3.2
26::COMC;;import mpl_toolkits.mplot3d # noqa: F401
31::COMO;;# %%
32::COMO;;# Let's look at the original data. Also define some helping
33::COMO;;# functions, which we will use further on.
62::COMO;;# %%
63::COMO;;# Define algorithms for the manifold learning
64::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------
65::COMO;;#
66::COMO;;# Manifold learning is an approach to non-linear dimensionality reduction.
67::COMO;;# Algorithms for this task are based on the idea that the dimensionality of
68::COMO;;# many data sets is only artificially high.
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <manifold>`.
71::COMC;;n_neighbors = 12 # neighborhood which is used to recover the locally linear structure
72::COMC;;n_components = 2 # number of coordinates for the manifold
73::COMO;;# %%
74::COMO;;# Locally Linear Embeddings
75::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
76::COMO;;#
77::COMO;;# Locally linear embedding (LLE) can be thought of as a series of local
78::COMO;;# Principal Component Analyses which are globally compared to find the
79::COMO;;# best non-linear embedding.
80::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <locally_linear_embedding>`.
95::COMO;;# %%
110::COMO;;# %%
111::COMO;;# Isomap Embedding
112::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# Non-linear dimensionality reduction through Isometric Mapping.
115::COMO;;# Isomap seeks a lower-dimensional embedding which maintains geodesic
116::COMO;;# distances between all points. Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <isomap>`.
120::COMO;;# %%
121::COMO;;# Multidimensional scaling
122::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# Multidimensional scaling (MDS) seeks a low-dimensional representation
125::COMO;;# of the data in which the distances respect well the distances in the
126::COMO;;# original high-dimensional space.
127::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <multidimensional_scaling>`.
149::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# %%
164::COMO;;# Spectral embedding for non-linear dimensionality reduction
165::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
166::COMO;;#
167::COMO;;# This implementation uses Laplacian Eigenmaps, which finds a low dimensional
168::COMO;;# representation of the data using a spectral decomposition of the graph Laplacian.
169::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <spectral_embedding>`.
175::COMO;;# %%
176::COMO;;# T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding
177::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
178::COMO;;#
179::COMO;;# It converts similarities between data points to joint probabilities and
180::COMO;;# tries to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the joint probabilities
181::COMO;;# of the low-dimensional embedding and the high-dimensional data. t-SNE has a cost
182::COMO;;# function that is not convex, i.e. with different initializations we can get
183::COMO;;# different results. Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <t_sne>`.
193::COMO;;# %%
2::COMM;;=============================================================================

81::COMO;;# generated by PCA in this example. It ensures global stability of the embedding,
82::COMO;;# i.e., the embedding does not depend on random initialization.
