2::COMM;;===================================
3::COMM;;Swiss Roll And Swiss-Hole Reduction
4::COMM;;===================================
5::COMM;;This notebook seeks to compare two popular non-linear dimensionality
6::COMM;;techniques, T-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) and
7::COMM;;Locally Linear Embedding (LLE), on the classic Swiss Roll dataset.
8::COMM;;Then, we will explore how they both deal with the addition of a hole
9::COMM;;in the data.
11::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
12::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
13::COMO;;# %%
14::COMO;;# Swiss Roll
15::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
16::COMO;;#
17::COMO;;# We start by generating the Swiss Roll dataset.
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# Now, let's take a look at our data:
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# Computing the LLE and t-SNE embeddings, we find that LLE seems to unroll the
34::COMO;;# Swiss Roll pretty effectively. t-SNE on the other hand, is able
35::COMO;;# to preserve the general structure of the data, but, poorly represents the
36::COMO;;# continuous nature of our original data. Instead, it seems to unnecessarily
37::COMO;;# clump sections of points together.
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# .. note::
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# LLE seems to be stretching the points from the center (purple)
53::COMO;;# of the swiss roll. However, we observe that this is simply a byproduct
54::COMO;;# of how the data was generated. There is a higher density of points near the
55::COMO;;# center of the roll, which ultimately affects how LLE reconstructs the
56::COMO;;# data in a lower dimension.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# Swiss-Hole
59::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
60::COMO;;#

2::COMM;;============================================================================
3::COMM;;Comparing anomaly detection algorithms for outlier detection on toy datasets
4::COMM;;============================================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows characteristics of different anomaly detection algorithms
6::COMM;;on 2D datasets. Datasets contain one or two modes (regions of high density)
7::COMM;;to illustrate the ability of algorithms to cope with multimodal data.
8::COMM;;For each dataset, 15% of samples are generated as random uniform noise. This
9::COMM;;proportion is the value given to the nu parameter of the OneClassSVM and the
10::COMM;;contamination parameter of the other outlier detection algorithms.
11::COMM;;Decision boundaries between inliers and outliers are displayed in black
12::COMM;;except for Local Outlier Factor (LOF) as it has no predict method to be applied
13::COMM;;on new data when it is used for outlier detection.
14::COMM;;The :class:`~sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM` is known to be sensitive to outliers and
15::COMM;;thus does not perform very well for outlier detection. This estimator is best
16::COMM;;suited for novelty detection when the training set is not contaminated by
17::COMM;;outliers. That said, outlier detection in high-dimension, or without any
18::COMM;;assumptions on the distribution of the inlying data is very challenging, and a
19::COMM;;One-class SVM might give useful results in these situations depending on the
20::COMM;;value of its hyperparameters.
21::COMM;;The :class:`sklearn.linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` is an implementation of the
22::COMM;;One-Class SVM based on stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Combined with kernel
23::COMM;;approximation, this estimator can be used to approximate the solution
24::COMM;;of a kernelized :class:`sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM`. We note that, although not
25::COMM;;identical, the decision boundaries of the
26::COMM;;:class:`sklearn.linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` and the ones of
27::COMM;;:class:`sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM` are very similar. The main advantage of using
28::COMM;;:class:`sklearn.linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` is that it scales linearly with
29::COMM;;the number of samples.
30::COMM;;:class:`sklearn.covariance.EllipticEnvelope` assumes the data is Gaussian and
31::COMM;;learns an ellipse. It thus degrades when the data is not unimodal. Notice
32::COMM;;however that this estimator is robust to outliers.
33::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest` and
34::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor` seem to perform reasonably well
35::COMM;;for multi-modal data sets. The advantage of
36::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor` over the other estimators is
37::COMM;;shown for the third data set, where the two modes have different densities.
38::COMM;;This advantage is explained by the local aspect of LOF, meaning that it only
39::COMM;;compares the score of abnormality of one sample with the scores of its
40::COMM;;neighbors.
41::COMM;;Finally, for the last data set, it is hard to say that one sample is more
42::COMM;;abnormal than another sample as they are uniformly distributed in a
43::COMM;;hypercube. Except for the :class:`~sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM` which overfits a
44::COMM;;little, all estimators present decent solutions for this situation. In such a
45::COMM;;case, it would be wise to look more closely at the scores of abnormality of
46::COMM;;the samples as a good estimator should assign similar scores to all the
47::COMM;;samples.
48::COMM;;While these examples give some intuition about the algorithms, this
49::COMM;;intuition might not apply to very high dimensional data.
50::COMM;;Finally, note that parameters of the models have been here handpicked but
51::COMM;;that in practice they need to be adjusted. In the absence of labelled data,
52::COMM;;the problem is completely unsupervised so model selection can be a challenge.
54::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
55::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;=====================================================================
3::COMM;;The Johnson-Lindenstrauss bound for embedding with random projections
4::COMM;;=====================================================================
5::COMM;;The `Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma`_ states that any high dimensional
6::COMM;;dataset can be randomly projected into a lower dimensional Euclidean
7::COMM;;space while controlling the distortion in the pairwise distances.
8::COMM;;.. _`Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma`: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/\
9::COMM;;Johnson%E2%80%93Lindenstrauss_lemma
11::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
12::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
23::COMO;;# %%
24::COMO;;# Theoretical bounds
25::COMO;;# ==================
26::COMO;;# The distortion introduced by a random projection `p` is asserted by
27::COMO;;# the fact that `p` is defining an eps-embedding with good probability
28::COMO;;# as defined by:
29::COMO;;#
30::COMO;;# .. math::
31::COMO;;# (1 - eps) \|u - v\|^2 < \|p(u) - p(v)\|^2 < (1 + eps) \|u - v\|^2
32::COMO;;#
33::COMO;;# Where `u` and `v` are any rows taken from a dataset of shape `(n_samples,
34::COMO;;# n_features)` and `p` is a projection by a random Gaussian `N(0, 1)` matrix
35::COMO;;# of shape `(n_components, n_features)` (or a sparse Achlioptas matrix).
36::COMO;;#
37::COMO;;# The minimum number of components to guarantees the eps-embedding is
38::COMO;;# given by:
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# .. math::
41::COMO;;# n\_components \geq 4 log(n\_samples) / (eps^2 / 2 - eps^3 / 3)
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;#
44::COMO;;# The first plot shows that with an increasing number of samples ``n_samples``,
45::COMO;;# the minimal number of dimensions ``n_components`` increased logarithmically
46::COMO;;# in order to guarantee an ``eps``-embedding.
47::COMO;;# range of admissible distortions
50::COMO;;# range of number of samples (observation) to embed
61::COMO;;# %%
62::COMO;;# The second plot shows that an increase of the admissible
63::COMO;;# distortion ``eps`` allows to reduce drastically the minimal number of
64::COMO;;# dimensions ``n_components`` for a given number of samples ``n_samples``
65::COMO;;# range of admissible distortions
67::COMO;;# range of number of samples (observation) to embed
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# Empirical validation
81::COMO;;# ====================
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# We validate the above bounds on the 20 newsgroups text document
84::COMO;;# (TF-IDF word frequencies) dataset or on the digits dataset:
85::COMO;;#
86::COMO;;# - for the 20 newsgroups dataset some 300 documents with 100k
87::COMO;;# features in total are projected using a sparse random matrix to smaller
88::COMO;;# euclidean spaces with various values for the target number of dimensions
89::COMO;;# ``n_components``.
90::COMO;;#
91::COMO;;# - for the digits dataset, some 8x8 gray level pixels data for 300
92::COMO;;# handwritten digits pictures are randomly projected to spaces for various
93::COMO;;# larger number of dimensions ``n_components``.
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# The default dataset is the 20 newsgroups dataset. To run the example on the
96::COMO;;# digits dataset, pass the ``--use-digits-dataset`` command line argument to
97::COMO;;# this script.
102::COMO;;# %%
103::COMO;;# For each value of ``n_components``, we plot:
104::COMO;;#
105::COMO;;# - 2D distribution of sample pairs with pairwise distances in original
106::COMO;;# and projected spaces as x- and y-axis respectively.
107::COMO;;#
108::COMO;;# - 1D histogram of the ratio of those distances (projected / original).
116::COMO;;# select only non-identical samples pairs
154::COMO;;# TODO: compute the expected value of eps and add them to the previous plot
155::COMO;;# as vertical lines / region
157::COMO;;# %%
158::COMO;;# We can see that for low values of ``n_components`` the distribution is wide
159::COMO;;# with many distorted pairs and a skewed distribution (due to the hard
160::COMO;;# limit of zero ratio on the left as distances are always positives)
161::COMO;;# while for larger values of `n_components` the distortion is controlled
162::COMO;;# and the distances are well preserved by the random projection.
163::COMO;;#
164::COMO;;# Remarks
165::COMO;;# =======
166::COMO;;#
167::COMO;;# According to the JL lemma, projecting 300 samples without too much distortion
168::COMO;;# will require at least several thousands dimensions, irrespective of the
169::COMO;;# number of features of the original dataset.
170::COMO;;#
171::COMO;;# Hence using random projections on the digits dataset which only has 64
172::COMO;;# features in the input space does not make sense: it does not allow
173::COMO;;# for dimensionality reduction in this case.
174::COMO;;#
175::COMO;;# On the twenty newsgroups on the other hand the dimensionality can be
176::COMO;;# decreased from 56,436 down to 10,000 while reasonably preserving
177::COMO;;# pairwise distances.

3::COMM;;Explicit feature map approximation for RBF kernels
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;An example illustrating the approximation of the feature map
6::COMM;;of an RBF kernel.
7::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.kernel_approximation
8::COMM;;It shows how to use :class:`RBFSampler` and :class:`Nystroem` to
9::COMM;;approximate the feature map of an RBF kernel for classification with an SVM on
10::COMM;;the digits dataset. Results using a linear SVM in the original space, a linear
11::COMM;;SVM using the approximate mappings and using a kernelized SVM are compared.
12::COMM;;Timings and accuracy for varying amounts of Monte Carlo samplings (in the case
13::COMM;;of :class:`RBFSampler`, which uses random Fourier features) and different sized
14::COMM;;subsets of the training set (for :class:`Nystroem`) for the approximate mapping
15::COMM;;are shown.
16::COMM;;Please note that the dataset here is not large enough to show the benefits
17::COMM;;of kernel approximation, as the exact SVM is still reasonably fast.
18::COMM;;Sampling more dimensions clearly leads to better classification results, but
19::COMM;;comes at a greater cost. This means there is a tradeoff between runtime and
20::COMM;;accuracy, given by the parameter n_components. Note that solving the Linear
21::COMM;;SVM and also the approximate kernel SVM could be greatly accelerated by using
22::COMM;;stochastic gradient descent via :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.SGDClassifier`.
23::COMM;;This is not easily possible for the case of the kernelized SVM.

2::COMM;;=============================================
3::COMM;;Comparison of kernel ridge regression and SVR
4::COMM;;=============================================
5::COMM;;Both kernel ridge regression (KRR) and SVR learn a non-linear function by
6::COMM;;employing the kernel trick, i.e., they learn a linear function in the space
7::COMM;;induced by the respective kernel which corresponds to a non-linear function in
8::COMM;;the original space. They differ in the loss functions (ridge versus
9::COMM;;epsilon-insensitive loss). In contrast to SVR, fitting a KRR can be done in
10::COMM;;closed-form and is typically faster for medium-sized datasets. On the other
11::COMM;;hand, the learned model is non-sparse and thus slower than SVR at
12::COMM;;prediction-time.
13::COMM;;This example illustrates both methods on an artificial dataset, which
14::COMM;;consists of a sinusoidal target function and strong noise added to every fifth
15::COMM;;datapoint.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

21::COMO;;# --------------------

46::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------------
68::COMO;;# %%
69::COMO;;# Look at the results
70::COMO;;# -------------------
96::COMO;;# %%
97::COMO;;# The previous figure compares the learned model of KRR and SVR when both
98::COMO;;# complexity/regularization and bandwidth of the RBF kernel are optimized using
99::COMO;;# grid-search. The learned functions are very similar; however, fitting KRR is
100::COMO;;# approximately 3-4 times faster than fitting SVR (both with grid-search).
101::COMO;;#
102::COMO;;# Prediction of 100000 target values could be in theory approximately three
103::COMO;;# times faster with SVR since it has learned a sparse model using only
104::COMO;;# approximately 1/3 of the training datapoints as support vectors. However, in
105::COMO;;# practice, this is not necessarily the case because of implementation details
106::COMO;;# in the way the kernel function is computed for each model that can make the
107::COMO;;# KRR model as fast or even faster despite computing more arithmetic
108::COMO;;# operations.

149::COMO;;# different sizes of the training set. Fitting KRR is faster than SVR for
150::COMO;;# medium-sized training sets (less than a few thousand samples); however, for
151::COMO;;# larger training sets SVR scales better. With regard to prediction time, SVR
152::COMO;;# should be faster than KRR for all sizes of the training set because of the
153::COMO;;# learned sparse solution, however this is not necessarily the case in practice
154::COMO;;# because of implementation details. Note that the degree of sparsity and thus
155::COMO;;# the prediction time depends on the parameters epsilon and C of the SVR.

2::COMM;;================
3::COMM;;Metadata Routing
4::COMM;;================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
6::COMM;;This document shows how you can use the :ref:`metadata routing mechanism
7::COMM;;<metadata_routing>` in scikit-learn to route metadata to the estimators,
8::COMM;;scorers, and CV splitters consuming them.
9::COMM;;To better understand the following document, we need to introduce two concepts:
10::COMM;;routers and consumers. A router is an object which forwards some given data and
11::COMM;;metadata to other objects. In most cases, a router is a :term:`meta-estimator`,
12::COMM;;i.e. an estimator which takes another estimator as a parameter. A function such
13::COMM;;as :func:`sklearn.model_selection.cross_validate` which takes an estimator as a
14::COMM;;parameter and forwards data and metadata, is also a router.
15::COMM;;A consumer, on the other hand, is an object which accepts and uses some given
16::COMM;;metadata. For instance, an estimator taking into account ``sample_weight`` in
17::COMM;;its :term:`fit` method is a consumer of ``sample_weight``.
18::COMM;;It is possible for an object to be both a router and a consumer. For instance,
19::COMM;;a meta-estimator may take into account ``sample_weight`` in certain
20::COMM;;calculations, but it may also route it to the underlying estimator.
21::COMM;;First a few imports and some random data for the rest of the script.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# %%
55::COMO;;# Metadata routing is only available if explicitly enabled:
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# This utility function is a dummy to check if a metadata is passed:
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# A utility function to nicely print the routing information of an object:
71::COMO;;# %%
72::COMO;;# Consuming Estimator
73::COMO;;# -------------------
74::COMO;;# Here we demonstrate how an estimator can expose the required API to support
75::COMO;;# metadata routing as a consumer. Imagine a simple classifier accepting
76::COMO;;# ``sample_weight`` as a metadata on its ``fit`` and ``groups`` in its
77::COMO;;# ``predict`` method:
81::COMO;;# all classifiers need to expose a classes_ attribute once they're fit.
86::COMO;;# return a constant value of 1, not a very smart classifier!
88::COMO;;# %%
89::COMO;;# The above estimator now has all it needs to consume metadata. This is
90::COMO;;# accomplished by some magic done in :class:`~base.BaseEstimator`. There are
91::COMO;;# now three methods exposed by the above class: ``set_fit_request``,
92::COMO;;# ``set_predict_request``, and ``get_metadata_routing``. There is also a
93::COMO;;# ``set_score_request`` for ``sample_weight`` which is present since
94::COMO;;# :class:`~base.ClassifierMixin` implements a ``score`` method accepting
95::COMO;;# ``sample_weight``. The same applies to regressors which inherit from
96::COMO;;# :class:`~base.RegressorMixin`.
97::COMO;;#
98::COMO;;# By default, no metadata is requested, which we can see as:
100::COMO;;# %%
101::COMO;;# The above output means that ``sample_weight`` and ``groups`` are not
102::COMO;;# requested by `ExampleClassifier`, and if a router is given those metadata, it
103::COMO;;# should raise an error, since the user has not explicitly set whether they are
104::COMO;;# required or not. The same is true for ``sample_weight`` in the ``score``
105::COMO;;# method, which is inherited from :class:`~base.ClassifierMixin`. In order to
106::COMO;;# explicitly set request values for those metadata, we can use these methods:
114::COMO;;# %%

117::COMO;;# meta-estimator, the user does not need to set any requests for the
118::COMO;;# metadata and the set values are ignored, since a consumer does not
119::COMO;;# validate or route given metadata. A simple usage of the above estimator
120::COMO;;# would work as expected.
124::COMO;;# %%
125::COMO;;# Routing Meta-Estimator
126::COMO;;# ----------------------
127::COMO;;# Now, we show how to design a meta-estimator to be a router. As a simplified
128::COMO;;# example, here is a meta-estimator, which doesn't do much other than routing
129::COMO;;# the metadata.
134::COMO;;# This method defines the routing for this meta-estimator.
135::COMO;;# In order to do so, a `MetadataRouter` instance is created, and the
136::COMO;;# routing is added to it. More explanations follow below.
146::COMO;;# `get_routing_for_object` returns a copy of the `MetadataRouter`
147::COMO;;# constructed by the above `get_metadata_routing` method, that is
148::COMO;;# internally called.
150::COMO;;# Meta-estimators are responsible for validating the given metadata.
151::COMO;;# `method` refers to the parent's method, i.e. `fit` in this example.
153::COMO;;# `MetadataRouter.route_params` maps the given metadata to the metadata
154::COMO;;# required by the underlying estimator based on the routing information
155::COMO;;# defined by the MetadataRouter. The output of type `Bunch` has a key
156::COMO;;# for each consuming object and those hold keys for their consuming
157::COMO;;# methods, which then contain key for the metadata which should be
158::COMO;;# routed to them.
160::COMO;;# A sub-estimator is fitted and its classes are attributed to the
161::COMO;;# meta-estimator.
167::COMO;;# As in `fit`, we get a copy of the object's MetadataRouter,
169::COMO;;# then we validate the given metadata,
171::COMO;;# and then prepare the input to the underlying `predict` method.
176::COMO;;# %%
177::COMO;;# Let's break down different parts of the above code.
178::COMO;;#
179::COMO;;# First, the :meth:`~utils.metadata_routing.get_routing_for_object` takes our
180::COMO;;# meta-estimator (``self``) and returns a
181::COMO;;# :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRouter` or, a
182::COMO;;# :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRequest` if the object is a consumer,
183::COMO;;# based on the output of the estimator's ``get_metadata_routing`` method.
184::COMO;;#
185::COMO;;# Then in each method, we use the ``route_params`` method to construct a
186::COMO;;# dictionary of the form ``{"object_name": {"method_name": {"metadata":
187::COMO;;# value}}}`` to pass to the underlying estimator's method. The ``object_name``
188::COMO;;# (``estimator`` in the above ``routed_params.estimator.fit`` example) is the
189::COMO;;# same as the one added in the ``get_metadata_routing``. ``validate_metadata``
190::COMO;;# makes sure all given metadata are requested to avoid silent bugs.
191::COMO;;#
192::COMO;;# Next, we illustrate the different behaviors and notably the type of errors
193::COMO;;# raised.
198::COMO;;# %%
199::COMO;;# Note that the above example is calling our utility function
200::COMO;;# `check_metadata()` via the `ExampleClassifier`. It checks that
201::COMO;;# ``sample_weight`` is correctly passed to it. If it is not, like in the
202::COMO;;# following example, it would print that ``sample_weight`` is ``None``:
204::COMO;;# %%
205::COMO;;# If we pass an unknown metadata, an error is raised:
210::COMO;;# %%
211::COMO;;# And if we pass a metadata which is not explicitly requested:
216::COMO;;# %%
217::COMO;;# Also, if we explicitly set it as not requested, but it is provided:
227::COMO;;# %%
228::COMO;;# Another concept to introduce is **aliased metadata**. This is when an
229::COMO;;# estimator requests a metadata with a different variable name than the default
230::COMO;;# variable name. For instance, in a setting where there are two estimators in a
231::COMO;;# pipeline, one could request ``sample_weight1`` and the other
232::COMO;;# ``sample_weight2``. Note that this doesn't change what the estimator expects,
233::COMO;;# it only tells the meta-estimator how to map the provided metadata to what is
234::COMO;;# required. Here's an example, where we pass ``aliased_sample_weight`` to the
235::COMO;;# meta-estimator, but the meta-estimator understands that
236::COMO;;# ``aliased_sample_weight`` is an alias for ``sample_weight``, and passes it as
237::COMO;;# ``sample_weight`` to the underlying estimator:
242::COMO;;# %%
243::COMO;;# Passing ``sample_weight`` here will fail since it is requested with an
244::COMO;;# alias and ``sample_weight`` with that name is not requested:
249::COMO;;# %%
250::COMO;;# This leads us to the ``get_metadata_routing``. The way routing works in
251::COMO;;# scikit-learn is that consumers request what they need, and routers pass that
252::COMO;;# along. Additionally, a router exposes what it requires itself so that it can
253::COMO;;# be used inside another router, e.g. a pipeline inside a grid search object.
254::COMO;;# The output of the ``get_metadata_routing`` which is a dictionary
255::COMO;;# representation of a :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRouter`, includes
256::COMO;;# the complete tree of requested metadata by all nested objects and their
257::COMO;;# corresponding method routings, i.e. which method of a sub-estimator is used
258::COMO;;# in which method of a meta-estimator:
260::COMO;;# %%
261::COMO;;# As you can see, the only metadata requested for method ``fit`` is
262::COMO;;# ``"sample_weight"`` with ``"aliased_sample_weight"`` as the alias. The
263::COMO;;# ``~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRouter`` class enables us to easily create
264::COMO;;# the routing object which would create the output we need for our
265::COMO;;# ``get_metadata_routing``.
266::COMO;;#
267::COMO;;# In order to understand how aliases work in meta-estimators, imagine our
268::COMO;;# meta-estimator inside another one:
272::COMO;;# %%
273::COMO;;# In the above example, this is how the ``fit`` method of `meta_meta_est`
274::COMO;;# will call their sub-estimator's ``fit`` methods::
275::COMO;;#
276::COMO;;# # user feeds `my_weights` as `aliased_sample_weight` into `meta_meta_est`:
277::COMO;;# meta_meta_est.fit(X, y, aliased_sample_weight=my_weights):
278::COMO;;# ...
279::COMO;;#
280::COMO;;# # the first sub-estimator (`meta_est`) expects `aliased_sample_weight`
281::COMO;;# self.estimator_.fit(X, y, aliased_sample_weight=aliased_sample_weight):
282::COMO;;# ...
283::COMO;;#
284::COMO;;# # the second sub-estimator (`est`) expects `sample_weight`
285::COMO;;# self.estimator_.fit(X, y, sample_weight=aliased_sample_weight):
286::COMO;;# ...
287::COMO;;# %%
288::COMO;;# Consuming and routing Meta-Estimator
289::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
290::COMO;;# For a slightly more complex example, consider a meta-estimator that routes
291::COMO;;# metadata to an underlying estimator as before, but it also uses some metadata
292::COMO;;# in its own methods. This meta-estimator is a consumer and a router at the
293::COMO;;# same time. Implementing one is very similar to what we had before, but with a
294::COMO;;# few tweaks.
301::COMO;;# defining metadata routing request values for usage in the meta-estimator
303::COMO;;# defining metadata routing request values for usage in the sub-estimator
313::COMO;;# Since `sample_weight` is used and consumed here, it should be defined as
314::COMO;;# an explicit argument in the method's signature. All other metadata which
315::COMO;;# are only routed, will be passed as `**fit_params`:
320::COMO;;# We add `sample_weight` to the `fit_params` dictionary.
331::COMO;;# As in `fit`, we get a copy of the object's MetadataRouter,
333::COMO;;# we validate the given metadata,
335::COMO;;# and then prepare the input to the underlying ``predict`` method.
340::COMO;;# %%
341::COMO;;# The key parts where the above meta-estimator differs from our previous
342::COMO;;# meta-estimator is accepting ``sample_weight`` explicitly in ``fit`` and
343::COMO;;# including it in ``fit_params``. Since ``sample_weight`` is an explicit
344::COMO;;# argument, we can be sure that ``set_fit_request(sample_weight=...)`` is
345::COMO;;# present for this method. The meta-estimator is both a consumer, as well as a
346::COMO;;# router of ``sample_weight``.
347::COMO;;#
348::COMO;;# In ``get_metadata_routing``, we add ``self`` to the routing using
349::COMO;;# ``add_self_request`` to indicate this estimator is consuming
350::COMO;;# ``sample_weight`` as well as being a router; which also adds a
351::COMO;;# ``$self_request`` key to the routing info as illustrated below. Now let's
352::COMO;;# look at some examples:

371::COMO;;#
372::COMO;;# - We can also alias the metadata to pass different values to the fit methods
373::COMO;;# of the meta- and the sub-estimator:
378::COMO;;# %%
379::COMO;;# However, ``fit`` of the meta-estimator only needs the alias for the
380::COMO;;# sub-estimator and addresses their own sample weight as `sample_weight`, since
381::COMO;;# it doesn't validate and route its own required metadata:
383::COMO;;# %%
384::COMO;;# - Alias only on the sub-estimator:
385::COMO;;#
386::COMO;;# This is useful when we don't want the meta-estimator to use the metadata, but
387::COMO;;# the sub-estimator should.
392::COMO;;# %%
393::COMO;;# The meta-estimator cannot use `aliased_sample_weight`, because it expects
394::COMO;;# it passed as `sample_weight`. This would apply even if

396::COMO;;# %%
397::COMO;;# Simple Pipeline
398::COMO;;# ---------------
399::COMO;;# A slightly more complicated use-case is a meta-estimator resembling a
400::COMO;;# :class:`~pipeline.Pipeline`. Here is a meta-estimator, which accepts a
401::COMO;;# transformer and a classifier. When calling its `fit` method, it applies the
402::COMO;;# transformer's `fit` and `transform` before running the classifier on the
403::COMO;;# transformed data. Upon `predict`, it applies the transformer's `transform`
404::COMO;;# before predicting with the classifier's `predict` method on the transformed
405::COMO;;# new data.
413::COMO;;# We add the routing for the transformer.
417::COMO;;# The metadata is routed such that it retraces how
418::COMO;;# `SimplePipeline` internally calls the transformer's `fit` and
419::COMO;;# `transform` methods in its own methods (`fit` and `predict`).
424::COMO;;# We add the routing for the classifier.
453::COMO;;# %%
454::COMO;;# Note the usage of :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MethodMapping` to
455::COMO;;# declare which methods of the child estimator (callee) are used in which
456::COMO;;# methods of the meta estimator (caller). As you can see, `SimplePipeline` uses
457::COMO;;# the transformer's ``transform`` and ``fit`` methods in ``fit``, and its
458::COMO;;# ``transform`` method in ``predict``, and that's what you see implemented in
459::COMO;;# the routing structure of the pipeline class.
460::COMO;;#
461::COMO;;# Another difference in the above example with the previous ones is the usage
462::COMO;;# of :func:`~utils.metadata_routing.process_routing`, which processes the input
463::COMO;;# parameters, does the required validation, and returns the `routed_params`
464::COMO;;# which we had created in previous examples. This reduces the boilerplate code
465::COMO;;# a developer needs to write in each meta-estimator's method. Developers are
466::COMO;;# strongly recommended to use this function unless there is a good reason
467::COMO;;# against it.
468::COMO;;#
469::COMO;;# In order to test the above pipeline, let's add an example transformer.
479::COMO;;# %%
480::COMO;;# Note that in the above example, we have implemented ``fit_transform`` which
481::COMO;;# calls ``fit`` and ``transform`` with the appropriate metadata. This is only
482::COMO;;# required if ``transform`` accepts metadata, since the default ``fit_transform``
483::COMO;;# implementation in :class:`~base.TransformerMixin` doesn't pass metadata to
484::COMO;;# ``transform``.
485::COMO;;#
486::COMO;;# Now we can test our pipeline, and see if metadata is correctly passed around.

488::COMO;;# `RouterConsumerClassifier` which uses our `ExampleClassifier`.

493::COMO;;# we set transformer's transform to receive groups
497::COMO;;# we want this sub-estimator to receive sample_weight in fit
499::COMO;;# but not groups in predict

586::COMO;;# Third Party Development and scikit-learn Dependency
587::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
588::COMO;;#
589::COMO;;# As seen above, information is communicated between classes using
590::COMO;;# :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRequest` and
591::COMO;;# :class:`~utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRouter`. It is strongly not advised,
592::COMO;;# but possible to vendor the tools related to metadata-routing if you strictly
593::COMO;;# want to have a scikit-learn compatible estimator, without depending on the
594::COMO;;# scikit-learn package. If all of the following conditions are met, you do NOT
595::COMO;;# need to modify your code at all:
596::COMO;;#
597::COMO;;# - your estimator inherits from :class:`~base.BaseEstimator`
598::COMO;;# - the parameters consumed by your estimator's methods, e.g. ``fit``, are
599::COMO;;# explicitly defined in the method's signature, as opposed to being
600::COMO;;# ``*args`` or ``*kwargs``.
601::COMO;;# - your estimator does not route any metadata to the underlying objects, i.e.
602::COMO;;# it's not a *router*.
2::COMM;;=========================
3::COMM;;Multilabel classification
4::COMM;;=========================
5::COMM;;This example simulates a multi-label document classification problem. The
6::COMM;;dataset is generated randomly based on the following process:
7::COMM;;- pick the number of labels: n ~ Poisson(n_labels)
8::COMM;;- n times, choose a class c: c ~ Multinomial(theta)
9::COMM;;- pick the document length: k ~ Poisson(length)
10::COMM;;- k times, choose a word: w ~ Multinomial(theta_c)
11::COMM;;In the above process, rejection sampling is used to make sure that n is more
12::COMM;;than 2, and that the document length is never zero. Likewise, we reject classes
13::COMM;;which have already been chosen. The documents that are assigned to both
14::COMM;;classes are plotted surrounded by two colored circles.
15::COMM;;The classification is performed by projecting to the first two principal
16::COMM;;components found by PCA and CCA for visualisation purposes, followed by using
17::COMM;;the :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier` metaclassifier using two
18::COMM;;SVCs with linear kernels to learn a discriminative model for each class.
19::COMM;;Note that PCA is used to perform an unsupervised dimensionality reduction,
20::COMM;;while CCA is used to perform a supervised one.
21::COMM;;Note: in the plot, "unlabeled samples" does not mean that we don't know the
22::COMM;;labels (as in semi-supervised learning) but that the samples simply do *not*
23::COMM;;have a label.
25::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
26::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
35::COMO;;# get the separating hyperplane
38::COMC;;xx = np.linspace(min_x - 5, max_x + 5) # make sure the line is long enough

2::COMM;;==========================================
3::COMM;;Evaluation of outlier detection estimators
4::COMM;;==========================================
5::COMM;;This example compares two outlier detection algorithms, namely
6::COMM;;:ref:`local_outlier_factor` (LOF) and :ref:`isolation_forest` (IForest), on
7::COMM;;real-world datasets available in :class:`sklearn.datasets`. The goal is to show
8::COMM;;that different algorithms perform well on different datasets and contrast their
9::COMM;;training speed and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
10::COMM;;The algorithms are trained (without labels) on the whole dataset assumed to
11::COMM;;contain outliers.
12::COMM;;1. The ROC curves are computed using knowledge of the ground-truth labels
13::COMM;;and displayed using :class:`~sklearn.metrics.RocCurveDisplay`.
14::COMM;;2. The performance is assessed in terms of the ROC-AUC.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMO;;# %%
19::COMO;;# Dataset preprocessing and model training
20::COMO;;# ========================================
21::COMO;;#
22::COMO;;# Different outlier detection models require different preprocessing. In the
23::COMO;;# presence of categorical variables,
24::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder` is often a good strategy for
25::COMO;;# tree-based models such as :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest`, whereas
26::COMO;;# neighbors-based models such as :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor`
27::COMO;;# would be impacted by the ordering induced by ordinal encoding. To avoid
28::COMO;;# inducing an ordering, on should rather use
29::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder`.
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# Neighbors-based models may also require scaling of the numerical features (see
32::COMO;;# for instance :ref:`neighbors_scaling`). In the presence of outliers, a good
33::COMO;;# option is to use a :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler`.
45::COMM;;if name == "LOF":
46::COMM;;outlier_detector = LocalOutlierFactor(**(lof_kw or {}))
47::COMM;;if categorical_columns is None:
48::COMM;;preprocessor = RobustScaler()
49::COMM;;else:
50::COMM;;preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
51::COMM;;transformers=[("categorical", OneHotEncoder(), categorical_columns)],
52::COMM;;remainder=RobustScaler(),
53::COMM;;)
54::COMM;;else: # name == "IForest"
55::COMM;;outlier_detector = IsolationForest(**(iforest_kw or {}))
56::COMM;;if categorical_columns is None:
57::COMM;;preprocessor = None
58::COMM;;else:
59::COMM;;ordinal_encoder = OrdinalEncoder(
60::COMM;;handle_unknown="use_encoded_value", unknown_value=-1
61::COMM;;)
62::COMM;;preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
63::COMM;;transformers=[
64::COMM;;("categorical", ordinal_encoder, categorical_columns),
65::COMM;;],
66::COMM;;remainder="passthrough",
67::COMM;;)
68::COMM;;return make_pipeline(preprocessor, outlier_detector)
69::COMM;;# %%
70::COMM;;# The following `fit_predict` function returns the average outlier score of X.
71::COMM;;from time import perf_counter
72::COMM;;def fit_predict(estimator, X):
73::COMM;;tic = perf_counter()
74::COMM;;if estimator[-1].__class__.__name__ == "LocalOutlierFactor":
75::COMM;;estimator.fit(X)
76::COMM;;y_score = estimator[-1].negative_outlier_factor_
77::COMM;;else: # "IsolationForest"
78::COMM;;y_score = estimator.fit(X).decision_function(X)
79::COMM;;toc = perf_counter()
80::COMM;;print(f"Duration for {model_name}: {toc - tic:.2f} s")
81::COMM;;return y_score
82::COMM;;# %%
83::COMM;;# On the rest of the example we process one dataset per section. After loading
84::COMM;;# the data, the targets are modified to consist of two classes: 0 representing
85::COMM;;# inliers and 1 representing outliers. Due to computational constraints of the
86::COMM;;# scikit-learn documentation, the sample size of some datasets is reduced using
87::COMM;;# a stratified :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split`.
88::COMM;;#
89::COMM;;# Furthermore, we set `n_neighbors` to match the expected number of anomalies
90::COMM;;# `expected_n_anomalies = n_samples * expected_anomaly_fraction`. This is a good
91::COMM;;# heuristic as long as the proportion of outliers is not very low, the reason
92::COMM;;# being that `n_neighbors` should be at least greater than the number of samples
93::COMM;;# in the less populated cluster (see
94::COMM;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neighbors_plot_lof_outlier_detection.py`).
95::COMM;;#
96::COMM;;# KDDCup99 - SA dataset
97::COMM;;# ---------------------
98::COMM;;#
99::COMM;;# The :ref:`kddcup99_dataset` was generated using a closed network and
100::COMM;;# hand-injected attacks. The SA dataset is a subset of it obtained by simply
101::COMM;;# selecting all the normal data and an anomaly proportion of around 3%.
102::COMM;;# %%
103::COMM;;import numpy as np
104::COMM;;from sklearn.datasets import fetch_kddcup99
105::COMM;;from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
106::COMM;;X, y = fetch_kddcup99(
107::COMM;;subset="SA", percent10=True, random_state=42, return_X_y=True, as_frame=True
108::COMM;;)
109::COMM;;y = (y != b"normal.").astype(np.int32)
110::COMM;;X, _, y, _ = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=0.1, stratify=y, random_state=42)
111::COMM;;n_samples, anomaly_frac = X.shape[0], y.mean()
112::COMM;;print(f"{n_samples} datapoints with {y.sum()} anomalies ({anomaly_frac:.02%})")
113::COMM;;# %%
114::COMM;;# The SA dataset contains 41 features out of which 3 are categorical:
115::COMM;;# "protocol_type", "service" and "flag".
116::COMM;;# %%
117::COMM;;y_true = {}
118::COMM;;y_score = {"LOF": {}, "IForest": {}}
119::COMM;;model_names = ["LOF", "IForest"]
120::COMM;;cat_columns = ["protocol_type", "service", "flag"]
121::COMM;;y_true["KDDCup99 - SA"] = y
122::COMM;;for model_name in model_names:
123::COMM;;model = make_estimator(
124::COMM;;name=model_name,
125::COMM;;categorical_columns=cat_columns,
126::COMM;;lof_kw={"n_neighbors": int(n_samples * anomaly_frac)},
127::COMM;;iforest_kw={"random_state": 42},
128::COMM;;)
129::COMM;;y_score[model_name]["KDDCup99 - SA"] = fit_predict(model, X)
130::COMM;;# %%
131::COMM;;# Forest covertypes dataset
132::COMM;;# -------------------------
133::COMM;;#
134::COMM;;# The :ref:`covtype_dataset` is a multiclass dataset where the target is the
135::COMM;;# dominant species of tree in a given patch of forest. It contains 54 features,
136::COMM;;# some of which ("Wilderness_Area" and "Soil_Type") are already binary encoded.
137::COMM;;# Though originally meant as a classification task, one can regard inliers as
138::COMM;;# samples encoded with label 2 and outliers as those with label 4.
139::COMM;;# %%
140::COMM;;from sklearn.datasets import fetch_covtype
141::COMM;;X, y = fetch_covtype(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
142::COMM;;s = (y == 2) + (y == 4)
143::COMM;;X = X.loc[s]
144::COMM;;y = y.loc[s]
145::COMM;;y = (y != 2).astype(np.int32)
146::COMM;;X, _, y, _ = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=0.05, stratify=y, random_state=42)
147::COMM;;X_forestcover = X # save X for later use
148::COMM;;n_samples, anomaly_frac = X.shape[0], y.mean()
149::COMM;;print(f"{n_samples} datapoints with {y.sum()} anomalies ({anomaly_frac:.02%})")
150::COMM;;# %%
151::COMM;;y_true["forestcover"] = y
152::COMM;;for model_name in model_names:
153::COMM;;model = make_estimator(
154::COMM;;name=model_name,
155::COMM;;lof_kw={"n_neighbors": int(n_samples * anomaly_frac)},
156::COMM;;iforest_kw={"random_state": 42},
157::COMM;;)
158::COMM;;y_score[model_name]["forestcover"] = fit_predict(model, X)
159::COMM;;# %%
160::COMM;;# Ames Housing dataset
161::COMM;;# --------------------
162::COMM;;#
163::COMM;;# The `Ames housing dataset <http://www.openml.org/d/43926>`_ is originally a
164::COMM;;# regression dataset where the target are sales prices of houses in Ames, Iowa.
165::COMM;;# Here we convert it into an outlier detection problem by regarding houses with
166::COMM;;# price over 70 USD/sqft. To make the problem easier, we drop intermediate
167::COMM;;# prices between 40 and 70 USD/sqft.
168::COMM;;# %%
169::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
170::COMM;;from sklearn.datasets import fetch_openml
171::COMM;;X, y = fetch_openml(name="ames_housing", version=1, return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
172::COMM;;y = y.div(X["Lot_Area"])
173::COMM;;# None values in pandas 1.5.1 were mapped to np.nan in pandas 2.0.1
174::COMM;;X["Misc_Feature"] = X["Misc_Feature"].cat.add_categories("NoInfo").fillna("NoInfo")
175::COMM;;X["Mas_Vnr_Type"] = X["Mas_Vnr_Type"].cat.add_categories("NoInfo").fillna("NoInfo")
176::COMM;;X.drop(columns="Lot_Area", inplace=True)
177::COMM;;mask = (y < 40) | (y > 70)
178::COMM;;X = X.loc[mask]
179::COMM;;y = y.loc[mask]
180::COMM;;y.hist(bins=20, edgecolor="black")
181::COMM;;plt.xlabel("House price in USD/sqft")
182::COMM;;_ = plt.title("Distribution of house prices in Ames")
183::COMM;;# %%
184::COMM;;y = (y > 70).astype(np.int32)
185::COMM;;n_samples, anomaly_frac = X.shape[0], y.mean()
186::COMM;;print(f"{n_samples} datapoints with {y.sum()} anomalies ({anomaly_frac:.02%})")
187::COMM;;# %%
188::COMM;;# The dataset contains 46 categorical features. In this case it is easier use a
189::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.compose.make_column_selector` to find them instead of passing
190::COMM;;# a list made by hand.
191::COMM;;# %%
192::COMM;;from sklearn.compose import make_column_selector as selector
193::COMM;;categorical_columns_selector = selector(dtype_include="category")
194::COMM;;cat_columns = categorical_columns_selector(X)
195::COMM;;y_true["ames_housing"] = y
196::COMM;;for model_name in model_names:
197::COMM;;model = make_estimator(
198::COMM;;name=model_name,
199::COMM;;categorical_columns=cat_columns,
200::COMM;;lof_kw={"n_neighbors": int(n_samples * anomaly_frac)},
201::COMM;;iforest_kw={"random_state": 42},
202::COMM;;)
203::COMM;;y_score[model_name]["ames_housing"] = fit_predict(model, X)
204::COMM;;# %%
205::COMM;;# Cardiotocography dataset
206::COMM;;# ------------------------
207::COMM;;#
208::COMM;;# The `Cardiotocography dataset <http://www.openml.org/d/1466>`_ is a multiclass
209::COMM;;# dataset of fetal cardiotocograms, the classes being the fetal heart rate (FHR)
210::COMM;;# pattern encoded with labels from 1 to 10. Here we set class 3 (the minority
211::COMM;;# class) to represent the outliers. It contains 30 numerical features, some of
212::COMM;;# which are binary encoded and some are continuous.
213::COMM;;# %%
214::COMM;;X, y = fetch_openml(name="cardiotocography", version=1, return_X_y=True, as_frame=False)
215::COMM;;X_cardiotocography = X # save X for later use
216::COMM;;s = y == "3"
217::COMM;;y = s.astype(np.int32)
218::COMM;;n_samples, anomaly_frac = X.shape[0], y.mean()
219::COMM;;print(f"{n_samples} datapoints with {y.sum()} anomalies ({anomaly_frac:.02%})")
220::COMM;;# %%
221::COMM;;y_true["cardiotocography"] = y
222::COMM;;for model_name in model_names:
223::COMM;;model = make_estimator(
224::COMM;;name=model_name,
225::COMM;;lof_kw={"n_neighbors": int(n_samples * anomaly_frac)},
226::COMM;;iforest_kw={"random_state": 42},
227::COMM;;)
228::COMM;;y_score[model_name]["cardiotocography"] = fit_predict(model, X)
229::COMM;;# %%
230::COMM;;# Plot and interpret results
231::COMM;;# ==========================
232::COMM;;#
233::COMM;;# The algorithm performance relates to how good the true positive rate (TPR) is
234::COMM;;# at low value of the false positive rate (FPR). The best algorithms have the
235::COMM;;# curve on the top-left of the plot and the area under curve (AUC) close to 1.
236::COMM;;# The diagonal dashed line represents a random classification of outliers and
237::COMM;;# inliers.
238::COMM;;# %%
239::COMM;;import math
240::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import RocCurveDisplay
241::COMM;;cols = 2
242::COMM;;pos_label = 0 # mean 0 belongs to positive class
243::COMM;;datasets_names = y_true.keys()
244::COMM;;rows = math.ceil(len(datasets_names) / cols)
245::COMM;;fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=rows, ncols=cols, squeeze=False, figsize=(10, rows * 4))
246::COMM;;for ax, dataset_name in zip(axs.ravel(), datasets_names):
247::COMM;;for model_idx, model_name in enumerate(model_names):
248::COMM;;display = RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
249::COMM;;y_true[dataset_name],
250::COMM;;y_score[model_name][dataset_name],
251::COMM;;pos_label=pos_label,
252::COMM;;name=model_name,
253::COMM;;ax=ax,
254::COMM;;plot_chance_level=(model_idx == len(model_names) - 1),
255::COMM;;chance_level_kw={"linestyle": ":"},
256::COMM;;)
257::COMM;;ax.set_title(dataset_name)
258::COMM;;_ = plt.tight_layout(pad=2.0) # spacing between subplots
259::COMM;;# %%
260::COMM;;# We observe that once the number of neighbors is tuned, LOF and IForest perform
261::COMM;;# similarly in terms of ROC AUC for the forestcover and cardiotocography
262::COMM;;# datasets. The score for IForest is slightly better for the SA dataset and LOF
263::COMM;;# performs considerably better on the Ames housing dataset than IForest.
264::COMM;;#
265::COMM;;# Recall however that Isolation Forest tends to train much faster than LOF on
266::COMM;;# datasets with a large number of samples. LOF needs to compute pairwise
267::COMM;;# distances to find nearest neighbors, which has a quadratic complexity with respect
268::COMM;;# to the number of observations. This can make this method prohibitive on large
269::COMM;;# datasets.
270::COMM;;#
271::COMM;;# Ablation study
272::COMM;;# ==============
273::COMM;;#
274::COMM;;# In this section we explore the impact of the hyperparameter `n_neighbors` and
275::COMM;;# the choice of scaling the numerical variables on the LOF model. Here we use
276::COMM;;# the :ref:`covtype_dataset` dataset as the binary encoded categories introduce
277::COMM;;# a natural scale of euclidean distances between 0 and 1. We then want a scaling
278::COMM;;# method to avoid granting a privilege to non-binary features and that is robust
279::COMM;;# enough to outliers so that the task of finding them does not become too
280::COMM;;# difficult.
281::COMM;;# %%
282::COMM;;X = X_forestcover
283::COMM;;y = y_true["forestcover"]
284::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
285::COMM;;n_neighbors_list = (n_samples * np.array([0.2, 0.02, 0.01, 0.001])).astype(np.int32)
286::COMM;;model = make_pipeline(RobustScaler(), LocalOutlierFactor())
287::COMM;;linestyles = ["solid", "dashed", "dashdot", ":", (5, (10, 3))]
288::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots()
289::COMM;;for model_idx, (linestyle, n_neighbors) in enumerate(zip(linestyles, n_neighbors_list)):
290::COMM;;model.set_params(localoutlierfactor__n_neighbors=n_neighbors)
291::COMM;;model.fit(X)
292::COMM;;y_score = model[-1].negative_outlier_factor_
293::COMM;;display = RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
294::COMM;;y,
295::COMM;;y_score,
296::COMM;;pos_label=pos_label,
297::COMM;;name=f"n_neighbors = {n_neighbors}",
298::COMM;;ax=ax,
299::COMM;;plot_chance_level=(model_idx == len(n_neighbors_list) - 1),
300::COMM;;chance_level_kw={"linestyle": (0, (1, 10))},
301::COMM;;curve_kwargs=dict(linestyle=linestyle, linewidth=2),
302::COMM;;)
303::COMM;;_ = ax.set_title("RobustScaler with varying n_neighbors\non forestcover dataset")
304::COMM;;# %%
305::COMM;;# We observe that the number of neighbors has a big impact on the performance of
306::COMM;;# the model. If one has access to (at least some) ground truth labels, it is
307::COMM;;# then important to tune `n_neighbors` accordingly. A convenient way to do so is
308::COMM;;# to explore values for `n_neighbors` of the order of magnitud of the expected
309::COMM;;# contamination.
310::COMM;;# %%
311::COMM;;from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler, SplineTransformer, StandardScaler
312::COMM;;preprocessor_list = [
313::COMM;;None,
314::COMM;;RobustScaler(),
315::COMM;;StandardScaler(),
316::COMM;;MinMaxScaler(),
317::COMM;;SplineTransformer(),
318::COMM;;]
319::COMM;;expected_anomaly_fraction = 0.02
320::COMM;;lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=int(n_samples * expected_anomaly_fraction))
321::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots()
322::COMM;;for model_idx, (linestyle, preprocessor) in enumerate(
323::COMM;;zip(linestyles, preprocessor_list)
324::COMM;;):
325::COMM;;model = make_pipeline(preprocessor, lof)
326::COMM;;model.fit(X)
327::COMM;;y_score = model[-1].negative_outlier_factor_
328::COMM;;display = RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
329::COMM;;y,
330::COMM;;y_score,
331::COMM;;pos_label=pos_label,
332::COMM;;name=str(preprocessor).split("(")[0],
333::COMM;;ax=ax,
334::COMM;;plot_chance_level=(model_idx == len(preprocessor_list) - 1),
335::COMM;;chance_level_kw={"linestyle": (0, (1, 10))},
336::COMM;;curve_kwargs=dict(linestyle=linestyle, linewidth=2),
337::COMM;;)
338::COMM;;_ = ax.set_title("Fixed n_neighbors with varying preprocessing\non forestcover dataset")
339::COMM;;# %%
340::COMM;;# On the one hand, :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler` scales each
341::COMM;;# feature independently by using the interquartile range (IQR) by default, which
342::COMM;;# is the range between the 25th and 75th percentiles of the data. It centers the
343::COMM;;# data by subtracting the median and then scale it by dividing by the IQR. The
344::COMM;;# IQR is robust to outliers: the median and interquartile range are less
345::COMM;;# affected by extreme values than the range, the mean and the standard
346::COMM;;# deviation. Furthermore, :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler` does not
347::COMM;;# squash marginal outlier values, contrary to
348::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler`.
349::COMM;;#
350::COMM;;# On the other hand, :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler` scales each
351::COMM;;# feature individually such that its range maps into the range between zero and
352::COMM;;# one. If there are outliers in the data, they can skew it towards either the
353::COMM;;# minimum or maximum values, leading to a completely different distribution of
354::COMM;;# data with large marginal outliers: all non-outlier values can be collapsed
355::COMM;;# almost together as a result.
356::COMM;;#
357::COMM;;# We also evaluated no preprocessing at all (by passing `None` to the pipeline),
358::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` and
359::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.SplineTransformer`. Please refer to their
360::COMM;;# respective documentation for more details.
361::COMM;;#
362::COMM;;# Note that the optimal preprocessing depends on the dataset, as shown below:
363::COMM;;# %%
364::COMM;;X = X_cardiotocography
365::COMM;;y = y_true["cardiotocography"]
366::COMM;;n_samples, expected_anomaly_fraction = X.shape[0], 0.025
367::COMM;;lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=int(n_samples * expected_anomaly_fraction))
368::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots()
369::COMM;;for model_idx, (linestyle, preprocessor) in enumerate(
370::COMM;;zip(linestyles, preprocessor_list)
371::COMM;;):
372::COMM;;model = make_pipeline(preprocessor, lof)
373::COMM;;model.fit(X)
374::COMM;;y_score = model[-1].negative_outlier_factor_
375::COMM;;display = RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(
376::COMM;;y,
377::COMM;;y_score,
378::COMM;;pos_label=pos_label,
379::COMM;;name=str(preprocessor).split("(")[0],
380::COMM;;ax=ax,
381::COMM;;plot_chance_level=(model_idx == len(preprocessor_list) - 1),
382::COMM;;chance_level_kw={"linestyle": (0, (1, 10))},
383::COMM;;curve_kwargs=dict(linestyle=linestyle, linewidth=2),
384::COMM;;)
385::COMM;;ax.set_title(
386::COMM;;"Fixed n_neighbors with varying preprocessing\non cardiotocography dataset"
387::COMM;;)
388::COMM;;plt.show()
2::COMM;;=========================================
3::COMM;;Advanced Plotting With Partial Dependence
4::COMM;;=========================================
5::COMM;;The :class:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay` object can be used
6::COMM;;for plotting without needing to recalculate the partial dependence. In this
7::COMM;;example, we show how to plot partial dependence plots and how to quickly
8::COMM;;customize the plot with the visualization API.
9::COMM;;.. note::
10::COMM;;See also :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_miscellaneous_plot_roc_curve_visualization_api.py`
12::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
13::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
22::COMO;;# %%
23::COMO;;# Train models on the diabetes dataset
24::COMO;;# ================================================
25::COMO;;#
26::COMO;;# First, we train a decision tree and a multi-layer perceptron on the diabetes
27::COMO;;# dataset.
38::COMO;;# %%
39::COMO;;# Plotting partial dependence for two features
40::COMO;;# ============================================
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# We plot partial dependence curves for features "age" and "bmi" (body mass
43::COMO;;# index) for the decision tree. With two features,
44::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator` expects to plot
45::COMO;;# two curves. Here the plot function place a grid of two plots using the space
46::COMO;;# defined by `ax` .
50::COMO;;# %%
51::COMO;;# The partial dependence curves can be plotted for the multi-layer perceptron.
52::COMO;;# In this case, `line_kw` is passed to
53::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator` to change the
54::COMO;;# color of the curve.
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# Plotting partial dependence of the two models together
62::COMO;;# ======================================================
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# The `tree_disp` and `mlp_disp`
65::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay` objects contain all the
66::COMO;;# computed information needed to recreate the partial dependence curves. This
67::COMO;;# means we can easily create additional plots without needing to recompute the
68::COMO;;# curves.
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# One way to plot the curves is to place them in the same figure, with the
71::COMO;;# curves of each model on each row. First, we create a figure with two axes
72::COMO;;# within two rows and one column. The two axes are passed to the
73::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.plot` functions of
74::COMO;;# `tree_disp` and `mlp_disp`. The given axes will be used by the plotting
75::COMO;;# function to draw the partial dependence. The resulting plot places the
76::COMO;;# decision tree partial dependence curves in the first row of the
77::COMO;;# multi-layer perceptron in the second row.
83::COMO;;# %%
84::COMO;;# Another way to compare the curves is to plot them on top of each other. Here,
85::COMO;;# we create a figure with one row and two columns. The axes are passed into the
86::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.plot` function as a list,
87::COMO;;# which will plot the partial dependence curves of each model on the same axes.
88::COMO;;# The length of the axes list must be equal to the number of plots drawn.
89::COMO;;# sphinx_gallery_thumbnail_number = 4
97::COMO;;# %%
98::COMO;;# `tree_disp.axes_` is a numpy array container the axes used to draw the
99::COMO;;# partial dependence plots. This can be passed to `mlp_disp` to have the same
100::COMO;;# affect of drawing the plots on top of each other. Furthermore, the
101::COMO;;# `mlp_disp.figure_` stores the figure, which allows for resizing the figure
102::COMO;;# after calling `plot`. In this case `tree_disp.axes_` has two dimensions, thus
103::COMO;;# `plot` will only show the y label and y ticks on the left most plot.
112::COMO;;# %%
113::COMO;;# Plotting partial dependence for one feature
114::COMO;;# ===========================================
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# Here, we plot the partial dependence curves for a single feature, "age", on
117::COMO;;# the same axes. In this case, `tree_disp.axes_` is passed into the second
118::COMO;;# plot function.

2::COMM;;================================
3::COMM;;ROC Curve with Visualization API
4::COMM;;================================
5::COMM;;Scikit-learn defines a simple API for creating visualizations for machine
6::COMM;;learning. The key features of this API is to allow for quick plotting and
7::COMM;;visual adjustments without recalculation. In this example, we will demonstrate
8::COMM;;how to use the visualization API by comparing ROC curves.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# Load Data and Train a SVC
14::COMO;;# -------------------------
15::COMO;;# First, we load the wine dataset and convert it to a binary classification
16::COMO;;# problem. Then, we train a support vector classifier on a training dataset.
28::COMO;;# %%
29::COMO;;# Plotting the ROC Curve
30::COMO;;# ----------------------
31::COMO;;# Next, we plot the ROC curve with a single call to
32::COMO;;# :func:`sklearn.metrics.RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator`. The returned
33::COMO;;# `svc_disp` object allows us to continue using the already computed ROC curve
34::COMO;;# for the SVC in future plots.
37::COMO;;# %%
38::COMO;;# Training a Random Forest and Plotting the ROC Curve
39::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
40::COMO;;# We train a random forest classifier and create a plot comparing it to the SVC
41::COMO;;# ROC curve. Notice how `svc_disp` uses
42::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.RocCurveDisplay.plot` to plot the SVC ROC curve
43::COMO;;# without recomputing the values of the roc curve itself. Furthermore, we
44::COMO;;# pass `alpha=0.8` to the plot functions to adjust the alpha values of the
45::COMO;;# curves.
2::COMM;;================================
3::COMM;;Introducing the `set_output` API
4::COMM;;================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn
6::COMM;;This example will demonstrate the `set_output` API to configure transformers to
7::COMM;;output pandas DataFrames. `set_output` can be configured per estimator by calling
8::COMM;;the `set_output` method or globally by setting `set_config(transform_output="pandas")`.
9::COMM;;For details, see
10::COMM;;`SLEP018 <https://scikit-learn-enhancement-proposals.readthedocs.io/en/latest/slep018/proposal.html>`__.
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# First, we load the iris dataset as a DataFrame to demonstrate the `set_output` API.
19::COMO;;# %%
20::COMO;;# To configure an estimator such as :class:`preprocessing.StandardScaler` to return
21::COMO;;# DataFrames, call `set_output`. This feature requires pandas to be installed.
27::COMO;;# %%
28::COMO;;# `set_output` can be called after `fit` to configure `transform` after the fact.
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# In a :class:`pipeline.Pipeline`, `set_output` configures all steps to output
38::COMO;;# DataFrames.
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# Each transformer in the pipeline is configured to return DataFrames. This
49::COMO;;# means that the final logistic regression step contains the feature names of the input.
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# .. note:: If one uses the method `set_params`, the transformer will be
53::COMO;;# replaced by a new one with the default output format.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# To keep the intended behavior, use `set_output` on the new transformer
59::COMO;;# beforehand
64::COMO;;# %%
65::COMO;;# Next we load the titanic dataset to demonstrate `set_output` with
66::COMO;;# :class:`compose.ColumnTransformer` and heterogeneous data.
70::COMO;;# %%
71::COMO;;# The `set_output` API can be configured globally by using :func:`set_config` and
72::COMO;;# setting `transform_output` to `"pandas"`.
96::COMO;;# %%
97::COMO;;# With the global configuration, all transformers output DataFrames. This allows us to
98::COMO;;# easily plot the logistic regression coefficients with the corresponding feature names.
103::COMO;;# %%
104::COMO;;# In order to demonstrate the :func:`config_context` functionality below, let
105::COMO;;# us first reset `transform_output` to its default value.
107::COMO;;# %%
108::COMO;;# When configuring the output type with :func:`config_context` the
109::COMO;;# configuration at the time when `transform` or `fit_transform` are
110::COMO;;# called is what counts. Setting these only when you construct or fit
111::COMO;;# the transformer has no effect.
115::COMO;;# %%

3::COMM;;Concentration Prior Type Analysis of Variation Bayesian Gaussian Mixture
4::COMM;;========================================================================
5::COMM;;This example plots the ellipsoids obtained from a toy dataset (mixture of three
6::COMM;;Gaussians) fitted by the ``BayesianGaussianMixture`` class models with a
7::COMM;;Dirichlet distribution prior
8::COMM;;(``weight_concentration_prior_type='dirichlet_distribution'``) and a Dirichlet
9::COMM;;process prior (``weight_concentration_prior_type='dirichlet_process'``). On
10::COMM;;each figure, we plot the results for three different values of the weight
11::COMM;;concentration prior.
12::COMM;;The ``BayesianGaussianMixture`` class can adapt its number of mixture
13::COMM;;components automatically. The parameter ``weight_concentration_prior`` has a
14::COMM;;direct link with the resulting number of components with non-zero weights.
15::COMM;;Specifying a low value for the concentration prior will make the model put most
16::COMM;;of the weight on few components set the remaining components weights very close
17::COMM;;to zero. High values of the concentration prior will allow a larger number of
18::COMM;;components to be active in the mixture.
19::COMM;;The Dirichlet process prior allows to define an infinite number of components
20::COMM;;and automatically selects the correct number of components: it activates a
21::COMM;;component only if it is necessary.
22::COMM;;On the contrary the classical finite mixture model with a Dirichlet
23::COMM;;distribution prior will favor more uniformly weighted components and therefore
24::COMM;;tends to divide natural clusters into unnecessary sub-components.

2::COMM;;================================
3::COMM;;Gaussian Mixture Model Selection
4::COMM;;================================
5::COMM;;This example shows that model selection can be performed with Gaussian Mixture
6::COMM;;Models (GMM) using :ref:`information-theory criteria <aic_bic>`. Model selection
7::COMM;;concerns both the covariance type and the number of components in the model.
8::COMM;;In this case, both the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayes
9::COMM;;Information Criterion (BIC) provide the right result, but we only demo the
10::COMM;;latter as BIC is better suited to identify the true model among a set of
11::COMM;;candidates. Unlike Bayesian procedures, such inferences are prior-free.
13::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
14::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

16::COMO;;# Data generation
17::COMO;;# ---------------
18::COMO;;#
19::COMO;;# We generate two components (each one containing `n_samples`) by randomly
20::COMO;;# sampling the standard normal distribution as returned by `numpy.random.randn`.
21::COMO;;# One component is kept spherical yet shifted and re-scaled. The other one is
22::COMO;;# deformed to have a more general covariance matrix.
27::COMC;;component_1 = np.dot(np.random.randn(n_samples, 2), C) # general
28::COMC;;component_2 = 0.7 * np.random.randn(n_samples, 2) + np.array([-4, 1]) # spherical

41::COMO;;#

43::COMO;;# parameters to use:
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# - `"full"`: each component has its own general covariance matrix.
46::COMO;;# - `"tied"`: all components share the same general covariance matrix.
47::COMO;;# - `"diag"`: each component has its own diagonal covariance matrix.
48::COMO;;# - `"spherical"`: each component has its own single variance.
49::COMO;;#

51::COMO;;# is done by using :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` and a
52::COMO;;# user-defined score function which returns the negative BIC score, as
53::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` is designed to **maximize** a
54::COMO;;# score (maximizing the negative BIC is equivalent to minimizing the BIC).
55::COMO;;#
56::COMO;;# The best set of parameters and estimator are stored in `best_parameters_` and
57::COMO;;# `best_estimator_`, respectively.

63::COMM;;return -estimator.bic(X)

2::COMM;;=================================
3::COMM;;Gaussian Mixture Model Sine Curve
4::COMM;;=================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates the behavior of Gaussian mixture models fit on data
6::COMM;;that was not sampled from a mixture of Gaussian random variables. The dataset
7::COMM;;is formed by 100 points loosely spaced following a noisy sine curve. There is
8::COMM;;therefore no ground truth value for the number of Gaussian components.
9::COMM;;The first model is a classical Gaussian Mixture Model with 10 components fit
10::COMM;;with the Expectation-Maximization algorithm.
11::COMM;;The second model is a Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Model with a Dirichlet process
12::COMM;;prior fit with variational inference. The low value of the concentration prior
13::COMM;;makes the model favor a lower number of active components. This models
14::COMM;;"decides" to focus its modeling power on the big picture of the structure of
15::COMM;;the dataset: groups of points with alternating directions modeled by
16::COMM;;non-diagonal covariance matrices. Those alternating directions roughly capture
17::COMM;;the alternating nature of the original sine signal.
18::COMM;;The third model is also a Bayesian Gaussian mixture model with a Dirichlet
19::COMM;;process prior but this time the value of the concentration prior is higher
20::COMM;;giving the model more liberty to model the fine-grained structure of the data.
21::COMM;;The result is a mixture with a larger number of active components that is
22::COMM;;similar to the first model where we arbitrarily decided to fix the number of
23::COMM;;components to 10.
24::COMM;;Which model is the best is a matter of subjective judgment: do we want to
25::COMM;;favor models that only capture the big picture to summarize and explain most of
26::COMM;;the structure of the data while ignoring the details or do we prefer models
27::COMM;;that closely follow the high density regions of the signal?
28::COMM;;The last two panels show how we can sample from the last two models. The
29::COMM;;resulting samples distributions do not look exactly like the original data
30::COMM;;distribution. The difference primarily stems from the approximation error we
31::COMM;;made by using a model that assumes that the data was generated by a finite
32::COMM;;number of Gaussian components instead of a continuous noisy sine curve.
