2::COMM;;==============================================================
3::COMM;;Post-tuning the decision threshold for cost-sensitive learning
4::COMM;;==============================================================
5::COMM;;Once a classifier is trained, the output of the :term:`predict` method outputs class
6::COMM;;label predictions corresponding to a thresholding of either the
7::COMM;;:term:`decision_function` or the :term:`predict_proba` output. For a binary classifier,
8::COMM;;the default threshold is defined as a posterior probability estimate of 0.5 or a
9::COMM;;decision score of 0.0.
10::COMM;;However, this default strategy is most likely not optimal for the task at hand.
11::COMM;;Here, we use the "Statlog" German credit dataset [1]_ to illustrate a use case.
12::COMM;;In this dataset, the task is to predict whether a person has a "good" or "bad" credit.
13::COMM;;In addition, a cost-matrix is provided that specifies the cost of
14::COMM;;misclassification. Specifically, misclassifying a "bad" credit as "good" is five
15::COMM;;times more costly on average than misclassifying a "good" credit as "bad".
16::COMM;;We use the :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` to select the
17::COMM;;cut-off point of the decision function that minimizes the provided business
18::COMM;;cost.
19::COMM;;In the second part of the example, we further extend this approach by
20::COMM;;considering the problem of fraud detection in credit card transactions: in this
21::COMM;;case, the business metric depends on the amount of each individual transaction.
22::COMM;;.. rubric :: References
23::COMM;;.. [1] "Statlog (German Credit Data) Data Set", UCI Machine Learning Repository,
24::COMM;;`Link <https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Statlog+%28German+Credit+Data%29>`_.
25::COMM;;.. [2] `Charles Elkan, "The Foundations of Cost-Sensitive Learning",
26::COMM;;International joint conference on artificial intelligence.
27::COMM;;Vol. 17. No. 1. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates Ltd, 2001.
28::COMM;;<https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~elkan/rescale.pdf>`_
30::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
31::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# Cost-sensitive learning with constant gains and costs
34::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------
35::COMO;;#
36::COMO;;# In this first section, we illustrate the use of the
37::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` in a setting of
38::COMO;;# cost-sensitive learning when the gains and costs associated to each entry of the
39::COMO;;# confusion matrix are constant. We use the problematic presented in [2]_ using the
40::COMO;;# "Statlog" German credit dataset [1]_.
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# "Statlog" German credit dataset
43::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# We fetch the German credit dataset from OpenML.
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# We check the feature types available in `X`.
54::COMO;;# %%
55::COMO;;# Many features are categorical and usually string-encoded. We need to encode
56::COMO;;# these categories when we develop our predictive model. Let's check the targets.
58::COMO;;# %%
59::COMO;;# Another observation is that the dataset is imbalanced. We would need to be careful
60::COMO;;# when evaluating our predictive model and use a family of metrics that are adapted
61::COMO;;# to this setting.
62::COMO;;#
63::COMO;;# In addition, we observe that the target is string-encoded. Some metrics
64::COMO;;# (e.g. precision and recall) require to provide the label of interest also called
65::COMO;;# the "positive label". Here, we define that our goal is to predict whether or not
66::COMO;;# a sample is a "bad" credit.
68::COMO;;# %%
69::COMO;;# To carry our analysis, we split our dataset using a single stratified split.
72::COMO;;# %%
73::COMO;;# We are ready to design our predictive model and the associated evaluation strategy.
74::COMO;;#
75::COMO;;# Evaluation metrics
76::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;# In this section, we define a set of metrics that we use later. To see
79::COMO;;# the effect of tuning the cut-off point, we evaluate the predictive model using
80::COMO;;# the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the Precision-Recall curve.
81::COMO;;# The values reported on these plots are therefore the true positive rate (TPR),
82::COMO;;# also known as the recall or the sensitivity, and the false positive rate (FPR),
83::COMO;;# also known as the specificity, for the ROC curve and the precision and recall for
84::COMO;;# the Precision-Recall curve.
85::COMO;;#
86::COMO;;# From these four metrics, scikit-learn does not provide a scorer for the FPR. We
87::COMO;;# therefore need to define a small custom function to compute it.
94::COMO;;# %%
95::COMO;;# As previously stated, the "positive label" is not defined as the value "1" and calling
96::COMO;;# some of the metrics with this non-standard value raise an error. We need to
97::COMO;;# provide the indication of the "positive label" to the metrics.
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# We therefore need to define a scikit-learn scorer using
100::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.make_scorer` where the information is passed. We store all
101::COMO;;# the custom scorers in a dictionary. To use them, we need to pass the fitted model,
102::COMO;;# the data and the target on which we want to evaluate the predictive model.
104::COMC;;tpr_score = recall_score # TPR and recall are the same metric
111::COMO;;# %%
112::COMO;;# In addition, the original research [1]_ defines a custom business metric. We
113::COMO;;# call a "business metric" any metric function that aims at quantifying how the
114::COMO;;# predictions (correct or wrong) might impact the business value of deploying a
115::COMO;;# given machine learning model in a specific application context. For our
116::COMO;;# credit prediction task, the authors provide a custom cost-matrix which
117::COMO;;# encodes that classifying a "bad" credit as "good" is 5 times more costly on
118::COMO;;# average than the opposite: it is less costly for the financing institution to
119::COMO;;# not grant a credit to a potential customer that will not default (and
120::COMO;;# therefore miss a good customer that would have otherwise both reimbursed the
121::COMO;;# credit and paid interests) than to grant a credit to a customer that will
122::COMO;;# default.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# We define a python function that weighs the confusion matrix and returns the
125::COMO;;# overall cost.
126::COMO;;# The rows of the confusion matrix hold the counts of observed classes
127::COMO;;# while the columns hold counts of predicted classes. Recall that here we
128::COMO;;# consider "bad" as the positive class (second row and column).
129::COMO;;# Scikit-learn model selection tools expect that we follow a convention
130::COMO;;# that "higher" means "better", hence the following gain matrix assigns
131::COMO;;# negative gains (costs) to the two kinds of prediction errors:
132::COMO;;#
133::COMO;;# - a gain of `-1` for each false positive ("good" credit labeled as "bad"),
134::COMO;;# - a gain of `-5` for each false negative ("bad" credit labeled as "good"),
135::COMO;;# - a `0` gain for true positives and true negatives.
136::COMO;;#
137::COMO;;# Note that theoretically, given that our model is calibrated and our data
138::COMO;;# set representative and large enough, we do not need to tune the
139::COMO;;# threshold, but can safely set it to 1/5 of the cost ratio, as stated by
140::COMO;;# Eq. (2) in Elkan's paper [2]_.
146::COMC;;[0, -1], # -1 gain for false positives
147::COMC;;[-5, 0], # -5 gain for false negatives
154::COMO;;# %%
155::COMO;;# Vanilla predictive model
156::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
157::COMO;;#
158::COMO;;# We use :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier` as a predictive model
159::COMO;;# that natively handles categorical features and missing values.
165::COMO;;# %%
166::COMO;;# We evaluate the performance of our predictive model using the ROC and Precision-Recall
167::COMO;;# curves.
204::COMO;;# %%
205::COMO;;# We recall that these curves give insights on the statistical performance of the
206::COMO;;# predictive model for different cut-off points. For the Precision-Recall curve, the
207::COMO;;# reported metrics are the precision and recall and for the ROC curve, the reported
208::COMO;;# metrics are the TPR (same as recall) and FPR.
209::COMO;;#
210::COMO;;# Here, the different cut-off points correspond to different levels of posterior
211::COMO;;# probability estimates ranging between 0 and 1. By default, `model.predict` uses a
212::COMO;;# cut-off point at a probability estimate of 0.5. The metrics for such a cut-off point
213::COMO;;# are reported with the blue dot on the curves: it corresponds to the statistical
214::COMO;;# performance of the model when using `model.predict`.
215::COMO;;#
216::COMO;;# However, we recall that the original aim was to minimize the cost (or maximize the
217::COMO;;# gain) as defined by the business metric. We can compute the value of the business
218::COMO;;# metric:
220::COMO;;# %%
221::COMO;;# At this stage we don't know if any other cut-off can lead to a greater gain. To find
222::COMO;;# the optimal one, we need to compute the cost-gain using the business metric for all
223::COMO;;# possible cut-off points and choose the best. This strategy can be quite tedious to
224::COMO;;# implement by hand, but the
225::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` class is here to help us.
226::COMO;;# It automatically computes the cost-gain for all possible cut-off points and optimizes
227::COMO;;# for the `scoring`.
228::COMO;;#
229::COMO;;# .. _cost_sensitive_learning_example:
230::COMO;;#
231::COMO;;# Tuning the cut-off point
232::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
233::COMO;;#
234::COMO;;# We use :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` to tune the
235::COMO;;# cut-off point. We need to provide the business metric to optimize as well as the
236::COMO;;# positive label. Internally, the optimum cut-off point is chosen such that it maximizes
237::COMO;;# the business metric via cross-validation. By default a 5-fold stratified
238::COMO;;# cross-validation is used.
243::COMC;;store_cv_results=True, # necessary to inspect all results
247::COMO;;# %%
248::COMO;;# We plot the ROC and Precision-Recall curves for the vanilla model and the tuned model.
249::COMO;;# Also we plot the cut-off points that would be used by each model. Because, we are
250::COMO;;# reusing the same code later, we define a function that generates the plots.
319::COMO;;# %%
322::COMO;;# %%
323::COMO;;# The first remark is that both classifiers have exactly the same ROC and
324::COMO;;# Precision-Recall curves. It is expected because by default, the classifier is fitted
325::COMO;;# on the same training data. In a later section, we discuss more in detail the
326::COMO;;# available options regarding model refitting and cross-validation.
327::COMO;;#
328::COMO;;# The second remark is that the cut-off points of the vanilla and tuned model are
329::COMO;;# different. To understand why the tuned model has chosen this cut-off point, we can
330::COMO;;# look at the right-hand side plot that plots the objective score that is our exactly
331::COMO;;# the same as our business metric. We see that the optimum threshold corresponds to the
332::COMO;;# maximum of the objective score. This maximum is reached for a decision threshold
333::COMO;;# much lower than 0.5: the tuned model enjoys a much higher recall at the cost of
334::COMO;;# of significantly lower precision: the tuned model is much more eager to
335::COMO;;# predict the "bad" class label to larger fraction of individuals.
336::COMO;;#
337::COMO;;# We can now check if choosing this cut-off point leads to a better score on the testing
338::COMO;;# set:
340::COMO;;# %%
341::COMO;;# We observe that tuning the decision threshold almost improves our business gains
342::COMO;;# by factor of 2.
343::COMO;;#
344::COMO;;# .. _TunedThresholdClassifierCV_no_cv:
345::COMO;;#
346::COMO;;# Consideration regarding model refitting and cross-validation
347::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
348::COMO;;#
349::COMO;;# In the above experiment, we used the default setting of the
350::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV`. In particular, the
351::COMO;;# cut-off point is tuned using a 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Also, the
352::COMO;;# underlying predictive model is refitted on the entire training data once the cut-off
353::COMO;;# point is chosen.
354::COMO;;#
355::COMO;;# These two strategies can be changed by providing the `refit` and `cv` parameters.
356::COMO;;# For instance, one could provide a fitted `estimator` and set `cv="prefit"`, in which
357::COMO;;# case the cut-off point is found on the entire dataset provided at fitting time.
358::COMO;;# Also, the underlying classifier is not be refitted by setting `refit=False`. Here, we
359::COMO;;# can try to do such experiment.
363::COMO;;# %%
364::COMO;;# Then, we evaluate our model with the same approach as before:
367::COMO;;# %%
368::COMO;;# We observe the that the optimum cut-off point is different from the one found
369::COMO;;# in the previous experiment. If we look at the right-hand side plot, we
370::COMO;;# observe that the business gain has large plateau of near-optimal 0 gain for a
371::COMO;;# large span of decision thresholds. This behavior is symptomatic of an
372::COMO;;# overfitting. Because we disable cross-validation, we tuned the cut-off point
373::COMO;;# on the same set as the model was trained on, and this is the reason for the
374::COMO;;# observed overfitting.
375::COMO;;#
376::COMO;;# This option should therefore be used with caution. One needs to make sure that the
377::COMO;;# data provided at fitting time to the
378::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` is not the same as the
379::COMO;;# data used to train the underlying classifier. This could happen sometimes when the
380::COMO;;# idea is just to tune the predictive model on a completely new validation set without a
381::COMO;;# costly complete refit.
382::COMO;;#
383::COMO;;# When cross-validation is too costly, a potential alternative is to use a
384::COMO;;# single train-test split by providing a floating number in range `[0, 1]` to the `cv`
385::COMO;;# parameter. It splits the data into a training and testing set. Let's explore this
386::COMO;;# option:
388::COMO;;# %%
391::COMO;;# %%
392::COMO;;# Regarding the cut-off point, we observe that the optimum is similar to the multiple
393::COMO;;# repeated cross-validation case. However, be aware that a single split does not account
394::COMO;;# for the variability of the fit/predict process and thus we are unable to know if there
395::COMO;;# is any variance in the cut-off point. The repeated cross-validation averages out
396::COMO;;# this effect.
397::COMO;;#
398::COMO;;# Another observation concerns the ROC and Precision-Recall curves of the tuned model.
399::COMO;;# As expected, these curves differ from those of the vanilla model, given that we
400::COMO;;# trained the underlying classifier on a subset of the data provided during fitting and
401::COMO;;# reserved a validation set for tuning the cut-off point.
402::COMO;;#
403::COMO;;# Cost-sensitive learning when gains and costs are not constant
404::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------
405::COMO;;#
406::COMO;;# As stated in [2]_, gains and costs are generally not constant in real-world problems.
407::COMO;;# In this section, we use a similar example as in [2]_ for the problem of
408::COMO;;# detecting fraud in credit card transaction records.
409::COMO;;#
410::COMO;;# The credit card dataset
411::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
414::COMO;;# %%
415::COMO;;# The dataset contains information about credit card records from which some are
416::COMO;;# fraudulent and others are legitimate. The goal is therefore to predict whether or
417::COMO;;# not a credit card record is fraudulent.
421::COMO;;# %%
422::COMO;;# First, we check the class distribution of the datasets.
424::COMO;;# %%
425::COMO;;# The dataset is highly imbalanced with fraudulent transaction representing only 0.17%
426::COMO;;# of the data. Since we are interested in training a machine learning model, we should
427::COMO;;# also make sure that we have enough samples in the minority class to train the model.
429::COMO;;# %%
430::COMO;;# We observe that we have around 500 samples that is on the low end of the number of
431::COMO;;# samples required to train a machine learning model. In addition of the target
432::COMO;;# distribution, we check the distribution of the amount of the
433::COMO;;# fraudulent transactions.
440::COMO;;# %%
441::COMO;;# Addressing the problem with a business metric
442::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
443::COMO;;#
444::COMO;;# Now, we create the business metric that depends on the amount of each transaction. We
445::COMO;;# define the cost matrix similarly to [2]_. Accepting a legitimate transaction provides
446::COMO;;# a gain of 2% of the amount of the transaction. However, accepting a fraudulent
447::COMO;;# transaction result in a loss of the amount of the transaction. As stated in [2]_, the
448::COMO;;# gain and loss related to refusals (of fraudulent and legitimate transactions) are not
449::COMO;;# trivial to define. Here, we define that a refusal of a legitimate transaction
450::COMO;;# is estimated to a loss of 5€ while the refusal of a fraudulent transaction is
451::COMO;;# estimated to a gain of 50€. Therefore, we define the following function to
452::COMO;;# compute the total benefit of a given decision:
463::COMO;;# %%
464::COMO;;# From this business metric, we create a scikit-learn scorer that given a fitted
465::COMO;;# classifier and a test set compute the business metric. In this regard, we use
466::COMO;;# the :func:`~sklearn.metrics.make_scorer` factory. The variable `amount` is an
467::COMO;;# additional metadata to be passed to the scorer and we need to use
468::COMO;;# :ref:`metadata routing <metadata_routing>` to take into account this information.
471::COMO;;# %%
472::COMO;;# So at this stage, we observe that the amount of the transaction is used twice: once
473::COMO;;# as a feature to train our predictive model and once as a metadata to compute the
474::COMO;;# the business metric and thus the statistical performance of our model. When used as a
475::COMO;;# feature, we are only required to have a column in `data` that contains the amount of
476::COMO;;# each transaction. To use this information as metadata, we need to have an external
477::COMO;;# variable that we can pass to the scorer or the model that internally routes this
478::COMO;;# metadata to the scorer. So let's create this variable.
480::COMO;;# %%
487::COMO;;# %%
488::COMO;;# We first evaluate some baseline policies to serve as reference. Recall that
489::COMO;;# class "0" is the legitimate class and class "1" is the fraudulent class.
497::COMO;;# %%
498::COMO;;# A policy that considers all transactions as legitimate would create a profit of
499::COMO;;# around 220,000€. We make the same evaluation for a classifier that predicts all
500::COMO;;# transactions as fraudulent.
507::COMO;;# %%
508::COMO;;# Such a policy would entail a catastrophic loss: around 670,000€. This is
509::COMO;;# expected since the vast majority of the transactions are legitimate and the
510::COMO;;# policy would refuse them at a non-trivial cost.
511::COMO;;#
512::COMO;;# A predictive model that adapts the accept/reject decisions on a per
513::COMO;;# transaction basis should ideally allow us to make a profit larger than the
514::COMO;;# 220,000€ of the best of our constant baseline policies.
515::COMO;;#
516::COMO;;# We start with a logistic regression model with the default decision threshold
517::COMO;;# at 0.5. Here we tune the hyperparameter `C` of the logistic regression with a
518::COMO;;# proper scoring rule (the log loss) to ensure that the model's probabilistic
519::COMO;;# predictions returned by its `predict_proba` method are as accurate as
520::COMO;;# possible, irrespectively of the choice of the value of the decision
521::COMO;;# threshold.
532::COMO;;# %%
537::COMO;;# %%
538::COMO;;# The business metric shows that our predictive model with a default decision
539::COMO;;# threshold is already winning over the baseline in terms of profit and it would be
540::COMO;;# already beneficial to use it to accept or reject transactions instead of
541::COMO;;# accepting all transactions.
542::COMO;;#
543::COMO;;# Tuning the decision threshold
544::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
545::COMO;;#
546::COMO;;# Now the question is: is our model optimum for the type of decision that we want to do?
547::COMO;;# Up to now, we did not optimize the decision threshold. We use the
548::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` to optimize the decision
549::COMO;;# given our business scorer. To avoid a nested cross-validation, we will use the
550::COMO;;# best estimator found during the previous grid-search.
557::COMO;;# %%
558::COMO;;# Since our business scorer requires the amount of each transaction, we need to pass
559::COMO;;# this information in the `fit` method. The
560::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` is in charge of
561::COMO;;# automatically dispatching this metadata to the underlying scorer.
563::COMO;;# %%
564::COMO;;# We observe that the tuned decision threshold is far away from the default 0.5:
566::COMO;;# %%
571::COMO;;# %%
572::COMO;;# We observe that tuning the decision threshold increases the expected profit
573::COMO;;# when deploying our model - as indicated by the business metric. It is therefore
574::COMO;;# valuable, whenever possible, to optimize the decision threshold with respect
575::COMO;;# to the business metric.
576::COMO;;#
577::COMO;;# Manually setting the decision threshold instead of tuning it
578::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
579::COMO;;#
580::COMO;;# In the previous example, we used the
581::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` to find the optimal
582::COMO;;# decision threshold. However, in some cases, we might have some prior knowledge about
583::COMO;;# the problem at hand and we might be happy to set the decision threshold manually.
584::COMO;;#
585::COMO;;# The class :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.FixedThresholdClassifier` allows us to
586::COMO;;# manually set the decision threshold. At prediction time, it behave as the previous
587::COMO;;# tuned model but no search is performed during the fitting process. Note that here
588::COMO;;# we use :class:`~sklearn.frozen.FrozenEstimator` to wrap the predictive model to
589::COMO;;# avoid any refitting.
590::COMO;;#
591::COMO;;# Here, we will reuse the decision threshold found in the previous section to create a
592::COMO;;# new model and check that it gives the same results.
598::COMO;;# %%
603::COMO;;# %%
604::COMO;;# We observe that we obtained the exact same results but the fitting process
605::COMO;;# was much faster since we did not perform any hyper-parameter search.
606::COMO;;#
607::COMO;;# Finally, the estimate of the (average) business metric itself can be unreliable, in
608::COMO;;# particular when the number of data points in the minority class is very small.
609::COMO;;# Any business impact estimated by cross-validation of a business metric on
610::COMO;;# historical data (offline evaluation) should ideally be confirmed by A/B testing
611::COMO;;# on live data (online evaluation). Note however that A/B testing models is
612::COMO;;# beyond the scope of the scikit-learn library itself.
613::COMO;;#
614::COMO;;# At the end, we disable the configuration flag for metadata routing::
2::COMM;;Visualizing cross-validation behavior in scikit-learn
3::COMM;;=====================================================
4::COMM;;Choosing the right cross-validation object is a crucial part of fitting a
5::COMM;;model properly. There are many ways to split data into training and test
6::COMM;;sets in order to avoid model overfitting, to standardize the number of
7::COMM;;groups in test sets, etc.
8::COMM;;This example visualizes the behavior of several common scikit-learn objects
9::COMM;;for comparison.
11::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
12::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# Visualize our data
32::COMO;;# ------------------
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# First, we must understand the structure of our data. It has 100 randomly
35::COMO;;# generated input datapoints, 3 classes split unevenly across datapoints,
36::COMO;;# and 10 "groups" split evenly across datapoints.
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# As we'll see, some cross-validation objects do specific things with
39::COMO;;# labeled data, others behave differently with grouped data, and others
40::COMO;;# do not use this information.
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# To begin, we'll visualize our data.
43::COMO;;# Generate the class/group data
48::COMO;;# Generate uneven groups
52::COMO;;# Visualize dataset groups

82::COMO;;# cross-validation object. We'll perform 4 splits of the data. On each
83::COMO;;# split, we'll visualize the indices chosen for the training set
84::COMO;;# (in blue) and the test set (in red).
87::COMM;;use_groups = "Group" in type(cv).__name__

109::COMM;;)

127::COMM;;# cross-validation object:

133::COMM;;# take either datapoint class or group into consideration. We can change this
134::COMM;;# by using either:

140::COMM;;# attempting to return stratified folds.

2::COMM;;====================================
3::COMM;;Plotting Cross-Validated Predictions
4::COMM;;====================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how to use
6::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_predict` together with
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.PredictionErrorDisplay` to visualize prediction
8::COMM;;errors.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMO;;# %%
13::COMO;;# We will load the diabetes dataset and create an instance of a linear
14::COMO;;# regression model.
19::COMO;;# %%
20::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_predict` returns an array of the
21::COMO;;# same size of `y` where each entry is a prediction obtained by cross
22::COMO;;# validation.
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Since `cv=10`, it means that we trained 10 models and each model was
27::COMO;;# used to predict on one of the 10 folds. We can now use the
28::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.PredictionErrorDisplay` to visualize the
29::COMO;;# prediction errors.
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# On the left axis, we plot the observed values :math:`y` vs. the predicted
32::COMO;;# values :math:`\hat{y}` given by the models. On the right axis, we plot the
33::COMO;;# residuals (i.e. the difference between the observed values and the predicted
34::COMO;;# values) vs. the predicted values.
59::COMO;;# %%
60::COMO;;# It is important to note that we used
61::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_predict` for visualization
62::COMO;;# purpose only in this example.
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# It would be problematic to
65::COMO;;# quantitatively assess the model performance by computing a single
66::COMO;;# performance metric from the concatenated predictions returned by
67::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_predict`
68::COMO;;# when the different CV folds vary by size and distributions.
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# It is recommended to compute per-fold performance metrics using:
71::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score` or
72::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_validate` instead.
2::COMM;;====================================
3::COMM;;Detection error tradeoff (DET) curve
4::COMM;;====================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we compare two binary classification multi-threshold metrics:
6::COMM;;the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) and the Detection Error Tradeoff
7::COMM;;(DET). For such purpose, we evaluate two different classifiers for the same
8::COMM;;classification task.
9::COMM;;ROC curves feature true positive rate (TPR) on the Y axis, and false positive
10::COMM;;rate (FPR) on the X axis. This means that the top left corner of the plot is the
11::COMM;;"ideal" point - a FPR of zero, and a TPR of one.
12::COMM;;DET curves are a variation of ROC curves where False Negative Rate (FNR) is
13::COMM;;plotted on the y-axis instead of the TPR. In this case the origin (bottom left
14::COMM;;corner) is the "ideal" point.
15::COMM;;.. note::
16::COMM;;- See :func:`sklearn.metrics.roc_curve` for further information about ROC
17::COMM;;curves.
18::COMM;;- See :func:`sklearn.metrics.det_curve` for further information about
19::COMM;;DET curves.
20::COMM;;- This example is loosely based on
21::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_classification_plot_classifier_comparison.py`
22::COMM;;example.
23::COMM;;- See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_roc_crossval.py` for
24::COMM;;an example estimating the variance of the ROC curves and ROC-AUC.

28::COMO;;# %%
29::COMO;;# Generate synthetic data
30::COMO;;# -----------------------
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# Define the classifiers
45::COMO;;# ----------------------
46::COMO;;#
47::COMO;;# Here we define two different classifiers. The goal is to visually compare their
48::COMO;;# statistical performance across thresholds using the ROC and DET curves.
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# Compare ROC and DET curves
62::COMO;;# --------------------------
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# DET curves are commonly plotted in normal deviate scale. To achieve this the
65::COMO;;# DET display transforms the error rates as returned by the
66::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.det_curve` and the axis scale using
67::COMO;;# `scipy.stats.norm`.
94::COMO;;# %%
95::COMO;;# Notice that it is easier to visually assess the overall performance of
96::COMO;;# different classification algorithms using DET curves than using ROC curves. As
97::COMO;;# ROC curves are plot in a linear scale, different classifiers usually appear
98::COMO;;# similar for a large part of the plot and differ the most in the top left
99::COMO;;# corner of the graph. On the other hand, because DET curves represent straight
100::COMO;;# lines in normal deviate scale, they tend to be distinguishable as a whole and
101::COMO;;# the area of interest spans a large part of the plot.
102::COMO;;#
103::COMO;;# DET curves give direct feedback of the detection error tradeoff to aid in
104::COMO;;# operating point analysis. The user can then decide the FNR they are willing to
105::COMO;;# accept at the expense of the FPR (or vice-versa).
106::COMO;;#
107::COMO;;# Non-informative classifier baseline for the ROC and DET curves
108::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# The diagonal black-dotted lines in the plots above correspond to a
111::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.dummy.DummyClassifier` using the default "prior" strategy, to
112::COMO;;# serve as baseline for comparison with other classifiers. This classifier makes
113::COMO;;# constant predictions, independent of the input features in `X`, making it a
114::COMO;;# non-informative classifier.
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# To further understand the non-informative baseline of the ROC and DET curves,
117::COMO;;# we recall the following mathematical definitions:
118::COMO;;#
119::COMO;;# :math:`\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}`
120::COMO;;#
121::COMO;;# :math:`\text{FNR} = \frac{\text{FN}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}`
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# :math:`\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}`
124::COMO;;#
125::COMO;;# A classifier that always predict the positive class would have no true
126::COMO;;# negatives nor false negatives, giving :math:`\text{FPR} = \text{TPR} = 1` and
127::COMO;;# :math:`\text{FNR} = 0`, i.e.:
128::COMO;;#
129::COMO;;# - a single point in the upper right corner of the ROC plane,
130::COMO;;# - a single point in the lower right corner of the DET plane.
131::COMO;;#
132::COMO;;# Similarly, a classifier that always predict the negative class would have no
133::COMO;;# true positives nor false positives, thus :math:`\text{FPR} = \text{TPR} = 0`
134::COMO;;# and :math:`\text{FNR} = 1`, i.e.:
135::COMO;;#
136::COMO;;# - a single point in the lower left corner of the ROC plane,
137::COMO;;# - a single point in the upper left corner of the DET plane.
2::COMM;;============================================================
3::COMM;;Custom refit strategy of a grid search with cross-validation
4::COMM;;============================================================
5::COMM;;This examples shows how a classifier is optimized by cross-validation,
6::COMM;;which is done using the :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` object
7::COMM;;on a development set that comprises only half of the available labeled data.
8::COMM;;The performance of the selected hyper-parameters and trained model is
9::COMM;;then measured on a dedicated evaluation set that was not used during
10::COMM;;the model selection step.
11::COMM;;More details on tools available for model selection can be found in the
12::COMM;;sections on :ref:`cross_validation` and :ref:`grid_search`.
14::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
15::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# The dataset
18::COMO;;# -----------
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# We will work with the `digits` dataset. The goal is to classify handwritten
21::COMO;;# digits images.
22::COMO;;# We transform the problem into a binary classification for easier
23::COMO;;# understanding: the goal is to identify whether a digit is `8` or not.
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# In order to train a classifier on images, we need to flatten them into vectors.
28::COMO;;# Each image of 8 by 8 pixels needs to be transformed to a vector of 64 pixels.
29::COMO;;# Thus, we will get a final data array of shape `(n_images, n_pixels)`.
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# As presented in the introduction, the data will be split into a training
38::COMO;;# and a testing set of equal size.
41::COMO;;# %%
42::COMO;;# Define our grid-search strategy
43::COMO;;# -------------------------------
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# We will select a classifier by searching the best hyper-parameters on folds
46::COMO;;# of the training set. To do this, we need to define
47::COMO;;# the scores to select the best candidate.
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# We can also define a function to be passed to the `refit` parameter of the
51::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` instance. It will implement the
52::COMO;;# custom strategy to select the best candidate from the `cv_results_` attribute
53::COMO;;# of the :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`. Once the candidate is
54::COMO;;# selected, it is automatically refitted by the
55::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` instance.
56::COMO;;#
57::COMO;;# Here, the strategy is to short-list the models which are the best in terms of
58::COMO;;# precision and recall. From the selected models, we finally select the fastest
59::COMO;;# model at predicting. Notice that these custom choices are completely
60::COMO;;# arbitrary.
64::COMM;;for mean_precision, std_precision, mean_recall, std_recall, params in zip(
65::COMM;;filtered_cv_results["mean_test_precision"],
66::COMM;;filtered_cv_results["std_test_precision"],
67::COMM;;filtered_cv_results["mean_test_recall"],
68::COMM;;filtered_cv_results["std_test_recall"],
69::COMM;;filtered_cv_results["params"],
70::COMM;;):
71::COMM;;print(
72::COMM;;f"precision: {mean_precision:0.3f} (±{std_precision:0.03f}),"
73::COMM;;f" recall: {mean_recall:0.3f} (±{std_recall:0.03f}),"
74::COMM;;f" for {params}"
75::COMM;;)
76::COMM;;print()
77::COMM;;def refit_strategy(cv_results):
92::COMM;;# print the info about the grid-search for the different scores
93::COMM;;precision_threshold = 0.98
94::COMM;;cv_results_ = pd.DataFrame(cv_results)
95::COMM;;print("All grid-search results:")
96::COMM;;print_dataframe(cv_results_)
97::COMM;;# Filter-out all results below the threshold
98::COMM;;high_precision_cv_results = cv_results_[
99::COMM;;cv_results_["mean_test_precision"] > precision_threshold
100::COMM;;]
101::COMM;;print(f"Models with a precision higher than {precision_threshold}:")
102::COMM;;print_dataframe(high_precision_cv_results)
103::COMM;;high_precision_cv_results = high_precision_cv_results[
104::COMM;;[
105::COMM;;"mean_score_time",
106::COMM;;"mean_test_recall",
107::COMM;;"std_test_recall",
108::COMM;;"mean_test_precision",
109::COMM;;"std_test_precision",
110::COMM;;"rank_test_recall",
111::COMM;;"rank_test_precision",
112::COMM;;"params",
113::COMM;;]
114::COMM;;]
115::COMM;;# Select the most performant models in terms of recall
116::COMM;;# (within 1 sigma from the best)
117::COMM;;best_recall_std = high_precision_cv_results["mean_test_recall"].std()
118::COMM;;best_recall = high_precision_cv_results["mean_test_recall"].max()
119::COMM;;best_recall_threshold = best_recall - best_recall_std
120::COMM;;high_recall_cv_results = high_precision_cv_results[
121::COMM;;high_precision_cv_results["mean_test_recall"] > best_recall_threshold
122::COMM;;]
123::COMM;;print(
124::COMM;;"Out of the previously selected high precision models, we keep all the\n"
125::COMM;;"the models within one standard deviation of the highest recall model:"
126::COMM;;)
127::COMM;;print_dataframe(high_recall_cv_results)
128::COMM;;# From the best candidates, select the fastest model to predict
129::COMM;;fastest_top_recall_high_precision_index = high_recall_cv_results[
130::COMM;;"mean_score_time"
131::COMM;;].idxmin()
132::COMM;;print(
133::COMM;;"\nThe selected final model is the fastest to predict out of the previously\n"
134::COMM;;"selected subset of best models based on precision and recall.\n"
135::COMM;;"Its scoring time is:\n\n"
136::COMM;;f"{high_recall_cv_results.loc[fastest_top_recall_high_precision_index]}"
137::COMM;;)
138::COMM;;return fastest_top_recall_high_precision_index
139::COMM;;# %%

145::COMM;;# of the hyper-parameters and create the grid-search instance:
146::COMM;;from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
147::COMM;;from sklearn.svm import SVC
148::COMM;;tuned_parameters = [
149::COMM;;{"kernel": ["rbf"], "gamma": [1e-3, 1e-4], "C": [1, 10, 100, 1000]},
150::COMM;;{"kernel": ["linear"], "C": [1, 10, 100, 1000]},

154::COMM;;)

160::COMM;;# %%
161::COMM;;#
162::COMM;;# Finally, we evaluate the fine-tuned model on the left-out evaluation set: the
163::COMM;;# `grid_search` object **has automatically been refit** on the full training
164::COMM;;# set with the parameters selected by our custom refit strategy.
165::COMM;;#
166::COMM;;# We can use the classification report to compute standard classification
167::COMM;;# metrics on the left-out set:
168::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

2::COMM;;==================================================
3::COMM;;Balance model complexity and cross-validated score
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates how to balance model complexity and cross-validated score by
6::COMM;;finding a decent accuracy within 1 standard deviation of the best accuracy score while
7::COMM;;minimising the number of :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` components [1]_. It uses
8::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` with a custom refit callable to select
9::COMM;;the optimal model.
10::COMM;;The figure shows the trade-off between cross-validated score and the number
11::COMM;;of PCA components. The balanced case is when `n_components=10` and `accuracy=0.88`,
12::COMM;;which falls into the range within 1 standard deviation of the best accuracy
13::COMM;;score.
14::COMM;;References
15::COMM;;----------
16::COMM;;.. [1] Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., Friedman, J. (2001). Model Assessment and
17::COMM;;Selection. The Elements of Statistical Learning (pp. 219-260). New York,
18::COMM;;NY, USA: Springer New York Inc.
20::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
21::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# Introduction
32::COMO;;# ------------
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# When tuning hyperparameters, we often want to balance model complexity and
35::COMO;;# performance. The "one-standard-error" rule is a common approach: select the simplest
36::COMO;;# model whose performance is within one standard error of the best model's performance.
37::COMO;;# This helps to avoid overfitting by preferring simpler models when their performance is
38::COMO;;# statistically comparable to more complex ones.
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# Helper functions
41::COMO;;# ----------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# We define two helper functions:
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# 1. `lower_bound`: Calculates the threshold for acceptable performance
46::COMO;;# (best score - 1 std)
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# 2. `best_low_complexity`: Selects the model with the fewest PCA components that
49::COMO;;# exceeds this threshold
52::COMM;;Calculate the lower bound within 1 standard deviation
53::COMM;;of the best `mean_test_scores`.
54::COMM;;Parameters
55::COMM;;----------
56::COMM;;cv_results : dict of numpy(masked) ndarrays
57::COMM;;See attribute cv_results_ of `GridSearchCV`
58::COMM;;Returns
59::COMM;;-------
60::COMM;;float
61::COMM;;Lower bound within 1 standard deviation of the
62::COMM;;best `mean_test_score`.
71::COMM;;Balance model complexity with cross-validated score.
72::COMM;;Parameters
73::COMM;;----------
74::COMM;;cv_results : dict of numpy(masked) ndarrays
75::COMM;;See attribute cv_results_ of `GridSearchCV`.
76::COMM;;Return
77::COMM;;------
78::COMM;;int
79::COMM;;Index of a model that has the fewest PCA components
80::COMM;;while has its test score within 1 standard deviation of the best
81::COMM;;`mean_test_score`.

90::COMO;;# Set up the pipeline and parameter grid
91::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
92::COMO;;#
93::COMO;;# We create a pipeline with two steps:
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# 1. Dimensionality reduction using PCA
96::COMO;;#
97::COMO;;# 2. Classification using LogisticRegression
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# We'll search over different numbers of PCA components to find the optimal complexity.
107::COMO;;# %%
108::COMO;;# Perform the search with GridSearchCV
109::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
110::COMO;;#
111::COMO;;# We use `GridSearchCV` with our custom `best_low_complexity` function as the refit
112::COMO;;# parameter. This function will select the model with the fewest PCA components that
113::COMO;;# still performs within one standard deviation of the best model.
116::COMO;;# Use a non-stratified CV strategy to make sure that the inter-fold
117::COMO;;# standard deviation of the test scores is informative.
119::COMC;;n_jobs=1, # increase this on your machine to use more physical cores

136::COMO;;# one-standard-deviation threshold.

312::COMO;;# %%
313::COMO;;# Conclusion
314::COMO;;# ----------
315::COMO;;#
316::COMO;;# The one-standard-error rule helps us select a simpler model (fewer PCA components)
317::COMO;;# while maintaining performance statistically comparable to the best model.
318::COMO;;# This approach can help prevent overfitting and improve model interpretability
319::COMO;;# and efficiency.
320::COMO;;#
321::COMO;;# In this example, we've seen how to implement this rule using a custom refit
322::COMO;;# callable with :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`.
323::COMO;;#
324::COMO;;# Key takeaways:
325::COMO;;#
326::COMO;;# 1. The one-standard-error rule provides a good rule of thumb to select simpler models
327::COMO;;#
328::COMO;;# 2. Custom refit callables in :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` allow for
329::COMO;;# flexible model selection strategies
330::COMO;;#
331::COMO;;# 3. Visualizing both train and test scores helps identify potential overfitting
332::COMO;;#
333::COMO;;# This approach can be applied to other model selection scenarios where balancing
334::COMO;;# complexity and performance is important, or in cases where a use-case specific
335::COMO;;# selection of the "best" model is desired.

2::COMM;;==================================================
3::COMM;;Statistical comparison of models using grid search
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates how to statistically compare the performance of models
6::COMM;;trained and evaluated using :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`.
8::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
9::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
10::COMO;;# %%
11::COMO;;# We will start by simulating moon shaped data (where the ideal separation
12::COMO;;# between classes is non-linear), adding to it a moderate degree of noise.
13::COMO;;# Datapoints will belong to one of two possible classes to be predicted by two
14::COMO;;# features. We will simulate 50 samples for each class:
23::COMO;;# %%
24::COMO;;# We will compare the performance of :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` estimators that
25::COMO;;# vary on their `kernel` parameter, to decide which choice of this
26::COMO;;# hyper-parameter predicts our simulated data best.
27::COMO;;# We will evaluate the performance of the models using
28::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RepeatedStratifiedKFold`, repeating 10 times
29::COMO;;# a 10-fold stratified cross validation using a different randomization of the
30::COMO;;# data in each repetition. The performance will be evaluated using
31::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score`.
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# We can now inspect the results of our search, sorted by their
45::COMO;;# `mean_test_score`:
53::COMO;;# %%
54::COMO;;# We can see that the estimator using the `'rbf'` kernel performed best,
55::COMO;;# closely followed by `'linear'`. Both estimators with a `'poly'` kernel
56::COMO;;# performed worse, with the one using a two-degree polynomial achieving a much
57::COMO;;# lower performance than all other models.
58::COMO;;#
59::COMO;;# Usually, the analysis just ends here, but half the story is missing. The
60::COMO;;# output of :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` does not provide
61::COMO;;# information on the certainty of the differences between the models.
62::COMO;;# We don't know if these are **statistically** significant.
63::COMO;;# To evaluate this, we need to conduct a statistical test.
64::COMO;;# Specifically, to contrast the performance of two models we should
65::COMO;;# statistically compare their AUC scores. There are 100 samples (AUC
66::COMO;;# scores) for each model as we repreated 10 times a 10-fold cross-validation.
67::COMO;;#
68::COMO;;# However, the scores of the models are not independent: all models are
69::COMO;;# evaluated on the **same** 100 partitions, increasing the correlation
70::COMO;;# between the performance of the models.
71::COMO;;# Since some partitions of the data can make the distinction of the classes
72::COMO;;# particularly easy or hard to find for all models, the models scores will
73::COMO;;# co-vary.
74::COMO;;#
75::COMO;;# Let's inspect this partition effect by plotting the performance of all models
76::COMO;;# in each fold, and calculating the correlation between models across folds:
77::COMO;;# create df of model scores ordered by performance
79::COMO;;# plot 30 examples of dependency between cv fold and AUC scores
93::COMO;;# print correlation of AUC scores across folds
95::COMO;;# %%
96::COMO;;# We can observe that the performance of the models highly depends on the fold.
97::COMO;;#
98::COMO;;# As a consequence, if we assume independence between samples we will be
99::COMO;;# underestimating the variance computed in our statistical tests, increasing
100::COMO;;# the number of false positive errors (i.e. detecting a significant difference
101::COMO;;# between models when such does not exist) [1]_.
102::COMO;;#
103::COMO;;# Several variance-corrected statistical tests have been developed for these
104::COMO;;# cases. In this example we will show how to implement one of them (the so
105::COMO;;# called Nadeau and Bengio's corrected t-test) under two different statistical
106::COMO;;# frameworks: frequentist and Bayesian.
107::COMO;;# %%
108::COMO;;# Comparing two models: frequentist approach
109::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------
110::COMO;;#
111::COMO;;# We can start by asking: "Is the first model significantly better than the
112::COMO;;# second model (when ranked by `mean_test_score`)?"
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# To answer this question using a frequentist approach we could
115::COMO;;# run a paired t-test and compute the p-value. This is also known as
116::COMO;;# Diebold-Mariano test in the forecast literature [5]_.
117::COMO;;# Many variants of such a t-test have been developed to account for the
118::COMO;;# 'non-independence of samples problem'
119::COMO;;# described in the previous section. We will use the one proven to obtain the
120::COMO;;# highest replicability scores (which rate how similar the performance of a
121::COMO;;# model is when evaluating it on different random partitions of the same
122::COMO;;# dataset) while maintaining a low rate of false positives and false negatives:
123::COMO;;# the Nadeau and Bengio's corrected t-test [2]_ that uses a 10 times repeated
124::COMO;;# 10-fold cross validation [3]_.
125::COMO;;#
126::COMO;;# This corrected paired t-test is computed as:
127::COMO;;#
128::COMO;;# .. math::
129::COMO;;# t=\frac{\frac{1}{k \cdot r}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{r}x_{ij}}
130::COMO;;# {\sqrt{(\frac{1}{k \cdot r}+\frac{n_{test}}{n_{train}})\hat{\sigma}^2}}
131::COMO;;#
132::COMO;;# where :math:`k` is the number of folds,
133::COMO;;# :math:`r` the number of repetitions in the cross-validation,
134::COMO;;# :math:`x` is the difference in performance of the models,
135::COMO;;# :math:`n_{test}` is the number of samples used for testing,
136::COMO;;# :math:`n_{train}` is the number of samples used for training,
137::COMO;;# and :math:`\hat{\sigma}^2` represents the variance of the observed
138::COMO;;# differences.
139::COMO;;#
140::COMO;;# Let's implement a corrected right-tailed paired t-test to evaluate if the
141::COMO;;# performance of the first model is significantly better than that of the
142::COMO;;# second model. Our null hypothesis is that the second model performs at least
143::COMO;;# as good as the first model.
148::COMM;;Parameters
149::COMM;;----------
150::COMM;;differences : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
151::COMM;;Vector containing the differences in the score metrics of two models.
152::COMM;;n_train : int
153::COMM;;Number of samples in the training set.
154::COMM;;n_test : int
155::COMM;;Number of samples in the testing set.
156::COMM;;Returns
157::COMM;;-------
158::COMM;;corrected_std : float
159::COMM;;Variance-corrected standard deviation of the set of differences.
161::COMO;;# kr = k times r, r times repeated k-fold crossvalidation,
162::COMO;;# kr equals the number of times the model was evaluated
169::COMM;;Parameters
170::COMM;;----------
171::COMM;;differences : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
172::COMM;;Vector containing the differences in the score metrics of two models.
173::COMM;;df : int
174::COMM;;Degrees of freedom.
175::COMM;;n_train : int
176::COMM;;Number of samples in the training set.
177::COMM;;n_test : int
178::COMM;;Number of samples in the testing set.
179::COMM;;Returns
180::COMM;;-------
181::COMM;;t_stat : float
182::COMM;;Variance-corrected t-statistic.
183::COMM;;p_val : float
184::COMM;;Variance-corrected p-value.
189::COMC;;p_val = t.sf(np.abs(t_stat), df) # right-tailed t-test
191::COMO;;# %%
192::COMC;;model_1_scores = model_scores.iloc[0].values # scores of the best model
193::COMC;;model_2_scores = model_scores.iloc[1].values # scores of the second-best model
195::COMC;;n = differences.shape[0] # number of test sets
201::COMO;;# %%
202::COMO;;# We can compare the corrected t- and p-values with the uncorrected ones:
209::COMO;;# %%
210::COMO;;# Using the conventional significance alpha level at `p=0.05`, we observe that
211::COMO;;# the uncorrected t-test concludes that the first model is significantly better
212::COMO;;# than the second.
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# With the corrected approach, in contrast, we fail to detect this difference.
215::COMO;;#
216::COMO;;# In the latter case, however, the frequentist approach does not let us
217::COMO;;# conclude that the first and second model have an equivalent performance. If
218::COMO;;# we wanted to make this assertion we need to use a Bayesian approach.
219::COMO;;# %%
220::COMO;;# Comparing two models: Bayesian approach
221::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------
222::COMO;;# We can use Bayesian estimation to calculate the probability that the first
223::COMO;;# model is better than the second. Bayesian estimation will output a
224::COMO;;# distribution followed by the mean :math:`\mu` of the differences in the
225::COMO;;# performance of two models.
226::COMO;;#
227::COMO;;# To obtain the posterior distribution we need to define a prior that models
228::COMO;;# our beliefs of how the mean is distributed before looking at the data,
229::COMO;;# and multiply it by a likelihood function that computes how likely our
230::COMO;;# observed differences are, given the values that the mean of differences
231::COMO;;# could take.
232::COMO;;#
233::COMO;;# Bayesian estimation can be carried out in many forms to answer our question,
234::COMO;;# but in this example we will implement the approach suggested by Benavoli and
235::COMO;;# colleagues [4]_.
236::COMO;;#
237::COMO;;# One way of defining our posterior using a closed-form expression is to select
238::COMO;;# a prior conjugate to the likelihood function. Benavoli and colleagues [4]_
239::COMO;;# show that when comparing the performance of two classifiers we can model the
240::COMO;;# prior as a Normal-Gamma distribution (with both mean and variance unknown)
241::COMO;;# conjugate to a normal likelihood, to thus express the posterior as a normal
242::COMO;;# distribution.
243::COMO;;# Marginalizing out the variance from this normal posterior, we can define the
244::COMO;;# posterior of the mean parameter as a Student's t-distribution. Specifically:
245::COMO;;#
246::COMO;;# .. math::
247::COMO;;# St(\mu;n-1,\overline{x},(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{n_{test}}{n_{train}})
248::COMO;;# \hat{\sigma}^2)
249::COMO;;#
250::COMO;;# where :math:`n` is the total number of samples,
251::COMO;;# :math:`\overline{x}` represents the mean difference in the scores,
252::COMO;;# :math:`n_{test}` is the number of samples used for testing,
253::COMO;;# :math:`n_{train}` is the number of samples used for training,
254::COMO;;# and :math:`\hat{\sigma}^2` represents the variance of the observed
255::COMO;;# differences.
256::COMO;;#
257::COMO;;# Notice that we are using Nadeau and Bengio's corrected variance in our
258::COMO;;# Bayesian approach as well.
259::COMO;;#
260::COMO;;# Let's compute and plot the posterior:
261::COMO;;# initialize random variable
265::COMO;;# %%
266::COMO;;# Let's plot the posterior distribution:
275::COMO;;# %%
276::COMO;;# We can calculate the probability that the first model is better than the
277::COMO;;# second by computing the area under the curve of the posterior distribution
278::COMO;;# from zero to infinity. And also the reverse: we can calculate the probability
279::COMO;;# that the second model is better than the first by computing the area under
280::COMO;;# the curve from minus infinity to zero.
290::COMO;;# %%
291::COMO;;# In contrast with the frequentist approach, we can compute the probability
292::COMO;;# that one model is better than the other.
293::COMO;;#
294::COMO;;# Note that we obtained similar results as those in the frequentist approach.
295::COMO;;# Given our choice of priors, we are essentially performing the same
296::COMO;;# computations, but we are allowed to make different assertions.
297::COMO;;# %%
298::COMO;;# Region of Practical Equivalence
299::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
300::COMO;;# Sometimes we are interested in determining the probabilities that our models
301::COMO;;# have an equivalent performance, where "equivalent" is defined in a practical
302::COMO;;# way. A naive approach [4]_ would be to define estimators as practically
303::COMO;;# equivalent when they differ by less than 1% in their accuracy. But we could
304::COMO;;# also define this practical equivalence taking into account the problem we are
305::COMO;;# trying to solve. For example, a difference of 5% in accuracy would mean an
306::COMO;;# increase of $1000 in sales, and we consider any quantity above that as
307::COMO;;# relevant for our business.
308::COMO;;#
309::COMO;;# In this example we are going to define the
310::COMO;;# Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE) to be :math:`[-0.01, 0.01]`. That is,
311::COMO;;# we will consider two models as practically equivalent if they differ by less
312::COMO;;# than 1% in their performance.
313::COMO;;#
314::COMO;;# To compute the probabilities of the classifiers being practically equivalent,
315::COMO;;# we calculate the area under the curve of the posterior over the ROPE
316::COMO;;# interval:
323::COMO;;# %%
324::COMO;;# We can plot how the posterior is distributed over the ROPE interval:
334::COMO;;# %%
335::COMO;;# As suggested in [4]_, we can further interpret these probabilities using the
336::COMO;;# same criteria as the frequentist approach: is the probability of falling
337::COMO;;# inside the ROPE bigger than 95% (alpha value of 5%)? In that case we can
338::COMO;;# conclude that both models are practically equivalent.
339::COMO;;# %%
340::COMO;;# The Bayesian estimation approach also allows us to compute how uncertain we
341::COMO;;# are about our estimation of the difference. This can be calculated using
342::COMO;;# credible intervals. For a given probability, they show the range of values
343::COMO;;# that the estimated quantity, in our case the mean difference in
344::COMO;;# performance, can take.
345::COMO;;# For example, a 50% credible interval [x, y] tells us that there is a 50%
346::COMO;;# probability that the true (mean) difference of performance between models is
347::COMO;;# between x and y.
348::COMO;;#
349::COMO;;# Let's determine the credible intervals of our data using 50%, 75% and 95%:
359::COMO;;# %%
360::COMO;;# As shown in the table, there is a 50% probability that the true mean
361::COMO;;# difference between models will be between 0.000977 and 0.019023, 70%
362::COMO;;# probability that it will be between -0.005422 and 0.025422, and 95%
363::COMO;;# probability that it will be between -0.016445 and 0.036445.
364::COMO;;# %%
365::COMO;;# Pairwise comparison of all models: frequentist approach
366::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------
367::COMO;;#
368::COMO;;# We could also be interested in comparing the performance of all our models
369::COMO;;# evaluated with :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`. In this case
370::COMO;;# we would be running our statistical test multiple times, which leads us to
371::COMO;;# the `multiple comparisons problem
372::COMO;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_comparisons_problem>`_.
373::COMO;;#
374::COMO;;# There are many possible ways to tackle this problem, but a standard approach
375::COMO;;# is to apply a `Bonferroni correction
376::COMO;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonferroni_correction>`_. Bonferroni can be
377::COMO;;# computed by multiplying the p-value by the number of comparisons we are
378::COMO;;# testing.
379::COMO;;#
380::COMO;;# Let's compare the performance of the models using the corrected t-test:
392::COMC;;p_val *= n_comparisons # implement Bonferroni correction
393::COMO;;# Bonferroni can output p-values higher than 1
402::COMO;;# %%
403::COMO;;# We observe that after correcting for multiple comparisons, the only model
404::COMO;;# that significantly differs from the others is `'2_poly'`.
405::COMO;;# `'rbf'`, the model ranked first by
406::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`, does not significantly
407::COMO;;# differ from `'linear'` or `'3_poly'`.
408::COMO;;# %%
409::COMO;;# Pairwise comparison of all models: Bayesian approach
410::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------------
411::COMO;;#
412::COMO;;# When using Bayesian estimation to compare multiple models, we don't need to
413::COMO;;# correct for multiple comparisons (for reasons why see [4]_).
414::COMO;;#
415::COMO;;# We can carry out our pairwise comparisons the same way as in the first
416::COMO;;# section:
434::COMO;;# %%
435::COMO;;# Using the Bayesian approach we can compute the probability that a model
436::COMO;;# performs better, worse or practically equivalent to another.
437::COMO;;#
438::COMO;;# Results show that the model ranked first by
439::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` `'rbf'`, has approximately a
440::COMO;;# 6.8% chance of being worse than `'linear'`, and a 1.8% chance of being worse
441::COMO;;# than `'3_poly'`.
442::COMO;;# `'rbf'` and `'linear'` have a 43% probability of being practically
443::COMO;;# equivalent, while `'rbf'` and `'3_poly'` have a 10% chance of being so.
444::COMO;;#
445::COMO;;# Similarly to the conclusions obtained using the frequentist approach, all
446::COMO;;# models have a 100% probability of being better than `'2_poly'`, and none have
447::COMO;;# a practically equivalent performance with the latter.
448::COMO;;# %%
449::COMO;;# Take-home messages
450::COMO;;# ------------------
451::COMO;;# - Small differences in performance measures might easily turn out to be
452::COMO;;# merely by chance, but not because one model predicts systematically better
453::COMO;;# than the other. As shown in this example, statistics can tell you how
454::COMO;;# likely that is.
455::COMO;;# - When statistically comparing the performance of two models evaluated in
456::COMO;;# GridSearchCV, it is necessary to correct the calculated variance which
457::COMO;;# could be underestimated since the scores of the models are not independent
458::COMO;;# from each other.
459::COMO;;# - A frequentist approach that uses a (variance-corrected) paired t-test can
460::COMO;;# tell us if the performance of one model is better than another with a
461::COMO;;# degree of certainty above chance.
462::COMO;;# - A Bayesian approach can provide the probabilities of one model being
463::COMO;;# better, worse or practically equivalent than another. It can also tell us
464::COMO;;# how confident we are of knowing that the true differences of our models
465::COMO;;# fall under a certain range of values.
466::COMO;;# - If multiple models are statistically compared, a multiple comparisons
467::COMO;;# correction is needed when using the frequentist approach.
468::COMO;;# %%

61::COMO;;# %%
62::COMO;;# We define a grid of hyperparameters to be explored by the
63::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RandomizedSearchCV`. Using a
64::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` instead would explore all the
65::COMO;;# possible combinations on the grid, which can be costly to compute, whereas the
66::COMO;;# parameter `n_iter` of the :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RandomizedSearchCV`
67::COMO;;# controls the number of different random combination that are evaluated. Notice
68::COMO;;# that setting `n_iter` larger than the number of possible combinations in a
69::COMO;;# grid would lead to repeating already-explored combinations. We search for the
70::COMO;;# best parameter combination for both the feature extraction (`vect__`) and the
71::COMO;;# classifier (`clf__`).
76::COMC;;"vect__ngram_range": ((1, 1), (1, 2)), # unigrams or bigrams
80::COMO;;# %%
81::COMO;;# In this case `n_iter=40` is not an exhaustive search of the hyperparameters'
82::COMO;;# grid. In practice it would be interesting to increase the parameter `n_iter`
83::COMO;;# to get a more informative analysis. As a consequence, the computional time
84::COMO;;# increases. We can reduce it by taking advantage of the parallelisation over
85::COMO;;# the parameter combinations evaluation by increasing the number of CPUs used
86::COMO;;# via the parameter `n_jobs`.

216::COMM;;# the top performing models do not seem to depend on the regularization `norm`,
217::COMM;;# but they do depend on a trade-off between `max_df`, `min_df` and the
218::COMM;;# regularization strength `alpha`. The reason is that including noisy features
219::COMM;;# (i.e. `max_df` close to :math:`1.0` or `min_df` close to :math:`0`) tend to
220::COMM;;# overfit and therefore require a stronger regularization to compensate. Having
221::COMM;;# less features require less regularization and less scoring time.
222::COMM;;#
223::COMM;;# The best accuracy scores are obtained when `alpha` is between :math:`10^{-6}`
224::COMM;;# and :math:`10^0`, regardless of the hyperparameter `norm`.
2::COMM;;=========================================================
3::COMM;;Plotting Learning Curves and Checking Models' Scalability
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we show how to use the class
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.LearningCurveDisplay` to easily plot learning
7::COMM;;curves. In addition, we give an interpretation to the learning curves obtained
8::COMM;;for a naive Bayes and SVM classifiers.
9::COMM;;Then, we explore and draw some conclusions about the scalability of these predictive
10::COMM;;models by looking at their computational cost and not only at their statistical
11::COMM;;accuracy.
13::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
14::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
15::COMO;;# %%
16::COMO;;# Learning Curve
17::COMO;;# ==============
18::COMO;;#
19::COMO;;# Learning curves show the effect of adding more samples during the training
20::COMO;;# process. The effect is depicted by checking the statistical performance of
21::COMO;;# the model in terms of training score and testing score.
22::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# Here, we compute the learning curve of a naive Bayes classifier and a SVM
24::COMO;;# classifier with a RBF kernel using the digits dataset.
31::COMO;;# %%
32::COMO;;# The :meth:`~sklearn.model_selection.LearningCurveDisplay.from_estimator`
33::COMO;;# displays the learning curve given the dataset and the predictive model to
34::COMO;;# analyze. To get an estimate of the scores uncertainty, this method uses
35::COMO;;# a cross-validation procedure.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# We first analyze the learning curve of the naive Bayes classifier. Its shape
58::COMO;;# can be found in more complex datasets very often: the training score is very
59::COMO;;# high when using few samples for training and decreases when increasing the
60::COMO;;# number of samples, whereas the test score is very low at the beginning and
61::COMO;;# then increases when adding samples. The training and test scores become more
62::COMO;;# realistic when all the samples are used for training.
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# We see another typical learning curve for the SVM classifier with RBF kernel.
65::COMO;;# The training score remains high regardless of the size of the training set.
66::COMO;;# On the other hand, the test score increases with the size of the training
67::COMO;;# dataset. Indeed, it increases up to a point where it reaches a plateau.
68::COMO;;# Observing such a plateau is an indication that it might not be useful to
69::COMO;;# acquire new data to train the model since the generalization performance of
70::COMO;;# the model will not increase anymore.
71::COMO;;#
72::COMO;;# Complexity analysis
73::COMO;;# ===================
74::COMO;;#
75::COMO;;# In addition to these learning curves, it is also possible to look at the
76::COMO;;# scalability of the predictive models in terms of training and scoring times.
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;# The :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.LearningCurveDisplay` class does not
79::COMO;;# provide such information. We need to resort to the
80::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.learning_curve` function instead and make
81::COMO;;# the plot manually.
82::COMO;;# %%
98::COMO;;# %%
107::COMO;;# scalability regarding the fit time
119::COMO;;# scalability regarding the score time
129::COMO;;# %%
130::COMO;;# We see that the scalability of the SVM and naive Bayes classifiers is very
131::COMO;;# different. The SVM classifier complexity at fit and score time increases
132::COMO;;# rapidly with the number of samples. Indeed, it is known that the fit time
133::COMO;;# complexity of this classifier is more than quadratic with the number of
134::COMO;;# samples which makes it hard to scale to dataset with more than a few
135::COMO;;# 10,000 samples. In contrast, the naive Bayes classifier scales much better
136::COMO;;# with a lower complexity at fit and score time.
137::COMO;;#
138::COMO;;# Subsequently, we can check the trade-off between increased training time and
139::COMO;;# the cross-validation score.
140::COMO;;# %%
162::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# In these plots, we can look for the inflection point for which the
164::COMO;;# cross-validation score does not increase anymore and only the training time
165::COMO;;# increases.
2::COMM;;=============================================================
3::COMM;;Class Likelihood Ratios to measure classification performance
4::COMM;;=============================================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates the :func:`~sklearn.metrics.class_likelihood_ratios`
6::COMM;;function, which computes the positive and negative likelihood ratios (`LR+`,
7::COMM;;`LR-`) to assess the predictive power of a binary classifier. As we will see,
8::COMM;;these metrics are independent of the proportion between classes in the test set,
9::COMM;;which makes them very useful when the available data for a study has a different
10::COMM;;class proportion than the target application.
11::COMM;;A typical use is a case-control study in medicine, which has nearly balanced
12::COMM;;classes while the general population has large class imbalance. In such
13::COMM;;application, the pre-test probability of an individual having the target
14::COMM;;condition can be chosen to be the prevalence, i.e. the proportion of a
15::COMM;;particular population found to be affected by a medical condition. The post-test
16::COMM;;probabilities represent then the probability that the condition is truly present
17::COMM;;given a positive test result.
18::COMM;;In this example we first discuss the link between pre-test and post-test odds
19::COMM;;given by the :ref:`class_likelihood_ratios`. Then we evaluate their behavior in
20::COMM;;some controlled scenarios. In the last section we plot them as a function of the
21::COMM;;prevalence of the positive class.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Pre-test vs. post-test analysis
27::COMO;;# ===============================
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# Suppose we have a population of subjects with physiological measurements `X`
30::COMO;;# that can hopefully serve as indirect bio-markers of the disease and actual
31::COMO;;# disease indicators `y` (ground truth). Most of the people in the population do
32::COMO;;# not carry the disease but a minority (in this case around 10%) does:
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# A machine learning model is built to diagnose if a person with some given
38::COMO;;# physiological measurements is likely to carry the disease of interest. To
39::COMO;;# evaluate the model, we need to assess its performance on a held-out test set:
42::COMO;;# %%
43::COMO;;# Then we can fit our diagnosis model and compute the positive likelihood
44::COMO;;# ratio to evaluate the usefulness of this classifier as a disease diagnosis
45::COMO;;# tool:
52::COMO;;# %%
53::COMO;;# Since the positive class likelihood ratio is much larger than 1.0, it means
54::COMO;;# that the machine learning-based diagnosis tool is useful: the post-test odds
55::COMO;;# that the condition is truly present given a positive test result are more than
56::COMO;;# 12 times larger than the pre-test odds.
57::COMO;;#
58::COMO;;# Cross-validation of likelihood ratios
59::COMO;;# =====================================
60::COMO;;#
61::COMO;;# We assess the variability of the measurements for the class likelihood ratios
62::COMO;;# in some particular cases.
76::COMO;;# %%
77::COMO;;# We first validate the :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` model
78::COMO;;# with default hyperparameters as used in the previous section.
82::COMO;;# %%
83::COMO;;# We confirm that the model is useful: the post-test odds are between 12 and 20
84::COMO;;# times larger than the pre-test odds.
85::COMO;;#
86::COMO;;# On the contrary, let's consider a dummy model that will output random
87::COMO;;# predictions with similar odds as the average disease prevalence in the
88::COMO;;# training set:
92::COMO;;# %%
93::COMO;;# Here both class likelihood ratios are compatible with 1.0 which makes this
94::COMO;;# classifier useless as a diagnostic tool to improve disease detection.
95::COMO;;#
96::COMO;;# Another option for the dummy model is to always predict the most frequent
97::COMO;;# class, which in this case is "no-disease".
100::COMO;;# %%
101::COMO;;# The absence of positive predictions means there will be no true positives nor
102::COMO;;# false positives, leading to an undefined `LR+` that by no means should be
103::COMO;;# interpreted as an infinite `LR+` (the classifier perfectly identifying
104::COMO;;# positive cases). In such situation the
105::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.class_likelihood_ratios` function returns `nan` and
106::COMO;;# raises a warning by default. Indeed, the value of `LR-` helps us discard this
107::COMO;;# model.
108::COMO;;#
109::COMO;;# A similar scenario may arise when cross-validating highly imbalanced data with
110::COMO;;# few samples: some folds will have no samples with the disease and therefore
111::COMO;;# they will output no true positives nor false negatives when used for testing.
112::COMO;;# Mathematically this leads to an infinite `LR+`, which should also not be
113::COMO;;# interpreted as the model perfectly identifying positive cases. Such event
114::COMO;;# leads to a higher variance of the estimated likelihood ratios, but can still
115::COMO;;# be interpreted as an increment of the post-test odds of having the condition.
119::COMO;;# %%
120::COMO;;# Invariance with respect to prevalence
121::COMO;;# =====================================
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# The likelihood ratios are independent of the disease prevalence and can be
124::COMO;;# extrapolated between populations regardless of any possible class imbalance,
125::COMO;;# **as long as the same model is applied to all of them**. Notice that in the
126::COMO;;# plots below **the decision boundary is constant** (see
127::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_svm_plot_separating_hyperplane_unbalanced.py` for
128::COMO;;# a study of the boundary decision for unbalanced classes).
129::COMO;;#
130::COMO;;# Here we train a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` base model
131::COMO;;# on a case-control study with a prevalence of 50%. It is then evaluated over
132::COMO;;# populations with varying prevalence. We use the
133::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.make_classification` function to ensure the
134::COMO;;# data-generating process is always the same as shown in the plots below. The
135::COMO;;# label `1` corresponds to the positive class "disease", whereas the label `0`
136::COMO;;# stands for "no-disease".
151::COMO;;# fit and evaluate base model on balanced classes
157::COMO;;# %%
158::COMO;;# We will now show the decision boundary for each level of prevalence. Note that
159::COMO;;# we only plot a subset of the original data to better assess the linear model
160::COMO;;# decision boundary.
