2::COMM;;=========================================
3::COMM;;Nested versus non-nested cross-validation
4::COMM;;=========================================
5::COMM;;This example compares non-nested and nested cross-validation strategies on a
6::COMM;;classifier of the iris data set. Nested cross-validation (CV) is often used to
7::COMM;;train a model in which hyperparameters also need to be optimized. Nested CV
8::COMM;;estimates the generalization error of the underlying model and its
9::COMM;;(hyper)parameter search. Choosing the parameters that maximize non-nested CV
10::COMM;;biases the model to the dataset, yielding an overly-optimistic score.
11::COMM;;Model selection without nested CV uses the same data to tune model parameters
12::COMM;;and evaluate model performance. Information may thus "leak" into the model
13::COMM;;and overfit the data. The magnitude of this effect is primarily dependent on
14::COMM;;the size of the dataset and the stability of the model. See Cawley and Talbot
15::COMM;;[1]_ for an analysis of these issues.
16::COMM;;To avoid this problem, nested CV effectively uses a series of
17::COMM;;train/validation/test set splits. In the inner loop (here executed by
18::COMM;;:class:`GridSearchCV <sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV>`), the score is
19::COMM;;approximately maximized by fitting a model to each training set, and then
20::COMM;;directly maximized in selecting (hyper)parameters over the validation set. In
21::COMM;;the outer loop (here in :func:`cross_val_score
22::COMM;;<sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score>`), generalization error is estimated
23::COMM;;by averaging test set scores over several dataset splits.
24::COMM;;The example below uses a support vector classifier with a non-linear kernel to
25::COMM;;build a model with optimized hyperparameters by grid search. We compare the
26::COMM;;performance of non-nested and nested CV strategies by taking the difference
27::COMM;;between their scores.
28::COMM;;.. seealso::
29::COMM;;- :ref:`cross_validation`
30::COMM;;- :ref:`grid_search`
31::COMM;;.. rubric:: References
32::COMM;;.. [1] `Cawley, G.C.; Talbot, N.L.C. On over-fitting in model selection and
33::COMM;;subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation.
34::COMM;;J. Mach. Learn. Res 2010,11, 2079-2107.
35::COMM;;<http://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume11/cawley10a/cawley10a.pdf>`_
37::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
38::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
44::COMO;;# Number of random trials
46::COMO;;# Load the dataset
50::COMO;;# Set up possible values of parameters to optimize over
52::COMO;;# We will use a Support Vector Classifier with "rbf" kernel
54::COMO;;# Arrays to store scores
57::COMO;;# Loop for each trial
59::COMO;;# Choose cross-validation techniques for the inner and outer loops,
60::COMO;;# independently of the dataset.
61::COMO;;# E.g "GroupKFold", "LeaveOneOut", "LeaveOneGroupOut", etc.

2::COMM;;=================================================================
3::COMM;;Test with permutations the significance of a classification score
4::COMM;;=================================================================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates the use of
6::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.model_selection.permutation_test_score` to evaluate the
7::COMM;;significance of a cross-validated score using permutations.
9::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
10::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
11::COMO;;# %%
12::COMO;;# Dataset
13::COMO;;# -------
14::COMO;;#
15::COMO;;# We will use the :ref:`iris_dataset`, which consists of measurements taken
16::COMO;;# from 3 Iris species. Our model will use the measurements to predict
17::COMO;;# the iris species.
22::COMO;;# %%
23::COMO;;# For comparison, we also generate some random feature data (i.e., 20 features),
24::COMO;;# uncorrelated with the class labels in the iris dataset.
28::COMO;;# Use same number of samples as in iris and 20 features
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# Permutation test score
32::COMO;;# ----------------------
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# Next, we calculate the
35::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.permutation_test_score` for both, the original
36::COMO;;# iris dataset (where there's a strong relationship between features and labels) and
37::COMO;;# the randomly generated features with iris labels (where no dependency between features
38::COMO;;# and labels is expected). We use the
39::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` classifier and :ref:`accuracy_score` to evaluate
40::COMO;;# the model at each round.
41::COMO;;#
42::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.permutation_test_score` generates a null
43::COMO;;# distribution by calculating the accuracy of the classifier
44::COMO;;# on 1000 different permutations of the dataset, where features
45::COMO;;# remain the same but labels undergo different random permutations. This is the
46::COMO;;# distribution for the null hypothesis which states there is no dependency
47::COMO;;# between the features and labels. An empirical p-value is then calculated as
48::COMO;;# the proportion of permutations, for which the score obtained by the model trained on
49::COMO;;# the permutation, is greater than or equal to the score obtained using the original
50::COMO;;# data.
61::COMO;;# %%
62::COMO;;# Original data
63::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
64::COMO;;#
65::COMO;;# Below we plot a histogram of the permutation scores (the null
66::COMO;;# distribution). The red line indicates the score obtained by the classifier
67::COMO;;# on the original data (without permuted labels). The score is much better than those
68::COMO;;# obtained by using permuted data and the p-value is thus very low. This indicates that
69::COMO;;# there is a low likelihood that this good score would be obtained by chance
70::COMO;;# alone. It provides evidence that the iris dataset contains real dependency
71::COMO;;# between features and labels and the classifier was able to utilize this
72::COMO;;# to obtain good results. The low p-value can lead us to reject the null hypothesis.
83::COMO;;# %%
84::COMO;;# Random data
85::COMO;;# ^^^^^^^^^^^
86::COMO;;#
87::COMO;;# Below we plot the null distribution for the randomized data. The permutation
88::COMO;;# scores are similar to those obtained using the original iris dataset
89::COMO;;# because the permutation always destroys any feature-label dependency present.
90::COMO;;# The score obtained on the randomized data in this case
91::COMO;;# though, is very poor. This results in a large p-value, confirming that there was no
92::COMO;;# feature-label dependency in the randomized data.
104::COMO;;# %%
105::COMO;;# Another possible reason for obtaining a high p-value could be that the classifier
106::COMO;;# was not able to use the structure in the data. In this case, the p-value
107::COMO;;# would only be low for classifiers that are able to utilize the dependency
108::COMO;;# present. In our case above, where the data is random, all classifiers would
109::COMO;;# have a high p-value as there is no structure present in the data. We might or might
110::COMO;;# not fail to reject the null hypothesis depending on whether the p-value is high on a
111::COMO;;# more appropriate estimator as well.
112::COMO;;#
113::COMO;;# Finally, note that this test has been shown to produce low p-values even
114::COMO;;# if there is only weak structure in the data [1]_.
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# .. rubric:: References
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# .. [1] Ojala and Garriga. `Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier
119::COMO;;# Performance
120::COMO;;# <http://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume11/ojala10a/ojala10a.pdf>`_. The
121::COMO;;# Journal of Machine Learning Research (2010) vol. 11
122::COMO;;#
2::COMM;;================
3::COMM;;Precision-Recall
4::COMM;;================
5::COMM;;Example of Precision-Recall metric to evaluate classifier output quality.
6::COMM;;Precision-Recall is a useful measure of success of prediction when the
7::COMM;;classes are very imbalanced. In information retrieval, precision is a
8::COMM;;measure of the fraction of relevant items among actually returned items while recall
9::COMM;;is a measure of the fraction of items that were returned among all items that should
10::COMM;;have been returned. 'Relevancy' here refers to items that are
11::COMM;;positively labeled, i.e., true positives and false negatives.
12::COMM;;Precision (:math:`P`) is defined as the number of true positives (:math:`T_p`)
13::COMM;;over the number of true positives plus the number of false positives
14::COMM;;(:math:`F_p`).
15::COMM;;.. math::
16::COMM;;P = \\frac{T_p}{T_p+F_p}
17::COMM;;Recall (:math:`R`) is defined as the number of true positives (:math:`T_p`)
18::COMM;;over the number of true positives plus the number of false negatives
19::COMM;;(:math:`F_n`).
20::COMM;;.. math::
21::COMM;;R = \\frac{T_p}{T_p + F_n}
22::COMM;;The precision-recall curve shows the tradeoff between precision and
23::COMM;;recall for different thresholds. A high area under the curve represents
24::COMM;;both high recall and high precision. High precision is achieved by having
25::COMM;;few false positives in the returned results, and high recall is achieved by
26::COMM;;having few false negatives in the relevant results.
27::COMM;;High scores for both show that the classifier is returning
28::COMM;;accurate results (high precision), as well as returning a majority of all relevant
29::COMM;;results (high recall).
30::COMM;;A system with high recall but low precision returns most of the relevant items, but
31::COMM;;the proportion of returned results that are incorrectly labeled is high. A
32::COMM;;system with high precision but low recall is just the opposite, returning very
33::COMM;;few of the relevant items, but most of its predicted labels are correct when compared
34::COMM;;to the actual labels. An ideal system with high precision and high recall will
35::COMM;;return most of the relevant items, with most results labeled correctly.
36::COMM;;The definition of precision (:math:`\\frac{T_p}{T_p + F_p}`) shows that lowering
37::COMM;;the threshold of a classifier may increase the denominator, by increasing the
38::COMM;;number of results returned. If the threshold was previously set too high, the
39::COMM;;new results may all be true positives, which will increase precision. If the
40::COMM;;previous threshold was about right or too low, further lowering the threshold
41::COMM;;will introduce false positives, decreasing precision.
42::COMM;;Recall is defined as :math:`\\frac{T_p}{T_p+F_n}`, where :math:`T_p+F_n` does
43::COMM;;not depend on the classifier threshold. Changing the classifier threshold can only
44::COMM;;change the numerator, :math:`T_p`. Lowering the classifier
45::COMM;;threshold may increase recall, by increasing the number of true positive
46::COMM;;results. It is also possible that lowering the threshold may leave recall
47::COMM;;unchanged, while the precision fluctuates. Thus, precision does not necessarily
48::COMM;;decrease with recall.
49::COMM;;The relationship between recall and precision can be observed in the
50::COMM;;stairstep area of the plot - at the edges of these steps a small change
51::COMM;;in the threshold considerably reduces precision, with only a minor gain in
52::COMM;;recall.
53::COMM;;**Average precision** (AP) summarizes such a plot as the weighted mean of
54::COMM;;precisions achieved at each threshold, with the increase in recall from the
55::COMM;;previous threshold used as the weight:
56::COMM;;:math:`\\text{AP} = \\sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1}) P_n`
57::COMM;;where :math:`P_n` and :math:`R_n` are the precision and recall at the
58::COMM;;nth threshold. A pair :math:`(R_k, P_k)` is referred to as an
59::COMM;;*operating point*.
60::COMM;;AP and the trapezoidal area under the operating points
61::COMM;;(:func:`sklearn.metrics.auc`) are common ways to summarize a precision-recall
62::COMM;;curve that lead to different results. Read more in the
63::COMM;;:ref:`User Guide <precision_recall_f_measure_metrics>`.
64::COMM;;Precision-recall curves are typically used in binary classification to study
65::COMM;;the output of a classifier. In order to extend the precision-recall curve and
66::COMM;;average precision to multi-class or multi-label classification, it is necessary
67::COMM;;to binarize the output. One curve can be drawn per label, but one can also draw
68::COMM;;a precision-recall curve by considering each element of the label indicator
69::COMM;;matrix as a binary prediction (:ref:`micro-averaging <average>`).
70::COMM;;.. note::
71::COMM;;See also :func:`sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score`,
72::COMM;;:func:`sklearn.metrics.recall_score`,
73::COMM;;:func:`sklearn.metrics.precision_score`,
74::COMM;;:func:`sklearn.metrics.f1_score`
76::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
77::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;==================================================
3::COMM;;Multiclass Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;This example describes the use of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC)
6::COMM;;metric to evaluate the quality of multiclass classifiers.
7::COMM;;ROC curves typically feature true positive rate (TPR) on the Y axis, and false
8::COMM;;positive rate (FPR) on the X axis. This means that the top left corner of the
9::COMM;;plot is the "ideal" point - a FPR of zero, and a TPR of one. This is not very
10::COMM;;realistic, but it does mean that a larger area under the curve (AUC) is usually
11::COMM;;better. The "steepness" of ROC curves is also important, since it is ideal to
12::COMM;;maximize the TPR while minimizing the FPR.
13::COMM;;ROC curves are typically used in binary classification, where the TPR and FPR
14::COMM;;can be defined unambiguously. In the case of multiclass classification, a notion
15::COMM;;of TPR or FPR is obtained only after binarizing the output. This can be done in
16::COMM;;2 different ways:
17::COMM;;- the One-vs-Rest scheme compares each class against all the others (assumed as
18::COMM;;one);
19::COMM;;- the One-vs-One scheme compares every unique pairwise combination of classes.
20::COMM;;In this example we explore both schemes and demo the concepts of micro and macro
21::COMM;;averaging as different ways of summarizing the information of the multiclass ROC
22::COMM;;curves.
23::COMM;;.. note::
24::COMM;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_roc_crossval.py` for
25::COMM;;an extension of the present example estimating the variance of the ROC
26::COMM;;curves and their respective AUC.
28::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
29::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# Load and prepare data
32::COMO;;# =====================
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# We import the :ref:`iris_dataset` which contains 3 classes, each one
35::COMO;;# corresponding to a type of iris plant. One class is linearly separable from
36::COMO;;# the other 2; the latter are **not** linearly separable from each other.
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# Here we binarize the output and add noisy features to make the problem harder.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# We train a :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` model which can
58::COMO;;# naturally handle multiclass problems, thanks to the use of the multinomial
59::COMO;;# formulation.
63::COMO;;# %%
64::COMO;;# One-vs-Rest multiclass ROC
65::COMO;;# ==========================
66::COMO;;#
67::COMO;;# The One-vs-the-Rest (OvR) multiclass strategy, also known as one-vs-all,
68::COMO;;# consists in computing a ROC curve per each of the `n_classes`. In each step, a
69::COMO;;# given class is regarded as the positive class and the remaining classes are
70::COMO;;# regarded as the negative class as a bulk.
71::COMO;;#
72::COMO;;# .. note:: One should not confuse the OvR strategy used for the **evaluation**
73::COMO;;# of multiclass classifiers with the OvR strategy used to **train** a
74::COMO;;# multiclass classifier by fitting a set of binary classifiers (for instance
75::COMO;;# via the :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier` meta-estimator).
76::COMO;;# The OvR ROC evaluation can be used to scrutinize any kind of classification
77::COMO;;# models irrespectively of how they were trained (see :ref:`multiclass`).
78::COMO;;#
79::COMO;;# In this section we use a :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.LabelBinarizer` to
80::COMO;;# binarize the target by one-hot-encoding in a OvR fashion. This means that the
81::COMO;;# target of shape (`n_samples`,) is mapped to a target of shape (`n_samples`,
82::COMO;;# `n_classes`).
86::COMC;;y_onehot_test.shape # (n_samples, n_classes)
87::COMO;;# %%
88::COMO;;# We can as well easily check the encoding of a specific class:
90::COMO;;# %%
91::COMO;;# ROC curve showing a specific class
92::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
93::COMO;;#
94::COMO;;# In the following plot we show the resulting ROC curve when regarding the iris
95::COMO;;# flowers as either "virginica" (`class_id=2`) or "non-virginica" (the rest).
99::COMO;;# %%
115::COMO;;# %%
116::COMO;;# ROC curve using micro-averaged OvR
117::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
118::COMO;;#
119::COMO;;# Micro-averaging aggregates the contributions from all the classes (using
120::COMO;;# :func:`numpy.ravel`) to compute the average metrics as follows:
121::COMO;;#
122::COMO;;# :math:`TPR=\frac{\sum_{c}TP_c}{\sum_{c}(TP_c + FN_c)}` ;
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# :math:`FPR=\frac{\sum_{c}FP_c}{\sum_{c}(FP_c + TN_c)}` .
125::COMO;;#
126::COMO;;# We can briefly demo the effect of :func:`numpy.ravel`:
130::COMO;;# %%
131::COMO;;# In a multi-class classification setup with highly imbalanced classes,
132::COMO;;# micro-averaging is preferable over macro-averaging. In such cases, one can
133::COMO;;# alternatively use a weighted macro-averaging, not demonstrated here.
147::COMO;;# %%
148::COMO;;# In the case where the main interest is not the plot but the ROC-AUC score
149::COMO;;# itself, we can reproduce the value shown in the plot using
150::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score`.
159::COMO;;# %%
160::COMO;;# This is equivalent to computing the ROC curve with
161::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.roc_curve` and then the area under the curve with
162::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.auc` for the raveled true and predicted classes.
164::COMO;;# store the fpr, tpr, and roc_auc for all averaging strategies
166::COMO;;# Compute micro-average ROC curve and ROC area
170::COMO;;# %%
171::COMO;;# .. note:: By default, the computation of the ROC curve adds a single point at
172::COMO;;# the maximal false positive rate by using linear interpolation and the
173::COMO;;# McClish correction [:doi:`Analyzing a portion of the ROC curve Med Decis
174::COMO;;# Making. 1989 Jul-Sep; 9(3):190-5.<10.1177/0272989x8900900307>`].
175::COMO;;#
176::COMO;;# ROC curve using the OvR macro-average
177::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
178::COMO;;#
179::COMO;;# Obtaining the macro-average requires computing the metric independently for
180::COMO;;# each class and then taking the average over them, hence treating all classes
181::COMO;;# equally a priori. We first aggregate the true/false positive rates per class:
182::COMO;;#
183::COMO;;# :math:`TPR=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c}\frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}` ;
184::COMO;;#
185::COMO;;# :math:`FPR=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c}\frac{FP_c}{FP_c + TN_c}` .
186::COMO;;#
187::COMO;;# where `C` is the total number of classes.
192::COMO;;# Interpolate all ROC curves at these points
195::COMC;;mean_tpr += np.interp(fpr_grid, fpr[i], tpr[i]) # linear interpolation
196::COMO;;# Average it and compute AUC
202::COMO;;# %%
203::COMO;;# This computation is equivalent to simply calling
211::COMO;;# %%
212::COMO;;# Plot all OvR ROC curves together
213::COMO;;# --------------------------------
248::COMO;;# %%
249::COMO;;# One-vs-One multiclass ROC
250::COMO;;# =========================
251::COMO;;#
252::COMO;;# The One-vs-One (OvO) multiclass strategy consists in fitting one classifier
253::COMO;;# per class pair. Since it requires to train `n_classes` * (`n_classes` - 1) / 2
254::COMO;;# classifiers, this method is usually slower than One-vs-Rest due to its
255::COMO;;# O(`n_classes` ^2) complexity.
256::COMO;;#
257::COMO;;# In this section, we demonstrate the macro-averaged AUC using the OvO scheme
258::COMO;;# for the 3 possible combinations in the :ref:`iris_dataset`: "setosa" vs
259::COMO;;# "versicolor", "versicolor" vs "virginica" and "virginica" vs "setosa". Notice
260::COMO;;# that micro-averaging is not defined for the OvO scheme.
261::COMO;;#
262::COMO;;# ROC curve using the OvO macro-average
263::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
264::COMO;;#
265::COMO;;# In the OvO scheme, the first step is to identify all possible unique
266::COMO;;# combinations of pairs. The computation of scores is done by treating one of
267::COMO;;# the elements in a given pair as the positive class and the other element as
268::COMO;;# the negative class, then re-computing the score by inversing the roles and
269::COMO;;# taking the mean of both scores.
273::COMO;;# %%
320::COMO;;# %%
321::COMO;;# One can also assert that the macro-average we computed "by hand" is equivalent
322::COMO;;# to the implemented `average="macro"` option of the
323::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score` function.
331::COMO;;# %%
332::COMO;;# Plot all OvO ROC curves together
333::COMO;;# --------------------------------
360::COMO;;# %%
361::COMO;;# We confirm that the classes "versicolor" and "virginica" are not well
362::COMO;;# identified by a linear classifier. Notice that the "virginica"-vs-the-rest
363::COMO;;# ROC-AUC score (0.77) is between the OvO ROC-AUC scores for "versicolor" vs
364::COMO;;# "virginica" (0.64) and "setosa" vs "virginica" (0.90). Indeed, the OvO
365::COMO;;# strategy gives additional information on the confusion between a pair of
366::COMO;;# classes, at the expense of computational cost when the number of classes
367::COMO;;# is large.
368::COMO;;#
369::COMO;;# The OvO strategy is recommended if the user is mainly interested in correctly
370::COMO;;# identifying a particular class or subset of classes, whereas evaluating the
371::COMO;;# global performance of a classifier can still be summarized via a given
372::COMO;;# averaging strategy.
373::COMO;;#
374::COMO;;# When dealing with imbalanced datasets, choosing the appropriate metric based on
375::COMO;;# the business context or problem you are addressing is crucial.
376::COMO;;# It is also essential to select an appropriate averaging method (micro vs. macro)
377::COMO;;# depending on the desired outcome:
378::COMO;;#
379::COMO;;# - Micro-averaging aggregates metrics across all instances, treating each
380::COMO;;# individual instance equally, regardless of its class. This approach is useful
381::COMO;;# when evaluating overall performance, but note that it can be dominated by
382::COMO;;# the majority class in imbalanced datasets.
383::COMO;;#
384::COMO;;# - Macro-averaging calculates metrics for each class independently and then
385::COMO;;# averages them, giving equal weight to each class. This is particularly useful
386::COMO;;# when you want under-represented classes to be considered as important as highly
387::COMO;;# populated classes.
2::COMM;;=============================================================
3::COMM;;Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) with cross validation
4::COMM;;=============================================================
5::COMM;;This example presents how to estimate and visualize the variance of the Receiver
6::COMM;;Operating Characteristic (ROC) metric using cross-validation.
7::COMM;;ROC curves typically feature true positive rate (TPR) on the Y axis, and false
8::COMM;;positive rate (FPR) on the X axis. This means that the top left corner of the
9::COMM;;plot is the "ideal" point - a FPR of zero, and a TPR of one. This is not very
10::COMM;;realistic, but it does mean that a larger Area Under the Curve (AUC) is usually
11::COMM;;better. The "steepness" of ROC curves is also important, since it is ideal to
12::COMM;;maximize the TPR while minimizing the FPR.
13::COMM;;This example shows the ROC response of different datasets, created from K-fold
14::COMM;;cross-validation. Taking all of these curves, it is possible to calculate the
15::COMM;;mean AUC, and see the variance of the curve when the
16::COMM;;training set is split into different subsets. This roughly shows how the
17::COMM;;classifier output is affected by changes in the training data, and how different
18::COMM;;the splits generated by K-fold cross-validation are from one another.
19::COMM;;.. note::
20::COMM;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_roc.py` for a
21::COMM;;complement of the present example explaining the averaging strategies to
22::COMM;;generalize the metrics for multiclass classifiers.
24::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
25::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# Load and prepare data
28::COMO;;# =====================
29::COMO;;#
30::COMO;;# We import the :ref:`iris_dataset` which contains 3 classes, each one
31::COMO;;# corresponding to a type of iris plant. One class is linearly separable from
32::COMO;;# the other 2; the latter are **not** linearly separable from each other.
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# In the following we binarize the dataset by dropping the "virginica" class
35::COMO;;# (`class_id=2`). This means that the "versicolor" class (`class_id=1`) is
36::COMO;;# regarded as the positive class and "setosa" as the negative class
37::COMO;;# (`class_id=0`).
45::COMO;;# %%
46::COMO;;# We also add noisy features to make the problem harder.
49::COMO;;# %%
50::COMO;;# Classification and ROC analysis
51::COMO;;# -------------------------------
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# Here we run :func:`~sklearn.model_selection.cross_validate` on a
54::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` classifier, then use the computed cross-validation results
55::COMO;;# to plot the ROC curves fold-wise. Notice that the baseline to define the chance
56::COMO;;# level (dashed ROC curve) is a classifier that would always predict the most
57::COMO;;# frequent class.

2::COMM;;Successive Halving Iterations
3::COMM;;=============================
4::COMM;;This example illustrates how a successive halving search
5::COMM;;(:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.HalvingGridSearchCV` and
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.HalvingRandomSearchCV`)
7::COMM;;iteratively chooses the best parameter combination out of
8::COMM;;multiple candidates.
10::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
11::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMC;;from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv # noqa: F401
20::COMO;;# %%
21::COMO;;# We first define the parameter space and train a
22::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.HalvingRandomSearchCV` instance.
37::COMO;;# %%
38::COMO;;# We can now use the `cv_results_` attribute of the search estimator to inspect
39::COMO;;# and plot the evolution of the search.
58::COMO;;# %%
59::COMO;;# Number of candidates and amount of resource at each iteration
60::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------
61::COMO;;#
62::COMO;;# At the first iteration, a small amount of resources is used. The resource
63::COMO;;# here is the number of samples that the estimators are trained on. All
64::COMO;;# candidates are evaluated.
65::COMO;;#
66::COMO;;# At the second iteration, only the best half of the candidates is evaluated.
67::COMO;;# The number of allocated resources is doubled: candidates are evaluated on
68::COMO;;# twice as many samples.
69::COMO;;#
70::COMO;;# This process is repeated until the last iteration, where only 2 candidates
71::COMO;;# are left. The best candidate is the candidate that has the best score at the
72::COMO;;# last iteration.
2::COMM;;=========================================================
3::COMM;;Effect of model regularization on training and test error
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we evaluate the impact of the regularization parameter in a
6::COMM;;linear model called :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet`. To carry out this
7::COMM;;evaluation, we use a validation curve using
8::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.ValidationCurveDisplay`. This curve shows the
9::COMM;;training and test scores of the model for different values of the regularization
10::COMM;;parameter.
11::COMM;;Once we identify the optimal regularization parameter, we compare the true and
12::COMM;;estimated coefficients of the model to determine if the model is able to recover
13::COMM;;the coefficients from the noisy input data.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMO;;# %%
18::COMO;;# Generate sample data
19::COMO;;# --------------------
20::COMO;;#
21::COMO;;# We generate a regression dataset that contains many features relative to the
22::COMO;;# number of samples. However, only 10% of the features are informative. In this context,
23::COMO;;# linear models exposing L1 penalization are commonly used to recover a sparse
24::COMO;;# set of coefficients.
40::COMO;;# %%
41::COMO;;# Model definition
42::COMO;;# ----------------
43::COMO;;#
44::COMO;;# Here, we do not use a model that only exposes an L1 penalty. Instead, we use
45::COMO;;# an :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet` model that exposes both L1 and L2
46::COMO;;# penalties.
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# We fix the `l1_ratio` parameter such that the solution found by the model is still
49::COMO;;# sparse. Therefore, this type of model tries to find a sparse solution but at the same
50::COMO;;# time also tries to shrink all coefficients towards zero.
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# In addition, we force the coefficients of the model to be positive since we know that
53::COMO;;# `make_regression` generates a response with a positive signal. So we use this
54::COMO;;# pre-knowledge to get a better model.
57::COMO;;# %%
58::COMO;;# Evaluate the impact of the regularization parameter
59::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
60::COMO;;#
61::COMO;;# To evaluate the impact of the regularization parameter, we use a validation
62::COMO;;# curve. This curve shows the training and test scores of the model for different
63::COMO;;# values of the regularization parameter.
64::COMO;;#
65::COMO;;# The regularization `alpha` is a parameter applied to the coefficients of the model:
66::COMO;;# when it tends to zero, no regularization is applied and the model tries to fit the
67::COMO;;# training data with the least amount of error. However, it leads to overfitting when
68::COMO;;# features are noisy. When `alpha` increases, the model coefficients are constrained,
69::COMO;;# and thus the model cannot fit the training data as closely, avoiding overfitting.
70::COMO;;# However, if too much regularization is applied, the model underfits the data and
71::COMO;;# is not able to properly capture the signal.
72::COMO;;#
73::COMO;;# The validation curve helps in finding a good trade-off between both extremes: the
74::COMO;;# model is not regularized and thus flexible enough to fit the signal, but not too
75::COMO;;# flexible to overfit. The :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.ValidationCurveDisplay`
76::COMO;;# allows us to display the training and validation scores across a range of alpha
77::COMO;;# values.
108::COMO;;# %%
109::COMO;;# To find the optimal regularization parameter, we can select the value of `alpha`
110::COMO;;# that maximizes the validation score.
111::COMO;;#
112::COMO;;# Coefficients comparison
113::COMO;;# -----------------------
114::COMO;;#
115::COMO;;# Now that we have identified the optimal regularization parameter, we can compare the
116::COMO;;# true coefficients and the estimated coefficients.
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# First, let's set the regularization parameter to the optimal value and fit the
119::COMO;;# model on the training data. In addition, we'll show the test score for this model.
124::COMO;;# %%
125::COMO;;# Now, we plot the true coefficients and the estimated coefficients.
140::COMO;;# %%
141::COMO;;# While the original coefficients are sparse, the estimated coefficients are not
142::COMO;;# as sparse. The reason is that we fixed the `l1_ratio` parameter to 0.9. We could
143::COMO;;# force the model to get a sparser solution by increasing the `l1_ratio` parameter.
144::COMO;;#
145::COMO;;# However, we observed that for the estimated coefficients that are close to zero in
146::COMO;;# the true generative model, our model shrinks them towards zero. So we don't recover
147::COMO;;# the true coefficients, but we get a sensible outcome in line with the performance
148::COMO;;# obtained on the test set.
2::COMM;;======================================================
3::COMM;;Post-hoc tuning the cut-off point of decision function
4::COMM;;======================================================
5::COMM;;Once a binary classifier is trained, the :term:`predict` method outputs class label
6::COMM;;predictions corresponding to a thresholding of either the :term:`decision_function` or
7::COMM;;the :term:`predict_proba` output. The default threshold is defined as a posterior
8::COMM;;probability estimate of 0.5 or a decision score of 0.0. However, this default strategy
9::COMM;;may not be optimal for the task at hand.
10::COMM;;This example shows how to use the
11::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` to tune the decision
12::COMM;;threshold, depending on a metric of interest.
14::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
15::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# The diabetes dataset
18::COMO;;# --------------------
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# To illustrate the tuning of the decision threshold, we will use the diabetes dataset.
21::COMO;;# This dataset is available on OpenML: https://www.openml.org/d/37. We use the
22::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml` function to fetch this dataset.
26::COMO;;# %%
27::COMO;;# We look at the target to understand the type of problem we are dealing with.
29::COMO;;# %%
30::COMO;;# We can see that we are dealing with a binary classification problem. Since the
31::COMO;;# labels are not encoded as 0 and 1, we make it explicit that we consider the class
32::COMO;;# labeled "tested_negative" as the negative class (which is also the most frequent)
33::COMO;;# and the class labeled "tested_positive" the positive as the positive class:
35::COMO;;# %%
36::COMO;;# We can also observe that this binary problem is slightly imbalanced where we have
37::COMO;;# around twice more samples from the negative class than from the positive class. When
38::COMO;;# it comes to evaluation, we should consider this aspect to interpret the results.
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# Our vanilla classifier
41::COMO;;# ----------------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# We define a basic predictive model composed of a scaler followed by a logistic
44::COMO;;# regression classifier.
50::COMO;;# %%
51::COMO;;# We evaluate our model using cross-validation. We use the accuracy and the balanced
52::COMO;;# accuracy to report the performance of our model. The balanced accuracy is a metric
53::COMO;;# that is less sensitive to class imbalance and will allow us to put the accuracy
54::COMO;;# score in perspective.
55::COMO;;#
56::COMO;;# Cross-validation allows us to study the variance of the decision threshold across
57::COMO;;# different splits of the data. However, the dataset is rather small and it would be
58::COMO;;# detrimental to use more than 5 folds to evaluate the dispersion. Therefore, we use
59::COMO;;# a :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RepeatedStratifiedKFold` where we apply several
60::COMO;;# repetitions of 5-fold cross-validation.
83::COMO;;# %%
84::COMO;;# Our predictive model succeeds to grasp the relationship between the data and the
85::COMO;;# target. The training and testing scores are close to each other, meaning that our
86::COMO;;# predictive model is not overfitting. We can also observe that the balanced accuracy is
87::COMO;;# lower than the accuracy, due to the class imbalance previously mentioned.
88::COMO;;#
89::COMO;;# For this classifier, we let the decision threshold, used convert the probability of
90::COMO;;# the positive class into a class prediction, to its default value: 0.5. However, this
91::COMO;;# threshold might not be optimal. If our interest is to maximize the balanced accuracy,
92::COMO;;# we should select another threshold that would maximize this metric.
93::COMO;;#
94::COMO;;# The :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` meta-estimator allows
95::COMO;;# to tune the decision threshold of a classifier given a metric of interest.
96::COMO;;#
97::COMO;;# Tuning the decision threshold
98::COMO;;# -----------------------------
99::COMO;;#
100::COMO;;# We create a :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV` and
101::COMO;;# configure it to maximize the balanced accuracy. We evaluate the model using the same
102::COMO;;# cross-validation strategy as previously.
117::COMO;;# %%
118::COMO;;# In comparison with the vanilla model, we observe that the balanced accuracy score
119::COMO;;# increased. Of course, it comes at the cost of a lower accuracy score. It means that
120::COMO;;# our model is now more sensitive to the positive class but makes more mistakes on the
121::COMO;;# negative class.
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# However, it is important to note that this tuned predictive model is internally the
124::COMO;;# same model as the vanilla model: they have the same fitted coefficients.
141::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# Only the decision threshold of each model was changed during the cross-validation.
158::COMO;;# %%
159::COMO;;# In average, a decision threshold around 0.32 maximizes the balanced accuracy, which is
160::COMO;;# different from the default decision threshold of 0.5. Thus tuning the decision
161::COMO;;# threshold is particularly important when the output of the predictive model
162::COMO;;# is used to make decisions. Besides, the metric used to tune the decision threshold
163::COMO;;# should be chosen carefully. Here, we used the balanced accuracy but it might not be
164::COMO;;# the most appropriate metric for the problem at hand. The choice of the "right" metric
165::COMO;;# is usually problem-dependent and might require some domain knowledge. Refer to the
166::COMO;;# example entitled,
167::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_cost_sensitive_learning.py`,
168::COMO;;# for more details.
2::COMM;;============================
3::COMM;;Underfitting vs. Overfitting
4::COMM;;============================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates the problems of underfitting and overfitting and
6::COMM;;how we can use linear regression with polynomial features to approximate
7::COMM;;nonlinear functions. The plot shows the function that we want to approximate,
8::COMM;;which is a part of the cosine function. In addition, the samples from the
9::COMM;;real function and the approximations of different models are displayed. The
10::COMM;;models have polynomial features of different degrees. We can see that a
11::COMM;;linear function (polynomial with degree 1) is not sufficient to fit the
12::COMM;;training samples. This is called **underfitting**. A polynomial of degree 4
13::COMM;;approximates the true function almost perfectly. However, for higher degrees
14::COMM;;the model will **overfit** the training data, i.e. it learns the noise of the
15::COMM;;training data.
16::COMM;;We evaluate quantitatively **overfitting** / **underfitting** by using
17::COMM;;cross-validation. We calculate the mean squared error (MSE) on the validation
18::COMM;;set, the higher, the less likely the model generalizes correctly from the
19::COMM;;training data.
21::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
22::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
49::COMO;;# Evaluate the models using crossvalidation
2::COMM;;===============================================
3::COMM;;Overview of multiclass training meta-estimators
4::COMM;;===============================================
5::COMM;;In this example, we discuss the problem of classification when the target
6::COMM;;variable is composed of more than two classes. This is called multiclass
7::COMM;;classification.
8::COMM;;In scikit-learn, all estimators support multiclass classification out of the
9::COMM;;box: the most sensible strategy was implemented for the end-user. The
10::COMM;;:mod:`sklearn.multiclass` module implements various strategies that one can use
11::COMM;;for experimenting or developing third-party estimators that only support binary
12::COMM;;classification.
13::COMM;;:mod:`sklearn.multiclass` includes OvO/OvR strategies used to train a
14::COMM;;multiclass classifier by fitting a set of binary classifiers (the
15::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier` and
16::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier` meta-estimators). This example
17::COMM;;will review them.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# The Yeast UCI dataset
23::COMO;;# ---------------------
24::COMO;;#
25::COMO;;# In this example, we use a UCI dataset [1]_, generally referred as the Yeast
26::COMO;;# dataset. We use the :func:`sklearn.datasets.fetch_openml` function to load
27::COMO;;# the dataset from OpenML.
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# To know the type of data science problem we are dealing with, we can check
32::COMO;;# the target for which we want to build a predictive model.
34::COMO;;# %%
35::COMO;;# We see that the target is discrete and composed of 10 classes. We therefore
36::COMO;;# deal with a multiclass classification problem.
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# Strategies comparison
39::COMO;;# ---------------------
40::COMO;;#
41::COMO;;# In the following experiment, we use a
42::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` and a
43::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RepeatedStratifiedKFold` cross-validation
44::COMO;;# with 3 splits and 5 repetitions.
45::COMO;;#
46::COMO;;# We compare the following strategies:
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` can handle multiclass
49::COMO;;# classification without needing any special adjustments. It works by breaking
50::COMO;;# down the training data into smaller subsets and focusing on the most common
51::COMO;;# class in each subset. By repeating this process, the model can accurately
52::COMO;;# classify input data into multiple different classes.
53::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsOneClassifier` trains a set of binary
54::COMO;;# classifiers where each classifier is trained to distinguish between
55::COMO;;# two classes.
56::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`: trains a set of binary
57::COMO;;# classifiers where each classifier is trained to distinguish between
58::COMO;;# one class and the rest of the classes.
59::COMO;;# * :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OutputCodeClassifier`: trains a set of binary
60::COMO;;# classifiers where each classifier is trained to distinguish between
61::COMO;;# a set of classes from the rest of the classes. The set of classes is
62::COMO;;# defined by a codebook, which is randomly generated in scikit-learn. This
63::COMO;;# method exposes a parameter `code_size` to control the size of the codebook.
64::COMO;;# We set it above one since we are not interested in compressing the class
65::COMO;;# representation.
83::COMO;;# %%
84::COMO;;# We can now compare the statistical performance of the different strategies.
85::COMO;;# We plot the score distribution of the different strategies.
101::COMO;;# %%
102::COMO;;# At a first glance, we can see that the built-in strategy of the decision
103::COMO;;# tree classifier is working quite well. One-vs-one and the error-correcting
104::COMO;;# output code strategies are working even better. However, the
105::COMO;;# one-vs-rest strategy is not working as well as the other strategies.
106::COMO;;#
107::COMO;;# Indeed, these results reproduce something reported in the literature
108::COMO;;# as in [2]_. However, the story is not as simple as it seems.
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# The importance of hyperparameters search
111::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
112::COMO;;#
113::COMO;;# It was later shown in [3]_ that the multiclass strategies would show similar
114::COMO;;# scores if the hyperparameters of the base classifiers are first optimized.
115::COMO;;#
116::COMO;;# Here we try to reproduce such result by at least optimizing the depth of the
117::COMO;;# base decision tree.
143::COMO;;# %%
144::COMO;;# We can see that once the hyperparameters are optimized, all multiclass
145::COMO;;# strategies have similar performance as discussed in [3]_.
146::COMO;;#
147::COMO;;# Conclusion
148::COMO;;# ----------
149::COMO;;#
150::COMO;;# We can get some intuition behind those results.
151::COMO;;#
152::COMO;;# First, the reason for which one-vs-one and error-correcting output code are
153::COMO;;# outperforming the tree when the hyperparameters are not optimized relies on
154::COMO;;# fact that they ensemble a larger number of classifiers. The ensembling
155::COMO;;# improves the generalization performance. This is a bit similar why a bagging
156::COMO;;# classifier generally performs better than a single decision tree if no care
157::COMO;;# is taken to optimize the hyperparameters.
158::COMO;;#
159::COMO;;# Then, we see the importance of optimizing the hyperparameters. Indeed, it
160::COMO;;# should be regularly explored when developing predictive models even if
161::COMO;;# techniques such as ensembling help at reducing this impact.
162::COMO;;#
163::COMO;;# Finally, it is important to recall that the estimators in scikit-learn
164::COMO;;# are developed with a specific strategy to handle multiclass classification
165::COMO;;# out of the box. So for these estimators, it means that there is no need to
166::COMO;;# use different strategies. These strategies are mainly useful for third-party
167::COMO;;# estimators supporting only binary classification. In all cases, we also show
168::COMO;;# that the hyperparameters should be optimized.
169::COMO;;#
170::COMO;;# References
171::COMO;;# ----------
172::COMO;;#
173::COMO;;# .. [1] https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Yeast
174::COMO;;#
175::COMO;;# .. [2] `"Reducing multiclass to binary: A unifying approach for margin classifiers."
176::COMO;;# Allwein, Erin L., Robert E. Schapire, and Yoram Singer.
177::COMO;;# Journal of machine learning research. 1 Dec (2000): 113-141.
178::COMO;;# <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume1/allwein00a/allwein00a.pdf>`_
179::COMO;;#
180::COMO;;# .. [3] `"In defense of one-vs-all classification."
181::COMO;;# Journal of Machine Learning Research. 5 Jan (2004): 101-141.
182::COMO;;# <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume5/rifkin04a/rifkin04a.pdf>`_
2::COMM;;==================================================
3::COMM;;Multilabel classification using a classifier chain
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how to use :class:`~sklearn.multioutput.ClassifierChain` to solve
6::COMM;;a multilabel classification problem.
7::COMM;;The most naive strategy to solve such a task is to independently train a binary
8::COMM;;classifier on each label (i.e. each column of the target variable). At prediction
9::COMM;;time, the ensemble of binary classifiers is used to assemble multitask prediction.
10::COMM;;This strategy does not allow to model relationship between different tasks. The
11::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.multioutput.ClassifierChain` is the meta-estimator (i.e. an estimator
12::COMM;;taking an inner estimator) that implements a more advanced strategy. The ensemble
13::COMM;;of binary classifiers are used as a chain where the prediction of a classifier in the
14::COMM;;chain is used as a feature for training the next classifier on a new label. Therefore,
15::COMM;;these additional features allow each chain to exploit correlations among labels.
16::COMM;;The :ref:`Jaccard similarity <jaccard_similarity_score>` score for chain tends to be
17::COMM;;greater than that of the set independent base models.
19::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
20::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
21::COMO;;# %%
22::COMO;;# Loading a dataset
23::COMO;;# -----------------
24::COMO;;# For this example, we use the `yeast
25::COMO;;# <https://www.openml.org/d/40597>`_ dataset which contains
26::COMO;;# 2,417 datapoints each with 103 features and 14 possible labels. Each
27::COMO;;# data point has at least one label. As a baseline we first train a logistic
28::COMO;;# regression classifier for each of the 14 labels. To evaluate the performance of
29::COMO;;# these classifiers we predict on a held-out test set and calculate the
30::COMO;;# Jaccard similarity for each sample.
35::COMO;;# Load a multi-label dataset from https://www.openml.org/d/40597
39::COMO;;# %%
40::COMO;;# Fit models
41::COMO;;# ----------
42::COMO;;# We fit :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` wrapped by
43::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier` and ensemble of multiple
44::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.multioutput.ClassifierChain`.
45::COMO;;#
46::COMO;;# LogisticRegression wrapped by OneVsRestClassifier
47::COMO;;# **************************************************
48::COMO;;# Since by default :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` can't
49::COMO;;# handle data with multiple targets, we need to use
50::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`.
51::COMO;;# After fitting the model we calculate Jaccard similarity.
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# Chain of binary classifiers
62::COMO;;# ***************************
63::COMO;;# Because the models in each chain are arranged randomly there is significant
64::COMO;;# variation in performance among the chains. Presumably there is an optimal
65::COMO;;# ordering of the classes in a chain that will yield the best performance.
66::COMO;;# However, we do not know that ordering a priori. Instead, we can build a
67::COMO;;# voting ensemble of classifier chains by averaging the binary predictions of
68::COMO;;# the chains and apply a threshold of 0.5. The Jaccard similarity score of the
69::COMO;;# ensemble is greater than that of the independent models and tends to exceed
70::COMO;;# the score of each chain in the ensemble (although this is not guaranteed
71::COMO;;# with randomly ordered chains).
85::COMO;;# %%
86::COMO;;# Plot results
87::COMO;;# ------------
88::COMO;;# Plot the Jaccard similarity scores for the independent model, each of the
89::COMO;;# chains, and the ensemble (note that the vertical axis on this plot does
90::COMO;;# not begin at 0).
118::COMO;;# %%
119::COMO;;# Results interpretation
120::COMO;;# ----------------------
121::COMO;;# There are three main takeaways from this plot:
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# - Independent model wrapped by :class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`
124::COMO;;# performs worse than the ensemble of classifier chains and some of individual chains.
125::COMO;;# This is caused by the fact that the logistic regression doesn't model relationship
126::COMO;;# between the labels.
127::COMO;;# - :class:`~sklearn.multioutput.ClassifierChain` takes advantage of correlation
128::COMO;;# among labels but due to random nature of labels ordering, it could yield worse
129::COMO;;# result than an independent model.
130::COMO;;# - An ensemble of chains performs better because it not only captures relationship
131::COMO;;# between labels but also does not make strong assumptions about their correct order.
2::COMM;;=====================================
3::COMM;;Approximate nearest neighbors in TSNE
4::COMM;;=====================================
5::COMM;;This example presents how to chain KNeighborsTransformer and TSNE in a pipeline.
6::COMM;;It also shows how to wrap the packages `nmslib` and `pynndescent` to replace
7::COMM;;KNeighborsTransformer and perform approximate nearest neighbors. These packages
8::COMM;;can be installed with `pip install nmslib pynndescent`.
9::COMM;;Note: In KNeighborsTransformer we use the definition which includes each
10::COMM;;training point as its own neighbor in the count of `n_neighbors`, and for
11::COMM;;compatibility reasons, one extra neighbor is computed when `mode == 'distance'`.
12::COMM;;Please note that we do the same in the proposed `nmslib` wrapper.
14::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
15::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# First we try to import the packages and warn the user in case they are
18::COMO;;# missing.
30::COMO;;# %%
31::COMO;;# We define a wrapper class for implementing the scikit-learn API to the
32::COMO;;# `nmslib`, as well as a loading function.
41::COMM;;def __init__(self, n_neighbors=5, metric="euclidean", method="sw-graph", n_jobs=-1):
42::COMM;;self.n_neighbors = n_neighbors
43::COMM;;self.method = method
44::COMM;;self.metric = metric
45::COMM;;self.n_jobs = n_jobs
46::COMM;;def fit(self, X):
47::COMM;;self.n_samples_fit_ = X.shape[0]
48::COMM;;# see more metric in the manual
49::COMM;;# https://github.com/nmslib/nmslib/tree/master/manual
50::COMM;;space = {
51::COMM;;"euclidean": "l2",
52::COMM;;"cosine": "cosinesimil",
53::COMM;;"l1": "l1",
54::COMM;;"l2": "l2",
55::COMM;;}[self.metric]
56::COMM;;self.nmslib_ = nmslib.init(method=self.method, space=space)
57::COMM;;self.nmslib_.addDataPointBatch(X.copy())
58::COMM;;self.nmslib_.createIndex()
59::COMM;;return self
60::COMM;;def transform(self, X):
61::COMM;;n_samples_transform = X.shape[0]
62::COMM;;# For compatibility reasons, as each sample is considered as its own
63::COMM;;# neighbor, one extra neighbor will be computed.
64::COMM;;n_neighbors = self.n_neighbors + 1
65::COMM;;if self.n_jobs < 0:
66::COMM;;# Same handling as done in joblib for negative values of n_jobs:
67::COMM;;# in particular, `n_jobs == -1` means "as many threads as CPUs".
68::COMM;;num_threads = joblib.cpu_count() + self.n_jobs + 1
69::COMM;;else:
70::COMM;;num_threads = self.n_jobs
71::COMM;;results = self.nmslib_.knnQueryBatch(
72::COMM;;X.copy(), k=n_neighbors, num_threads=num_threads
73::COMM;;)
74::COMM;;indices, distances = zip(*results)
75::COMM;;indices, distances = np.vstack(indices), np.vstack(distances)
76::COMM;;indptr = np.arange(0, n_samples_transform * n_neighbors + 1, n_neighbors)
77::COMM;;kneighbors_graph = csr_matrix(
78::COMM;;(distances.ravel(), indices.ravel(), indptr),
79::COMM;;shape=(n_samples_transform, self.n_samples_fit_),
80::COMM;;)
81::COMM;;return kneighbors_graph
82::COMM;;def load_mnist(n_samples):

159::COMO;;# PyNNDescentTransformer 4.884 sec (transform)

164::COMO;;# KNeighborsTransformer 0.011 sec (fit)
165::COMO;;# KNeighborsTransformer 5.769 sec (transform)
166::COMO;;# NMSlibTransformer 0.733 sec (fit)

169::COMO;;# PyNNDescentTransformer 7.103 sec (transform)
170::COMO;;# PyNNDescentTransformer 1.759 sec (transform)
171::COMO;;#
172::COMO;;# Notice that the `PyNNDescentTransformer` takes more time during the first
173::COMO;;# `fit` and the first `transform` due to the overhead of the numba just in time
174::COMO;;# compiler. But after the first call, the compiled Python code is kept in a
175::COMO;;# cache by numba and subsequent calls do not suffer from this initial overhead.
176::COMO;;# Both :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsTransformer` and `NMSlibTransformer`
177::COMO;;# are only run once here as they would show more stable `fit` and `transform`
178::COMO;;# times (they don't have the cold start problem of PyNNDescentTransformer).
179::COMO;;# %%
201::COMO;;# init the plot
221::COMO;;# plot TSNE embedding which should be very similar across methods
236::COMO;;# %%
237::COMO;;# Sample output::
238::COMO;;#
239::COMO;;# Benchmarking on MNIST_10000:
240::COMO;;# ----------------------------
241::COMO;;# TSNE with internal NearestNeighbors 24.828 sec (fit_transform)
242::COMO;;# TSNE with KNeighborsTransformer 20.111 sec (fit_transform)
243::COMO;;# TSNE with NMSlibTransformer 21.757 sec (fit_transform)
244::COMO;;#
245::COMO;;# Benchmarking on MNIST_20000:
246::COMO;;# ----------------------------
247::COMO;;# TSNE with internal NearestNeighbors 51.955 sec (fit_transform)
248::COMO;;# TSNE with KNeighborsTransformer 50.994 sec (fit_transform)
249::COMO;;# TSNE with NMSlibTransformer 43.536 sec (fit_transform)
250::COMO;;#
251::COMO;;# We can observe that the default :class:`~sklearn.manifold.TSNE` estimator with
252::COMO;;# its internal :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors` implementation is
253::COMO;;# roughly equivalent to the pipeline with :class:`~sklearn.manifold.TSNE` and
254::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsTransformer` in terms of performance.
255::COMO;;# This is expected because both pipelines rely internally on the same
256::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors` implementation that performs
257::COMO;;# exacts neighbors search. The approximate `NMSlibTransformer` is already
258::COMO;;# slightly faster than the exact search on the smallest dataset but this speed
259::COMO;;# difference is expected to become more significant on datasets with a larger
260::COMO;;# number of samples.
261::COMO;;#
262::COMO;;# Notice however that not all approximate search methods are guaranteed to
263::COMO;;# improve the speed of the default exact search method: indeed the exact search
264::COMO;;# implementation significantly improved since scikit-learn 1.1. Furthermore, the
265::COMO;;# brute-force exact search method does not require building an index at `fit`
266::COMO;;# time. So, to get an overall performance improvement in the context of the
267::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.manifold.TSNE` pipeline, the gains of the approximate search
268::COMO;;# at `transform` need to be larger than the extra time spent to build the
269::COMO;;# approximate search index at `fit` time.
270::COMO;;#
271::COMO;;# Finally, the TSNE algorithm itself is also computationally intensive,
272::COMO;;# irrespective of the nearest neighbors search. So speeding-up the nearest
273::COMO;;# neighbors search step by a factor of 5 would not result in a speed up by a
274::COMO;;# factor of 5 for the overall pipeline.
2::COMM;;=========================
3::COMM;;Caching nearest neighbors
4::COMM;;=========================
5::COMM;;This example demonstrates how to precompute the k nearest neighbors before
6::COMM;;using them in KNeighborsClassifier. KNeighborsClassifier can compute the
7::COMM;;nearest neighbors internally, but precomputing them can have several benefits,
8::COMM;;such as finer parameter control, caching for multiple use, or custom
9::COMM;;implementations.
10::COMM;;Here we use the caching property of pipelines to cache the nearest neighbors
11::COMM;;graph between multiple fits of KNeighborsClassifier. The first call is slow
12::COMM;;since it computes the neighbors graph, while subsequent calls are faster as they
13::COMM;;do not need to recompute the graph. Here the durations are small since the
14::COMM;;dataset is small, but the gain can be more substantial when the dataset grows
15::COMM;;larger, or when the grid of parameter to search is large.
17::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
18::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
27::COMO;;# The transformer computes the nearest neighbors graph using the maximum number
28::COMO;;# of neighbors necessary in the grid search. The classifier model filters the
29::COMO;;# nearest neighbors graph as required by its own n_neighbors parameter.
32::COMO;;# Note that we give `memory` a directory to cache the graph computation
33::COMO;;# that will be used several times when tuning the hyperparameters of the
34::COMO;;# classifier.
42::COMO;;# Plot the results of the grid search.

2::COMM;;===================================
3::COMM;;Simple 1D Kernel Density Estimation
4::COMM;;===================================
5::COMM;;This example uses the :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.KernelDensity` class to
6::COMM;;demonstrate the principles of Kernel Density Estimation in one dimension.
7::COMM;;The first plot shows one of the problems with using histograms to visualize
8::COMM;;the density of points in 1D. Intuitively, a histogram can be thought of as a
9::COMM;;scheme in which a unit "block" is stacked above each point on a regular grid.
10::COMM;;As the top two panels show, however, the choice of gridding for these blocks
11::COMM;;can lead to wildly divergent ideas about the underlying shape of the density
12::COMM;;distribution. If we instead center each block on the point it represents, we
13::COMM;;get the estimate shown in the bottom left panel. This is a kernel density
14::COMM;;estimation with a "top hat" kernel. This idea can be generalized to other
15::COMM;;kernel shapes: the bottom-right panel of the first figure shows a Gaussian
16::COMM;;kernel density estimate over the same distribution.
17::COMM;;Scikit-learn implements efficient kernel density estimation using either
18::COMM;;a Ball Tree or KD Tree structure, through the
19::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.neighbors.KernelDensity` estimator. The available kernels
20::COMM;;are shown in the second figure of this example.
21::COMM;;The third figure compares kernel density estimates for a distribution of 100
22::COMM;;samples in 1 dimension. Though this example uses 1D distributions, kernel
23::COMM;;density estimation is easily and efficiently extensible to higher dimensions
24::COMM;;as well.
26::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
27::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;=================================================
3::COMM;;Novelty detection with Local Outlier Factor (LOF)
4::COMM;;=================================================
5::COMM;;The Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithm is an unsupervised anomaly detection
6::COMM;;method which computes the local density deviation of a given data point with
7::COMM;;respect to its neighbors. It considers as outliers the samples that have a
8::COMM;;substantially lower density than their neighbors. This example shows how to
9::COMM;;use LOF for novelty detection. Note that when LOF is used for novelty
10::COMM;;detection you MUST not use predict, decision_function and score_samples on the
11::COMM;;training set as this would lead to wrong results. You must only use these
12::COMM;;methods on new unseen data (which are not in the training set). See
13::COMM;;:ref:`User Guide <outlier_detection>`: for details on the difference between
14::COMM;;outlier detection and novelty detection and how to use LOF for outlier
15::COMM;;detection.
16::COMM;;The number of neighbors considered, (parameter n_neighbors) is typically
17::COMM;;set 1) greater than the minimum number of samples a cluster has to contain,
18::COMM;;so that other samples can be local outliers relative to this cluster, and 2)
19::COMM;;smaller than the maximum number of close by samples that can potentially be
20::COMM;;local outliers.
21::COMM;;In practice, such information is generally not available, and taking
22::COMM;;n_neighbors=20 appears to work well in general.

2::COMM;;=================================================
3::COMM;;Outlier detection with Local Outlier Factor (LOF)
4::COMM;;=================================================
5::COMM;;The Local Outlier Factor (LOF) algorithm is an unsupervised anomaly detection
6::COMM;;method which computes the local density deviation of a given data point with
7::COMM;;respect to its neighbors. It considers as outliers the samples that have a
8::COMM;;substantially lower density than their neighbors. This example shows how to use
9::COMM;;LOF for outlier detection which is the default use case of this estimator in
10::COMM;;scikit-learn. Note that when LOF is used for outlier detection it has no
11::COMM;;`predict`, `decision_function` and `score_samples` methods. See the :ref:`User

15::COMM;;greater than the minimum number of samples a cluster has to contain, so that
16::COMM;;other samples can be local outliers relative to this cluster, and 2) smaller
17::COMM;;than the maximum number of close by samples that can potentially be local
18::COMM;;outliers. In practice, such information is generally not available, and taking
19::COMM;;`n_neighbors=20` appears to work well in general.

12::COMM;;feature space) that account for the most variance in the data. Here we
13::COMM;;plot the different samples on the 2 first principal components.

15::COMM;;account for the most variance *between classes*. In particular,
16::COMM;;LDA, in contrast to PCA, is a supervised method, using known class labels.
17::COMM;;Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) tries to find a feature space such
18::COMM;;that a stochastic nearest neighbor algorithm will give the best accuracy.
19::COMM;;Like LDA, it is a supervised method.
20::COMM;;One can see that NCA enforces a clustering of the data that is visually
21::COMM;;meaningful despite the large reduction in dimension.

7::COMM;;decision functions.

13::COMM;;encouraging larger weights, potentially resulting in a more complicated
14::COMM;;decision boundary.

2::COMM;;=============================================================
3::COMM;;Compare the effect of different scalers on data with outliers
4::COMM;;=============================================================
5::COMM;;Feature 0 (median income in a block) and feature 5 (average house occupancy) of
6::COMM;;the :ref:`california_housing_dataset` have very
7::COMM;;different scales and contain some very large outliers. These two
8::COMM;;characteristics lead to difficulties to visualize the data and, more
9::COMM;;importantly, they can degrade the predictive performance of many machine
10::COMM;;learning algorithms. Unscaled data can also slow down or even prevent the
11::COMM;;convergence of many gradient-based estimators.
12::COMM;;Indeed many estimators are designed with the assumption that each feature takes
13::COMM;;values close to zero or more importantly that all features vary on comparable
14::COMM;;scales. In particular, metric-based and gradient-based estimators often assume
15::COMM;;approximately standardized data (centered features with unit variances). A
16::COMM;;notable exception are decision tree-based estimators that are robust to
17::COMM;;arbitrary scaling of the data.
18::COMM;;This example uses different scalers, transformers, and normalizers to bring the
19::COMM;;data within a pre-defined range.
20::COMM;;Scalers are linear (or more precisely affine) transformers and differ from each
21::COMM;;other in the way they estimate the parameters used to shift and scale each
22::COMM;;feature.
23::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer` provides non-linear
24::COMM;;transformations in which distances
25::COMM;;between marginal outliers and inliers are shrunk.
26::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer` provides
27::COMM;;non-linear transformations in which data is mapped to a normal distribution to
28::COMM;;stabilize variance and minimize skewness.
29::COMM;;Unlike the previous transformations, normalization refers to a per sample
30::COMM;;transformation instead of a per feature transformation.
31::COMM;;The following code is a bit verbose, feel free to jump directly to the analysis
32::COMM;;of the results_.
34::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
35::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
64::COMO;;# Take only 2 features to make visualization easier
65::COMO;;# Feature MedInc has a long tail distribution.
66::COMO;;# Feature AveOccup has a few but very large outliers.
101::COMO;;# scale the output between 0 and 1 for the colorbar
103::COMO;;# plasma does not exist in matplotlib < 1.5
108::COMO;;# define the axis for the first plot
119::COMO;;# define the axis for the zoomed-in plot
128::COMO;;# define the axis for the colorbar
142::COMO;;# The scatter plot
145::COMO;;# Removing the top and the right spine for aesthetics
146::COMO;;# make nice axis layout
153::COMO;;# Histogram for axis X1 (feature 5)
159::COMO;;# Histogram for axis X0 (feature 0)
165::COMO;;# %%
166::COMO;;# Two plots will be shown for each scaler/normalizer/transformer. The left
167::COMO;;# figure will show a scatter plot of the full data set while the right figure
168::COMO;;# will exclude the extreme values considering only 99 % of the data set,
169::COMO;;# excluding marginal outliers. In addition, the marginal distributions for each
170::COMO;;# feature will be shown on the sides of the scatter plot.

209::COMO;;# .. _results:
210::COMO;;#
211::COMO;;# Original data
212::COMO;;# -------------
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# Each transformation is plotted showing two transformed features, with the
215::COMO;;# left plot showing the entire dataset, and the right zoomed-in to show the
216::COMO;;# dataset without the marginal outliers. A large majority of the samples are
217::COMO;;# compacted to a specific range, [0, 10] for the median income and [0, 6] for
218::COMO;;# the average house occupancy. Note that there are some marginal outliers (some
219::COMO;;# blocks have average occupancy of more than 1200). Therefore, a specific
220::COMO;;# pre-processing can be very beneficial depending of the application. In the
221::COMO;;# following, we present some insights and behaviors of those pre-processing
222::COMO;;# methods in the presence of marginal outliers.
224::COMO;;# %%
225::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_standard_scaler_section:
226::COMO;;#
227::COMO;;# StandardScaler
228::COMO;;# --------------
229::COMO;;#
230::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` removes the mean and scales
231::COMO;;# the data to unit variance. The scaling shrinks the range of the feature
232::COMO;;# values as shown in the left figure below.
233::COMO;;# However, the outliers have an influence when computing the empirical mean and
234::COMO;;# standard deviation. Note in particular that because the outliers on each
235::COMO;;# feature have different magnitudes, the spread of the transformed data on
236::COMO;;# each feature is very different: most of the data lie in the [-2, 4] range for
237::COMO;;# the transformed median income feature while the same data is squeezed in the
238::COMO;;# smaller [-0.2, 0.2] range for the transformed average house occupancy.
239::COMO;;#
240::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` therefore cannot guarantee
241::COMO;;# balanced feature scales in the
242::COMO;;# presence of outliers.
244::COMO;;# %%
245::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_minmax_scaler_section:
246::COMO;;#
247::COMO;;# MinMaxScaler
248::COMO;;# ------------
249::COMO;;#
250::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler` rescales the data set such that
251::COMO;;# all feature values are in
252::COMO;;# the range [0, 1] as shown in the right panel below. However, this scaling
253::COMO;;# compresses all inliers into the narrow range [0, 0.005] for the transformed
254::COMO;;# average house occupancy.
255::COMO;;#
256::COMO;;# Both :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` and
257::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler` are very sensitive to the
258::COMO;;# presence of outliers.
260::COMO;;# %%
261::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_max_abs_scaler_section:
262::COMO;;#
263::COMO;;# MaxAbsScaler
264::COMO;;# ------------
265::COMO;;#
266::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MaxAbsScaler` is similar to
267::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler` except that the
268::COMO;;# values are mapped across several ranges depending on whether negative
269::COMO;;# OR positive values are present. If only positive values are present, the
270::COMO;;# range is [0, 1]. If only negative values are present, the range is [-1, 0].
271::COMO;;# If both negative and positive values are present, the range is [-1, 1].
272::COMO;;# On positive only data, both :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler`
273::COMO;;# and :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MaxAbsScaler` behave similarly.
274::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MaxAbsScaler` therefore also suffers from
275::COMO;;# the presence of large outliers.
277::COMO;;# %%
278::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_robust_scaler_section:
279::COMO;;#
280::COMO;;# RobustScaler
281::COMO;;# ------------
282::COMO;;#
283::COMO;;# Unlike the previous scalers, the centering and scaling statistics of
284::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler`
285::COMO;;# are based on percentiles and are therefore not influenced by a small
286::COMO;;# number of very large marginal outliers. Consequently, the resulting range of
287::COMO;;# the transformed feature values is larger than for the previous scalers and,
288::COMO;;# more importantly, are approximately similar: for both features most of the
289::COMO;;# transformed values lie in a [-2, 3] range as seen in the zoomed-in figure.
290::COMO;;# Note that the outliers themselves are still present in the transformed data.
291::COMO;;# If a separate outlier clipping is desirable, a non-linear transformation is
292::COMO;;# required (see below).
294::COMO;;# %%
295::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_power_transformer_section:
296::COMO;;#
297::COMO;;# PowerTransformer
298::COMO;;# ----------------
299::COMO;;#
300::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer` applies a power
301::COMO;;# transformation to each feature to make the data more Gaussian-like in order
302::COMO;;# to stabilize variance and minimize skewness. Currently the Yeo-Johnson
303::COMO;;# and Box-Cox transforms are supported and the optimal
304::COMO;;# scaling factor is determined via maximum likelihood estimation in both
305::COMO;;# methods. By default, :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PowerTransformer` applies
306::COMO;;# zero-mean, unit variance normalization. Note that
307::COMO;;# Box-Cox can only be applied to strictly positive data. Income and average
308::COMO;;# house occupancy happen to be strictly positive, but if negative values are
309::COMO;;# present the Yeo-Johnson transformed is preferred.
312::COMO;;# %%
313::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_quantile_transformer_section:
314::COMO;;#
315::COMO;;# QuantileTransformer (uniform output)
316::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
317::COMO;;#
318::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer` applies a non-linear
319::COMO;;# transformation such that the
320::COMO;;# probability density function of each feature will be mapped to a uniform
321::COMO;;# or Gaussian distribution. In this case, all the data, including outliers,
322::COMO;;# will be mapped to a uniform distribution with the range [0, 1], making
323::COMO;;# outliers indistinguishable from inliers.
324::COMO;;#
325::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler` and
326::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer` are robust to outliers in
327::COMO;;# the sense that adding or removing outliers in the training set will yield
328::COMO;;# approximately the same transformation. But contrary to
329::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler`,
330::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.QuantileTransformer` will also automatically
331::COMO;;# collapse any outlier by setting them to the a priori defined range boundaries
332::COMO;;# (0 and 1). This can result in saturation artifacts for extreme values.
334::COMO;;##############################################################################
335::COMO;;# QuantileTransformer (Gaussian output)
336::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
337::COMO;;#
338::COMO;;# To map to a Gaussian distribution, set the parameter
339::COMO;;# ``output_distribution='normal'``.
341::COMO;;# %%
342::COMO;;# .. _plot_all_scaling_normalizer_section:
343::COMO;;#
344::COMO;;# Normalizer
345::COMO;;# ----------
346::COMO;;#
347::COMO;;# The :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.Normalizer` rescales the vector for each
348::COMO;;# sample to have unit norm,
349::COMO;;# independently of the distribution of the samples. It can be seen on both
350::COMO;;# figures below where all samples are mapped onto the unit circle. In our
351::COMO;;# example the two selected features have only positive values; therefore the
352::COMO;;# transformed data only lie in the positive quadrant. This would not be the
353::COMO;;# case if some original features had a mix of positive and negative values.
2::COMM;;================================================================
3::COMM;;Using KBinsDiscretizer to discretize continuous features
4::COMM;;================================================================
5::COMM;;The example compares prediction result of linear regression (linear model)
6::COMM;;and decision tree (tree based model) with and without discretization of
7::COMM;;real-valued features.
8::COMM;;As is shown in the result before discretization, linear model is fast to
9::COMM;;build and relatively straightforward to interpret, but can only model
10::COMM;;linear relationships, while decision tree can build a much more complex model
11::COMM;;of the data. One way to make linear model more powerful on continuous data
12::COMM;;is to use discretization (also known as binning). In the example, we
13::COMM;;discretize the feature and one-hot encode the transformed data. Note that if
14::COMM;;the bins are not reasonably wide, there would appear to be a substantially
15::COMM;;increased risk of overfitting, so the discretizer parameters should usually
16::COMM;;be tuned under cross validation.
17::COMM;;After discretization, linear regression and decision tree make exactly the
18::COMM;;same prediction. As features are constant within each bin, any model must
19::COMM;;predict the same value for all points within a bin. Compared with the result
20::COMM;;before discretization, linear model become much more flexible while decision
21::COMM;;tree gets much less flexible. Note that binning features generally has no
22::COMM;;beneficial effect for tree-based models, as these models can learn to split
23::COMM;;up the data anywhere.

26::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
