2::COMM;;======================
3::COMM;;Feature discretization
4::COMM;;======================
5::COMM;;A demonstration of feature discretization on synthetic classification datasets.
6::COMM;;Feature discretization decomposes each feature into a set of bins, here equally
7::COMM;;distributed in width. The discrete values are then one-hot encoded, and given
8::COMM;;to a linear classifier. This preprocessing enables a non-linear behavior even
9::COMM;;though the classifier is linear.
10::COMM;;On this example, the first two rows represent linearly non-separable datasets
11::COMM;;(moons and concentric circles) while the third is approximately linearly
12::COMM;;separable. On the two linearly non-separable datasets, feature discretization
13::COMM;;largely increases the performance of linear classifiers. On the linearly
14::COMM;;separable dataset, feature discretization decreases the performance of linear
15::COMM;;classifiers. Two non-linear classifiers are also shown for comparison.
16::COMM;;This example should be taken with a grain of salt, as the intuition conveyed
17::COMM;;does not necessarily carry over to real datasets. Particularly in
18::COMM;;high-dimensional spaces, data can more easily be separated linearly. Moreover,
19::COMM;;using feature discretization and one-hot encoding increases the number of
20::COMM;;features, which easily lead to overfitting when the number of samples is small.
21::COMM;;The plots show training points in solid colors and testing points
22::COMM;;semi-transparent. The lower right shows the classification accuracy on the test
23::COMM;;set.

48::COMO;;# its runtime. In a real use case, a broader search space for the algorithms
49::COMO;;# should be used.

3::COMM;;Demonstrating the different strategies of KBinsDiscretizer
4::COMM;;==========================================================
5::COMM;;This example presents the different strategies implemented in KBinsDiscretizer:
6::COMM;;- 'uniform': The discretization is uniform in each feature, which means that
7::COMM;;the bin widths are constant in each dimension.
8::COMM;;- 'quantile': The discretization is done on the quantiled values, which means
9::COMM;;that each bin has approximately the same number of samples.
10::COMM;;- 'kmeans': The discretization is based on the centroids of a KMeans clustering
11::COMM;;procedure.
12::COMM;;The plot shows the regions where the discretized encoding is constant.

2::COMM;;=================================
3::COMM;;Map data to a normal distribution
4::COMM;;=================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.preprocessing
6::COMM;;This example demonstrates the use of the Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson transforms
7::COMM;;through :class:`~PowerTransformer` to map data from various
8::COMM;;distributions to a normal distribution.
9::COMM;;The power transform is useful as a transformation in modeling problems where
10::COMM;;homoscedasticity and normality are desired. Below are examples of Box-Cox and
11::COMM;;Yeo-Johnwon applied to six different probability distributions: Lognormal,
12::COMM;;Chi-squared, Weibull, Gaussian, Uniform, and Bimodal.
13::COMM;;Note that the transformations successfully map the data to a normal
14::COMM;;distribution when applied to certain datasets, but are ineffective with others.
15::COMM;;This highlights the importance of visualizing the data before and after
16::COMM;;transformation.
17::COMM;;Also note that even though Box-Cox seems to perform better than Yeo-Johnson for
18::COMM;;lognormal and chi-squared distributions, keep in mind that Box-Cox does not
19::COMM;;support inputs with negative values.
20::COMM;;For comparison, we also add the output from
21::COMM;;:class:`~QuantileTransformer`. It can force any arbitrary
22::COMM;;distribution into a gaussian, provided that there are enough training samples
23::COMM;;(thousands). Because it is a non-parametric method, it is harder to interpret
24::COMM;;than the parametric ones (Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson).
25::COMM;;On "small" datasets (less than a few hundred points), the quantile transformer
26::COMM;;is prone to overfitting. The use of the power transform is then recommended.

2::COMM;;=============================
3::COMM;;Importance of Feature Scaling
4::COMM;;=============================
5::COMM;;Feature scaling through standardization, also called Z-score normalization, is
6::COMM;;an important preprocessing step for many machine learning algorithms. It
7::COMM;;involves rescaling each feature such that it has a standard deviation of 1 and a
8::COMM;;mean of 0.
9::COMM;;Even if tree based models are (almost) not affected by scaling, many other
10::COMM;;algorithms require features to be normalized, often for different reasons: to
11::COMM;;ease the convergence (such as a non-penalized logistic regression), to create a
12::COMM;;completely different model fit compared to the fit with unscaled data (such as
13::COMM;;KNeighbors models). The latter is demonstrated on the first part of the present
14::COMM;;example.
15::COMM;;On the second part of the example we show how Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
16::COMM;;is impacted by normalization of features. To illustrate this, we compare the
17::COMM;;principal components found using :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` on unscaled
18::COMM;;data with those obtained when using a
19::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` to scale data first.
20::COMM;;In the last part of the example we show the effect of the normalization on the
21::COMM;;accuracy of a model trained on PCA-reduced data.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Load and prepare data
27::COMO;;# =====================
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# The dataset used is the :ref:`wine_dataset` available at UCI. This dataset has
30::COMO;;# continuous features that are heterogeneous in scale due to differing
31::COMO;;# properties that they measure (e.g. alcohol content and malic acid).
41::COMO;;# %%
42::COMO;;# .. _neighbors_scaling:
43::COMO;;#
44::COMO;;# Effect of rescaling on a k-neighbors models
45::COMO;;# ===========================================
46::COMO;;#
47::COMO;;# For the sake of visualizing the decision boundary of a
48::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier`, in this section we select a
49::COMO;;# subset of 2 features that have values with different orders of magnitude.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Keep in mind that using a subset of the features to train the model may likely
52::COMO;;# leave out feature with high predictive impact, resulting in a decision
53::COMO;;# boundary that is much worse in comparison to a model trained on the full set
54::COMO;;# of features.
81::COMO;;# %%
82::COMO;;# Here the decision boundary shows that fitting scaled or non-scaled data lead
83::COMO;;# to completely different models. The reason is that the variable "proline" has
84::COMO;;# values which vary between 0 and 1,000; whereas the variable "hue" varies
85::COMO;;# between 1 and 10. Because of this, distances between samples are mostly
86::COMO;;# impacted by differences in values of "proline", while values of the "hue" will
87::COMO;;# be comparatively ignored. If one uses
88::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` to normalize this database,
89::COMO;;# both scaled values lay approximately between -3 and 3 and the neighbors
90::COMO;;# structure will be impacted more or less equivalently by both variables.
91::COMO;;#
92::COMO;;# Effect of rescaling on a PCA dimensional reduction
93::COMO;;# ==================================================
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# Dimensional reduction using :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` consists of
96::COMO;;# finding the features that maximize the variance. If one feature varies more
97::COMO;;# than the others only because of their respective scales,
98::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` would determine that such feature
99::COMO;;# dominates the direction of the principal components.
100::COMO;;#
101::COMO;;# We can inspect the first principal components using all the original features:
116::COMO;;# %%
117::COMO;;# Indeed we find that the "proline" feature dominates the direction of the first
118::COMO;;# principal component without scaling, being about two orders of magnitude above
119::COMO;;# the other features. This is contrasted when observing the first principal
120::COMO;;# component for the scaled version of the data, where the orders of magnitude
121::COMO;;# are roughly the same across all the features.
122::COMO;;#
123::COMO;;# We can visualize the distribution of the principal components in both cases:
153::COMO;;# %%
154::COMO;;# From the plot above we observe that scaling the features before reducing the
155::COMO;;# dimensionality results in components with the same order of magnitude. In this
156::COMO;;# case it also improves the separability of the classes. Indeed, in the next
157::COMO;;# section we confirm that a better separability has a good repercussion on the
158::COMO;;# overall model's performance.
159::COMO;;#
160::COMO;;# Effect of rescaling on model's performance
161::COMO;;# ==========================================
162::COMO;;#
163::COMO;;# First we show how the optimal regularization of a
164::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegressionCV` depends on the scaling or
165::COMO;;# non-scaling of the data:
180::COMO;;# %%
181::COMO;;# The need for regularization is higher (lower values of `C`) for the data that
182::COMO;;# was not scaled before applying PCA. We now evaluate the effect of scaling on
183::COMO;;# the accuracy and the mean log-loss of the optimal models:
197::COMO;;# %%
198::COMO;;# A clear difference in prediction accuracies is observed when the data is
199::COMO;;# scaled before :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, as it vastly outperforms
200::COMO;;# the unscaled version. This corresponds to the intuition obtained from the plot
201::COMO;;# in the previous section, where the components become linearly separable when
202::COMO;;# scaling before using :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`.
203::COMO;;#
204::COMO;;# Notice that in this case the models with scaled features perform better than
205::COMO;;# the models with non-scaled features because all the variables are expected to
206::COMO;;# be predictive and we rather avoid some of them being comparatively ignored.
207::COMO;;#
208::COMO;;# If the variables in lower scales were not predictive, one may experience a
209::COMO;;# decrease of the performance after scaling the features: noisy features would
210::COMO;;# contribute more to the prediction after scaling and therefore scaling would
211::COMO;;# increase overfitting.
212::COMO;;#
213::COMO;;# Last but not least, we observe that one achieves a lower log-loss by means of
214::COMO;;# the scaling step.
2::COMM;;============================================
3::COMM;;Comparing Target Encoder with Other Encoders
4::COMM;;============================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.preprocessing
6::COMM;;The :class:`TargetEncoder` uses the value of the target to encode each
7::COMM;;categorical feature. In this example, we will compare three different approaches
8::COMM;;for handling categorical features: :class:`TargetEncoder`,
9::COMM;;:class:`OrdinalEncoder`, :class:`OneHotEncoder` and dropping the category.
10::COMM;;.. note::
11::COMM;;`fit(X, y).transform(X)` does not equal `fit_transform(X, y)` because a
12::COMM;;cross fitting scheme is used in `fit_transform` for encoding. See the
13::COMM;;:ref:`User Guide <target_encoder>` for details.

43::COMO;;# Training and Evaluating Pipelines with Different Encoders
44::COMO;;# =========================================================
45::COMO;;# In this section, we will evaluate pipelines with
46::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` with different encoding
47::COMO;;# strategies. First, we list out the encoders we will be using to preprocess
48::COMO;;# the categorical features:

99::COMO;;# %%
100::COMO;;# Native Categorical Feature Support
101::COMO;;# ==================================
102::COMO;;# In this section, we build and evaluate a pipeline that uses native categorical
103::COMO;;# feature support in :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`,
104::COMO;;# which only supports up to 255 unique categories. In our dataset, the most of
105::COMO;;# the categorical features have more than 255 unique categories:
108::COMO;;# %%
109::COMO;;# To workaround the limitation above, we group the categorical features into
110::COMO;;# low cardinality and high cardinality features. The high cardinality features
111::COMO;;# will be target encoded and the low cardinality features will use the native
112::COMO;;# categorical feature in gradient boosting.
131::COMO;;# The output of the of the preprocessor must be set to pandas so the
132::COMO;;# gradient boosting model can detect the low cardinality features.
141::COMO;;# %%
142::COMO;;# Finally, we evaluate the pipeline using cross validation and record the results:
144::COMO;;# %%
145::COMO;;# Plotting the Results
146::COMO;;# ====================
147::COMO;;# In this section, we display the results by plotting the test and train scores:
176::COMO;;# %%
177::COMO;;# When evaluating the predictive performance on the test set, dropping the
178::COMO;;# categories perform the worst and the target encoders performs the best. This
179::COMO;;# can be explained as follows:
180::COMO;;#
181::COMO;;# - Dropping the categorical features makes the pipeline less expressive and
182::COMO;;# underfitting as a result;
183::COMO;;# - Due to the high cardinality and to reduce the training time, the one-hot
184::COMO;;# encoding scheme uses `max_categories=20` which prevents the features from
185::COMO;;# expanding too much, which can result in underfitting.
186::COMO;;# - If we had not set `max_categories=20`, the one-hot encoding scheme would have
187::COMO;;# likely made the pipeline overfitting as the number of features explodes with rare
188::COMO;;# category occurrences that are correlated with the target by chance (on the training
189::COMO;;# set only);
190::COMO;;# - The ordinal encoding imposes an arbitrary order to the features which are then
191::COMO;;# treated as numerical values by the
192::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`. Since this
193::COMO;;# model groups numerical features in 256 bins per feature, many unrelated categories
194::COMO;;# can be grouped together and as a result overall pipeline can underfit;
195::COMO;;# - When using the target encoder, the same binning happens, but since the encoded
196::COMO;;# values are statistically ordered by marginal association with the target variable,
197::COMO;;# the binning use by the :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`
198::COMO;;# makes sense and leads to good results: the combination of smoothed target
199::COMO;;# encoding and binning works as a good regularizing strategy against
200::COMO;;# overfitting while not limiting the expressiveness of the pipeline too much.
2::COMM;;=======================================
3::COMM;;Target Encoder's Internal Cross fitting
4::COMM;;=======================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.preprocessing
6::COMM;;The :class:`TargetEncoder` replaces each category of a categorical feature with
7::COMM;;the shrunk mean of the target variable for that category. This method is useful
8::COMM;;in cases where there is a strong relationship between the categorical feature
9::COMM;;and the target. To prevent overfitting, :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` uses
10::COMM;;an internal :term:`cross fitting` scheme to encode the training data to be used
11::COMM;;by a downstream model. This scheme involves splitting the data into *k* folds
12::COMM;;and encoding each fold using the encodings learnt using the *other k-1* folds.
13::COMM;;In this example, we demonstrate the importance of the cross
14::COMM;;fitting procedure to prevent overfitting.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
18::COMO;;# %%

22::COMO;;#
23::COMO;;# * an informative feature with medium cardinality ("informative")
24::COMO;;# * an uninformative feature with medium cardinality ("shuffled")
25::COMO;;# * an uninformative feature with high cardinality ("near_unique")
26::COMO;;#
27::COMO;;# First, we generate the informative feature:

44::COMO;;# values of X_informative:

48::COMO;;# The uninformative feature with medium cardinality is generated by permuting the
49::COMO;;# informative feature and removing the relationship with the target:
51::COMO;;# %%
52::COMO;;# The uninformative feature with high cardinality is generated so that it is
53::COMO;;# independent of the target variable. We will show that target encoding without
54::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting` will cause catastrophic overfitting for the downstream
55::COMO;;# regressor. These high cardinality features are basically unique identifiers
56::COMO;;# for samples which should generally be removed from machine learning datasets.
57::COMO;;# In this example, we generate them to show how :class:`TargetEncoder`'s default
58::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting` behavior mitigates the overfitting issue automatically.

79::COMO;;# internal :term:`cross fitting`. First, we see the Ridge model trained on the
80::COMO;;# raw features will have low performance. This is because we permuted the order
81::COMO;;# of the informative feature meaning `X_informative` is not informative when
82::COMO;;# raw:
85::COMO;;# Configure transformers to always output DataFrames
91::COMO;;# %%
92::COMO;;# Next, we create a pipeline with the target encoder and ridge model. The pipeline
93::COMO;;# uses :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` which uses :term:`cross fitting`. We
94::COMO;;# see that the model fits the data well and generalizes to the test set:
101::COMO;;# %%
102::COMO;;# The coefficients of the linear model shows that most of the weight is on the
103::COMO;;# feature at column index 0, which is the informative feature
116::COMO;;# %%
117::COMO;;# While :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` uses an internal
118::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting` scheme to learn encodings for the training set,
119::COMO;;# :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit` followed by :meth:`TargetEncoder.transform` does not.
120::COMO;;# It uses the complete training set to learn encodings and to transform the
121::COMO;;# categorical features. Thus, we can use :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit` followed by
122::COMO;;# :meth:`TargetEncoder.transform` to disable the :term:`cross fitting`. This
123::COMO;;# encoding is then passed to the ridge model.
129::COMO;;# %%
130::COMO;;# We evaluate the model that did not use :term:`cross fitting` when encoding and
131::COMO;;# see that it overfits:
143::COMO;;# %%
144::COMO;;# The ridge model overfits because it assigns much more weight to the
145::COMO;;# uninformative extremely high cardinality ("near_unique") and medium
146::COMO;;# cardinality ("shuffled") features than when the model used
147::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting` to encode the features.
157::COMO;;# %%
158::COMO;;# Conclusion
159::COMO;;# ==========
160::COMO;;# This example demonstrates the importance of :class:`TargetEncoder`'s internal
161::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting`. It is important to use
162::COMO;;# :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` to encode training data before passing it
163::COMO;;# to a machine learning model. When a :class:`TargetEncoder` is a part of a
164::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline` and the pipeline is fitted, the pipeline
165::COMO;;# will correctly call :meth:`TargetEncoder.fit_transform` and use
166::COMO;;# :term:`cross fitting` when encoding the training data.

52::COMO;;# %%
53::COMO;;# Stacking Classifier and Regressor
54::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
55::COMO;;# :class:`~ensemble.StackingClassifier` and
56::COMO;;# :class:`~ensemble.StackingRegressor`
57::COMO;;# allow you to have a stack of estimators with a final classifier or
58::COMO;;# a regressor.
59::COMO;;# Stacked generalization consists in stacking the output of individual
60::COMO;;# estimators and use a classifier to compute the final prediction. Stacking
61::COMO;;# allows to use the strength of each individual estimator by using their output
62::COMO;;# as input of a final estimator.
63::COMO;;# Base estimators are fitted on the full ``X`` while
64::COMO;;# the final estimator is trained using cross-validated predictions of the
65::COMO;;# base estimators using ``cross_val_predict``.
66::COMO;;#
67::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <stacking>`.

88::COMO;;# estimate of the importance of each feature, for any fitted estimator:

115::COMO;;# %%
116::COMO;;# Native support for missing values for gradient boosting
117::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------
118::COMO;;#
119::COMO;;# The :class:`ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier`
120::COMO;;# and :class:`ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` now have native
121::COMO;;# support for missing values (NaNs). This means that there is no need for

128::COMO;;# %%
129::COMO;;# Precomputed sparse nearest neighbors graph
130::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------
131::COMO;;# Most estimators based on nearest neighbors graphs now accept precomputed
132::COMO;;# sparse graphs as input, to reuse the same graph for multiple estimator fits.
133::COMO;;# To use this feature in a pipeline, one can use the `memory` parameter, along
134::COMO;;# with one of the two new transformers,
135::COMO;;# :class:`neighbors.KNeighborsTransformer` and
136::COMO;;# :class:`neighbors.RadiusNeighborsTransformer`. The precomputation
137::COMO;;# can also be performed by custom estimators to use alternative
138::COMO;;# implementations, such as approximate nearest neighbors methods.
139::COMO;;# See more details in the :ref:`User Guide <neighbors_transformer>`.
152::COMO;;# We can decrease the number of neighbors and the graph will not be
153::COMO;;# recomputed.
156::COMO;;# %%
157::COMO;;# KNN Based Imputation
158::COMO;;# ------------------------------------
159::COMO;;# We now support imputation for completing missing values using k-Nearest
160::COMO;;# Neighbors.
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# Each sample's missing values are imputed using the mean value from
163::COMO;;# ``n_neighbors`` nearest neighbors found in the training set. Two samples are
164::COMO;;# close if the features that neither is missing are close.
165::COMO;;# By default, a euclidean distance metric
166::COMO;;# that supports missing values,
167::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.nan_euclidean_distances`, is used to find the nearest
168::COMO;;# neighbors.
169::COMO;;#
170::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <knnimpute>`.
175::COMO;;# %%
176::COMO;;# Tree pruning
177::COMO;;# ------------
178::COMO;;#
179::COMO;;# It is now possible to prune most tree-based estimators once the trees are
180::COMO;;# built. The pruning is based on minimal cost-complexity. Read more in the
181::COMO;;# :ref:`User Guide <minimal_cost_complexity_pruning>` for details.

222::COMO;;# %%
223::COMO;;# ROC AUC now supports multiclass classification
224::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------
225::COMO;;# The :func:`~sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score` function can also be used in multi-class
226::COMO;;# classification. Two averaging strategies are currently supported: the
227::COMO;;# one-vs-one algorithm computes the average of the pairwise ROC AUC scores, and
228::COMO;;# the one-vs-rest algorithm computes the average of the ROC AUC scores for each
229::COMO;;# class against all other classes. In both cases, the multiclass ROC AUC scores
230::COMO;;# are computed from the probability estimates that a sample belongs to a
231::COMO;;# particular class according to the model. The OvO and OvR algorithms support
232::COMO;;# weighting uniformly (``average='macro'``) and weighting by the prevalence
233::COMO;;# (``average='weighted'``).
234::COMO;;#
235::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <roc_metrics>`.

16::COMO;;##############################################################################
17::COMO;;# Successive Halving estimators for tuning hyper-parameters
18::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
19::COMO;;# Successive Halving, a state of the art method, is now available to
20::COMO;;# explore the space of the parameters and identify their best combination.
21::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.HalvingGridSearchCV` and
22::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.HalvingRandomSearchCV` can be
23::COMO;;# used as drop-in replacement for
24::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` and
25::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.RandomizedSearchCV`.
26::COMO;;# Successive Halving is an iterative selection process illustrated in the
27::COMO;;# figure below. The first iteration is run with a small amount of resources,
28::COMO;;# where the resource typically corresponds to the number of training samples,
29::COMO;;# but can also be an arbitrary integer parameter such as `n_estimators` in a
30::COMO;;# random forest. Only a subset of the parameter candidates are selected for the
31::COMO;;# next iteration, which will be run with an increasing amount of allocated
32::COMO;;# resources. Only a subset of candidates will last until the end of the
33::COMO;;# iteration process, and the best parameter candidate is the one that has the
34::COMO;;# highest score on the last iteration.
35::COMO;;#
36::COMO;;# Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <successive_halving_user_guide>` (note:
37::COMO;;# the Successive Halving estimators are still :term:`experimental
38::COMO;;# <experimental>`).
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# .. figure:: ../model_selection/images/sphx_glr_plot_successive_halving_iterations_001.png
41::COMO;;# :target: ../model_selection/plot_successive_halving_iterations.html
42::COMO;;# :align: center
47::COMC;;from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv # noqa: F401

21::COMO;;##############################################################################
22::COMO;;# Keyword and positional arguments
23::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
24::COMO;;# The scikit-learn API exposes many functions and methods which have many input
25::COMO;;# parameters. For example, before this release, one could instantiate a
26::COMO;;# :class:`~ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor` as::
27::COMO;;#
28::COMO;;# HistGradientBoostingRegressor("squared_error", 0.1, 100, 31, None,
29::COMO;;# 20, 0.0, 255, None, None, False, "auto", "loss", 0.1, 10, 1e-7,
30::COMO;;# 0, None)
31::COMO;;#
32::COMO;;# Understanding the above code requires the reader to go to the API
33::COMO;;# documentation and to check each and every parameter for its position and
34::COMO;;# its meaning. To improve the readability of code written based on scikit-learn,
35::COMO;;# now users have to provide most parameters with their names, as keyword
36::COMO;;# arguments, instead of positional arguments. For example, the above code would
37::COMO;;# be::
38::COMO;;#
39::COMO;;# HistGradientBoostingRegressor(
40::COMO;;# loss="squared_error",
41::COMO;;# learning_rate=0.1,
42::COMO;;# max_iter=100,
43::COMO;;# max_leaf_nodes=31,
44::COMO;;# max_depth=None,
45::COMO;;# min_samples_leaf=20,
46::COMO;;# l2_regularization=0.0,
47::COMO;;# max_bins=255,
48::COMO;;# categorical_features=None,
49::COMO;;# monotonic_cst=None,
50::COMO;;# warm_start=False,
51::COMO;;# early_stopping="auto",
52::COMO;;# scoring="loss",
53::COMO;;# validation_fraction=0.1,
54::COMO;;# n_iter_no_change=10,
55::COMO;;# tol=1e-7,
56::COMO;;# verbose=0,
57::COMO;;# random_state=None,
58::COMO;;# )
59::COMO;;#
60::COMO;;# which is much more readable. Positional arguments have been deprecated since
61::COMO;;# version 0.23 and will now raise a ``TypeError``. A limited number of
62::COMO;;# positional arguments are still allowed in some cases, for example in
63::COMO;;# :class:`~decomposition.PCA`, where ``PCA(10)`` is still allowed, but ``PCA(10,
64::COMO;;# False)`` is not allowed.
65::COMO;;##############################################################################
66::COMO;;# Spline Transformers
67::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------
68::COMO;;# One way to add nonlinear terms to a dataset's feature set is to generate
69::COMO;;# spline basis functions for continuous/numerical features with the new
70::COMO;;# :class:`~preprocessing.SplineTransformer`. Splines are piecewise polynomials,
71::COMO;;# parametrized by their polynomial degree and the positions of the knots. The
72::COMO;;# :class:`~preprocessing.SplineTransformer` implements a B-spline basis.
73::COMO;;#
74::COMO;;# .. figure:: ../linear_model/images/sphx_glr_plot_polynomial_interpolation_001.png
75::COMO;;# :target: ../linear_model/plot_polynomial_interpolation.html
76::COMO;;# :align: center
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;# The following code shows splines in action, for more information, please
79::COMO;;# refer to the :ref:`User Guide <spline_transformer>`.
85::COMO;;##############################################################################
86::COMO;;# Quantile Regressor
87::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
88::COMO;;# Quantile regression estimates the median or other quantiles of :math:`y`
89::COMO;;# conditional on :math:`X`, while ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates the
90::COMO;;# conditional mean.
91::COMO;;#
92::COMO;;# As a linear model, the new :class:`~linear_model.QuantileRegressor` gives
93::COMO;;# linear predictions :math:`\hat{y}(w, X) = Xw` for the :math:`q`-th quantile,
94::COMO;;# :math:`q \in (0, 1)`. The weights or coefficients :math:`w` are then found by
95::COMO;;# the following minimization problem:
96::COMO;;#
97::COMO;;# .. math::
98::COMO;;# \min_{w} {\frac{1}{n_{\text{samples}}}
99::COMO;;# \sum_i PB_q(y_i - X_i w) + \alpha ||w||_1}.
100::COMO;;#
101::COMO;;# This consists of the pinball loss (also known as linear loss),
102::COMO;;# see also :class:`~sklearn.metrics.mean_pinball_loss`,
103::COMO;;#
104::COMO;;# .. math::
105::COMO;;# PB_q(t) = q \max(t, 0) + (1 - q) \max(-t, 0) =
106::COMO;;# \begin{cases}
107::COMO;;# q t, & t > 0, \\
108::COMO;;# 0, & t = 0, \\
109::COMO;;# (1-q) t, & t < 0
110::COMO;;# \end{cases}
111::COMO;;#
112::COMO;;# and the L1 penalty controlled by parameter ``alpha``, similar to
113::COMO;;# :class:`linear_model.Lasso`.
114::COMO;;#
115::COMO;;# Please check the following example to see how it works, and the :ref:`User
116::COMO;;# Guide <quantile_regression>` for more details.
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# .. figure:: ../linear_model/images/sphx_glr_plot_quantile_regression_002.png
119::COMO;;# :target: ../linear_model/plot_quantile_regression.html
120::COMO;;# :align: center
121::COMO;;# :scale: 50%
122::COMO;;##############################################################################
123::COMO;;# Feature Names Support
124::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
125::COMO;;# When an estimator is passed a `pandas' dataframe
126::COMO;;# <https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe>`_ during
127::COMO;;# :term:`fit`, the estimator will set a `feature_names_in_` attribute
128::COMO;;# containing the feature names. This is a part of
129::COMO;;# `SLEP007 <https://scikit-learn-enhancement-proposals.readthedocs.io/en/latest/slep007/proposal.html>`__.
130::COMO;;# Note that feature names support is only enabled
131::COMO;;# when the column names in the dataframe are all strings. `feature_names_in_`
132::COMO;;# is used to check that the column names of the dataframe passed in
133::COMO;;# non-:term:`fit`, such as :term:`predict`, are consistent with features in
134::COMO;;# :term:`fit`:
140::COMO;;# %%
141::COMO;;# The support of :term:`get_feature_names_out` is available for transformers
142::COMO;;# that already had `get_feature_names` and transformers with a one-to-one
143::COMO;;# correspondence between input and output such as
144::COMO;;# :class:`~preprocessing.StandardScaler`. :term:`get_feature_names_out` support
145::COMO;;# will be added to all other transformers in future releases. Additionally,
146::COMO;;# :meth:`compose.ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` is available to
147::COMO;;# combine feature names of its transformers:
160::COMO;;# %%
161::COMO;;# When this ``preprocessor`` is used with a pipeline, the feature names used
162::COMO;;# by the classifier are obtained by slicing and calling
163::COMO;;# :term:`get_feature_names_out`:

171::COMO;;# A more flexible plotting API
172::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
173::COMO;;# :class:`metrics.ConfusionMatrixDisplay`,
174::COMO;;# :class:`metrics.PrecisionRecallDisplay`, :class:`metrics.DetCurveDisplay`,
175::COMO;;# and :class:`inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay` now expose two class
176::COMO;;# methods: `from_estimator` and `from_predictions` which allow users to create
177::COMO;;# a plot given the predictions or an estimator. This means the corresponding

183::COMO;;##############################################################################
184::COMO;;# Online One-Class SVM
185::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
186::COMO;;# The new class :class:`~linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` implements an online
187::COMO;;# linear version of the One-Class SVM using a stochastic gradient descent.
188::COMO;;# Combined with kernel approximation techniques,
189::COMO;;# :class:`~linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` can be used to approximate the solution
190::COMO;;# of a kernelized One-Class SVM, implemented in :class:`~svm.OneClassSVM`, with
191::COMO;;# a fit time complexity linear in the number of samples. Note that the
192::COMO;;# complexity of a kernelized One-Class SVM is at best quadratic in the number
193::COMO;;# of samples. :class:`~linear_model.SGDOneClassSVM` is thus well suited for
194::COMO;;# datasets with a large number of training samples (> 10,000) for which the SGD
195::COMO;;# variant can be several orders of magnitude faster. Please check this
196::COMO;;# :ref:`example
197::COMO;;# <sphx_glr_auto_examples_miscellaneous_plot_anomaly_comparison.py>` to see how
198::COMO;;# it's used, and the :ref:`User Guide <sgd_online_one_class_svm>` for more
199::COMO;;# details.
200::COMO;;#
201::COMO;;# .. figure:: ../miscellaneous/images/sphx_glr_plot_anomaly_comparison_001.png
202::COMO;;# :target: ../miscellaneous/plot_anomaly_comparison.html
203::COMO;;# :align: center

110::COMO;;# %%
111::COMO;;# Performance improvements
112::COMO;;# ------------------------
113::COMO;;# Reductions on pairwise distances for dense float64 datasets has been refactored
114::COMO;;# to better take advantage of non-blocking thread parallelism. For example,
115::COMO;;# :meth:`neighbors.NearestNeighbors.kneighbors` and
116::COMO;;# :meth:`neighbors.NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors` can respectively be up to ×20 and
117::COMO;;# ×5 faster than previously. In summary, the following functions and estimators
118::COMO;;# now benefit from improved performance:
119::COMO;;#
120::COMO;;# - :func:`metrics.pairwise_distances_argmin`
121::COMO;;# - :func:`metrics.pairwise_distances_argmin_min`
122::COMO;;# - :class:`cluster.AffinityPropagation`
123::COMO;;# - :class:`cluster.Birch`
124::COMO;;# - :class:`cluster.MeanShift`
125::COMO;;# - :class:`cluster.OPTICS`
126::COMO;;# - :class:`cluster.SpectralClustering`
127::COMO;;# - :func:`feature_selection.mutual_info_regression`
128::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier`
129::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.KNeighborsRegressor`
130::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.RadiusNeighborsClassifier`
131::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.RadiusNeighborsRegressor`
132::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor`
133::COMO;;# - :class:`neighbors.NearestNeighbors`
134::COMO;;# - :class:`manifold.Isomap`
135::COMO;;# - :class:`manifold.LocallyLinearEmbedding`
136::COMO;;# - :class:`manifold.TSNE`
137::COMO;;# - :func:`manifold.trustworthiness`
138::COMO;;# - :class:`semi_supervised.LabelPropagation`
139::COMO;;# - :class:`semi_supervised.LabelSpreading`
140::COMO;;#
141::COMO;;# To know more about the technical details of this work, you can read
142::COMO;;# `this suite of blog posts <https://blog.scikit-learn.org/technical/performances/>`_.
143::COMO;;#
144::COMO;;# Moreover, the computation of loss functions has been refactored using
145::COMO;;# Cython resulting in performance improvements for the following estimators:
146::COMO;;#
147::COMO;;# - :class:`linear_model.LogisticRegression`
148::COMO;;# - :class:`linear_model.GammaRegressor`
149::COMO;;# - :class:`linear_model.PoissonRegressor`
150::COMO;;# - :class:`linear_model.TweedieRegressor`
151::COMO;;# %%
152::COMO;;# :class:`~decomposition.MiniBatchNMF`: an online version of NMF
153::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------
154::COMO;;# The new class :class:`~decomposition.MiniBatchNMF` implements a faster but
155::COMO;;# less accurate version of non-negative matrix factorization
156::COMO;;# (:class:`~decomposition.NMF`). :class:`~decomposition.MiniBatchNMF` divides the
157::COMO;;# data into mini-batches and optimizes the NMF model in an online manner by
158::COMO;;# cycling over the mini-batches, making it better suited for large datasets. In
159::COMO;;# particular, it implements `partial_fit`, which can be used for online
160::COMO;;# learning when the data is not readily available from the start, or when the
161::COMO;;# data does not fit into memory.
179::COMO;;# %%
180::COMO;;# :class:`~cluster.BisectingKMeans`: divide and cluster
181::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------
182::COMO;;# The new class :class:`~cluster.BisectingKMeans` is a variant of
183::COMO;;# :class:`~cluster.KMeans`, using divisive hierarchical clustering. Instead of
184::COMO;;# creating all centroids at once, centroids are picked progressively based on a
185::COMO;;# previous clustering: a cluster is split into two new clusters repeatedly
186::COMO;;# until the target number of clusters is reached, giving a hierarchical
187::COMO;;# structure to the clustering.

16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# FixedThresholdClassifier: Setting the decision threshold of a binary classifier
18::COMO;;# -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
19::COMO;;# All binary classifiers of scikit-learn use a fixed decision threshold of 0.5
20::COMO;;# to convert probability estimates (i.e. output of `predict_proba`) into class
21::COMO;;# predictions. However, 0.5 is almost never the desired threshold for a given
22::COMO;;# problem. :class:`~model_selection.FixedThresholdClassifier` allows wrapping any
23::COMO;;# binary classifier and setting a custom decision threshold.
32::COMO;;# %%
33::COMO;;# Lowering the threshold, i.e. allowing more samples to be classified as the positive
34::COMO;;# class, increases the number of true positives at the cost of more false positives
35::COMO;;# (as is well known from the concavity of the ROC curve).
40::COMO;;# %%
41::COMO;;# TunedThresholdClassifierCV: Tuning the decision threshold of a binary classifier
42::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
43::COMO;;# The decision threshold of a binary classifier can be tuned to optimize a
44::COMO;;# given metric, using :class:`~model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV`.
45::COMO;;#
46::COMO;;# It is particularly useful to find the best decision threshold when the model
47::COMO;;# is meant to be deployed in a specific application context where we can assign
48::COMO;;# different gains or costs for true positives, true negatives, false positives,
49::COMO;;# and false negatives.
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# Let's illustrate this by considering an arbitrary case where:
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# - each true positive gains 1 unit of profit, e.g. euro, year of life in good
54::COMO;;# health, etc.;
55::COMO;;# - true negatives gain or cost nothing;
56::COMO;;# - each false negative costs 2;
57::COMO;;# - each false positive costs 0.1.
58::COMO;;#
59::COMO;;# Our metric quantifies the average profit per sample, which is defined by the
60::COMO;;# following Python function:
67::COMO;;# %%
68::COMO;;# It is interesting to observe that the average gain per prediction is negative
69::COMO;;# which means that this decision system is making a loss on average.
70::COMO;;#
71::COMO;;# Tuning the threshold to optimize this custom metric gives a smaller threshold
72::COMO;;# that allows more samples to be classified as the positive class. As a result,
73::COMO;;# the average gain per prediction improves.
84::COMO;;# %%
85::COMO;;# We observe that tuning the decision threshold can turn a machine
86::COMO;;# learning-based system that makes a loss on average into a beneficial one.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# In practice, defining a meaningful application-specific metric might involve
89::COMO;;# making those costs for bad predictions and gains for good predictions depend on
90::COMO;;# auxiliary metadata specific to each individual data point such as the amount
91::COMO;;# of a transaction in a fraud detection system.
92::COMO;;#
93::COMO;;# To achieve this, :class:`~model_selection.TunedThresholdClassifierCV`
94::COMO;;# leverages metadata routing support (:ref:`Metadata Routing User
95::COMO;;# Guide<metadata_routing>`) allowing to optimize complex business metrics as
96::COMO;;# detailed in :ref:`Post-tuning the decision threshold for cost-sensitive
97::COMO;;# learning
98::COMO;;# <sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_cost_sensitive_learning.py>`.
99::COMO;;# %%
100::COMO;;# Performance improvements in PCA
101::COMO;;# -------------------------------
102::COMO;;# :class:`~decomposition.PCA` has a new solver, `"covariance_eigh"`, which is
103::COMO;;# up to an order of magnitude faster and more memory efficient than the other
104::COMO;;# solvers for datasets with many data points and few features.
112::COMO;;# %%
113::COMO;;# The new solver also accepts sparse input data:
118::COMO;;# %%
119::COMO;;# The `"full"` solver has also been improved to use less memory and allows
120::COMO;;# faster transformation. The default `svd_solver="auto"` option takes
121::COMO;;# advantage of the new solver and is now able to select an appropriate solver
122::COMO;;# for sparse datasets.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# Similarly to most other PCA solvers, the new `"covariance_eigh"` solver can leverage
125::COMO;;# GPU computation if the input data is passed as a PyTorch or CuPy array by
126::COMO;;# enabling the experimental support for :ref:`Array API <array_api>`.
127::COMO;;# %%
128::COMO;;# ColumnTransformer is subscriptable
129::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
130::COMO;;# The transformers of a :class:`~compose.ColumnTransformer` can now be directly
131::COMO;;# accessed using indexing by name.

146::COMO;;# using a callable that computes a scalar value from the non missing values of
147::COMO;;# a column vector.

16::COMO;;# %%
17::COMO;;# FrozenEstimator: Freezing an estimator
18::COMO;;# --------------------------------------
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# This meta-estimator allows you to take an estimator and freeze its fit method, meaning
21::COMO;;# that calling `fit` does not perform any operations; also, `fit_predict` and
22::COMO;;# `fit_transform` call `predict` and `transform` respectively without calling `fit`. The
23::COMO;;# original estimator's other methods and properties are left unchanged. An interesting
24::COMO;;# use case for this is to use a pre-fitted model as a transformer step in a pipeline
25::COMO;;# or to pass a pre-fitted model to some of the meta-estimators. Here's a short example:
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# Fitting the threshold classifier skipped fitting the inner `SGDClassifier`. For more
45::COMO;;# details refer to the example :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_frozen_plot_frozen_examples.py`.
46::COMO;;# %%
47::COMO;;# Transforming data other than X in a Pipeline
48::COMO;;# --------------------------------------------
49::COMO;;#
50::COMO;;# The :class:`~pipeline.Pipeline` now supports transforming passed data other than `X`
51::COMO;;# if necessary. This can be done by setting the new `transform_input` parameter. This
52::COMO;;# is particularly useful when passing a validation set through the pipeline.
53::COMO;;#
54::COMO;;# As an example, imagine `EstimatorWithValidationSet` is an estimator which accepts
55::COMO;;# a validation set. We can now have a pipeline which will transform the validation set
56::COMO;;# and pass it to the estimator::
57::COMO;;#
58::COMO;;# with sklearn.config_context(enable_metadata_routing=True):
59::COMO;;# est_gs = GridSearchCV(
60::COMO;;# Pipeline(
61::COMO;;# (
62::COMO;;# StandardScaler(),
63::COMO;;# EstimatorWithValidationSet(...).set_fit_request(X_val=True, y_val=True),
64::COMO;;# ),
65::COMO;;# # telling pipeline to transform these inputs up to the step which is
66::COMO;;# # requesting them.
67::COMO;;# transform_input=["X_val"],
68::COMO;;# ),
69::COMO;;# param_grid={"estimatorwithvalidationset__param_to_optimize": list(range(5))},
70::COMO;;# cv=5,
71::COMO;;# ).fit(X, y, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val)
72::COMO;;#
73::COMO;;# In the above code, the key parts are the call to `set_fit_request` to specify that
74::COMO;;# `X_val` and `y_val` are required by the `EstimatorWithValidationSet.fit` method, and
75::COMO;;# the `transform_input` parameter to tell the pipeline to transform `X_val` before
76::COMO;;# passing it to `EstimatorWithValidationSet.fit`.
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;# Note that at this time scikit-learn estimators have not yet been extended to accept
79::COMO;;# user specified validation sets. This feature is released early to collect feedback
80::COMO;;# from third-party libraries who might benefit from it.
81::COMO;;# %%
82::COMO;;# Multiclass support for `LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky")`
83::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
84::COMO;;#
85::COMO;;# The `"newton-cholesky"` solver (originally introduced in scikit-learn version
86::COMO;;# 1.2) was previously limited to binary
87::COMO;;# :class:`~linear_model.LogisticRegression` and some other generalized linear
88::COMO;;# regression estimators (namely :class:`~linear_model.PoissonRegressor`,
89::COMO;;# :class:`~linear_model.GammaRegressor` and
90::COMO;;# :class:`~linear_model.TweedieRegressor`).
91::COMO;;#
92::COMO;;# This new release includes support for multiclass (multinomial)
93::COMO;;# :class:`~linear_model.LogisticRegression`.
94::COMO;;#
95::COMO;;# This solver is particularly useful when the number of features is small to
96::COMO;;# medium. It has been empirically shown to converge more reliably and faster
97::COMO;;# than other solvers on some medium sized datasets with one-hot encoded
98::COMO;;# categorical features as can be seen in the `benchmark results of the
99::COMO;;# pull-request
100::COMO;;# <https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/28840#issuecomment-2065368727>`_.

103::COMO;;# -------------------------------------
104::COMO;;#
105::COMO;;# The classes :class:`ensemble.ExtraTreesClassifier` and
106::COMO;;# :class:`ensemble.ExtraTreesRegressor` now support missing values. More details in the
107::COMO;;# :ref:`User Guide <tree_missing_value_support>`.
114::COMO;;# %%
115::COMO;;# Download any dataset from the web
116::COMO;;# ---------------------------------
117::COMO;;#
118::COMO;;# The function :func:`datasets.fetch_file` allows downloading a file from any given URL.
119::COMO;;# This convenience function provides built-in local disk caching, sha256 digest
120::COMO;;# integrity check and an automated retry mechanism on network error.
121::COMO;;#
122::COMO;;# The goal is to provide the same convenience and reliability as dataset fetchers while
123::COMO;;# giving the flexibility to work with data from arbitrary online sources and file
124::COMO;;# formats.
125::COMO;;#
126::COMO;;# The downloaded file can then be loaded with generic or domain specific functions such
127::COMO;;# as `pandas.read_csv`, `pandas.read_parquet`, etc.

147::COMO;;# Free-threaded CPython 3.13 support
148::COMO;;# ----------------------------------
149::COMO;;#
150::COMO;;# scikit-learn has preliminary support for free-threaded CPython, in particular
151::COMO;;# free-threaded wheels are available for all of our supported platforms.
152::COMO;;#
153::COMO;;# Free-threaded (also known as nogil) CPython 3.13 is an experimental version of
154::COMO;;# CPython 3.13 which aims at enabling efficient multi-threaded use cases by
155::COMO;;# removing the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL).
156::COMO;;#
157::COMO;;# For more details about free-threaded CPython see `py-free-threading doc <https://py-free-threading.github.io>`_,
158::COMO;;# in particular `how to install a free-threaded CPython <https://py-free-threading.github.io/installing_cpython/>`_
159::COMO;;# and `Ecosystem compatibility tracking <https://py-free-threading.github.io/tracking/>`_.
160::COMO;;#
161::COMO;;# Feel free to try free-threaded CPython on your use case and report any issues!
162::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# Improvements to the developer API for third party libraries
164::COMO;;# -----------------------------------------------------------
165::COMO;;#
166::COMO;;# We have been working on improving the developer API for third party libraries.
167::COMO;;# This is still a work in progress, but a fair amount of work has been done in this
168::COMO;;# release. This release includes:
169::COMO;;#
170::COMO;;# - :func:`sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data` is introduced and replaces the
171::COMO;;# previously private `BaseEstimator._validate_data` method. This function extends
172::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.utils.validation.check_array` and adds support for remembering
173::COMO;;# input feature counts and names.
174::COMO;;# - Estimator tags are now revamped and a part of the public API via
175::COMO;;# :class:`sklearn.utils.Tags`. Estimators should now override the
176::COMO;;# :meth:`BaseEstimator.__sklearn_tags__` method instead of implementing a `_more_tags`
177::COMO;;# method. If you'd like to support multiple scikit-learn versions, you can implement
178::COMO;;# both methods in your class.
179::COMO;;# - As a consequence of developing a public tag API, we've removed the `_xfail_checks`
180::COMO;;# tag and tests which are expected to fail are directly passed to
181::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.check_estimator` and
182::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks`. See their
183::COMO;;# corresponding API docs for more details.
184::COMO;;# - Many tests in the common test suite are updated and raise more helpful error
185::COMO;;# messages. We've also added some new tests, which should help you more easily fix
186::COMO;;# potential issues with your estimators.
187::COMO;;#
188::COMO;;# An updated version of our :ref:`develop` is also available, which we recommend you
189::COMO;;# check out.

8::COMM;;dataset, with varying thresholds.
9::COMM;;The upper graph shows the amount of labeled samples that the classifier has
10::COMM;;available by the end of fit, and the accuracy of the classifier. The lower
11::COMM;;graph shows the last iteration in which a sample was labeled. All values are
12::COMM;;cross validated with 3 folds.
13::COMM;;At low thresholds (in [0.4, 0.5]), the classifier learns from samples that were
14::COMM;;labeled with a low confidence. These low-confidence samples are likely have
15::COMM;;incorrect predicted labels, and as a result, fitting on these incorrect labels
16::COMM;;produces a poor accuracy. Note that the classifier labels almost all of the
17::COMM;;samples, and only takes one iteration.
18::COMM;;For very high thresholds (in [0.9, 1)) we observe that the classifier does not
19::COMM;;augment its dataset (the amount of self-labeled samples is 0). As a result, the
20::COMM;;accuracy achieved with a threshold of 0.9999 is the same as a normal supervised
21::COMM;;classifier would achieve.
22::COMM;;The optimal accuracy lies in between both of these extremes at a threshold of
23::COMM;;around 0.7.

50::COMO;;# class when computing accuracy

10::COMM;;scenario)

12::COMM;;- Represents the best possible performance when labeled data is abundant

14::COMM;;- Same model as the best-case scenario but trained on a random 20% subset of
15::COMM;;the labeled training data

17::COMM;;limited labeled data

19::COMM;;- Uses 20% labeled data + 80% unlabeled data for training
20::COMM;;- Iteratively predicts labels for unlabeled data
21::COMM;;- Demonstrates how self-training can improve performance
22::COMM;;4. :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` (semi-supervised)
23::COMM;;- Uses 20% labeled data + 80% unlabeled data for training
24::COMM;;- Propagates labels through the data manifold
25::COMM;;- Shows how graph-based methods can leverage unlabeled data
26::COMM;;The example uses the 20 newsgroups dataset, focusing on five categories.
27::COMM;;The results demonstrate how semi-supervised methods can achieve better
28::COMM;;performance than supervised learning with limited labeled data by
29::COMM;;effectively utilizing unlabeled samples.

2::COMM;;===============================================================================
3::COMM;;Decision boundary of semi-supervised classifiers versus SVM on the Iris dataset
4::COMM;;===============================================================================
5::COMM;;This example compares decision boundaries learned by two semi-supervised
6::COMM;;methods, namely :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` and
7::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier`, while varying the
8::COMM;;proportion of labeled training data from small fractions up to the full dataset.
9::COMM;;Both methods rely on RBF kernels: :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` uses
10::COMM;;it by default, and :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier` is paired
11::COMM;;here with :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` as base estimator (also RBF-based by default) to
12::COMM;;allow a fair comparison. With 100% labeled data,
13::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier` reduces to a fully supervised
14::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC`, since there are no unlabeled points left to pseudo-label.
15::COMM;;In a second section, we explain how `predict_proba` is computed in
16::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` and
17::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier`.
18::COMM;;See
19::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_semi_supervised_plot_semi_supervised_newsgroups.py`
20::COMM;;for a comparison of `LabelSpreading` and `SelfTrainingClassifier` in terms of
21::COMM;;performance.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
39::COMC;;y_10[y_rand > 0.1] = -1 # set random samples to be unlabeled
91::COMO;;# %%
92::COMO;;# We observe that the decision boundaries are already quite similar to those
93::COMO;;# using the full labeled data available for training, even when using a very
94::COMO;;# small subset of the labels.
95::COMO;;#
96::COMO;;# Interpretation of `predict_proba`
97::COMO;;# =================================
98::COMO;;#
99::COMO;;# `predict_proba` in `LabelSpreading`
100::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
101::COMO;;#
102::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` constructs a similarity graph
103::COMO;;# from the data, by default using an RBF kernel. This means each sample is
104::COMO;;# connected to every other with a weight that decays with their squared
105::COMO;;# Euclidean distance, scaled by a parameter `gamma`.
106::COMO;;#
107::COMO;;# Once we have that weighted graph, labels are propagated along the graph
108::COMO;;# edges. Each sample gradually takes on a soft label distribution that reflects
109::COMO;;# a weighted average of the labels of its neighbors until the process converges.
110::COMO;;# These per-sample distributions are stored in `label_distributions_`.
111::COMO;;#
112::COMO;;# `predict_proba` computes the class probabilities for a new point by taking a
113::COMO;;# weighted average of the rows in `label_distributions_`, where the weights come
114::COMO;;# from the RBF kernel similarities between the new point and the training
115::COMO;;# samples. The averaged values are then renormalized so that they sum to one.
116::COMO;;#
117::COMO;;# Just keep in mind that these "probabilities" are graph-based scores, not
118::COMO;;# calibrated posteriors. Don't over-interpret their absolute values.
120::COMC;;ls = ls100[0] # fitted LabelSpreading instance
121::COMC;;x_query = np.array([[3.5, 1.5]]) # point in the soft blue region
122::COMO;;# Step 1: similarities between query and all training samples
123::COMC;;W = rbf_kernel(x_query, X, gamma=ls.gamma) # `gamma=20` by default
124::COMO;;# Step 2: weighted average of label distributions
126::COMO;;# Step 3: normalize to sum to 1
130::COMO;;# %%
131::COMO;;# `predict_proba` in `SelfTrainingClassifier`
132::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------
133::COMO;;#
134::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier` works by repeatedly
135::COMO;;# fitting its base estimator on the currently labeled data, then adding
136::COMO;;# pseudo-labels for unlabeled points whose predicted probabilities exceed a
137::COMO;;# confidence threshold. This process continues until no new points can be
138::COMO;;# labeled, at which point the classifier has a final fitted base estimator
139::COMO;;# stored in the attribute `estimator_`.
140::COMO;;#
141::COMO;;# When you call `predict_proba` on the `SelfTrainingClassifier`, it simply
142::COMO;;# delegates to this final estimator.
146::COMO;;# %%
147::COMO;;# In both methods, semi-supervised learning can be understood as constructing a
148::COMO;;# categorical distribution over classes for each sample.
149::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.LabelSpreading` keeps these distributions soft and
150::COMO;;# updates them through graph-based propagation.
151::COMO;;# Predictions (including `predict_proba`) remain tied to the training set, which
152::COMO;;# must be stored for inference.
153::COMO;;#
154::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.semi_supervised.SelfTrainingClassifier` instead uses these
155::COMO;;# distributions internally to decide which unlabeled points to assign pseudo-labels
156::COMO;;# during training, but at prediction time the returned probabilities come directly from
157::COMO;;# the final fitted estimator, and therefore the decision rule does not require storing
158::COMO;;# the training data.

3::COMM;;Plot different SVM classifiers in the iris dataset
4::COMM;;==================================================
5::COMM;;Comparison of different linear SVM classifiers on a 2D projection of the iris
6::COMM;;dataset. We only consider the first 2 features of this dataset:
7::COMM;;- Sepal length

9::COMM;;This example shows how to plot the decision surface for four SVM classifiers
10::COMM;;with different kernels.
11::COMM;;The linear models ``LinearSVC()`` and ``SVC(kernel='linear')`` yield slightly
12::COMM;;different decision boundaries. This can be a consequence of the following
13::COMM;;differences:
14::COMM;;- ``LinearSVC`` minimizes the squared hinge loss while ``SVC`` minimizes the
15::COMM;;regular hinge loss.
16::COMM;;- ``LinearSVC`` uses the One-vs-All (also known as One-vs-Rest) multiclass
17::COMM;;reduction while ``SVC`` uses the One-vs-One multiclass reduction.
18::COMM;;Both linear models have linear decision boundaries (intersecting hyperplanes)
19::COMM;;while the non-linear kernel models (polynomial or Gaussian RBF) have more
20::COMM;;flexible non-linear decision boundaries with shapes that depend on the kind of
21::COMM;;kernel and its parameters.
22::COMM;;.. NOTE:: while plotting the decision function of classifiers for toy 2D
23::COMM;;datasets can help get an intuitive understanding of their respective
24::COMM;;expressive power, be aware that those intuitions don't always generalize to
25::COMM;;more realistic high-dimensional problems.

2::COMM;;==================
3::COMM;;RBF SVM parameters
4::COMM;;==================
5::COMM;;This example illustrates the effect of the parameters ``gamma`` and ``C`` of
6::COMM;;the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel SVM.
7::COMM;;Intuitively, the ``gamma`` parameter defines how far the influence of a single
8::COMM;;training example reaches, with low values meaning 'far' and high values meaning
9::COMM;;'close'. The ``gamma`` parameters can be seen as the inverse of the radius of
10::COMM;;influence of samples selected by the model as support vectors.
11::COMM;;The ``C`` parameter trades off correct classification of training examples
12::COMM;;against maximization of the decision function's margin. For larger values of
13::COMM;;``C``, a smaller margin will be accepted if the decision function is better at
14::COMM;;classifying all training points correctly. A lower ``C`` will encourage a
15::COMM;;larger margin, therefore a simpler decision function, at the cost of training
16::COMM;;accuracy. In other words ``C`` behaves as a regularization parameter in the
17::COMM;;SVM.
18::COMM;;The first plot is a visualization of the decision function for a variety of
19::COMM;;parameter values on a simplified classification problem involving only 2 input
20::COMM;;features and 2 possible target classes (binary classification). Note that this
21::COMM;;kind of plot is not possible to do for problems with more features or target
22::COMM;;classes.
23::COMM;;The second plot is a heatmap of the classifier's cross-validation accuracy as a
24::COMM;;function of ``C`` and ``gamma``. For this example we explore a relatively large
25::COMM;;grid for illustration purposes. In practice, a logarithmic grid from
26::COMM;;:math:`10^{-3}` to :math:`10^3` is usually sufficient. If the best parameters
27::COMM;;lie on the boundaries of the grid, it can be extended in that direction in a
28::COMM;;subsequent search.
29::COMM;;Note that the heat map plot has a special colorbar with a midpoint value close
30::COMM;;to the score values of the best performing models so as to make it easy to tell
31::COMM;;them apart in the blink of an eye.
32::COMM;;The behavior of the model is very sensitive to the ``gamma`` parameter. If
33::COMM;;``gamma`` is too large, the radius of the area of influence of the support
34::COMM;;vectors only includes the support vector itself and no amount of
35::COMM;;regularization with ``C`` will be able to prevent overfitting.
36::COMM;;When ``gamma`` is very small, the model is too constrained and cannot capture
37::COMM;;the complexity or "shape" of the data. The region of influence of any selected
38::COMM;;support vector would include the whole training set. The resulting model will
39::COMM;;behave similarly to a linear model with a set of hyperplanes that separate the
40::COMM;;centers of high density of any pair of two classes.
41::COMM;;For intermediate values, we can see on the second plot that good models can
42::COMM;;be found on a diagonal of ``C`` and ``gamma``. Smooth models (lower ``gamma``
43::COMM;;values) can be made more complex by increasing the importance of classifying
44::COMM;;each point correctly (larger ``C`` values) hence the diagonal of good
45::COMM;;performing models.
46::COMM;;Finally, one can also observe that for some intermediate values of ``gamma`` we
47::COMM;;get equally performing models when ``C`` becomes very large. This suggests that
48::COMM;;the set of support vectors does not change anymore. The radius of the RBF
49::COMM;;kernel alone acts as a good structural regularizer. Increasing ``C`` further
50::COMM;;doesn't help, likely because there are no more training points in violation
51::COMM;;(inside the margin or wrongly classified), or at least no better solution can
52::COMM;;be found. Scores being equal, it may make sense to use the smaller ``C``
53::COMM;;values, since very high ``C`` values typically increase fitting time.
54::COMM;;On the other hand, lower ``C`` values generally lead to more support vectors,
55::COMM;;which may increase prediction time. Therefore, lowering the value of ``C``
56::COMM;;involves a trade-off between fitting time and prediction time.
57::COMM;;We should also note that small differences in scores results from the random
58::COMM;;splits of the cross-validation procedure. Those spurious variations can be
59::COMM;;smoothed out by increasing the number of CV iterations ``n_splits`` at the
60::COMM;;expense of compute time. Increasing the value number of ``C_range`` and
61::COMM;;``gamma_range`` steps will increase the resolution of the hyper-parameter heat
62::COMM;;map.
64::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
65::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

2::COMM;;=========================================================
3::COMM;;Plot classification boundaries with different SVM Kernels
4::COMM;;=========================================================
5::COMM;;This example shows how different kernels in a :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` (Support Vector
6::COMM;;Classifier) influence the classification boundaries in a binary, two-dimensional
7::COMM;;classification problem.
8::COMM;;SVCs aim to find a hyperplane that effectively separates the classes in their training
9::COMM;;data by maximizing the margin between the outermost data points of each class. This is
10::COMM;;achieved by finding the best weight vector :math:`w` that defines the decision boundary
11::COMM;;hyperplane and minimizes the sum of hinge losses for misclassified samples, as measured
12::COMM;;by the :func:`~sklearn.metrics.hinge_loss` function. By default, regularization is
13::COMM;;applied with the parameter `C=1`, which allows for a certain degree of misclassification
14::COMM;;tolerance.
15::COMM;;If the data is not linearly separable in the original feature space, a non-linear kernel
16::COMM;;parameter can be set. Depending on the kernel, the process involves adding new features
17::COMM;;or transforming existing features to enrich and potentially add meaning to the data.
18::COMM;;When a kernel other than `"linear"` is set, the SVC applies the `kernel trick
19::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_method#Mathematics:_the_kernel_trick>`__, which
20::COMM;;computes the similarity between pairs of data points using the kernel function without
21::COMM;;explicitly transforming the entire dataset. The kernel trick surpasses the otherwise
22::COMM;;necessary matrix transformation of the whole dataset by only considering the relations
23::COMM;;between all pairs of data points. The kernel function maps two vectors (each pair of
24::COMM;;observations) to their similarity using their dot product.
25::COMM;;The hyperplane can then be calculated using the kernel function as if the dataset were
26::COMM;;represented in a higher-dimensional space. Using a kernel function instead of an
27::COMM;;explicit matrix transformation improves performance, as the kernel function has a time
28::COMM;;complexity of :math:`O({n}^2)`, whereas matrix transformation scales according to the
29::COMM;;specific transformation being applied.
30::COMM;;In this example, we compare the most common kernel types of Support Vector Machines: the
31::COMM;;linear kernel (`"linear"`), the polynomial kernel (`"poly"`), the radial basis function
32::COMM;;kernel (`"rbf"`) and the sigmoid kernel (`"sigmoid"`).
34::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
35::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
36::COMO;;# %%
37::COMO;;# Creating a dataset
38::COMO;;# ------------------
39::COMO;;# We create a two-dimensional classification dataset with 16 samples and two classes. We
40::COMO;;# plot the samples with the colors matching their respective targets.
64::COMO;;# Plotting settings
68::COMO;;# Plot samples by color and add legend
73::COMO;;# %%
74::COMO;;# We can see that the samples are not clearly separable by a straight line.
75::COMO;;#
76::COMO;;# Training SVC model and plotting decision boundaries
77::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------
78::COMO;;# We define a function that fits a :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` classifier,
79::COMO;;# allowing the `kernel` parameter as an input, and then plots the decision
80::COMO;;# boundaries learned by the model using
81::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.inspection.DecisionBoundaryDisplay`.
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# Notice that for the sake of simplicity, the `C` parameter is set to its
84::COMO;;# default value (`C=1`) in this example and the `gamma` parameter is set to
85::COMO;;# `gamma=2` across all kernels, although it is automatically ignored for the
86::COMO;;# linear kernel. In a real classification task, where performance matters,
87::COMO;;# parameter tuning (by using :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` for
88::COMO;;# instance) is highly recommended to capture different structures within the
89::COMO;;# data.
90::COMO;;#
91::COMO;;# Setting `response_method="predict"` in
92::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.inspection.DecisionBoundaryDisplay` colors the areas based
93::COMO;;# on their predicted class. Using `response_method="decision_function"` allows
94::COMO;;# us to also plot the decision boundary and the margins to both sides of it.
95::COMO;;# Finally the support vectors used during training (which always lay on the
96::COMO;;# margins) are identified by means of the `support_vectors_` attribute of
97::COMO;;# the trained SVCs, and plotted as well.
103::COMO;;# Train the SVC
105::COMO;;# Settings for plotting
110::COMO;;# Plot decision boundary and margins
127::COMO;;# Plot bigger circles around samples that serve as support vectors
135::COMO;;# Plot samples by color and add legend
144::COMO;;# %%
145::COMO;;# Linear kernel
146::COMO;;# *************
147::COMO;;# Linear kernel is the dot product of the input samples:
148::COMO;;#
149::COMO;;# .. math:: K(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = \mathbf{x}_1^\top \mathbf{x}_2
150::COMO;;#
151::COMO;;# It is then applied to any combination of two data points (samples) in the
152::COMO;;# dataset. The dot product of the two points determines the
153::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity` between both points. The
154::COMO;;# higher the value, the more similar the points are.
156::COMO;;# %%
157::COMO;;# Training a :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` on a linear kernel results in an
158::COMO;;# untransformed feature space, where the hyperplane and the margins are
159::COMO;;# straight lines. Due to the lack of expressivity of the linear kernel, the
160::COMO;;# trained classes do not perfectly capture the training data.
161::COMO;;#
162::COMO;;# Polynomial kernel
163::COMO;;# *****************
164::COMO;;# The polynomial kernel changes the notion of similarity. The kernel function
165::COMO;;# is defined as:
166::COMO;;#
167::COMO;;# .. math::
168::COMO;;# K(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = (\gamma \cdot \
169::COMO;;# \mathbf{x}_1^\top\mathbf{x}_2 + r)^d
170::COMO;;#
171::COMO;;# where :math:`{d}` is the degree (`degree`) of the polynomial, :math:`{\gamma}`
172::COMO;;# (`gamma`) controls the influence of each individual training sample on the
173::COMO;;# decision boundary and :math:`{r}` is the bias term (`coef0`) that shifts the
174::COMO;;# data up or down. Here, we use the default value for the degree of the
175::COMO;;# polynomial in the kernel function (`degree=3`). When `coef0=0` (the default),
176::COMO;;# the data is only transformed, but no additional dimension is added. Using a
177::COMO;;# polynomial kernel is equivalent to creating
178::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.PolynomialFeatures` and then fitting a
179::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC` with a linear kernel on the transformed data,
180::COMO;;# although this alternative approach would be computationally expensive for most
181::COMO;;# datasets.
183::COMO;;# %%
184::COMO;;# The polynomial kernel with `gamma=2` adapts well to the training data,
185::COMO;;# causing the margins on both sides of the hyperplane to bend accordingly.
186::COMO;;#
187::COMO;;# RBF kernel
188::COMO;;# **********
189::COMO;;# The radial basis function (RBF) kernel, also known as the Gaussian kernel, is
190::COMO;;# the default kernel for Support Vector Machines in scikit-learn. It measures
191::COMO;;# similarity between two data points in infinite dimensions and then approaches
192::COMO;;# classification by majority vote. The kernel function is defined as:
193::COMO;;#
194::COMO;;# .. math::
195::COMO;;# K(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = \exp\left(-\gamma \cdot
196::COMO;;# {\|\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2\|^2}\right)
197::COMO;;#
198::COMO;;# where :math:`{\gamma}` (`gamma`) controls the influence of each individual
199::COMO;;# training sample on the decision boundary.
200::COMO;;#
201::COMO;;# The larger the euclidean distance between two points
202::COMO;;# :math:`\|\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2\|^2`
203::COMO;;# the closer the kernel function is to zero. This means that two points far away
204::COMO;;# are more likely to be dissimilar.
206::COMO;;# %%
207::COMO;;# In the plot we can see how the decision boundaries tend to contract around
208::COMO;;# data points that are close to each other.
209::COMO;;#
210::COMO;;# Sigmoid kernel
211::COMO;;# **************
212::COMO;;# The sigmoid kernel function is defined as:
213::COMO;;#
214::COMO;;# .. math::
215::COMO;;# K(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) = \tanh(\gamma \cdot
216::COMO;;# \mathbf{x}_1^\top\mathbf{x}_2 + r)
217::COMO;;#
218::COMO;;# where the kernel coefficient :math:`{\gamma}` (`gamma`) controls the influence
219::COMO;;# of each individual training sample on the decision boundary and :math:`{r}` is
220::COMO;;# the bias term (`coef0`) that shifts the data up or down.
221::COMO;;#
222::COMO;;# In the sigmoid kernel, the similarity between two data points is computed
223::COMO;;# using the hyperbolic tangent function (:math:`\tanh`). The kernel function
224::COMO;;# scales and possibly shifts the dot product of the two points
225::COMO;;# (:math:`\mathbf{x}_1` and :math:`\mathbf{x}_2`).
227::COMO;;# %%
228::COMO;;# We can see that the decision boundaries obtained with the sigmoid kernel
229::COMO;;# appear curved and irregular. The decision boundary tries to separate the
230::COMO;;# classes by fitting a sigmoid-shaped curve, resulting in a complex boundary
231::COMO;;# that may not generalize well to unseen data. From this example it becomes
232::COMO;;# obvious, that the sigmoid kernel has very specific use cases, when dealing
233::COMO;;# with data that exhibits a sigmoidal shape. In this example, careful fine
234::COMO;;# tuning might find more generalizable decision boundaries. Because of its
235::COMO;;# specificity, the sigmoid kernel is less commonly used in practice compared to
236::COMO;;# other kernels.
237::COMO;;#
238::COMO;;# Conclusion
239::COMO;;# ----------
240::COMO;;# In this example, we have visualized the decision boundaries trained with the
241::COMO;;# provided dataset. The plots serve as an intuitive demonstration of how
242::COMO;;# different kernels utilize the training data to determine the classification
243::COMO;;# boundaries.
244::COMO;;#
245::COMO;;# The hyperplanes and margins, although computed indirectly, can be imagined as
246::COMO;;# planes in the transformed feature space. However, in the plots, they are
247::COMO;;# represented relative to the original feature space, resulting in curved
248::COMO;;# decision boundaries for the polynomial, RBF, and sigmoid kernels.
249::COMO;;#
250::COMO;;# Please note that the plots do not evaluate the individual kernel's accuracy or
251::COMO;;# quality. They are intended to provide a visual understanding of how the
252::COMO;;# different kernels use the training data.
253::COMO;;#
254::COMO;;# For a comprehensive evaluation, fine-tuning of :class:`~sklearn.svm.SVC`
255::COMO;;# parameters using techniques such as
256::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` is recommended to capture the
257::COMO;;# underlying structures within the data.
258::COMO;;# %%
259::COMO;;# XOR dataset
260::COMO;;# -----------
261::COMO;;# A classical example of a dataset which is not linearly separable is the XOR
262::COMO;;# pattern. HEre we demonstrate how different kernels work on such a dataset.
274::COMO;;# %%
275::COMO;;# As you can see from the plots above, only the `rbf` kernel can find a
276::COMO;;# reasonable decision boundary for the above dataset.
