2::COMM;;==============================================
3::COMM;;Scaling the regularization parameter for SVCs
4::COMM;;==============================================
5::COMM;;The following example illustrates the effect of scaling the regularization
6::COMM;;parameter when using :ref:`svm` for :ref:`classification <svm_classification>`.
7::COMM;;For SVC classification, we are interested in a risk minimization for the
8::COMM;;equation:
9::COMM;;.. math::
10::COMM;;C \sum_{i=1, n} \mathcal{L} (f(x_i), y_i) + \Omega (w)
11::COMM;;where
12::COMM;;- :math:`C` is used to set the amount of regularization
13::COMM;;- :math:`\mathcal{L}` is a `loss` function of our samples and our model parameters.
14::COMM;;- :math:`\Omega` is a `penalty` function of our model parameters
15::COMM;;If we consider the loss function to be the individual error per sample, then the
16::COMM;;data-fit term, or the sum of the error for each sample, increases as we add more
17::COMM;;samples. The penalization term, however, does not increase.
18::COMM;;When using, for example, :ref:`cross validation <cross_validation>`, to set the
19::COMM;;amount of regularization with `C`, there would be a different amount of samples
20::COMM;;between the main problem and the smaller problems within the folds of the cross
21::COMM;;validation.
22::COMM;;Since the loss function dependens on the amount of samples, the latter
23::COMM;;influences the selected value of `C`. The question that arises is "How do we
24::COMM;;optimally adjust C to account for the different amount of training samples?"
26::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
27::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
28::COMO;;# %%
29::COMO;;# Data generation
30::COMO;;# ---------------
31::COMO;;#
32::COMO;;# In this example we investigate the effect of reparametrizing the regularization
33::COMO;;# parameter `C` to account for the number of samples when using either L1 or L2
34::COMO;;# penalty. For such purpose we create a synthetic dataset with a large number of
35::COMO;;# features, out of which only a few are informative. We therefore expect the
36::COMO;;# regularization to shrink the coefficients towards zero (L2 penalty) or exactly
37::COMO;;# zero (L1 penalty).
43::COMO;;# %%
44::COMO;;# L1-penalty case
45::COMO;;# ---------------
46::COMO;;# In the L1 case, theory says that provided a strong regularization, the
47::COMO;;# estimator cannot predict as well as a model knowing the true distribution
48::COMO;;# (even in the limit where the sample size grows to infinity) as it may set some
49::COMO;;# weights of otherwise predictive features to zero, which induces a bias. It does
50::COMO;;# say, however, that it is possible to find the right set of non-zero parameters
51::COMO;;# as well as their signs by tuning `C`.
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# We define a linear SVC with the L1 penalty.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# We compute the mean test score for different values of `C` via
58::COMO;;# cross-validation.
84::COMO;;# %%
87::COMO;;# plot results without scaling C
94::COMO;;# plot results by scaling C
105::COMO;;# %%
106::COMO;;# In the region of small `C` (strong regularization) all the coefficients
107::COMO;;# learned by the models are zero, leading to severe underfitting. Indeed, the
108::COMO;;# accuracy in this region is at the chance level.
109::COMO;;#
110::COMO;;# Using the default scale results in a somewhat stable optimal value of `C`,
111::COMO;;# whereas the transition out of the underfitting region depends on the number of
112::COMO;;# training samples. The reparametrization leads to even more stable results.
113::COMO;;#
114::COMO;;# See e.g. theorem 3 of :arxiv:`On the prediction performance of the Lasso
115::COMO;;# <1402.1700>` or :arxiv:`Simultaneous analysis of Lasso and Dantzig selector
116::COMO;;# <0801.1095>` where the regularization parameter is always assumed to be
117::COMO;;# proportional to 1 / sqrt(n_samples).
118::COMO;;#
119::COMO;;# L2-penalty case
120::COMO;;# ---------------
121::COMO;;# We can do a similar experiment with the L2 penalty. In this case, the
122::COMO;;# theory says that in order to achieve prediction consistency, the penalty
123::COMO;;# parameter should be kept constant as the number of samples grow.
141::COMO;;# %%
144::COMO;;# plot results without scaling C
151::COMO;;# plot results by scaling C
162::COMO;;# %%
163::COMO;;# For the L2 penalty case, the reparametrization seems to have a smaller impact
164::COMO;;# on the stability of the optimal value for the regularization. The transition
165::COMO;;# out of the overfitting region occurs in a more spread range and the accuracy
166::COMO;;# does not seem to be degraded up to chance level.
167::COMO;;#
168::COMO;;# Try increasing the value to `n_splits=1_000` for better results in the L2
169::COMO;;# case, which is not shown here due to the limitations on the documentation
170::COMO;;# builder.

3::COMM;;Classification of text documents using sparse features
4::COMM;;======================================================
5::COMM;;This is an example showing how scikit-learn can be used to classify documents by
6::COMM;;topics using a `Bag of Words approach
7::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bag-of-words_model>`_. This example uses a
8::COMM;;Tf-idf-weighted document-term sparse matrix to encode the features and
9::COMM;;demonstrates various classifiers that can efficiently handle sparse matrices.
10::COMM;;For document analysis via an unsupervised learning approach, see the example
11::COMM;;script :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_clustering.py`.

20::COMO;;# comprises around 18,000 newsgroups posts on 20 topics split in two subsets:
21::COMO;;# one for training (or development) and the other one for testing (or for
22::COMO;;# performance evaluation). Note that, by default, the text samples contain some

92::COMM;;# %%
93::COMM;;# Analysis of a bag-of-words document classifier
94::COMM;;# ==============================================
95::COMM;;#
96::COMM;;# We will now train a classifier twice, once on the text samples including
97::COMM;;# metadata and once after stripping the metadata. For both cases we will analyze
98::COMM;;# the classification errors on a test set using a confusion matrix and inspect
99::COMM;;# the coefficients that define the classification function of the trained
100::COMM;;# models.
101::COMM;;#
102::COMM;;# Model without metadata stripping
103::COMM;;# --------------------------------
104::COMM;;#
105::COMM;;# We start by using the custom function `load_dataset` to load the data without
106::COMM;;# metadata stripping.
107::COMM;;X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, feature_names, target_names = load_dataset(
108::COMM;;verbose=True
109::COMM;;)
110::COMM;;# %%
111::COMM;;# Our first model is an instance of the
112::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.RidgeClassifier` class. This is a linear
113::COMM;;# classification model that uses the mean squared error on {-1, 1} encoded
114::COMM;;# targets, one for each possible class. Contrary to
115::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression`,
116::COMM;;# :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.RidgeClassifier` does not
117::COMM;;# provide probabilistic predictions (no `predict_proba` method),
118::COMM;;# but it is often faster to train.
119::COMM;;from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
120::COMM;;clf = RidgeClassifier(tol=1e-2, solver="sparse_cg")
121::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
122::COMM;;pred = clf.predict(X_test)
123::COMM;;# %%
124::COMM;;# We plot the confusion matrix of this classifier to find if there is a pattern
125::COMM;;# in the classification errors.
126::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
127::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay
128::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
129::COMM;;ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, pred, ax=ax)
130::COMM;;ax.xaxis.set_ticklabels(target_names)
131::COMM;;ax.yaxis.set_ticklabels(target_names)
132::COMM;;_ = ax.set_title(
133::COMM;;f"Confusion Matrix for {clf.__class__.__name__}\non the original documents"
134::COMM;;)
135::COMM;;# %%
136::COMM;;# The confusion matrix highlights that documents of the `alt.atheism` class are
137::COMM;;# often confused with documents with the class `talk.religion.misc` class and
138::COMM;;# vice-versa which is expected since the topics are semantically related.
139::COMM;;#
140::COMM;;# We also observe that some documents of the `sci.space` class can be misclassified as
141::COMM;;# `comp.graphics` while the converse is much rarer. A manual inspection of those
142::COMM;;# badly classified documents would be required to get some insights on this
143::COMM;;# asymmetry. It could be the case that the vocabulary of the space topic could
144::COMM;;# be more specific than the vocabulary for computer graphics.
145::COMM;;#
146::COMM;;# We can gain a deeper understanding of how this classifier makes its decisions
147::COMM;;# by looking at the words with the highest average feature effects:
148::COMM;;import numpy as np
149::COMM;;import pandas as pd
150::COMM;;def plot_feature_effects():
151::COMM;;# learned coefficients weighted by frequency of appearance
152::COMM;;average_feature_effects = clf.coef_ * np.asarray(X_train.mean(axis=0)).ravel()
153::COMM;;for i, label in enumerate(target_names):
154::COMM;;top5 = np.argsort(average_feature_effects[i])[-5:][::-1]
155::COMM;;if i == 0:
156::COMM;;top = pd.DataFrame(feature_names[top5], columns=[label])
157::COMM;;top_indices = top5
158::COMM;;else:
159::COMM;;top[label] = feature_names[top5]
160::COMM;;top_indices = np.concatenate((top_indices, top5), axis=None)
161::COMM;;top_indices = np.unique(top_indices)
162::COMM;;predictive_words = feature_names[top_indices]
163::COMM;;# plot feature effects
164::COMM;;bar_size = 0.25
165::COMM;;padding = 0.75
166::COMM;;y_locs = np.arange(len(top_indices)) * (4 * bar_size + padding)
167::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
168::COMM;;for i, label in enumerate(target_names):
169::COMM;;ax.barh(
170::COMM;;y_locs + (i - 2) * bar_size,
171::COMM;;average_feature_effects[i, top_indices],
172::COMM;;height=bar_size,
173::COMM;;label=label,
174::COMM;;)
175::COMM;;ax.set(
176::COMM;;yticks=y_locs,
177::COMM;;yticklabels=predictive_words,
178::COMM;;ylim=[
179::COMM;;0 - 4 * bar_size,
180::COMM;;len(top_indices) * (4 * bar_size + padding) - 4 * bar_size,
181::COMM;;],
182::COMM;;)
183::COMM;;ax.legend(loc="lower right")
184::COMM;;print("top 5 keywords per class:")
185::COMM;;print(top)
186::COMM;;return ax
187::COMM;;_ = plot_feature_effects().set_title("Average feature effect on the original data")
188::COMM;;# %%
189::COMM;;# We can observe that the most predictive words are often strongly positively
190::COMM;;# associated with a single class and negatively associated with all the other
191::COMM;;# classes. Most of those positive associations are quite easy to interpret.
192::COMM;;# However, some words such as `"god"` and `"people"` are positively associated to
193::COMM;;# both `"talk.misc.religion"` and `"alt.atheism"` as those two classes expectedly
194::COMM;;# share some common vocabulary. Notice however that there are also words such as
195::COMM;;# `"christian"` and `"morality"` that are only positively associated with
196::COMM;;# `"talk.misc.religion"`. Furthermore, in this version of the dataset, the word
197::COMM;;# `"caltech"` is one of the top predictive features for atheism due to pollution
198::COMM;;# in the dataset coming from some sort of metadata such as the email addresses
199::COMM;;# of the sender of previous emails in the discussion as can be seen below:
200::COMM;;data_train = fetch_20newsgroups(
201::COMM;;subset="train", categories=categories, shuffle=True, random_state=42
202::COMM;;)
203::COMM;;for doc in data_train.data:
204::COMM;;if "caltech" in doc:
205::COMM;;print(doc)
206::COMM;;break
207::COMM;;# %%
208::COMM;;# Such headers, signature footers (and quoted metadata from previous messages)
209::COMM;;# can be considered side information that artificially reveals the newsgroup by
210::COMM;;# identifying the registered members and one would rather want our text
211::COMM;;# classifier to only learn from the "main content" of each text document instead
212::COMM;;# of relying on the leaked identity of the writers.
213::COMM;;#
214::COMM;;# Model with metadata stripping
215::COMM;;# -----------------------------
216::COMM;;#
217::COMM;;# The `remove` option of the 20 newsgroups dataset loader in scikit-learn allows
218::COMM;;# to heuristically attempt to filter out some of this unwanted metadata that
219::COMM;;# makes the classification problem artificially easier. Be aware that such
220::COMM;;# filtering of the text contents is far from perfect.
221::COMM;;#
222::COMM;;# Let us try to leverage this option to train a text classifier that does not
223::COMM;;# rely too much on this kind of metadata to make its decisions:
224::COMM;;(
225::COMM;;X_train,
226::COMM;;X_test,
227::COMM;;y_train,
228::COMM;;y_test,
229::COMM;;feature_names,
230::COMM;;target_names,
231::COMM;;) = load_dataset(remove=("headers", "footers", "quotes"))
232::COMM;;clf = RidgeClassifier(tol=1e-2, solver="sparse_cg")
233::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
234::COMM;;pred = clf.predict(X_test)
235::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
236::COMM;;ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, pred, ax=ax)
237::COMM;;ax.xaxis.set_ticklabels(target_names)
238::COMM;;ax.yaxis.set_ticklabels(target_names)
239::COMM;;_ = ax.set_title(
240::COMM;;f"Confusion Matrix for {clf.__class__.__name__}\non filtered documents"
241::COMM;;)
242::COMM;;# %%
243::COMM;;# By looking at the confusion matrix, it is more evident that the scores of the
244::COMM;;# model trained with metadata were over-optimistic. The classification problem
245::COMM;;# without access to the metadata is less accurate but more representative of the
246::COMM;;# intended text classification problem.
247::COMM;;_ = plot_feature_effects().set_title("Average feature effects on filtered documents")
248::COMM;;# %%
249::COMM;;# In the next section we keep the dataset without metadata to compare several
250::COMM;;# classifiers.
251::COMM;;# %%
252::COMM;;# Benchmarking classifiers
253::COMM;;# ========================
254::COMM;;#
255::COMM;;# Scikit-learn provides many different kinds of classification algorithms. In
256::COMM;;# this section we will train a selection of those classifiers on the same text
257::COMM;;# classification problem and measure both their generalization performance
258::COMM;;# (accuracy on the test set) and their computation performance (speed), both at
259::COMM;;# training time and testing time. For such purpose we define the following
260::COMM;;# benchmarking utilities:
261::COMM;;from sklearn import metrics
262::COMM;;from sklearn.utils.extmath import density
263::COMM;;def benchmark(clf, custom_name=False):
264::COMM;;print("_" * 80)
265::COMM;;print("Training: ")
266::COMM;;print(clf)
267::COMM;;t0 = time()
268::COMM;;clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
269::COMM;;train_time = time() - t0
270::COMM;;print(f"train time: {train_time:.3}s")
271::COMM;;t0 = time()
272::COMM;;pred = clf.predict(X_test)
273::COMM;;test_time = time() - t0
274::COMM;;print(f"test time: {test_time:.3}s")
275::COMM;;score = metrics.accuracy_score(y_test, pred)
276::COMM;;print(f"accuracy: {score:.3}")
277::COMM;;if hasattr(clf, "coef_"):
278::COMM;;print(f"dimensionality: {clf.coef_.shape[1]}")
279::COMM;;print(f"density: {density(clf.coef_)}")
280::COMM;;print()
281::COMM;;print()
282::COMM;;if custom_name:
283::COMM;;clf_descr = str(custom_name)
284::COMM;;else:
285::COMM;;clf_descr = clf.__class__.__name__
286::COMM;;return clf_descr, score, train_time, test_time
287::COMM;;# %%
288::COMM;;# We now train and test the datasets with 8 different classification models and
289::COMM;;# get performance results for each model. The goal of this study is to highlight
290::COMM;;# the computation/accuracy tradeoffs of different types of classifiers for
291::COMM;;# such a multi-class text classification problem.
292::COMM;;#
293::COMM;;# Notice that the most important hyperparameters values were tuned using a grid
294::COMM;;# search procedure not shown in this notebook for the sake of simplicity. See
295::COMM;;# the example script
296::COMM;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_model_selection_plot_grid_search_text_feature_extraction.py` # noqa: E501
297::COMM;;# for a demo on how such tuning can be done.
298::COMM;;from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

300::COMM;;from sklearn.naive_bayes import ComplementNB

327::COMM;;# Plot accuracy, training and test time of each classifier

329::COMM;;#

331::COMM;;# training and testing time of each classifier.
332::COMM;;indices = np.arange(len(results))

334::COMM;;clf_names, score, training_time, test_time = results

341::COMM;;yscale="log",
342::COMM;;xlabel="test accuracy",
343::COMM;;ylabel="training time (s)",
344::COMM;;)
345::COMM;;fig, ax2 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8))
346::COMM;;ax2.scatter(score, test_time, s=60)
347::COMM;;ax2.set(
348::COMM;;title="Score-test time trade-off",
349::COMM;;yscale="log",
350::COMM;;xlabel="test accuracy",
351::COMM;;ylabel="test time (s)",
352::COMM;;)
353::COMM;;for i, txt in enumerate(clf_names):

356::COMM;;# %%
357::COMM;;# The naive Bayes model has the best trade-off between score and
358::COMM;;# training/testing time, while Random Forest is both slow to train, expensive to
359::COMM;;# predict and has a comparatively bad accuracy. This is expected: for
360::COMM;;# high-dimensional prediction problems, linear models are often better suited as
361::COMM;;# most problems become linearly separable when the feature space has 10,000
362::COMM;;# dimensions or more.
363::COMM;;#
364::COMM;;# The difference in training speed and accuracy of the linear models can be
365::COMM;;# explained by the choice of the loss function they optimize and the kind of
366::COMM;;# regularization they use. Be aware that some linear models with the same loss
367::COMM;;# but a different solver or regularization configuration may yield different
368::COMM;;# fitting times and test accuracy. We can observe on the second plot that once
369::COMM;;# trained, all linear models have approximately the same prediction speed which
370::COMM;;# is expected because they all implement the same prediction function.
371::COMM;;#
372::COMM;;# KNeighborsClassifier has a relatively low accuracy and has the highest testing
373::COMM;;# time. The long prediction time is also expected: for each prediction the model
374::COMM;;# has to compute the pairwise distances between the testing sample and each
375::COMM;;# document in the training set, which is computationally expensive. Furthermore,
376::COMM;;# the "curse of dimensionality" harms the ability of this model to yield
377::COMM;;# competitive accuracy in the high dimensional feature space of text
378::COMM;;# classification problems.
2::COMM;;=======================================
3::COMM;;Clustering text documents using k-means
4::COMM;;=======================================
5::COMM;;This is an example showing how the scikit-learn API can be used to cluster
6::COMM;;documents by topics using a `Bag of Words approach
7::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bag-of-words_model>`_.
8::COMM;;Two algorithms are demonstrated, namely :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` and its more
9::COMM;;scalable variant, :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`. Additionally,
10::COMM;;latent semantic analysis is used to reduce dimensionality and discover latent
11::COMM;;patterns in the data.
12::COMM;;This example uses two different text vectorizers: a
13::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` and a
14::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer`. See the example
15::COMM;;notebook :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_hashing_vs_dict_vectorizer.py`
16::COMM;;for more information on vectorizers and a comparison of their processing times.
17::COMM;;For document analysis via a supervised learning approach, see the example script
18::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_classification_20newsgroups.py`.
20::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
21::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
22::COMO;;# %%
23::COMO;;# Loading text data
24::COMO;;# =================
25::COMO;;#
26::COMO;;# We load data from :ref:`20newsgroups_dataset`, which comprises around 18,000
27::COMO;;# newsgroups posts on 20 topics. For illustrative purposes and to reduce the
28::COMO;;# computational cost, we select a subset of 4 topics only accounting for around
29::COMO;;# 3,400 documents. See the example
30::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_classification_20newsgroups.py`
31::COMO;;# to gain intuition on the overlap of such topics.
32::COMO;;#
33::COMO;;# Notice that, by default, the text samples contain some message metadata such
34::COMO;;# as `"headers"`, `"footers"` (signatures) and `"quotes"` to other posts. We use
35::COMO;;# the `remove` parameter from :func:`~sklearn.datasets.fetch_20newsgroups` to
36::COMO;;# strip those features and have a more sensible clustering problem.
56::COMO;;# %%
57::COMO;;# Quantifying the quality of clustering results
58::COMO;;# =============================================
59::COMO;;#
60::COMO;;# In this section we define a function to score different clustering pipelines
61::COMO;;# using several metrics.
62::COMO;;#
63::COMO;;# Clustering algorithms are fundamentally unsupervised learning methods.
64::COMO;;# However, since we happen to have class labels for this specific dataset, it is
65::COMO;;# possible to use evaluation metrics that leverage this "supervised" ground
66::COMO;;# truth information to quantify the quality of the resulting clusters. Examples
67::COMO;;# of such metrics are the following:
68::COMO;;#
69::COMO;;# - homogeneity, which quantifies how much clusters contain only members of a
70::COMO;;# single class;
71::COMO;;#
72::COMO;;# - completeness, which quantifies how much members of a given class are
73::COMO;;# assigned to the same clusters;
74::COMO;;#
75::COMO;;# - V-measure, the harmonic mean of completeness and homogeneity;
76::COMO;;#
77::COMO;;# - Rand-Index, which measures how frequently pairs of data points are grouped
78::COMO;;# consistently according to the result of the clustering algorithm and the
79::COMO;;# ground truth class assignment;
80::COMO;;#
81::COMO;;# - Adjusted Rand-Index, a chance-adjusted Rand-Index such that random cluster
82::COMO;;# assignment have an ARI of 0.0 in expectation.
83::COMO;;#
84::COMO;;# If the ground truth labels are not known, evaluation can only be performed
85::COMO;;# using the model results itself. In that case, the Silhouette Coefficient comes in
86::COMO;;# handy. See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_kmeans_silhouette_analysis.py`
87::COMO;;# for an example on how to do it.
88::COMO;;#
89::COMO;;# For more reference, see :ref:`clustering_evaluation`.
130::COMO;;# %%
131::COMO;;# K-means clustering on text features
132::COMO;;# ===================================
133::COMO;;#
134::COMO;;# Two feature extraction methods are used in this example:
135::COMO;;#
136::COMO;;# - :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` uses an in-memory
137::COMO;;# vocabulary (a Python dict) to map the most frequent words to features
138::COMO;;# indices and hence compute a word occurrence frequency (sparse) matrix. The
139::COMO;;# word frequencies are then reweighted using the Inverse Document Frequency
140::COMO;;# (IDF) vector collected feature-wise over the corpus.
141::COMO;;#
142::COMO;;# - :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer` hashes word
143::COMO;;# occurrences to a fixed dimensional space, possibly with collisions. The word
144::COMO;;# count vectors are then normalized to each have l2-norm equal to one
145::COMO;;# (projected to the euclidean unit-sphere) which seems to be important for
146::COMO;;# k-means to work in high dimensional space.
147::COMO;;#
148::COMO;;# Furthermore it is possible to post-process those extracted features using
149::COMO;;# dimensionality reduction. We will explore the impact of those choices on the
150::COMO;;# clustering quality in the following.
151::COMO;;#
152::COMO;;# Feature Extraction using TfidfVectorizer
153::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------
154::COMO;;#
155::COMO;;# We first benchmark the estimators using a dictionary vectorizer along with an
156::COMO;;# IDF normalization as provided by
157::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer`.
168::COMO;;# %%
169::COMO;;# After ignoring terms that appear in more than 50% of the documents (as set by
170::COMO;;# `max_df=0.5`) and terms that are not present in at least 5 documents (set by
171::COMO;;# `min_df=5`), the resulting number of unique terms `n_features` is around
172::COMO;;# 8,000. We can additionally quantify the sparsity of the `X_tfidf` matrix as
173::COMO;;# the fraction of non-zero entries divided by the total number of elements.
175::COMO;;# %%
176::COMO;;# We find that around 0.7% of the entries of the `X_tfidf` matrix are non-zero.
177::COMO;;#
178::COMO;;# .. _kmeans_sparse_high_dim:
179::COMO;;#
180::COMO;;# Clustering sparse data with k-means
181::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
182::COMO;;#
183::COMO;;# As both :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` and
184::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans` optimize a non-convex objective
185::COMO;;# function, their clustering is not guaranteed to be optimal for a given random
186::COMO;;# init. Even further, on sparse high-dimensional data such as text vectorized
187::COMO;;# using the Bag of Words approach, k-means can initialize centroids on extremely
188::COMO;;# isolated data points. Those data points can stay their own centroids all
189::COMO;;# along.
190::COMO;;#
191::COMO;;# The following code illustrates how the previous phenomenon can sometimes lead
192::COMO;;# to highly imbalanced clusters, depending on the random initialization:
208::COMO;;# %%
209::COMO;;# To avoid this problem, one possibility is to increase the number of runs with
210::COMO;;# independent random initiations `n_init`. In such case the clustering with the
211::COMO;;# best inertia (objective function of k-means) is chosen.
218::COMO;;# %%
219::COMO;;# All those clustering evaluation metrics have a maximum value of 1.0 (for a
220::COMO;;# perfect clustering result). Higher values are better. Values of the Adjusted
221::COMO;;# Rand-Index close to 0.0 correspond to a random labeling. Notice from the
222::COMO;;# scores above that the cluster assignment is indeed well above chance level,
223::COMO;;# but the overall quality can certainly improve.
224::COMO;;#
225::COMO;;# Keep in mind that the class labels may not reflect accurately the document
226::COMO;;# topics and therefore metrics that use labels are not necessarily the best to
227::COMO;;# evaluate the quality of our clustering pipeline.
228::COMO;;#
229::COMO;;# Performing dimensionality reduction using LSA
230::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------
231::COMO;;#
232::COMO;;# A `n_init=1` can still be used as long as the dimension of the vectorized
233::COMO;;# space is reduced first to make k-means more stable. For such purpose we use
234::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.TruncatedSVD`, which works on term count/tf-idf
235::COMO;;# matrices. Since SVD results are not normalized, we redo the normalization to
236::COMO;;# improve the :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` result. Using SVD to reduce the
237::COMO;;# dimensionality of TF-IDF document vectors is often known as `latent semantic
238::COMO;;# analysis <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_semantic_analysis>`_ (LSA) in
239::COMO;;# the information retrieval and text mining literature.
249::COMO;;# %%
250::COMO;;# Using a single initialization means the processing time will be reduced for
251::COMO;;# both :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` and
252::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`.
259::COMO;;# %%
260::COMO;;# We can observe that clustering on the LSA representation of the document is
261::COMO;;# significantly faster (both because of `n_init=1` and because the
262::COMO;;# dimensionality of the LSA feature space is much smaller). Furthermore, all the
263::COMO;;# clustering evaluation metrics have improved. We repeat the experiment with
264::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`.
277::COMO;;# %%
278::COMO;;# Top terms per cluster
279::COMO;;# ---------------------
280::COMO;;#
281::COMO;;# Since :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` can be
282::COMO;;# inverted we can identify the cluster centers, which provide an intuition of
283::COMO;;# the most influential words **for each cluster**. See the example script
284::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_classification_20newsgroups.py`
285::COMO;;# for a comparison with the most predictive words **for each target class**.
294::COMO;;# %%
295::COMO;;# HashingVectorizer
296::COMO;;# -----------------
297::COMO;;# An alternative vectorization can be done using a
298::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer` instance, which
299::COMO;;# does not provide IDF weighting as this is a stateless model (the fit method
300::COMO;;# does nothing). When IDF weighting is needed it can be added by pipelining the
301::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer` output to a
302::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfTransformer` instance. In this
303::COMO;;# case we also add LSA to the pipeline to reduce the dimension and sparcity of
304::COMO;;# the hashed vector space.
315::COMO;;# %%
316::COMO;;# One can observe that the LSA step takes a relatively long time to fit,
317::COMO;;# especially with hashed vectors. The reason is that a hashed space is typically
318::COMO;;# large (set to `n_features=50_000` in this example). One can try lowering the
319::COMO;;# number of features at the expense of having a larger fraction of features with
320::COMO;;# hash collisions as shown in the example notebook
321::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_hashing_vs_dict_vectorizer.py`.
322::COMO;;#
323::COMO;;# We now fit and evaluate the `kmeans` and `minibatch_kmeans` instances on this
324::COMO;;# hashed-lsa-reduced data:
326::COMO;;# %%
332::COMO;;# %%
333::COMO;;# Both methods lead to good results that are similar to running the same models
334::COMO;;# on the traditional LSA vectors (without hashing).
335::COMO;;#
336::COMO;;# Clustering evaluation summary
337::COMO;;# ==============================
352::COMO;;# %%
353::COMO;;# :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` and :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`
354::COMO;;# suffer from the phenomenon called the `Curse of Dimensionality
355::COMO;;# <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_dimensionality>`_ for high dimensional
356::COMO;;# datasets such as text data. That is the reason why the overall scores improve
357::COMO;;# when using LSA. Using LSA reduced data also improves the stability and
358::COMO;;# requires lower clustering time, though keep in mind that the LSA step itself
359::COMO;;# takes a long time, especially with hashed vectors.
360::COMO;;#
361::COMO;;# The Silhouette Coefficient is defined between 0 and 1. In all cases we obtain
362::COMO;;# values close to 0 (even if they improve a bit after using LSA) because its
363::COMO;;# definition requires measuring distances, in contrast with other evaluation
364::COMO;;# metrics such as the V-measure and the Adjusted Rand Index which are only based
365::COMO;;# on cluster assignments rather than distances. Notice that strictly speaking,
366::COMO;;# one should not compare the Silhouette Coefficient between spaces of different
367::COMO;;# dimension, due to the different notions of distance they imply.
368::COMO;;#
369::COMO;;# The homogeneity, completeness and hence v-measure metrics do not yield a
370::COMO;;# baseline with regards to random labeling: this means that depending on the
371::COMO;;# number of samples, clusters and ground truth classes, a completely random
372::COMO;;# labeling will not always yield the same values. In particular random labeling
373::COMO;;# won't yield zero scores, especially when the number of clusters is large. This
374::COMO;;# problem can safely be ignored when the number of samples is more than a
375::COMO;;# thousand and the number of clusters is less than 10, which is the case of the
376::COMO;;# present example. For smaller sample sizes or larger number of clusters it is
377::COMO;;# safer to use an adjusted index such as the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). See the
378::COMO;;# example
379::COMO;;# :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_adjusted_for_chance_measures.py` for
380::COMO;;# a demo on the effect of random labeling.
381::COMO;;#
382::COMO;;# The size of the error bars show that :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`
383::COMO;;# is less stable than :class:`~sklearn.cluster.KMeans` for this relatively small
384::COMO;;# dataset. It is more interesting to use when the number of samples is much
385::COMO;;# bigger, but it can come at the expense of a small degradation in clustering
386::COMO;;# quality compared to the traditional k-means algorithm.
2::COMM;;===========================================
3::COMM;;FeatureHasher and DictVectorizer Comparison
4::COMM;;===========================================
5::COMM;;In this example we illustrate text vectorization, which is the process of
6::COMM;;representing non-numerical input data (such as dictionaries or text documents)
7::COMM;;as vectors of real numbers.
8::COMM;;We first compare :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` and
9::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer` by using both methods to
10::COMM;;vectorize text documents that are preprocessed (tokenized) with the help of a
11::COMM;;custom Python function.
12::COMM;;Later we introduce and analyze the text-specific vectorizers
13::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer`,
14::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` and
15::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` that handle both the
16::COMM;;tokenization and the assembling of the feature matrix within a single class.
17::COMM;;The objective of the example is to demonstrate the usage of text vectorization
18::COMM;;API and to compare their processing time. See the example scripts
19::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_classification_20newsgroups.py`
20::COMM;;and :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_clustering.py` for actual
21::COMM;;learning on text documents.
23::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
24::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
25::COMO;;# %%
26::COMO;;# Load Data
27::COMO;;# ---------
28::COMO;;#
29::COMO;;# We load data from :ref:`20newsgroups_dataset`, which comprises around
30::COMO;;# 18000 newsgroups posts on 20 topics split in two subsets: one for training and
31::COMO;;# one for testing. For the sake of simplicity and reducing the computational
32::COMO;;# cost, we select a subset of 7 topics and use the training set only.
47::COMO;;# %%
48::COMO;;# Define preprocessing functions
49::COMO;;# ------------------------------
50::COMO;;#
51::COMO;;# A token may be a word, part of a word or anything comprised between spaces or
52::COMO;;# symbols in a string. Here we define a function that extracts the tokens using
53::COMO;;# a simple regular expression (regex) that matches Unicode word characters. This
54::COMO;;# includes most characters that can be part of a word in any language, as well
55::COMO;;# as numbers and the underscore:
59::COMM;;This uses a simple regex that matches word characters to break strings
60::COMM;;into tokens. For a more principled approach, see CountVectorizer or
61::COMM;;TfidfVectorizer.
65::COMO;;# %%
66::COMO;;# We define an additional function that counts the (frequency of) occurrence of
67::COMO;;# each token in a given document. It returns a frequency dictionary to be used
68::COMO;;# by the vectorizers.
72::COMM;;freq = defaultdict(int)
73::COMM;;for tok in tokenize(doc):
74::COMM;;freq[tok] += 1
75::COMM;;return freq
76::COMM;;token_freqs("That is one example, but this is another one")
77::COMM;;# %%
78::COMM;;# Observe in particular that the repeated token `"is"` is counted twice for
79::COMM;;# instance.
80::COMM;;#
81::COMM;;# Breaking a text document into word tokens, potentially losing the order
82::COMM;;# information between the words in a sentence is often called a `Bag of Words
83::COMM;;# representation <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bag-of-words_model>`_.
84::COMM;;# %%
85::COMM;;# DictVectorizer
86::COMM;;# --------------
87::COMM;;#
88::COMM;;# First we benchmark the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer`,
89::COMM;;# then we compare it to :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` as
90::COMM;;# both of them receive dictionaries as input.
91::COMM;;from time import time
92::COMM;;from sklearn.feature_extraction import DictVectorizer
93::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers = defaultdict(list)
94::COMM;;t0 = time()
95::COMM;;vectorizer = DictVectorizer()
96::COMM;;vectorizer.fit_transform(token_freqs(d) for d in raw_data)
97::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
98::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(
99::COMM;;vectorizer.__class__.__name__ + "\non freq dicts"
100::COMM;;)
101::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
102::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
103::COMM;;print(f"Found {len(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())} unique terms")
104::COMM;;# %%
105::COMM;;# The actual mapping from text token to column index is explicitly stored in
106::COMM;;# the `.vocabulary_` attribute which is a potentially very large Python
107::COMM;;# dictionary:
108::COMM;;type(vectorizer.vocabulary_)
109::COMM;;# %%
110::COMM;;len(vectorizer.vocabulary_)
111::COMM;;# %%
112::COMM;;vectorizer.vocabulary_["example"]
113::COMM;;# %%
114::COMM;;# FeatureHasher
115::COMM;;# -------------
116::COMM;;#
117::COMM;;# Dictionaries take up a large amount of storage space and grow in size as the
118::COMM;;# training set grows. Instead of growing the vectors along with a dictionary,
119::COMM;;# feature hashing builds a vector of pre-defined length by applying a hash
120::COMM;;# function `h` to the features (e.g., tokens), then using the hash values
121::COMM;;# directly as feature indices and updating the resulting vector at those
122::COMM;;# indices. When the feature space is not large enough, hashing functions tend to
123::COMM;;# map distinct values to the same hash code (hash collisions). As a result, it
124::COMM;;# is impossible to determine what object generated any particular hash code.
125::COMM;;#
126::COMM;;# Because of the above it is impossible to recover the original tokens from the
127::COMM;;# feature matrix and the best approach to estimate the number of unique terms in
128::COMM;;# the original dictionary is to count the number of active columns in the
129::COMM;;# encoded feature matrix. For such a purpose we define the following function:
130::COMM;;import numpy as np
131::COMM;;def n_nonzero_columns(X):
136::COMM;;return len(np.unique(X.nonzero()[1]))
137::COMM;;# %%
138::COMM;;# The default number of features for the
139::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` is 2**20. Here we set
140::COMM;;# `n_features = 2**18` to illustrate hash collisions.
141::COMM;;#
142::COMM;;# **FeatureHasher on frequency dictionaries**
143::COMM;;from sklearn.feature_extraction import FeatureHasher
144::COMM;;t0 = time()
145::COMM;;hasher = FeatureHasher(n_features=2**18)
146::COMM;;X = hasher.transform(token_freqs(d) for d in raw_data)
147::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
148::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(
149::COMM;;hasher.__class__.__name__ + "\non freq dicts"
150::COMM;;)
151::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
152::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
153::COMM;;print(f"Found {n_nonzero_columns(X)} unique tokens")
154::COMM;;# %%
155::COMM;;# The number of unique tokens when using the
156::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` is lower than those obtained
157::COMM;;# using the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer`. This is due to
158::COMM;;# hash collisions.
159::COMM;;#
160::COMM;;# The number of collisions can be reduced by increasing the feature space.
161::COMM;;# Notice that the speed of the vectorizer does not change significantly when
162::COMM;;# setting a large number of features, though it causes larger coefficient
163::COMM;;# dimensions and then requires more memory usage to store them, even if a
164::COMM;;# majority of them is inactive.
165::COMM;;t0 = time()
166::COMM;;hasher = FeatureHasher(n_features=2**22)
167::COMM;;X = hasher.transform(token_freqs(d) for d in raw_data)
168::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
169::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
170::COMM;;print(f"Found {n_nonzero_columns(X)} unique tokens")
171::COMM;;# %%
172::COMM;;# We confirm that the number of unique tokens gets closer to the number of
173::COMM;;# unique terms found by the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer`.
174::COMM;;#
175::COMM;;# **FeatureHasher on raw tokens**
176::COMM;;#
177::COMM;;# Alternatively, one can set `input_type="string"` in the
178::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` to vectorize the strings
179::COMM;;# output directly from the customized `tokenize` function. This is equivalent to
180::COMM;;# passing a dictionary with an implied frequency of 1 for each feature name.
181::COMM;;t0 = time()
182::COMM;;hasher = FeatureHasher(n_features=2**18, input_type="string")
183::COMM;;X = hasher.transform(tokenize(d) for d in raw_data)
184::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
185::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(
186::COMM;;hasher.__class__.__name__ + "\non raw tokens"
187::COMM;;)
188::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
189::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
190::COMM;;print(f"Found {n_nonzero_columns(X)} unique tokens")
191::COMM;;# %%
192::COMM;;# We now plot the speed of the above methods for vectorizing.
193::COMM;;import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
194::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
195::COMM;;y_pos = np.arange(len(dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"]))
196::COMM;;ax.barh(y_pos, dict_count_vectorizers["speed"], align="center")
197::COMM;;ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
198::COMM;;ax.set_yticklabels(dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"])
199::COMM;;ax.invert_yaxis()
200::COMM;;_ = ax.set_xlabel("speed (MB/s)")
201::COMM;;# %%
202::COMM;;# In both cases :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` is
203::COMM;;# approximately twice as fast as
204::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer`. This is handy when dealing
205::COMM;;# with large amounts of data, with the downside of losing the invertibility of
206::COMM;;# the transformation, which in turn makes the interpretation of a model a more
207::COMM;;# complex task.
208::COMM;;#
209::COMM;;# The `FeatureHeasher` with `input_type="string"` is slightly faster than the
210::COMM;;# variant that works on frequency dict because it does not count repeated
211::COMM;;# tokens: each token is implicitly counted once, even if it was repeated.
212::COMM;;# Depending on the downstream machine learning task, it can be a limitation or
213::COMM;;# not.
214::COMM;;#
215::COMM;;# Comparison with special purpose text vectorizers
216::COMM;;# ------------------------------------------------
217::COMM;;#
218::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` accepts raw data as
219::COMM;;# it internally implements tokenization and occurrence counting. It is similar
220::COMM;;# to the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer` when used along with
221::COMM;;# the customized function `token_freqs` as done in the previous section. The
222::COMM;;# difference being that :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer`
223::COMM;;# is more flexible. In particular it accepts various regex patterns through the
224::COMM;;# `token_pattern` parameter.
225::COMM;;from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
226::COMM;;t0 = time()
227::COMM;;vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
228::COMM;;vectorizer.fit_transform(raw_data)
229::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
230::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(vectorizer.__class__.__name__)
231::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
232::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
233::COMM;;print(f"Found {len(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())} unique terms")
234::COMM;;# %%
235::COMM;;# We see that using the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer`
236::COMM;;# implementation is approximately twice as fast as using the
237::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer` along with the simple
238::COMM;;# function we defined for mapping the tokens. The reason is that
239::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` is optimized by
240::COMM;;# reusing a compiled regular expression for the full training set instead of
241::COMM;;# creating one per document as done in our naive tokenize function.
242::COMM;;#
243::COMM;;# Now we make a similar experiment with the
244::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer`, which is
245::COMM;;# equivalent to combining the "hashing trick" implemented by the
246::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` class and the text
247::COMM;;# preprocessing and tokenization of the
248::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer`.
249::COMM;;from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import HashingVectorizer
250::COMM;;t0 = time()
251::COMM;;vectorizer = HashingVectorizer(n_features=2**18)
252::COMM;;vectorizer.fit_transform(raw_data)
253::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
254::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(vectorizer.__class__.__name__)
255::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
256::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
257::COMM;;# %%
258::COMM;;# We can observe that this is the fastest text tokenization strategy so far,
259::COMM;;# assuming that the downstream machine learning task can tolerate a few
260::COMM;;# collisions.
261::COMM;;#
262::COMM;;# TfidfVectorizer
263::COMM;;# ---------------
264::COMM;;#
265::COMM;;# In a large text corpus, some words appear with higher frequency (e.g. "the",
266::COMM;;# "a", "is" in English) and do not carry meaningful information about the actual
267::COMM;;# contents of a document. If we were to feed the word count data directly to a
268::COMM;;# classifier, those very common terms would shadow the frequencies of rarer yet
269::COMM;;# more informative terms. In order to re-weight the count features into floating
270::COMM;;# point values suitable for usage by a classifier it is very common to use the
271::COMM;;# tf-idf transform as implemented by the
272::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfTransformer`. TF stands for
273::COMM;;# "term-frequency" while "tf-idf" means term-frequency times inverse
274::COMM;;# document-frequency.
275::COMM;;#
276::COMM;;# We now benchmark the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer`,
277::COMM;;# which is equivalent to combining the tokenization and occurrence counting of
278::COMM;;# the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` along with the
279::COMM;;# normalizing and weighting from a
280::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfTransformer`.
281::COMM;;from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
282::COMM;;t0 = time()
283::COMM;;vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer()
284::COMM;;vectorizer.fit_transform(raw_data)
285::COMM;;duration = time() - t0
286::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"].append(vectorizer.__class__.__name__)
287::COMM;;dict_count_vectorizers["speed"].append(data_size_mb / duration)
288::COMM;;print(f"done in {duration:.3f} s at {data_size_mb / duration:.1f} MB/s")
289::COMM;;print(f"Found {len(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())} unique terms")
290::COMM;;# %%
291::COMM;;# Summary
292::COMM;;# -------
293::COMM;;# Let's conclude this notebook by summarizing all the recorded processing speeds
294::COMM;;# in a single plot:
295::COMM;;fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))
296::COMM;;y_pos = np.arange(len(dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"]))
297::COMM;;ax.barh(y_pos, dict_count_vectorizers["speed"], align="center")
298::COMM;;ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
299::COMM;;ax.set_yticklabels(dict_count_vectorizers["vectorizer"])
300::COMM;;ax.invert_yaxis()
301::COMM;;_ = ax.set_xlabel("speed (MB/s)")
302::COMM;;# %%
303::COMM;;# Notice from the plot that
304::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer` is slightly slower
305::COMM;;# than :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` because of the
306::COMM;;# extra operation induced by the
307::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfTransformer`.
308::COMM;;#
309::COMM;;# Also notice that, by setting the number of features `n_features = 2**18`, the
310::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer` performs better
311::COMM;;# than the :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` at the
312::COMM;;# expense of inversibility of the transformation due to hash collisions.
313::COMM;;#
314::COMM;;# We highlight that :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.CountVectorizer` and
315::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.HashingVectorizer` perform better than
316::COMM;;# their equivalent :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.DictVectorizer` and
317::COMM;;# :func:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.FeatureHasher` on manually tokenized
318::COMM;;# documents since the internal tokenization step of the former vectorizers
319::COMM;;# compiles a regular expression once and then reuses it for all the documents.
2::COMM;;========================================================
3::COMM;;Post pruning decision trees with cost complexity pruning
4::COMM;;========================================================
5::COMM;;.. currentmodule:: sklearn.tree
6::COMM;;The :class:`DecisionTreeClassifier` provides parameters such as
7::COMM;;``min_samples_leaf`` and ``max_depth`` to prevent a tree from overfiting. Cost
8::COMM;;complexity pruning provides another option to control the size of a tree. In
9::COMM;;:class:`DecisionTreeClassifier`, this pruning technique is parameterized by the
10::COMM;;cost complexity parameter, ``ccp_alpha``. Greater values of ``ccp_alpha``
11::COMM;;increase the number of nodes pruned. Here we only show the effect of
12::COMM;;``ccp_alpha`` on regularizing the trees and how to choose a ``ccp_alpha``
13::COMM;;based on validation scores.
14::COMM;;See also :ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details on pruning.
16::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
17::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
22::COMO;;# %%
23::COMO;;# Total impurity of leaves vs effective alphas of pruned tree
24::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------------------------------
25::COMO;;# Minimal cost complexity pruning recursively finds the node with the "weakest
26::COMO;;# link". The weakest link is characterized by an effective alpha, where the
27::COMO;;# nodes with the smallest effective alpha are pruned first. To get an idea of
28::COMO;;# what values of ``ccp_alpha`` could be appropriate, scikit-learn provides
29::COMO;;# :func:`DecisionTreeClassifier.cost_complexity_pruning_path` that returns the
30::COMO;;# effective alphas and the corresponding total leaf impurities at each step of
31::COMO;;# the pruning process. As alpha increases, more of the tree is pruned, which
32::COMO;;# increases the total impurity of its leaves.
38::COMO;;# %%
39::COMO;;# In the following plot, the maximum effective alpha value is removed, because
40::COMO;;# it is the trivial tree with only one node.
46::COMO;;# %%
47::COMO;;# Next, we train a decision tree using the effective alphas. The last value
48::COMO;;# in ``ccp_alphas`` is the alpha value that prunes the whole tree,
49::COMO;;# leaving the tree, ``clfs[-1]``, with one node.
60::COMO;;# %%
61::COMO;;# For the remainder of this example, we remove the last element in
62::COMO;;# ``clfs`` and ``ccp_alphas``, because it is the trivial tree with only one
63::COMO;;# node. Here we show that the number of nodes and tree depth decreases as alpha
64::COMO;;# increases.
79::COMO;;# %%
80::COMO;;# Accuracy vs alpha for training and testing sets
81::COMO;;# ----------------------------------------------------
82::COMO;;# When ``ccp_alpha`` is set to zero and keeping the other default parameters
83::COMO;;# of :class:`DecisionTreeClassifier`, the tree overfits, leading to
84::COMO;;# a 100% training accuracy and 88% testing accuracy. As alpha increases, more
85::COMO;;# of the tree is pruned, thus creating a decision tree that generalizes better.
86::COMO;;# In this example, setting ``ccp_alpha=0.015`` maximizes the testing accuracy.

104::COMO;;# Plot the results
105::COMO;;# ----------------
126::COMO;;# %%
127::COMO;;# As you can see, the higher the value of `max_depth`, the more details of the data
128::COMO;;# are caught by the model. However, the model also overfits to the data and is
129::COMO;;# influenced by the noise.
2::COMM;;=========================================
3::COMM;;Understanding the decision tree structure
4::COMM;;=========================================
5::COMM;;The decision tree structure can be analysed to gain further insight on the
6::COMM;;relation between the features and the target to predict. In this example, we
7::COMM;;show how to retrieve:
8::COMM;;- the binary tree structure;
9::COMM;;- the depth of each node and whether or not it's a leaf;
10::COMM;;- the nodes that were reached by a sample using the ``decision_path`` method;
11::COMM;;- the leaf that was reached by a sample using the apply method;
12::COMM;;- the rules that were used to predict a sample;
13::COMM;;- the decision path shared by a group of samples.
15::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
23::COMO;;##############################################################################
24::COMO;;# Train tree classifier
25::COMO;;# ---------------------
26::COMO;;# First, we fit a :class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier` using the
27::COMO;;# :func:`~sklearn.datasets.load_iris` dataset.
34::COMO;;##############################################################################
35::COMO;;# Tree structure
36::COMO;;# --------------
37::COMO;;#
38::COMO;;# The decision classifier has an attribute called ``tree_`` which allows access
39::COMO;;# to low level attributes such as ``node_count``, the total number of nodes,
40::COMO;;# and ``max_depth``, the maximal depth of the tree. The
41::COMO;;# ``tree_.compute_node_depths()`` method computes the depth of each node in the
42::COMO;;# tree. `tree_` also stores the entire binary tree structure, represented as a
43::COMO;;# number of parallel arrays. The i-th element of each array holds information
44::COMO;;# about the node ``i``. Node 0 is the tree's root. Some of the arrays only
45::COMO;;# apply to either leaves or split nodes. In this case the values of the nodes
46::COMO;;# of the other type is arbitrary. For example, the arrays ``feature`` and
47::COMO;;# ``threshold`` only apply to split nodes. The values for leaf nodes in these
48::COMO;;# arrays are therefore arbitrary.
49::COMO;;#
50::COMO;;# Among these arrays, we have:
51::COMO;;#
52::COMO;;# - ``children_left[i]``: id of the left child of node ``i`` or -1 if leaf node
53::COMO;;# - ``children_right[i]``: id of the right child of node ``i`` or -1 if leaf node
54::COMO;;# - ``feature[i]``: feature used for splitting node ``i``
55::COMO;;# - ``threshold[i]``: threshold value at node ``i``
56::COMO;;# - ``n_node_samples[i]``: the number of training samples reaching node ``i``
57::COMO;;# - ``impurity[i]``: the impurity at node ``i``
58::COMO;;# - ``weighted_n_node_samples[i]``: the weighted number of training samples
59::COMO;;# reaching node ``i``
60::COMO;;# - ``value[i, j, k]``: the summary of the training samples that reached node i for
61::COMO;;# output j and class k (for regression tree, class is set to 1). See below
62::COMO;;# for more information about ``value``.
63::COMO;;#
64::COMO;;# Using the arrays, we can traverse the tree structure to compute various
65::COMO;;# properties. Below, we will compute the depth of each node and whether or not
66::COMO;;# it is a leaf.
75::COMC;;stack = [(0, 0)] # start with the root node id (0) and its depth (0)
77::COMO;;# `pop` ensures each node is only visited once
80::COMO;;# If the left and right child of a node is not the same we have a split
81::COMO;;# node
83::COMO;;# If a split node, append left and right children and depth to `stack`
84::COMO;;# so we can loop through them
115::COMO;;# %%
116::COMO;;# What is the values array used here?
117::COMO;;# -----------------------------------
118::COMO;;# The `tree_.value` array is a 3D array of shape
119::COMO;;# [``n_nodes``, ``n_classes``, ``n_outputs``] which provides the proportion of samples
120::COMO;;# reaching a node for each class and for each output.
121::COMO;;# Each node has a ``value`` array which is the proportion of weighted samples reaching
122::COMO;;# this node for each output and class with respect to the parent node.
123::COMO;;#
124::COMO;;# One could convert this to the absolute weighted number of samples reaching a node,
125::COMO;;# by multiplying this number by `tree_.weighted_n_node_samples[node_idx]` for the
126::COMO;;# given node. Note sample weights are not used in this example, so the weighted
127::COMO;;# number of samples is the number of samples reaching the node because each sample
128::COMO;;# has a weight of 1 by default.
129::COMO;;#
130::COMO;;# For example, in the above tree built on the iris dataset, the root node has
131::COMO;;# ``value = [0.33, 0.304, 0.366]`` indicating there are 33% of class 0 samples,
132::COMO;;# 30.4% of class 1 samples, and 36.6% of class 2 samples at the root node. One can
133::COMO;;# convert this to the absolute number of samples by multiplying by the number of
134::COMO;;# samples reaching the root node, which is `tree_.weighted_n_node_samples[0]`.
135::COMO;;# Then the root node has ``value = [37, 34, 41]``, indicating there are 37 samples
136::COMO;;# of class 0, 34 samples of class 1, and 41 samples of class 2 at the root node.
137::COMO;;#
138::COMO;;# Traversing the tree, the samples are split and as a result, the ``value`` array
139::COMO;;# reaching each node changes. The left child of the root node has ``value = [1., 0, 0]``
140::COMO;;# (or ``value = [37, 0, 0]`` when converted to the absolute number of samples)
141::COMO;;# because all 37 samples in the left child node are from class 0.
142::COMO;;#
143::COMO;;# Note: In this example, `n_outputs=1`, but the tree classifier can also handle
144::COMO;;# multi-output problems. The `value` array at each node would just be a 2D
145::COMO;;# array instead.
146::COMO;;##############################################################################
147::COMO;;# We can compare the above output to the plot of the decision tree.
148::COMO;;# Here, we show the proportions of samples of each class that reach each
149::COMO;;# node corresponding to the actual elements of `tree_.value` array.
152::COMO;;##############################################################################
153::COMO;;# Decision path
154::COMO;;# -------------
155::COMO;;#
156::COMO;;# We can also retrieve the decision path of samples of interest. The
157::COMO;;# ``decision_path`` method outputs an indicator matrix that allows us to
158::COMO;;# retrieve the nodes the samples of interest traverse through. A non zero
159::COMO;;# element in the indicator matrix at position ``(i, j)`` indicates that
160::COMO;;# the sample ``i`` goes through the node ``j``. Or, for one sample ``i``, the
161::COMO;;# positions of the non zero elements in row ``i`` of the indicator matrix
162::COMO;;# designate the ids of the nodes that sample goes through.
163::COMO;;#
164::COMO;;# The leaf ids reached by samples of interest can be obtained with the
165::COMO;;# ``apply`` method. This returns an array of the node ids of the leaves
166::COMO;;# reached by each sample of interest. Using the leaf ids and the
167::COMO;;# ``decision_path`` we can obtain the splitting conditions that were used to
168::COMO;;# predict a sample or a group of samples. First, let's do it for one sample.
169::COMO;;# Note that ``node_index`` is a sparse matrix.
173::COMO;;# obtain ids of the nodes `sample_id` goes through, i.e., row `sample_id`
179::COMO;;# continue to the next node if it is a leaf node
182::COMO;;# check if value of the split feature for sample 0 is below threshold
198::COMO;;##############################################################################
199::COMO;;# For a group of samples, we can determine the common nodes the samples go
200::COMO;;# through.
202::COMO;;# boolean array indicating the nodes both samples go through
204::COMO;;# obtain node ids using position in array

68::COMM;;class BaseLink(ABC):
79::COMM;;is_multiclass = False # used for testing only
80::COMM;;# Usually, raw_prediction may be any real number and y_pred is an open
81::COMM;;# interval.
82::COMM;;# interval_raw_prediction = Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, False, False)
83::COMM;;interval_y_pred = Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, False, False)
84::COMM;;@abstractmethod
85::COMM;;def link(self, y_pred, out=None):
102::COMM;;@abstractmethod
103::COMM;;def inverse(self, raw_prediction, out=None):
120::COMM;;class IdentityLink(BaseLink):
131::COMM;;interval_y_pred = Interval(0, np.inf, False, False)
132::COMM;;def link(self, y_pred, out=None):
133::COMM;;return np.log(y_pred, out=out)
134::COMM;;def inverse(self, raw_prediction, out=None):
135::COMM;;return np.exp(raw_prediction, out=out)
136::COMM;;class LogitLink(BaseLink):
145::COMM;;Used for the exponential loss.
156::COMM;;Convention:
157::COMM;;- y_pred.shape = raw_prediction.shape = (n_samples, n_classes)
158::COMM;;Notes:
159::COMM;;- The inverse link h is the softmax function.
160::COMM;;- The sum is over the second axis, i.e. axis=1 (n_classes).
161::COMM;;We have to choose additional constraints in order to make
162::COMM;;y_pred[k] = exp(raw_pred[k]) / sum(exp(raw_pred[k]), k=0..n_classes-1)
163::COMM;;for n_classes classes identifiable and invertible.
164::COMM;;We choose the symmetric side constraint where the geometric mean response
165::COMM;;is set as reference category, see [2]:
166::COMM;;The symmetric multinomial logit link function for a single data point is
167::COMM;;then defined as
168::COMM;;raw_prediction[k] = g(y_pred[k]) = log(y_pred[k]/gmean(y_pred))
169::COMM;;= log(y_pred[k]) - mean(log(y_pred)).
170::COMM;;Note that this is equivalent to the definition in [1] and implies mean
171::COMM;;centered raw predictions:
172::COMM;;sum(raw_prediction[k], k=0..n_classes-1) = 0.
173::COMM;;For linear models with raw_prediction = X @ coef, this corresponds to
174::COMM;;sum(coef[k], k=0..n_classes-1) = 0, i.e. the sum over classes for every
175::COMM;;feature is zero.
176::COMM;;Reference
177::COMM;;---------
178::COMM;;.. [1] Friedman, Jerome; Hastie, Trevor; Tibshirani, Robert. "Additive
179::COMM;;logistic regression: a statistical view of boosting" Ann. Statist.
180::COMM;;28 (2000), no. 2, 337--407. doi:10.1214/aos/1016218223.
181::COMM;;https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aos/1016218223
182::COMM;;.. [2] Zahid, Faisal Maqbool and Gerhard Tutz. "Ridge estimation for
183::COMM;;multinomial logit models with symmetric side constraints."
184::COMM;;Computational Statistics 28 (2013): 1017-1034.
185::COMM;;http://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/11001/1/tr067.pdf
192::COMO;;# geometric mean as reference category
2::COMM;;This module contains loss classes suitable for fitting.
3::COMM;;It is not part of the public API.
4::COMM;;Specific losses are used for regression, binary classification or multiclass
5::COMM;;classification.

8::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
9::COMO;;# Goals:
10::COMO;;# - Provide a common private module for loss functions/classes.
11::COMO;;# - To be used in:
12::COMO;;# - LogisticRegression
13::COMO;;# - PoissonRegressor, GammaRegressor, TweedieRegressor
14::COMO;;# - HistGradientBoostingRegressor, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
15::COMO;;# - GradientBoostingRegressor, GradientBoostingClassifier
16::COMO;;# - SGDRegressor, SGDClassifier
17::COMO;;# - Replace link module of GLMs.
44::COMO;;# Note: The shape of raw_prediction for multiclass classifications are
45::COMO;;# - GradientBoostingClassifier: (n_samples, n_classes)
46::COMO;;# - HistGradientBoostingClassifier: (n_classes, n_samples)
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;# Note: Instead of inheritance like
49::COMO;;#
50::COMO;;# class BaseLoss(BaseLink, CyLossFunction):
51::COMO;;# ...
52::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# # Note: Naturally, we would inherit in the following order
54::COMO;;# # class HalfSquaredError(IdentityLink, CyHalfSquaredError, BaseLoss)
55::COMO;;# # But because of https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/4350 we set BaseLoss as
56::COMO;;# # the last one. This, of course, changes the MRO.
57::COMO;;# class HalfSquaredError(IdentityLink, CyHalfSquaredError, BaseLoss):
58::COMO;;#
59::COMO;;# we use composition. This way we improve maintainability by avoiding the above
60::COMO;;# mentioned Cython edge case and have easier to understand code (which method calls
61::COMO;;# which code).
64::COMM;;Conventions:
65::COMM;;- y_true.shape = sample_weight.shape = (n_samples,)
66::COMM;;- y_pred.shape = raw_prediction.shape = (n_samples,)
67::COMM;;- If is_multiclass is true (multiclass classification), then
68::COMM;;y_pred.shape = raw_prediction.shape = (n_samples, n_classes)
69::COMM;;Note that this corresponds to the return value of decision_function.
70::COMM;;y_true, y_pred, sample_weight and raw_prediction must either be all float64
71::COMM;;or all float32.
72::COMM;;gradient and hessian must be either both float64 or both float32.
73::COMM;;Note that y_pred = link.inverse(raw_prediction).
74::COMM;;Specific loss classes can inherit specific link classes to satisfy
75::COMM;;BaseLink's abstractmethods.

79::COMM;;If sample_weight is None, the hessian might be constant.
80::COMM;;n_classes : {None, int}
81::COMM;;The number of classes for classification, else None.

93::COMM;;need_update_leaves_values : bool
94::COMM;;Indicates whether decision trees in gradient boosting need to uptade
95::COMM;;leave values after having been fit to the (negative) gradients.
96::COMM;;approx_hessian : bool
97::COMM;;Indicates whether the hessian is approximated or exact. If,
98::COMM;;approximated, it should be larger or equal to the exact one.
99::COMM;;constant_hessian : bool
100::COMM;;Indicates whether the hessian is one for this loss.
101::COMM;;is_multiclass : bool
102::COMM;;Indicates whether n_classes > 2 is allowed.
104::COMO;;# For gradient boosted decision trees:
105::COMO;;# This variable indicates whether the loss requires the leaves values to
106::COMO;;# be updated once the tree has been trained. The trees are trained to
107::COMO;;# predict a Newton-Raphson step (see grower._finalize_leaf()). But for
108::COMO;;# some losses (e.g. least absolute deviation) we need to adjust the tree
109::COMO;;# values to account for the "line search" of the gradient descent
110::COMO;;# procedure. See the original paper Greedy Function Approximation: A
111::COMO;;# Gradient Boosting Machine by Friedman
112::COMO;;# (https://statweb.stanford.edu/~jhf/ftp/trebst.pdf) for the theory.

383::COMO;;# As default, take weighted average of the target over the samples

405::COMM;;With this term added, the loss of perfect predictions is zero.

422::COMM;;Parameters
