434::COMM;;(n_samples, n_classes)
435::COMM;;Empty array (allocated but not initialized) to be used as argument
436::COMM;;gradient_out.
437::COMM;;hessian : C-contiguous array of shape (n_samples,), array of shape
438::COMM;;(n_samples, n_classes) or shape (1,)
439::COMM;;Empty (allocated but not initialized) array to be used as argument
440::COMM;;hessian_out.
441::COMM;;If constant_hessian is True (e.g. `HalfSquaredError`), the array is
442::COMM;;initialized to ``1``.
455::COMO;;# If the hessians are constant, we consider them equal to 1.
456::COMO;;# - This is correct for HalfSquaredError
457::COMO;;# - For AbsoluteError, hessians are actually 0, but they are
458::COMO;;# always ignored anyway.
463::COMO;;# Note: Naturally, we would inherit in the following order
464::COMO;;# class HalfSquaredError(IdentityLink, CyHalfSquaredError, BaseLoss)
465::COMO;;# But because of https://github.com/cython/cython/issues/4350 we
466::COMO;;# set BaseLoss as the last one. This, of course, changes the MRO.
469::COMM;;Domain:
470::COMM;;y_true and y_pred all real numbers
471::COMM;;Link:
472::COMM;;y_pred = raw_prediction
473::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half squared error is defined as::
474::COMM;;loss(x_i) = 0.5 * (y_true_i - raw_prediction_i)**2
475::COMM;;The factor of 0.5 simplifies the computation of gradients and results in a
476::COMM;;unit hessian (and is consistent with what is done in LightGBM). It is also
477::COMM;;half the Normal distribution deviance.
484::COMM;;Domain:
485::COMM;;y_true and y_pred all real numbers
486::COMM;;Link:
487::COMM;;y_pred = raw_prediction
488::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, the absolute error is defined as::
489::COMM;;loss(x_i) = |y_true_i - raw_prediction_i|
490::COMM;;Note that the exact hessian = 0 almost everywhere (except at one point, therefore
491::COMM;;differentiable = False). Optimization routines like in HGBT, however, need a
492::COMM;;hessian > 0. Therefore, we assign 1.
502::COMM;;This is the weighted median of the target, i.e. over the samples
503::COMM;;axis=0.
511::COMM;;Domain:
512::COMM;;y_true and y_pred all real numbers
513::COMM;;quantile in (0, 1)
514::COMM;;Link:
515::COMM;;y_pred = raw_prediction
516::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, the pinball loss is defined as::
517::COMM;;loss(x_i) = rho_{quantile}(y_true_i - raw_prediction_i)
518::COMM;;rho_{quantile}(u) = u * (quantile - 1_{u<0})
519::COMM;;= -u *(1 - quantile) if u < 0
520::COMM;;u * quantile if u >= 0
521::COMM;;Note: 2 * PinballLoss(quantile=0.5) equals AbsoluteError().
522::COMM;;Note that the exact hessian = 0 almost everywhere (except at one point, therefore
523::COMM;;differentiable = False). Optimization routines like in HGBT, however, need a
524::COMM;;hessian > 0. Therefore, we assign 1.
525::COMM;;Additional Attributes
526::COMM;;---------------------
527::COMM;;quantile : float
528::COMM;;The quantile level of the quantile to be estimated. Must be in range (0, 1).
549::COMM;;This is the weighted median of the target, i.e. over the samples
550::COMM;;axis=0.
560::COMM;;Domain:
561::COMM;;y_true and y_pred all real numbers
562::COMM;;quantile in (0, 1)
563::COMM;;Link:
564::COMM;;y_pred = raw_prediction
565::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, the Huber loss is defined as::
566::COMM;;loss(x_i) = 1/2 * abserr**2 if abserr <= delta
567::COMM;;delta * (abserr - delta/2) if abserr > delta
568::COMM;;abserr = |y_true_i - raw_prediction_i|
569::COMM;;delta = quantile(abserr, self.quantile)
570::COMM;;Note: HuberLoss(quantile=1) equals HalfSquaredError and HuberLoss(quantile=0)
571::COMM;;equals delta * (AbsoluteError() - delta/2).
572::COMM;;Additional Attributes
573::COMM;;---------------------
574::COMM;;quantile : float
575::COMM;;The quantile level which defines the breaking point `delta` to distinguish
576::COMM;;between absolute error and squared error. Must be in range (0, 1).
577::COMM;;Reference
578::COMM;;---------
579::COMM;;.. [1] Friedman, J.H. (2001). :doi:`Greedy function approximation: A gradient
580::COMM;;boosting machine <10.1214/aos/1013203451>`.
581::COMM;;Annals of Statistics, 29, 1189-1232.
594::COMC;;self.quantile = quantile # This is better stored outside of Cython.
603::COMM;;This is the weighted median of the target, i.e. over the samples
604::COMM;;axis=0.
606::COMO;;# See formula before algo 4 in Friedman (2001), but we apply it to y_true,
607::COMO;;# not to the residual y_true - raw_prediction. An estimator like
608::COMO;;# HistGradientBoostingRegressor might then call it on the residual, e.g.
609::COMO;;# fit_intercept_only(y_true - raw_prediction).
619::COMM;;Domain:
620::COMM;;y_true in non-negative real numbers
621::COMM;;y_pred in positive real numbers
622::COMM;;Link:
623::COMM;;y_pred = exp(raw_prediction)
624::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half the Poisson deviance is defined as::
625::COMM;;loss(x_i) = y_true_i * log(y_true_i/exp(raw_prediction_i))
626::COMM;;- y_true_i + exp(raw_prediction_i)
627::COMM;;Half the Poisson deviance is actually the negative log-likelihood up to
628::COMM;;constant terms (not involving raw_prediction) and simplifies the
629::COMM;;computation of the gradients.
630::COMM;;We also skip the constant term `y_true_i * log(y_true_i) - y_true_i`.
642::COMM;;Domain:
643::COMM;;y_true and y_pred in positive real numbers
644::COMM;;Link:
645::COMM;;y_pred = exp(raw_prediction)
646::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half Gamma deviance loss is defined as::
647::COMM;;loss(x_i) = log(exp(raw_prediction_i)/y_true_i)
648::COMM;;+ y_true/exp(raw_prediction_i) - 1
649::COMM;;Half the Gamma deviance is actually proportional to the negative log-
650::COMM;;likelihood up to constant terms (not involving raw_prediction) and
651::COMM;;simplifies the computation of the gradients.
652::COMM;;We also skip the constant term `-log(y_true_i) - 1`.
664::COMM;;Domain:
665::COMM;;y_true in real numbers for power <= 0
666::COMM;;y_true in non-negative real numbers for 0 < power < 2
667::COMM;;y_true in positive real numbers for 2 <= power
668::COMM;;y_pred in positive real numbers
669::COMM;;power in real numbers
670::COMM;;Link:
671::COMM;;y_pred = exp(raw_prediction)
672::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half Tweedie deviance loss with p=power is defined
673::COMM;;as::
674::COMM;;loss(x_i) = max(y_true_i, 0)**(2-p) / (1-p) / (2-p)
675::COMM;;- y_true_i * exp(raw_prediction_i)**(1-p) / (1-p)
676::COMM;;+ exp(raw_prediction_i)**(2-p) / (2-p)
677::COMM;;Taking the limits for p=0, 1, 2 gives HalfSquaredError with a log link,
678::COMM;;HalfPoissonLoss and HalfGammaLoss.
679::COMM;;We also skip constant terms, but those are different for p=0, 1, 2.
680::COMM;;Therefore, the loss is not continuous in `power`.
681::COMM;;Note furthermore that although no Tweedie distribution exists for
682::COMM;;0 < power < 1, it still gives a strictly consistent scoring function for
683::COMM;;the expectation.
717::COMM;;Domain:
718::COMM;;y_true in real numbers for power <= 0
719::COMM;;y_true in non-negative real numbers for 0 < power < 2
720::COMM;;y_true in positive real numbers for 2 <= power
721::COMM;;y_pred in positive real numbers for power != 0
722::COMM;;y_pred in real numbers for power = 0
723::COMM;;power in real numbers
724::COMM;;Link:
725::COMM;;y_pred = raw_prediction
726::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half Tweedie deviance loss with p=power is defined
727::COMM;;as::
728::COMM;;loss(x_i) = max(y_true_i, 0)**(2-p) / (1-p) / (2-p)
729::COMM;;- y_true_i * raw_prediction_i**(1-p) / (1-p)
730::COMM;;+ raw_prediction_i**(2-p) / (2-p)
731::COMM;;Note that the minimum value of this loss is 0.
732::COMM;;Note furthermore that although no Tweedie distribution exists for
733::COMM;;0 < power < 1, it still gives a strictly consistent scoring function for
734::COMM;;the expectation.
753::COMM;;This is also know as binary cross entropy, log-loss and logistic loss.
754::COMM;;Domain:
755::COMM;;y_true in [0, 1], i.e. regression on the unit interval
756::COMM;;y_pred in (0, 1), i.e. boundaries excluded
757::COMM;;Link:
758::COMM;;y_pred = expit(raw_prediction)
759::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, half Binomial deviance is defined as the negative
760::COMM;;log-likelihood of the Binomial/Bernoulli distribution and can be expressed
761::COMM;;as::
762::COMM;;loss(x_i) = log(1 + exp(raw_pred_i)) - y_true_i * raw_pred_i
763::COMM;;See The Elements of Statistical Learning, by Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman,
764::COMM;;section 4.4.1 (about logistic regression).
765::COMM;;Note that the formulation works for classification, y = {0, 1}, as well as
766::COMM;;logistic regression, y = [0, 1].
767::COMM;;If you add `constant_to_optimal_zero` to the loss, you get half the
768::COMM;;Bernoulli/binomial deviance.
769::COMM;;More details: Inserting the predicted probability y_pred = expit(raw_prediction)
770::COMM;;in the loss gives the well known::
771::COMM;;loss(x_i) = - y_true_i * log(y_pred_i) - (1 - y_true_i) * log(1 - y_pred_i)
781::COMO;;# This is non-zero only if y_true is neither 0 nor 1.
788::COMM;;Parameters
789::COMM;;----------
790::COMM;;raw_prediction : array of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, 1)
791::COMM;;Raw prediction values (in link space).
792::COMM;;Returns
793::COMM;;-------
794::COMM;;proba : array of shape (n_samples, 2)
795::COMM;;Element-wise class probabilities.
797::COMO;;# Be graceful to shape (n_samples, 1) -> (n_samples,)
806::COMM;;Domain:
807::COMM;;y_true in {0, 1, 2, 3, .., n_classes - 1}
808::COMM;;y_pred has n_classes elements, each element in (0, 1)
809::COMM;;Link:
810::COMM;;y_pred = softmax(raw_prediction)
811::COMM;;Note: We assume y_true to be already label encoded. The inverse link is
812::COMM;;softmax. But the full link function is the symmetric multinomial logit
813::COMM;;function.
814::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, the categorical cross-entropy loss is defined as
815::COMM;;the negative log-likelihood of the multinomial distribution, it
816::COMM;;generalizes the binary cross-entropy to more than 2 classes::
817::COMM;;loss_i = log(sum(exp(raw_pred_{i, k}), k=0..n_classes-1))
818::COMM;;- sum(y_true_{i, k} * raw_pred_{i, k}, k=0..n_classes-1)
819::COMM;;See [1].
820::COMM;;Note that for the hessian, we calculate only the diagonal part in the
821::COMM;;classes: If the full hessian for classes k and l and sample i is H_i_k_l,
822::COMM;;we calculate H_i_k_k, i.e. k=l.
823::COMM;;Parameters
824::COMM;;----------
825::COMM;;sample_weight : {None, ndarray}
826::COMM;;If sample_weight is None, the hessian might be constant.
827::COMM;;n_classes : {None, int}
828::COMM;;The number of classes for classification, else None.
829::COMM;;References
830::COMM;;----------
831::COMM;;.. [1] :arxiv:`Simon, Noah, J. Friedman and T. Hastie.
832::COMM;;"A Blockwise Descent Algorithm for Group-penalized Multiresponse and
833::COMM;;Multinomial Regression".
834::COMM;;<1311.6529>`

895::COMM;;Parameters

897::COMM;;y_true : C-contiguous array of shape (n_samples,)

899::COMM;;raw_prediction : array of shape (n_samples, n_classes)

915::COMM;;proba : array of shape (n_samples, n_classes)

937::COMM;;This is also know as boosting loss.
938::COMM;;Domain:
939::COMM;;y_true in [0, 1], i.e. regression on the unit interval
940::COMM;;y_pred in (0, 1), i.e. boundaries excluded
941::COMM;;Link:
942::COMM;;y_pred = expit(2 * raw_prediction)
943::COMM;;For a given sample x_i, the exponential loss is defined as::
944::COMM;;loss(x_i) = y_true_i * exp(-raw_pred_i)) + (1 - y_true_i) * exp(raw_pred_i)
945::COMM;;See:
946::COMM;;- J. Friedman, T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani.
947::COMM;;"Additive logistic regression: a statistical view of boosting (With discussion
948::COMM;;and a rejoinder by the authors)." Ann. Statist. 28 (2) 337 - 407, April 2000.
949::COMM;;https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1016218223
950::COMM;;- A. Buja, W. Stuetzle, Y. Shen. (2005).
951::COMM;;"Loss Functions for Binary Class Probability Estimation and Classification:
952::COMM;;Structure and Applications."
953::COMM;;Note that the formulation works for classification, y = {0, 1}, as well as
954::COMM;;"exponential logistic" regression, y = [0, 1].
955::COMM;;Note that this is a proper scoring rule, but without it's canonical link.
956::COMM;;More details: Inserting the predicted probability
957::COMM;;y_pred = expit(2 * raw_prediction) in the loss gives::
958::COMM;;loss(x_i) = y_true_i * sqrt((1 - y_pred_i) / y_pred_i)
959::COMM;;+ (1 - y_true_i) * sqrt(y_pred_i / (1 - y_pred_i))
969::COMO;;# This is non-zero only if y_true is neither 0 nor 1.
976::COMM;;Parameters
977::COMM;;----------
978::COMM;;raw_prediction : array of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, 1)
979::COMM;;Raw prediction values (in link space).
980::COMM;;Returns
981::COMM;;-------
982::COMM;;proba : array of shape (n_samples, 2)
983::COMM;;Element-wise class probabilities.
985::COMO;;# Be graceful to shape (n_samples, 1) -> (n_samples,)
14::COMM;;with pytest.raises(
15::COMM;;ValueError, match="One must have low <= high; got low=1, high=0."
16::COMM;;):
17::COMM;;Interval(1, 0, False, False)
18::COMM;;@pytest.mark.parametrize(
19::COMM;;"interval",
20::COMM;;[
21::COMM;;Interval(0, 1, False, False),
22::COMM;;Interval(0, 1, False, True),
23::COMM;;Interval(0, 1, True, False),
24::COMM;;Interval(0, 1, True, True),
25::COMM;;Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, False, False),
26::COMM;;Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, False, True),
27::COMM;;Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, True, False),
28::COMM;;Interval(-np.inf, np.inf, True, True),
29::COMM;;Interval(-10, -1, False, False),

31::COMM;;Interval(-10, -1, True, False),

655::COMM;;def test_graceful_squeezing(loss):
686::COMM;;Loss of y_pred = y_true plus constant_to_optimal_zero should sums up to
687::COMM;;zero.
690::COMO;;# Use small values such that exp(value) is not nan.
692::COMO;;# If link is identity, we must respect the interval of y_pred:
704::COMO;;# HalfMultinomialLoss
706::COMO;;# raw_prediction with entries -exp(10), but +exp(10) on the diagonal
707::COMO;;# this is close enough to np.inf which would produce nan
724::COMO;;# Comparing loss_value + constant_term to zero would result in large
725::COMO;;# round-off errors.
731::COMM;;Gradient should equal the numerical derivatives of the loss function.
732::COMM;;Hessians should equal the numerical derivatives of gradients.
768::COMO;;# TODO: What could we test if loss.approx_hessian?
773::COMO;;# For multiclass loss, we should only change the predictions of the
774::COMO;;# class for which the derivative is taken for, e.g. offset[:, k] = eps
775::COMO;;# for class k.
776::COMO;;# As a softmax is computed, offsetting the whole array by a constant
777::COMO;;# would have no effect on the probabilities, and thus on the loss.
799::COMO;;# TODO: What could we test if loss.approx_hessian?
809::COMO;;# The argmin of binomial_loss for y_true=0 and y_true=1 is resp.
810::COMO;;# -inf and +inf due to logit, cf. "complete separation". Therefore, we
811::COMO;;# use 0 < y_true < 1.
823::COMM;;We check this on a single value/sample using Halley's method with the
824::COMM;;first and second order derivatives computed by the Loss instance.
825::COMM;;Note that methods of Loss instances operate on arrays while the newton
826::COMM;;root finder expects a scalar or a one-element array for this purpose.
833::COMM;;The constant term is such that the minimum function value is zero,
834::COMM;;which is required by the Newton method.
851::COMO;;# Need to ravel arrays because assert_allclose requires matching
852::COMO;;# dimensions.
862::COMM;;Also test that the gradient is zero at the minimum.
869::COMC;;y_true[::5] = 0 # exceedance of class 0
873::COMO;;# find minimum by optimization
893::COMC;;assert a.shape == tuple() # scalar
899::COMO;;# The constraint corresponds to sum(raw_prediction) = 0. Without it, we would
900::COMO;;# need to apply loss.symmetrize_raw_prediction to opt.x before comparing.
932::COMM;;We test the functional for specific, meaningful distributions, e.g.
933::COMM;;squared error estimates the expectation of a probability distribution.
941::COMO;;# Make sure baseline prediction is the expected functional=func, e.g. mean
942::COMO;;# or median.
948::COMO;;# Test baseline at boundary

961::COMM;;loss = HalfMultinomialLoss(n_classes=n_classes)

963::COMM;;# function = softmax and link function = log - symmetry term.

1170::COMM;;def test_loss_pickle(loss):
1188::COMM;;half_tweedie_log = HalfTweedieLoss(power=p)
1189::COMM;;half_tweedie_identity = HalfTweedieLossIdentity(power=p)
1190::COMM;;n_samples = 10
1191::COMM;;y_true, raw_prediction = random_y_true_raw_prediction(
1192::COMM;;loss=half_tweedie_log, n_samples=n_samples, seed=42
1193::COMM;;)
1194::COMM;;y_pred = half_tweedie_log.link.inverse(raw_prediction) # exp(raw_prediction)
1195::COMM;;# Let's compare the loss values, up to some constant term that is dropped
1196::COMM;;# in HalfTweedieLoss but not in HalfTweedieLossIdentity.
1197::COMM;;loss_log = half_tweedie_log.loss(
1198::COMM;;y_true=y_true, raw_prediction=raw_prediction
1199::COMM;;) + half_tweedie_log.constant_to_optimal_zero(y_true)
1200::COMM;;loss_identity = half_tweedie_identity.loss(
1201::COMM;;y_true=y_true, raw_prediction=y_pred
1202::COMM;;) + half_tweedie_identity.constant_to_optimal_zero(y_true)
1203::COMM;;# Note that HalfTweedieLoss ignores different constant terms than
1204::COMM;;# HalfTweedieLossIdentity. Constant terms means terms not depending on
1205::COMM;;# raw_prediction. By adding these terms, `constant_to_optimal_zero`, both losses
1206::COMM;;# give the same values.
1207::COMM;;assert_allclose(loss_log, loss_identity)
1208::COMM;;# For gradients and hessians, the constant terms do not matter. We have, however,
1209::COMM;;# to account for the chain rule, i.e. with x=raw_prediction
1210::COMM;;# gradient_log(x) = d/dx loss_log(x)
1211::COMM;;# = d/dx loss_identity(exp(x))
1212::COMM;;# = exp(x) * gradient_identity(exp(x))
1213::COMM;;# Similarly,
1214::COMM;;# hessian_log(x) = exp(x) * gradient_identity(exp(x))
1215::COMM;;# + exp(x)**2 * hessian_identity(x)
1216::COMM;;gradient_log, hessian_log = half_tweedie_log.gradient_hessian(
1217::COMM;;y_true=y_true, raw_prediction=raw_prediction
1218::COMM;;)
1219::COMM;;gradient_identity, hessian_identity = half_tweedie_identity.gradient_hessian(
1220::COMM;;y_true=y_true, raw_prediction=y_pred
1221::COMM;;)
1222::COMM;;assert_allclose(gradient_log, y_pred * gradient_identity)
1223::COMM;;assert_allclose(
1224::COMM;;hessian_log, y_pred * gradient_identity + y_pred**2 * hessian_identity
1225::COMM;;)

347::COMC;;lim = N_CHAR_MAX // 2 # apprx number of chars to keep on both ends
349::COMO;;# The regex '^(\s*\S){%d}' % n
350::COMO;;# matches from the start of the string until the nth non-blank
351::COMO;;# character:
352::COMO;;# - ^ matches the start of string
353::COMO;;# - (pattern){n} matches n repetitions of pattern
354::COMO;;# - \s*\S matches a non-blank char following zero or more blanks
358::COMO;;# The left side and right side aren't on the same line.
359::COMO;;# To avoid weird cuts, e.g.:
360::COMO;;# categoric...ore',
361::COMO;;# we need to start the right side with an appropriate newline
362::COMO;;# character so that it renders properly as:

429::COMM;;This mixin defines the following functionality:

464::COMM;;Return :ref:`accuracy <accuracy_score>` on provided data and labels.
465::COMM;;In multi-label classification, this is the subset accuracy
466::COMM;;which is a harsh metric since you require for each sample that
467::COMM;;each label set be correctly predicted.
468::COMM;;Parameters
469::COMM;;----------
470::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
471::COMM;;Test samples.
472::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_outputs)
473::COMM;;True labels for `X`.
474::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
475::COMM;;Sample weights.
476::COMM;;Returns
477::COMM;;-------
478::COMM;;score : float
479::COMM;;Mean accuracy of ``self.predict(X)`` w.r.t. `y`.
485::COMM;;This mixin defines the following functionality:
486::COMM;;- set estimator type to `"regressor"` through the `estimator_type` tag;
487::COMM;;- `score` method that default to :func:`~sklearn.metrics.r2_score`.
488::COMM;;- enforce that `fit` requires `y` to be passed through the `requires_y` tag,
489::COMM;;which is done by setting the regressor type tag.
490::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <rolling_your_own_estimator>`.
491::COMM;;Examples
492::COMM;;--------
493::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
494::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, RegressorMixin
495::COMM;;>>> # Mixin classes should always be on the left-hand side for a correct MRO
496::COMM;;>>> class MyEstimator(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
497::COMM;;... def __init__(self, *, param=1):
498::COMM;;... self.param = param
499::COMM;;... def fit(self, X, y=None):
500::COMM;;... self.is_fitted_ = True
501::COMM;;... return self
502::COMM;;... def predict(self, X):
503::COMM;;... return np.full(shape=X.shape[0], fill_value=self.param)
504::COMM;;>>> estimator = MyEstimator(param=0)
505::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]])
506::COMM;;>>> y = np.array([-1, 0, 1])
507::COMM;;>>> estimator.fit(X, y).predict(X)
508::COMM;;array([0, 0, 0])
509::COMM;;>>> estimator.score(X, y)
510::COMM;;0.0
520::COMM;;The coefficient of determination, :math:`R^2`, is defined as
521::COMM;;:math:`(1 - \\frac{u}{v})`, where :math:`u` is the residual
522::COMM;;sum of squares ``((y_true - y_pred)** 2).sum()`` and :math:`v`
523::COMM;;is the total sum of squares ``((y_true - y_true.mean()) ** 2).sum()``.
524::COMM;;The best possible score is 1.0 and it can be negative (because the
525::COMM;;model can be arbitrarily worse). A constant model that always predicts
526::COMM;;the expected value of `y`, disregarding the input features, would get
527::COMM;;a :math:`R^2` score of 0.0.
528::COMM;;Parameters
529::COMM;;----------
530::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
531::COMM;;Test samples. For some estimators this may be a precomputed
532::COMM;;kernel matrix or a list of generic objects instead with shape
533::COMM;;``(n_samples, n_samples_fitted)``, where ``n_samples_fitted``
534::COMM;;is the number of samples used in the fitting for the estimator.
535::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_outputs)
536::COMM;;True values for `X`.
537::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
538::COMM;;Sample weights.
539::COMM;;Returns
540::COMM;;-------
541::COMM;;score : float
542::COMM;;:math:`R^2` of ``self.predict(X)`` w.r.t. `y`.
543::COMM;;Notes
544::COMM;;-----
545::COMM;;The :math:`R^2` score used when calling ``score`` on a regressor uses
546::COMM;;``multioutput='uniform_average'`` from version 0.23 to keep consistent
547::COMM;;with default value of :func:`~sklearn.metrics.r2_score`.
548::COMM;;This influences the ``score`` method of all the multioutput
549::COMM;;regressors (except for
550::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.multioutput.MultiOutputRegressor`).
557::COMM;;- set estimator type to `"clusterer"` through the `estimator_type` tag;
558::COMM;;- `fit_predict` method returning the cluster labels associated to each sample.
559::COMM;;Examples

600::COMM;;This mixin defines the following functionality:

674::COMM;;Works with sparse matrices. Only works if ``rows_`` and
675::COMM;;``columns_`` attributes exist.
682::COMM;;This mixin defines the following functionality:
683::COMM;;- a `fit_transform` method that delegates to `fit` and `transform`;
684::COMM;;- a `set_output` method to output `X` as a specific container type.
685::COMM;;If :term:`get_feature_names_out` is defined, then :class:`BaseEstimator` will
686::COMM;;automatically wrap `transform` and `fit_transform` to follow the `set_output`
687::COMM;;API. See the :ref:`developer_api_set_output` for details.

713::COMM;;Fit to data, then transform it.
714::COMM;;Fits transformer to `X` and `y` with optional parameters `fit_params`
715::COMM;;and returns a transformed version of `X`.
716::COMM;;Parameters
717::COMM;;----------
718::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
719::COMM;;Input samples.
720::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_outputs), \
721::COMM;;default=None
722::COMM;;Target values (None for unsupervised transformations).
723::COMM;;**fit_params : dict
724::COMM;;Additional fit parameters.
725::COMM;;Pass only if the estimator accepts additional params in its `fit` method.
726::COMM;;Returns
727::COMM;;-------
728::COMM;;X_new : ndarray array of shape (n_samples, n_features_new)
729::COMM;;Transformed array.
731::COMO;;# non-optimized default implementation; override when a better
732::COMO;;# method is possible for a given clustering algorithm
733::COMO;;# we do not route parameters here, since consumers don't route. But
734::COMO;;# since it's possible for a `transform` method to also consume
735::COMO;;# metadata, we check if that's the case, and we raise a warning telling
736::COMO;;# users that they should implement a custom `fit_transform` method
737::COMO;;# to forward metadata to `transform` as well.
738::COMO;;#
739::COMO;;# For that, we calculate routing and check if anything would be routed
740::COMO;;# to `transform` if we were to route them.
759::COMO;;# fit method of arity 1 (unsupervised transformation)
762::COMO;;# fit method of arity 2 (supervised transformation)
766::COMM;;This mixin assumes there's a 1-to-1 correspondence between input features
767::COMM;;and output features, such as :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler`.
768::COMM;;Examples
769::COMM;;--------
770::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
771::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.base import OneToOneFeatureMixin, BaseEstimator
772::COMM;;>>> class MyEstimator(OneToOneFeatureMixin, BaseEstimator):
773::COMM;;... def fit(self, X, y=None):
774::COMM;;... self.n_features_in_ = X.shape[1]
775::COMM;;... return self
776::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
777::COMM;;>>> MyEstimator().fit(X).get_feature_names_out()
778::COMM;;array(['x0', 'x1'], dtype=object)
782::COMM;;Parameters
783::COMM;;----------
784::COMM;;input_features : array-like of str or None, default=None
785::COMM;;Input features.
786::COMM;;- If `input_features` is `None`, then `feature_names_in_` is
787::COMM;;used as feature names in. If `feature_names_in_` is not defined,
788::COMM;;then the following input feature names are generated:
789::COMM;;`["x0", "x1", ..., "x(n_features_in_ - 1)"]`.
790::COMM;;- If `input_features` is an array-like, then `input_features` must
791::COMM;;match `feature_names_in_` if `feature_names_in_` is defined.
792::COMM;;Returns
793::COMM;;-------
794::COMM;;feature_names_out : ndarray of str objects
795::COMM;;Same as input features.
797::COMO;;# Note that passing attributes="n_features_in_" forces check_is_fitted
798::COMO;;# to check if the attribute is present. Otherwise it will pass on
799::COMO;;# stateless estimators (requires_fit=False)
804::COMM;;This mixin is useful when the transformer needs to generate its own feature
805::COMM;;names out, such as :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`. For example, if
806::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` outputs 3 features, then the generated feature
807::COMM;;names out are: `["pca0", "pca1", "pca2"]`.
808::COMM;;This mixin assumes that a `_n_features_out` attribute is defined when the
809::COMM;;transformer is fitted. `_n_features_out` is the number of output features
810::COMM;;that the transformer will return in `transform` of `fit_transform`.
811::COMM;;Examples
812::COMM;;--------
813::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
814::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.base import ClassNamePrefixFeaturesOutMixin, BaseEstimator
815::COMM;;>>> class MyEstimator(ClassNamePrefixFeaturesOutMixin, BaseEstimator):
816::COMM;;... def fit(self, X, y=None):
817::COMM;;... self._n_features_out = X.shape[1]
818::COMM;;... return self
819::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
820::COMM;;>>> MyEstimator().fit(X).get_feature_names_out()
821::COMM;;array(['myestimator0', 'myestimator1'], dtype=object)
825::COMM;;The feature names out will prefixed by the lowercased class name. For
826::COMM;;example, if the transformer outputs 3 features, then the feature names
827::COMM;;out are: `["class_name0", "class_name1", "class_name2"]`.
828::COMM;;Parameters
829::COMM;;----------
830::COMM;;input_features : array-like of str or None, default=None
831::COMM;;Only used to validate feature names with the names seen in `fit`.
832::COMM;;Returns
833::COMM;;-------
834::COMM;;feature_names_out : ndarray of str objects
835::COMM;;Transformed feature names.

1035::COMM;;pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None
1036::COMM;;The label of the positive class.
1037::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
1038::COMM;;n_bins : int, default=5
1039::COMM;;Number of bins to discretize the [0, 1] interval. A bigger number
1040::COMM;;requires more data. Bins with no samples (i.e. without
1041::COMM;;corresponding values in `y_prob`) will not be returned, thus the
1042::COMM;;returned arrays may have less than `n_bins` values.
1043::COMM;;strategy : {'uniform', 'quantile'}, default='uniform'
1044::COMM;;Strategy used to define the widths of the bins.
1045::COMM;;uniform
1046::COMM;;The bins have identical widths.
1047::COMM;;quantile
1048::COMM;;The bins have the same number of samples and depend on `y_prob`.
1049::COMM;;Returns

1052::COMM;;The proportion of samples whose class is the positive class, in each
1053::COMM;;bin (fraction of positives).
1054::COMM;;prob_pred : ndarray of shape (n_bins,) or smaller
1055::COMM;;The mean predicted probability in each bin.

14::COMM;;def _equal_similarities_and_preferences(S, preference):
15::COMM;;def all_equal_preferences():
16::COMM;;return np.all(preference == preference.flat[0])
17::COMM;;def all_equal_similarities():
18::COMM;;# Create mask to ignore diagonal of S
19::COMM;;mask = np.ones(S.shape, dtype=bool)
20::COMM;;np.fill_diagonal(mask, 0)
21::COMM;;return np.all(S[mask].flat == S[mask].flat[0])
22::COMM;;return all_equal_preferences() and all_equal_similarities()
23::COMM;;def _affinity_propagation(
24::COMM;;S,
25::COMM;;*,
26::COMM;;preference,
27::COMM;;convergence_iter,
28::COMM;;max_iter,
29::COMM;;damping,
30::COMM;;verbose,
31::COMM;;return_n_iter,
32::COMM;;random_state,
33::COMM;;):
37::COMO;;# It makes no sense to run the algorithm in this case, so return 1 or
38::COMO;;# n_samples clusters, depending on preferences
55::COMO;;# Place preference on the diagonal of S
58::COMC;;R = np.zeros((n_samples, n_samples)) # Initialize messages
59::COMO;;# Intermediate results
61::COMO;;# Remove degeneracies
65::COMO;;# Execute parallel affinity propagation updates
69::COMO;;# tmp = A + S; compute responsibilities
72::COMC;;Y = tmp[ind, I] # np.max(A + S, axis=1)
75::COMO;;# tmp = Rnew
78::COMO;;# Damping
82::COMO;;# tmp = Rp; compute availabilities
85::COMO;;# tmp = -Anew
90::COMO;;# Damping
94::COMO;;# Check for convergence
111::COMC;;K = I.size # Identify exemplars
122::COMC;;c[I] = np.arange(K) # Identify clusters
123::COMO;;# Refine the final set of exemplars and clusters and return results
131::COMO;;# Reduce labels to a sorted, gapless, list
148::COMO;;###############################################################################
149::COMO;;# Public API
170::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <affinity_propagation>`.
171::COMM;;Parameters
172::COMM;;----------
173::COMM;;S : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
174::COMM;;Matrix of similarities between points.
175::COMM;;preference : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or float, default=None
176::COMM;;Preferences for each point - points with larger values of
177::COMM;;preferences are more likely to be chosen as exemplars. The number of
178::COMM;;exemplars, i.e. of clusters, is influenced by the input preferences
179::COMM;;value. If the preferences are not passed as arguments, they will be
180::COMM;;set to the median of the input similarities (resulting in a moderate
181::COMM;;number of clusters). For a smaller amount of clusters, this can be set
182::COMM;;to the minimum value of the similarities.
183::COMM;;convergence_iter : int, default=15
184::COMM;;Number of iterations with no change in the number
185::COMM;;of estimated clusters that stops the convergence.
186::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=200
187::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations.
188::COMM;;damping : float, default=0.5
189::COMM;;Damping factor between 0.5 and 1.
190::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
191::COMM;;If copy is False, the affinity matrix is modified inplace by the
192::COMM;;algorithm, for memory efficiency.
193::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
194::COMM;;The verbosity level.
195::COMM;;return_n_iter : bool, default=False
196::COMM;;Whether or not to return the number of iterations.
197::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
198::COMM;;Pseudo-random number generator to control the starting state.
199::COMM;;Use an int for reproducible results across function calls.
200::COMM;;See the :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
201::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
202::COMM;;this parameter was previously hardcoded as 0.
203::COMM;;Returns
204::COMM;;-------
205::COMM;;cluster_centers_indices : ndarray of shape (n_clusters,)
206::COMM;;Index of clusters centers.
207::COMM;;labels : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
208::COMM;;Cluster labels for each point.
209::COMM;;n_iter : int
210::COMM;;Number of iterations run. Returned only if `return_n_iter` is
211::COMM;;set to True.
212::COMM;;Notes
213::COMM;;-----
214::COMM;;For an example usage,
215::COMM;;see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_affinity_propagation.py`.
216::COMM;;You may also check out,
217::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_applications_plot_stock_market.py`
218::COMM;;When the algorithm does not converge, it will still return an array of
219::COMM;;``cluster_center_indices`` and labels if there are any exemplars/clusters,
220::COMM;;however they may be degenerate and should be used with caution.
221::COMM;;When all training samples have equal similarities and equal preferences,
222::COMM;;the assignment of cluster centers and labels depends on the preference.
223::COMM;;If the preference is smaller than the similarities, a single cluster center
224::COMM;;and label ``0`` for every sample will be returned. Otherwise, every
225::COMM;;training sample becomes its own cluster center and is assigned a unique
226::COMM;;label.
227::COMM;;References
228::COMM;;----------
229::COMM;;Brendan J. Frey and Delbert Dueck, "Clustering by Passing Messages
230::COMM;;Between Data Points", Science Feb. 2007
231::COMM;;Examples
232::COMM;;--------
233::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
234::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.cluster import affinity_propagation
235::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidean_distances
236::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0],
237::COMM;;... [4, 2], [4, 4], [4, 0]])
238::COMM;;>>> S = -euclidean_distances(X, squared=True)
239::COMM;;>>> cluster_centers_indices, labels = affinity_propagation(S, random_state=0)

243::COMM;;array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
260::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <affinity_propagation>`.
261::COMM;;Parameters
262::COMM;;----------
263::COMM;;damping : float, default=0.5
264::COMM;;Damping factor in the range `[0.5, 1.0)` is the extent to
265::COMM;;which the current value is maintained relative to
266::COMM;;incoming values (weighted 1 - damping). This in order
267::COMM;;to avoid numerical oscillations when updating these
268::COMM;;values (messages).
269::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=200
270::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations.
271::COMM;;convergence_iter : int, default=15
272::COMM;;Number of iterations with no change in the number
273::COMM;;of estimated clusters that stops the convergence.
274::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
275::COMM;;Make a copy of input data.
276::COMM;;preference : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or float, default=None
277::COMM;;Preferences for each point - points with larger values of
278::COMM;;preferences are more likely to be chosen as exemplars. The number
279::COMM;;of exemplars, ie of clusters, is influenced by the input
280::COMM;;preferences value. If the preferences are not passed as arguments,
281::COMM;;they will be set to the median of the input similarities.
282::COMM;;affinity : {'euclidean', 'precomputed'}, default='euclidean'
283::COMM;;Which affinity to use. At the moment 'precomputed' and
284::COMM;;``euclidean`` are supported. 'euclidean' uses the
285::COMM;;negative squared euclidean distance between points.
286::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
287::COMM;;Whether to be verbose.
288::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
289::COMM;;Pseudo-random number generator to control the starting state.
290::COMM;;Use an int for reproducible results across function calls.
291::COMM;;See the :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
292::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
293::COMM;;this parameter was previously hardcoded as 0.
294::COMM;;Attributes
295::COMM;;----------
296::COMM;;cluster_centers_indices_ : ndarray of shape (n_clusters,)
297::COMM;;Indices of cluster centers.
298::COMM;;cluster_centers_ : ndarray of shape (n_clusters, n_features)
299::COMM;;Cluster centers (if affinity != ``precomputed``).
300::COMM;;labels_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
301::COMM;;Labels of each point.
302::COMM;;affinity_matrix_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
303::COMM;;Stores the affinity matrix used in ``fit``.
304::COMM;;n_iter_ : int

306::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int

309::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)

320::COMM;;MiniBatchKMeans : Mini-Batch K-Means clustering.
321::COMM;;MeanShift : Mean shift clustering using a flat kernel.
322::COMM;;SpectralClustering : Apply clustering to a projection
323::COMM;;of the normalized Laplacian.
324::COMM;;Notes
325::COMM;;-----
326::COMM;;The algorithmic complexity of affinity propagation is quadratic
327::COMM;;in the number of points.
328::COMM;;When the algorithm does not converge, it will still return an array of
329::COMM;;``cluster_center_indices`` and labels if there are any exemplars/clusters,
330::COMM;;however they may be degenerate and should be used with caution.
331::COMM;;When ``fit`` does not converge, ``cluster_centers_`` is still populated
332::COMM;;however it may be degenerate. In such a case, proceed with caution.
333::COMM;;If ``fit`` does not converge and fails to produce any ``cluster_centers_``
334::COMM;;then ``predict`` will label every sample as ``-1``.
335::COMM;;When all training samples have equal similarities and equal preferences,
336::COMM;;the assignment of cluster centers and labels depends on the preference.
337::COMM;;If the preference is smaller than the similarities, ``fit`` will result in
338::COMM;;a single cluster center and label ``0`` for every sample. Otherwise, every
339::COMM;;training sample becomes its own cluster center and is assigned a unique
340::COMM;;label.
341::COMM;;References
342::COMM;;----------
343::COMM;;Brendan J. Frey and Delbert Dueck, "Clustering by Passing Messages
344::COMM;;Between Data Points", Science Feb. 2007
345::COMM;;Examples
346::COMM;;--------
347::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.cluster import AffinityPropagation
348::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
349::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0],
350::COMM;;... [4, 2], [4, 4], [4, 0]])
351::COMM;;>>> clustering = AffinityPropagation(random_state=5).fit(X)
352::COMM;;>>> clustering
353::COMM;;AffinityPropagation(random_state=5)
354::COMM;;>>> clustering.labels_
355::COMM;;array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])
356::COMM;;>>> clustering.predict([[0, 0], [4, 4]])
357::COMM;;array([0, 1])
358::COMM;;>>> clustering.cluster_centers_
359::COMM;;array([[1, 2],
360::COMM;;[4, 2]])
361::COMM;;For an example usage,
362::COMM;;see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_affinity_propagation.py`.
363::COMM;;For a comparison of Affinity Propagation with other clustering algorithms, see
364::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_cluster_comparison.py`

145::COMO;;# Hierarchical tree building functions
157::COMM;;Recursively merges the pair of clusters that minimally increases
158::COMM;;within-cluster variance.
159::COMM;;The inertia matrix uses a Heapq-based representation.
160::COMM;;This is the structured version, that takes into account some topological
161::COMM;;structure between samples.
162::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <hierarchical_clustering>`.
163::COMM;;Parameters
164::COMM;;----------
165::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
166::COMM;;Feature matrix representing `n_samples` samples to be clustered.
167::COMM;;connectivity : {array-like, sparse matrix}, default=None
168::COMM;;Connectivity matrix. Defines for each sample the neighboring samples
169::COMM;;following a given structure of the data. The matrix is assumed to
170::COMM;;be symmetric and only the upper triangular half is used.
171::COMM;;Default is None, i.e, the Ward algorithm is unstructured.
172::COMM;;n_clusters : int, default=None
173::COMM;;`n_clusters` should be less than `n_samples`. Stop early the
174::COMM;;construction of the tree at `n_clusters.` This is useful to decrease
175::COMM;;computation time if the number of clusters is not small compared to the
176::COMM;;number of samples. In this case, the complete tree is not computed, thus
177::COMM;;the 'children' output is of limited use, and the 'parents' output should
178::COMM;;rather be used. This option is valid only when specifying a connectivity
179::COMM;;matrix.
180::COMM;;return_distance : bool, default=False
181::COMM;;If `True`, return the distance between the clusters.
182::COMM;;Returns
183::COMM;;-------
184::COMM;;children : ndarray of shape (n_nodes-1, 2)
185::COMM;;The children of each non-leaf node. Values less than `n_samples`
186::COMM;;correspond to leaves of the tree which are the original samples.
187::COMM;;A node `i` greater than or equal to `n_samples` is a non-leaf
188::COMM;;node and has children `children_[i - n_samples]`. Alternatively
189::COMM;;at the i-th iteration, children[i][0] and children[i][1]
190::COMM;;are merged to form node `n_samples + i`.
191::COMM;;n_connected_components : int
192::COMM;;The number of connected components in the graph.
193::COMM;;n_leaves : int
194::COMM;;The number of leaves in the tree.
195::COMM;;parents : ndarray of shape (n_nodes,) or None
196::COMM;;The parent of each node. Only returned when a connectivity matrix
197::COMM;;is specified, elsewhere 'None' is returned.
198::COMM;;distances : ndarray of shape (n_nodes-1,)
199::COMM;;Only returned if `return_distance` is set to `True` (for compatibility).
200::COMM;;The distances between the centers of the nodes. `distances[i]`
201::COMM;;corresponds to a weighted Euclidean distance between
202::COMM;;the nodes `children[i, 1]` and `children[i, 2]`. If the nodes refer to
203::COMM;;leaves of the tree, then `distances[i]` is their unweighted Euclidean
204::COMM;;distance. Distances are updated in the following way
205::COMM;;(from scipy.hierarchy.linkage):
206::COMM;;The new entry :math:`d(u,v)` is computed as follows,
207::COMM;;.. math::
208::COMM;;d(u,v) = \\sqrt{\\frac{|v|+|s|}
209::COMM;;{T}d(v,s)^2
210::COMM;;+ \\frac{|v|+|t|}
211::COMM;;{T}d(v,t)^2
212::COMM;;- \\frac{|v|}
213::COMM;;{T}d(s,t)^2}
214::COMM;;where :math:`u` is the newly joined cluster consisting of
215::COMM;;clusters :math:`s` and :math:`t`, :math:`v` is an unused
216::COMM;;cluster in the forest, :math:`T=|v|+|s|+|t|`, and
217::COMM;;:math:`|*|` is the cardinality of its argument. This is also
218::COMM;;known as the incremental algorithm.
219::COMM;;Examples
220::COMM;;--------
221::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
222::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.cluster import ward_tree
223::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 0],
224::COMM;;... [4, 2], [4, 4], [4, 0]])
225::COMM;;>>> children, n_connected_components, n_leaves, parents = ward_tree(X)
226::COMM;;>>> children
227::COMM;;array([[0, 1],
228::COMM;;[3, 5],
229::COMM;;[2, 6],
230::COMM;;[4, 7],
231::COMM;;[8, 9]])
232::COMM;;>>> n_connected_components
233::COMM;;1
234::COMM;;>>> n_leaves
235::COMM;;6

650::COMM;;Agglomerative Clustering.
651::COMM;;Recursively merges pair of clusters of sample data; uses linkage distance.
652::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <hierarchical_clustering>`.
653::COMM;;Parameters
654::COMM;;----------
655::COMM;;n_clusters : int or None, default=2
656::COMM;;The number of clusters to find. It must be ``None`` if
657::COMM;;``distance_threshold`` is not ``None``.
658::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default="euclidean"
659::COMM;;Metric used to compute the linkage. Can be "euclidean", "l1", "l2",
660::COMM;;"manhattan", "cosine", or "precomputed". If linkage is "ward", only
661::COMM;;"euclidean" is accepted. If "precomputed", a distance matrix is needed
662::COMM;;as input for the fit method. If connectivity is None, linkage is
663::COMM;;"single" and affinity is not "precomputed" any valid pairwise distance
664::COMM;;metric can be assigned.
665::COMM;;For an example of agglomerative clustering with different metrics, see
666::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_agglomerative_clustering_metrics.py`.
667::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
668::COMM;;memory : str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None
669::COMM;;Used to cache the output of the computation of the tree.
670::COMM;;By default, no caching is done. If a string is given, it is the
671::COMM;;path to the caching directory.
672::COMM;;connectivity : array-like, sparse matrix, or callable, default=None
673::COMM;;Connectivity matrix. Defines for each sample the neighboring
674::COMM;;samples following a given structure of the data.
675::COMM;;This can be a connectivity matrix itself or a callable that transforms
676::COMM;;the data into a connectivity matrix, such as derived from
677::COMM;;`kneighbors_graph`. Default is ``None``, i.e, the
678::COMM;;hierarchical clustering algorithm is unstructured.
679::COMM;;For an example of connectivity matrix using
680::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.neighbors.kneighbors_graph`, see
681::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_ward_structured_vs_unstructured.py`.
682::COMM;;compute_full_tree : 'auto' or bool, default='auto'
683::COMM;;Stop early the construction of the tree at ``n_clusters``. This is
684::COMM;;useful to decrease computation time if the number of clusters is not
685::COMM;;small compared to the number of samples. This option is useful only
686::COMM;;when specifying a connectivity matrix. Note also that when varying the
687::COMM;;number of clusters and using caching, it may be advantageous to compute
688::COMM;;the full tree. It must be ``True`` if ``distance_threshold`` is not
689::COMM;;``None``. By default `compute_full_tree` is "auto", which is equivalent
690::COMM;;to `True` when `distance_threshold` is not `None` or that `n_clusters`
691::COMM;;is inferior to the maximum between 100 or `0.02 * n_samples`.
692::COMM;;Otherwise, "auto" is equivalent to `False`.
693::COMM;;linkage : {'ward', 'complete', 'average', 'single'}, default='ward'
694::COMM;;Which linkage criterion to use. The linkage criterion determines which
695::COMM;;distance to use between sets of observation. The algorithm will merge
696::COMM;;the pairs of cluster that minimize this criterion.
697::COMM;;- 'ward' minimizes the variance of the clusters being merged.
698::COMM;;- 'average' uses the average of the distances of each observation of
699::COMM;;the two sets.
700::COMM;;- 'complete' or 'maximum' linkage uses the maximum distances between
701::COMM;;all observations of the two sets.
702::COMM;;- 'single' uses the minimum of the distances between all observations
703::COMM;;of the two sets.
704::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
705::COMM;;Added the 'single' option
706::COMM;;For examples comparing different `linkage` criteria, see
707::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_linkage_comparison.py`.
708::COMM;;distance_threshold : float, default=None
709::COMM;;The linkage distance threshold at or above which clusters will not be
710::COMM;;merged. If not ``None``, ``n_clusters`` must be ``None`` and
711::COMM;;``compute_full_tree`` must be ``True``.
712::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
713::COMM;;compute_distances : bool, default=False
714::COMM;;Computes distances between clusters even if `distance_threshold` is not
715::COMM;;used. This can be used to make dendrogram visualization, but introduces
716::COMM;;a computational and memory overhead.
717::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
718::COMM;;For an example of dendrogram visualization, see
719::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_agglomerative_dendrogram.py`.
720::COMM;;Attributes

930::COMM;;Recursively merges pair of clusters of features.
931::COMM;;Refer to
932::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_feature_agglomeration_vs_univariate_selection.py`
933::COMM;;for an example comparison of :class:`FeatureAgglomeration` strategy with a
934::COMM;;univariate feature selection strategy (based on ANOVA).

936::COMM;;Parameters
937::COMM;;----------
938::COMM;;n_clusters : int or None, default=2
939::COMM;;The number of clusters to find. It must be ``None`` if
940::COMM;;``distance_threshold`` is not ``None``.
941::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default="euclidean"
942::COMM;;Metric used to compute the linkage. Can be "euclidean", "l1", "l2",
943::COMM;;"manhattan", "cosine", or "precomputed". If linkage is "ward", only
944::COMM;;"euclidean" is accepted. If "precomputed", a distance matrix is needed
945::COMM;;as input for the fit method.
946::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
947::COMM;;memory : str or object with the joblib.Memory interface, default=None
948::COMM;;Used to cache the output of the computation of the tree.
949::COMM;;By default, no caching is done. If a string is given, it is the
950::COMM;;path to the caching directory.
951::COMM;;connectivity : array-like, sparse matrix, or callable, default=None
952::COMM;;Connectivity matrix. Defines for each feature the neighboring
953::COMM;;features following a given structure of the data.
954::COMM;;This can be a connectivity matrix itself or a callable that transforms
955::COMM;;the data into a connectivity matrix, such as derived from
956::COMM;;`kneighbors_graph`. Default is `None`, i.e, the
957::COMM;;hierarchical clustering algorithm is unstructured.
958::COMM;;compute_full_tree : 'auto' or bool, default='auto'
959::COMM;;Stop early the construction of the tree at `n_clusters`. This is useful
960::COMM;;to decrease computation time if the number of clusters is not small
961::COMM;;compared to the number of features. This option is useful only when
962::COMM;;specifying a connectivity matrix. Note also that when varying the
963::COMM;;number of clusters and using caching, it may be advantageous to compute
964::COMM;;the full tree. It must be ``True`` if ``distance_threshold`` is not
965::COMM;;``None``. By default `compute_full_tree` is "auto", which is equivalent
966::COMM;;to `True` when `distance_threshold` is not `None` or that `n_clusters`
967::COMM;;is inferior to the maximum between 100 or `0.02 * n_samples`.
968::COMM;;Otherwise, "auto" is equivalent to `False`.
969::COMM;;linkage : {"ward", "complete", "average", "single"}, default="ward"
970::COMM;;Which linkage criterion to use. The linkage criterion determines which
971::COMM;;distance to use between sets of features. The algorithm will merge
972::COMM;;the pairs of cluster that minimize this criterion.
973::COMM;;- "ward" minimizes the variance of the clusters being merged.
974::COMM;;- "complete" or maximum linkage uses the maximum distances between
975::COMM;;all features of the two sets.
976::COMM;;- "average" uses the average of the distances of each feature of
977::COMM;;the two sets.
978::COMM;;- "single" uses the minimum of the distances between all features
979::COMM;;of the two sets.
980::COMM;;pooling_func : callable, default=np.mean
981::COMM;;This combines the values of agglomerated features into a single
982::COMM;;value, and should accept an array of shape [M, N] and the keyword
983::COMM;;argument `axis=1`, and reduce it to an array of size [M].
984::COMM;;distance_threshold : float, default=None
985::COMM;;The linkage distance threshold at or above which clusters will not be
986::COMM;;merged. If not ``None``, ``n_clusters`` must be ``None`` and
987::COMM;;``compute_full_tree`` must be ``True``.
988::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
989::COMM;;compute_distances : bool, default=False
990::COMM;;Computes distances between clusters even if `distance_threshold` is not
991::COMM;;used. This can be used to make dendrogram visualization, but introduces
992::COMM;;a computational and memory overhead.
993::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
994::COMM;;Attributes
995::COMM;;----------

998::COMM;;``distance_threshold=None``, it will be equal to the given
999::COMM;;``n_clusters``.
1000::COMM;;labels_ : array-like of (n_features,)
1001::COMM;;Cluster labels for each feature.
1002::COMM;;n_leaves_ : int
1003::COMM;;Number of leaves in the hierarchical tree.
1004::COMM;;n_connected_components_ : int

1006::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.21

1010::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1011::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
1012::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
1013::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
1014::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0

1016::COMM;;The children of each non-leaf node. Values less than `n_features`
1017::COMM;;correspond to leaves of the tree which are the original samples.
1018::COMM;;A node `i` greater than or equal to `n_features` is a non-leaf
1019::COMM;;node and has children `children_[i - n_features]`. Alternatively
1020::COMM;;at the i-th iteration, children[i][0] and children[i][1]
1021::COMM;;are merged to form node `n_features + i`.
1022::COMM;;distances_ : array-like of shape (n_nodes-1,)
1023::COMM;;Distances between nodes in the corresponding place in `children_`.
1024::COMM;;Only computed if `distance_threshold` is used or `compute_distances`
1025::COMM;;is set to `True`.

176::COMM;;Clusters rows and columns of an array `X` to solve the relaxed
177::COMM;;normalized cut of the bipartite graph created from `X` as follows:
178::COMM;;the edge between row vertex `i` and column vertex `j` has weight
179::COMM;;`X[i, j]`.
180::COMM;;The resulting bicluster structure is block-diagonal, since each
181::COMM;;row and each column belongs to exactly one bicluster.
182::COMM;;Supports sparse matrices, as long as they are nonnegative.
183::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <spectral_coclustering>`.
184::COMM;;Parameters

192::COMM;;for large matrices. If 'arpack', use

300::COMM;;Partitions rows and columns under the assumption that the data has
301::COMM;;an underlying checkerboard structure. For instance, if there are
302::COMM;;two row partitions and three column partitions, each row will
303::COMM;;belong to three biclusters, and each column will belong to two
304::COMM;;biclusters. The outer product of the corresponding row and column
305::COMM;;label vectors gives this checkerboard structure.

147::COMO;;# if we change init_centroids and init_sq_norm_, it is
148::COMO;;# sufficient,
153::COMM;;split subclusters.

167::COMM;;# We need to find the closest subcluster among all the
168::COMM;;# subclusters so that we can insert our new subcluster.
169::COMM;;dist_matrix = np.dot(self.centroids_, subcluster.centroid_)
170::COMM;;dist_matrix *= -2.0

185::COMM;;closest_index

265::COMM;;def merge_subcluster(self, nominee_cluster, threshold):
269::COMM;;new_ss = self.squared_sum_ + nominee_cluster.squared_sum_
270::COMM;;new_ls = self.linear_sum_ + nominee_cluster.linear_sum_
271::COMM;;new_n = self.n_samples_ + nominee_cluster.n_samples_
272::COMM;;new_centroid = (1 / new_n) * new_ls
273::COMM;;new_sq_norm = np.dot(new_centroid, new_centroid)
274::COMM;;# The squared radius of the cluster is defined:
275::COMM;;# r^2 = sum_i ||x_i - c||^2 / n
276::COMM;;# with x_i the n points assigned to the cluster and c its centroid:
277::COMM;;# c = sum_i x_i / n
278::COMM;;# This can be expanded to:
279::COMM;;# r^2 = sum_i ||x_i||^2 / n - 2 < sum_i x_i / n, c> + n ||c||^2 / n
280::COMM;;# and therefore simplifies to:
281::COMM;;# r^2 = sum_i ||x_i||^2 / n - ||c||^2
282::COMM;;sq_radius = new_ss / new_n - new_sq_norm

294::COMM;;def radius(self):
296::COMO;;# Because of numerical issues, this could become negative
303::COMM;;It is a memory-efficient, online-learning algorithm provided as an
304::COMM;;alternative to :class:`MiniBatchKMeans`. It constructs a tree
305::COMM;;data structure with the cluster centroids being read off the leaf.
306::COMM;;These can be either the final cluster centroids or can be provided as input
307::COMM;;to another clustering algorithm such as :class:`AgglomerativeClustering`.
308::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <birch>`.
309::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.16
310::COMM;;Parameters
311::COMM;;----------
312::COMM;;threshold : float, default=0.5
313::COMM;;The radius of the subcluster obtained by merging a new sample and the
314::COMM;;closest subcluster should be lesser than the threshold. Otherwise a new
315::COMM;;subcluster is started. Setting this value to be very low promotes
316::COMM;;splitting and vice-versa.
317::COMM;;branching_factor : int, default=50
318::COMM;;Maximum number of CF subclusters in each node. If a new samples enters
319::COMM;;such that the number of subclusters exceed the branching_factor then
320::COMM;;that node is split into two nodes with the subclusters redistributed
321::COMM;;in each. The parent subcluster of that node is removed and two new
322::COMM;;subclusters are added as parents of the 2 split nodes.
323::COMM;;n_clusters : int, instance of sklearn.cluster model or None, default=3
324::COMM;;Number of clusters after the final clustering step, which treats the
325::COMM;;subclusters from the leaves as new samples.
326::COMM;;- `None` : the final clustering step is not performed and the
327::COMM;;subclusters are returned as they are.
328::COMM;;- :mod:`sklearn.cluster` Estimator : If a model is provided, the model
329::COMM;;is fit treating the subclusters as new samples and the initial data
330::COMM;;is mapped to the label of the closest subcluster.
331::COMM;;- `int` : the model fit is :class:`AgglomerativeClustering` with
332::COMM;;`n_clusters` set to be equal to the int.
333::COMM;;compute_labels : bool, default=True
334::COMM;;Whether or not to compute labels for each fit.
335::COMM;;Attributes
336::COMM;;----------
337::COMM;;root_ : _CFNode
338::COMM;;Root of the CFTree.
339::COMM;;dummy_leaf_ : _CFNode
340::COMM;;Start pointer to all the leaves.
341::COMM;;subcluster_centers_ : ndarray
342::COMM;;Centroids of all subclusters read directly from the leaves.
343::COMM;;subcluster_labels_ : ndarray
344::COMM;;Labels assigned to the centroids of the subclusters after
345::COMM;;they are clustered globally.
346::COMM;;labels_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
347::COMM;;Array of labels assigned to the input data.
348::COMM;;if partial_fit is used instead of fit, they are assigned to the
349::COMM;;last batch of data.
350::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
351::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
352::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
353::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
354::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
355::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
356::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
357::COMM;;See Also
358::COMM;;--------
359::COMM;;MiniBatchKMeans : Alternative implementation that does incremental updates
360::COMM;;of the centers' positions using mini-batches.
361::COMM;;Notes
362::COMM;;-----
363::COMM;;The tree data structure consists of nodes with each node consisting of
364::COMM;;a number of subclusters. The maximum number of subclusters in a node
365::COMM;;is determined by the branching factor. Each subcluster maintains a
366::COMM;;linear sum, squared sum and the number of samples in that subcluster.
367::COMM;;In addition, each subcluster can also have a node as its child, if the
368::COMM;;subcluster is not a member of a leaf node.
369::COMM;;For a new point entering the root, it is merged with the subcluster closest
370::COMM;;to it and the linear sum, squared sum and the number of samples of that
371::COMM;;subcluster are updated. This is done recursively till the properties of
372::COMM;;the leaf node are updated.
373::COMM;;See :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_birch_vs_minibatchkmeans.py` for a
374::COMM;;comparison with :class:`~sklearn.cluster.MiniBatchKMeans`.
375::COMM;;References
376::COMM;;----------
377::COMM;;* Tian Zhang, Raghu Ramakrishnan, Maron Livny
378::COMM;;BIRCH: An efficient data clustering method for large databases.
379::COMM;;https://www.cs.sfu.ca/CourseCentral/459/han/papers/zhang96.pdf
380::COMM;;* Roberto Perdisci
381::COMM;;JBirch - Java implementation of BIRCH clustering algorithm
382::COMM;;https://code.google.com/archive/p/jbirch
383::COMM;;Examples

67::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <bisect_k_means>`.
68::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
69::COMM;;Parameters
70::COMM;;----------
71::COMM;;n_clusters : int, default=8
72::COMM;;The number of clusters to form as well as the number of
73::COMM;;centroids to generate.
74::COMM;;init : {'k-means++', 'random'} or callable, default='random'
75::COMM;;Method for initialization:
76::COMM;;'k-means++' : selects initial cluster centers for k-mean
77::COMM;;clustering in a smart way to speed up convergence. See section
78::COMM;;Notes in k_init for more details.
79::COMM;;'random': choose `n_clusters` observations (rows) at random from data
80::COMM;;for the initial centroids.
81::COMM;;If a callable is passed, it should take arguments X, n_clusters and a
82::COMM;;random state and return an initialization.
83::COMM;;n_init : int, default=1
84::COMM;;Number of time the inner k-means algorithm will be run with different
85::COMM;;centroid seeds in each bisection.
86::COMM;;That will result producing for each bisection best output of n_init
87::COMM;;consecutive runs in terms of inertia.
88::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
89::COMM;;Determines random number generation for centroid initialization
90::COMM;;in inner K-Means. Use an int to make the randomness deterministic.
91::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
92::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
93::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations of the inner k-means algorithm at each
94::COMM;;bisection.
95::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
96::COMM;;Verbosity mode.
97::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
98::COMM;;Relative tolerance with regards to Frobenius norm of the difference
99::COMM;;in the cluster centers of two consecutive iterations to declare
100::COMM;;convergence. Used in inner k-means algorithm at each bisection to pick
101::COMM;;best possible clusters.
102::COMM;;copy_x : bool, default=True
103::COMM;;When pre-computing distances it is more numerically accurate to center
104::COMM;;the data first. If copy_x is True (default), then the original data is
105::COMM;;not modified. If False, the original data is modified, and put back
106::COMM;;before the function returns, but small numerical differences may be
107::COMM;;introduced by subtracting and then adding the data mean. Note that if
108::COMM;;the original data is not C-contiguous, a copy will be made even if
109::COMM;;copy_x is False. If the original data is sparse, but not in CSR format,
110::COMM;;a copy will be made even if copy_x is False.
111::COMM;;algorithm : {"lloyd", "elkan"}, default="lloyd"
112::COMM;;Inner K-means algorithm used in bisection.
113::COMM;;The classical EM-style algorithm is `"lloyd"`.
114::COMM;;The `"elkan"` variation can be more efficient on some datasets with
115::COMM;;well-defined clusters, by using the triangle inequality. However it's
116::COMM;;more memory intensive due to the allocation of an extra array of shape
117::COMM;;`(n_samples, n_clusters)`.
118::COMM;;bisecting_strategy : {"biggest_inertia", "largest_cluster"},\
119::COMM;;default="biggest_inertia"
120::COMM;;Defines how bisection should be performed:
121::COMM;;- "biggest_inertia" means that BisectingKMeans will always check
122::COMM;;all calculated cluster for cluster with biggest SSE
123::COMM;;(Sum of squared errors) and bisect it. This approach concentrates on
124::COMM;;precision, but may be costly in terms of execution time (especially for
125::COMM;;larger amount of data points).
126::COMM;;- "largest_cluster" - BisectingKMeans will always split cluster with
127::COMM;;largest amount of points assigned to it from all clusters
128::COMM;;previously calculated. That should work faster than picking by SSE
129::COMM;;('biggest_inertia') and may produce similar results in most cases.
130::COMM;;Attributes
131::COMM;;----------
132::COMM;;cluster_centers_ : ndarray of shape (n_clusters, n_features)
133::COMM;;Coordinates of cluster centers. If the algorithm stops before fully
134::COMM;;converging (see ``tol`` and ``max_iter``), these will not be
135::COMM;;consistent with ``labels_``.
136::COMM;;labels_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
137::COMM;;Labels of each point.
138::COMM;;inertia_ : float
139::COMM;;Sum of squared distances of samples to their closest cluster center,
140::COMM;;weighted by the sample weights if provided.
141::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
142::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
143::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
144::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
145::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
146::COMM;;See Also

2::COMM;;DBSCAN: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
37::COMM;;This function is a wrapper around :class:`~cluster.DBSCAN`, suitable for
38::COMM;;quick, standalone clustering tasks. For estimator-based workflows, where
39::COMM;;estimator attributes or pipeline integration is required, prefer
40::COMM;;:class:`~cluster.DBSCAN`.
41::COMM;;DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) is a
42::COMM;;density-based clustering algorithm that groups together points that are
43::COMM;;closely packed while marking points in low-density regions as outliers.
44::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <dbscan>`.
45::COMM;;Parameters
46::COMM;;----------
47::COMM;;X : {array-like, scipy sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features) or \
48::COMM;;(n_samples, n_samples)
49::COMM;;A feature array, or array of distances between samples if
50::COMM;;``metric='precomputed'``. When using precomputed distances, X must
51::COMM;;be a square symmetric matrix.
52::COMM;;eps : float, default=0.5
53::COMM;;The maximum distance between two samples for one to be considered
54::COMM;;as in the neighborhood of the other. This is not a maximum bound
55::COMM;;on the distances of points within a cluster. This is the most
56::COMM;;important DBSCAN parameter to choose appropriately for your data set
57::COMM;;and distance function. Smaller values result in more clusters,
58::COMM;;while larger values result in fewer, larger clusters.
59::COMM;;min_samples : int, default=5
60::COMM;;The number of samples (or total weight) in a neighborhood for a point
61::COMM;;to be considered as a core point. This includes the point itself.
62::COMM;;Higher values yield fewer, denser clusters, while lower values yield
63::COMM;;more, sparser clusters.
64::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default='minkowski'
65::COMM;;The metric to use when calculating distance between instances in a
66::COMM;;feature array. If metric is a string or callable, it must be one of
67::COMM;;the options allowed by :func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances` for
68::COMM;;its metric parameter.
69::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
70::COMM;;must be square during fit.
71::COMM;;X may be a :term:`sparse graph <sparse graph>`,
72::COMM;;in which case only "nonzero" elements may be considered neighbors.
73::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
74::COMM;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
75::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
76::COMM;;algorithm : {'auto', 'ball_tree', 'kd_tree', 'brute'}, default='auto'
77::COMM;;The algorithm to be used by the NearestNeighbors module
78::COMM;;to compute pointwise distances and find nearest neighbors.
79::COMM;;'auto' will attempt to decide the most appropriate algorithm
80::COMM;;based on the values passed to :meth:`fit` method.
81::COMM;;See :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors` documentation for
82::COMM;;details.
83::COMM;;leaf_size : int, default=30
84::COMM;;Leaf size passed to BallTree or cKDTree. This can affect the speed
85::COMM;;of the construction and query, as well as the memory required
86::COMM;;to store the tree. The optimal value depends
87::COMM;;on the nature of the problem. Generally, smaller leaf sizes
88::COMM;;lead to faster queries but slower construction.
89::COMM;;p : float, default=2
90::COMM;;Power parameter for the Minkowski metric. When p = 1, this is equivalent
91::COMM;;to using manhattan_distance (l1), and euclidean_distance (l2) for p = 2.
92::COMM;;For arbitrary p, minkowski_distance (l_p) is used. This parameter is expected
93::COMM;;to be positive.
94::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
95::COMM;;Weight of each sample, such that a sample with a weight of at least
96::COMM;;``min_samples`` is by itself a core sample; a sample with negative
97::COMM;;weight may inhibit its eps-neighbor from being core.
98::COMM;;Note that weights are absolute, and default to 1.
99::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
100::COMM;;The number of parallel jobs to run for neighbors search. ``None`` means
101::COMM;;1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context. ``-1`` means
102::COMM;;using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>` for more details.
103::COMM;;If precomputed distances are used, parallel execution is not available
104::COMM;;and thus n_jobs will have no effect.
105::COMM;;Returns
106::COMM;;-------
107::COMM;;core_samples : ndarray of shape (n_core_samples,)
108::COMM;;Indices of core samples.
109::COMM;;labels : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
110::COMM;;Cluster labels for each point. Noisy samples are given the label -1.
111::COMM;;Non-negative integers indicate cluster membership.
112::COMM;;See Also
113::COMM;;--------
114::COMM;;DBSCAN : An estimator interface for this clustering algorithm.
115::COMM;;OPTICS : A similar estimator interface clustering at multiple values of
116::COMM;;eps. Our implementation is optimized for memory usage.
117::COMM;;Notes
118::COMM;;-----
119::COMM;;For an example, see :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_cluster_plot_dbscan.py`.
120::COMM;;This implementation bulk-computes all neighborhood queries, which increases
121::COMM;;the memory complexity to O(n.d) where d is the average number of neighbors,
122::COMM;;while original DBSCAN had memory complexity O(n). It may attract a higher
123::COMM;;memory complexity when querying these nearest neighborhoods, depending
124::COMM;;on the ``algorithm``.
125::COMM;;One way to avoid the query complexity is to pre-compute sparse
126::COMM;;neighborhoods in chunks using
127::COMM;;:func:`NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors_graph
128::COMM;;<sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors_graph>` with
129::COMM;;``mode='distance'``, then using ``metric='precomputed'`` here.
130::COMM;;Another way to reduce memory and computation time is to remove
131::COMM;;(near-)duplicate points and use ``sample_weight`` instead.
132::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.cluster.OPTICS` provides a similar clustering with lower
133::COMM;;memory usage.
134::COMM;;References
135::COMM;;----------
136::COMM;;Ester, M., H. P. Kriegel, J. Sander, and X. Xu, `"A Density-Based
137::COMM;;Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise"
138::COMM;;<https://www.dbs.ifi.lmu.de/Publikationen/Papers/KDD-96.final.frame.pdf>`_.
139::COMM;;In: Proceedings of the 2nd International Conference on Knowledge Discovery
140::COMM;;and Data Mining, Portland, OR, AAAI Press, pp. 226-231. 1996
141::COMM;;Schubert, E., Sander, J., Ester, M., Kriegel, H. P., & Xu, X. (2017).
142::COMM;;:doi:`"DBSCAN revisited, revisited: why and how you should (still) use DBSCAN."
143::COMM;;<10.1145/3068335>`
144::COMM;;ACM Transactions on Database Systems (TODS), 42(3), 19.
145::COMM;;Examples
146::COMM;;--------
147::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.cluster import dbscan
148::COMM;;>>> X = [[1, 2], [2, 2], [2, 3], [8, 7], [8, 8], [25, 80]]
149::COMM;;>>> core_samples, labels = dbscan(X, eps=3, min_samples=2)
150::COMM;;>>> core_samples
151::COMM;;array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
152::COMM;;>>> labels
153::COMM;;array([ 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, -1])
169::COMM;;DBSCAN - Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise.
170::COMM;;Finds core samples of high density and expands clusters from them.
171::COMM;;This algorithm is particularly good for data which contains clusters of
172::COMM;;similar density and can find clusters of arbitrary shape.
173::COMM;;Unlike K-means, DBSCAN does not require specifying the number of clusters
174::COMM;;in advance and can identify outliers as noise points.
175::COMM;;This implementation has a worst case memory complexity of :math:`O({n}^2)`,
176::COMM;;which can occur when the `eps` param is large and `min_samples` is low,
177::COMM;;while the original DBSCAN only uses linear memory.
178::COMM;;For further details, see the Notes below.
179::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <dbscan>`.
180::COMM;;Parameters
181::COMM;;----------
182::COMM;;eps : float, default=0.5
183::COMM;;The maximum distance between two samples for one to be considered
184::COMM;;as in the neighborhood of the other. This is not a maximum bound
185::COMM;;on the distances of points within a cluster. This is the most
186::COMM;;important DBSCAN parameter to choose appropriately for your data set
187::COMM;;and distance function. Smaller values generally lead to more clusters.
188::COMM;;min_samples : int, default=5
189::COMM;;The number of samples (or total weight) in a neighborhood for a point to
190::COMM;;be considered as a core point. This includes the point itself. If
191::COMM;;`min_samples` is set to a higher value, DBSCAN will find denser clusters,
192::COMM;;whereas if it is set to a lower value, the found clusters will be more
193::COMM;;sparse.
194::COMM;;metric : str, or callable, default='euclidean'
195::COMM;;The metric to use when calculating distance between instances in a
196::COMM;;feature array. If metric is a string or callable, it must be one of
197::COMM;;the options allowed by :func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances` for
198::COMM;;its metric parameter.
199::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
200::COMM;;must be square. X may be a :term:`sparse graph`, in which
201::COMM;;case only "nonzero" elements may be considered neighbors for DBSCAN.
202::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
203::COMM;;metric *precomputed* to accept precomputed sparse matrix.
204::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
205::COMM;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
206::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
207::COMM;;algorithm : {'auto', 'ball_tree', 'kd_tree', 'brute'}, default='auto'
208::COMM;;The algorithm to be used by the NearestNeighbors module
209::COMM;;to compute pointwise distances and find nearest neighbors.
210::COMM;;'auto' will attempt to decide the most appropriate algorithm
211::COMM;;based on the values passed to :meth:`fit` method.
212::COMM;;See :class:`~sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors` documentation for
213::COMM;;details.
214::COMM;;leaf_size : int, default=30
215::COMM;;Leaf size passed to BallTree or cKDTree. This can affect the speed
216::COMM;;of the construction and query, as well as the memory required
217::COMM;;to store the tree. The optimal value depends
218::COMM;;on the nature of the problem.
219::COMM;;p : float, default=None
220::COMM;;The power of the Minkowski metric to be used to calculate distance
221::COMM;;between points. If None, then ``p=2`` (equivalent to the Euclidean
222::COMM;;distance). When p=1, this is equivalent to Manhattan distance.
223::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
224::COMM;;The number of parallel jobs to run.
225::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
226::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
227::COMM;;for more details.
228::COMM;;Attributes
229::COMM;;----------
230::COMM;;core_sample_indices_ : ndarray of shape (n_core_samples,)
231::COMM;;Indices of core samples.
232::COMM;;components_ : ndarray of shape (n_core_samples, n_features)
233::COMM;;Copy of each core sample found by training.
234::COMM;;labels_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
235::COMM;;Cluster labels for each point in the dataset given to fit().
236::COMM;;Noisy samples are given the label -1. Non-negative integers
237::COMM;;indicate cluster membership.
238::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
239::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
240::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
241::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
242::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
243::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
244::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
245::COMM;;See Also
246::COMM;;--------
247::COMM;;OPTICS : A similar clustering at multiple values of eps. Our implementation
248::COMM;;is optimized for memory usage.
249::COMM;;Notes
250::COMM;;-----
251::COMM;;This implementation bulk-computes all neighborhood queries, which increases
252::COMM;;the memory complexity to O(n.d) where d is the average number of neighbors,
253::COMM;;while original DBSCAN had memory complexity O(n). It may attract a higher
254::COMM;;memory complexity when querying these nearest neighborhoods, depending
255::COMM;;on the ``algorithm``.
256::COMM;;One way to avoid the query complexity is to pre-compute sparse
257::COMM;;neighborhoods in chunks using
258::COMM;;:func:`NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors_graph
