388::COMM;;Get the array API compatible namespace for the arrays `xs`.
389::COMM;;Parameters
390::COMM;;----------
391::COMM;;xs: arrays
392::COMM;;one or more arrays. xs can also be Python scalars (bool, int, float,
393::COMM;;complex, or None), which are ignored.
394::COMM;;api_version: str
395::COMM;;The newest version of the spec that you need support for (currently
396::COMM;;the compat library wrapped APIs support v2024.12).
397::COMM;;use_compat: bool or None
398::COMM;;If None (the default), the native namespace will be returned if it is
399::COMM;;already array API compatible, otherwise a compat wrapper is used. If
400::COMM;;True, the compat library wrapped library will be returned. If False,
401::COMM;;the native library namespace is returned.
402::COMM;;Returns
403::COMM;;-------
404::COMM;;out: namespace
405::COMM;;The array API compatible namespace corresponding to the arrays in `xs`.
406::COMM;;Raises
407::COMM;;------
408::COMM;;TypeError
409::COMM;;If `xs` contains arrays from different array libraries or contains a
410::COMM;;non-array.
411::COMM;;Typical usage is to pass the arguments of a function to
412::COMM;;`array_namespace()` at the top of a function to get the corresponding
413::COMM;;array API namespace:
414::COMM;;.. code:: python
415::COMM;;def your_function(x, y):
416::COMM;;xp = array_api_compat.array_namespace(x, y)
417::COMM;;# Now use xp as the array library namespace
418::COMM;;return xp.mean(x, axis=0) + 2*xp.std(y, axis=0)
419::COMM;;Wrapped array namespaces can also be imported directly. For example,
420::COMM;;`array_namespace(np.array(...))` will return `array_api_compat.numpy`.
421::COMM;;This function will also work for any array library not wrapped by
422::COMM;;array-api-compat if it explicitly defines `__array_namespace__
423::COMM;;<https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/API_specification/generated/array_api.array.__array_namespace__.html>`__
424::COMM;;(the wrapped namespace is always preferred if it exists).
425::COMM;;See Also

206::COMM;;from ._funcs import apply_where # pylint: disable=cyclic-import
207::COMM;;x, idx = self._x, self._idx

218::COMM;;raise ValueError(msg)
219::COMM;;if copy not in (True, False, None):
220::COMM;;msg = f"copy must be True, False, or None; got {copy!r}"
221::COMM;;raise ValueError(msg)
222::COMM;;writeable = None if copy else is_writeable_array(x)
223::COMM;;# JAX inside jax.jit doesn't support in-place updates with boolean
224::COMM;;# masks; Dask exclusively supports __setitem__ but not iops.
225::COMM;;# We can handle the common special case of 0-dimensional y
226::COMM;;# with where(idx, y, x) instead.
227::COMM;;if (
228::COMM;;(is_dask_array(idx) or is_jax_array(idx))
229::COMM;;and idx.dtype == xp.bool
230::COMM;;and idx.shape == x.shape
231::COMM;;):

233::COMM;;if y_xp.ndim == 0:

235::COMM;;# suppress inf warnings on Dask
236::COMM;;out = apply_where(
237::COMM;;idx, (x, y_xp), out_of_place_op, fill_value=x, xp=xp
238::COMM;;)
239::COMM;;# Undo int->float promotion on JAX after _AtOp.DIVIDE
240::COMM;;out = xp.astype(out, x.dtype, copy=False)
241::COMM;;else: # set()

243::COMM;;if copy is False:
244::COMM;;x[()] = out
245::COMM;;return x
246::COMM;;return out
247::COMM;;# else: this will work on eager JAX and crash on jax.jit and Dask
248::COMM;;if copy or (copy is None and not writeable):
249::COMM;;if is_jax_array(x):
250::COMM;;# Use JAX's at[]
251::COMM;;func = cast(
252::COMM;;Callable[[Array | complex], Array],

255::COMM;;out = func(y)
256::COMM;;# Undo int->float promotion on JAX after _AtOp.DIVIDE

258::COMM;;# Emulate at[] behaviour for non-JAX arrays
259::COMM;;# with a copy followed by an update
260::COMM;;x = xp.asarray(x, copy=True)
261::COMM;;# A copy of a read-only numpy array is writeable
262::COMM;;# Note: this assumes that a copy of a writeable array is writeable
263::COMM;;assert not writeable
264::COMM;;writeable = None
265::COMM;;if writeable is None:

267::COMM;;if not writeable:
268::COMM;;# sparse crashes here
269::COMM;;msg = f"Can't update read-only array {x}"
270::COMM;;raise ValueError(msg)

272::COMM;;# always support mismatched dtypes
273::COMM;;# https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/150017
274::COMM;;if is_torch_array(y):
275::COMM;;y = xp.astype(y, x.dtype, copy=False)
276::COMM;;# Backends without boolean indexing (other than JAX) crash here
277::COMM;;if in_place_op: # add(), subtract(), ...
278::COMM;;x[idx] = in_place_op(x[idx], y)
279::COMM;;else: # set()
280::COMM;;x[idx] = y
281::COMM;;return x

154::COMM;;Recursively expand the dimension of an array to at least `ndim`.
155::COMM;;Parameters
156::COMM;;----------
157::COMM;;x : array
158::COMM;;Input array.
159::COMM;;ndim : int
160::COMM;;The minimum number of dimensions for the result.
161::COMM;;xp : array_namespace, optional
162::COMM;;The standard-compatible namespace for `x`. Default: infer.
163::COMM;;Returns
164::COMM;;-------
165::COMM;;array
166::COMM;;An array with ``res.ndim`` >= `ndim`.
167::COMM;;If ``x.ndim`` >= `ndim`, `x` is returned.
168::COMM;;If ``x.ndim`` < `ndim`, `x` is expanded by prepending new axes
169::COMM;;until ``res.ndim`` equals `ndim`.
170::COMM;;Examples
171::COMM;;--------
172::COMM;;>>> import array_api_strict as xp
173::COMM;;>>> import array_api_extra as xpx

175::COMM;;>>> xpx.atleast_nd(x, ndim=3, xp=xp)

178::COMM;;... [3, 4]]])
179::COMM;;>>> xpx.atleast_nd(x, ndim=1, xp=xp) is x
180::COMM;;True
188::COMO;;# `float` in signature to accept `math.nan` for Dask.
189::COMO;;# `int`s are still accepted as `float` is a superclass of `int` in typing
192::COMM;;Compute the shape of the broadcasted arrays.
193::COMM;;Duplicates :func:`numpy.broadcast_shapes`, with additional support for
194::COMM;;None and NaN sizes.
195::COMM;;This is equivalent to ``xp.broadcast_arrays(arr1, arr2, ...)[0].shape``
196::COMM;;without needing to worry about the backend potentially deep copying
197::COMM;;the arrays.

242::COMM;;Estimate a covariance matrix.
243::COMM;;Covariance indicates the level to which two variables vary together.
244::COMM;;If we examine N-dimensional samples, :math:`X = [x_1, x_2, ... x_N]^T`,
245::COMM;;then the covariance matrix element :math:`C_{ij}` is the covariance of
246::COMM;;:math:`x_i` and :math:`x_j`. The element :math:`C_{ii}` is the variance
247::COMM;;of :math:`x_i`.
248::COMM;;This provides a subset of the functionality of ``numpy.cov``.
249::COMM;;Parameters
250::COMM;;----------
251::COMM;;m : array
252::COMM;;A 1-D or 2-D array containing multiple variables and observations.
253::COMM;;Each row of `m` represents a variable, and each column a single
254::COMM;;observation of all those variables.
255::COMM;;xp : array_namespace, optional
256::COMM;;The standard-compatible namespace for `m`. Default: infer.
257::COMM;;Returns
258::COMM;;-------
259::COMM;;array
260::COMM;;The covariance matrix of the variables.
261::COMM;;Examples
262::COMM;;--------
263::COMM;;>>> import array_api_strict as xp
264::COMM;;>>> import array_api_extra as xpx
265::COMM;;Consider two variables, :math:`x_0` and :math:`x_1`, which
266::COMM;;correlate perfectly, but in opposite directions:
267::COMM;;>>> x = xp.asarray([[0, 2], [1, 1], [2, 0]]).T
268::COMM;;>>> x
269::COMM;;Array([[0, 1, 2],
270::COMM;;[2, 1, 0]], dtype=array_api_strict.int64)
271::COMM;;Note how :math:`x_0` increases while :math:`x_1` decreases. The covariance
272::COMM;;matrix shows this clearly:
273::COMM;;>>> xpx.cov(x, xp=xp)
274::COMM;;Array([[ 1., -1.],
275::COMM;;[-1., 1.]], dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
276::COMM;;Note that element :math:`C_{0,1}`, which shows the correlation between
277::COMM;;:math:`x_0` and :math:`x_1`, is negative.
278::COMM;;Further, note how `x` and `y` are combined:
279::COMM;;>>> x = xp.asarray([-2.1, -1, 4.3])
280::COMM;;>>> y = xp.asarray([3, 1.1, 0.12])
281::COMM;;>>> X = xp.stack((x, y), axis=0)
282::COMM;;>>> xpx.cov(X, xp=xp)
283::COMM;;Array([[11.71 , -4.286 ],
284::COMM;;[-4.286 , 2.14413333]], dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
285::COMM;;>>> xpx.cov(x, xp=xp)
286::COMM;;Array(11.71, dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
287::COMM;;>>> xpx.cov(y, xp=xp)
288::COMM;;Array(2.14413333, dtype=array_api_strict.float64)

533::COMM;;Kronecker product of two arrays.
534::COMM;;Computes the Kronecker product, a composite array made of blocks of the
535::COMM;;second array scaled by the first.
536::COMM;;Equivalent to ``numpy.kron`` for NumPy arrays.
537::COMM;;Parameters
538::COMM;;----------
539::COMM;;a, b : Array | int | float | complex
540::COMM;;Input arrays or scalars. At least one must be an array.
541::COMM;;xp : array_namespace, optional
542::COMM;;The standard-compatible namespace for `a` and `b`. Default: infer.
543::COMM;;Returns
544::COMM;;-------
545::COMM;;array
546::COMM;;The Kronecker product of `a` and `b`.
547::COMM;;Notes
548::COMM;;-----
549::COMM;;The function assumes that the number of dimensions of `a` and `b`
550::COMM;;are the same, if necessary prepending the smallest with ones.
551::COMM;;If ``a.shape = (r0,r1,..,rN)`` and ``b.shape = (s0,s1,...,sN)``,
552::COMM;;the Kronecker product has shape ``(r0*s0, r1*s1, ..., rN*SN)``.
553::COMM;;The elements are products of elements from `a` and `b`, organized
554::COMM;;explicitly by::
555::COMM;;kron(a,b)[k0,k1,...,kN] = a[i0,i1,...,iN] * b[j0,j1,...,jN]
556::COMM;;where::
557::COMM;;kt = it * st + jt, t = 0,...,N
558::COMM;;In the common 2-D case (N=1), the block structure can be visualized::
559::COMM;;[[ a[0,0]*b, a[0,1]*b, ... , a[0,-1]*b ],
560::COMM;;[ ... ... ],
561::COMM;;[ a[-1,0]*b, a[-1,1]*b, ... , a[-1,-1]*b ]]
562::COMM;;Examples
563::COMM;;--------
564::COMM;;>>> import array_api_strict as xp
565::COMM;;>>> import array_api_extra as xpx
566::COMM;;>>> xpx.kron(xp.asarray([1, 10, 100]), xp.asarray([5, 6, 7]), xp=xp)
567::COMM;;Array([ 5, 6, 7, 50, 60, 70, 500,
568::COMM;;600, 700], dtype=array_api_strict.int64)
569::COMM;;>>> xpx.kron(xp.asarray([5, 6, 7]), xp.asarray([1, 10, 100]), xp=xp)
570::COMM;;Array([ 5, 50, 500, 6, 60, 600, 7,
571::COMM;;70, 700], dtype=array_api_strict.int64)
572::COMM;;>>> xpx.kron(xp.eye(2), xp.ones((2, 2)), xp=xp)
573::COMM;;Array([[1., 1., 0., 0.],
574::COMM;;[1., 1., 0., 0.],
575::COMM;;[0., 0., 1., 1.],
576::COMM;;[0., 0., 1., 1.]], dtype=array_api_strict.float64)
577::COMM;;>>> a = xp.reshape(xp.arange(100), (2, 5, 2, 5))
578::COMM;;>>> b = xp.reshape(xp.arange(24), (2, 3, 4))
579::COMM;;>>> c = xpx.kron(a, b, xp=xp)
580::COMM;;>>> c.shape
581::COMM;;(2, 10, 6, 20)
582::COMM;;>>> I = (1, 3, 0, 2)
583::COMM;;>>> J = (0, 2, 1)
584::COMM;;>>> J1 = (0,) + J # extend to ndim=4
585::COMM;;>>> S1 = (1,) + b.shape
586::COMM;;>>> K = tuple(xp.asarray(I) * xp.asarray(S1) + xp.asarray(J1))
587::COMM;;>>> c[K] == a[I]*b[J]
588::COMM;;Array(True, dtype=array_api_strict.bool)

270::COMM;;class CountingDaskScheduler(SchedulerGetCallable):
282::COMM;;count: int

293::COMM;;import dask

296::COMM;;# offending line in the user's code

299::COMM;;def _dask_wrap(
300::COMM;;func: Callable[P, T], n: int
301::COMM;;) -> Callable[P, T]: # numpydoc ignore=PR01,RT01
306::COMM;;import dask
307::COMM;;import dask.array as da

309::COMM;;n_str = f"only up to {n}" if n else "no"
310::COMM;;msg = (
311::COMM;;f"Called `dask.compute()` or `dask.persist()` {n + 1} times, "
312::COMM;;f"but {n_str} calls are allowed. Set "
313::COMM;;f"`lazy_xp_function({func_name}, allow_dask_compute={n + 1})` "
314::COMM;;"to allow for more (but note that this will harm performance). "
315::COMM;;)

319::COMM;;with dask.config.set({"scheduler": scheduler}): # pyright: ignore[reportPrivateImportUsage]

322::COMM;;# `pytest.raises` and `pytest.warns` to work as expected. Note that this would
323::COMM;;# not work on scheduler='distributed', as it would not block.
324::COMM;;arrays, rest = pickle_flatten(out, da.Array)
325::COMM;;arrays = dask.persist(arrays, scheduler="threads")[0] # type: ignore[attr-defined,no-untyped-call] # pyright: ignore[reportPrivateImportUsage]

1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers

14::COMM;;This transformer turns lists of mappings (dict-like objects) of feature
15::COMM;;names to feature values into Numpy arrays or scipy.sparse matrices for use
16::COMM;;with scikit-learn estimators.
17::COMM;;When feature values are strings, this transformer will do a binary one-hot
18::COMM;;(aka one-of-K) coding: one boolean-valued feature is constructed for each
19::COMM;;of the possible string values that the feature can take on. For instance,
20::COMM;;a feature "f" that can take on the values "ham" and "spam" will become two
21::COMM;;features in the output, one signifying "f=ham", the other "f=spam".
22::COMM;;If a feature value is a sequence or set of strings, this transformer
23::COMM;;will iterate over the values and will count the occurrences of each string
24::COMM;;value.
25::COMM;;However, note that this transformer will only do a binary one-hot encoding
26::COMM;;when feature values are of type string. If categorical features are
27::COMM;;represented as numeric values such as int or iterables of strings, the
28::COMM;;DictVectorizer can be followed by
29::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.OneHotEncoder` to complete
30::COMM;;binary one-hot encoding.
31::COMM;;Features that do not occur in a sample (mapping) will have a zero value
32::COMM;;in the resulting array/matrix.
33::COMM;;For an efficiency comparison of the different feature extractors, see
34::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_hashing_vs_dict_vectorizer.py`.
35::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <dict_feature_extraction>`.
36::COMM;;Parameters
37::COMM;;----------
38::COMM;;dtype : dtype, default=np.float64
39::COMM;;The type of feature values. Passed to Numpy array/scipy.sparse matrix
40::COMM;;constructors as the dtype argument.
41::COMM;;separator : str, default="="
42::COMM;;Separator string used when constructing new features for one-hot
43::COMM;;coding.
44::COMM;;sparse : bool, default=True
45::COMM;;Whether transform should produce scipy.sparse matrices.
46::COMM;;sort : bool, default=True
47::COMM;;Whether ``feature_names_`` and ``vocabulary_`` should be
48::COMM;;sorted when fitting.
49::COMM;;Attributes
50::COMM;;----------
51::COMM;;vocabulary_ : dict
52::COMM;;A dictionary mapping feature names to feature indices.
53::COMM;;feature_names_ : list
54::COMM;;A list of length n_features containing the feature names (e.g., "f=ham"
55::COMM;;and "f=spam").
56::COMM;;See Also
57::COMM;;--------
58::COMM;;FeatureHasher : Performs vectorization using only a hash function.
59::COMM;;sklearn.preprocessing.OrdinalEncoder : Handles nominal/categorical
60::COMM;;features encoded as columns of arbitrary data types.
61::COMM;;Examples
62::COMM;;--------
63::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.feature_extraction import DictVectorizer
64::COMM;;>>> v = DictVectorizer(sparse=False)
65::COMM;;>>> D = [{'foo': 1, 'bar': 2}, {'foo': 3, 'baz': 1}]
66::COMM;;>>> X = v.fit_transform(D)
67::COMM;;>>> X
68::COMM;;array([[2., 0., 1.],
69::COMM;;[0., 1., 3.]])
70::COMM;;>>> v.inverse_transform(X) == [{'bar': 2.0, 'foo': 1.0},
71::COMM;;... {'baz': 1.0, 'foo': 3.0}]
72::COMM;;True
73::COMM;;>>> v.transform({'foo': 4, 'unseen_feature': 3})
74::COMM;;array([[0., 0., 4.]])
76::COMO;;# This isn't something that people should be routing / using in a pipeline.

105::COMM;;vv = 1
106::COMM;;else:
107::COMM;;raise TypeError(

162::COMM;;def _transform(self, X, fitting):
163::COMM;;# Sanity check: Python's array has no way of explicitly requesting the
164::COMM;;# signed 32-bit integers that scipy.sparse needs, so we use the next
165::COMM;;# best thing: typecode "i" (int). However, if that gives larger or
166::COMM;;# smaller integers than 32-bit ones, np.frombuffer screws up.
167::COMM;;assert array("i").itemsize == 4, (
168::COMM;;"sizeof(int) != 4 on your platform; please report this at"
169::COMM;;" https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues and"
170::COMM;;" include the output from platform.platform() in your bug report"
171::COMM;;)
172::COMM;;dtype = self.dtype
173::COMM;;if fitting:
174::COMM;;feature_names = []
175::COMM;;vocab = {}
176::COMM;;else:
177::COMM;;feature_names = self.feature_names_
178::COMM;;vocab = self.vocabulary_
179::COMM;;transforming = True
180::COMM;;# Process everything as sparse regardless of setting
181::COMM;;X = [X] if isinstance(X, Mapping) else X
182::COMM;;indices = array("i")
183::COMM;;indptr = [0]
184::COMM;;# XXX we could change values to an array.array as well, but it
185::COMM;;# would require (heuristic) conversion of dtype to typecode...
186::COMM;;values = []
187::COMM;;# collect all the possible feature names and build sparse matrix at
188::COMM;;# same time
189::COMM;;for x in X:
190::COMM;;for f, v in x.items():
191::COMM;;if isinstance(v, str):
192::COMM;;feature_name = "%s%s%s" % (f, self.separator, v)
193::COMM;;v = 1
194::COMM;;elif isinstance(v, Number) or (v is None):
195::COMM;;feature_name = f
196::COMM;;elif not isinstance(v, Mapping) and isinstance(v, Iterable):
197::COMM;;feature_name = None
198::COMM;;self._add_iterable_element(
199::COMM;;f,
200::COMM;;v,
201::COMM;;feature_names,
202::COMM;;vocab,
203::COMM;;fitting=fitting,
204::COMM;;transforming=transforming,
205::COMM;;indices=indices,
206::COMM;;values=values,
207::COMM;;)
208::COMM;;else:
209::COMM;;raise TypeError(
210::COMM;;f"Unsupported value Type {type(v)} "
211::COMM;;f"for {f}: {v}.\n"
212::COMM;;f"{type(v)} objects are not supported."
213::COMM;;)
214::COMM;;if feature_name is not None:
215::COMM;;if fitting and feature_name not in vocab:
216::COMM;;vocab[feature_name] = len(feature_names)
217::COMM;;feature_names.append(feature_name)
218::COMM;;if feature_name in vocab:
219::COMM;;indices.append(vocab[feature_name])
220::COMM;;values.append(self.dtype(v))
221::COMM;;indptr.append(len(indices))
222::COMM;;if len(indptr) == 1:
223::COMM;;raise ValueError("Sample sequence X is empty.")
224::COMM;;indices = np.frombuffer(indices, dtype=np.intc)
225::COMM;;shape = (len(indptr) - 1, len(vocab))
226::COMM;;result_matrix = sp.csr_matrix(
227::COMM;;(values, indices, indptr), shape=shape, dtype=dtype
228::COMM;;)
229::COMM;;# Sort everything if asked
230::COMM;;if fitting and self.sort:
231::COMM;;feature_names.sort()
232::COMM;;map_index = np.empty(len(feature_names), dtype=np.int32)
233::COMM;;for new_val, f in enumerate(feature_names):
234::COMM;;map_index[new_val] = vocab[f]
235::COMM;;vocab[f] = new_val
236::COMM;;result_matrix = result_matrix[:, map_index]
237::COMM;;if self.sparse:
238::COMM;;result_matrix.sort_indices()
239::COMM;;else:
240::COMM;;result_matrix = result_matrix.toarray()
241::COMM;;if fitting:

243::COMM;;self.vocabulary_ = vocab

26::COMM;;# From an image to a graph
27::COMM;;def _make_edges_3d(n_x, n_y, n_z=1):
38::COMM;;vertices = np.arange(n_x * n_y * n_z).reshape((n_x, n_y, n_z))
39::COMM;;edges_deep = np.vstack((vertices[:, :, :-1].ravel(), vertices[:, :, 1:].ravel()))
40::COMM;;edges_right = np.vstack((vertices[:, :-1].ravel(), vertices[:, 1:].ravel()))
41::COMM;;edges_down = np.vstack((vertices[:-1].ravel(), vertices[1:].ravel()))
42::COMM;;edges = np.hstack((edges_deep, edges_right, edges_down))
43::COMM;;return edges
44::COMM;;def _compute_gradient_3d(edges, img):
45::COMM;;_, n_y, n_z = img.shape
46::COMM;;gradient = np.abs(
47::COMM;;img[
48::COMM;;edges[0] // (n_y * n_z),
49::COMM;;(edges[0] % (n_y * n_z)) // n_z,
50::COMM;;(edges[0] % (n_y * n_z)) % n_z,
51::COMM;;]
52::COMM;;- img[
53::COMM;;edges[1] // (n_y * n_z),
54::COMM;;(edges[1] % (n_y * n_z)) // n_z,
55::COMM;;(edges[1] % (n_y * n_z)) % n_z,
56::COMM;;]
57::COMM;;)
58::COMM;;return gradient
59::COMM;;# XXX: Why mask the image after computing the weights?
60::COMM;;def _mask_edges_weights(mask, edges, weights=None):
82::COMM;;edges = _make_edges_3d(n_x, n_y, n_z)
83::COMM;;if dtype is None: # To not overwrite input dtype
84::COMM;;if img is None:
85::COMM;;dtype = int
86::COMM;;else:
87::COMM;;dtype = img.dtype
88::COMM;;if img is not None:
89::COMM;;img = np.atleast_3d(img)
90::COMM;;weights = _compute_gradient_3d(edges, img)
91::COMM;;if mask is not None:
92::COMM;;edges, weights = _mask_edges_weights(mask, edges, weights)
93::COMM;;diag = img.squeeze()[mask]
94::COMM;;else:
95::COMM;;diag = img.ravel()
96::COMM;;n_voxels = diag.size
97::COMM;;else:
98::COMM;;if mask is not None:
99::COMM;;mask = mask.astype(dtype=bool, copy=False)
100::COMM;;edges = _mask_edges_weights(mask, edges)
101::COMM;;n_voxels = np.sum(mask)
102::COMM;;else:
103::COMM;;n_voxels = n_x * n_y * n_z
104::COMM;;weights = np.ones(edges.shape[1], dtype=dtype)
105::COMM;;diag = np.ones(n_voxels, dtype=dtype)
106::COMM;;diag_idx = np.arange(n_voxels)
107::COMM;;i_idx = np.hstack((edges[0], edges[1]))
108::COMM;;j_idx = np.hstack((edges[1], edges[0]))
109::COMM;;graph = sparse.coo_matrix(
110::COMM;;(
111::COMM;;np.hstack((weights, weights, diag)),
112::COMM;;(np.hstack((i_idx, diag_idx)), np.hstack((j_idx, diag_idx))),
113::COMM;;),
114::COMM;;(n_voxels, n_voxels),
115::COMM;;dtype=dtype,
116::COMM;;)
117::COMM;;if return_as is np.ndarray:
118::COMM;;return graph.toarray()
119::COMM;;return return_as(graph)

219::COMM;;# From an image to a set of small image patches
220::COMM;;def _compute_n_patches(i_h, i_w, p_h, p_w, max_patches=None):
238::COMM;;n_h = i_h - p_h + 1
239::COMM;;n_w = i_w - p_w + 1
240::COMM;;all_patches = n_h * n_w
241::COMM;;if max_patches:
242::COMM;;if isinstance(max_patches, (Integral)) and max_patches < all_patches:
243::COMM;;return max_patches
244::COMM;;elif isinstance(max_patches, (Integral)) and max_patches >= all_patches:
245::COMM;;return all_patches
246::COMM;;elif isinstance(max_patches, (Real)) and 0 < max_patches < 1:
247::COMM;;return int(max_patches * all_patches)
248::COMM;;else:
249::COMM;;raise ValueError("Invalid value for max_patches: %r" % max_patches)
250::COMM;;else:
251::COMM;;return all_patches
252::COMM;;def _extract_patches(arr, patch_shape=8, extraction_step=1):
280::COMM;;arr_ndim = arr.ndim
281::COMM;;if isinstance(patch_shape, Number):
282::COMM;;patch_shape = tuple([patch_shape] * arr_ndim)
283::COMM;;if isinstance(extraction_step, Number):
284::COMM;;extraction_step = tuple([extraction_step] * arr_ndim)
285::COMM;;patch_strides = arr.strides
286::COMM;;slices = tuple(slice(None, None, st) for st in extraction_step)
287::COMM;;indexing_strides = arr[slices].strides
288::COMM;;patch_indices_shape = (
289::COMM;;(np.array(arr.shape) - np.array(patch_shape)) // np.array(extraction_step)
290::COMM;;) + 1
291::COMM;;shape = tuple(list(patch_indices_shape) + list(patch_shape))
292::COMM;;strides = tuple(list(indexing_strides) + list(patch_strides))
293::COMM;;patches = as_strided(arr, shape=shape, strides=strides)
294::COMM;;return patches
295::COMM;;@validate_params(
296::COMM;;{
297::COMM;;"image": [np.ndarray],
298::COMM;;"patch_size": [tuple, list],
299::COMM;;"max_patches": [
300::COMM;;Interval(RealNotInt, 0, 1, closed="neither"),
301::COMM;;Interval(Integral, 1, None, closed="left"),
302::COMM;;None,
303::COMM;;],
304::COMM;;"random_state": ["random_state"],

308::COMM;;def extract_patches_2d(image, patch_size, *, max_patches=None, random_state=None):
341::COMC;;>>> # Use the array data from the first image in this dataset:
348::COMC;;>>> # Here are just two of these patches:
360::COMM;;i_h, i_w = image.shape[:2]
361::COMM;;p_h, p_w = patch_size
362::COMM;;if p_h > i_h:
363::COMM;;raise ValueError(
364::COMM;;"Height of the patch should be less than the height of the image."
365::COMM;;)
366::COMM;;if p_w > i_w:
367::COMM;;raise ValueError(
368::COMM;;"Width of the patch should be less than the width of the image."
369::COMM;;)
370::COMM;;image = check_array(image, allow_nd=True)
371::COMM;;image = image.reshape((i_h, i_w, -1))
372::COMM;;n_colors = image.shape[-1]
373::COMM;;extracted_patches = _extract_patches(
374::COMM;;image, patch_shape=(p_h, p_w, n_colors), extraction_step=1
375::COMM;;)
376::COMM;;n_patches = _compute_n_patches(i_h, i_w, p_h, p_w, max_patches)
377::COMM;;if max_patches:
378::COMM;;rng = check_random_state(random_state)
379::COMM;;i_s = rng.randint(i_h - p_h + 1, size=n_patches)
380::COMM;;j_s = rng.randint(i_w - p_w + 1, size=n_patches)
381::COMM;;patches = extracted_patches[i_s, j_s, 0]
382::COMM;;else:
383::COMM;;patches = extracted_patches
384::COMM;;patches = patches.reshape(-1, p_h, p_w, n_colors)
385::COMM;;# remove the color dimension if useless
386::COMM;;if patches.shape[-1] == 1:
387::COMM;;return patches.reshape((n_patches, p_h, p_w))
388::COMM;;else:
389::COMM;;return patches
390::COMM;;@validate_params(
391::COMM;;{"patches": [np.ndarray], "image_size": [tuple, Hidden(list)]},
392::COMM;;prefer_skip_nested_validation=True,
393::COMM;;)
394::COMM;;def reconstruct_from_patches_2d(patches, image_size):
431::COMM;;i_h, i_w = image_size[:2]
432::COMM;;p_h, p_w = patches.shape[1:3]
433::COMM;;img = np.zeros(image_size)
434::COMM;;# compute the dimensions of the patches array
435::COMM;;n_h = i_h - p_h + 1
436::COMM;;n_w = i_w - p_w + 1
437::COMM;;for p, (i, j) in zip(patches, product(range(n_h), range(n_w))):
438::COMM;;img[i : i + p_h, j : j + p_w] += p
439::COMM;;for i in range(i_h):
440::COMM;;for j in range(i_w):
441::COMM;;# divide by the amount of overlap
442::COMM;;# XXX: is this the most efficient way? memory-wise yes, cpu wise?
443::COMM;;img[i, j] /= float(min(i + 1, p_h, i_h - i) * min(j + 1, p_w, i_w - j))
444::COMM;;return img

67::COMM;;doc,
68::COMM;;analyzer=None,
69::COMM;;tokenizer=None,
70::COMM;;ngrams=None,
71::COMM;;preprocessor=None,
72::COMM;;decoder=None,

74::COMM;;):
92::COMM;;if decoder is not None:

98::COMM;;doc = preprocessor(doc)

100::COMM;;doc = tokenizer(doc)

104::COMM;;else:

107::COMM;;def strip_accents_unicode(s):
125::COMM;;try:
126::COMM;;# If `s` is ASCII-compatible, then it does not contain any accented
127::COMM;;# characters and we can avoid an expensive list comprehension
128::COMM;;s.encode("ASCII", errors="strict")
129::COMM;;return s
130::COMM;;except UnicodeEncodeError:
131::COMM;;normalized = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", s)
132::COMM;;return "".join([c for c in normalized if not unicodedata.combining(c)])
133::COMM;;def strip_accents_ascii(s):
149::COMM;;nkfd_form = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", s)

428::COMM;;def _validate_ngram_range(self):
479::COMM;;It turns a collection of text documents into a scipy.sparse matrix holding
480::COMM;;token occurrence counts (or binary occurrence information), possibly
481::COMM;;normalized as token frequencies if norm='l1' or projected on the euclidean
482::COMM;;unit sphere if norm='l2'.
483::COMM;;This text vectorizer implementation uses the hashing trick to find the
484::COMM;;token string name to feature integer index mapping.
485::COMM;;This strategy has several advantages:
486::COMM;;- it is very low memory scalable to large datasets as there is no need to
487::COMM;;store a vocabulary dictionary in memory.
488::COMM;;- it is fast to pickle and un-pickle as it holds no state besides the
489::COMM;;constructor parameters.
490::COMM;;- it can be used in a streaming (partial fit) or parallel pipeline as there
491::COMM;;is no state computed during fit.
492::COMM;;There are also a couple of cons (vs using a CountVectorizer with an
493::COMM;;in-memory vocabulary):
494::COMM;;- there is no way to compute the inverse transform (from feature indices to
495::COMM;;string feature names) which can be a problem when trying to introspect
496::COMM;;which features are most important to a model.
497::COMM;;- there can be collisions: distinct tokens can be mapped to the same
498::COMM;;feature index. However in practice this is rarely an issue if n_features
499::COMM;;is large enough (e.g. 2 ** 18 for text classification problems).
500::COMM;;- no IDF weighting as this would render the transformer stateful.
501::COMM;;The hash function employed is the signed 32-bit version of Murmurhash3.
502::COMM;;For an efficiency comparison of the different feature extractors, see
503::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_hashing_vs_dict_vectorizer.py`.
504::COMM;;For an example of document clustering and comparison with
505::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer`, see
506::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_text_plot_document_clustering.py`.
507::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <text_feature_extraction>`.
508::COMM;;Parameters
509::COMM;;----------
510::COMM;;input : {'filename', 'file', 'content'}, default='content'
511::COMM;;- If `'filename'`, the sequence passed as an argument to fit is
512::COMM;;expected to be a list of filenames that need reading to fetch
513::COMM;;the raw content to analyze.
514::COMM;;- If `'file'`, the sequence items must have a 'read' method (file-like
515::COMM;;object) that is called to fetch the bytes in memory.
516::COMM;;- If `'content'`, the input is expected to be a sequence of items that
517::COMM;;can be of type string or byte.
518::COMM;;encoding : str, default='utf-8'
519::COMM;;If bytes or files are given to analyze, this encoding is used to
520::COMM;;decode.
521::COMM;;decode_error : {'strict', 'ignore', 'replace'}, default='strict'
522::COMM;;Instruction on what to do if a byte sequence is given to analyze that
523::COMM;;contains characters not of the given `encoding`. By default, it is
524::COMM;;'strict', meaning that a UnicodeDecodeError will be raised. Other
525::COMM;;values are 'ignore' and 'replace'.
526::COMM;;strip_accents : {'ascii', 'unicode'} or callable, default=None
527::COMM;;Remove accents and perform other character normalization
528::COMM;;during the preprocessing step.
529::COMM;;'ascii' is a fast method that only works on characters that have
530::COMM;;a direct ASCII mapping.
531::COMM;;'unicode' is a slightly slower method that works on any character.
532::COMM;;None (default) means no character normalization is performed.
533::COMM;;Both 'ascii' and 'unicode' use NFKD normalization from
534::COMM;;:func:`unicodedata.normalize`.
535::COMM;;lowercase : bool, default=True
536::COMM;;Convert all characters to lowercase before tokenizing.
537::COMM;;preprocessor : callable, default=None
538::COMM;;Override the preprocessing (string transformation) stage while
539::COMM;;preserving the tokenizing and n-grams generation steps.
540::COMM;;Only applies if ``analyzer`` is not callable.
541::COMM;;tokenizer : callable, default=None
542::COMM;;Override the string tokenization step while preserving the
543::COMM;;preprocessing and n-grams generation steps.
544::COMM;;Only applies if ``analyzer == 'word'``.
545::COMM;;stop_words : {'english'}, list, default=None
546::COMM;;If 'english', a built-in stop word list for English is used.
547::COMM;;There are several known issues with 'english' and you should
548::COMM;;consider an alternative (see :ref:`stop_words`).
549::COMM;;If a list, that list is assumed to contain stop words, all of which
550::COMM;;will be removed from the resulting tokens.
551::COMM;;Only applies if ``analyzer == 'word'``.
552::COMM;;token_pattern : str or None, default=r"(?u)\\b\\w\\w+\\b"
553::COMM;;Regular expression denoting what constitutes a "token", only used
554::COMM;;if ``analyzer == 'word'``. The default regexp selects tokens of 2
555::COMM;;or more alphanumeric characters (punctuation is completely ignored
556::COMM;;and always treated as a token separator).
557::COMM;;If there is a capturing group in token_pattern then the
558::COMM;;captured group content, not the entire match, becomes the token.
559::COMM;;At most one capturing group is permitted.
560::COMM;;ngram_range : tuple (min_n, max_n), default=(1, 1)
561::COMM;;The lower and upper boundary of the range of n-values for different
562::COMM;;n-grams to be extracted. All values of n such that min_n <= n <= max_n
563::COMM;;will be used. For example an ``ngram_range`` of ``(1, 1)`` means only
564::COMM;;unigrams, ``(1, 2)`` means unigrams and bigrams, and ``(2, 2)`` means
565::COMM;;only bigrams.
566::COMM;;Only applies if ``analyzer`` is not callable.
567::COMM;;analyzer : {'word', 'char', 'char_wb'} or callable, default='word'
568::COMM;;Whether the feature should be made of word or character n-grams.
569::COMM;;Option 'char_wb' creates character n-grams only from text inside
570::COMM;;word boundaries; n-grams at the edges of words are padded with space.
571::COMM;;If a callable is passed it is used to extract the sequence of features
572::COMM;;out of the raw, unprocessed input.
573::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.21
574::COMM;;Since v0.21, if ``input`` is ``'filename'`` or ``'file'``, the data
575::COMM;;is first read from the file and then passed to the given callable
576::COMM;;analyzer.
577::COMM;;n_features : int, default=(2 ** 20)
578::COMM;;The number of features (columns) in the output matrices. Small numbers
579::COMM;;of features are likely to cause hash collisions, but large numbers
580::COMM;;will cause larger coefficient dimensions in linear learners.
581::COMM;;binary : bool, default=False
582::COMM;;If True, all non zero counts are set to 1. This is useful for discrete
583::COMM;;probabilistic models that model binary events rather than integer
584::COMM;;counts.
585::COMM;;norm : {'l1', 'l2'}, default='l2'
586::COMM;;Norm used to normalize term vectors. None for no normalization.
587::COMM;;alternate_sign : bool, default=True
588::COMM;;When True, an alternating sign is added to the features as to
589::COMM;;approximately conserve the inner product in the hashed space even for
590::COMM;;small n_features. This approach is similar to sparse random projection.
591::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
592::COMM;;dtype : type, default=np.float64
593::COMM;;Type of the matrix returned by fit_transform() or transform().
594::COMM;;See Also
595::COMM;;--------
596::COMM;;CountVectorizer : Convert a collection of text documents to a matrix of
597::COMM;;token counts.
598::COMM;;TfidfVectorizer : Convert a collection of raw documents to a matrix of
599::COMM;;TF-IDF features.
600::COMM;;Notes
601::COMM;;-----
602::COMM;;This estimator is :term:`stateless` and does not need to be fitted.
603::COMM;;However, we recommend to call :meth:`fit_transform` instead of
604::COMM;;:meth:`transform`, as parameter validation is only performed in

1023::COMM;;dfs = _document_frequency(X)
1024::COMM;;mask = np.ones(len(dfs), dtype=bool)
1025::COMM;;if high is not None:

1036::COMM;;for term, old_index in list(vocabulary.items()):

188::COMM;;Number of neighbors to use for MI estimation for continuous variables,
189::COMM;;see [1]_ and [2]_. Higher values reduce variance of the estimation, but
190::COMM;;could introduce a bias.
191::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
192::COMM;;Whether to make a copy of the given data. If set to False, the initial
193::COMM;;data will be overwritten.
194::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
195::COMM;;Determines random number generation for adding small noise to
196::COMM;;continuous variables in order to remove repeated values.
197::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
198::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
199::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
200::COMM;;The number of jobs to use for computing the mutual information.
201::COMM;;The parallelization is done on the columns of `X`.
202::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
203::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
204::COMM;;for more details.
205::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
206::COMM;;Returns
207::COMM;;-------
208::COMM;;mi : ndarray, shape (n_features,)
209::COMM;;Estimated mutual information between each feature and the target in
210::COMM;;nat units. A negative value will be replaced by 0.
211::COMM;;References
212::COMM;;----------
213::COMM;;.. [1] A. Kraskov, H. Stogbauer and P. Grassberger, "Estimating mutual
214::COMM;;information". Phys. Rev. E 69, 2004.
215::COMM;;.. [2] B. C. Ross "Mutual Information between Discrete and Continuous
216::COMM;;Data Sets". PLoS ONE 9(2), 2014.
244::COMO;;# Add small noise to continuous features as advised in Kraskov et. al.
286::COMM;;Mutual information (MI) [1]_ between two random variables is a non-negative
287::COMM;;value, which measures the dependency between the variables. It is equal
288::COMM;;to zero if and only if two random variables are independent, and higher
289::COMM;;values mean higher dependency.
290::COMM;;The function relies on nonparametric methods based on entropy estimation
291::COMM;;from k-nearest neighbors distances as described in [2]_ and [3]_. Both
292::COMM;;methods are based on the idea originally proposed in [4]_.
293::COMM;;It can be used for univariate features selection, read more in the
294::COMM;;:ref:`User Guide <univariate_feature_selection>`.
295::COMM;;Parameters
296::COMM;;----------
297::COMM;;X : array-like or sparse matrix, shape (n_samples, n_features)
298::COMM;;Feature matrix.
299::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
300::COMM;;Target vector.
301::COMM;;discrete_features : {'auto', bool, array-like}, default='auto'
302::COMM;;If bool, then determines whether to consider all features discrete
303::COMM;;or continuous. If array, then it should be either a boolean mask
304::COMM;;with shape (n_features,) or array with indices of discrete features.
305::COMM;;If 'auto', it is assigned to False for dense `X` and to True for
306::COMM;;sparse `X`.
307::COMM;;n_neighbors : int, default=3
308::COMM;;Number of neighbors to use for MI estimation for continuous variables,
309::COMM;;see [2]_ and [3]_. Higher values reduce variance of the estimation, but
310::COMM;;could introduce a bias.
311::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
312::COMM;;Whether to make a copy of the given data. If set to False, the initial
313::COMM;;data will be overwritten.
314::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
315::COMM;;Determines random number generation for adding small noise to
316::COMM;;continuous variables in order to remove repeated values.
317::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
318::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
319::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
320::COMM;;The number of jobs to use for computing the mutual information.
321::COMM;;The parallelization is done on the columns of `X`.
322::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
323::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
324::COMM;;for more details.
325::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
326::COMM;;Returns
327::COMM;;-------
328::COMM;;mi : ndarray, shape (n_features,)
329::COMM;;Estimated mutual information between each feature and the target in
330::COMM;;nat units.
331::COMM;;Notes
332::COMM;;-----
333::COMM;;1. The term "discrete features" is used instead of naming them
334::COMM;;"categorical", because it describes the essence more accurately.
335::COMM;;For example, pixel intensities of an image are discrete features
336::COMM;;(but hardly categorical) and you will get better results if mark them
337::COMM;;as such. Also note, that treating a continuous variable as discrete and
338::COMM;;vice versa will usually give incorrect results, so be attentive about
339::COMM;;that.
340::COMM;;2. True mutual information can't be negative. If its estimate turns out
341::COMM;;to be negative, it is replaced by zero.
342::COMM;;References
343::COMM;;----------
344::COMM;;.. [1] `Mutual Information
345::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_information>`_
346::COMM;;on Wikipedia.
347::COMM;;.. [2] A. Kraskov, H. Stogbauer and P. Grassberger, "Estimating mutual
348::COMM;;information". Phys. Rev. E 69, 2004.
349::COMM;;.. [3] B. C. Ross "Mutual Information between Discrete and Continuous
350::COMM;;Data Sets". PLoS ONE 9(2), 2014.
351::COMM;;.. [4] L. F. Kozachenko, N. N. Leonenko, "Sample Estimate of the Entropy
352::COMM;;of a Random Vector", Probl. Peredachi Inf., 23:2 (1987), 9-16
353::COMM;;Examples
354::COMM;;--------

229::COMM;;def _fit(self, X, y, step_score=None, **fit_params):
230::COMM;;# Parameter step_score controls the calculation of self.step_scores_
231::COMM;;# step_score is not exposed to users and is used when implementing RFECV
232::COMM;;# self.step_scores_ will not be calculated when calling _fit through fit
233::COMM;;X, y = validate_data(
234::COMM;;self,
235::COMM;;X,
236::COMM;;y,
237::COMM;;accept_sparse="csc",
238::COMM;;ensure_min_features=2,
239::COMM;;ensure_all_finite=False,
240::COMM;;multi_output=True,
241::COMM;;)
242::COMM;;# Initialization
243::COMM;;n_features = X.shape[1]
244::COMM;;if self.n_features_to_select is None:
245::COMM;;n_features_to_select = n_features // 2
246::COMM;;elif isinstance(self.n_features_to_select, Integral): # int
247::COMM;;n_features_to_select = self.n_features_to_select
248::COMM;;if n_features_to_select > n_features:
249::COMM;;warnings.warn(
250::COMM;;(
251::COMM;;f"Found {n_features_to_select=} > {n_features=}. There will be"
252::COMM;;" no feature selection and all features will be kept."
253::COMM;;),
254::COMM;;UserWarning,
255::COMM;;)
256::COMM;;else: # float
257::COMM;;n_features_to_select = int(n_features * self.n_features_to_select)
258::COMM;;if 0.0 < self.step < 1.0:
259::COMM;;step = int(max(1, self.step * n_features))
260::COMM;;else:
261::COMM;;step = int(self.step)
262::COMM;;support_ = np.ones(n_features, dtype=bool)
263::COMM;;ranking_ = np.ones(n_features, dtype=int)
264::COMM;;if step_score:
265::COMM;;self.step_n_features_ = []
266::COMM;;self.step_scores_ = []
267::COMM;;self.step_support_ = []
268::COMM;;self.step_ranking_ = []
269::COMM;;# Elimination
270::COMM;;while np.sum(support_) > n_features_to_select:
271::COMM;;# Remaining features
272::COMM;;features = np.arange(n_features)[support_]
273::COMM;;# Rank the remaining features
274::COMM;;estimator = clone(self.estimator)
275::COMM;;if self.verbose > 0:
276::COMM;;print("Fitting estimator with %d features." % np.sum(support_))
277::COMM;;estimator.fit(X[:, features], y, **fit_params)
278::COMM;;# Compute step values on the previous selection iteration because
279::COMM;;# 'estimator' must use features that have not been eliminated yet
280::COMM;;if step_score:
281::COMM;;self.step_n_features_.append(len(features))
282::COMM;;self.step_scores_.append(step_score(estimator, features))
283::COMM;;self.step_support_.append(list(support_))
284::COMM;;self.step_ranking_.append(list(ranking_))
285::COMM;;# Get importance and rank them
286::COMM;;importances = _get_feature_importances(
287::COMM;;estimator,
288::COMM;;self.importance_getter,
289::COMM;;transform_func="square",
290::COMM;;)
291::COMM;;ranks = np.argsort(importances)
292::COMM;;# for sparse case ranks is matrix
293::COMM;;ranks = np.ravel(ranks)
294::COMM;;# Eliminate the worse features
295::COMM;;threshold = min(step, np.sum(support_) - n_features_to_select)
296::COMM;;support_[features[ranks][:threshold]] = False
297::COMM;;ranking_[np.logical_not(support_)] += 1
298::COMM;;# Set final attributes
299::COMM;;features = np.arange(n_features)[support_]
300::COMM;;self.estimator_ = clone(self.estimator)
301::COMM;;self.estimator_.fit(X[:, features], y, **fit_params)
302::COMM;;# Compute step values when only n_features_to_select features left
303::COMM;;if step_score:
304::COMM;;self.step_n_features_.append(len(features))
305::COMM;;self.step_scores_.append(step_score(self.estimator_, features))
306::COMM;;self.step_support_.append(support_)
307::COMM;;self.step_ranking_.append(ranking_)
308::COMM;;self.n_features_ = support_.sum()
309::COMM;;self.support_ = support_
310::COMM;;self.ranking_ = ranking_
311::COMM;;return self

713::COMM;;)
714::COMM;;# Determine the number of subsets of features by fitting across
715::COMM;;# the train folds and choosing the "features_to_select" parameter
716::COMM;;# that gives the least averaged error across all folds.
717::COMM;;# Note that joblib raises a non-picklable error for bound methods
718::COMM;;# even if n_jobs is set to 1 with the default multiprocessing
719::COMM;;# backend.
720::COMM;;# This branching is done so that to
721::COMM;;# make sure that user code that sets n_jobs to 1
722::COMM;;# and provides bound methods as scorers is not broken with the
723::COMM;;# addition of n_jobs parameter in version 0.18.
724::COMM;;if effective_n_jobs(self.n_jobs) == 1:
725::COMM;;parallel, func = list, _rfe_single_fit
726::COMM;;else:
727::COMM;;parallel = Parallel(n_jobs=self.n_jobs)
728::COMM;;func = delayed(_rfe_single_fit)
729::COMM;;step_results = parallel(
730::COMM;;func(clone(rfe), self.estimator, X, y, train, test, scorer, routed_params)
731::COMM;;for train, test in cv.split(X, y, **routed_params.splitter.split)
732::COMM;;)
733::COMM;;scores, supports, rankings, step_n_features = zip(*step_results)
734::COMM;;step_n_features_rev = np.array(step_n_features[0])[::-1]
735::COMM;;scores = np.array(scores)
736::COMM;;rankings = np.array(rankings)
737::COMM;;supports = np.array(supports)
738::COMM;;# Reverse order such that lowest number of features is selected in case of tie.
739::COMM;;scores_sum_rev = np.sum(scores, axis=0)[::-1]
740::COMM;;n_features_to_select = step_n_features_rev[np.argmax(scores_sum_rev)]
741::COMM;;# Re-execute an elimination with best_k over the whole set
742::COMM;;rfe = RFE(
743::COMM;;estimator=self.estimator,
744::COMM;;n_features_to_select=n_features_to_select,
745::COMM;;step=self.step,
746::COMM;;importance_getter=self.importance_getter,
747::COMM;;verbose=self.verbose,
748::COMM;;)
749::COMM;;rfe.fit(X, y, **routed_params.estimator.fit)
750::COMM;;# Set final attributes
751::COMM;;self.support_ = rfe.support_
752::COMM;;self.n_features_ = rfe.n_features_
753::COMM;;self.ranking_ = rfe.ranking_
754::COMM;;self.estimator_ = clone(self.estimator)
755::COMM;;self.estimator_.fit(self._transform(X), y, **routed_params.estimator.fit)
756::COMM;;# reverse to stay consistent with before
757::COMM;;scores_rev = scores[:, ::-1]
758::COMM;;supports_rev = supports[:, ::-1]
759::COMM;;rankings_rev = rankings[:, ::-1]
760::COMM;;self.cv_results_ = {
761::COMM;;"mean_test_score": np.mean(scores_rev, axis=0),
762::COMM;;"std_test_score": np.std(scores_rev, axis=0),
763::COMM;;**{f"split{i}_test_score": scores_rev[i] for i in range(scores.shape[0])},
764::COMM;;**{f"split{i}_ranking": rankings_rev[i] for i in range(rankings.shape[0])},
765::COMM;;**{f"split{i}_support": supports_rev[i] for i in range(supports.shape[0])},
766::COMM;;"n_features": step_n_features_rev,
767::COMM;;}
768::COMM;;return self
769::COMM;;def score(self, X, y, **score_params):
790::COMM;;_raise_for_params(score_params, self, "score")
791::COMM;;scoring = self._get_scorer()
792::COMM;;if _routing_enabled():
793::COMM;;routed_params = process_routing(self, "score", **score_params)
794::COMM;;else:
795::COMM;;routed_params = Bunch()
796::COMM;;routed_params.scorer = Bunch(score={})
797::COMM;;return scoring(self, X, y, **routed_params.scorer.score)
798::COMM;;def get_metadata_routing(self):

816::COMM;;method_mapping=MethodMapping().add(

819::COMM;;),

2::COMM;;Sequential feature selection
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
30::COMM;;This Sequential Feature Selector adds (forward selection) or
31::COMM;;removes (backward selection) features to form a feature subset in a
32::COMM;;greedy fashion. At each stage, this estimator chooses the best feature to
33::COMM;;add or remove based on the cross-validation score of an estimator. In
34::COMM;;the case of unsupervised learning, this Sequential Feature Selector
35::COMM;;looks only at the features (X), not the desired outputs (y).
36::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <sequential_feature_selection>`.
37::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
38::COMM;;Parameters
39::COMM;;----------
40::COMM;;estimator : estimator instance
41::COMM;;An unfitted estimator.
42::COMM;;n_features_to_select : "auto", int or float, default="auto"
43::COMM;;If `"auto"`, the behaviour depends on the `tol` parameter:
44::COMM;;- if `tol` is not `None`, then features are selected while the score
45::COMM;;change does not exceed `tol`.
46::COMM;;- otherwise, half of the features are selected.
47::COMM;;If integer, the parameter is the absolute number of features to select.
48::COMM;;If float between 0 and 1, it is the fraction of features to select.
49::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
50::COMM;;The option `"auto"` was added in version 1.1.
51::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.3
52::COMM;;The default changed from `"warn"` to `"auto"` in 1.3.
53::COMM;;tol : float, default=None
54::COMM;;If the score is not incremented by at least `tol` between two
55::COMM;;consecutive feature additions or removals, stop adding or removing.
56::COMM;;`tol` can be negative when removing features using `direction="backward"`.
57::COMM;;`tol` is required to be strictly positive when doing forward selection.
58::COMM;;It can be useful to reduce the number of features at the cost of a small
59::COMM;;decrease in the score.
60::COMM;;`tol` is enabled only when `n_features_to_select` is `"auto"`.
61::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
62::COMM;;direction : {'forward', 'backward'}, default='forward'
63::COMM;;Whether to perform forward selection or backward selection.
64::COMM;;scoring : str or callable, default=None
65::COMM;;Scoring method to use for cross-validation. Options:
66::COMM;;- str: see :ref:`scoring_string_names` for options.
67::COMM;;- callable: a scorer callable object (e.g., function) with signature
68::COMM;;``scorer(estimator, X, y)`` that returns a single value.
69::COMM;;See :ref:`scoring_callable` for details.
70::COMM;;- `None`: the `estimator`'s
71::COMM;;:ref:`default evaluation criterion <scoring_api_overview>` is used.
72::COMM;;cv : int, cross-validation generator or an iterable, default=None
73::COMM;;Determines the cross-validation splitting strategy.
74::COMM;;Possible inputs for cv are:
75::COMM;;- None, to use the default 5-fold cross validation,
76::COMM;;- integer, to specify the number of folds in a `(Stratified)KFold`,
77::COMM;;- :term:`CV splitter`,
78::COMM;;- An iterable yielding (train, test) splits as arrays of indices.
79::COMM;;For integer/None inputs, if the estimator is a classifier and ``y`` is
80::COMM;;either binary or multiclass,
81::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.StratifiedKFold` is used. In all other
82::COMM;;cases, :class:`~sklearn.model_selection.KFold` is used. These splitters
83::COMM;;are instantiated with `shuffle=False` so the splits will be the same
84::COMM;;across calls.
85::COMM;;Refer :ref:`User Guide <cross_validation>` for the various
86::COMM;;cross-validation strategies that can be used here.
87::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
88::COMM;;Number of jobs to run in parallel. When evaluating a new feature to
89::COMM;;add or remove, the cross-validation procedure is parallel over the
90::COMM;;folds.
91::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
92::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
93::COMM;;for more details.
94::COMM;;Attributes
95::COMM;;----------
96::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
97::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
98::COMM;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
99::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
100::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
101::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
102::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
103::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
104::COMM;;n_features_to_select_ : int
105::COMM;;The number of features that were selected.
106::COMM;;support_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,), dtype=bool
107::COMM;;The mask of selected features.
108::COMM;;See Also
109::COMM;;--------
110::COMM;;GenericUnivariateSelect : Univariate feature selector with configurable
111::COMM;;strategy.
112::COMM;;RFE : Recursive feature elimination based on importance weights.
113::COMM;;RFECV : Recursive feature elimination based on importance weights, with
114::COMM;;automatic selection of the number of features.
115::COMM;;SelectFromModel : Feature selection based on thresholds of importance
116::COMM;;weights.
117::COMM;;Examples
118::COMM;;--------
119::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import SequentialFeatureSelector
120::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
121::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
122::COMM;;>>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
123::COMM;;>>> knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)
124::COMM;;>>> sfs = SequentialFeatureSelector(knn, n_features_to_select=3)
125::COMM;;>>> sfs.fit(X, y)
126::COMM;;SequentialFeatureSelector(estimator=KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3),
127::COMM;;n_features_to_select=3)
128::COMM;;>>> sfs.get_support()
129::COMM;;array([ True, False, True, True])
130::COMM;;>>> sfs.transform(X).shape
131::COMM;;(150, 3)
165::COMO;;# SequentialFeatureSelector.estimator is not validated yet
170::COMM;;Parameters
171::COMM;;----------
172::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
173::COMM;;Training vectors, where `n_samples` is the number of samples and
174::COMM;;`n_features` is the number of predictors.
175::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
176::COMM;;Target values. This parameter may be ignored for
177::COMM;;unsupervised learning.
178::COMM;;**params : dict, default=None
179::COMM;;Parameters to be passed to the underlying `estimator`, `cv`
180::COMM;;and `scorer` objects.
181::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
182::COMM;;Only available if `enable_metadata_routing=True`,
183::COMM;;which can be set by using
184::COMM;;``sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)``.
185::COMM;;See :ref:`Metadata Routing User Guide <metadata_routing>` for
186::COMM;;more details.

204::COMO;;# With auto feature selection, `n_features_to_select_` will be updated

222::COMO;;# - that we have already *selected* if we do forward selection

254::COMO;;# Feature will be added if the current score and past score are greater
255::COMO;;# than tol when n_feature is auto,

27::COMM;;# Scoring functions
28::COMM;;# The following function is a rewriting of scipy.stats.f_oneway
29::COMM;;# Contrary to the scipy.stats.f_oneway implementation it does not
30::COMM;;# copy the data while keeping the inputs unchanged.
31::COMM;;def f_oneway(*args):
69::COMM;;n_classes = len(args)
70::COMM;;args = [as_float_array(a) for a in args]
71::COMM;;n_samples_per_class = np.array([a.shape[0] for a in args])
72::COMM;;n_samples = np.sum(n_samples_per_class)
73::COMM;;ss_alldata = sum(safe_sqr(a).sum(axis=0) for a in args)
74::COMM;;sums_args = [np.asarray(a.sum(axis=0)) for a in args]
75::COMM;;square_of_sums_alldata = sum(sums_args) ** 2
76::COMM;;square_of_sums_args = [s**2 for s in sums_args]
77::COMM;;sstot = ss_alldata - square_of_sums_alldata / float(n_samples)
78::COMM;;ssbn = 0.0
79::COMM;;for k, _ in enumerate(args):
80::COMM;;ssbn += square_of_sums_args[k] / n_samples_per_class[k]
81::COMM;;ssbn -= square_of_sums_alldata / float(n_samples)
82::COMM;;sswn = sstot - ssbn
83::COMM;;dfbn = n_classes - 1
84::COMM;;dfwn = n_samples - n_classes
85::COMM;;msb = ssbn / float(dfbn)
86::COMM;;msw = sswn / float(dfwn)
87::COMM;;constant_features_idx = np.where(msw == 0.0)[0]
88::COMM;;if np.nonzero(msb)[0].size != msb.size and constant_features_idx.size:
89::COMM;;warnings.warn("Features %s are constant." % constant_features_idx, UserWarning)
90::COMM;;f = msb / msw
91::COMM;;# flatten matrix to vector in sparse case
92::COMM;;f = np.asarray(f).ravel()
93::COMM;;prob = special.fdtrc(dfbn, dfwn, f)
94::COMM;;return f, prob
95::COMM;;@validate_params(
96::COMM;;{
97::COMM;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
98::COMM;;"y": ["array-like"],
99::COMM;;},

101::COMM;;)
102::COMM;;def f_classif(X, y):
139::COMM;;X, y = check_X_y(X, y, accept_sparse=["csr", "csc", "coo"])
140::COMM;;args = [X[safe_mask(X, y == k)] for k in np.unique(y)]
141::COMM;;return f_oneway(*args)
142::COMM;;def _chisquare(f_obs, f_exp):
147::COMM;;f_obs = np.asarray(f_obs, dtype=np.float64)
148::COMM;;k = len(f_obs)
149::COMM;;# Reuse f_obs for chi-squared statistics
150::COMM;;chisq = f_obs
151::COMM;;chisq -= f_exp
152::COMM;;chisq **= 2
153::COMM;;with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):
154::COMM;;chisq /= f_exp
155::COMM;;chisq = chisq.sum(axis=0)
156::COMM;;return chisq, special.chdtrc(k - 1, chisq)
157::COMM;;@validate_params(
158::COMM;;{
159::COMM;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
160::COMM;;"y": ["array-like"],
161::COMM;;},

163::COMM;;)
164::COMM;;def chi2(X, y):
213::COMM;;# XXX: we might want to do some of the following in logspace instead for
214::COMM;;# numerical stability.
215::COMM;;# Converting X to float allows getting better performance for the
216::COMM;;# safe_sparse_dot call made below.
217::COMM;;X = check_array(X, accept_sparse="csr", dtype=(np.float64, np.float32))
218::COMM;;if np.any((X.data if issparse(X) else X) < 0):
219::COMM;;raise ValueError("Input X must be non-negative.")
220::COMM;;# Use a sparse representation for Y by default to reduce memory usage when
221::COMM;;# y has many unique classes.
222::COMM;;Y = LabelBinarizer(sparse_output=True).fit_transform(y)
223::COMM;;if Y.shape[1] == 1:
224::COMM;;Y = Y.toarray()
225::COMM;;Y = np.append(1 - Y, Y, axis=1)
226::COMM;;observed = safe_sparse_dot(Y.T, X) # n_classes * n_features
227::COMM;;if issparse(observed):
228::COMM;;# convert back to a dense array before calling _chisquare
229::COMM;;# XXX: could _chisquare be reimplement to accept sparse matrices for
230::COMM;;# cases where both n_classes and n_features are large (and X is
231::COMM;;# sparse)?
232::COMM;;observed = observed.toarray()
233::COMM;;feature_count = X.sum(axis=0).reshape(1, -1)
234::COMM;;class_prob = Y.mean(axis=0).reshape(1, -1)
235::COMM;;expected = np.dot(class_prob.T, feature_count)
236::COMM;;return _chisquare(observed, expected)
237::COMM;;@validate_params(
238::COMM;;{
239::COMM;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
240::COMM;;"y": ["array-like"],
241::COMM;;"center": ["boolean"],
242::COMM;;"force_finite": ["boolean"],
243::COMM;;},
244::COMM;;prefer_skip_nested_validation=True,
245::COMM;;)
246::COMM;;def r_regression(X, y, *, center=True, force_finite=True):
295::COMM;;X, y = check_X_y(X, y, accept_sparse=["csr", "csc", "coo"], dtype=np.float64)
296::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
297::COMM;;# Compute centered values
298::COMM;;# Note that E[(x - mean(x))*(y - mean(y))] = E[x*(y - mean(y))], so we
299::COMM;;# need not center X
300::COMM;;if center:
301::COMM;;y = y - np.mean(y)
302::COMM;;# TODO: for Scipy <= 1.10, `isspmatrix(X)` returns `True` for sparse arrays.
303::COMM;;# Here, we check the output of the `.mean` operation that returns a `np.matrix`
304::COMM;;# for sparse matrices while a `np.array` for dense and sparse arrays.
305::COMM;;# We can reconsider using `isspmatrix` when the minimum version is
306::COMM;;# SciPy >= 1.11
307::COMM;;X_means = X.mean(axis=0)
308::COMM;;X_means = X_means.getA1() if isinstance(X_means, np.matrix) else X_means
309::COMM;;# Compute the scaled standard deviations via moments
310::COMM;;X_norms = np.sqrt(row_norms(X.T, squared=True) - n_samples * X_means**2)
311::COMM;;else:
312::COMM;;X_norms = row_norms(X.T)
313::COMM;;correlation_coefficient = safe_sparse_dot(y, X)
314::COMM;;with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
315::COMM;;correlation_coefficient /= X_norms
316::COMM;;correlation_coefficient /= np.linalg.norm(y)
317::COMM;;if force_finite and not np.isfinite(correlation_coefficient).all():
318::COMM;;# case where the target or some features are constant
319::COMM;;# the correlation coefficient(s) is/are set to the minimum (i.e. 0.0)
320::COMM;;nan_mask = np.isnan(correlation_coefficient)
321::COMM;;correlation_coefficient[nan_mask] = 0.0
322::COMM;;return correlation_coefficient
323::COMM;;@validate_params(
324::COMM;;{
325::COMM;;"X": ["array-like", "sparse matrix"],
326::COMM;;"y": ["array-like"],
327::COMM;;"center": ["boolean"],
328::COMM;;"force_finite": ["boolean"],
329::COMM;;},
330::COMM;;prefer_skip_nested_validation=True,
331::COMM;;)
332::COMM;;def f_regression(X, y, *, center=True, force_finite=True):
406::COMM;;correlation_coefficient = r_regression(
407::COMM;;X, y, center=center, force_finite=force_finite
408::COMM;;)
409::COMM;;deg_of_freedom = y.size - (2 if center else 1)
410::COMM;;corr_coef_squared = correlation_coefficient**2
411::COMM;;with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
412::COMM;;f_statistic = corr_coef_squared / (1 - corr_coef_squared) * deg_of_freedom
413::COMM;;p_values = stats.f.sf(f_statistic, 1, deg_of_freedom)
414::COMM;;if force_finite and not np.isfinite(f_statistic).all():
415::COMM;;# case where there is a perfect (anti-)correlation
416::COMM;;# f-statistics can be set to the maximum and p-values to zero
417::COMM;;mask_inf = np.isinf(f_statistic)
418::COMM;;f_statistic[mask_inf] = np.finfo(f_statistic.dtype).max
419::COMM;;# case where the target or some features are constant
420::COMM;;# f-statistics would be minimum and thus p-values large
421::COMM;;mask_nan = np.isnan(f_statistic)
422::COMM;;f_statistic[mask_nan] = 0.0
423::COMM;;p_values[mask_nan] = 1.0
424::COMM;;return f_statistic, p_values

546::COMM;;return np.ones(len(self.scores_), dtype=bool)
547::COMM;;elif self.percentile == 0:
548::COMM;;return np.zeros(len(self.scores_), dtype=bool)
549::COMM;;scores = _clean_nans(self.scores_)
550::COMM;;threshold = np.percentile(scores, 100 - self.percentile)
551::COMM;;mask = scores > threshold
552::COMM;;ties = np.where(scores == threshold)[0]
553::COMM;;if len(ties):
554::COMM;;max_feats = int(len(scores) * self.percentile / 100)
555::COMM;;kept_ties = ties[: max_feats - mask.sum()]
556::COMM;;mask[kept_ties] = True
557::COMM;;return mask
558::COMM;;def __sklearn_tags__(self):
559::COMM;;tags = super().__sklearn_tags__()
560::COMM;;tags.target_tags.required = False
561::COMM;;return tags

650::COMM;;class SelectFpr(_BaseFilter):

712::COMM;;class SelectFdr(_BaseFilter):
767::COMM;;_parameter_constraints: dict = {
768::COMM;;**_BaseFilter._parameter_constraints,
769::COMM;;"alpha": [Interval(Real, 0, 1, closed="both")],
770::COMM;;}
771::COMM;;def __init__(self, score_func=f_classif, *, alpha=5e-2):
772::COMM;;super().__init__(score_func=score_func)
773::COMM;;self.alpha = alpha
774::COMM;;def _get_support_mask(self):
775::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
776::COMM;;n_features = len(self.pvalues_)
777::COMM;;sv = np.sort(self.pvalues_)
778::COMM;;selected = sv[
779::COMM;;sv <= float(self.alpha) / n_features * np.arange(1, n_features + 1)
780::COMM;;]
781::COMM;;if selected.size == 0:

783::COMM;;return self.pvalues_ <= selected.max()

1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
12::COMM;;This feature selection algorithm looks only at the features (X), not the
13::COMM;;desired outputs (y), and can thus be used for unsupervised learning.
14::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <variance_threshold>`.
15::COMM;;Parameters
16::COMM;;----------
17::COMM;;threshold : float, default=0
18::COMM;;Features with a training-set variance lower than this threshold will
19::COMM;;be removed. The default is to keep all features with non-zero variance,
20::COMM;;i.e. remove the features that have the same value in all samples.
21::COMM;;Attributes
22::COMM;;----------
23::COMM;;variances_ : array, shape (n_features,)
24::COMM;;Variances of individual features.
25::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
26::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
27::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
28::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
29::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
30::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
31::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
32::COMM;;See Also
33::COMM;;--------
34::COMM;;SelectFromModel: Meta-transformer for selecting features based on
35::COMM;;importance weights.
36::COMM;;SelectPercentile : Select features according to a percentile of the highest
37::COMM;;scores.
38::COMM;;SequentialFeatureSelector : Transformer that performs Sequential Feature
39::COMM;;Selection.
40::COMM;;Notes
41::COMM;;-----
42::COMM;;Allows NaN in the input.
43::COMM;;Raises ValueError if no feature in X meets the variance threshold.
44::COMM;;Examples
45::COMM;;--------
46::COMM;;The following dataset has integer features, two of which are the same
47::COMM;;in every sample. These are removed with the default setting for threshold::
48::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.feature_selection import VarianceThreshold
49::COMM;;>>> X = [[0, 2, 0, 3], [0, 1, 4, 3], [0, 1, 1, 3]]
50::COMM;;>>> selector = VarianceThreshold()
51::COMM;;>>> selector.fit_transform(X)
52::COMM;;array([[2, 0],
53::COMM;;[1, 4],
54::COMM;;[1, 1]])
64::COMM;;Parameters
65::COMM;;----------
66::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix}, shape (n_samples, n_features)
67::COMM;;Data from which to compute variances, where `n_samples` is
68::COMM;;the number of samples and `n_features` is the number of features.
69::COMM;;y : any, default=None
70::COMM;;Ignored. This parameter exists only for compatibility with
71::COMM;;sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.
72::COMM;;Returns
73::COMM;;-------
74::COMM;;self : object
75::COMM;;Returns the instance itself.
84::COMC;;if hasattr(X, "toarray"): # sparse matrix

13::COMO;;# In discrete case computations are straightforward and can be done

22::COMO;;# For two continuous variables a good approach is to test on bivariate
23::COMO;;# normal distribution, where mutual information is known.
24::COMO;;# Mean of the distribution, irrelevant for mutual information.
26::COMO;;# Setup covariance matrix with correlation coeff. equal 0.5.
36::COMO;;# True theoretical mutual information.
41::COMO;;# Theory and computed values won't be very close
42::COMO;;# We here check with a large relative tolerance
49::COMO;;# To test define a joint distribution as follows:
50::COMO;;# p(x, y) = p(x) p(y | x)
51::COMO;;# X ~ Bernoulli(p)
52::COMO;;# (Y | x = 0) ~ Uniform(-1, 1)
53::COMO;;# (Y | x = 1) ~ Uniform(0, 2)
54::COMO;;# Use the following formula for mutual information:
55::COMO;;# I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y | X)
56::COMO;;# Two entropies can be computed by hand:
57::COMO;;# H(Y) = -(1-p)/2 * ln((1-p)/2) - p/2*log(p/2) - 1/2*log(1/2)
58::COMO;;# H(Y | X) = ln(2)
59::COMO;;# Now we need to implement sampling from out distribution, which is
60::COMO;;# done easily using conditional distribution logic.
72::COMO;;# Assert the same tolerance.
79::COMO;;# Test that adding unique label doesn't change MI.
91::COMO;;# We are going test that feature ordering by MI matches our expectations.
97::COMO;;# Here X[:, 0] is the most informative feature, and X[:, 1] is weakly
98::COMO;;# informative.
102::COMO;;# We generate sample from multivariate normal distribution, using
103::COMO;;# transformation from initially uncorrelated variables. The zero
104::COMO;;# variables after transformation is selected as the target vector,
105::COMO;;# it has the strongest correlation with the variable 2, and
106::COMO;;# the weakest correlation with the variable 1.

117::COMO;;# up-casting float32 inputs to float64?

11::COMM;;Used together with `available_if`.
14::COMO;;# raise original `AttributeError` if `attr` does not exist
20::COMM;;This meta-estimator takes an estimator and freezes it, in the sense that calling
21::COMM;;`fit` on it has no effect. `fit_predict` and `fit_transform` are also disabled.
22::COMM;;All other methods are delegated to the original estimator and original estimator's
23::COMM;;attributes are accessible as well.
24::COMM;;This is particularly useful when you have a fitted or a pre-trained model as a
25::COMM;;transformer in a pipeline, and you'd like `pipeline.fit` to have no effect on this
26::COMM;;step.
27::COMM;;Parameters
28::COMM;;----------
29::COMM;;estimator : estimator
30::COMM;;The estimator which is to be kept frozen.
31::COMM;;See Also
32::COMM;;--------
33::COMM;;None: No similar entry in the scikit-learn documentation.
34::COMM;;Examples
35::COMM;;--------
36::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
37::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.frozen import FrozenEstimator
38::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
39::COMM;;>>> X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
40::COMM;;>>> clf = LogisticRegression(random_state=0).fit(X, y)
41::COMM;;>>> frozen_clf = FrozenEstimator(clf)
42::COMM;;>>> frozen_clf.fit(X, y) # No-op
43::COMM;;FrozenEstimator(estimator=LogisticRegression(random_state=0))
44::COMM;;>>> frozen_clf.predict(X) # Predictions from `clf.predict`
45::COMM;;array(...)
52::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.compose.ColumnTransformer`.

151::COMM;;if self.kernel is None: # Use an RBF kernel as default
152::COMM;;self.kernel_ = C(1.0, constant_value_bounds="fixed") * RBF(
153::COMM;;1.0, length_scale_bounds="fixed"

157::COMM;;self.rng = check_random_state(self.random_state)

159::COMM;;# Encode class labels and check that it is a binary classification
160::COMM;;# problem
161::COMM;;label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
162::COMM;;self.y_train_ = label_encoder.fit_transform(y)
163::COMM;;self.classes_ = label_encoder.classes_
164::COMM;;if self.classes_.size > 2:
165::COMM;;raise ValueError(
166::COMM;;"%s supports only binary classification. y contains classes %s"
167::COMM;;% (self.__class__.__name__, self.classes_)
168::COMM;;)
169::COMM;;elif self.classes_.size == 1:
170::COMM;;raise ValueError(
171::COMM;;"{0:s} requires 2 classes; got {1:d} class".format(
172::COMM;;self.__class__.__name__, self.classes_.size
173::COMM;;)
174::COMM;;)
175::COMM;;if self.optimizer is not None and self.kernel_.n_dims > 0:
176::COMM;;# Choose hyperparameters based on maximizing the log-marginal
177::COMM;;# likelihood (potentially starting from several initial values)
178::COMM;;def obj_func(theta, eval_gradient=True):
179::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
180::COMM;;lml, grad = self.log_marginal_likelihood(
181::COMM;;theta, eval_gradient=True, clone_kernel=False
182::COMM;;)
183::COMM;;return -lml, -grad
184::COMM;;else:
185::COMM;;return -self.log_marginal_likelihood(theta, clone_kernel=False)
186::COMM;;# First optimize starting from theta specified in kernel
187::COMM;;optima = [
188::COMM;;self._constrained_optimization(
189::COMM;;obj_func, self.kernel_.theta, self.kernel_.bounds
190::COMM;;)
191::COMM;;]
192::COMM;;# Additional runs are performed from log-uniform chosen initial
193::COMM;;# theta
194::COMM;;if self.n_restarts_optimizer > 0:
195::COMM;;if not np.isfinite(self.kernel_.bounds).all():
196::COMM;;raise ValueError(
197::COMM;;"Multiple optimizer restarts (n_restarts_optimizer>0) "
198::COMM;;"requires that all bounds are finite."
199::COMM;;)
200::COMM;;bounds = self.kernel_.bounds
201::COMM;;for iteration in range(self.n_restarts_optimizer):
202::COMM;;theta_initial = np.exp(self.rng.uniform(bounds[:, 0], bounds[:, 1]))
203::COMM;;optima.append(
204::COMM;;self._constrained_optimization(obj_func, theta_initial, bounds)
205::COMM;;)
206::COMM;;# Select result from run with minimal (negative) log-marginal
207::COMM;;# likelihood
208::COMM;;lml_values = list(map(itemgetter(1), optima))
209::COMM;;self.kernel_.theta = optima[np.argmin(lml_values)][0]
210::COMM;;self.kernel_._check_bounds_params()
211::COMM;;self.log_marginal_likelihood_value_ = -np.min(lml_values)
212::COMM;;else:

214::COMM;;self.kernel_.theta

217::COMM;;# of actual query points

223::COMM;;def predict(self, X):
234::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
235::COMM;;# As discussed on Section 3.4.2 of GPML, for making hard binary
236::COMM;;# decisions, it is enough to compute the MAP of the posterior and
237::COMM;;# pass it through the link function
238::COMM;;K_star = self.kernel_(self.X_train_, X) # K_star =k(x_star)
239::COMM;;f_star = K_star.T.dot(self.y_train_ - self.pi_) # Algorithm 3.2,Line 4
240::COMM;;return np.where(f_star > 0, self.classes_[1], self.classes_[0])
241::COMM;;def predict_proba(self, X):
254::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
255::COMM;;# Compute the mean and variance of the latent function
256::COMM;;# (Lines 4-6 of Algorithm 3.2 of GPML)
257::COMM;;latent_mean, latent_var = self.latent_mean_and_variance(X)
258::COMM;;# Line 7:
259::COMM;;# Approximate \int log(z) * N(z | f_star, var_f_star)
260::COMM;;# Approximation is due to Williams & Barber, "Bayesian Classification
261::COMM;;# with Gaussian Processes", Appendix A: Approximate the logistic
262::COMM;;# sigmoid by a linear combination of 5 error functions.
263::COMM;;# For information on how this integral can be computed see
264::COMM;;# blitiri.blogspot.de/2012/11/gaussian-integral-of-error-function.html
265::COMM;;alpha = 1 / (2 * latent_var)
266::COMM;;gamma = LAMBDAS * latent_mean
267::COMM;;integrals = (
268::COMM;;np.sqrt(np.pi / alpha)
269::COMM;;* erf(gamma * np.sqrt(alpha / (alpha + LAMBDAS**2)))
270::COMM;;/ (2 * np.sqrt(latent_var * 2 * np.pi))
271::COMM;;)
272::COMM;;pi_star = (COEFS * integrals).sum(axis=0) + 0.5 * COEFS.sum()
273::COMM;;return np.vstack((1 - pi_star, pi_star)).T
274::COMM;;def log_marginal_likelihood(
275::COMM;;self, theta=None, eval_gradient=False, clone_kernel=True
276::COMM;;):
301::COMM;;if theta is None:
302::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
303::COMM;;raise ValueError("Gradient can only be evaluated for theta!=None")
304::COMM;;return self.log_marginal_likelihood_value_
305::COMM;;if clone_kernel:
306::COMM;;kernel = self.kernel_.clone_with_theta(theta)
307::COMM;;else:
308::COMM;;kernel = self.kernel_
309::COMM;;kernel.theta = theta
310::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
311::COMM;;K, K_gradient = kernel(self.X_train_, eval_gradient=True)
312::COMM;;else:
313::COMM;;K = kernel(self.X_train_)
314::COMM;;# Compute log-marginal-likelihood Z and also store some temporaries
315::COMM;;# which can be reused for computing Z's gradient
316::COMM;;Z, (pi, W_sr, L, b, a) = self._posterior_mode(K, return_temporaries=True)
317::COMM;;if not eval_gradient:
318::COMM;;return Z
319::COMM;;# Compute gradient based on Algorithm 5.1 of GPML
320::COMM;;d_Z = np.empty(theta.shape[0])
321::COMM;;# XXX: Get rid of the np.diag() in the next line
322::COMM;;R = W_sr[:, np.newaxis] * cho_solve((L, True), np.diag(W_sr)) # Line 7
323::COMM;;C = solve(L, W_sr[:, np.newaxis] * K) # Line 8
324::COMM;;# Line 9: (use einsum to compute np.diag(C.T.dot(C))))
325::COMM;;s_2 = (
326::COMM;;-0.5
327::COMM;;* (np.diag(K) - np.einsum("ij, ij -> j", C, C))
328::COMM;;* (pi * (1 - pi) * (1 - 2 * pi))
329::COMM;;) # third derivative
330::COMM;;for j in range(d_Z.shape[0]):
331::COMM;;C = K_gradient[:, :, j] # Line 11
332::COMM;;# Line 12: (R.T.ravel().dot(C.ravel()) = np.trace(R.dot(C)))
333::COMM;;s_1 = 0.5 * a.T.dot(C).dot(a) - 0.5 * R.T.ravel().dot(C.ravel())
334::COMM;;b = C.dot(self.y_train_ - pi) # Line 13
335::COMM;;s_3 = b - K.dot(R.dot(b)) # Line 14
336::COMM;;d_Z[j] = s_1 + s_2.T.dot(s_3) # Line 15
337::COMM;;return Z, d_Z
338::COMM;;def latent_mean_and_variance(self, X):
355::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
356::COMM;;# Based on Algorithm 3.2 of GPML
357::COMM;;K_star = self.kernel_(self.X_train_, X) # K_star =k(x_star)
358::COMM;;latent_mean = K_star.T.dot(self.y_train_ - self.pi_) # Line 4
359::COMM;;v = solve(self.L_, self.W_sr_[:, np.newaxis] * K_star) # Line 5
360::COMM;;# Line 6 (compute np.diag(v.T.dot(v)) via einsum)
361::COMM;;latent_var = self.kernel_.diag(X) - np.einsum("ij,ij->j", v, v)
362::COMM;;return latent_mean, latent_var
363::COMM;;def _posterior_mode(self, K, return_temporaries=False):
369::COMM;;# Based on Algorithm 3.1 of GPML
370::COMM;;# If warm_start are enabled, we reuse the last solution for the
371::COMM;;# posterior mode as initialization; otherwise, we initialize with 0
372::COMM;;if (
373::COMM;;self.warm_start
374::COMM;;and hasattr(self, "f_cached")
375::COMM;;and self.f_cached.shape == self.y_train_.shape
376::COMM;;):
377::COMM;;f = self.f_cached
378::COMM;;else:
379::COMM;;f = np.zeros_like(self.y_train_, dtype=np.float64)
380::COMM;;# Use Newton's iteration method to find mode of Laplace approximation
381::COMM;;log_marginal_likelihood = -np.inf
382::COMM;;for _ in range(self.max_iter_predict):
383::COMM;;# Line 4
384::COMM;;pi = expit(f)
385::COMM;;W = pi * (1 - pi)
386::COMM;;# Line 5
387::COMM;;W_sr = np.sqrt(W)
388::COMM;;W_sr_K = W_sr[:, np.newaxis] * K
389::COMM;;B = np.eye(W.shape[0]) + W_sr_K * W_sr
390::COMM;;L = cholesky(B, lower=True)
391::COMM;;# Line 6
392::COMM;;b = W * f + (self.y_train_ - pi)
393::COMM;;# Line 7
394::COMM;;a = b - W_sr * cho_solve((L, True), W_sr_K.dot(b))
395::COMM;;# Line 8

398::COMM;;# convergence criterion

400::COMM;;-0.5 * a.T.dot(f)
401::COMM;;- np.log1p(np.exp(-(self.y_train_ * 2 - 1) * f)).sum()
402::COMM;;- np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
403::COMM;;)
404::COMM;;# Check if we have converged (log marginal likelihood does
405::COMM;;# not decrease)
406::COMM;;# XXX: more complex convergence criterion
407::COMM;;if lml - log_marginal_likelihood < 1e-10:
408::COMM;;break
409::COMM;;log_marginal_likelihood = lml
410::COMM;;self.f_cached = f # Remember solution for later warm-starts
411::COMM;;if return_temporaries:
412::COMM;;return log_marginal_likelihood, (pi, W_sr, L, b, a)
413::COMM;;else:
414::COMM;;return log_marginal_likelihood

416::COMM;;if self.optimizer == "fmin_l_bfgs_b":
417::COMM;;opt_res = scipy.optimize.minimize(
418::COMM;;obj_func, initial_theta, method="L-BFGS-B", jac=True, bounds=bounds
419::COMM;;)
420::COMM;;_check_optimize_result("lbfgs", opt_res)
421::COMM;;theta_opt, func_min = opt_res.x, opt_res.fun
