700::COMM;;def kernel_(self):
712::COMM;;In the case of multi-class classification, the mean log-marginal
713::COMM;;likelihood of the one-versus-rest classifiers are returned.
714::COMM;;Parameters
715::COMM;;----------
716::COMM;;theta : array-like of shape (n_kernel_params,), default=None
717::COMM;;Kernel hyperparameters for which the log-marginal likelihood is
718::COMM;;evaluated. In the case of multi-class classification, theta may
719::COMM;;be the hyperparameters of the compound kernel or of an individual
720::COMM;;kernel. In the latter case, all individual kernel get assigned the
721::COMM;;same theta values. If None, the precomputed log_marginal_likelihood
722::COMM;;of ``self.kernel_.theta`` is returned.
723::COMM;;eval_gradient : bool, default=False
724::COMM;;If True, the gradient of the log-marginal likelihood with respect
725::COMM;;to the kernel hyperparameters at position theta is returned
726::COMM;;additionally. Note that gradient computation is not supported
727::COMM;;for non-binary classification. If True, theta must not be None.
728::COMM;;clone_kernel : bool, default=True
729::COMM;;If True, the kernel attribute is copied. If False, the kernel
730::COMM;;attribute is modified, but may result in a performance improvement.
731::COMM;;Returns

733::COMM;;log_likelihood : float
734::COMM;;Log-marginal likelihood of theta for training data.
735::COMM;;log_likelihood_gradient : ndarray of shape (n_kernel_params,), optional
736::COMM;;Gradient of the log-marginal likelihood with respect to the kernel
737::COMM;;hyperparameters at position theta.
738::COMM;;Only returned when `eval_gradient` is True.

449::COMM;;rng.multivariate_normal(
450::COMM;;y_mean[:, target], y_cov[..., target], n_samples
451::COMM;;).T[:, np.newaxis]
452::COMM;;for target in range(y_mean.shape[1])
453::COMM;;]
454::COMM;;y_samples = np.hstack(y_samples)
455::COMM;;return y_samples
456::COMM;;def log_marginal_likelihood(
457::COMM;;self, theta=None, eval_gradient=False, clone_kernel=True
458::COMM;;):
482::COMM;;if theta is None:
483::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
484::COMM;;raise ValueError("Gradient can only be evaluated for theta!=None")
485::COMM;;return self.log_marginal_likelihood_value_
486::COMM;;if clone_kernel:
487::COMM;;kernel = self.kernel_.clone_with_theta(theta)
488::COMM;;else:
489::COMM;;kernel = self.kernel_
490::COMM;;kernel.theta = theta
491::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
492::COMM;;K, K_gradient = kernel(self.X_train_, eval_gradient=True)
493::COMM;;else:
494::COMM;;K = kernel(self.X_train_)
495::COMM;;# Alg. 2.1, page 19, line 2 -> L = cholesky(K + sigma^2 I)
496::COMM;;K[np.diag_indices_from(K)] += self.alpha
497::COMM;;try:
498::COMM;;L = cholesky(K, lower=GPR_CHOLESKY_LOWER, check_finite=False)
499::COMM;;except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
500::COMM;;return (-np.inf, np.zeros_like(theta)) if eval_gradient else -np.inf
501::COMM;;# Support multi-dimensional output of self.y_train_
502::COMM;;y_train = self.y_train_
503::COMM;;if y_train.ndim == 1:
504::COMM;;y_train = y_train[:, np.newaxis]
505::COMM;;# Alg 2.1, page 19, line 3 -> alpha = L^T \ (L \ y)
506::COMM;;alpha = cho_solve((L, GPR_CHOLESKY_LOWER), y_train, check_finite=False)
507::COMM;;# Alg 2.1, page 19, line 7
508::COMM;;# -0.5 . y^T . alpha - sum(log(diag(L))) - n_samples / 2 log(2*pi)
509::COMM;;# y is originally thought to be a (1, n_samples) row vector. However,
510::COMM;;# in multioutputs, y is of shape (n_samples, 2) and we need to compute
511::COMM;;# y^T . alpha for each output, independently using einsum. Thus, it
512::COMM;;# is equivalent to:
513::COMM;;# for output_idx in range(n_outputs):
514::COMM;;# log_likelihood_dims[output_idx] = (
515::COMM;;# y_train[:, [output_idx]] @ alpha[:, [output_idx]]
516::COMM;;# )
517::COMM;;log_likelihood_dims = -0.5 * np.einsum("ik,ik->k", y_train, alpha)
518::COMM;;log_likelihood_dims -= np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
519::COMM;;log_likelihood_dims -= K.shape[0] / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi)
520::COMM;;# the log likelihood is sum-up across the outputs
521::COMM;;log_likelihood = log_likelihood_dims.sum(axis=-1)
522::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
523::COMM;;# Eq. 5.9, p. 114, and footnote 5 in p. 114
524::COMM;;# 0.5 * trace((alpha . alpha^T - K^-1) . K_gradient)
525::COMM;;# alpha is supposed to be a vector of (n_samples,) elements. With
526::COMM;;# multioutputs, alpha is a matrix of size (n_samples, n_outputs).
527::COMM;;# Therefore, we want to construct a matrix of
528::COMM;;# (n_samples, n_samples, n_outputs) equivalent to
529::COMM;;# for output_idx in range(n_outputs):
530::COMM;;# output_alpha = alpha[:, [output_idx]]
531::COMM;;# inner_term[..., output_idx] = output_alpha @ output_alpha.T
532::COMM;;inner_term = np.einsum("ik,jk->ijk", alpha, alpha)
533::COMM;;# compute K^-1 of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
534::COMM;;K_inv = cho_solve(
535::COMM;;(L, GPR_CHOLESKY_LOWER), np.eye(K.shape[0]), check_finite=False
536::COMM;;)
537::COMM;;# create a new axis to use broadcasting between inner_term and
538::COMM;;# K_inv
539::COMM;;inner_term -= K_inv[..., np.newaxis]
540::COMM;;# Since we are interested about the trace of
541::COMM;;# inner_term @ K_gradient, we don't explicitly compute the
542::COMM;;# matrix-by-matrix operation and instead use an einsum. Therefore
543::COMM;;# it is equivalent to:
544::COMM;;# for param_idx in range(n_kernel_params):
545::COMM;;# for output_idx in range(n_output):
546::COMM;;# log_likehood_gradient_dims[param_idx, output_idx] = (
547::COMM;;# inner_term[..., output_idx] @
548::COMM;;# K_gradient[..., param_idx]
549::COMM;;# )
550::COMM;;log_likelihood_gradient_dims = 0.5 * np.einsum(
551::COMM;;"ijl,jik->kl", inner_term, K_gradient
552::COMM;;)
553::COMM;;# the log likelihood gradient is the sum-up across the outputs
554::COMM;;log_likelihood_gradient = log_likelihood_gradient_dims.sum(axis=-1)
555::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
556::COMM;;return log_likelihood, log_likelihood_gradient
557::COMM;;else:
558::COMM;;return log_likelihood
559::COMM;;def _constrained_optimization(self, obj_func, initial_theta, bounds):
560::COMM;;if self.optimizer == "fmin_l_bfgs_b":
561::COMM;;opt_res = scipy.optimize.minimize(
562::COMM;;obj_func,
563::COMM;;initial_theta,
564::COMM;;method="L-BFGS-B",
565::COMM;;jac=True,
566::COMM;;bounds=bounds,
567::COMM;;)
568::COMM;;_check_optimize_result("lbfgs", opt_res)
569::COMM;;theta_opt, func_min = opt_res.x, opt_res.fun
570::COMM;;elif callable(self.optimizer):
571::COMM;;theta_opt, func_min = self.optimizer(obj_func, initial_theta, bounds=bounds)
572::COMM;;else:
573::COMM;;raise ValueError(f"Unknown optimizer {self.optimizer}.")
574::COMM;;return theta_opt, func_min

576::COMM;;tags = super().__sklearn_tags__()

2::COMM;;# Kernels for Gaussian process regression and classification.
3::COMM;;#
4::COMM;;# The kernels in this module allow kernel-engineering, i.e., they can be
5::COMM;;# combined via the "+" and "*" operators or be exponentiated with a scalar
6::COMM;;# via "**". These sum and product expressions can also contain scalar values,
7::COMM;;# which are automatically converted to a constant kernel.
8::COMM;;#
9::COMM;;# All kernels allow (analytic) gradient-based hyperparameter optimization.
10::COMM;;# The space of hyperparameters can be specified by giving lower und upper
11::COMM;;# boundaries for the value of each hyperparameter (the search space is thus
12::COMM;;# rectangular). Instead of specifying bounds, hyperparameters can also be
13::COMM;;# declared to be "fixed", which causes these hyperparameters to be excluded from
14::COMM;;# optimization.
15::COMM;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
16::COMM;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMM;;# Note: this module is strongly inspired by the kernel module of the george
18::COMM;;# package.
19::COMM;;import math
20::COMM;;import warnings
21::COMM;;from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
22::COMM;;from collections import namedtuple
23::COMM;;from inspect import signature
24::COMM;;import numpy as np
25::COMM;;from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist, pdist, squareform
26::COMM;;from scipy.special import gamma, kv
27::COMM;;from sklearn.base import clone
28::COMM;;from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning
29::COMM;;from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import pairwise_kernels
30::COMM;;from sklearn.utils.validation import _num_samples
31::COMM;;def _check_length_scale(X, length_scale):
32::COMM;;length_scale = np.squeeze(length_scale).astype(float)
33::COMM;;if np.ndim(length_scale) > 1:
34::COMM;;raise ValueError("length_scale cannot be of dimension greater than 1")
35::COMM;;if np.ndim(length_scale) == 1 and X.shape[1] != length_scale.shape[0]:
36::COMM;;raise ValueError(
37::COMM;;"Anisotropic kernel must have the same number of "
38::COMM;;"dimensions as data (%d!=%d)" % (length_scale.shape[0], X.shape[1])
39::COMM;;)
40::COMM;;return length_scale
41::COMM;;class Hyperparameter(
42::COMM;;namedtuple(
43::COMM;;"Hyperparameter", ("name", "value_type", "bounds", "n_elements", "fixed")
44::COMM;;)
45::COMM;;):
90::COMM;;# A raw namedtuple is very memory efficient as it packs the attributes
91::COMM;;# in a struct to get rid of the __dict__ of attributes in particular it
92::COMM;;# does not copy the string for the keys on each instance.
93::COMM;;# By deriving a namedtuple class just to introduce the __init__ method we
94::COMM;;# would also reintroduce the __dict__ on the instance. By telling the
95::COMM;;# Python interpreter that this subclass uses static __slots__ instead of
96::COMM;;# dynamic attributes. Furthermore we don't need any additional slot in the
97::COMM;;# subclass so we set __slots__ to the empty tuple.
98::COMM;;__slots__ = ()
99::COMM;;def __new__(cls, name, value_type, bounds, n_elements=1, fixed=None):
100::COMM;;if not isinstance(bounds, str) or bounds != "fixed":
101::COMM;;bounds = np.atleast_2d(bounds)
102::COMM;;if n_elements > 1: # vector-valued parameter
103::COMM;;if bounds.shape[0] == 1:
104::COMM;;bounds = np.repeat(bounds, n_elements, 0)
105::COMM;;elif bounds.shape[0] != n_elements:
106::COMM;;raise ValueError(
107::COMM;;"Bounds on %s should have either 1 or "
108::COMM;;"%d dimensions. Given are %d"
109::COMM;;% (name, n_elements, bounds.shape[0])
110::COMM;;)
111::COMM;;if fixed is None:
112::COMM;;fixed = isinstance(bounds, str) and bounds == "fixed"
113::COMM;;return super().__new__(cls, name, value_type, bounds, n_elements, fixed)
114::COMM;;# This is mainly a testing utility to check that two hyperparameters
115::COMM;;# are equal.
116::COMM;;def __eq__(self, other):
117::COMM;;return (
118::COMM;;self.name == other.name
119::COMM;;and self.value_type == other.value_type
120::COMM;;and np.all(self.bounds == other.bounds)
121::COMM;;and self.n_elements == other.n_elements
122::COMM;;and self.fixed == other.fixed

162::COMM;;# to represent

165::COMM;;init_sign = signature(init)

167::COMM;;for parameter in init_sign.parameters.values():
168::COMM;;if parameter.kind != parameter.VAR_KEYWORD and parameter.name != "self":
169::COMM;;args.append(parameter.name)

171::COMM;;varargs.append(parameter.name)

178::COMM;;)

182::COMM;;def set_params(self, **params):

973::COMM;;Can be used as part of a product-kernel where it scales the magnitude of
974::COMM;;the other factor (kernel) or as part of a sum-kernel, where it modifies
975::COMM;;the mean of the Gaussian process.

1171::COMM;;Diagonal of kernel k(X, X)
1182::COMM;;The RBF kernel is a stationary kernel. It is also known as the
1183::COMM;;"squared exponential" kernel. It is parameterized by a length scale
1184::COMM;;parameter :math:`l>0`, which can either be a scalar (isotropic variant
1185::COMM;;of the kernel) or a vector with the same number of dimensions as the inputs
1186::COMM;;X (anisotropic variant of the kernel). The kernel is given by:
1187::COMM;;.. math::
1188::COMM;;k(x_i, x_j) = \\exp\\left(- \\frac{d(x_i, x_j)^2}{2l^2} \\right)
1189::COMM;;where :math:`l` is the length scale of the kernel and
1190::COMM;;:math:`d(\\cdot,\\cdot)` is the Euclidean distance.
1191::COMM;;For advice on how to set the length scale parameter, see e.g. [1]_.
1192::COMM;;This kernel is infinitely differentiable, which implies that GPs with this
1193::COMM;;kernel as covariance function have mean square derivatives of all orders,
1194::COMM;;and are thus very smooth.
1195::COMM;;See [2]_, Chapter 4, Section 4.2, for further details of the RBF kernel.
1196::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gp_kernels>`.
1197::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1198::COMM;;Parameters
1199::COMM;;----------
1200::COMM;;length_scale : float or ndarray of shape (n_features,), default=1.0
1201::COMM;;The length scale of the kernel. If a float, an isotropic kernel is
1202::COMM;;used. If an array, an anisotropic kernel is used where each dimension
1203::COMM;;of l defines the length-scale of the respective feature dimension.
1204::COMM;;length_scale_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1205::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'length_scale'.
1206::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'length_scale' cannot be changed during
1207::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.
1208::COMM;;References
1209::COMM;;----------
1210::COMM;;.. [1] `David Duvenaud (2014). "The Kernel Cookbook:
1211::COMM;;Advice on Covariance functions".
1212::COMM;;<https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~duvenaud/cookbook/>`_
1213::COMM;;.. [2] `Carl Edward Rasmussen, Christopher K. I. Williams (2006).
1214::COMM;;"Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning". The MIT Press.
1215::COMM;;<http://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/>`_
1216::COMM;;Examples
1217::COMM;;--------

1219::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessClassifier

1291::COMO;;# We need to recompute the pairwise dimension-wise distances
1305::COMC;;else: # isotropic
1311::COMM;;The class of Matern kernels is a generalization of the :class:`RBF`.
1312::COMM;;It has an additional parameter :math:`\\nu` which controls the
1313::COMM;;smoothness of the resulting function. The smaller :math:`\\nu`,
1314::COMM;;the less smooth the approximated function is.
1315::COMM;;As :math:`\\nu\\rightarrow\\infty`, the kernel becomes equivalent to
1316::COMM;;the :class:`RBF` kernel. When :math:`\\nu = 1/2`, the Matérn kernel
1317::COMM;;becomes identical to the absolute exponential kernel.
1318::COMM;;Important intermediate values are
1319::COMM;;:math:`\\nu=1.5` (once differentiable functions)
1320::COMM;;and :math:`\\nu=2.5` (twice differentiable functions).
1321::COMM;;The kernel is given by:
1322::COMM;;.. math::
1323::COMM;;k(x_i, x_j) = \\frac{1}{\\Gamma(\\nu)2^{\\nu-1}}\\Bigg(
1324::COMM;;\\frac{\\sqrt{2\\nu}}{l} d(x_i , x_j )
1325::COMM;;\\Bigg)^\\nu K_\\nu\\Bigg(
1326::COMM;;\\frac{\\sqrt{2\\nu}}{l} d(x_i , x_j )\\Bigg)
1327::COMM;;where :math:`d(\\cdot,\\cdot)` is the Euclidean distance,
1328::COMM;;:math:`K_{\\nu}(\\cdot)` is a modified Bessel function and
1329::COMM;;:math:`\\Gamma(\\cdot)` is the gamma function.
1330::COMM;;See [1]_, Chapter 4, Section 4.2, for details regarding the different
1331::COMM;;variants of the Matern kernel.
1332::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gp_kernels>`.
1333::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1334::COMM;;Parameters
1335::COMM;;----------
1336::COMM;;length_scale : float or ndarray of shape (n_features,), default=1.0
1337::COMM;;The length scale of the kernel. If a float, an isotropic kernel is
1338::COMM;;used. If an array, an anisotropic kernel is used where each dimension
1339::COMM;;of l defines the length-scale of the respective feature dimension.
1340::COMM;;length_scale_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1341::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'length_scale'.
1342::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'length_scale' cannot be changed during
1343::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.
1344::COMM;;nu : float, default=1.5
1345::COMM;;The parameter nu controlling the smoothness of the learned function.
1346::COMM;;The smaller nu, the less smooth the approximated function is.
1347::COMM;;For nu=inf, the kernel becomes equivalent to the RBF kernel and for
1348::COMM;;nu=0.5 to the absolute exponential kernel. Important intermediate
1349::COMM;;values are nu=1.5 (once differentiable functions) and nu=2.5
1350::COMM;;(twice differentiable functions). Note that values of nu not in
1351::COMM;;[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, inf] incur a considerably higher computational cost
1352::COMM;;(appr. 10 times higher) since they require to evaluate the modified
1353::COMM;;Bessel function. Furthermore, in contrast to l, nu is kept fixed to
1354::COMM;;its initial value and not optimized.
1355::COMM;;References
1356::COMM;;----------
1357::COMM;;.. [1] `Carl Edward Rasmussen, Christopher K. I. Williams (2006).
1358::COMM;;"Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning". The MIT Press.
1359::COMM;;<http://www.gaussianprocess.org/gpml/>`_

1365::COMM;;>>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
1366::COMM;;>>> kernel = 1.0 * Matern(length_scale=1.0, nu=1.5)
1367::COMM;;>>> gpc = GaussianProcessClassifier(kernel=kernel,

1481::COMM;;The RationalQuadratic kernel can be seen as a scale mixture (an infinite
1482::COMM;;sum) of RBF kernels with different characteristic length scales. It is
1483::COMM;;parameterized by a length scale parameter :math:`l>0` and a scale
1484::COMM;;mixture parameter :math:`\\alpha>0`. Only the isotropic variant
1485::COMM;;where length_scale :math:`l` is a scalar is supported at the moment.
1486::COMM;;The kernel is given by:
1487::COMM;;.. math::
1488::COMM;;k(x_i, x_j) = \\left(
1489::COMM;;1 + \\frac{d(x_i, x_j)^2 }{ 2\\alpha l^2}\\right)^{-\\alpha}
1490::COMM;;where :math:`\\alpha` is the scale mixture parameter, :math:`l` is
1491::COMM;;the length scale of the kernel and :math:`d(\\cdot,\\cdot)` is the
1492::COMM;;Euclidean distance.
1493::COMM;;For advice on how to set the parameters, see e.g. [1]_.
1494::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gp_kernels>`.
1495::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1496::COMM;;Parameters
1497::COMM;;----------
1498::COMM;;length_scale : float > 0, default=1.0
1499::COMM;;The length scale of the kernel.
1500::COMM;;alpha : float > 0, default=1.0
1501::COMM;;Scale mixture parameter
1502::COMM;;length_scale_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1503::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'length_scale'.
1504::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'length_scale' cannot be changed during
1505::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.
1506::COMM;;alpha_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1507::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'alpha'.
1508::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'alpha' cannot be changed during
1509::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.

1611::COMM;;The ExpSineSquared kernel allows one to model functions which repeat
1612::COMM;;themselves exactly. It is parameterized by a length scale
1613::COMM;;parameter :math:`l>0` and a periodicity parameter :math:`p>0`.
1614::COMM;;Only the isotropic variant where :math:`l` is a scalar is
1615::COMM;;supported at the moment. The kernel is given by:
1616::COMM;;.. math::
1617::COMM;;k(x_i, x_j) = \text{exp}\left(-
1618::COMM;;\frac{ 2\sin^2(\pi d(x_i, x_j)/p) }{ l^ 2} \right)
1619::COMM;;where :math:`l` is the length scale of the kernel, :math:`p` the
1620::COMM;;periodicity of the kernel and :math:`d(\cdot,\cdot)` is the
1621::COMM;;Euclidean distance.
1622::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <gp_kernels>`.
1623::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1624::COMM;;Parameters
1625::COMM;;----------
1626::COMM;;length_scale : float > 0, default=1.0
1627::COMM;;The length scale of the kernel.
1628::COMM;;periodicity : float > 0, default=1.0
1629::COMM;;The periodicity of the kernel.
1630::COMM;;length_scale_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1631::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'length_scale'.
1632::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'length_scale' cannot be changed during
1633::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.
1634::COMM;;periodicity_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1635::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'periodicity'.
1636::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'periodicity' cannot be changed during
1637::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.

1670::COMM;;def __call__(self, X, Y=None, eval_gradient=False):
1693::COMM;;X = np.atleast_2d(X)
1694::COMM;;if Y is None:
1695::COMM;;dists = squareform(pdist(X, metric="euclidean"))
1696::COMM;;arg = np.pi * dists / self.periodicity
1697::COMM;;sin_of_arg = np.sin(arg)
1698::COMM;;K = np.exp(-2 * (sin_of_arg / self.length_scale) ** 2)
1699::COMM;;else:
1700::COMM;;if eval_gradient:
1701::COMM;;raise ValueError("Gradient can only be evaluated when Y is None.")
1702::COMM;;dists = cdist(X, Y, metric="euclidean")
1703::COMM;;K = np.exp(
1704::COMM;;-2 * (np.sin(np.pi / self.periodicity * dists) / self.length_scale) ** 2
1705::COMM;;)

1708::COMM;;# gradient with respect to length_scale
1709::COMM;;if not self.hyperparameter_length_scale.fixed:
1710::COMM;;length_scale_gradient = 4 / self.length_scale**2 * sin_of_arg**2 * K
1711::COMM;;length_scale_gradient = length_scale_gradient[:, :, np.newaxis]
1712::COMM;;else: # length_scale is kept fixed
1713::COMM;;length_scale_gradient = np.empty((K.shape[0], K.shape[1], 0))
1714::COMM;;# gradient with respect to p
1715::COMM;;if not self.hyperparameter_periodicity.fixed:

1717::COMM;;4 * arg / self.length_scale**2 * cos_of_arg * sin_of_arg * K

1840::COMO;;# adapted from scipy/optimize/optimize.py for functions with 2d output
1853::COMM;;A thin wrapper around the functionality of the kernels in
1854::COMM;;sklearn.metrics.pairwise.
1855::COMM;;Note: Evaluation of eval_gradient is not analytic but numeric and all
1856::COMM;;kernels support only isotropic distances. The parameter gamma is
1857::COMM;;considered to be a hyperparameter and may be optimized. The other
1858::COMM;;kernel parameters are set directly at initialization and are kept
1859::COMM;;fixed.
1860::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
1861::COMM;;Parameters
1862::COMM;;----------
1863::COMM;;gamma : float, default=1.0
1864::COMM;;Parameter gamma of the pairwise kernel specified by metric. It should
1865::COMM;;be positive.
1866::COMM;;gamma_bounds : pair of floats >= 0 or "fixed", default=(1e-5, 1e5)
1867::COMM;;The lower and upper bound on 'gamma'.
1868::COMM;;If set to "fixed", 'gamma' cannot be changed during
1869::COMM;;hyperparameter tuning.
1870::COMM;;metric : {"linear", "additive_chi2", "chi2", "poly", "polynomial", \
1871::COMM;;"rbf", "laplacian", "sigmoid", "cosine"} or callable, \
1872::COMM;;default="linear"
1873::COMM;;The metric to use when calculating kernel between instances in a
1874::COMM;;feature array. If metric is a string, it must be one of the metrics
1875::COMM;;in pairwise.PAIRWISE_KERNEL_FUNCTIONS.
1876::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a kernel matrix.
1877::COMM;;Alternatively, if metric is a callable function, it is called on each
1878::COMM;;pair of instances (rows) and the resulting value recorded. The callable
1879::COMM;;should take two arrays from X as input and return a value indicating
1880::COMM;;the distance between them.
1881::COMM;;pairwise_kernels_kwargs : dict, default=None
1882::COMM;;All entries of this dict (if any) are passed as keyword arguments to
1883::COMM;;the pairwise kernel function.
1884::COMM;;Examples
1885::COMM;;--------
1886::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
1887::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessClassifier
1888::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import PairwiseKernel
1889::COMM;;>>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
1890::COMM;;>>> kernel = PairwiseKernel(metric='rbf')
1891::COMM;;>>> gpc = GaussianProcessClassifier(kernel=kernel,
1892::COMM;;... random_state=0).fit(X, y)
1893::COMM;;>>> gpc.score(X, y)
1894::COMM;;0.9733
1895::COMM;;>>> gpc.predict_proba(X[:2,:])
1896::COMM;;array([[0.8880, 0.05663, 0.05532],
1897::COMM;;[0.8676, 0.07073, 0.06165]])
1915::COMM;;Parameters
1916::COMM;;----------
1917::COMM;;X : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
1918::COMM;;Left argument of the returned kernel k(X, Y)
1919::COMM;;Y : ndarray of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features), default=None
1920::COMM;;Right argument of the returned kernel k(X, Y). If None, k(X, X)
1921::COMM;;if evaluated instead.
1922::COMM;;eval_gradient : bool, default=False
1923::COMM;;Determines whether the gradient with respect to the log of
1924::COMM;;the kernel hyperparameter is computed.
1925::COMM;;Only supported when Y is None.
1926::COMM;;Returns
1927::COMM;;-------
1928::COMM;;K : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_Y)
1929::COMM;;Kernel k(X, Y)
1930::COMM;;K_gradient : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_X, n_dims),\
1931::COMM;;optional
1932::COMM;;The gradient of the kernel k(X, X) with respect to the log of the
1933::COMM;;hyperparameter of the kernel. Only returned when `eval_gradient`
1934::COMM;;is True.

1970::COMM;;Parameters

144::COMM;;Replace missing values using a descriptive statistic (e.g. mean, median, or
145::COMM;;most frequent) along each column, or using a constant value.
146::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <impute>`.
147::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
148::COMM;;`SimpleImputer` replaces the previous `sklearn.preprocessing.Imputer`
149::COMM;;estimator which is now removed.
150::COMM;;Parameters
151::COMM;;----------
152::COMM;;missing_values : int, float, str, np.nan, None or pandas.NA, default=np.nan
153::COMM;;The placeholder for the missing values. All occurrences of
154::COMM;;`missing_values` will be imputed. For pandas' dataframes with
155::COMM;;nullable integer dtypes with missing values, `missing_values`
156::COMM;;can be set to either `np.nan` or `pd.NA`.
157::COMM;;strategy : str or Callable, default='mean'
158::COMM;;The imputation strategy.
159::COMM;;- If "mean", then replace missing values using the mean along
160::COMM;;each column. Can only be used with numeric data.
161::COMM;;- If "median", then replace missing values using the median along
162::COMM;;each column. Can only be used with numeric data.
163::COMM;;- If "most_frequent", then replace missing using the most frequent
164::COMM;;value along each column. Can be used with strings or numeric data.
165::COMM;;If there is more than one such value, only the smallest is returned.
166::COMM;;- If "constant", then replace missing values with fill_value. Can be
167::COMM;;used with strings or numeric data.
168::COMM;;- If an instance of Callable, then replace missing values using the
169::COMM;;scalar statistic returned by running the callable over a dense 1d
170::COMM;;array containing non-missing values of each column.
171::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
172::COMM;;strategy="constant" for fixed value imputation.
173::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
174::COMM;;strategy=callable for custom value imputation.
175::COMM;;fill_value : str or numerical value, default=None
176::COMM;;When strategy == "constant", `fill_value` is used to replace all
177::COMM;;occurrences of missing_values. For string or object data types,
178::COMM;;`fill_value` must be a string.
179::COMM;;If `None`, `fill_value` will be 0 when imputing numerical
180::COMM;;data and "missing_value" for strings or object data types.
181::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
182::COMM;;If True, a copy of X will be created. If False, imputation will
183::COMM;;be done in-place whenever possible. Note that, in the following cases,
184::COMM;;a new copy will always be made, even if `copy=False`:
185::COMM;;- If `X` is not an array of floating values;
186::COMM;;- If `X` is encoded as a CSR matrix;
187::COMM;;- If `add_indicator=True`.
188::COMM;;add_indicator : bool, default=False
189::COMM;;If True, a :class:`MissingIndicator` transform will stack onto output
190::COMM;;of the imputer's transform. This allows a predictive estimator
191::COMM;;to account for missingness despite imputation. If a feature has no
192::COMM;;missing values at fit/train time, the feature won't appear on
193::COMM;;the missing indicator even if there are missing values at
194::COMM;;transform/test time.
195::COMM;;keep_empty_features : bool, default=False
196::COMM;;If True, features that consist exclusively of missing values when
197::COMM;;`fit` is called are returned in results when `transform` is called.
198::COMM;;The imputed value is always `0` except when `strategy="constant"`
199::COMM;;in which case `fill_value` will be used instead.
200::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
201::COMM;;Attributes
202::COMM;;----------
203::COMM;;statistics_ : array of shape (n_features,)
204::COMM;;The imputation fill value for each feature.
205::COMM;;Computing statistics can result in `np.nan` values.
206::COMM;;During :meth:`transform`, features corresponding to `np.nan`
207::COMM;;statistics will be discarded.
208::COMM;;indicator_ : :class:`~sklearn.impute.MissingIndicator`
209::COMM;;Indicator used to add binary indicators for missing values.
210::COMM;;`None` if `add_indicator=False`.
211::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
212::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
213::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
214::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
215::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
216::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
217::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
218::COMM;;See Also
219::COMM;;--------
220::COMM;;IterativeImputer : Multivariate imputer that estimates values to impute for
221::COMM;;each feature with missing values from all the others.
222::COMM;;KNNImputer : Multivariate imputer that estimates missing features using
223::COMM;;nearest samples.
224::COMM;;Notes
225::COMM;;-----
226::COMM;;Columns which only contained missing values at :meth:`fit` are discarded
227::COMM;;upon :meth:`transform` if strategy is not `"constant"`.
228::COMM;;In a prediction context, simple imputation usually performs poorly when
229::COMM;;associated with a weak learner. However, with a powerful learner, it can
230::COMM;;lead to as good or better performance than complex imputation such as
231::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.impute.IterativeImputer` or :class:`~sklearn.impute.KNNImputer`.
232::COMM;;Examples
233::COMM;;--------
234::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
235::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
236::COMM;;>>> imp_mean = SimpleImputer(missing_values=np.nan, strategy='mean')
237::COMM;;>>> imp_mean.fit([[7, 2, 3], [4, np.nan, 6], [10, 5, 9]])
238::COMM;;SimpleImputer()

51::COMM;;A strategy for imputing missing values by modeling each feature with
52::COMM;;missing values as a function of other features in a round-robin fashion.
53::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <iterative_imputer>`.
54::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
55::COMM;;.. note::
56::COMM;;This estimator is still **experimental** for now: the predictions
57::COMM;;and the API might change without any deprecation cycle. To use it,
58::COMM;;you need to explicitly import `enable_iterative_imputer`::
59::COMM;;>>> # explicitly require this experimental feature
60::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer # noqa
61::COMM;;>>> # now you can import normally from sklearn.impute
62::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputer
63::COMM;;Parameters
64::COMM;;----------
65::COMM;;estimator : estimator object, default=BayesianRidge()
66::COMM;;The estimator to use at each step of the round-robin imputation.
67::COMM;;If `sample_posterior=True`, the estimator must support
68::COMM;;`return_std` in its `predict` method.
69::COMM;;missing_values : int or np.nan, default=np.nan
70::COMM;;The placeholder for the missing values. All occurrences of
71::COMM;;`missing_values` will be imputed. For pandas' dataframes with
72::COMM;;nullable integer dtypes with missing values, `missing_values`
73::COMM;;should be set to `np.nan`, since `pd.NA` will be converted to `np.nan`.
74::COMM;;sample_posterior : bool, default=False
75::COMM;;Whether to sample from the (Gaussian) predictive posterior of the
76::COMM;;fitted estimator for each imputation. Estimator must support
77::COMM;;`return_std` in its `predict` method if set to `True`. Set to
78::COMM;;`True` if using `IterativeImputer` for multiple imputations.
79::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=10
80::COMM;;Maximum number of imputation rounds to perform before returning the
81::COMM;;imputations computed during the final round. A round is a single
82::COMM;;imputation of each feature with missing values. The stopping criterion
83::COMM;;is met once `max(abs(X_t - X_{t-1}))/max(abs(X[known_vals])) < tol`,
84::COMM;;where `X_t` is `X` at iteration `t`. Note that early stopping is only
85::COMM;;applied if `sample_posterior=False`.
86::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-3
87::COMM;;Tolerance of the stopping condition.
88::COMM;;n_nearest_features : int, default=None
89::COMM;;Number of other features to use to estimate the missing values of
90::COMM;;each feature column. Nearness between features is measured using
91::COMM;;the absolute correlation coefficient between each feature pair (after
92::COMM;;initial imputation). To ensure coverage of features throughout the
93::COMM;;imputation process, the neighbor features are not necessarily nearest,
94::COMM;;but are drawn with probability proportional to correlation for each
95::COMM;;imputed target feature. Can provide significant speed-up when the
96::COMM;;number of features is huge. If `None`, all features will be used.
97::COMM;;initial_strategy : {'mean', 'median', 'most_frequent', 'constant'}, \
98::COMM;;default='mean'
99::COMM;;Which strategy to use to initialize the missing values. Same as the
100::COMM;;`strategy` parameter in :class:`~sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer`.
101::COMM;;fill_value : str or numerical value, default=None
102::COMM;;When `strategy="constant"`, `fill_value` is used to replace all
103::COMM;;occurrences of missing_values. For string or object data types,
104::COMM;;`fill_value` must be a string.
105::COMM;;If `None`, `fill_value` will be 0 when imputing numerical
106::COMM;;data and "missing_value" for strings or object data types.
107::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
108::COMM;;imputation_order : {'ascending', 'descending', 'roman', 'arabic', \
109::COMM;;'random'}, default='ascending'
110::COMM;;The order in which the features will be imputed. Possible values:
111::COMM;;- `'ascending'`: From features with fewest missing values to most.
112::COMM;;- `'descending'`: From features with most missing values to fewest.
113::COMM;;- `'roman'`: Left to right.
114::COMM;;- `'arabic'`: Right to left.
115::COMM;;- `'random'`: A random order for each round.
116::COMM;;skip_complete : bool, default=False
117::COMM;;If `True` then features with missing values during :meth:`transform`
118::COMM;;which did not have any missing values during :meth:`fit` will be
119::COMM;;imputed with the initial imputation method only. Set to `True` if you
120::COMM;;have many features with no missing values at both :meth:`fit` and
121::COMM;;:meth:`transform` time to save compute.
122::COMM;;min_value : float or array-like of shape (n_features,), default=-np.inf
123::COMM;;Minimum possible imputed value. Broadcast to shape `(n_features,)` if
124::COMM;;scalar. If array-like, expects shape `(n_features,)`, one min value for
125::COMM;;each feature. The default is `-np.inf`.
126::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.23
127::COMM;;Added support for array-like.
128::COMM;;max_value : float or array-like of shape (n_features,), default=np.inf
129::COMM;;Maximum possible imputed value. Broadcast to shape `(n_features,)` if
130::COMM;;scalar. If array-like, expects shape `(n_features,)`, one max value for
131::COMM;;each feature. The default is `np.inf`.
132::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.23
133::COMM;;Added support for array-like.
134::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
135::COMM;;Verbosity flag, controls the debug messages that are issued
136::COMM;;as functions are evaluated. The higher, the more verbose. Can be 0, 1,
137::COMM;;or 2.
138::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
139::COMM;;The seed of the pseudo random number generator to use. Randomizes
140::COMM;;selection of estimator features if `n_nearest_features` is not `None`,
141::COMM;;the `imputation_order` if `random`, and the sampling from posterior if
142::COMM;;`sample_posterior=True`. Use an integer for determinism.
143::COMM;;See :term:`the Glossary <random_state>`.
144::COMM;;add_indicator : bool, default=False
145::COMM;;If `True`, a :class:`MissingIndicator` transform will stack onto output
146::COMM;;of the imputer's transform. This allows a predictive estimator
147::COMM;;to account for missingness despite imputation. If a feature has no
148::COMM;;missing values at fit/train time, the feature won't appear on
149::COMM;;the missing indicator even if there are missing values at
150::COMM;;transform/test time.
151::COMM;;keep_empty_features : bool, default=False
152::COMM;;If True, features that consist exclusively of missing values when
153::COMM;;`fit` is called are returned in results when `transform` is called.
154::COMM;;The imputed value is always `0` except when
155::COMM;;`initial_strategy="constant"` in which case `fill_value` will be
156::COMM;;used instead.
157::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
158::COMM;;Attributes
159::COMM;;----------
160::COMM;;initial_imputer_ : object of type :class:`~sklearn.impute.SimpleImputer`
161::COMM;;Imputer used to initialize the missing values.
162::COMM;;imputation_sequence_ : list of tuples
163::COMM;;Each tuple has `(feat_idx, neighbor_feat_idx, estimator)`, where
164::COMM;;`feat_idx` is the current feature to be imputed,
165::COMM;;`neighbor_feat_idx` is the array of other features used to impute the
166::COMM;;current feature, and `estimator` is the trained estimator used for
167::COMM;;the imputation. Length is `self.n_features_with_missing_ *
168::COMM;;self.n_iter_`.
169::COMM;;n_iter_ : int
170::COMM;;Number of iteration rounds that occurred. Will be less than
171::COMM;;`self.max_iter` if early stopping criterion was reached.
172::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
173::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
174::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
175::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
176::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
177::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
178::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
179::COMM;;n_features_with_missing_ : int
180::COMM;;Number of features with missing values.
181::COMM;;indicator_ : :class:`~sklearn.impute.MissingIndicator`
182::COMM;;Indicator used to add binary indicators for missing values.
183::COMM;;`None` if `add_indicator=False`.
184::COMM;;random_state_ : RandomState instance
185::COMM;;RandomState instance that is generated either from a seed, the random
186::COMM;;number generator or by `np.random`.
187::COMM;;See Also
188::COMM;;--------
189::COMM;;SimpleImputer : Univariate imputer for completing missing values
190::COMM;;with simple strategies.
191::COMM;;KNNImputer : Multivariate imputer that estimates missing features using
192::COMM;;nearest samples.
193::COMM;;Notes
194::COMM;;-----
195::COMM;;To support imputation in inductive mode we store each feature's estimator
196::COMM;;during the :meth:`fit` phase, and predict without refitting (in order)
197::COMM;;during the :meth:`transform` phase.
198::COMM;;Features which contain all missing values at :meth:`fit` are discarded upon
199::COMM;;:meth:`transform`.
200::COMM;;Using defaults, the imputer scales in :math:`\\mathcal{O}(knp^3\\min(n,p))`
201::COMM;;where :math:`k` = `max_iter`, :math:`n` the number of samples and
202::COMM;;:math:`p` the number of features. It thus becomes prohibitively costly when
203::COMM;;the number of features increases. Setting
204::COMM;;`n_nearest_features << n_features`, `skip_complete=True` or increasing `tol`
205::COMM;;can help to reduce its computational cost.
206::COMM;;Depending on the nature of missing values, simple imputers can be
207::COMM;;preferable in a prediction context.
208::COMM;;References
209::COMM;;----------
210::COMM;;.. [1] `Stef van Buuren, Karin Groothuis-Oudshoorn (2011). "mice:
211::COMM;;Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations in R". Journal of
212::COMM;;Statistical Software 45: 1-67.
213::COMM;;<https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v045i03>`_
214::COMM;;.. [2] `S. F. Buck, (1960). "A Method of Estimation of Missing Values in
215::COMM;;Multivariate Data Suitable for use with an Electronic Computer".
216::COMM;;Journal of the Royal Statistical Society 22(2): 302-306.
217::COMM;;<https://www.jstor.org/stable/2984099>`_

402::COMM;;number of features, then use a probability proportional to the absolute
403::COMM;;correlation between `feat_idx` and each other feature to randomly

21::COMM;;Each sample's missing values are imputed using the mean value from
22::COMM;;`n_neighbors` nearest neighbors found in the training set. Two samples are
23::COMM;;close if the features that neither is missing are close.
24::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <knnimpute>`.
25::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
26::COMM;;Parameters
27::COMM;;----------
28::COMM;;missing_values : int, float, str, np.nan or None, default=np.nan
29::COMM;;The placeholder for the missing values. All occurrences of
30::COMM;;`missing_values` will be imputed. For pandas' dataframes with
31::COMM;;nullable integer dtypes with missing values, `missing_values`
32::COMM;;should be set to np.nan, since `pd.NA` will be converted to np.nan.
33::COMM;;n_neighbors : int, default=5
34::COMM;;Number of neighboring samples to use for imputation.
35::COMM;;weights : {'uniform', 'distance'} or callable, default='uniform'
36::COMM;;Weight function used in prediction. Possible values:
37::COMM;;- 'uniform' : uniform weights. All points in each neighborhood are
38::COMM;;weighted equally.
39::COMM;;- 'distance' : weight points by the inverse of their distance.
40::COMM;;in this case, closer neighbors of a query point will have a
41::COMM;;greater influence than neighbors which are further away.
42::COMM;;- callable : a user-defined function which accepts an
43::COMM;;array of distances, and returns an array of the same shape
44::COMM;;containing the weights.
45::COMM;;metric : {'nan_euclidean'} or callable, default='nan_euclidean'
46::COMM;;Distance metric for searching neighbors. Possible values:
47::COMM;;- 'nan_euclidean'
48::COMM;;- callable : a user-defined function which conforms to the definition
49::COMM;;of ``func_metric(x, y, *, missing_values=np.nan)``. `x` and `y`
50::COMM;;corresponds to a row (i.e. 1-D arrays) of `X` and `Y`, respectively.
51::COMM;;The callable should returns a scalar distance value.
52::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
53::COMM;;If True, a copy of X will be created. If False, imputation will
54::COMM;;be done in-place whenever possible.
55::COMM;;add_indicator : bool, default=False
56::COMM;;If True, a :class:`MissingIndicator` transform will stack onto the
57::COMM;;output of the imputer's transform. This allows a predictive estimator
58::COMM;;to account for missingness despite imputation. If a feature has no
59::COMM;;missing values at fit/train time, the feature won't appear on the
60::COMM;;missing indicator even if there are missing values at transform/test
61::COMM;;time.
62::COMM;;keep_empty_features : bool, default=False
63::COMM;;If True, features that consist exclusively of missing values when
64::COMM;;`fit` is called are returned in results when `transform` is called.
65::COMM;;The imputed value is always `0`.

265::COMM;;predictions.append(pred)
266::COMM;;# average over samples
267::COMM;;averaged_predictions.append(np.average(pred, axis=0, weights=sample_weight))
268::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
269::COMM;;# reshape to (n_targets, n_instances, n_points) where n_targets is:
270::COMM;;# - 1 for non-multioutput regression and binary classification (shape is
271::COMM;;# already correct in those cases)
272::COMM;;# - n_tasks for multi-output regression
273::COMM;;# - n_classes for multiclass classification.
274::COMM;;predictions = np.array(predictions).T
275::COMM;;if is_regressor(est) and predictions.ndim == 2:
276::COMM;;# non-multioutput regression, shape is (n_instances, n_points,)
277::COMM;;predictions = predictions.reshape(n_samples, -1)
278::COMM;;elif is_classifier(est) and predictions.shape[0] == 2:
279::COMM;;# Binary classification, shape is (2, n_instances, n_points).
280::COMM;;# we output the effect of **positive** class
281::COMM;;predictions = predictions[1]
282::COMM;;predictions = predictions.reshape(n_samples, -1)
283::COMM;;# reshape averaged_predictions to (n_targets, n_points) where n_targets is:
284::COMM;;# - 1 for non-multioutput regression and binary classification (shape is
285::COMM;;# already correct in those cases)
286::COMM;;# - n_tasks for multi-output regression
287::COMM;;# - n_classes for multiclass classification.
288::COMM;;averaged_predictions = np.array(averaged_predictions).T
289::COMM;;if averaged_predictions.ndim == 1:
290::COMM;;# reshape to (1, n_points) for consistency with
291::COMM;;# _partial_dependence_recursion
292::COMM;;averaged_predictions = averaged_predictions.reshape(1, -1)
293::COMM;;return averaged_predictions, predictions

23::COMM;;def _calculate_permutation_scores(
24::COMM;;estimator,
25::COMM;;X,
26::COMM;;y,
27::COMM;;sample_weight,
28::COMM;;col_idx,
29::COMM;;random_state,
30::COMM;;n_repeats,
31::COMM;;scorer,
32::COMM;;max_samples,
33::COMM;;):
36::COMO;;# Work on a copy of X to ensure thread-safety in case of threading based
37::COMO;;# parallelism. Furthermore, making a copy is also useful when the joblib
38::COMO;;# backend is 'loky' (default) or the old 'multiprocessing': in those cases,
39::COMO;;# if X is large it will be automatically be backed by a readonly memory map
40::COMO;;# (memmap). X.copy() on the other hand is always guaranteed to return a
41::COMO;;# writable data-structure whose columns can be shuffled inplace.
73::COMM;;Parameters
74::COMM;;----------
75::COMM;;baseline_score : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
76::COMM;;The baseline score without permutation.
77::COMM;;permuted_score : ndarray of shape (n_features, n_repeats)
78::COMM;;The permuted scores for the `n` repetitions.
79::COMM;;Returns
80::COMM;;-------
81::COMM;;importances : :class:`~sklearn.utils.Bunch`
82::COMM;;Dictionary-like object, with the following attributes.
83::COMM;;importances_mean : ndarray, shape (n_features, )
84::COMM;;Mean of feature importance over `n_repeats`.
85::COMM;;importances_std : ndarray, shape (n_features, )
86::COMM;;Standard deviation over `n_repeats`.
87::COMM;;importances : ndarray, shape (n_features, n_repeats)
88::COMM;;Raw permutation importance scores.
133::COMM;;The :term:`estimator` is required to be a fitted estimator. `X` can be the
134::COMM;;data set used to train the estimator or a hold-out set. The permutation
135::COMM;;importance of a feature is calculated as follows. First, a baseline metric,
136::COMM;;defined by :term:`scoring`, is evaluated on a (potentially different)
137::COMM;;dataset defined by the `X`. Next, a feature column from the validation set
138::COMM;;is permuted and the metric is evaluated again. The permutation importance
139::COMM;;is defined to be the difference between the baseline metric and metric from
140::COMM;;permutating the feature column.
141::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <permutation_importance>`.
142::COMM;;Parameters
143::COMM;;----------
144::COMM;;estimator : object
145::COMM;;An estimator that has already been :term:`fitted` and is compatible
146::COMM;;with :term:`scorer`.
147::COMM;;X : ndarray or DataFrame, shape (n_samples, n_features)
148::COMM;;Data on which permutation importance will be computed.
149::COMM;;y : array-like or None, shape (n_samples, ) or (n_samples, n_classes)
150::COMM;;Targets for supervised or `None` for unsupervised.
151::COMM;;scoring : str, callable, list, tuple, or dict, default=None
152::COMM;;Scorer to use.
153::COMM;;If `scoring` represents a single score, one can use:
154::COMM;;- str: see :ref:`scoring_string_names` for options.
155::COMM;;- callable: a scorer callable object (e.g., function) with signature
156::COMM;;``scorer(estimator, X, y)``. See :ref:`scoring_callable` for details.
157::COMM;;- `None`: the `estimator`'s
158::COMM;;:ref:`default evaluation criterion <scoring_api_overview>` is used.
159::COMM;;If `scoring` represents multiple scores, one can use:
160::COMM;;- a list or tuple of unique strings;
161::COMM;;- a callable returning a dictionary where the keys are the metric
162::COMM;;names and the values are the metric scores;
163::COMM;;- a dictionary with metric names as keys and callables a values.
164::COMM;;Passing multiple scores to `scoring` is more efficient than calling
165::COMM;;`permutation_importance` for each of the scores as it reuses
166::COMM;;predictions to avoid redundant computation.
167::COMM;;n_repeats : int, default=5
168::COMM;;Number of times to permute a feature.
169::COMM;;n_jobs : int or None, default=None
170::COMM;;Number of jobs to run in parallel. The computation is done by computing
171::COMM;;permutation score for each columns and parallelized over the columns.
172::COMM;;`None` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
173::COMM;;`-1` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
174::COMM;;for more details.
175::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
176::COMM;;Pseudo-random number generator to control the permutations of each
177::COMM;;feature.
178::COMM;;Pass an int to get reproducible results across function calls.
179::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
180::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
181::COMM;;Sample weights used in scoring.
182::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
183::COMM;;max_samples : int or float, default=1.0
184::COMM;;The number of samples to draw from X to compute feature importance
185::COMM;;in each repeat (without replacement).
186::COMM;;- If int, then draw `max_samples` samples.
187::COMM;;- If float, then draw `max_samples * X.shape[0]` samples.
188::COMM;;- If `max_samples` is equal to `1.0` or `X.shape[0]`, all samples
189::COMM;;will be used.
190::COMM;;While using this option may provide less accurate importance estimates,
191::COMM;;it keeps the method tractable when evaluating feature importance on
192::COMM;;large datasets. In combination with `n_repeats`, this allows to control
193::COMM;;the computational speed vs statistical accuracy trade-off of this method.
194::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
195::COMM;;Returns
196::COMM;;-------
197::COMM;;result : :class:`~sklearn.utils.Bunch` or dict of such instances
198::COMM;;Dictionary-like object, with the following attributes.
199::COMM;;importances_mean : ndarray of shape (n_features, )
200::COMM;;Mean of feature importance over `n_repeats`.
201::COMM;;importances_std : ndarray of shape (n_features, )
202::COMM;;Standard deviation over `n_repeats`.
203::COMM;;importances : ndarray of shape (n_features, n_repeats)
204::COMM;;Raw permutation importance scores.
205::COMM;;If there are multiple scoring metrics in the scoring parameter
206::COMM;;`result` is a dict with scorer names as keys (e.g. 'roc_auc') and
207::COMM;;`Bunch` objects like above as values.
208::COMM;;References
209::COMM;;----------
210::COMM;;.. [BRE] :doi:`L. Breiman, "Random Forests", Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32,
211::COMM;;2001. <10.1023/A:1010933404324>`
212::COMM;;Examples
213::COMM;;--------
214::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
215::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

217::COMM;;... [0, 9, 9],[0, 9, 9],[0, 9, 9]]
218::COMM;;>>> y = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]

220::COMM;;>>> result = permutation_importance(clf, X, y, n_repeats=10,
221::COMM;;... random_state=0)

99::COMM;;Axes with decision boundary.
100::COMM;;figure_ : matplotlib Figure
101::COMM;;Figure containing the decision boundary.
102::COMM;;See Also
103::COMM;;--------
104::COMM;;DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator : Plot decision boundary given an estimator.
105::COMM;;Examples
106::COMM;;--------
107::COMM;;>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
108::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
109::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
110::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import DecisionBoundaryDisplay

114::COMM;;... np.linspace(iris.data[:, 0].min(), iris.data[:, 0].max()),
115::COMM;;... np.linspace(iris.data[:, 1].min(), iris.data[:, 1].max())
116::COMM;;... )
117::COMM;;>>> grid = np.vstack([feature_1.ravel(), feature_2.ravel()]).T
118::COMM;;>>> tree = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(iris.data[:, :2], iris.target)
119::COMM;;>>> y_pred = np.reshape(tree.predict(grid), feature_1.shape)
120::COMM;;>>> display = DecisionBoundaryDisplay(
121::COMM;;... xx0=feature_1, xx1=feature_2, response=y_pred
122::COMM;;... )
123::COMM;;>>> display.plot()
124::COMM;;<...>
125::COMM;;>>> display.ax_.scatter(
126::COMM;;... iris.data[:, 0], iris.data[:, 1], c=iris.target, edgecolor="black"
127::COMM;;... )
128::COMM;;<...>
129::COMM;;>>> plt.show()

19::COMM;;It is recommended to use
20::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator` to create a
21::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay`. All parameters are stored
22::COMM;;as attributes.
23::COMM;;For general information regarding `scikit-learn` visualization tools, see
24::COMM;;the :ref:`Visualization Guide <visualizations>`.
25::COMM;;For guidance on interpreting these plots, refer to the
26::COMM;;:ref:`Inspection Guide <partial_dependence>`.
27::COMM;;For an example on how to use this class, see the following example:
28::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_miscellaneous_plot_partial_dependence_visualization_api.py`.
29::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
30::COMM;;Parameters
31::COMM;;----------
32::COMM;;pd_results : list of Bunch
33::COMM;;Results of :func:`~sklearn.inspection.partial_dependence` for
34::COMM;;``features``.
35::COMM;;features : list of (int,) or list of (int, int)
36::COMM;;Indices of features for a given plot. A tuple of one integer will plot
37::COMM;;a partial dependence curve of one feature. A tuple of two integers will
38::COMM;;plot a two-way partial dependence curve as a contour plot.
39::COMM;;feature_names : list of str
40::COMM;;Feature names corresponding to the indices in ``features``.
41::COMM;;target_idx : int
42::COMM;;- In a multiclass setting, specifies the class for which the PDPs
43::COMM;;should be computed. Note that for binary classification, the
44::COMM;;positive class (index 1) is always used.
45::COMM;;- In a multioutput setting, specifies the task for which the PDPs
46::COMM;;should be computed.
47::COMM;;Ignored in binary classification or classical regression settings.
48::COMM;;deciles : dict
49::COMM;;Deciles for feature indices in ``features``.
50::COMM;;kind : {'average', 'individual', 'both'} or list of such str, \
51::COMM;;default='average'
52::COMM;;Whether to plot the partial dependence averaged across all the samples
53::COMM;;in the dataset or one line per sample or both.
54::COMM;;- ``kind='average'`` results in the traditional PD plot;
55::COMM;;- ``kind='individual'`` results in the ICE plot;
56::COMM;;- ``kind='both'`` results in plotting both the ICE and PD on the same
57::COMM;;plot.
58::COMM;;A list of such strings can be provided to specify `kind` on a per-plot
59::COMM;;basis. The length of the list should be the same as the number of
60::COMM;;interaction requested in `features`.
61::COMM;;.. note::
62::COMM;;ICE ('individual' or 'both') is not a valid option for 2-ways
63::COMM;;interactions plot. As a result, an error will be raised.
64::COMM;;2-ways interaction plots should always be configured to
65::COMM;;use the 'average' kind instead.
66::COMM;;.. note::
67::COMM;;The fast ``method='recursion'`` option is only available for
68::COMM;;`kind='average'` and `sample_weights=None`. Computing individual
69::COMM;;dependencies and doing weighted averages requires using the slower
70::COMM;;`method='brute'`.
71::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
72::COMM;;Add `kind` parameter with `'average'`, `'individual'`, and `'both'`
73::COMM;;options.
74::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
75::COMM;;Add the possibility to pass a list of string specifying `kind`
76::COMM;;for each plot.
77::COMM;;subsample : float, int or None, default=1000
78::COMM;;Sampling for ICE curves when `kind` is 'individual' or 'both'.
79::COMM;;If float, should be between 0.0 and 1.0 and represent the proportion
80::COMM;;of the dataset to be used to plot ICE curves. If int, represents the
81::COMM;;maximum absolute number of samples to use.
82::COMM;;Note that the full dataset is still used to calculate partial
83::COMM;;dependence when `kind='both'`.
84::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
85::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
86::COMM;;Controls the randomness of the selected samples when subsamples is not
87::COMM;;`None`. See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
88::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
89::COMM;;is_categorical : list of (bool,) or list of (bool, bool), default=None
90::COMM;;Whether each target feature in `features` is categorical or not.
91::COMM;;The list should be same size as `features`. If `None`, all features
92::COMM;;are assumed to be continuous.
93::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
94::COMM;;Attributes
95::COMM;;----------
96::COMM;;bounding_ax_ : matplotlib Axes or None

98::COMM;;grid of partial dependence plots are drawn. If `ax` is a list of axes

103::COMM;;in `ax`. Elements that are None correspond to a nonexisting axes in
104::COMM;;that position.

106::COMM;;If `ax` is an axes or None, `lines_[i, j]` is the partial dependence
107::COMM;;curve on the i-th row and j-th column. If `ax` is a list of axes,
108::COMM;;`lines_[i]` is the partial dependence curve corresponding to the i-th
109::COMM;;item in `ax`. Elements that are None correspond to a nonexisting axes

121::COMM;;`ax` is a list of axes, `vlines_[i]` corresponds to the i-th item in
122::COMM;;`ax`. Elements that are None correspond to a nonexisting axes or an
123::COMM;;axes that does not include a 2-way plot.

127::COMM;;plot on the i-th row and j-th column. If `ax` is a list of axes,
128::COMM;;`contours_[i]` is the partial dependence plot corresponding to the i-th
129::COMM;;item in `ax`. Elements that are None correspond to a nonexisting axes
130::COMM;;or an axes that does not include a contour plot.

135::COMM;;plot corresponding to the i-th item in `ax`. Elements that are None
136::COMM;;correspond to a nonexisting axes or an axes that does not include a
137::COMM;;bar plot.

139::COMM;;heatmaps_ : ndarray of matplotlib Artists

141::COMM;;heatmap on the i-th row and j-th column (for a pair of categorical
142::COMM;;features) . If `ax` is a list of axes, `heatmaps_[i]` is the partial
143::COMM;;dependence heatmap corresponding to the i-th item in `ax`. Elements
144::COMM;;that are None correspond to a nonexisting axes or an axes that does not

149::COMM;;See Also
150::COMM;;--------
151::COMM;;partial_dependence : Compute Partial Dependence values.
152::COMM;;PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator : Plot Partial Dependence.
153::COMM;;Examples
154::COMM;;--------
155::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
156::COMM;;>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
157::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
158::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
159::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay
160::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence
161::COMM;;>>> X, y = make_friedman1()
162::COMM;;>>> clf = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=10).fit(X, y)
163::COMM;;>>> features, feature_names = [(0,)], [f"Features #{i}" for i in range(X.shape[1])]
164::COMM;;>>> deciles = {0: np.linspace(0, 1, num=5)}
165::COMM;;>>> pd_results = partial_dependence(
166::COMM;;... clf, X, features=0, kind="average", grid_resolution=5)
167::COMM;;>>> display = PartialDependenceDisplay(
168::COMM;;... [pd_results], features=features, feature_names=feature_names,
169::COMM;;... target_idx=0, deciles=deciles
170::COMM;;... )
171::COMM;;>>> display.plot(pdp_lim={1: (-1.38, 0.66)})
172::COMM;;<...>
173::COMM;;>>> plt.show()
227::COMM;;Partial dependence plots, individual conditional expectation plots, or an
228::COMM;;overlay of both can be plotted by setting the `kind` parameter.
229::COMM;;This method generates one plot for each entry in `features`. The plots
230::COMM;;are arranged in a grid with `n_cols` columns. For one-way partial
231::COMM;;dependence plots, the deciles of the feature values are shown on the
232::COMM;;x-axis. For two-way plots, the deciles are shown on both axes and PDPs
233::COMM;;are contour plots.
234::COMM;;For general information regarding `scikit-learn` visualization tools, see
235::COMM;;the :ref:`Visualization Guide <visualizations>`.
236::COMM;;For guidance on interpreting these plots, refer to the
237::COMM;;:ref:`Inspection Guide <partial_dependence>`.
238::COMM;;For an example on how to use this class method, see
239::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_inspection_plot_partial_dependence.py`.
240::COMM;;.. note::
241::COMM;;:func:`PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator` does not support using the
242::COMM;;same axes with multiple calls. To plot the partial dependence for
243::COMM;;multiple estimators, please pass the axes created by the first call to the
244::COMM;;second call::
245::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay
246::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_friedman1
247::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
248::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
249::COMM;;>>> X, y = make_friedman1()
250::COMM;;>>> est1 = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
251::COMM;;>>> est2 = RandomForestRegressor().fit(X, y)
252::COMM;;>>> disp1 = PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(est1, X,
253::COMM;;... [1, 2])
254::COMM;;>>> disp2 = PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(est2, X, [1, 2],
255::COMM;;... ax=disp1.axes_)
256::COMM;;.. warning::
257::COMM;;For :class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier` and
258::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`, the
259::COMM;;`'recursion'` method (used by default) will not account for the `init`
260::COMM;;predictor of the boosting process. In practice, this will produce
261::COMM;;the same values as `'brute'` up to a constant offset in the target
262::COMM;;response, provided that `init` is a constant estimator (which is the
263::COMM;;default). However, if `init` is not a constant estimator, the
264::COMM;;partial dependence values are incorrect for `'recursion'` because the
265::COMM;;offset will be sample-dependent. It is preferable to use the `'brute'`
266::COMM;;method. Note that this only applies to
267::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier` and
268::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`, not to
269::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier` and
270::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`.
271::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
272::COMM;;Parameters
273::COMM;;----------
274::COMM;;estimator : BaseEstimator
275::COMM;;A fitted estimator object implementing :term:`predict`,
276::COMM;;:term:`predict_proba`, or :term:`decision_function`.
277::COMM;;Multioutput-multiclass classifiers are not supported.
278::COMM;;X : {array-like, dataframe} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
279::COMM;;``X`` is used to generate a grid of values for the target
280::COMM;;``features`` (where the partial dependence will be evaluated), and
281::COMM;;also to generate values for the complement features when the
282::COMM;;`method` is `'brute'`.
283::COMM;;features : list of {int, str, pair of int, pair of str}
284::COMM;;The target features for which to create the PDPs.
285::COMM;;If `features[i]` is an integer or a string, a one-way PDP is created;
286::COMM;;if `features[i]` is a tuple, a two-way PDP is created (only supported
287::COMM;;with `kind='average'`). Each tuple must be of size 2.
288::COMM;;If any entry is a string, then it must be in ``feature_names``.
289::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
290::COMM;;Sample weights are used to calculate weighted means when averaging the
291::COMM;;model output. If `None`, then samples are equally weighted. If
292::COMM;;`sample_weight` is not `None`, then `method` will be set to `'brute'`.
293::COMM;;Note that `sample_weight` is ignored for `kind='individual'`.
294::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
295::COMM;;categorical_features : array-like of shape (n_features,) or shape \
296::COMM;;(n_categorical_features,), dtype={bool, int, str}, default=None
297::COMM;;Indicates the categorical features.
298::COMM;;- `None`: no feature will be considered categorical;
299::COMM;;- boolean array-like: boolean mask of shape `(n_features,)`
300::COMM;;indicating which features are categorical. Thus, this array has
301::COMM;;the same shape has `X.shape[1]`;
302::COMM;;- integer or string array-like: integer indices or strings
303::COMM;;indicating categorical features.
304::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
305::COMM;;feature_names : array-like of shape (n_features,), dtype=str, default=None
306::COMM;;Name of each feature; `feature_names[i]` holds the name of the feature
307::COMM;;with index `i`.
308::COMM;;By default, the name of the feature corresponds to their numerical
309::COMM;;index for NumPy array and their column name for pandas dataframe.
310::COMM;;target : int, default=None
311::COMM;;- In a multiclass setting, specifies the class for which the PDPs
312::COMM;;should be computed. Note that for binary classification, the
313::COMM;;positive class (index 1) is always used.
314::COMM;;- In a multioutput setting, specifies the task for which the PDPs
315::COMM;;should be computed.
316::COMM;;Ignored in binary classification or classical regression settings.
317::COMM;;response_method : {'auto', 'predict_proba', 'decision_function'}, \
318::COMM;;default='auto'
319::COMM;;Specifies whether to use :term:`predict_proba` or
320::COMM;;:term:`decision_function` as the target response. For regressors
321::COMM;;this parameter is ignored and the response is always the output of
322::COMM;;:term:`predict`. By default, :term:`predict_proba` is tried first
323::COMM;;and we revert to :term:`decision_function` if it doesn't exist. If
324::COMM;;``method`` is `'recursion'`, the response is always the output of
325::COMM;;:term:`decision_function`.
326::COMM;;n_cols : int, default=3
327::COMM;;The maximum number of columns in the grid plot. Only active when `ax`
328::COMM;;is a single axis or `None`.
329::COMM;;grid_resolution : int, default=100
330::COMM;;The number of equally spaced points on the axes of the plots, for each
331::COMM;;target feature.
332::COMM;;This parameter is overridden by `custom_values` if that parameter is set.
333::COMM;;percentiles : tuple of float, default=(0.05, 0.95)
334::COMM;;The lower and upper percentile used to create the extreme values
335::COMM;;for the PDP axes. Must be in [0, 1].
336::COMM;;This parameter is overridden by `custom_values` if that parameter is set.
337::COMM;;custom_values : dict
338::COMM;;A dictionary mapping the index of an element of `features` to an
339::COMM;;array of values where the partial dependence should be calculated
340::COMM;;for that feature. Setting a range of values for a feature overrides
341::COMM;;`grid_resolution` and `percentiles`.
342::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
343::COMM;;method : str, default='auto'
344::COMM;;The method used to calculate the averaged predictions:
345::COMM;;- `'recursion'` is only supported for some tree-based estimators
346::COMM;;(namely
347::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier`,
348::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor`,
349::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier`,
350::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor`,
351::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeRegressor`,
352::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestRegressor`
353::COMM;;but is more efficient in terms of speed.
354::COMM;;With this method, the target response of a
355::COMM;;classifier is always the decision function, not the predicted
356::COMM;;probabilities. Since the `'recursion'` method implicitly computes
357::COMM;;the average of the ICEs by design, it is not compatible with ICE and
358::COMM;;thus `kind` must be `'average'`.
359::COMM;;- `'brute'` is supported for any estimator, but is more
360::COMM;;computationally intensive.
361::COMM;;- `'auto'`: the `'recursion'` is used for estimators that support it,
362::COMM;;and `'brute'` is used otherwise. If `sample_weight` is not `None`,
363::COMM;;then `'brute'` is used regardless of the estimator.
364::COMM;;Please see :ref:`this note <pdp_method_differences>` for
365::COMM;;differences between the `'brute'` and `'recursion'` method.
366::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
367::COMM;;The number of CPUs to use to compute the partial dependences.
368::COMM;;Computation is parallelized over features specified by the `features`
369::COMM;;parameter.
370::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
371::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
372::COMM;;for more details.
373::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
374::COMM;;Verbose output during PD computations.
375::COMM;;line_kw : dict, default=None
376::COMM;;Dict with keywords passed to the ``matplotlib.pyplot.plot`` call.
377::COMM;;For one-way partial dependence plots. It can be used to define common
378::COMM;;properties for both `ice_lines_kw` and `pdp_line_kw`.
379::COMM;;ice_lines_kw : dict, default=None
380::COMM;;Dictionary with keywords passed to the `matplotlib.pyplot.plot` call.
381::COMM;;For ICE lines in the one-way partial dependence plots.
382::COMM;;The key value pairs defined in `ice_lines_kw` takes priority over
383::COMM;;`line_kw`.
384::COMM;;pd_line_kw : dict, default=None
385::COMM;;Dictionary with keywords passed to the `matplotlib.pyplot.plot` call.
386::COMM;;For partial dependence in one-way partial dependence plots.
387::COMM;;The key value pairs defined in `pd_line_kw` takes priority over
388::COMM;;`line_kw`.
389::COMM;;contour_kw : dict, default=None
390::COMM;;Dict with keywords passed to the ``matplotlib.pyplot.contourf`` call.
391::COMM;;For two-way partial dependence plots.
392::COMM;;ax : Matplotlib axes or array-like of Matplotlib axes, default=None
393::COMM;;- If a single axis is passed in, it is treated as a bounding axes
394::COMM;;and a grid of partial dependence plots will be drawn within
395::COMM;;these bounds. The `n_cols` parameter controls the number of
396::COMM;;columns in the grid.
397::COMM;;- If an array-like of axes are passed in, the partial dependence
398::COMM;;plots will be drawn directly into these axes.
399::COMM;;- If `None`, a figure and a bounding axes is created and treated
400::COMM;;as the single axes case.
401::COMM;;kind : {'average', 'individual', 'both'}, default='average'
402::COMM;;Whether to plot the partial dependence averaged across all the samples
403::COMM;;in the dataset or one line per sample or both.
404::COMM;;- ``kind='average'`` results in the traditional PD plot;
405::COMM;;- ``kind='individual'`` results in the ICE plot.
406::COMM;;Note that the fast `method='recursion'` option is only available for
407::COMM;;`kind='average'` and `sample_weights=None`. Computing individual
408::COMM;;dependencies and doing weighted averages requires using the slower
409::COMM;;`method='brute'`.
410::COMM;;centered : bool, default=False
411::COMM;;If `True`, the ICE and PD lines will start at the origin of the
412::COMM;;y-axis. By default, no centering is done.
413::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.1
414::COMM;;subsample : float, int or None, default=1000
415::COMM;;Sampling for ICE curves when `kind` is 'individual' or 'both'.
416::COMM;;If `float`, should be between 0.0 and 1.0 and represent the proportion
417::COMM;;of the dataset to be used to plot ICE curves. If `int`, represents the
418::COMM;;absolute number samples to use.
419::COMM;;Note that the full dataset is still used to calculate averaged partial
420::COMM;;dependence when `kind='both'`.
421::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
422::COMM;;Controls the randomness of the selected samples when subsamples is not
423::COMM;;`None` and `kind` is either `'both'` or `'individual'`.
424::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
425::COMM;;Returns
426::COMM;;-------
427::COMM;;display : :class:`~sklearn.inspection.PartialDependenceDisplay`
428::COMM;;See Also
429::COMM;;--------
430::COMM;;partial_dependence : Compute Partial Dependence values.
431::COMM;;Examples

435::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
436::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay

439::COMM;;>>> PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(clf, X, [0, (0, 1)])
440::COMM;;<...>
441::COMM;;>>> plt.show()

24::COMM;;def check_increasing(x, y):
58::COMM;;# Calculate Spearman rho estimate and set return accordingly.
59::COMM;;rho, _ = spearmanr(x, y)
60::COMM;;increasing_bool = rho >= 0
61::COMM;;# Run Fisher transform to get the rho CI, but handle rho=+/-1
62::COMM;;if rho not in [-1.0, 1.0] and len(x) > 3:
63::COMM;;F = 0.5 * math.log((1.0 + rho) / (1.0 - rho))
64::COMM;;F_se = 1 / math.sqrt(len(x) - 3)
65::COMM;;# Use a 95% CI, i.e., +/-1.96 S.E.
66::COMM;;# https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher_transformation
67::COMM;;rho_0 = math.tanh(F - 1.96 * F_se)
68::COMM;;rho_1 = math.tanh(F + 1.96 * F_se)
69::COMM;;# Warn if the CI spans zero.
70::COMM;;if np.sign(rho_0) != np.sign(rho_1):
71::COMM;;warnings.warn(
72::COMM;;"Confidence interval of the Spearman "
73::COMM;;"correlation coefficient spans zero. "
74::COMM;;"Determination of ``increasing`` may be "
75::COMM;;"suspect."
76::COMM;;)
77::COMM;;return increasing_bool

29::COMM;;class PolynomialCountSketch(
30::COMM;;ClassNamePrefixFeaturesOutMixin, TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator
31::COMM;;):
100::COMM;;_parameter_constraints: dict = {
101::COMM;;"gamma": [Interval(Real, 0, None, closed="left")],
102::COMM;;"degree": [Interval(Integral, 1, None, closed="left")],
103::COMM;;"coef0": [Interval(Real, None, None, closed="neither")],
104::COMM;;"n_components": [Interval(Integral, 1, None, closed="left")],
105::COMM;;"random_state": ["random_state"],
106::COMM;;}
107::COMM;;def __init__(
108::COMM;;self, *, gamma=1.0, degree=2, coef0=0, n_components=100, random_state=None
109::COMM;;):
110::COMM;;self.gamma = gamma
111::COMM;;self.degree = degree
112::COMM;;self.coef0 = coef0
113::COMM;;self.n_components = n_components
114::COMM;;self.random_state = random_state
115::COMM;;@_fit_context(prefer_skip_nested_validation=True)
116::COMM;;def fit(self, X, y=None):
133::COMM;;X = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csc")
134::COMM;;random_state = check_random_state(self.random_state)
135::COMM;;n_features = X.shape[1]
136::COMM;;if self.coef0 != 0:
137::COMM;;n_features += 1
138::COMM;;self.indexHash_ = random_state.randint(
139::COMM;;0, high=self.n_components, size=(self.degree, n_features)
140::COMM;;)
141::COMM;;self.bitHash_ = random_state.choice(a=[-1, 1], size=(self.degree, n_features))
142::COMM;;self._n_features_out = self.n_components
143::COMM;;return self
144::COMM;;def transform(self, X):
156::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
157::COMM;;X = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csc", reset=False)
158::COMM;;X_gamma = np.sqrt(self.gamma) * X
159::COMM;;if sp.issparse(X_gamma) and self.coef0 != 0:
160::COMM;;X_gamma = sp.hstack(
161::COMM;;[X_gamma, np.sqrt(self.coef0) * np.ones((X_gamma.shape[0], 1))],
162::COMM;;format="csc",
163::COMM;;)
164::COMM;;elif not sp.issparse(X_gamma) and self.coef0 != 0:
165::COMM;;X_gamma = np.hstack(
166::COMM;;[X_gamma, np.sqrt(self.coef0) * np.ones((X_gamma.shape[0], 1))]
167::COMM;;)
168::COMM;;if X_gamma.shape[1] != self.indexHash_.shape[1]:
169::COMM;;raise ValueError(
170::COMM;;"Number of features of test samples does not"
171::COMM;;" match that of training samples."
172::COMM;;)
173::COMM;;count_sketches = np.zeros((X_gamma.shape[0], self.degree, self.n_components))
174::COMM;;if sp.issparse(X_gamma):
175::COMM;;for j in range(X_gamma.shape[1]):
176::COMM;;for d in range(self.degree):
177::COMM;;iHashIndex = self.indexHash_[d, j]
178::COMM;;iHashBit = self.bitHash_[d, j]
179::COMM;;count_sketches[:, d, iHashIndex] += (
180::COMM;;(iHashBit * X_gamma[:, [j]]).toarray().ravel()
181::COMM;;)
182::COMM;;else:
183::COMM;;for j in range(X_gamma.shape[1]):
184::COMM;;for d in range(self.degree):
185::COMM;;iHashIndex = self.indexHash_[d, j]
186::COMM;;iHashBit = self.bitHash_[d, j]
187::COMM;;count_sketches[:, d, iHashIndex] += iHashBit * X_gamma[:, j]
188::COMM;;# For each same, compute a count sketch of phi(x) using the polynomial
189::COMM;;# multiplication (via FFT) of p count sketches of x.
190::COMM;;count_sketches_fft = fft(count_sketches, axis=2, overwrite_x=True)
191::COMM;;count_sketches_fft_prod = np.prod(count_sketches_fft, axis=1)
192::COMM;;data_sketch = np.real(ifft(count_sketches_fft_prod, overwrite_x=True))
193::COMM;;return data_sketch

265::COMM;;"gamma": [
266::COMM;;StrOptions({"scale"}),
267::COMM;;Interval(Real, 0.0, None, closed="left"),
268::COMM;;],
269::COMM;;"n_components": [Interval(Integral, 1, None, closed="left")],
270::COMM;;"random_state": ["random_state"],
271::COMM;;}
272::COMM;;def __init__(self, *, gamma=1.0, n_components=100, random_state=None):
273::COMM;;self.gamma = gamma
274::COMM;;self.n_components = n_components
275::COMM;;self.random_state = random_state

277::COMM;;def fit(self, X, y=None):

294::COMM;;random_state = check_random_state(self.random_state)
295::COMM;;n_features = X.shape[1]
296::COMM;;sparse = sp.issparse(X)
297::COMM;;if self.gamma == "scale":
298::COMM;;# var = E[X^2] - E[X]^2 if sparse
299::COMM;;X_var = (X.multiply(X)).mean() - (X.mean()) ** 2 if sparse else X.var()
300::COMM;;self._gamma = 1.0 / (n_features * X_var) if X_var != 0 else 1.0
301::COMM;;else:
