304::COMM;;size=(n_features, self.n_components)
305::COMM;;)
306::COMM;;self.random_offset_ = random_state.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, size=self.n_components)
307::COMM;;if X.dtype == np.float32:
308::COMM;;# Setting the data type of the fitted attribute will ensure the
309::COMM;;# output data type during `transform`.
310::COMM;;self.random_weights_ = self.random_weights_.astype(X.dtype, copy=False)
311::COMM;;self.random_offset_ = self.random_offset_.astype(X.dtype, copy=False)
312::COMM;;self._n_features_out = self.n_components
313::COMM;;return self
314::COMM;;def transform(self, X):
326::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
327::COMM;;X = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csr", reset=False)
328::COMM;;projection = safe_sparse_dot(X, self.random_weights_)
329::COMM;;projection += self.random_offset_
330::COMM;;np.cos(projection, projection)
331::COMM;;projection *= (2.0 / self.n_components) ** 0.5
332::COMM;;return projection

469::COMM;;class AdditiveChi2Sampler(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):

538::COMM;;def fit(self, X, y=None):
555::COMM;;X = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csr", ensure_non_negative=True)
556::COMM;;if self.sample_interval is None and self.sample_steps not in (1, 2, 3):

562::COMM;;def transform(self, X):
576::COMM;;X = validate_data(
577::COMM;;self, X, accept_sparse="csr", reset=False, ensure_non_negative=True
578::COMM;;)
579::COMM;;sparse = sp.issparse(X)
580::COMM;;if self.sample_interval is None:
581::COMM;;# See figure 2 c) of "Efficient additive kernels via explicit feature maps"
582::COMM;;# <http://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vedaldi/assets/pubs/vedaldi11efficient.pdf>
583::COMM;;# A. Vedaldi and A. Zisserman, Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence,
584::COMM;;# 2011
585::COMM;;if self.sample_steps == 1:

587::COMM;;elif self.sample_steps == 2:

589::COMM;;elif self.sample_steps == 3:

591::COMM;;else:
592::COMM;;raise ValueError(

594::COMM;;" you need to provide sample_interval"
595::COMM;;)
596::COMM;;else:
597::COMM;;sample_interval = self.sample_interval
598::COMM;;# zeroth component
599::COMM;;# 1/cosh = sech
600::COMM;;# cosh(0) = 1.0
601::COMM;;transf = self._transform_sparse if sparse else self._transform_dense
602::COMM;;return transf(X, self.sample_steps, sample_interval)
603::COMM;;def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
614::COMM;;# Note that passing attributes="n_features_in_" forces check_is_fitted
615::COMM;;# to check if the attribute is present. Otherwise it will pass on this
616::COMM;;# stateless estimator (requires_fit=False)
617::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self, attributes="n_features_in_")
618::COMM;;input_features = _check_feature_names_in(
619::COMM;;self, input_features, generate_names=True
620::COMM;;)
621::COMM;;est_name = self.__class__.__name__.lower()
622::COMM;;names_list = [f"{est_name}_{name}_sqrt" for name in input_features]
623::COMM;;for j in range(1, self.sample_steps):
624::COMM;;cos_names = [f"{est_name}_{name}_cos{j}" for name in input_features]
625::COMM;;sin_names = [f"{est_name}_{name}_sin{j}" for name in input_features]
626::COMM;;names_list.extend(cos_names + sin_names)
627::COMM;;return np.asarray(names_list, dtype=object)
628::COMM;;@staticmethod
629::COMM;;def _transform_dense(X, sample_steps, sample_interval):
630::COMM;;non_zero = X != 0.0
631::COMM;;X_nz = X[non_zero]
632::COMM;;X_step = np.zeros_like(X)
633::COMM;;X_step[non_zero] = np.sqrt(X_nz * sample_interval)
634::COMM;;X_new = [X_step]
635::COMM;;log_step_nz = sample_interval * np.log(X_nz)
636::COMM;;step_nz = 2 * X_nz * sample_interval
637::COMM;;for j in range(1, sample_steps):
638::COMM;;factor_nz = np.sqrt(step_nz / np.cosh(np.pi * j * sample_interval))
639::COMM;;X_step = np.zeros_like(X)
640::COMM;;X_step[non_zero] = factor_nz * np.cos(j * log_step_nz)
641::COMM;;X_new.append(X_step)
642::COMM;;X_step = np.zeros_like(X)
643::COMM;;X_step[non_zero] = factor_nz * np.sin(j * log_step_nz)
644::COMM;;X_new.append(X_step)
645::COMM;;return np.hstack(X_new)
646::COMM;;@staticmethod
647::COMM;;def _transform_sparse(X, sample_steps, sample_interval):
648::COMM;;indices = X.indices.copy()
649::COMM;;indptr = X.indptr.copy()
650::COMM;;data_step = np.sqrt(X.data * sample_interval)
651::COMM;;X_step = sp.csr_matrix(
652::COMM;;(data_step, indices, indptr), shape=X.shape, dtype=X.dtype, copy=False
653::COMM;;)
654::COMM;;X_new = [X_step]
655::COMM;;log_step_nz = sample_interval * np.log(X.data)
656::COMM;;step_nz = 2 * X.data * sample_interval
657::COMM;;for j in range(1, sample_steps):
658::COMM;;factor_nz = np.sqrt(step_nz / np.cosh(np.pi * j * sample_interval))
659::COMM;;data_step = factor_nz * np.cos(j * log_step_nz)
660::COMM;;X_step = sp.csr_matrix(
661::COMM;;(data_step, indices, indptr), shape=X.shape, dtype=X.dtype, copy=False
662::COMM;;)
663::COMM;;X_new.append(X_step)
664::COMM;;data_step = factor_nz * np.sin(j * log_step_nz)
665::COMM;;X_step = sp.csr_matrix(
666::COMM;;(data_step, indices, indptr), shape=X.shape, dtype=X.dtype, copy=False
667::COMM;;)
668::COMM;;X_new.append(X_step)
669::COMM;;return sp.hstack(X_new)

672::COMM;;tags.requires_fit = False
673::COMM;;tags.input_tags.positive_only = True

780::COMM;;def __init__(
781::COMM;;self,
782::COMM;;kernel="rbf",

785::COMM;;coef0=None,

794::COMM;;self.coef0 = coef0

798::COMM;;self.random_state = random_state

801::COMM;;def fit(self, X, y=None):
818::COMM;;X = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csr")
819::COMM;;rnd = check_random_state(self.random_state)
820::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
821::COMM;;# get basis vectors
822::COMM;;if self.n_components > n_samples:
823::COMM;;# XXX should we just bail?
824::COMM;;n_components = n_samples
825::COMM;;warnings.warn(
826::COMM;;"n_components > n_samples. This is not possible.\n"
827::COMM;;"n_components was set to n_samples, which results"
828::COMM;;" in inefficient evaluation of the full kernel."
829::COMM;;)
830::COMM;;else:

832::COMM;;n_components = min(n_samples, n_components)
833::COMM;;inds = rnd.permutation(n_samples)
834::COMM;;basis_inds = inds[:n_components]
835::COMM;;basis = X[basis_inds]
836::COMM;;basis_kernel = pairwise_kernels(
837::COMM;;basis,
838::COMM;;metric=self.kernel,
839::COMM;;filter_params=True,
840::COMM;;n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
841::COMM;;**self._get_kernel_params(),
842::COMM;;)

844::COMM;;U, S, V = svd(basis_kernel)
845::COMM;;S = np.maximum(S, 1e-12)
846::COMM;;self.normalization_ = np.dot(U / np.sqrt(S), V)
847::COMM;;self.components_ = basis
848::COMM;;self.component_indices_ = basis_inds
849::COMM;;self._n_features_out = n_components
850::COMM;;return self

866::COMM;;kernel_params = self._get_kernel_params()

868::COMM;;X,
869::COMM;;self.components_,
870::COMM;;metric=self.kernel,
871::COMM;;filter_params=True,
872::COMM;;n_jobs=self.n_jobs,
873::COMM;;**kernel_params,
874::COMM;;)
875::COMM;;return np.dot(embedded, self.normalization_.T)
876::COMM;;def _get_kernel_params(self):
877::COMM;;params = self.kernel_params
878::COMM;;if params is None:
879::COMM;;params = {}
880::COMM;;if not callable(self.kernel) and self.kernel != "precomputed":
881::COMM;;for param in KERNEL_PARAMS[self.kernel]:
882::COMM;;if getattr(self, param) is not None:
883::COMM;;params[param] = getattr(self, param)
884::COMM;;else:

887::COMM;;or self.coef0 is not None

75::COMO;;# seed should never be 0 in SequentialDataset64
103::COMM;;This helper is in charge of the following steps:
104::COMM;;- `sample_weight` is assumed to be `None` or a validated array with same dtype as
105::COMM;;`X`.
106::COMM;;- If `check_input=True`, perform standard input validation of `X`, `y`.
107::COMM;;- Perform copies if requested to avoid side-effects in case of inplace
108::COMM;;modifications of the input.
109::COMM;;Then, if `fit_intercept=True` this preprocessing centers both `X` and `y` as
110::COMM;;follows:
111::COMM;;- if `X` is dense, center the data and
112::COMM;;store the mean vector in `X_offset`.
113::COMM;;- if `X` is sparse, store the mean in `X_offset`
114::COMM;;without centering `X`. The centering is expected to be handled by the
115::COMM;;linear solver where appropriate.
116::COMM;;- in either case, always center `y` and store the mean in `y_offset`.
117::COMM;;- both `X_offset` and `y_offset` are always weighted by `sample_weight`
118::COMM;;if not set to `None`.
119::COMM;;If `fit_intercept=False`, no centering is performed and `X_offset`, `y_offset`
120::COMM;;are set to zero.
121::COMM;;If `rescale_with_sw` is True, then X and y are rescaled with the square root of
122::COMM;;sample weights.
123::COMM;;Returns
124::COMM;;-------
125::COMM;;X_out : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
126::COMM;;If copy=True a copy of the input X is triggered, otherwise operations are
127::COMM;;inplace.
128::COMM;;If input X is dense, then X_out is centered.
129::COMM;;y_out : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_targets)
130::COMM;;Centered version of y. Possibly performed inplace on input y depending
131::COMM;;on the copy_y parameter.
132::COMM;;X_offset : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
133::COMM;;The mean per column of input X.
134::COMM;;y_offset : float or ndarray of shape (n_features,)
135::COMM;;X_scale : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
136::COMM;;Always an array of ones. TODO: refactor the code base to make it
137::COMM;;possible to remove this unused variable.
138::COMM;;sample_weight_sqrt : ndarray of shape (n_samples, ) or None
139::COMM;;`np.sqrt(sample_weight)`
172::COMO;;# X_scale is no longer needed. It is a historic artifact from the
173::COMO;;# time where linear model exposed the normalize parameter.
176::COMO;;# Sample weight can be implemented via a simple rescaling.
177::COMO;;# For sparse X and y, it triggers copies anyway.
178::COMO;;# For dense X and y that already have been copied, we safely do inplace
179::COMO;;# rescaling.
186::COMM;;For many linear models, this enables easy support for sample_weight because
187::COMM;;(y - X w)' S (y - X w)

189::COMM;;||y_rescaled - X_rescaled w||_2^2

625::COMM;;raise ValueError(

18::COMO;;# BayesianRidge regression
21::COMM;;Fit a Bayesian ridge model. See the Notes section for details on this
22::COMM;;implementation and the optimization of the regularization parameters
23::COMM;;lambda (precision of the weights) and alpha (precision of the noise).
24::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <bayesian_regression>`.
25::COMM;;For an intuitive visualization of how the sinusoid is approximated by
26::COMM;;a polynomial using different pairs of initial values, see
27::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_bayesian_ridge_curvefit.py`.
28::COMM;;Parameters
29::COMM;;----------
30::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
31::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations over the complete dataset before
32::COMM;;stopping independently of any early stopping criterion.
33::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.3
34::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-3
35::COMM;;Stop the algorithm if w has converged.
36::COMM;;alpha_1 : float, default=1e-6
37::COMM;;Hyper-parameter : shape parameter for the Gamma distribution prior
38::COMM;;over the alpha parameter.
39::COMM;;alpha_2 : float, default=1e-6
40::COMM;;Hyper-parameter : inverse scale parameter (rate parameter) for the
41::COMM;;Gamma distribution prior over the alpha parameter.
42::COMM;;lambda_1 : float, default=1e-6
43::COMM;;Hyper-parameter : shape parameter for the Gamma distribution prior
44::COMM;;over the lambda parameter.
45::COMM;;lambda_2 : float, default=1e-6
46::COMM;;Hyper-parameter : inverse scale parameter (rate parameter) for the
47::COMM;;Gamma distribution prior over the lambda parameter.
48::COMM;;alpha_init : float, default=None
49::COMM;;Initial value for alpha (precision of the noise).
50::COMM;;If not set, alpha_init is 1/Var(y).
51::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
52::COMM;;lambda_init : float, default=None
53::COMM;;Initial value for lambda (precision of the weights).
54::COMM;;If not set, lambda_init is 1.
55::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
56::COMM;;compute_score : bool, default=False
57::COMM;;If True, compute the log marginal likelihood at each iteration of the
58::COMM;;optimization.
59::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
60::COMM;;Whether to calculate the intercept for this model.
61::COMM;;The intercept is not treated as a probabilistic parameter
62::COMM;;and thus has no associated variance. If set
63::COMM;;to False, no intercept will be used in calculations
64::COMM;;(i.e. data is expected to be centered).
65::COMM;;copy_X : bool, default=True
66::COMM;;If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
67::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
68::COMM;;Verbose mode when fitting the model.

84::COMM;;maximized) at each iteration of the optimization. The array starts
85::COMM;;with the value of the log marginal likelihood obtained for the initial
86::COMM;;values of alpha and lambda and ends with the value obtained for the
87::COMM;;estimated alpha and lambda.

92::COMM;;zero mean. Set to np.zeros(n_features) otherwise.

100::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.

102::COMM;;See Also
103::COMM;;--------
104::COMM;;ARDRegression : Bayesian ARD regression.
105::COMM;;Notes
106::COMM;;-----
107::COMM;;There exist several strategies to perform Bayesian ridge regression. This
108::COMM;;implementation is based on the algorithm described in Appendix A of
109::COMM;;(Tipping, 2001) where updates of the regularization parameters are done as
110::COMM;;suggested in (MacKay, 1992). Note that according to A New
111::COMM;;View of Automatic Relevance Determination (Wipf and Nagarajan, 2008) these
112::COMM;;update rules do not guarantee that the marginal likelihood is increasing
113::COMM;;between two consecutive iterations of the optimization.
114::COMM;;References
115::COMM;;----------
116::COMM;;D. J. C. MacKay, Bayesian Interpolation, Computation and Neural Systems,
117::COMM;;Vol. 4, No. 3, 1992.
118::COMM;;M. E. Tipping, Sparse Bayesian Learning and the Relevance Vector Machine,
119::COMM;;Journal of Machine Learning Research, Vol. 1, 2001.
120::COMM;;Examples
121::COMM;;--------
122::COMM;;>>> from sklearn import linear_model
123::COMM;;>>> clf = linear_model.BayesianRidge()
124::COMM;;>>> clf.fit([[0,0], [1, 1], [2, 2]], [0, 1, 2])
125::COMM;;BayesianRidge()
126::COMM;;>>> clf.predict([[1, 1]])
127::COMM;;array([1.])

180::COMM;;sample_weight : ndarray of shape (n_samples,), default=None
181::COMM;;Individual weights for each sample.

310::COMM;;In addition to the mean of the predictive distribution, also its
311::COMM;;standard deviation can be returned.

314::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
315::COMM;;Samples.

317::COMM;;Whether to return the standard deviation of posterior prediction.
318::COMM;;Returns

322::COMM;;y_std : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
323::COMM;;Standard deviation of predictive distribution of query points.
336::COMM;;Posterior mean is given by coef_ = scaled_sigma_ * X.T * y where
337::COMM;;scaled_sigma_ = (lambda_/alpha_ * np.eye(n_features)
338::COMM;;+ np.dot(X.T, X))^-1
348::COMO;;# Note: we do not need to explicitly use the weights in this sum because
349::COMO;;# y and X were preprocessed by _rescale_data to handle the weights.
356::COMM;;alpha_1 = self.alpha_1
357::COMM;;alpha_2 = self.alpha_2
358::COMM;;lambda_1 = self.lambda_1
359::COMM;;lambda_2 = self.lambda_2
360::COMM;;# compute the log of the determinant of the posterior covariance.
361::COMM;;# posterior covariance is given by
362::COMM;;# sigma = (lambda_ * np.eye(n_features) + alpha_ * np.dot(X.T, X))^-1
363::COMM;;if n_samples > n_features:
364::COMM;;logdet_sigma = -np.sum(np.log(lambda_ + alpha_ * eigen_vals))
365::COMM;;else:
366::COMM;;logdet_sigma = np.full(n_features, lambda_, dtype=np.array(lambda_).dtype)
367::COMM;;logdet_sigma[:n_samples] += alpha_ * eigen_vals
368::COMM;;logdet_sigma = -np.sum(np.log(logdet_sigma))
369::COMM;;score = lambda_1 * log(lambda_) - lambda_2 * lambda_
370::COMM;;score += alpha_1 * log(alpha_) - alpha_2 * alpha_
371::COMM;;score += 0.5 * (
372::COMM;;n_features * log(lambda_)
373::COMM;;+ sw_sum * log(alpha_)
374::COMM;;- alpha_ * sse
375::COMM;;- lambda_ * np.sum(coef**2)
376::COMM;;+ logdet_sigma
377::COMM;;- sw_sum * log(2 * np.pi)
378::COMM;;)
379::COMM;;return score

535::COMM;;X, y = validate_data(
536::COMM;;self,
537::COMM;;X,
538::COMM;;y,
539::COMM;;dtype=[np.float64, np.float32],
540::COMM;;force_writeable=True,
541::COMM;;y_numeric=True,
542::COMM;;ensure_min_samples=2,
543::COMM;;)
544::COMM;;dtype = X.dtype
545::COMM;;n_samples, n_features = X.shape
546::COMM;;coef_ = np.zeros(n_features, dtype=dtype)
547::COMM;;X, y, X_offset_, y_offset_, X_scale_, _ = _preprocess_data(
548::COMM;;X, y, fit_intercept=self.fit_intercept, copy=self.copy_X
549::COMM;;)
550::COMM;;self.X_offset_ = X_offset_
551::COMM;;self.X_scale_ = X_scale_
552::COMM;;# Launch the convergence loop
553::COMM;;keep_lambda = np.ones(n_features, dtype=bool)
554::COMM;;lambda_1 = self.lambda_1
555::COMM;;lambda_2 = self.lambda_2
556::COMM;;alpha_1 = self.alpha_1
557::COMM;;alpha_2 = self.alpha_2
558::COMM;;verbose = self.verbose
559::COMM;;# Initialization of the values of the parameters
560::COMM;;eps = np.finfo(np.float64).eps
561::COMM;;# Add `eps` in the denominator to omit division by zero if `np.var(y)`
562::COMM;;# is zero.
563::COMM;;# Explicitly set dtype to avoid unintended type promotion with numpy 2.
564::COMM;;alpha_ = np.asarray(1.0 / (np.var(y) + eps), dtype=dtype)
565::COMM;;lambda_ = np.ones(n_features, dtype=dtype)
566::COMM;;self.scores_ = list()
567::COMM;;coef_old_ = None
568::COMM;;def update_coeff(X, y, coef_, alpha_, keep_lambda, sigma_):
569::COMM;;coef_[keep_lambda] = alpha_ * np.linalg.multi_dot(
570::COMM;;[sigma_, X[:, keep_lambda].T, y]
571::COMM;;)
572::COMM;;return coef_
573::COMM;;update_sigma = (
574::COMM;;self._update_sigma
575::COMM;;if n_samples >= n_features
576::COMM;;else self._update_sigma_woodbury
577::COMM;;)
578::COMM;;# Iterative procedure of ARDRegression
579::COMM;;for iter_ in range(self.max_iter):
580::COMM;;sigma_ = update_sigma(X, alpha_, lambda_, keep_lambda)
581::COMM;;coef_ = update_coeff(X, y, coef_, alpha_, keep_lambda, sigma_)
582::COMM;;# Update alpha and lambda
583::COMM;;sse_ = np.sum((y - np.dot(X, coef_)) ** 2)
584::COMM;;gamma_ = 1.0 - lambda_[keep_lambda] * np.diag(sigma_)
585::COMM;;lambda_[keep_lambda] = (gamma_ + 2.0 * lambda_1) / (
586::COMM;;(coef_[keep_lambda]) ** 2 + 2.0 * lambda_2
587::COMM;;)
588::COMM;;alpha_ = (n_samples - gamma_.sum() + 2.0 * alpha_1) / (sse_ + 2.0 * alpha_2)
589::COMM;;# Prune the weights with a precision over a threshold
590::COMM;;keep_lambda = lambda_ < self.threshold_lambda
591::COMM;;coef_[~keep_lambda] = 0
592::COMM;;# Compute the objective function
593::COMM;;if self.compute_score:
594::COMM;;s = (lambda_1 * np.log(lambda_) - lambda_2 * lambda_).sum()
595::COMM;;s += alpha_1 * log(alpha_) - alpha_2 * alpha_
596::COMM;;s += 0.5 * (
597::COMM;;fast_logdet(sigma_)
598::COMM;;+ n_samples * log(alpha_)
599::COMM;;+ np.sum(np.log(lambda_))
600::COMM;;)
601::COMM;;s -= 0.5 * (alpha_ * sse_ + (lambda_ * coef_**2).sum())
602::COMM;;self.scores_.append(s)
603::COMM;;# Check for convergence
604::COMM;;if iter_ > 0 and np.sum(np.abs(coef_old_ - coef_)) < self.tol:
605::COMM;;if verbose:
606::COMM;;print("Converged after %s iterations" % iter_)
607::COMM;;break
608::COMM;;coef_old_ = np.copy(coef_)
609::COMM;;if not keep_lambda.any():
610::COMM;;break
611::COMM;;self.n_iter_ = iter_ + 1
612::COMM;;if keep_lambda.any():
613::COMM;;# update sigma and mu using updated params from the last iteration
614::COMM;;sigma_ = update_sigma(X, alpha_, lambda_, keep_lambda)
615::COMM;;coef_ = update_coeff(X, y, coef_, alpha_, keep_lambda, sigma_)
616::COMM;;else:
617::COMM;;sigma_ = np.array([]).reshape(0, 0)
618::COMM;;self.coef_ = coef_
619::COMM;;self.alpha_ = alpha_
620::COMM;;self.sigma_ = sigma_
621::COMM;;self.lambda_ = lambda_
622::COMM;;self._set_intercept(X_offset_, y_offset_, X_scale_)
623::COMM;;return self
624::COMM;;def _update_sigma_woodbury(self, X, alpha_, lambda_, keep_lambda):
625::COMM;;# See slides as referenced in the docstring note
626::COMM;;# this function is used when n_samples < n_features and will invert
627::COMM;;# a matrix of shape (n_samples, n_samples) making use of the
628::COMM;;# woodbury formula:
629::COMM;;# https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbury_matrix_identity
630::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
631::COMM;;X_keep = X[:, keep_lambda]
632::COMM;;inv_lambda = 1 / lambda_[keep_lambda].reshape(1, -1)
633::COMM;;sigma_ = pinvh(
634::COMM;;np.eye(n_samples, dtype=X.dtype) / alpha_
635::COMM;;+ np.dot(X_keep * inv_lambda, X_keep.T)
636::COMM;;)
637::COMM;;sigma_ = np.dot(sigma_, X_keep * inv_lambda)
638::COMM;;sigma_ = -np.dot(inv_lambda.reshape(-1, 1) * X_keep.T, sigma_)
639::COMM;;sigma_[np.diag_indices(sigma_.shape[1])] += 1.0 / lambda_[keep_lambda]
640::COMM;;return sigma_
641::COMM;;def _update_sigma(self, X, alpha_, lambda_, keep_lambda):
642::COMM;;# See slides as referenced in the docstring note
643::COMM;;# this function is used when n_samples >= n_features and will
644::COMM;;# invert a matrix of shape (n_features, n_features)
645::COMM;;X_keep = X[:, keep_lambda]
646::COMM;;gram = np.dot(X_keep.T, X_keep)
647::COMM;;eye = np.eye(gram.shape[0], dtype=X.dtype)
648::COMM;;sigma_inv = lambda_[keep_lambda] * eye + alpha_ * gram
649::COMM;;sigma_ = pinvh(sigma_inv)
650::COMM;;return sigma_
651::COMM;;def predict(self, X, return_std=False):
668::COMM;;y_mean = self._decision_function(X)
669::COMM;;if return_std is False:
670::COMM;;return y_mean
671::COMM;;else:
672::COMM;;col_index = self.lambda_ < self.threshold_lambda
673::COMM;;X = _safe_indexing(X, indices=col_index, axis=1)
674::COMM;;sigmas_squared_data = (np.dot(X, self.sigma_) * X).sum(axis=1)
675::COMM;;y_std = np.sqrt(sigmas_squared_data + (1.0 / self.alpha_))
676::COMM;;return y_mean, y_std

201::COMM;;The Lasso optimization function varies for mono and multi-outputs.
202::COMM;;For mono-output tasks it is::
203::COMM;;(1 / (2 * n_samples)) * ||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha * ||w||_1
204::COMM;;For multi-output tasks it is::
205::COMM;;(1 / (2 * n_samples)) * ||Y - XW||^2_Fro + alpha * ||W||_21
206::COMM;;Where::
207::COMM;;||W||_21 = \\sum_i \\sqrt{\\sum_j w_{ij}^2}
208::COMM;;i.e. the sum of norm of each row.
209::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <lasso>`.

276::COMM;;<sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_lasso_lasso_lars_elasticnet_path.py>`.
277::COMM;;To avoid unnecessary memory duplication the X argument of the fit method
278::COMM;;should be directly passed as a Fortran-contiguous numpy array.
279::COMM;;Note that in certain cases, the Lars solver may be significantly
280::COMM;;faster to implement this functionality. In particular, linear
281::COMM;;interpolation can be used to retrieve model coefficients between the
282::COMM;;values output by lars_path.
283::COMM;;The underlying coordinate descent solver uses gap safe screening rules to speedup
284::COMM;;fitting time, see :ref:`User Guide on coordinate descent <coordinate_descent>`.
285::COMM;;Examples
286::COMM;;--------
287::COMM;;Comparing lasso_path and lars_path with interpolation:
288::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
289::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import lasso_path
290::COMM;;>>> X = np.array([[1, 2, 3.1], [2.3, 5.4, 4.3]]).T
291::COMM;;>>> y = np.array([1, 2, 3.1])
292::COMM;;>>> # Use lasso_path to compute a coefficient path
293::COMM;;>>> _, coef_path, _ = lasso_path(X, y, alphas=[5., 1., .5])
294::COMM;;>>> print(coef_path)
295::COMM;;[[0. 0. 0.46874778]
296::COMM;;[0.2159048 0.4425765 0.23689075]]
297::COMM;;>>> # Now use lars_path and 1D linear interpolation to compute the
298::COMM;;>>> # same path
299::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import lars_path
300::COMM;;>>> alphas, active, coef_path_lars = lars_path(X, y, method='lasso')
301::COMM;;>>> from scipy import interpolate
302::COMM;;>>> coef_path_continuous = interpolate.interp1d(alphas[::-1],
303::COMM;;... coef_path_lars[:, ::-1])
304::COMM;;>>> print(coef_path_continuous([5., 1., .5]))
305::COMM;;[[0. 0. 0.46915237]
306::COMM;;[0.2159048 0.4425765 0.23668876]]
362::COMM;;The elastic net optimization function varies for mono and multi-outputs.
363::COMM;;For mono-output tasks it is::
364::COMM;;1 / (2 * n_samples) * ||y - Xw||^2_2
365::COMM;;+ alpha * l1_ratio * ||w||_1
366::COMM;;+ 0.5 * alpha * (1 - l1_ratio) * ||w||^2_2
367::COMM;;For multi-output tasks it is::
368::COMM;;(1 / (2 * n_samples)) * ||Y - XW||_Fro^2
369::COMM;;+ alpha * l1_ratio * ||W||_21
370::COMM;;+ 0.5 * alpha * (1 - l1_ratio) * ||W||_Fro^2
371::COMM;;Where::
372::COMM;;||W||_21 = \\sum_i \\sqrt{\\sum_j w_{ij}^2}
373::COMM;;i.e. the sum of norm of each row.
374::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <elastic_net>`.
375::COMM;;Parameters
376::COMM;;----------
377::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
378::COMM;;Training data. Pass directly as Fortran-contiguous data to avoid
379::COMM;;unnecessary memory duplication. If ``y`` is mono-output then ``X``
380::COMM;;can be sparse.
381::COMM;;y : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples,) or \
382::COMM;;(n_samples, n_targets)
383::COMM;;Target values.
384::COMM;;l1_ratio : float, default=0.5
385::COMM;;Number between 0 and 1 passed to elastic net (scaling between
386::COMM;;l1 and l2 penalties). ``l1_ratio=1`` corresponds to the Lasso.
387::COMM;;eps : float, default=1e-3
388::COMM;;Length of the path. ``eps=1e-3`` means that
389::COMM;;``alpha_min / alpha_max = 1e-3``.
390::COMM;;n_alphas : int, default=100
391::COMM;;Number of alphas along the regularization path.
392::COMM;;alphas : array-like, default=None
393::COMM;;List of alphas where to compute the models.
394::COMM;;If None alphas are set automatically.
395::COMM;;precompute : 'auto', bool or array-like of shape \
396::COMM;;(n_features, n_features), default='auto'
397::COMM;;Whether to use a precomputed Gram matrix to speed up
398::COMM;;calculations. If set to ``'auto'`` let us decide. The Gram
399::COMM;;matrix can also be passed as argument.
400::COMM;;Xy : array-like of shape (n_features,) or (n_features, n_targets),\
401::COMM;;default=None
402::COMM;;Xy = np.dot(X.T, y) that can be precomputed. It is useful
403::COMM;;only when the Gram matrix is precomputed.
404::COMM;;copy_X : bool, default=True
405::COMM;;If ``True``, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
406::COMM;;coef_init : array-like of shape (n_features, ), default=None
407::COMM;;The initial values of the coefficients.
408::COMM;;verbose : bool or int, default=False
409::COMM;;Amount of verbosity.
410::COMM;;return_n_iter : bool, default=False
411::COMM;;Whether to return the number of iterations or not.
412::COMM;;positive : bool, default=False
413::COMM;;If set to True, forces coefficients to be positive.
414::COMM;;(Only allowed when ``y.ndim == 1``).
415::COMM;;check_input : bool, default=True
416::COMM;;If set to False, the input validation checks are skipped (including the
417::COMM;;Gram matrix when provided). It is assumed that they are handled
418::COMM;;by the caller.
419::COMM;;**params : kwargs
420::COMM;;Keyword arguments passed to the coordinate descent solver.
421::COMM;;Returns
422::COMM;;-------
423::COMM;;alphas : ndarray of shape (n_alphas,)
424::COMM;;The alphas along the path where models are computed.
425::COMM;;coefs : ndarray of shape (n_features, n_alphas) or \
426::COMM;;(n_targets, n_features, n_alphas)
427::COMM;;Coefficients along the path.
428::COMM;;dual_gaps : ndarray of shape (n_alphas,)
429::COMM;;The dual gaps at the end of the optimization for each alpha.
430::COMM;;n_iters : list of int
431::COMM;;The number of iterations taken by the coordinate descent optimizer to
432::COMM;;reach the specified tolerance for each alpha.
433::COMM;;(Is returned when ``return_n_iter`` is set to True).
434::COMM;;See Also
435::COMM;;--------
436::COMM;;MultiTaskElasticNet : Multi-task ElasticNet model trained with L1/L2 mixed-norm \
437::COMM;;as regularizer.
438::COMM;;MultiTaskElasticNetCV : Multi-task L1/L2 ElasticNet with built-in cross-validation.
439::COMM;;ElasticNet : Linear regression with combined L1 and L2 priors as regularizer.
440::COMM;;ElasticNetCV : Elastic Net model with iterative fitting along a regularization path.
441::COMM;;Notes
442::COMM;;-----
443::COMM;;For an example, see
444::COMM;;:ref:`examples/linear_model/plot_lasso_lasso_lars_elasticnet_path.py
445::COMM;;<sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_lasso_lasso_lars_elasticnet_path.py>`.
446::COMM;;The underlying coordinate descent solver uses gap safe screening rules to speedup
447::COMM;;fitting time, see :ref:`User Guide on coordinate descent <coordinate_descent>`.
448::COMM;;Examples
449::COMM;;--------
450::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import enet_path
451::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
452::COMM;;>>> X, y, true_coef = make_regression(
453::COMM;;... n_samples=100, n_features=5, n_informative=2, coef=True, random_state=0
454::COMM;;... )
455::COMM;;>>> true_coef
456::COMM;;array([ 0. , 0. , 0. , 97.9, 45.7])
457::COMM;;>>> alphas, estimated_coef, _ = enet_path(X, y, n_alphas=3)
458::COMM;;>>> alphas.shape
459::COMM;;(3,)
460::COMM;;>>> estimated_coef
461::COMM;;array([[ 0., 0.787, 0.568],
462::COMM;;[ 0., 1.120, 0.620],
463::COMM;;[-0., -2.129, -1.128],
464::COMM;;[ 0., 23.046, 88.939],
465::COMM;;[ 0., 10.637, 41.566]])
477::COMO;;# We expect X and y to be already Fortran ordered when bypassing
478::COMO;;# checks
496::COMO;;# Xy should be a 1d contiguous array or a 2D C ordered array
507::COMO;;# MultiTaskElasticNet does not support sparse matrices
510::COMO;;# As sparse matrices are not actually centered we need this to be passed to
511::COMO;;# the CD solver.
516::COMO;;# X should have been passed through _pre_fit already if function is called
517::COMO;;# from ElasticNet.fit
529::COMO;;# fit_intercept and sample_weight have already been dealt with in calling
530::COMO;;# methods like ElasticNet.fit.
541::COMC;;alphas = np.sort(alphas)[::-1] # make sure alphas are properly ordered
558::COMO;;# account for n_samples scaling in objectives between here and cd_fast
584::COMO;;# We expect precompute to be already Fortran ordered when bypassing
585::COMO;;# checks
623::COMO;;# we correct the scale of the returned dual gap, as the objective
624::COMO;;# in cd_fast is n_samples * the objective in this docstring.
637::COMO;;###############################################################################
638::COMO;;# ElasticNet model
641::COMM;;Minimizes the objective function:
642::COMM;;.. math::
643::COMM;;\\frac{1}{2 n_{\\rm samples}} \\cdot \\|y - X w\\|_2^2
644::COMM;;+ \\alpha \\cdot {\\rm l1\\_{ratio}} \\cdot \\|w\\|_1
645::COMM;;+ 0.5 \\cdot \\alpha \\cdot (1 - {\\rm l1\\_{ratio}}) \\cdot \\|w\\|_2^2
646::COMM;;If you are interested in controlling the L1 and L2 penalty
647::COMM;;separately, keep in mind that this is equivalent to:
648::COMM;;.. math::
649::COMM;;a \\cdot \\|w\\|_1 + 0.5 \\cdot b \\cdot \\|w\\|_2^2
650::COMM;;where:
651::COMM;;.. math::
652::COMM;;\\alpha = a + b, \\quad {\\rm l1\\_{ratio}} = \\frac{a}{a + b}
653::COMM;;The parameter l1_ratio corresponds to alpha in the glmnet R package while
654::COMM;;alpha corresponds to the lambda parameter in glmnet. Specifically, l1_ratio
655::COMM;;= 1 is the lasso penalty. Currently, l1_ratio <= 0.01 is not reliable,
656::COMM;;unless you supply your own sequence of alpha.
657::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <elastic_net>`.
658::COMM;;Parameters
659::COMM;;----------
660::COMM;;alpha : float, default=1.0
661::COMM;;Constant that multiplies the penalty terms. Defaults to 1.0.
662::COMM;;See the notes for the exact mathematical meaning of this
663::COMM;;parameter. ``alpha = 0`` is equivalent to an ordinary least square,
664::COMM;;solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
665::COMM;;reasons, using ``alpha = 0`` with the ``Lasso`` object is not advised.
666::COMM;;Given this, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object.
667::COMM;;l1_ratio : float, default=0.5
668::COMM;;The ElasticNet mixing parameter, with ``0 <= l1_ratio <= 1``. For
669::COMM;;``l1_ratio = 0`` the penalty is an L2 penalty. ``For l1_ratio = 1`` it
670::COMM;;is an L1 penalty. For ``0 < l1_ratio < 1``, the penalty is a
671::COMM;;combination of L1 and L2.
672::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
673::COMM;;Whether the intercept should be estimated or not. If ``False``, the
674::COMM;;data is assumed to be already centered.
675::COMM;;precompute : bool or array-like of shape (n_features, n_features),\
676::COMM;;default=False
677::COMM;;Whether to use a precomputed Gram matrix to speed up
678::COMM;;calculations. The Gram matrix can also be passed as argument.
679::COMM;;For sparse input this option is always ``False`` to preserve sparsity.
680::COMM;;Check :ref:`an example on how to use a precomputed Gram Matrix in ElasticNet
681::COMM;;<sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_elastic_net_precomputed_gram_matrix_with_weighted_samples.py>`
682::COMM;;for details.
683::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=1000
684::COMM;;The maximum number of iterations.
685::COMM;;copy_X : bool, default=True
686::COMM;;If ``True``, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
687::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
688::COMM;;The tolerance for the optimization: if the updates are smaller or equal to
689::COMM;;``tol``, the optimization code checks the dual gap for optimality and continues
690::COMM;;until it is smaller or equal to ``tol``, see Notes below.
691::COMM;;warm_start : bool, default=False
692::COMM;;When set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as
693::COMM;;initialization, otherwise, just erase the previous solution.
694::COMM;;See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
695::COMM;;positive : bool, default=False
696::COMM;;When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive.
697::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
698::COMM;;The seed of the pseudo random number generator that selects a random
699::COMM;;feature to update. Used when ``selection`` == 'random'.
700::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
701::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
702::COMM;;selection : {'cyclic', 'random'}, default='cyclic'
703::COMM;;If set to 'random', a random coefficient is updated every iteration
704::COMM;;rather than looping over features sequentially by default. This
705::COMM;;(setting to 'random') often leads to significantly faster convergence
706::COMM;;especially when tol is higher than 1e-4.
707::COMM;;Attributes
708::COMM;;----------
709::COMM;;coef_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or (n_targets, n_features)
710::COMM;;Parameter vector (w in the cost function formula).
711::COMM;;sparse_coef_ : sparse matrix of shape (n_features,) or \
712::COMM;;(n_targets, n_features)
713::COMM;;Sparse representation of the `coef_`.
714::COMM;;intercept_ : float or ndarray of shape (n_targets,)
715::COMM;;Independent term in decision function.
716::COMM;;n_iter_ : list of int
717::COMM;;Number of iterations run by the coordinate descent solver to reach
718::COMM;;the specified tolerance.
719::COMM;;dual_gap_ : float or ndarray of shape (n_targets,)
720::COMM;;Given param alpha, the dual gaps at the end of the optimization,
721::COMM;;same shape as each observation of y.
722::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
723::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
724::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
725::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
726::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
727::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
728::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
729::COMM;;See Also
730::COMM;;--------
731::COMM;;ElasticNetCV : Elastic net model with best model selection by
732::COMM;;cross-validation.
733::COMM;;SGDRegressor : Implements elastic net regression with incremental training.
734::COMM;;SGDClassifier : Implements logistic regression with elastic net penalty
735::COMM;;(``SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", penalty="elasticnet")``).
736::COMM;;Notes
737::COMM;;-----
738::COMM;;To avoid unnecessary memory duplication the X argument of the fit method
739::COMM;;should be directly passed as a Fortran-contiguous numpy array.
740::COMM;;The precise stopping criteria based on `tol` are the following: First, check that
741::COMM;;that maximum coordinate update, i.e. :math:`\\max_j |w_j^{new} - w_j^{old}|`
742::COMM;;is smaller or equal to `tol` times the maximum absolute coefficient,
743::COMM;;:math:`\\max_j |w_j|`. If so, then additionally check whether the dual gap is
744::COMM;;smaller or equal to `tol` times :math:`||y||_2^2 / n_{\\text{samples}}`.
745::COMM;;The underlying coordinate descent solver uses gap safe screening rules to speedup
746::COMM;;fitting time, see :ref:`User Guide on coordinate descent <coordinate_descent>`.
747::COMM;;Examples
748::COMM;;--------
749::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet
750::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
751::COMM;;>>> X, y = make_regression(n_features=2, random_state=0)
752::COMM;;>>> regr = ElasticNet(random_state=0)
753::COMM;;>>> regr.fit(X, y)
754::COMM;;ElasticNet(random_state=0)
755::COMM;;>>> print(regr.coef_)
756::COMM;;[18.83816048 64.55968825]
757::COMM;;>>> print(regr.intercept_)
758::COMM;;1.451
759::COMM;;>>> print(regr.predict([[0, 0]]))
760::COMM;;[1.451]
761::COMM;;- :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_lasso_and_elasticnet.py`
762::COMM;;showcases ElasticNet alongside Lasso and ARD Regression for sparse
763::COMM;;signal recovery in the presence of noise and feature correlation.
765::COMO;;# "check_input" is used for optimisation and isn't something to be passed
766::COMO;;# around in a pipeline.
811::COMM;;Parameters
812::COMM;;----------
813::COMM;;X : {ndarray, sparse matrix, sparse array} of (n_samples, n_features)
814::COMM;;Data.
815::COMM;;Note that large sparse matrices and arrays requiring `int64`
816::COMM;;indices are not accepted.
817::COMM;;y : ndarray of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_targets)
818::COMM;;Target. Will be cast to X's dtype if necessary.
819::COMM;;sample_weight : float or array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
820::COMM;;Sample weights. Internally, the `sample_weight` vector will be
821::COMM;;rescaled to sum to `n_samples`.
822::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
823::COMM;;check_input : bool, default=True
824::COMM;;Allow to bypass several input checking.
825::COMM;;Don't use this parameter unless you know what you do.
826::COMM;;Returns
827::COMM;;-------
828::COMM;;self : object
829::COMM;;Fitted estimator.
830::COMM;;Notes
831::COMM;;-----
832::COMM;;Coordinate descent is an algorithm that considers each column of
833::COMM;;data at a time hence it will automatically convert the X input
834::COMM;;as a Fortran-contiguous numpy array if necessary.
835::COMM;;To avoid memory re-allocation it is advised to allocate the
836::COMM;;initial data in memory directly using that format.
847::COMO;;# Remember if X is copied
849::COMO;;# We expect X and y to be float64 or float32 Fortran ordered arrays
850::COMO;;# when bypassing checks
876::COMO;;# TLDR: Rescale sw to sum up to n_samples.
877::COMO;;# Long: The objective function of Enet
878::COMO;;#
879::COMO;;# 1/2 * np.average(squared error, weights=sw)
880::COMO;;# + alpha * penalty (1)
881::COMO;;#
882::COMO;;# is invariant under rescaling of sw.
883::COMO;;# But enet_path coordinate descent minimizes
884::COMO;;#
885::COMO;;# 1/2 * sum(squared error) + alpha' * penalty (2)
886::COMO;;#
887::COMO;;# and therefore sets
888::COMO;;#
889::COMO;;# alpha' = n_samples * alpha (3)
890::COMO;;#
891::COMO;;# inside its function body, which results in objective (2) being
892::COMO;;# equivalent to (1) in case of no sw.
893::COMO;;# With sw, however, enet_path should set
894::COMO;;#
895::COMO;;# alpha' = sum(sw) * alpha (4)
896::COMO;;#
897::COMO;;# Therefore, we use the freedom of Eq. (1) to rescale sw before
898::COMO;;# calling enet_path, i.e.
899::COMO;;#
900::COMO;;# sw *= n_samples / sum(sw)
901::COMO;;#
902::COMO;;# such that sum(sw) = n_samples. This way, (3) and (4) are the same.
904::COMO;;# Note: Alternatively, we could also have rescaled alpha instead
905::COMO;;# of sample_weight:
906::COMO;;#
907::COMO;;# alpha *= np.sum(sample_weight) / n_samples
908::COMO;;# Ensure copying happens only once, don't do it again if done above.
909::COMO;;# X and y will be rescaled if sample_weight is not None, order='F'
910::COMO;;# ensures that the returned X and y are still F-contiguous.
922::COMO;;# coordinate descent needs F-ordered arrays and _pre_fit might have
923::COMO;;# called _rescale_data
959::COMO;;# from here on **params
979::COMO;;# check for finiteness of coefficients
986::COMO;;# return self for chaining fit and predict calls
991::COMM;;return sparse.csr_matrix(self.coef_)
992::COMM;;def _decision_function(self, X):
1002::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
1003::COMM;;if sparse.issparse(X):
1004::COMM;;return safe_sparse_dot(X, self.coef_.T, dense_output=True) + self.intercept_
1005::COMM;;else:
1006::COMM;;return super()._decision_function(X)
1007::COMM;;def __sklearn_tags__(self):
1008::COMM;;tags = super().__sklearn_tags__()
1009::COMM;;tags.input_tags.sparse = True
1010::COMM;;return tags

1164::COMM;;# Functions for CV with paths functions
1165::COMM;;def _path_residuals(
1166::COMM;;X,
1167::COMM;;y,
1168::COMM;;sample_weight,
1169::COMM;;train,
1170::COMM;;test,
1171::COMM;;fit_intercept,
1172::COMM;;path,
1173::COMM;;path_params,
1174::COMM;;alphas=None,
1175::COMM;;l1_ratio=1,
1176::COMM;;X_order=None,
1177::COMM;;dtype=None,
1178::COMM;;):
1212::COMM;;X_train = X[train]
1213::COMM;;y_train = y[train]
1214::COMM;;X_test = X[test]
1215::COMM;;y_test = y[test]
1216::COMM;;if sample_weight is None:
1217::COMM;;sw_train, sw_test = None, None
1218::COMM;;else:
1219::COMM;;sw_train = sample_weight[train]
1220::COMM;;sw_test = sample_weight[test]
1221::COMM;;n_samples = X_train.shape[0]
1222::COMM;;# TLDR: Rescale sw_train to sum up to n_samples on the training set.
1223::COMM;;# See TLDR and long comment inside ElasticNet.fit.
1224::COMM;;sw_train *= n_samples / np.sum(sw_train)
1225::COMM;;# Note: Alternatively, we could also have rescaled alpha instead
1226::COMM;;# of sample_weight:
1227::COMM;;#
1228::COMM;;# alpha *= np.sum(sample_weight) / n_samples
1229::COMM;;if not sparse.issparse(X):
1230::COMM;;for array, array_input in (
1231::COMM;;(X_train, X),
1232::COMM;;(y_train, y),
1233::COMM;;(X_test, X),
1234::COMM;;(y_test, y),
1235::COMM;;):
1236::COMM;;if array.base is not array_input and not array.flags["WRITEABLE"]:
1237::COMM;;# fancy indexing should create a writable copy but it doesn't
1238::COMM;;# for read-only memmaps (cf. numpy#14132).
1239::COMM;;array.setflags(write=True)
1240::COMM;;if y.ndim == 1:
1241::COMM;;precompute = path_params["precompute"]
1242::COMM;;else:
1243::COMM;;# No Gram variant of multi-task exists right now.
1244::COMM;;# Fall back to default enet_multitask
1245::COMM;;precompute = False
1246::COMM;;X_train, y_train, X_offset, y_offset, X_scale, precompute, Xy = _pre_fit(
1247::COMM;;X_train,
1248::COMM;;y_train,
1249::COMM;;None,
1250::COMM;;precompute,
1251::COMM;;fit_intercept=fit_intercept,
1252::COMM;;copy=False,
1253::COMM;;sample_weight=sw_train,
1254::COMM;;)
1255::COMM;;path_params = path_params.copy()
1256::COMM;;path_params["Xy"] = Xy
1257::COMM;;path_params["X_offset"] = X_offset
1258::COMM;;path_params["X_scale"] = X_scale
1259::COMM;;path_params["precompute"] = precompute
1260::COMM;;path_params["copy_X"] = False
1261::COMM;;path_params["alphas"] = alphas
1262::COMM;;# needed for sparse cd solver
1263::COMM;;path_params["sample_weight"] = sw_train
1264::COMM;;if "l1_ratio" in path_params:
1265::COMM;;path_params["l1_ratio"] = l1_ratio
1266::COMM;;# Do the ordering and type casting here, as if it is done in the path,
1267::COMM;;# X is copied and a reference is kept here
1268::COMM;;X_train = check_array(X_train, accept_sparse="csc", dtype=dtype, order=X_order)
1269::COMM;;alphas, coefs, _ = path(X_train, y_train, **path_params)
1270::COMM;;del X_train, y_train
1271::COMM;;if y.ndim == 1:

4::COMM;;Newton solver for Generalized Linear Models
18::COMM;;This class implements Newton/2nd-order optimization routines for GLMs. Each Newton
19::COMM;;iteration aims at finding the Newton step which is done by the inner solver. With
20::COMM;;Hessian H, gradient g and coefficients coef, one step solves:
21::COMM;;H @ coef_newton = -g
22::COMM;;For our GLM / LinearModelLoss, we have gradient g and Hessian H:
23::COMM;;g = X.T @ loss.gradient + l2_reg_strength * coef
24::COMM;;H = X.T @ diag(loss.hessian) @ X + l2_reg_strength * identity
25::COMM;;Backtracking line search updates coef = coef_old + t * coef_newton for some t in
26::COMM;;(0, 1].
27::COMM;;This is a base class, actual implementations (child classes) may deviate from the
28::COMM;;above pattern and use structure specific tricks.
29::COMM;;Usage pattern:
30::COMM;;- initialize solver: sol = NewtonSolver(...)
31::COMM;;- solve the problem: sol.solve(X, y, sample_weight)
32::COMM;;References
33::COMM;;----------
34::COMM;;- Jorge Nocedal, Stephen J. Wright. (2006) "Numerical Optimization"
35::COMM;;2nd edition
36::COMM;;https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-40065-5
37::COMM;;- Stephen P. Boyd, Lieven Vandenberghe. (2004) "Convex Optimization."
38::COMM;;Cambridge University Press, 2004.
39::COMM;;https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf
40::COMM;;Parameters
41::COMM;;----------
42::COMM;;coef : ndarray of shape (n_dof,), (n_classes, n_dof) or (n_classes * n_dof,)
43::COMM;;Initial coefficients of a linear model.
44::COMM;;If shape (n_classes * n_dof,), the classes of one feature are contiguous,
45::COMM;;i.e. one reconstructs the 2d-array via
46::COMM;;coef.reshape((n_classes, -1), order="F").
47::COMM;;linear_loss : LinearModelLoss
48::COMM;;The loss to be minimized.
49::COMM;;l2_reg_strength : float, default=0.0
50::COMM;;L2 regularization strength.
51::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
52::COMM;;The optimization problem is solved when each of the following condition is
53::COMM;;fulfilled:
54::COMM;;1. maximum |gradient| <= tol
55::COMM;;2. Newton decrement d: 1/2 * d^2 <= tol
56::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=100
57::COMM;;Maximum number of Newton steps allowed.
58::COMM;;n_threads : int, default=1
59::COMM;;Number of OpenMP threads to use for the computation of the Hessian and gradient
60::COMM;;of the loss function.
61::COMM;;Attributes
62::COMM;;----------
63::COMM;;coef_old : ndarray of shape coef.shape
64::COMM;;Coefficient of previous iteration.
65::COMM;;coef_newton : ndarray of shape coef.shape
66::COMM;;Newton step.
67::COMM;;gradient : ndarray of shape coef.shape
68::COMM;;Gradient of the loss w.r.t. the coefficients.
69::COMM;;gradient_old : ndarray of shape coef.shape
70::COMM;;Gradient of previous iteration.
71::COMM;;loss_value : float
72::COMM;;Value of objective function = loss + penalty.
73::COMM;;loss_value_old : float
74::COMM;;Value of objective function of previous itertion.
75::COMM;;raw_prediction : ndarray of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_classes)
76::COMM;;converged : bool
77::COMM;;Indicator for convergence of the solver.
78::COMM;;iteration : int
79::COMM;;Number of Newton steps, i.e. calls to inner_solve
80::COMM;;use_fallback_lbfgs_solve : bool
81::COMM;;If set to True, the solver will resort to call LBFGS to finish the optimisation
82::COMM;;procedure in case of convergence issues.
83::COMM;;gradient_times_newton : float
84::COMM;;gradient @ coef_newton, set in inner_solve and used by line_search. If the
85::COMM;;Newton step is a descent direction, this is negative.
107::COMM;;If None, initializes:
108::COMM;;- self.coef
109::COMM;;Sets:
110::COMM;;- self.raw_prediction

264::COMM;;# convergence criterion because even a large step could have brought us close

380::COMM;;# As with LinearModelLoss, we always are contiguous in n_classes.

382::COMM;;# Note that the computation of gradient in LinearModelLoss follows the shape of

385::COMM;;# But the hessian is always 2d.
386::COMM;;n = self.coef.size

388::COMM;;# To help case distinctions.

391::COMM;;)
392::COMM;;self.is_multinomial_no_penalty = (

394::COMM;;)
395::COMM;;if self.is_multinomial_no_penalty:
396::COMM;;# See inner_solve. The provided coef might not adhere to the convention
397::COMM;;# that the last class is set to zero.
398::COMM;;# This is done by the usual freedom of a (overparametrized) multinomial to
399::COMM;;# add a constant to all classes which doesn't change predictions.
400::COMM;;n_classes = self.linear_loss.base_loss.n_classes
401::COMM;;coef = self.coef.reshape(n_classes, -1, order="F") # easier as 2d
402::COMM;;coef -= coef[-1, :] # coef -= coef of last class
403::COMM;;elif self.is_multinomial_with_intercept:
404::COMM;;# See inner_solve. Same as above, but only for the intercept.

408::COMM;;def update_gradient_hessian(self, X, y, sample_weight):
409::COMM;;_, _, self.hessian_warning = self.linear_loss.gradient_hessian(

437::COMM;;# Note: The following case distinction could also be shifted to the
438::COMM;;# implementation of HalfMultinomialLoss instead of here within the solver.
439::COMM;;if self.is_multinomial_no_penalty:
440::COMM;;# The multinomial loss is overparametrized for each unpenalized feature, so
441::COMM;;# at least the intercepts. This can be seen by noting that predicted
442::COMM;;# probabilities are invariant under shifting all coefficients of a single
443::COMM;;# feature j for all classes by the same amount c:
444::COMM;;# coef[k, :] -> coef[k, :] + c => proba stays the same
445::COMM;;# where we have assumed coef.shape = (n_classes, n_features).
446::COMM;;# Therefore, also the loss (-log-likelihood), gradient and hessian stay the
447::COMM;;# same, see
448::COMM;;# Noah Simon and Jerome Friedman and Trevor Hastie. (2013) "A Blockwise
449::COMM;;# Descent Algorithm for Group-penalized Multiresponse and Multinomial
450::COMM;;# Regression". https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1311.6529
451::COMM;;#
452::COMM;;# We choose the standard approach and set all the coefficients of the last
453::COMM;;# class to zero, for all features including the intercept.
454::COMM;;# Note that coef was already dealt with in setup.
455::COMM;;n_classes = self.linear_loss.base_loss.n_classes
456::COMM;;n_dof = self.coef.size // n_classes # degree of freedom per class
457::COMM;;n = self.coef.size - n_dof # effective size
458::COMM;;self.gradient[n_classes - 1 :: n_classes] = 0
459::COMM;;self.hessian[n_classes - 1 :: n_classes, :] = 0
460::COMM;;self.hessian[:, n_classes - 1 :: n_classes] = 0
461::COMM;;# We also need the reduced variants of gradient and hessian where the
462::COMM;;# entries set to zero are removed. For 2 features and 3 classes with
463::COMM;;# arbitrary values, "x" means removed:
464::COMM;;# gradient = [0, 1, x, 3, 4, x]
465::COMM;;#
466::COMM;;# hessian = [0, 1, x, 3, 4, x]
467::COMM;;# [1, 7, x, 9, 10, x]
468::COMM;;# [x, x, x, x, x, x]
469::COMM;;# [3, 9, x, 21, 22, x]
470::COMM;;# [4, 10, x, 22, 28, x]
471::COMM;;# [x, x, x, x, x, x]
472::COMM;;# The following slicing triggers copies of gradient and hessian.
473::COMM;;gradient = self.gradient.reshape(-1, n_classes)[:, :-1].flatten()
474::COMM;;hessian = self.hessian.reshape(n_dof, n_classes, n_dof, n_classes)[
475::COMM;;:, :-1, :, :-1
476::COMM;;].reshape(n, n)
477::COMM;;elif self.is_multinomial_with_intercept:
478::COMM;;# Here, only intercepts are unpenalized. We again choose the last class and
479::COMM;;# set its intercept to zero.
480::COMM;;# Note that coef was already dealt with in setup.
481::COMM;;self.gradient[-1] = 0
482::COMM;;self.hessian[-1, :] = 0
483::COMM;;self.hessian[:, -1] = 0
484::COMM;;gradient, hessian = self.gradient[:-1], self.hessian[:-1, :-1]
485::COMM;;else:
486::COMM;;gradient, hessian = self.gradient, self.hessian
487::COMM;;try:
488::COMM;;with warnings.catch_warnings():
489::COMM;;warnings.simplefilter("error", scipy.linalg.LinAlgWarning)
490::COMM;;self.coef_newton = scipy.linalg.solve(
491::COMM;;hessian, -gradient, check_finite=False, assume_a="sym"
492::COMM;;)
493::COMM;;if self.is_multinomial_no_penalty:
494::COMM;;self.coef_newton = np.c_[
495::COMM;;self.coef_newton.reshape(n_dof, n_classes - 1), np.zeros(n_dof)
496::COMM;;].reshape(-1)
497::COMM;;assert self.coef_newton.flags.f_contiguous
498::COMM;;elif self.is_multinomial_with_intercept:
499::COMM;;self.coef_newton = np.r_[self.coef_newton, 0]
500::COMM;;self.gradient_times_newton = self.gradient @ self.coef_newton
501::COMM;;if self.gradient_times_newton > 0:
502::COMM;;if self.verbose:
503::COMM;;print(
504::COMM;;" The inner solver found a Newton step that is not a "
505::COMM;;"descent direction and resorts to LBFGS steps instead."
506::COMM;;)
507::COMM;;self.use_fallback_lbfgs_solve = True
508::COMM;;return
509::COMM;;except (np.linalg.LinAlgError, scipy.linalg.LinAlgWarning) as e:
510::COMM;;warnings.warn(
511::COMM;;f"The inner solver of {self.__class__.__name__} stumbled upon a "
512::COMM;;"singular or very ill-conditioned Hessian matrix at iteration "
513::COMM;;f"{self.iteration}. It will now resort to lbfgs instead.\n"
514::COMM;;"Further options are to use another solver or to avoid such situation "
515::COMM;;"in the first place. Possible remedies are removing collinear features"
516::COMM;;" of X or increasing the penalization strengths.\n"
517::COMM;;"The original Linear Algebra message was:\n" + str(e),
518::COMM;;scipy.linalg.LinAlgWarning,
519::COMM;;)
520::COMM;;# Possible causes:
521::COMM;;# 1. hess_pointwise is negative. But this is already taken care in
522::COMM;;# LinearModelLoss.gradient_hessian.
523::COMM;;# 2. X is singular or ill-conditioned
524::COMM;;# This might be the most probable cause.
525::COMM;;#
526::COMM;;# There are many possible ways to deal with this situation. Most of them
527::COMM;;# add, explicitly or implicitly, a matrix to the hessian to make it
528::COMM;;# positive definite, confer to Chapter 3.4 of Nocedal & Wright 2nd ed.
529::COMM;;# Instead, we resort to lbfgs.
530::COMM;;if self.verbose:
531::COMM;;print(
532::COMM;;" The inner solver stumbled upon a singular or ill-conditioned "
533::COMM;;"Hessian matrix and resorts to LBFGS instead."
534::COMM;;)
535::COMM;;self.use_fallback_lbfgs_solve = True
536::COMM;;return
537::COMM;;def finalize(self, X, y, sample_weight):
538::COMM;;if self.is_multinomial_no_penalty:
539::COMM;;# Our convention is usually the symmetric parametrization where
540::COMM;;# sum(coef[classes, features], axis=0) = 0.
541::COMM;;# We convert now to this convention. Note that it does not change
542::COMM;;# the predicted probabilities.
543::COMM;;n_classes = self.linear_loss.base_loss.n_classes
544::COMM;;self.coef = self.coef.reshape(n_classes, -1, order="F")
545::COMM;;self.coef -= np.mean(self.coef, axis=0)
546::COMM;;elif self.is_multinomial_with_intercept:
547::COMM;;# Only the intercept needs an update to the symmetric parametrization.
548::COMM;;n_classes = self.linear_loss.base_loss.n_classes
549::COMM;;self.coef[-n_classes:] -= np.mean(self.coef[-n_classes:])

4::COMM;;Generalized Linear Models with Exponential Dispersion Family
31::COMM;;GLMs based on a reproductive Exponential Dispersion Model (EDM) aim at fitting and
32::COMM;;predicting the mean of the target y as y_pred=h(X*w) with coefficients w.
33::COMM;;Therefore, the fit minimizes the following objective function with L2 priors as
34::COMM;;regularizer::
35::COMM;;1/(2*sum(s_i)) * sum(s_i * deviance(y_i, h(x_i*w)) + 1/2 * alpha * ||w||_2^2
36::COMM;;with inverse link function h, s=sample_weight and per observation (unit) deviance
37::COMM;;deviance(y_i, h(x_i*w)). Note that for an EDM, 1/2 * deviance is the negative
38::COMM;;log-likelihood up to a constant (in w) term.
39::COMM;;The parameter ``alpha`` corresponds to the lambda parameter in glmnet.
40::COMM;;Instead of implementing the EDM family and a link function separately, we directly
41::COMM;;use the loss functions `from sklearn._loss` which have the link functions included
42::COMM;;in them for performance reasons. We pick the loss functions that implement
43::COMM;;(1/2 times) EDM deviances.
44::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <Generalized_linear_models>`.
45::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
46::COMM;;Parameters
47::COMM;;----------
48::COMM;;alpha : float, default=1
49::COMM;;Constant that multiplies the penalty term and thus determines the
50::COMM;;regularization strength. ``alpha = 0`` is equivalent to unpenalized
51::COMM;;GLMs. In this case, the design matrix `X` must have full column rank
52::COMM;;(no collinearities).
53::COMM;;Values must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
54::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
55::COMM;;Specifies if a constant (a.k.a. bias or intercept) should be
56::COMM;;added to the linear predictor (X @ coef + intercept).
57::COMM;;solver : {'lbfgs', 'newton-cholesky'}, default='lbfgs'
58::COMM;;Algorithm to use in the optimization problem:
59::COMM;;'lbfgs'
60::COMM;;Calls scipy's L-BFGS-B optimizer.
61::COMM;;'newton-cholesky'
62::COMM;;Uses Newton-Raphson steps (in arbitrary precision arithmetic equivalent to
63::COMM;;iterated reweighted least squares) with an inner Cholesky based solver.
64::COMM;;This solver is a good choice for `n_samples` >> `n_features`, especially
65::COMM;;with one-hot encoded categorical features with rare categories. Be aware
66::COMM;;that the memory usage of this solver has a quadratic dependency on
67::COMM;;`n_features` because it explicitly computes the Hessian matrix.
68::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
69::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=100
70::COMM;;The maximal number of iterations for the solver.
71::COMM;;Values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
72::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
73::COMM;;Stopping criterion. For the lbfgs solver,
74::COMM;;the iteration will stop when ``max{|g_j|, j = 1, ..., d} <= tol``
75::COMM;;where ``g_j`` is the j-th component of the gradient (derivative) of
76::COMM;;the objective function.
77::COMM;;Values must be in the range `(0.0, inf)`.
78::COMM;;warm_start : bool, default=False
79::COMM;;If set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to ``fit``
80::COMM;;as initialization for ``coef_`` and ``intercept_``.
81::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
82::COMM;;For the lbfgs solver set verbose to any positive number for verbosity.
83::COMM;;Values must be in the range `[0, inf)`.
84::COMM;;Attributes
85::COMM;;----------
86::COMM;;coef_ : array of shape (n_features,)
87::COMM;;Estimated coefficients for the linear predictor (`X @ coef_ +
88::COMM;;intercept_`) in the GLM.
89::COMM;;intercept_ : float
90::COMM;;Intercept (a.k.a. bias) added to linear predictor.
91::COMM;;n_iter_ : int
92::COMM;;Actual number of iterations used in the solver.
93::COMM;;_base_loss : BaseLoss, default=HalfSquaredError()
94::COMM;;This is set during fit via `self._get_loss()`.
95::COMM;;A `_base_loss` contains a specific loss function as well as the link
96::COMM;;function. The loss to be minimized specifies the distributional assumption of
97::COMM;;the GLM, i.e. the distribution from the EDM. Here are some examples:
98::COMM;;======================= ======== ==========================
99::COMM;;_base_loss Link Target Domain
100::COMM;;======================= ======== ==========================
101::COMM;;HalfSquaredError identity y any real number
102::COMM;;HalfPoissonLoss log 0 <= y
103::COMM;;HalfGammaLoss log 0 < y
104::COMM;;HalfTweedieLoss log dependent on tweedie power
105::COMM;;HalfTweedieLossIdentity identity dependent on tweedie power
106::COMM;;======================= ======== ==========================
107::COMM;;The link function of the GLM, i.e. mapping from linear predictor
108::COMM;;`X @ coeff + intercept` to prediction `y_pred`. For instance, with a log link,
109::COMM;;we have `y_pred = exp(X @ coeff + intercept)`.
111::COMO;;# We allow for NewtonSolver classes for the "solver" parameter but do not
112::COMO;;# make them public in the docstrings. This facilitates testing and
113::COMO;;# benchmarking.
147::COMM;;Parameters
148::COMM;;----------
149::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
150::COMM;;Training data.
151::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
152::COMM;;Target values.
153::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
154::COMM;;Sample weights.
155::COMM;;Returns
156::COMM;;-------
157::COMM;;self : object
158::COMM;;Fitted model.
169::COMO;;# required by losses
171::COMO;;# lbfgs will force coef and therefore raw_prediction to be float64. The
172::COMO;;# base_loss needs y, X @ coef and sample_weight all of same dtype
173::COMO;;# (and contiguous).
179::COMO;;# Note that _check_sample_weight calls check_array(order="C") required by
180::COMO;;# losses.
193::COMO;;# TODO: if alpha=0 check that X is not rank deficient
194::COMO;;# NOTE: Rescaling of sample_weight:
195::COMO;;# We want to minimize
196::COMO;;# obj = 1/(2 * sum(sample_weight)) * sum(sample_weight * deviance)
197::COMO;;# + 1/2 * alpha * L2,
198::COMO;;# with
199::COMO;;# deviance = 2 * loss.
200::COMO;;# The objective is invariant to multiplying sample_weight by a constant. We
201::COMO;;# could choose this constant such that sum(sample_weight) = 1 in order to end
202::COMO;;# up with
203::COMO;;# obj = sum(sample_weight * loss) + 1/2 * alpha * L2.
204::COMO;;# But LinearModelLoss.loss() already computes
205::COMO;;# average(loss, weights=sample_weight)
206::COMO;;# Thus, without rescaling, we have
207::COMO;;# obj = LinearModelLoss.loss(...)
210::COMO;;# LinearModelLoss needs intercept at the end of coefficient array.
223::COMO;;# Algorithms for optimization:
224::COMO;;# Note again that our losses implement 1/2 * deviance.
234::COMC;;"maxls": 50, # default is 20
236::COMO;;# The constant 64 was found empirically to pass the test suite.
237::COMO;;# The point is that ftol is very small, but a bit larger than
238::COMO;;# machine precision for float64, which is the dtype used by lbfgs.
277::COMO;;# set intercept to zero as the other linear models do
283::COMM;;Note that we often use the term raw_prediction instead of linear predictor.
284::COMM;;Parameters
285::COMM;;----------
286::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
287::COMM;;Samples.
288::COMM;;Returns
289::COMM;;-------
290::COMM;;y_pred : array of shape (n_samples,)
291::COMM;;Returns predicted values of linear predictor.

313::COMM;;Returns predicted values.
315::COMO;;# check_array is done in _linear_predictor
321::COMM;;D^2 is a generalization of the coefficient of determination R^2.
322::COMM;;R^2 uses squared error and D^2 uses the deviance of this GLM, see the
323::COMM;;:ref:`User Guide <regression_metrics>`.
324::COMM;;D^2 is defined as
325::COMM;;:math:`D^2 = 1-\\frac{D(y_{true},y_{pred})}{D_{null}}`,
326::COMM;;:math:`D_{null}` is the null deviance, i.e. the deviance of a model
327::COMM;;with intercept alone, which corresponds to :math:`y_{pred} = \\bar{y}`.
328::COMM;;The mean :math:`\\bar{y}` is averaged by sample_weight.
329::COMM;;Best possible score is 1.0 and it can be negative (because the model
330::COMM;;can be arbitrarily worse).
331::COMM;;Parameters
332::COMM;;----------
333::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
334::COMM;;Test samples.
335::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
336::COMM;;True values of target.
337::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
338::COMM;;Sample weights.

614::COMM;;This estimator can be used to model different GLMs depending on the
615::COMM;;``power`` parameter, which determines the underlying distribution.
616::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <Generalized_linear_models>`.
617::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.23
618::COMM;;Parameters
619::COMM;;----------
620::COMM;;power : float, default=0
621::COMM;;The power determines the underlying target distribution according
622::COMM;;to the following table:
623::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
624::COMM;;| Power | Distribution |
625::COMM;;+=======+========================+
626::COMM;;| 0 | Normal |
627::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
628::COMM;;| 1 | Poisson |
629::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
630::COMM;;| (1,2) | Compound Poisson Gamma |
631::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
632::COMM;;| 2 | Gamma |
633::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
634::COMM;;| 3 | Inverse Gaussian |
635::COMM;;+-------+------------------------+
636::COMM;;For ``0 < power < 1``, no distribution exists.
637::COMM;;alpha : float, default=1
638::COMM;;Constant that multiplies the L2 penalty term and determines the
639::COMM;;regularization strength. ``alpha = 0`` is equivalent to unpenalized
640::COMM;;GLMs. In this case, the design matrix `X` must have full column rank
641::COMM;;(no collinearities).
642::COMM;;Values of `alpha` must be in the range `[0.0, inf)`.
643::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
644::COMM;;Specifies if a constant (a.k.a. bias or intercept) should be
645::COMM;;added to the linear predictor (`X @ coef + intercept`).
646::COMM;;link : {'auto', 'identity', 'log'}, default='auto'
647::COMM;;The link function of the GLM, i.e. mapping from linear predictor
648::COMM;;`X @ coeff + intercept` to prediction `y_pred`. Option 'auto' sets
649::COMM;;the link depending on the chosen `power` parameter as follows:
650::COMM;;- 'identity' for ``power <= 0``, e.g. for the Normal distribution
651::COMM;;- 'log' for ``power > 0``, e.g. for Poisson, Gamma and Inverse Gaussian
652::COMM;;distributions
653::COMM;;solver : {'lbfgs', 'newton-cholesky'}, default='lbfgs'
654::COMM;;Algorithm to use in the optimization problem:
655::COMM;;'lbfgs'
656::COMM;;Calls scipy's L-BFGS-B optimizer.
657::COMM;;'newton-cholesky'
658::COMM;;Uses Newton-Raphson steps (in arbitrary precision arithmetic equivalent to
659::COMM;;iterated reweighted least squares) with an inner Cholesky based solver.
660::COMM;;This solver is a good choice for `n_samples` >> `n_features`, especially
661::COMM;;with one-hot encoded categorical features with rare categories. Be aware
662::COMM;;that the memory usage of this solver has a quadratic dependency on
663::COMM;;`n_features` because it explicitly computes the Hessian matrix.
664::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
665::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=100
666::COMM;;The maximal number of iterations for the solver.
667::COMM;;Values must be in the range `[1, inf)`.
668::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
669::COMM;;Stopping criterion. For the lbfgs solver,
670::COMM;;the iteration will stop when ``max{|g_j|, j = 1, ..., d} <= tol``
671::COMM;;where ``g_j`` is the j-th component of the gradient (derivative) of
672::COMM;;the objective function.
673::COMM;;Values must be in the range `(0.0, inf)`.
674::COMM;;warm_start : bool, default=False
675::COMM;;If set to ``True``, reuse the solution of the previous call to ``fit``
676::COMM;;as initialization for ``coef_`` and ``intercept_`` .
677::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
678::COMM;;For the lbfgs solver set verbose to any positive number for verbosity.
679::COMM;;Values must be in the range `[0, inf)`.
680::COMM;;Attributes
681::COMM;;----------
682::COMM;;coef_ : array of shape (n_features,)
683::COMM;;Estimated coefficients for the linear predictor (`X @ coef_ +
684::COMM;;intercept_`) in the GLM.
685::COMM;;intercept_ : float
686::COMM;;Intercept (a.k.a. bias) added to linear predictor.
687::COMM;;n_iter_ : int
688::COMM;;Actual number of iterations used in the solver.
689::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
690::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
691::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
692::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
693::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
694::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
695::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
696::COMM;;See Also
697::COMM;;--------
698::COMM;;PoissonRegressor : Generalized Linear Model with a Poisson distribution.
699::COMM;;GammaRegressor : Generalized Linear Model with a Gamma distribution.
700::COMM;;Examples
701::COMM;;--------
702::COMM;;>>> from sklearn import linear_model
703::COMM;;>>> clf = linear_model.TweedieRegressor()

705::COMM;;>>> y = [2, 3.5, 5, 5.5]
706::COMM;;>>> clf.fit(X, y)
707::COMM;;TweedieRegressor()

709::COMM;;np.float64(0.839)
710::COMM;;>>> clf.coef_
711::COMM;;array([0.599, 0.299])
712::COMM;;>>> clf.intercept_
713::COMM;;np.float64(1.600)
714::COMM;;>>> clf.predict([[1, 1], [3, 4]])
715::COMM;;array([2.500, 4.599])

752::COMO;;# log link

33::COMO;;# Find good starting point by Nelder-Mead
37::COMO;;# Now refine via root finding on the gradient of the function, which is
38::COMO;;# more precise than minimizing the function itself.
59::COMO;;# TweedieRegressor(power=3.0), # too difficult
60::COMO;;# TweedieRegressor(power=0, link="log"), # too difficult
68::COMM;;This is inspired by ols_ridge_dataset in test_ridge.py.
69::COMM;;The construction is based on the SVD decomposition of X = U S V'.
70::COMM;;Parameters
71::COMM;;----------
72::COMM;;type : {"long", "wide"}
73::COMM;;If "long", then n_samples > n_features.
74::COMM;;If "wide", then n_features > n_samples.
75::COMM;;model : a GLM model
76::COMM;;For "wide", we return the minimum norm solution:
77::COMM;;min ||w||_2 subject to w = argmin deviance(X, y, w)
78::COMM;;Note that the deviance is always minimized if y = inverse_link(X w) is possible to
79::COMM;;achieve, which it is in the wide data case. Therefore, we can construct the
80::COMM;;solution with minimum norm like (wide) OLS:
81::COMM;;min ||w||_2 subject to link(y) = raw_prediction = X w
82::COMM;;Returns
83::COMM;;-------
84::COMM;;model : GLM model
85::COMM;;X : ndarray
86::COMM;;Last column of 1, i.e. intercept.
87::COMM;;y : ndarray
88::COMM;;coef_unpenalized : ndarray
89::COMM;;Minimum norm solutions, i.e. min sum(loss(w)) (with minimum ||w||_2 in
90::COMM;;case of ambiguity)
91::COMM;;Last coefficient is intercept.
92::COMM;;coef_penalized : ndarray
93::COMM;;GLM solution with alpha=l2_reg_strength=1, i.e.
94::COMM;;min 1/n * sum(loss) + ||w[:-1]||_2^2.
95::COMM;;Last coefficient is intercept.
96::COMM;;l2_reg_strength : float
97::COMM;;Always equal 1.

101::COMO;;# This helps when constructing singular matrices like (X, X).

118::COMC;;assert np.max(s) / np.min(s) < 100 # condition number of X
125::COMO;;# minimum norm solution min ||w||_2 such that raw_prediction = X w:
126::COMO;;# w = X'(XX')^-1 raw_prediction = V s^-1 U' raw_prediction
131::COMO;;# Add penalty l2_reg_strength * ||coef||_2^2 for l2_reg_strength=1 and solve with
132::COMO;;# optimizer. Note that the problem is well conditioned such that we get accurate
133::COMO;;# results.

954::COMM;;warnings.simplefilter("ignore", ConvergenceWarning)
955::COMM;;sol.line_search(X=X, y=y, sample_weight=None)
956::COMM;;captured = capsys.readouterr()
957::COMM;;if verbose >= 1:
958::COMM;;assert (
959::COMM;;"Line search did not converge and resorts to lbfgs instead." in captured.out
960::COMM;;)
961::COMM;;# Set the Newton solver to a state with bad Newton step such that the loss
962::COMM;;# improvement in line search is tiny.
963::COMM;;sol = NewtonCholeskySolver(
964::COMM;;coef=np.array([1e-12, 0.69314758]),
965::COMM;;linear_loss=linear_loss,
966::COMM;;l2_reg_strength=0,
967::COMM;;verbose=verbose,
968::COMM;;)
969::COMM;;sol.setup(X=X, y=y, sample_weight=None)
970::COMM;;sol.iteration = 1
971::COMM;;sol.update_gradient_hessian(X=X, y=y, sample_weight=None)
972::COMM;;sol.coef_newton = np.array([1e-6, 0])
973::COMM;;sol.gradient_times_newton = sol.gradient @ sol.coef_newton
974::COMM;;with warnings.catch_warnings():
975::COMM;;warnings.simplefilter("ignore", ConvergenceWarning)
976::COMM;;sol.line_search(X=X, y=y, sample_weight=None)
977::COMM;;captured = capsys.readouterr()
978::COMM;;if verbose >= 2:
979::COMM;;msg = [
980::COMM;;"line search iteration=",
981::COMM;;"check loss improvement <= armijo term:",
982::COMM;;"check loss |improvement| <= eps * |loss_old|:",
983::COMM;;"check sum(|gradient|) < sum(|gradient_old|):",
984::COMM;;]
985::COMM;;for m in msg:
986::COMM;;assert m in captured.out
987::COMM;;# Test for a case with negative hessian. We badly initialize coef for a Tweedie
988::COMM;;# loss with non-canonical link, e.g. Inverse Gaussian deviance with a log link.
989::COMM;;linear_loss = LinearModelLoss(
990::COMM;;base_loss=HalfTweedieLoss(power=3), fit_intercept=False
991::COMM;;)

993::COMM;;coef=linear_loss.init_zero_coef(X) + 1,
994::COMM;;linear_loss=linear_loss,
995::COMM;;l2_reg_strength=0,
996::COMM;;verbose=verbose,
997::COMM;;)
998::COMM;;with warnings.catch_warnings():
999::COMM;;warnings.simplefilter("ignore", ConvergenceWarning)
1000::COMM;;sol.solve(X, y, None)
1001::COMM;;captured = capsys.readouterr()
