142::COMO;;# Note that centering y and X with _preprocess_data does not work
143::COMO;;# for quantile regression.
144::COMO;;# The objective is defined as 1/n * sum(pinball loss) + alpha * L1.
145::COMO;;# So we rescale the penalty term, which is equivalent.
156::COMO;;# make default solver more stable
161::COMO;;# After rescaling alpha, the minimization problem is
162::COMO;;# min sum(pinball loss) + alpha * L1
163::COMO;;# Use linear programming formulation of quantile regression
164::COMO;;# min_x c x
165::COMO;;# A_eq x = b_eq
166::COMO;;# 0 <= x
167::COMO;;# x = (s0, s, t0, t, u, v) = slack variables >= 0
168::COMO;;# intercept = s0 - t0
169::COMO;;# coef = s - t
170::COMO;;# c = (0, alpha * 1_p, 0, alpha * 1_p, quantile * 1_n, (1-quantile) * 1_n)
171::COMO;;# residual = y - X@coef - intercept = u - v
172::COMO;;# A_eq = (1_n, X, -1_n, -X, diag(1_n), -diag(1_n))
173::COMO;;# b_eq = y
174::COMO;;# p = n_features
175::COMO;;# n = n_samples
176::COMO;;# 1_n = vector of length n with entries equal one
177::COMO;;# see https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/384909/
178::COMO;;#
179::COMO;;# Filtering out zero sample weights from the beginning makes life
180::COMO;;# easier for the linprog solver.
182::COMC;;n_indices = len(indices) # use n_mask instead of n_samples
195::COMO;;# do not penalize the intercept
199::COMO;;# Note that highs methods always use a sparse CSC memory layout internally,
200::COMO;;# even for optimization problems parametrized using dense numpy arrays.
201::COMO;;# Therefore, we work with CSC matrices as early as possible to limit
202::COMO;;# unnecessary repeated memory copies.
241::COMO;;# positive slack - negative slack
242::COMO;;# solution is an array with (params_pos, params_neg, u, v)
1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
43::COMM;;sampled for the given inlier/outlier ratio.
44::COMM;;Parameters
45::COMM;;----------
46::COMM;;n_inliers : int
47::COMM;;Number of inliers in the data.
48::COMM;;n_samples : int
49::COMM;;Total number of samples in the data.
50::COMM;;min_samples : int
51::COMM;;Minimum number of samples chosen randomly from original data.
52::COMM;;probability : float
53::COMM;;Probability (confidence) that one outlier-free sample is generated.
54::COMM;;Returns
55::COMM;;-------
56::COMM;;trials : int
57::COMM;;Number of trials.
74::COMM;;RANSAC is an iterative algorithm for the robust estimation of parameters
75::COMM;;from a subset of inliers from the complete data set.
76::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <ransac_regression>`.
77::COMM;;Parameters
78::COMM;;----------
79::COMM;;estimator : object, default=None
80::COMM;;Base estimator object which implements the following methods:
81::COMM;;* `fit(X, y)`: Fit model to given training data and target values.
82::COMM;;* `score(X, y)`: Returns the mean accuracy on the given test data,
83::COMM;;which is used for the stop criterion defined by `stop_score`.
84::COMM;;Additionally, the score is used to decide which of two equally
85::COMM;;large consensus sets is chosen as the better one.
86::COMM;;* `predict(X)`: Returns predicted values using the linear model,
87::COMM;;which is used to compute residual error using loss function.
88::COMM;;If `estimator` is None, then
89::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` is used for
90::COMM;;target values of dtype float.
91::COMM;;Note that the current implementation only supports regression
92::COMM;;estimators.
93::COMM;;min_samples : int (>= 1) or float ([0, 1]), default=None
94::COMM;;Minimum number of samples chosen randomly from original data. Treated
95::COMM;;as an absolute number of samples for `min_samples >= 1`, treated as a
96::COMM;;relative number `ceil(min_samples * X.shape[0])` for
97::COMM;;`min_samples < 1`. This is typically chosen as the minimal number of
98::COMM;;samples necessary to estimate the given `estimator`. By default a
99::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` estimator is assumed and
100::COMM;;`min_samples` is chosen as ``X.shape[1] + 1``. This parameter is highly
101::COMM;;dependent upon the model, so if a `estimator` other than
102::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression` is used, the user must
103::COMM;;provide a value.
104::COMM;;residual_threshold : float, default=None
105::COMM;;Maximum residual for a data sample to be classified as an inlier.
106::COMM;;By default the threshold is chosen as the MAD (median absolute
107::COMM;;deviation) of the target values `y`. Points whose residuals are
108::COMM;;strictly equal to the threshold are considered as inliers.
109::COMM;;is_data_valid : callable, default=None
110::COMM;;This function is called with the randomly selected data before the
111::COMM;;model is fitted to it: `is_data_valid(X, y)`. If its return value is
112::COMM;;False the current randomly chosen sub-sample is skipped.
113::COMM;;is_model_valid : callable, default=None
114::COMM;;This function is called with the estimated model and the randomly
115::COMM;;selected data: `is_model_valid(model, X, y)`. If its return value is
116::COMM;;False the current randomly chosen sub-sample is skipped.
117::COMM;;Rejecting samples with this function is computationally costlier than
118::COMM;;with `is_data_valid`. `is_model_valid` should therefore only be used if
119::COMM;;the estimated model is needed for making the rejection decision.
120::COMM;;max_trials : int, default=100
121::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations for random sample selection.
122::COMM;;max_skips : int, default=np.inf
123::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations that can be skipped due to finding zero
124::COMM;;inliers or invalid data defined by ``is_data_valid`` or invalid models
125::COMM;;defined by ``is_model_valid``.
126::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
127::COMM;;stop_n_inliers : int, default=np.inf
128::COMM;;Stop iteration if at least this number of inliers are found.
129::COMM;;stop_score : float, default=np.inf
130::COMM;;Stop iteration if score is greater equal than this threshold.
131::COMM;;stop_probability : float in range [0, 1], default=0.99
132::COMM;;RANSAC iteration stops if at least one outlier-free set of the training
133::COMM;;data is sampled in RANSAC. This requires to generate at least N
134::COMM;;samples (iterations)::
135::COMM;;N >= log(1 - probability) / log(1 - e**m)
136::COMM;;where the probability (confidence) is typically set to high value such
137::COMM;;as 0.99 (the default) and e is the current fraction of inliers w.r.t.
138::COMM;;the total number of samples.
139::COMM;;loss : str, callable, default='absolute_error'
140::COMM;;String inputs, 'absolute_error' and 'squared_error' are supported which
141::COMM;;find the absolute error and squared error per sample respectively.
142::COMM;;If ``loss`` is a callable, then it should be a function that takes
143::COMM;;two arrays as inputs, the true and predicted value and returns a 1-D
144::COMM;;array with the i-th value of the array corresponding to the loss
145::COMM;;on ``X[i]``.
146::COMM;;If the loss on a sample is greater than the ``residual_threshold``,
147::COMM;;then this sample is classified as an outlier.
148::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
149::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
150::COMM;;The generator used to initialize the centers.
151::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
152::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
153::COMM;;Attributes
154::COMM;;----------
155::COMM;;estimator_ : object
156::COMM;;Final model fitted on the inliers predicted by the "best" model found
157::COMM;;during RANSAC sampling (copy of the `estimator` object).
158::COMM;;n_trials_ : int
159::COMM;;Number of random selection trials until one of the stop criteria is
160::COMM;;met. It is always ``<= max_trials``.
161::COMM;;inlier_mask_ : bool array of shape [n_samples]
162::COMM;;Boolean mask of inliers classified as ``True``.
163::COMM;;n_skips_no_inliers_ : int
164::COMM;;Number of iterations skipped due to finding zero inliers.
165::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
166::COMM;;n_skips_invalid_data_ : int
167::COMM;;Number of iterations skipped due to invalid data defined by
168::COMM;;``is_data_valid``.
169::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
170::COMM;;n_skips_invalid_model_ : int
171::COMM;;Number of iterations skipped due to an invalid model defined by
172::COMM;;``is_model_valid``.
173::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
174::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
175::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
176::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
177::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
178::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
179::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
180::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0

2::COMM;;Ridge regression
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
68::COMM;;Matrix product `LinearOperator @ coef` returns `(X - X_offset) @ coef`.
110::COMO;;# kernel ridge
111::COMO;;# w = X.T * inv(X X^t + alpha*Id) y
118::COMO;;# linear ridge
119::COMO;;# w = inv(X^t X + alpha*Id) * X.T y
146::COMM;;We expect that y is always mean centered.
147::COMM;;If X is dense, we expect it to be mean centered such that we can solve
148::COMM;;||y - Xw||_2^2 + alpha * ||w||_2^2
149::COMM;;If X is sparse, we expect X_offset to be given such that we can solve
150::COMM;;||y - (X - X_offset)w||_2^2 + alpha * ||w||_2^2
151::COMM;;With sample weights S=diag(sample_weight), this becomes
152::COMM;;||sqrt(S) (y - (X - X_offset) w)||_2^2 + alpha * ||w||_2^2
153::COMM;;and we expect y and X to already be rescaled, i.e. sqrt(S) @ y, sqrt(S) @ X. In
154::COMM;;this case, X_offset is the sample_weight weighted mean of X before scaling by
155::COMM;;sqrt(S). The objective then reads
156::COMM;;||y - (X - sqrt(S) X_offset) w)||_2^2 + alpha * ||w||_2^2
164::COMO;;# No need to touch anything
169::COMO;;# According to the lsqr documentation, alpha = damp^2.
180::COMO;;# w = inv(X^t X + alpha*Id) * X.T y
197::COMO;;# dual_coef = inv(X X^t + alpha*Id) y
206::COMO;;# Unlike other solvers, we need to support sample_weight directly
207::COMO;;# because K might be a pre-computed kernel.
212::COMO;;# Only one penalty, we can solve multi-target problems in one time.
215::COMO;;# Note: we must use overwrite_a=False in order to be able to
216::COMO;;# use the fall-back solution below in case a LinAlgError
217::COMO;;# is raised
225::COMO;;# K is expensive to compute and store in memory so change it back in
226::COMO;;# case it was user-given.
232::COMO;;# One penalty per target. We need to solve each target separately.
246::COMC;;idx = s > 1e-15 # same default value as scipy.linalg.pinv
265::COMM;;The main purpose is fitting with forcing coefficients to be positive.
266::COMM;;For unconstrained ridge regression, there are faster dedicated solver methods.
267::COMM;;Note that with positive bounds on the coefficients, LBFGS seems faster
268::COMM;;than scipy.optimize.lsq_linear.
360::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <ridge_regression>`.
361::COMM;;Parameters
362::COMM;;----------
363::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix, LinearOperator} of shape \
364::COMM;;(n_samples, n_features)
365::COMM;;Training data.
366::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_targets)
367::COMM;;Target values.
368::COMM;;alpha : float or array-like of shape (n_targets,)
369::COMM;;Constant that multiplies the L2 term, controlling regularization
370::COMM;;strength. `alpha` must be a non-negative float i.e. in `[0, inf)`.
371::COMM;;When `alpha = 0`, the objective is equivalent to ordinary least
372::COMM;;squares, solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
373::COMM;;reasons, using `alpha = 0` with the `Ridge` object is not advised.
374::COMM;;Instead, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object.
375::COMM;;If an array is passed, penalties are assumed to be specific to the
376::COMM;;targets. Hence they must correspond in number.
377::COMM;;sample_weight : float or array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
378::COMM;;Individual weights for each sample. If given a float, every sample
379::COMM;;will have the same weight. If sample_weight is not None and
380::COMM;;solver='auto', the solver will be set to 'cholesky'.
381::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
382::COMM;;solver : {'auto', 'svd', 'cholesky', 'lsqr', 'sparse_cg', \
383::COMM;;'sag', 'saga', 'lbfgs'}, default='auto'
384::COMM;;Solver to use in the computational routines:
385::COMM;;- 'auto' chooses the solver automatically based on the type of data.
386::COMM;;- 'svd' uses a Singular Value Decomposition of X to compute the Ridge
387::COMM;;coefficients. It is the most stable solver, in particular more stable
388::COMM;;for singular matrices than 'cholesky' at the cost of being slower.
389::COMM;;- 'cholesky' uses the standard scipy.linalg.solve function to
390::COMM;;obtain a closed-form solution via a Cholesky decomposition of
391::COMM;;dot(X.T, X)
392::COMM;;- 'sparse_cg' uses the conjugate gradient solver as found in
393::COMM;;scipy.sparse.linalg.cg. As an iterative algorithm, this solver is
394::COMM;;more appropriate than 'cholesky' for large-scale data
395::COMM;;(possibility to set `tol` and `max_iter`).
396::COMM;;- 'lsqr' uses the dedicated regularized least-squares routine
397::COMM;;scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr. It is the fastest and uses an iterative
398::COMM;;procedure.
399::COMM;;- 'sag' uses a Stochastic Average Gradient descent, and 'saga' uses
400::COMM;;its improved, unbiased version named SAGA. Both methods also use an
401::COMM;;iterative procedure, and are often faster than other solvers when
402::COMM;;both n_samples and n_features are large. Note that 'sag' and
403::COMM;;'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features with
404::COMM;;approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with a
405::COMM;;scaler from sklearn.preprocessing.
406::COMM;;- 'lbfgs' uses L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in
407::COMM;;`scipy.optimize.minimize`. It can be used only when `positive`
408::COMM;;is True.
409::COMM;;All solvers except 'svd' support both dense and sparse data. However, only
410::COMM;;'lsqr', 'sag', 'sparse_cg', and 'lbfgs' support sparse input when
411::COMM;;`fit_intercept` is True.
412::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
413::COMM;;Stochastic Average Gradient descent solver.
414::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
415::COMM;;SAGA solver.
416::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=None
417::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations for conjugate gradient solver.
418::COMM;;For the 'sparse_cg' and 'lsqr' solvers, the default value is determined
419::COMM;;by scipy.sparse.linalg. For 'sag' and saga solver, the default value is
420::COMM;;1000. For 'lbfgs' solver, the default value is 15000.
421::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
422::COMM;;Precision of the solution. Note that `tol` has no effect for solvers 'svd' and
423::COMM;;'cholesky'.
424::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
425::COMM;;Default value changed from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for consistency with other linear
426::COMM;;models.
427::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
428::COMM;;Verbosity level. Setting verbose > 0 will display additional
429::COMM;;information depending on the solver used.
430::COMM;;positive : bool, default=False
431::COMM;;When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive.
432::COMM;;Only 'lbfgs' solver is supported in this case.
433::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
434::COMM;;Used when ``solver`` == 'sag' or 'saga' to shuffle the data.
435::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
436::COMM;;return_n_iter : bool, default=False
437::COMM;;If True, the method also returns `n_iter`, the actual number of
438::COMM;;iteration performed by the solver.
439::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
440::COMM;;return_intercept : bool, default=False
441::COMM;;If True and if X is sparse, the method also returns the intercept,
442::COMM;;and the solver is automatically changed to 'sag'. This is only a
443::COMM;;temporary fix for fitting the intercept with sparse data. For dense
444::COMM;;data, use sklearn.linear_model._preprocess_data before your regression.
445::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
446::COMM;;check_input : bool, default=True
447::COMM;;If False, the input arrays X and y will not be checked.
448::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.21
449::COMM;;Returns
450::COMM;;-------
451::COMM;;coef : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or (n_targets, n_features)
452::COMM;;Weight vector(s).
453::COMM;;n_iter : int, optional
454::COMM;;The actual number of iteration performed by the solver.
455::COMM;;Only returned if `return_n_iter` is True.
456::COMM;;intercept : float or ndarray of shape (n_targets,)
457::COMM;;The intercept of the model. Only returned if `return_intercept`
458::COMM;;is True and if X is a scipy sparse array.
459::COMM;;Notes
460::COMM;;-----
461::COMM;;This function won't compute the intercept.
462::COMM;;Regularization improves the conditioning of the problem and
463::COMM;;reduces the variance of the estimates. Larger values specify stronger
464::COMM;;regularization. Alpha corresponds to ``1 / (2C)`` in other linear
465::COMM;;models such as :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` or
466::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`. If an array is passed, penalties are
467::COMM;;assumed to be specific to the targets. Hence they must correspond in
468::COMM;;number.
469::COMM;;Examples
470::COMM;;--------
471::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
472::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
473::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import ridge_regression
474::COMM;;>>> rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
475::COMM;;>>> X = rng.randn(100, 4)
476::COMM;;>>> y = 2.0 * X[:, 0] - 1.0 * X[:, 1] + 0.1 * rng.standard_normal(100)
477::COMM;;>>> coef, intercept = ridge_regression(X, y, alpha=1.0, return_intercept=True,
478::COMM;;... random_state=0)
479::COMM;;>>> coef
480::COMM;;array([ 1.97, -1., -2.69e-3, -9.27e-4 ])
481::COMM;;>>> intercept
482::COMM;;np.float64(-.0012)
571::COMO;;# SAG supports sample_weight directly. For other solvers,
572::COMO;;# we implement sample_weight via a simple rescaling.
574::COMO;;# Some callers of this method might pass alpha as single
575::COMO;;# element array which already has been validated.
584::COMO;;# There should be either 1 or n_targets penalties
627::COMO;;# use SVD solver if matrix is singular
633::COMO;;# use SVD solver if matrix is singular
636::COMO;;# precompute max_squared_sum for all targets
711::COMO;;# At the moment, Array API dispatch only supports the "svd" solver.
726::COMO;;# sag supports fitting intercept directly
807::COMO;;# when X is sparse we only remove offset from y
832::COMO;;# add the offset which was subtracted by _preprocess_data
836::COMO;;# required to fit intercept with sparse_cg and lbfgs solver
839::COMO;;# for dense matrices or when intercept is set to 0
862::COMM;;Minimizes the objective function::
863::COMM;;||y - Xw||^2_2 + alpha * ||w||^2_2
864::COMM;;This model solves a regression model where the loss function is
865::COMM;;the linear least squares function and regularization is given by
866::COMM;;the l2-norm. Also known as Ridge Regression or Tikhonov regularization.
867::COMM;;This estimator has built-in support for multi-variate regression
868::COMM;;(i.e., when y is a 2d-array of shape (n_samples, n_targets)).
869::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <ridge_regression>`.
870::COMM;;Parameters
871::COMM;;----------
872::COMM;;alpha : {float, ndarray of shape (n_targets,)}, default=1.0
873::COMM;;Constant that multiplies the L2 term, controlling regularization
874::COMM;;strength. `alpha` must be a non-negative float i.e. in `[0, inf)`.
875::COMM;;When `alpha = 0`, the objective is equivalent to ordinary least
876::COMM;;squares, solved by the :class:`LinearRegression` object. For numerical
877::COMM;;reasons, using `alpha = 0` with the `Ridge` object is not advised.
878::COMM;;Instead, you should use the :class:`LinearRegression` object.
879::COMM;;If an array is passed, penalties are assumed to be specific to the
880::COMM;;targets. Hence they must correspond in number.
881::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
882::COMM;;Whether to fit the intercept for this model. If set
883::COMM;;to false, no intercept will be used in calculations
884::COMM;;(i.e. ``X`` and ``y`` are expected to be centered).
885::COMM;;copy_X : bool, default=True
886::COMM;;If True, X will be copied; else, it may be overwritten.
887::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=None
888::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations for conjugate gradient solver.
889::COMM;;For 'sparse_cg' and 'lsqr' solvers, the default value is determined
890::COMM;;by scipy.sparse.linalg. For 'sag' solver, the default value is 1000.
891::COMM;;For 'lbfgs' solver, the default value is 15000.
892::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
893::COMM;;The precision of the solution (`coef_`) is determined by `tol` which
894::COMM;;specifies a different convergence criterion for each solver:
895::COMM;;- 'svd': `tol` has no impact.
896::COMM;;- 'cholesky': `tol` has no impact.
897::COMM;;- 'sparse_cg': norm of residuals smaller than `tol`.
898::COMM;;- 'lsqr': `tol` is set as atol and btol of scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr,
899::COMM;;which control the norm of the residual vector in terms of the norms of
900::COMM;;matrix and coefficients.
901::COMM;;- 'sag' and 'saga': relative change of coef smaller than `tol`.
902::COMM;;- 'lbfgs': maximum of the absolute (projected) gradient=max|residuals|
903::COMM;;smaller than `tol`.
904::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.2
905::COMM;;Default value changed from 1e-3 to 1e-4 for consistency with other linear
906::COMM;;models.
907::COMM;;solver : {'auto', 'svd', 'cholesky', 'lsqr', 'sparse_cg', \
908::COMM;;'sag', 'saga', 'lbfgs'}, default='auto'
909::COMM;;Solver to use in the computational routines:
910::COMM;;- 'auto' chooses the solver automatically based on the type of data.
911::COMM;;- 'svd' uses a Singular Value Decomposition of X to compute the Ridge
912::COMM;;coefficients. It is the most stable solver, in particular more stable
913::COMM;;for singular matrices than 'cholesky' at the cost of being slower.
914::COMM;;- 'cholesky' uses the standard :func:`scipy.linalg.solve` function to
915::COMM;;obtain a closed-form solution.
916::COMM;;- 'sparse_cg' uses the conjugate gradient solver as found in
917::COMM;;:func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.cg`. As an iterative algorithm, this solver is
918::COMM;;more appropriate than 'cholesky' for large-scale data
919::COMM;;(possibility to set `tol` and `max_iter`).
920::COMM;;- 'lsqr' uses the dedicated regularized least-squares routine
921::COMM;;:func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr`. It is the fastest and uses an iterative
922::COMM;;procedure.
923::COMM;;- 'sag' uses a Stochastic Average Gradient descent, and 'saga' uses
924::COMM;;its improved, unbiased version named SAGA. Both methods also use an
925::COMM;;iterative procedure, and are often faster than other solvers when
926::COMM;;both n_samples and n_features are large. Note that 'sag' and
927::COMM;;'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features with
928::COMM;;approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with a
929::COMM;;scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.
930::COMM;;- 'lbfgs' uses L-BFGS-B algorithm implemented in
931::COMM;;:func:`scipy.optimize.minimize`. It can be used only when `positive`
932::COMM;;is True.
933::COMM;;All solvers except 'svd' support both dense and sparse data. However, only
934::COMM;;'lsqr', 'sag', 'sparse_cg', and 'lbfgs' support sparse input when
935::COMM;;`fit_intercept` is True.
936::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
937::COMM;;Stochastic Average Gradient descent solver.
938::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
939::COMM;;SAGA solver.
940::COMM;;positive : bool, default=False
941::COMM;;When set to ``True``, forces the coefficients to be positive.
942::COMM;;Only 'lbfgs' solver is supported in this case.
943::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
944::COMM;;Used when ``solver`` == 'sag' or 'saga' to shuffle the data.
945::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
946::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
947::COMM;;`random_state` to support Stochastic Average Gradient.
948::COMM;;Attributes
949::COMM;;----------
950::COMM;;coef_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or (n_targets, n_features)
951::COMM;;Weight vector(s).
952::COMM;;intercept_ : float or ndarray of shape (n_targets,)
953::COMM;;Independent term in decision function. Set to 0.0 if
954::COMM;;``fit_intercept = False``.
955::COMM;;n_iter_ : None or ndarray of shape (n_targets,)
956::COMM;;Actual number of iterations for each target. Available only for
957::COMM;;'sag' and 'lsqr' solvers. Other solvers will return None.
958::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
959::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
960::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
961::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
962::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
963::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
964::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
965::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
966::COMM;;solver_ : str
967::COMM;;The solver that was used at fit time by the computational
968::COMM;;routines.
969::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
970::COMM;;See Also
971::COMM;;--------
972::COMM;;RidgeClassifier : Ridge classifier.
973::COMM;;RidgeCV : Ridge regression with built-in cross validation.
974::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.kernel_ridge.KernelRidge` : Kernel ridge regression
975::COMM;;combines ridge regression with the kernel trick.
976::COMM;;Notes
977::COMM;;-----
978::COMM;;Regularization improves the conditioning of the problem and
979::COMM;;reduces the variance of the estimates. Larger values specify stronger
980::COMM;;regularization. Alpha corresponds to ``1 / (2C)`` in other linear
981::COMM;;models such as :class:`~sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression` or
982::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.svm.LinearSVC`.

1663::COMO;;# when all samples have the same weight we add a column of 1
1670::COMO;;# remove eigenvalues and vectors in the null space of X^T.X
1678::COMM;;Used when we have a decomposition of X^T.X
1679::COMM;;(n_samples > n_features and X is sparse), and not fitting an intercept.
1687::COMO;;# handle case where y is 2-d
1694::COMM;;Used when we have a decomposition of X^T.X
1695::COMM;;(n_samples > n_features and X is sparse),
1696::COMM;;and we are fitting an intercept.
1698::COMO;;# the vector [0, 0, ..., 0, 1]
1699::COMO;;# is the eigenvector of X^TX which
1700::COMO;;# corresponds to the intercept; we cancel the regularization on
1701::COMO;;# this dimension. the corresponding eigenvalue is
1702::COMO;;# sum(sample_weight), e.g. n when uniform sample weights.
1709::COMO;;# add a column to X containing the square roots of sample weights
1714::COMO;;# return (1 - hat_diag), (y - y_hat)
1716::COMO;;# handle case where y is 2-d
1721::COMM;;Used when we have a decomposition of X^T.X
1722::COMM;;(n_samples > n_features and X is sparse).
1733::COMO;;# X already centered
1736::COMO;;# to emulate fit_intercept=True situation, add a column
1737::COMO;;# containing the square roots of the sample weights
1738::COMO;;# by centering, the other columns are orthogonal to that one
1747::COMM;;Used when we have an SVD decomposition of X
1748::COMM;;(n_samples > n_features and X is dense).
1753::COMO;;# detect intercept column
1756::COMO;;# cancel the regularization for the intercept
1761::COMO;;# handle case where y is 2-d

12::COMM;;def get_auto_step_size(
13::COMM;;max_squared_sum, alpha_scaled, loss, fit_intercept, n_samples=None, is_saga=False
14::COMM;;):
48::COMM;;if loss in ("log", "multinomial"):
49::COMM;;L = 0.25 * (max_squared_sum + int(fit_intercept)) + alpha_scaled
50::COMM;;elif loss == "squared":
51::COMM;;# inverse Lipschitz constant for squared loss
52::COMM;;L = max_squared_sum + int(fit_intercept) + alpha_scaled
53::COMM;;else:
54::COMM;;raise ValueError(
55::COMM;;"Unknown loss function for SAG solver, got %s instead of 'log' or 'squared'"
56::COMM;;% loss
57::COMM;;)
58::COMM;;if is_saga:
59::COMM;;# SAGA theoretical step size is 1/3L or 1 / (2 * (L + mu n))
60::COMM;;# See Defazio et al. 2014
61::COMM;;mun = min(2 * n_samples * alpha_scaled, L)
62::COMM;;step = 1.0 / (2 * L + mun)
63::COMM;;else:
64::COMM;;# SAG theoretical step size is 1/16L but it is recommended to use 1 / L
65::COMM;;# see http://www.birs.ca//workshops//2014/14w5003/files/schmidt.pdf,
66::COMM;;# slide 65
67::COMM;;step = 1.0 / L
68::COMM;;return step

65::COMM;;The spatial median is member of a class of so-called M-estimators which
66::COMM;;are defined by an optimization problem. Given a number of p points in an
67::COMM;;n-dimensional space, the point x minimizing the sum of all distances to the
68::COMM;;p other points is called spatial median.

132::COMM;;This function calculates the least squares method on a subset of rows of X
133::COMM;;and y defined by the indices array. Optionally, an intercept column is
134::COMM;;added if intercept is set to true.
135::COMM;;Parameters
136::COMM;;----------
137::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
138::COMM;;Design matrix, where `n_samples` is the number of samples and
139::COMM;;`n_features` is the number of features.
140::COMM;;y : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
141::COMM;;Target vector, where `n_samples` is the number of samples.
142::COMM;;indices : ndarray of shape (n_subpopulation, n_subsamples)
143::COMM;;Indices of all subsamples with respect to the chosen subpopulation.
144::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool
145::COMM;;Fit intercept or not.
146::COMM;;Returns
147::COMM;;-------
148::COMM;;weights : ndarray of shape (n_subpopulation, n_features + intercept)
149::COMM;;Solution matrix of n_subpopulation solved least square problems.
156::COMO;;# gelss need to pad y_subpopulation to be of the max dim of X_subpopulation
166::COMM;;The algorithm calculates least square solutions on subsets with size
167::COMM;;n_subsamples of the samples in X. Any value of n_subsamples between the
168::COMM;;number of features and samples leads to an estimator with a compromise
169::COMM;;between robustness and efficiency. Since the number of least square
170::COMM;;solutions is "n_samples choose n_subsamples", it can be extremely large
171::COMM;;and can therefore be limited with max_subpopulation. If this limit is
172::COMM;;reached, the subsets are chosen randomly. In a final step, the spatial
173::COMM;;median (or L1 median) is calculated of all least square solutions.
174::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <theil_sen_regression>`.
175::COMM;;Parameters
176::COMM;;----------
177::COMM;;fit_intercept : bool, default=True
178::COMM;;Whether to calculate the intercept for this model. If set
179::COMM;;to false, no intercept will be used in calculations.
180::COMM;;max_subpopulation : int, default=1e4
181::COMM;;Instead of computing with a set of cardinality 'n choose k', where n is
182::COMM;;the number of samples and k is the number of subsamples (at least
183::COMM;;number of features), consider only a stochastic subpopulation of a
184::COMM;;given maximal size if 'n choose k' is larger than max_subpopulation.
185::COMM;;For other than small problem sizes this parameter will determine
186::COMM;;memory usage and runtime if n_subsamples is not changed. Note that the
187::COMM;;data type should be int but floats such as 1e4 can be accepted too.
188::COMM;;n_subsamples : int, default=None
189::COMM;;Number of samples to calculate the parameters. This is at least the
190::COMM;;number of features (plus 1 if fit_intercept=True) and the number of
191::COMM;;samples as a maximum. A lower number leads to a higher breakdown
192::COMM;;point and a low efficiency while a high number leads to a low
193::COMM;;breakdown point and a high efficiency. If None, take the
194::COMM;;minimum number of subsamples leading to maximal robustness.
195::COMM;;If n_subsamples is set to n_samples, Theil-Sen is identical to least
196::COMM;;squares.
197::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
198::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations for the calculation of spatial median.
199::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-3
200::COMM;;Tolerance when calculating spatial median.
201::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
202::COMM;;A random number generator instance to define the state of the random
203::COMM;;permutations generator. Pass an int for reproducible output across
204::COMM;;multiple function calls.
205::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
206::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
207::COMM;;Number of CPUs to use during the cross validation.
208::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
209::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
210::COMM;;for more details.
211::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
212::COMM;;Verbose mode when fitting the model.

505::COMM;;# Numbers are with skglm version 0.5.
506::COMM;;n_samples, n_features, n_tasks = 5, 4, 3
507::COMM;;X = np.vander(np.arange(n_samples), n_features)
508::COMM;;Y = np.arange(n_samples * n_tasks).reshape(n_samples, n_tasks)
509::COMM;;def obj(W, X, y, alpha):
510::COMM;;intercept = W[:, -1]
511::COMM;;W = W[:, :-1]
512::COMM;;l21_norm = np.sqrt(np.sum(W**2, axis=0)).sum()
513::COMM;;return (
514::COMM;;np.linalg.norm(Y - X @ W.T - intercept, ord="fro") ** 2 / (2 * n_samples)
515::COMM;;+ alpha * l21_norm
516::COMM;;)
517::COMM;;alpha = 0.1
518::COMM;;# TODO: The high number of iterations are required for convergence and show room
519::COMM;;# for improvement of the CD algorithm.
520::COMM;;m = MultiTaskLasso(alpha=alpha, tol=1e-10, max_iter=5000).fit(X, Y)
521::COMM;;assert_allclose(
522::COMM;;obj(np.c_[m.coef_, m.intercept_], X, Y, alpha=alpha),
523::COMM;;0.4965993692547902,
524::COMM;;rtol=1e-10,
525::COMM;;)
526::COMM;;assert_allclose(
527::COMM;;m.intercept_, [0.219942959407, 1.219942959407, 2.219942959407], rtol=1e-7
528::COMM;;)
529::COMM;;assert_allclose(
530::COMM;;m.coef_,
531::COMM;;np.tile([-0.032075014794, 0.25430904614, 2.44785152982, 0], (n_tasks, 1)),
532::COMM;;rtol=1e-6,
533::COMM;;)

665::COMM;;def test_elasticnet_precompute_gram_weighted_samples():
666::COMM;;# check the equivalence between passing a precomputed Gram matrix and
667::COMM;;# internal computation using sample weights.
668::COMM;;X, y, _, _ = build_dataset()
669::COMM;;rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
670::COMM;;sample_weight = rng.lognormal(size=y.shape)
671::COMM;;w_norm = sample_weight * (y.shape / np.sum(sample_weight))
672::COMM;;X_c = X - np.average(X, axis=0, weights=w_norm)
673::COMM;;X_r = X_c * np.sqrt(w_norm)[:, np.newaxis]
674::COMM;;gram = np.dot(X_r.T, X_r)
675::COMM;;clf1 = ElasticNet(alpha=0.01, precompute=gram)
676::COMM;;clf1.fit(X_c, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
677::COMM;;clf2 = ElasticNet(alpha=0.01, precompute=False)
678::COMM;;clf2.fit(X, y, sample_weight=sample_weight)
679::COMM;;assert_allclose(clf1.coef_, clf2.coef_)

239::COMM;;Gradient should equal the numerical derivatives of the loss function.
240::COMM;;Hessians should equal the numerical derivatives of gradients.
250::COMC;;coef = coef.ravel(order="F") # this is important only for multinomial loss
253::COMO;;# 1. Check gradients numerically
258::COMO;;# Use a trick to get central finite difference of accuracy 4 (five-point stencil)
259::COMO;;# https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_differentiation
260::COMO;;# https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_difference_coefficient
261::COMO;;# approx_g1 = (f(x + eps) - f(x - eps)) / (2*eps)
273::COMO;;# approx_g2 = (f(x + 2*eps) - f(x - 2*eps)) / (4*eps)
285::COMO;;# Five-point stencil approximation
286::COMO;;# See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five-point_stencil#1D_first_derivative
289::COMO;;# 2. Check hessp numerically along the second direction of the gradient
293::COMO;;# Computation of the Hessian is particularly fragile to numerical errors when doing
294::COMO;;# simple finite differences. Here we compute the grad along a path in the direction
295::COMO;;# of the vector and then use a least-square regression to estimate the slope
316::COMM;;loss = LinearModelLoss(base_loss=HalfMultinomialLoss(), fit_intercept=fit_intercept)
317::COMM;;n_samples, n_features = 10, 5
318::COMM;;X, y, coef = random_X_y_coef(
319::COMM;;linear_model_loss=loss,
320::COMM;;n_samples=n_samples,
321::COMM;;n_features=n_features,
322::COMM;;seed=global_random_seed,

1548::COMM;;# Check that training with a penalty matching the objective leads

1550::COMM;;# Here we train a logistic regression with l2 (a) and elasticnet (b)

1552::COMM;;# greater than that of b (both objectives are convex).
1553::COMM;;X, y = make_classification(
1554::COMM;;n_samples=1000,
1555::COMM;;n_classes=2,
1556::COMM;;n_features=20,
1557::COMM;;n_informative=10,

1560::COMM;;random_state=0,

1564::COMM;;penalty="elasticnet",
1565::COMM;;solver="saga",
1566::COMM;;random_state=0,
1567::COMM;;C=C,

1569::COMM;;fit_intercept=False,

1573::COMM;;)

1577::COMM;;coef = lr.coef_.ravel()

1581::COMM;;return obj

1189::COMM;;# SGD One Class SVM Test Case
1190::COMM;;# a simple implementation of ASGD to use for testing SGDOneClassSVM
1191::COMM;;def asgd_oneclass(klass, X, eta, nu, coef_init=None, offset_init=0.0):
1192::COMM;;if coef_init is None:
1193::COMM;;coef = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
1194::COMM;;else:
1195::COMM;;coef = coef_init
1196::COMM;;average_coef = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
1197::COMM;;offset = offset_init
1198::COMM;;intercept = 1 - offset
1199::COMM;;average_intercept = 0.0
1200::COMM;;decay = 1.0
1201::COMM;;# sparse data has a fixed decay of .01
1202::COMM;;if klass == SparseSGDOneClassSVM:
1203::COMM;;decay = 0.01
1204::COMM;;for i, entry in enumerate(X):
1205::COMM;;p = np.dot(entry, coef)
1206::COMM;;p += intercept
1207::COMM;;if p <= 1.0:
1208::COMM;;gradient = -1
1209::COMM;;else:
1210::COMM;;gradient = 0
1211::COMM;;coef *= max(0, 1.0 - (eta * nu / 2))
1212::COMM;;coef += -(eta * gradient * entry)
1213::COMM;;intercept += -(eta * (nu + gradient)) * decay
1214::COMM;;average_coef *= i
1215::COMM;;average_coef += coef
1216::COMM;;average_coef /= i + 1.0
1217::COMM;;average_intercept *= i
1218::COMM;;average_intercept += intercept
1219::COMM;;average_intercept /= i + 1.0
1220::COMM;;return average_coef, 1 - average_intercept
1221::COMM;;@pytest.mark.parametrize("klass", [SGDOneClassSVM, SparseSGDOneClassSVM])
1222::COMM;;def _test_warm_start_oneclass(klass, X, lr):
1223::COMM;;# Test that explicit warm restart...
1224::COMM;;clf = klass(nu=0.5, eta0=0.01, shuffle=False, learning_rate=lr)
1225::COMM;;clf.fit(X)
1226::COMM;;clf2 = klass(nu=0.1, eta0=0.01, shuffle=False, learning_rate=lr)
1227::COMM;;clf2.fit(X, coef_init=clf.coef_.copy(), offset_init=clf.offset_.copy())
1228::COMM;;# ... and implicit warm restart are equivalent.
1229::COMM;;clf3 = klass(nu=0.5, eta0=0.01, shuffle=False, warm_start=True, learning_rate=lr)
1230::COMM;;clf3.fit(X)

2::COMM;;Classical multi-dimensional scaling (classical MDS).
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
17::COMM;;This is also known as principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) or
18::COMM;;Torgerson's scaling. It is a version of MDS that has exact solution
19::COMM;;in terms of eigendecomposition. If the input dissimilarity matrix
20::COMM;;consists of the pairwise Euclidean distances between some vectors,
21::COMM;;then classical MDS is equivalent to PCA applied to this set of vectors.
22::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <multidimensional_scaling>`.
23::COMM;;Parameters
24::COMM;;----------
25::COMM;;n_components : int, default=2
26::COMM;;Number of embedding dimensions.
27::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default='euclidean'
28::COMM;;Metric to use for dissimilarity computation. Default is "euclidean".
29::COMM;;If metric is a string, it must be one of the options allowed by
30::COMM;;`scipy.spatial.distance.pdist` for its metric parameter, or a metric
31::COMM;;listed in :func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics`
32::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
33::COMM;;must be square during fit.
34::COMM;;If metric is a callable function, it takes two arrays representing 1D
35::COMM;;vectors as inputs and must return one value indicating the distance
36::COMM;;between those vectors. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
37::COMM;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
38::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
39::COMM;;Additional keyword arguments for the dissimilarity computation.
40::COMM;;Attributes
41::COMM;;----------
42::COMM;;embedding_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components)
43::COMM;;Stores the position of the dataset in the embedding space.
44::COMM;;dissimilarity_matrix_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
45::COMM;;Pairwise dissimilarities between the points.
46::COMM;;eigenvalues_ : ndarray of shape (n_components,)
47::COMM;;Eigenvalues of the double-centered dissimilarity matrix, corresponding
48::COMM;;to each of the selected components. They are equal to the squared 2-norms
49::COMM;;of the `n_components` variables in the embedding space.
50::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
51::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
52::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
53::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
54::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
55::COMM;;See Also
56::COMM;;--------
57::COMM;;sklearn.decomposition.PCA : Principal component analysis.
58::COMM;;MDS : Metric and non-metric MDS.
59::COMM;;References
60::COMM;;----------
61::COMM;;.. [1] "Modern Multidimensional Scaling - Theory and Applications" Borg, I.;
62::COMM;;Groenen P. Springer Series in Statistics (1997)
63::COMM;;Examples
64::COMM;;--------
65::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
66::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.manifold import ClassicalMDS
67::COMM;;>>> X, _ = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
68::COMM;;>>> X.shape

21::COMM;;def barycenter_weights(X, Y, indices, reg=1e-3):
41::COMM;;X = check_array(X, dtype=FLOAT_DTYPES)
42::COMM;;Y = check_array(Y, dtype=FLOAT_DTYPES)
43::COMM;;indices = check_array(indices, dtype=int)
44::COMM;;n_samples, n_neighbors = indices.shape
45::COMM;;assert X.shape[0] == n_samples
46::COMM;;B = np.empty((n_samples, n_neighbors), dtype=X.dtype)
47::COMM;;v = np.ones(n_neighbors, dtype=X.dtype)
48::COMM;;# this might raise a LinalgError if G is singular and has trace
49::COMM;;# zero
50::COMM;;for i, ind in enumerate(indices):
51::COMM;;A = Y[ind]
52::COMM;;C = A - X[i] # broadcasting
53::COMM;;G = np.dot(C, C.T)
54::COMM;;trace = np.trace(G)
55::COMM;;if trace > 0:
56::COMM;;R = reg * trace
57::COMM;;else:
58::COMM;;R = reg
59::COMM;;G.flat[:: n_neighbors + 1] += R
60::COMM;;w = solve(G, v, assume_a="pos")
61::COMM;;B[i, :] = w / np.sum(w)
62::COMM;;return B

97::COMM;;def null_space(
98::COMM;;M, k, k_skip=1, eigen_solver="arpack", tol=1e-6, max_iter=100, random_state=None
99::COMM;;):
132::COMM;;if eigen_solver == "auto":
133::COMM;;if M.shape[0] > 200 and k + k_skip < 10:
134::COMM;;eigen_solver = "arpack"
135::COMM;;else:
136::COMM;;eigen_solver = "dense"

141::COMM;;M, k + k_skip, sigma=0.0, tol=tol, maxiter=max_iter, v0=v0
142::COMM;;)
143::COMM;;except RuntimeError as e:

145::COMM;;"Error in determining null-space with ARPACK. Error message: "
146::COMM;;"'%s'. Note that eigen_solver='arpack' can fail when the "
147::COMM;;"weight matrix is singular or otherwise ill-behaved. In that "
148::COMM;;"case, eigen_solver='dense' is recommended. See online "
149::COMM;;"documentation for more information." % e
150::COMM;;) from e
151::COMM;;return eigen_vectors[:, k_skip:], np.sum(eigen_values[k_skip:])
152::COMM;;elif eigen_solver == "dense":

154::COMM;;M = M.toarray()

156::COMM;;M, subset_by_index=(k_skip, k + k_skip - 1), overwrite_a=True
157::COMM;;)
158::COMM;;index = np.argsort(np.abs(eigen_values))
159::COMM;;return eigen_vectors[:, index], np.sum(eigen_values)
160::COMM;;else:

162::COMM;;def _locally_linear_embedding(
163::COMM;;X,
164::COMM;;*,
165::COMM;;n_neighbors,
166::COMM;;n_components,
167::COMM;;reg=1e-3,
168::COMM;;eigen_solver="auto",
169::COMM;;tol=1e-6,
170::COMM;;max_iter=100,
171::COMM;;method="standard",
172::COMM;;hessian_tol=1e-4,
173::COMM;;modified_tol=1e-12,
174::COMM;;random_state=None,
175::COMM;;n_jobs=None,
176::COMM;;):
177::COMM;;nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=n_neighbors + 1, n_jobs=n_jobs)
178::COMM;;nbrs.fit(X)
179::COMM;;X = nbrs._fit_X
180::COMM;;N, d_in = X.shape
181::COMM;;if n_components > d_in:
182::COMM;;raise ValueError(
183::COMM;;"output dimension must be less than or equal to input dimension"
184::COMM;;)
185::COMM;;if n_neighbors >= N:
186::COMM;;raise ValueError(
187::COMM;;"Expected n_neighbors < n_samples, but n_samples = %d, n_neighbors = %d"
188::COMM;;% (N, n_neighbors)
189::COMM;;)
190::COMM;;M_sparse = eigen_solver != "dense"
191::COMM;;M_container_constructor = lil_matrix if M_sparse else np.zeros
192::COMM;;if method == "standard":
193::COMM;;W = barycenter_kneighbors_graph(
194::COMM;;nbrs, n_neighbors=n_neighbors, reg=reg, n_jobs=n_jobs
195::COMM;;)
196::COMM;;# we'll compute M = (I-W)'(I-W)
197::COMM;;# depending on the solver, we'll do this differently
198::COMM;;if M_sparse:
199::COMM;;M = eye(*W.shape, format=W.format) - W
200::COMM;;M = M.T @ M
201::COMM;;else:
202::COMM;;M = (W.T @ W - W.T - W).toarray()
203::COMM;;M.flat[:: M.shape[0] + 1] += 1 # M = W' W - W' - W + I
204::COMM;;elif method == "hessian":
205::COMM;;dp = n_components * (n_components + 1) // 2
206::COMM;;if n_neighbors <= n_components + dp:
207::COMM;;raise ValueError(
208::COMM;;"for method='hessian', n_neighbors must be "
209::COMM;;"greater than "
210::COMM;;"[n_components * (n_components + 3) / 2]"
211::COMM;;)
212::COMM;;neighbors = nbrs.kneighbors(
213::COMM;;X, n_neighbors=n_neighbors + 1, return_distance=False
214::COMM;;)
215::COMM;;neighbors = neighbors[:, 1:]
216::COMM;;Yi = np.empty((n_neighbors, 1 + n_components + dp), dtype=np.float64)
217::COMM;;Yi[:, 0] = 1
218::COMM;;M = M_container_constructor((N, N), dtype=np.float64)
219::COMM;;use_svd = n_neighbors > d_in
220::COMM;;for i in range(N):
221::COMM;;Gi = X[neighbors[i]]
222::COMM;;Gi -= Gi.mean(0)
223::COMM;;# build Hessian estimator
224::COMM;;if use_svd:
225::COMM;;U = svd(Gi, full_matrices=0)[0]
226::COMM;;else:
227::COMM;;Ci = np.dot(Gi, Gi.T)
228::COMM;;U = eigh(Ci)[1][:, ::-1]
229::COMM;;Yi[:, 1 : 1 + n_components] = U[:, :n_components]
230::COMM;;j = 1 + n_components
231::COMM;;for k in range(n_components):
232::COMM;;Yi[:, j : j + n_components - k] = U[:, k : k + 1] * U[:, k:n_components]
233::COMM;;j += n_components - k
234::COMM;;Q, R = qr(Yi)
235::COMM;;w = Q[:, n_components + 1 :]
236::COMM;;S = w.sum(0)
237::COMM;;S[np.where(abs(S) < hessian_tol)] = 1
238::COMM;;w /= S
239::COMM;;nbrs_x, nbrs_y = np.meshgrid(neighbors[i], neighbors[i])
240::COMM;;M[nbrs_x, nbrs_y] += np.dot(w, w.T)
241::COMM;;elif method == "modified":
242::COMM;;if n_neighbors < n_components:
243::COMM;;raise ValueError("modified LLE requires n_neighbors >= n_components")
244::COMM;;neighbors = nbrs.kneighbors(
245::COMM;;X, n_neighbors=n_neighbors + 1, return_distance=False
246::COMM;;)
247::COMM;;neighbors = neighbors[:, 1:]
248::COMM;;# find the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of each local covariance
249::COMM;;# matrix. We want V[i] to be a [n_neighbors x n_neighbors] matrix,
250::COMM;;# where the columns are eigenvectors
251::COMM;;V = np.zeros((N, n_neighbors, n_neighbors))
252::COMM;;nev = min(d_in, n_neighbors)
253::COMM;;evals = np.zeros([N, nev])
254::COMM;;# choose the most efficient way to find the eigenvectors
255::COMM;;use_svd = n_neighbors > d_in
256::COMM;;if use_svd:
257::COMM;;for i in range(N):
258::COMM;;X_nbrs = X[neighbors[i]] - X[i]
259::COMM;;V[i], evals[i], _ = svd(X_nbrs, full_matrices=True)
260::COMM;;evals **= 2
261::COMM;;else:
262::COMM;;for i in range(N):
263::COMM;;X_nbrs = X[neighbors[i]] - X[i]
264::COMM;;C_nbrs = np.dot(X_nbrs, X_nbrs.T)
265::COMM;;evi, vi = eigh(C_nbrs)
266::COMM;;evals[i] = evi[::-1]
267::COMM;;V[i] = vi[:, ::-1]
268::COMM;;# find regularized weights: this is like normal LLE.
269::COMM;;# because we've already computed the SVD of each covariance matrix,
270::COMM;;# it's faster to use this rather than np.linalg.solve
271::COMM;;reg = 1e-3 * evals.sum(1)
272::COMM;;tmp = np.dot(V.transpose(0, 2, 1), np.ones(n_neighbors))
273::COMM;;tmp[:, :nev] /= evals + reg[:, None]
274::COMM;;tmp[:, nev:] /= reg[:, None]
275::COMM;;w_reg = np.zeros((N, n_neighbors))
276::COMM;;for i in range(N):
277::COMM;;w_reg[i] = np.dot(V[i], tmp[i])
278::COMM;;w_reg /= w_reg.sum(1)[:, None]
279::COMM;;# calculate eta: the median of the ratio of small to large eigenvalues
280::COMM;;# across the points. This is used to determine s_i, below
281::COMM;;rho = evals[:, n_components:].sum(1) / evals[:, :n_components].sum(1)
282::COMM;;eta = np.median(rho)
283::COMM;;# find s_i, the size of the "almost null space" for each point:
284::COMM;;# this is the size of the largest set of eigenvalues
285::COMM;;# such that Sum[v; v in set]/Sum[v; v not in set] < eta
286::COMM;;s_range = np.zeros(N, dtype=int)
287::COMM;;evals_cumsum = np.cumsum(evals, 1)
288::COMM;;eta_range = evals_cumsum[:, -1:] / evals_cumsum[:, :-1] - 1
289::COMM;;for i in range(N):
290::COMM;;s_range[i] = np.searchsorted(eta_range[i, ::-1], eta)
291::COMM;;s_range += n_neighbors - nev # number of zero eigenvalues
292::COMM;;# Now calculate M.
293::COMM;;# This is the [N x N] matrix whose null space is the desired embedding
294::COMM;;M = M_container_constructor((N, N), dtype=np.float64)
295::COMM;;for i in range(N):
296::COMM;;s_i = s_range[i]
297::COMM;;# select bottom s_i eigenvectors and calculate alpha
298::COMM;;Vi = V[i, :, n_neighbors - s_i :]
299::COMM;;alpha_i = np.linalg.norm(Vi.sum(0)) / np.sqrt(s_i)
300::COMM;;# compute Householder matrix which satisfies
301::COMM;;# Hi*Vi.T*ones(n_neighbors) = alpha_i*ones(s)
302::COMM;;# using prescription from paper
303::COMM;;h = np.full(s_i, alpha_i) - np.dot(Vi.T, np.ones(n_neighbors))
304::COMM;;norm_h = np.linalg.norm(h)
305::COMM;;if norm_h < modified_tol:
306::COMM;;h *= 0
307::COMM;;else:
308::COMM;;h /= norm_h
309::COMM;;# Householder matrix is
310::COMM;;# >> Hi = np.identity(s_i) - 2*np.outer(h,h)
311::COMM;;# Then the weight matrix is
312::COMM;;# >> Wi = np.dot(Vi,Hi) + (1-alpha_i) * w_reg[i,:,None]
313::COMM;;# We do this much more efficiently:
314::COMM;;Wi = Vi - 2 * np.outer(np.dot(Vi, h), h) + (1 - alpha_i) * w_reg[i, :, None]
315::COMM;;# Update M as follows:
316::COMM;;# >> W_hat = np.zeros( (N,s_i) )
317::COMM;;# >> W_hat[neighbors[i],:] = Wi
318::COMM;;# >> W_hat[i] -= 1
319::COMM;;# >> M += np.dot(W_hat,W_hat.T)
320::COMM;;# We can do this much more efficiently:
321::COMM;;nbrs_x, nbrs_y = np.meshgrid(neighbors[i], neighbors[i])
322::COMM;;M[nbrs_x, nbrs_y] += np.dot(Wi, Wi.T)
323::COMM;;Wi_sum1 = Wi.sum(1)
324::COMM;;M[i, neighbors[i]] -= Wi_sum1
325::COMM;;M[neighbors[i], [i]] -= Wi_sum1
326::COMM;;M[i, i] += s_i
327::COMM;;elif method == "ltsa":
328::COMM;;neighbors = nbrs.kneighbors(
329::COMM;;X, n_neighbors=n_neighbors + 1, return_distance=False
330::COMM;;)
331::COMM;;neighbors = neighbors[:, 1:]
332::COMM;;M = M_container_constructor((N, N), dtype=np.float64)
333::COMM;;use_svd = n_neighbors > d_in
334::COMM;;for i in range(N):
335::COMM;;Xi = X[neighbors[i]]
336::COMM;;Xi -= Xi.mean(0)
337::COMM;;# compute n_components largest eigenvalues of Xi @ Xi^T
338::COMM;;if use_svd:
339::COMM;;v = svd(Xi, full_matrices=True)[0]
340::COMM;;else:
341::COMM;;Ci = np.dot(Xi, Xi.T)
342::COMM;;v = eigh(Ci)[1][:, ::-1]
343::COMM;;Gi = np.zeros((n_neighbors, n_components + 1))
344::COMM;;Gi[:, 1:] = v[:, :n_components]
345::COMM;;Gi[:, 0] = 1.0 / np.sqrt(n_neighbors)
346::COMM;;GiGiT = np.dot(Gi, Gi.T)
347::COMM;;nbrs_x, nbrs_y = np.meshgrid(neighbors[i], neighbors[i])
348::COMM;;M[nbrs_x, nbrs_y] -= GiGiT
349::COMM;;M[neighbors[i], neighbors[i]] += np.ones(shape=n_neighbors)
350::COMM;;if M_sparse:
351::COMM;;M = M.tocsr()
352::COMM;;return null_space(
353::COMM;;M,
354::COMM;;n_components,
355::COMM;;k_skip=1,
356::COMM;;eigen_solver=eigen_solver,
357::COMM;;tol=tol,

359::COMM;;random_state=random_state,
360::COMM;;)

2::COMM;;Multi-dimensional Scaling (MDS).
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers

35::COMM;;Parameters
36::COMM;;----------
37::COMM;;dissimilarities : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
38::COMM;;Pairwise dissimilarities between the points. Must be symmetric.
39::COMM;;metric : bool, default=True
40::COMM;;Compute metric or nonmetric SMACOF algorithm.
41::COMM;;When ``False`` (i.e. non-metric MDS), dissimilarities with 0 are considered as
42::COMM;;missing values.
43::COMM;;n_components : int, default=2
44::COMM;;Number of dimensions in which to immerse the dissimilarities. If an
45::COMM;;``init`` array is provided, this option is overridden and the shape of
46::COMM;;``init`` is used to determine the dimensionality of the embedding
47::COMM;;space.
48::COMM;;init : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components), default=None
49::COMM;;Starting configuration of the embedding to initialize the algorithm. By
50::COMM;;default, the algorithm is initialized with a randomly chosen array.
51::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
52::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations of the SMACOF algorithm for a single run.
53::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
54::COMM;;Level of verbosity.
55::COMM;;eps : float, default=1e-6
56::COMM;;The tolerance with respect to stress (normalized by the sum of squared
57::COMM;;embedding distances) at which to declare convergence.
58::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
59::COMM;;The default value for `eps` has changed from 1e-3 to 1e-6, as a result
60::COMM;;of a bugfix in the computation of the convergence criterion.
61::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
62::COMM;;Determines the random number generator used to initialize the centers.
63::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
64::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
65::COMM;;normalized_stress : bool, default=False
66::COMM;;Whether to return normalized stress value (Stress-1) instead of raw
67::COMM;;stress.

73::COMM;;X : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components)
74::COMM;;Coordinates of the points in a ``n_components``-space.
75::COMM;;stress : float
76::COMM;;The final value of the stress (sum of squared distance of the
77::COMM;;disparities and the distances for all constrained points).
78::COMM;;If `normalized_stress=True`, returns Stress-1.
79::COMM;;A value of 0 indicates "perfect" fit, 0.025 excellent, 0.05 good,
80::COMM;;0.1 fair, and 0.2 poor [1]_.
81::COMM;;n_iter : int
82::COMM;;The number of iterations corresponding to the best stress.

196::COMM;;The SMACOF (Scaling by MAjorizing a COmplicated Function) algorithm is a
197::COMM;;multidimensional scaling algorithm which minimizes an objective function
198::COMM;;(the *stress*) using a majorization technique. Stress majorization, also
199::COMM;;known as the Guttman Transform, guarantees a monotone convergence of
200::COMM;;stress, and is more powerful than traditional techniques such as gradient
201::COMM;;descent.
202::COMM;;The SMACOF algorithm for metric MDS can be summarized by the following
203::COMM;;steps:
204::COMM;;1. Set an initial start configuration, randomly or not.
205::COMM;;2. Compute the stress
206::COMM;;3. Compute the Guttman Transform
207::COMM;;4. Iterate 2 and 3 until convergence.
208::COMM;;The nonmetric algorithm adds a monotonic regression step before computing
209::COMM;;the stress.
210::COMM;;Parameters
211::COMM;;----------
212::COMM;;dissimilarities : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
213::COMM;;Pairwise dissimilarities between the points. Must be symmetric.
214::COMM;;metric : bool, default=True
215::COMM;;Compute metric or nonmetric SMACOF algorithm.
216::COMM;;When ``False`` (i.e. non-metric MDS), dissimilarities with 0 are considered as
217::COMM;;missing values.
218::COMM;;n_components : int, default=2
219::COMM;;Number of dimensions in which to immerse the dissimilarities. If an
220::COMM;;``init`` array is provided, this option is overridden and the shape of
221::COMM;;``init`` is used to determine the dimensionality of the embedding
222::COMM;;space.
223::COMM;;init : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_components), default=None
224::COMM;;Starting configuration of the embedding to initialize the algorithm. By
225::COMM;;default, the algorithm is initialized with a randomly chosen array.
226::COMM;;n_init : int, default=8
227::COMM;;Number of times the SMACOF algorithm will be run with different
228::COMM;;initializations. The final results will be the best output of the runs,
229::COMM;;determined by the run with the smallest final stress. If ``init`` is
230::COMM;;provided, this option is overridden and a single run is performed.
231::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.9
232::COMM;;The default value for `n_iter` will change from 8 to 1 in version 1.9.
233::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
234::COMM;;The number of jobs to use for the computation. If multiple
235::COMM;;initializations are used (``n_init``), each run of the algorithm is
236::COMM;;computed in parallel.
237::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
238::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
239::COMM;;for more details.
240::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
241::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations of the SMACOF algorithm for a single run.
242::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
243::COMM;;Level of verbosity.
244::COMM;;eps : float, default=1e-6
245::COMM;;The tolerance with respect to stress (normalized by the sum of squared
246::COMM;;embedding distances) at which to declare convergence.
247::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
248::COMM;;The default value for `eps` has changed from 1e-3 to 1e-6, as a result
249::COMM;;of a bugfix in the computation of the convergence criterion.
250::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
251::COMM;;Determines the random number generator used to initialize the centers.
252::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
253::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
254::COMM;;return_n_iter : bool, default=False
255::COMM;;Whether or not to return the number of iterations.
256::COMM;;normalized_stress : bool or "auto", default="auto"
257::COMM;;Whether to return normalized stress value (Stress-1) instead of raw
258::COMM;;stress. By default, metric MDS returns raw stress while non-metric MDS
259::COMM;;returns normalized stress.
260::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
261::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.4
262::COMM;;The default value changed from `False` to `"auto"` in version 1.4.
263::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
264::COMM;;Normalized stress is now supported for metric MDS as well.
265::COMM;;Returns
266::COMM;;-------
267::COMM;;X : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components)
268::COMM;;Coordinates of the points in a ``n_components``-space.
269::COMM;;stress : float
270::COMM;;The final value of the stress (sum of squared distance of the
271::COMM;;disparities and the distances for all constrained points).
272::COMM;;If `normalized_stress=True`, returns Stress-1.
273::COMM;;A value of 0 indicates "perfect" fit, 0.025 excellent, 0.05 good,
274::COMM;;0.1 fair, and 0.2 poor [1]_.
275::COMM;;n_iter : int
276::COMM;;The number of iterations corresponding to the best stress. Returned
277::COMM;;only if ``return_n_iter`` is set to ``True``.
278::COMM;;References
279::COMM;;----------
280::COMM;;.. [1] "Nonmetric multidimensional scaling: a numerical method" Kruskal, J.
281::COMM;;Psychometrika, 29 (1964)
282::COMM;;.. [2] "Multidimensional scaling by optimizing goodness of fit to a nonmetric

287::COMM;;--------
288::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np

369::COMM;;Parameters
370::COMM;;----------
371::COMM;;n_components : int, default=2
372::COMM;;Number of dimensions in which to immerse the dissimilarities.
373::COMM;;metric_mds : bool, default=True
374::COMM;;If ``True``, perform metric MDS; otherwise, perform nonmetric MDS.
375::COMM;;When ``False`` (i.e. non-metric MDS), dissimilarities with 0 are considered as
376::COMM;;missing values.
377::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.8
378::COMM;;The parameter `metric` was renamed into `metric_mds`.
379::COMM;;n_init : int, default=4
380::COMM;;Number of times the SMACOF algorithm will be run with different
381::COMM;;initializations. The final results will be the best output of the runs,
382::COMM;;determined by the run with the smallest final stress.
383::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.9
384::COMM;;The default value for `n_init` will change from 4 to 1 in version 1.9.
385::COMM;;init : {'random', 'classical_mds'}, default='random'
386::COMM;;The initialization approach. If `random`, random initialization is used.
387::COMM;;If `classical_mds`, then classical MDS is run and used as initialization
388::COMM;;for MDS (in this case, the value of `n_init` is ignored).
389::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.8
390::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.10
391::COMM;;The default value for `init` will change to `classical_mds`.
392::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=300
393::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations of the SMACOF algorithm for a single run.
394::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
395::COMM;;Level of verbosity.
396::COMM;;eps : float, default=1e-6
397::COMM;;The tolerance with respect to stress (normalized by the sum of squared
398::COMM;;embedding distances) at which to declare convergence.
399::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
400::COMM;;The default value for `eps` has changed from 1e-3 to 1e-6, as a result
401::COMM;;of a bugfix in the computation of the convergence criterion.
402::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
403::COMM;;The number of jobs to use for the computation. If multiple
404::COMM;;initializations are used (``n_init``), each run of the algorithm is
405::COMM;;computed in parallel.
406::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
407::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
408::COMM;;for more details.
409::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
410::COMM;;Determines the random number generator used to initialize the centers.
411::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
412::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
413::COMM;;dissimilarity : {'euclidean', 'precomputed'}
414::COMM;;Dissimilarity measure to use:
415::COMM;;- 'euclidean':
416::COMM;;Pairwise Euclidean distances between points in the dataset.
417::COMM;;- 'precomputed':
418::COMM;;Pre-computed dissimilarities are passed directly to ``fit`` and
419::COMM;;``fit_transform``.
420::COMM;;.. deprecated:: 1.8
421::COMM;;`dissimilarity` was renamed `metric` in 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10.
422::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default='euclidean'
423::COMM;;Metric to use for dissimilarity computation. Default is "euclidean".
424::COMM;;If metric is a string, it must be one of the options allowed by
425::COMM;;`scipy.spatial.distance.pdist` for its metric parameter, or a metric
426::COMM;;listed in :func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics`
427::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
428::COMM;;must be square during fit.
429::COMM;;If metric is a callable function, it takes two arrays representing 1D
430::COMM;;vectors as inputs and must return one value indicating the distance
431::COMM;;between those vectors. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
432::COMM;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
433::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.8
434::COMM;;Prior to 1.8, `metric=True/False` was used to select metric/non-metric
435::COMM;;MDS, which is now the role of `metric_mds`. The support for ``True``
436::COMM;;and ``False`` will be dropped in version 1.10, use `metric_mds` instead.
437::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
438::COMM;;Additional keyword arguments for the dissimilarity computation.
439::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.8
440::COMM;;normalized_stress : bool or "auto" default="auto"
441::COMM;;Whether to return normalized stress value (Stress-1) instead of raw
442::COMM;;stress. By default, metric MDS returns raw stress while non-metric MDS
443::COMM;;returns normalized stress.
444::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
445::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.4
446::COMM;;The default value changed from `False` to `"auto"` in version 1.4.
447::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
448::COMM;;Normalized stress is now supported for metric MDS as well.
449::COMM;;Attributes
450::COMM;;----------
451::COMM;;embedding_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_components)
452::COMM;;Stores the position of the dataset in the embedding space.
453::COMM;;stress_ : float
454::COMM;;The final value of the stress (sum of squared distance of the
455::COMM;;disparities and the distances for all constrained points).
456::COMM;;If `normalized_stress=True`, returns Stress-1.
457::COMM;;A value of 0 indicates "perfect" fit, 0.025 excellent, 0.05 good,
458::COMM;;0.1 fair, and 0.2 poor [1]_.
459::COMM;;dissimilarity_matrix_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_samples)
460::COMM;;Pairwise dissimilarities between the points. Symmetric matrix that:
461::COMM;;- either uses a custom dissimilarity matrix by setting `dissimilarity`

463::COMM;;- or constructs a dissimilarity matrix from data using

21::COMM;;def _graph_connected_component(graph, node_id):
38::COMM;;n_node = graph.shape[0]
39::COMM;;if sparse.issparse(graph):
40::COMM;;# speed up row-wise access to boolean connection mask
41::COMM;;graph = graph.tocsr()
42::COMM;;connected_nodes = np.zeros(n_node, dtype=bool)
43::COMM;;nodes_to_explore = np.zeros(n_node, dtype=bool)
44::COMM;;nodes_to_explore[node_id] = True
45::COMM;;for _ in range(n_node):
46::COMM;;last_num_component = connected_nodes.sum()
47::COMM;;np.logical_or(connected_nodes, nodes_to_explore, out=connected_nodes)
48::COMM;;if last_num_component >= connected_nodes.sum():
49::COMM;;break
50::COMM;;indices = np.where(nodes_to_explore)[0]
51::COMM;;nodes_to_explore.fill(False)
52::COMM;;for i in indices:
53::COMM;;if sparse.issparse(graph):
54::COMM;;# scipy not yet implemented 1D sparse slices; can be changed back to
55::COMM;;# `neighbors = graph[i].toarray().ravel()` once implemented
56::COMM;;neighbors = graph[[i], :].toarray().ravel()
57::COMM;;else:
58::COMM;;neighbors = graph[i]
59::COMM;;np.logical_or(nodes_to_explore, neighbors, out=nodes_to_explore)
60::COMM;;return connected_nodes
61::COMM;;def _graph_is_connected(graph):
73::COMM;;if sparse.issparse(graph):
74::COMM;;# Before Scipy 1.11.3, `connected_components` only supports 32-bit indices.
75::COMM;;# PR: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/18913
76::COMM;;# First integration in 1.11.3: https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/19279
77::COMM;;# TODO(jjerphan): Once SciPy 1.11.3 is the minimum supported version, use
78::COMM;;# `accept_large_sparse=True`.
79::COMM;;accept_large_sparse = sp_version >= parse_version("1.11.3")
80::COMM;;graph = check_array(
81::COMM;;graph, accept_sparse=True, accept_large_sparse=accept_large_sparse
82::COMM;;)
83::COMM;;# sparse graph, find all the connected components
84::COMM;;n_connected_components, _ = connected_components(graph)
85::COMM;;return n_connected_components == 1
86::COMM;;else:
87::COMM;;# dense graph, find all connected components start from node 0
88::COMM;;return _graph_connected_component(graph, 0).sum() == graph.shape[0]
89::COMM;;def _set_diag(laplacian, value, norm_laplacian):
107::COMM;;n_nodes = laplacian.shape[0]
108::COMM;;# We need all entries in the diagonal to values
109::COMM;;if not sparse.issparse(laplacian):
110::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
111::COMM;;laplacian.flat[:: n_nodes + 1] = value
112::COMM;;else:
113::COMM;;laplacian = laplacian.tocoo()
114::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
115::COMM;;diag_idx = laplacian.row == laplacian.col
116::COMM;;laplacian.data[diag_idx] = value
117::COMM;;# If the matrix has a small number of diagonals (as in the
118::COMM;;# case of structured matrices coming from images), the
119::COMM;;# dia format might be best suited for matvec products:
120::COMM;;n_diags = np.unique(laplacian.row - laplacian.col).size
121::COMM;;if n_diags <= 7:
122::COMM;;# 3 or less outer diagonals on each side
123::COMM;;laplacian = laplacian.todia()
124::COMM;;else:
125::COMM;;# csr has the fastest matvec and is thus best suited to
126::COMM;;# arpack
127::COMM;;laplacian = laplacian.tocsr()
128::COMM;;return laplacian

250::COMM;;def _spectral_embedding(
251::COMM;;adjacency,
252::COMM;;*,
253::COMM;;n_components=8,
254::COMM;;eigen_solver=None,
255::COMM;;random_state=None,
256::COMM;;eigen_tol="auto",
257::COMM;;norm_laplacian=True,
258::COMM;;drop_first=True,
259::COMM;;):
260::COMM;;adjacency = check_symmetric(adjacency)
261::COMM;;if eigen_solver == "amg":
262::COMM;;try:
263::COMM;;from pyamg import smoothed_aggregation_solver
264::COMM;;except ImportError as e:
265::COMM;;raise ValueError(
266::COMM;;"The eigen_solver was set to 'amg', but pyamg is not available."
267::COMM;;) from e
268::COMM;;if eigen_solver is None:
269::COMM;;eigen_solver = "arpack"
270::COMM;;n_nodes = adjacency.shape[0]
271::COMM;;# Whether to drop the first eigenvector
272::COMM;;if drop_first:
273::COMM;;n_components = n_components + 1
274::COMM;;if not _graph_is_connected(adjacency):
275::COMM;;warnings.warn(
276::COMM;;"Graph is not fully connected, spectral embedding may not work as expected."
277::COMM;;)
278::COMM;;laplacian, dd = csgraph_laplacian(
279::COMM;;adjacency, normed=norm_laplacian, return_diag=True
280::COMM;;)
281::COMM;;if eigen_solver == "arpack" or (
282::COMM;;eigen_solver != "lobpcg"
283::COMM;;and (not sparse.issparse(laplacian) or n_nodes < 5 * n_components)
284::COMM;;):
285::COMM;;# lobpcg used with eigen_solver='amg' has bugs for low number of nodes
286::COMM;;# for details see the source code in scipy:
287::COMM;;# https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v0.11.0/scipy/sparse/linalg/eigen
288::COMM;;# /lobpcg/lobpcg.py#L237
289::COMM;;# or matlab:
290::COMM;;# https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/48-lobpcg-m
291::COMM;;laplacian = _set_diag(laplacian, 1, norm_laplacian)
292::COMM;;# Here we'll use shift-invert mode for fast eigenvalues
293::COMM;;# (see https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/tutorial/arpack.html
294::COMM;;# for a short explanation of what this means)
295::COMM;;# Because the normalized Laplacian has eigenvalues between 0 and 2,
296::COMM;;# I - L has eigenvalues between -1 and 1. ARPACK is most efficient
297::COMM;;# when finding eigenvalues of largest magnitude (keyword which='LM')
298::COMM;;# and when these eigenvalues are very large compared to the rest.
299::COMM;;# For very large, very sparse graphs, I - L can have many, many
300::COMM;;# eigenvalues very near 1.0. This leads to slow convergence. So
301::COMM;;# instead, we'll use ARPACK's shift-invert mode, asking for the
302::COMM;;# eigenvalues near 1.0. This effectively spreads-out the spectrum
303::COMM;;# near 1.0 and leads to much faster convergence: potentially an
304::COMM;;# orders-of-magnitude speedup over simply using keyword which='LA'
305::COMM;;# in standard mode.
306::COMM;;try:
307::COMM;;# We are computing the opposite of the laplacian inplace so as
308::COMM;;# to spare a memory allocation of a possibly very large array
309::COMM;;tol = 0 if eigen_tol == "auto" else eigen_tol
310::COMM;;laplacian *= -1
311::COMM;;v0 = _init_arpack_v0(laplacian.shape[0], random_state)
312::COMM;;laplacian = check_array(
313::COMM;;laplacian, accept_sparse="csr", accept_large_sparse=False
314::COMM;;)
315::COMM;;_, diffusion_map = eigsh(
316::COMM;;laplacian, k=n_components, sigma=1.0, which="LM", tol=tol, v0=v0
317::COMM;;)
318::COMM;;embedding = diffusion_map.T[n_components::-1]
319::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
320::COMM;;# recover u = D^-1/2 x from the eigenvector output x
321::COMM;;embedding = embedding / dd
322::COMM;;except RuntimeError:
323::COMM;;# When submatrices are exactly singular, an LU decomposition
324::COMM;;# in arpack fails. We fallback to lobpcg
325::COMM;;eigen_solver = "lobpcg"
326::COMM;;# Revert the laplacian to its opposite to have lobpcg work
327::COMM;;laplacian *= -1
328::COMM;;elif eigen_solver == "amg":
329::COMM;;# Use AMG to get a preconditioner and speed up the eigenvalue
330::COMM;;# problem.
331::COMM;;if not sparse.issparse(laplacian):
332::COMM;;warnings.warn("AMG works better for sparse matrices")
333::COMM;;laplacian = check_array(
334::COMM;;laplacian, dtype=[np.float64, np.float32], accept_sparse=True
335::COMM;;)
336::COMM;;laplacian = _set_diag(laplacian, 1, norm_laplacian)
337::COMM;;# The Laplacian matrix is always singular, having at least one zero
338::COMM;;# eigenvalue, corresponding to the trivial eigenvector, which is a
339::COMM;;# constant. Using a singular matrix for preconditioning may result in
340::COMM;;# random failures in LOBPCG and is not supported by the existing
341::COMM;;# theory:
342::COMM;;# see https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-015-9297-1
343::COMM;;# Shift the Laplacian so its diagononal is not all ones. The shift
344::COMM;;# does change the eigenpairs however, so we'll feed the shifted
345::COMM;;# matrix to the solver and afterward set it back to the original.
346::COMM;;diag_shift = 1e-5 * sparse.eye(laplacian.shape[0])
347::COMM;;laplacian += diag_shift
348::COMM;;if hasattr(sparse, "csr_array") and isinstance(laplacian, sparse.csr_array):
349::COMM;;# `pyamg` does not work with `csr_array` and we need to convert it to a
350::COMM;;# `csr_matrix` object.
351::COMM;;laplacian = sparse.csr_matrix(laplacian)
352::COMM;;ml = smoothed_aggregation_solver(check_array(laplacian, accept_sparse="csr"))
353::COMM;;laplacian -= diag_shift
354::COMM;;M = ml.aspreconditioner()
355::COMM;;# Create initial approximation X to eigenvectors
356::COMM;;X = random_state.standard_normal(size=(laplacian.shape[0], n_components + 1))
357::COMM;;X[:, 0] = dd.ravel()
358::COMM;;X = X.astype(laplacian.dtype)
359::COMM;;tol = None if eigen_tol == "auto" else eigen_tol
360::COMM;;_, diffusion_map = lobpcg(laplacian, X, M=M, tol=tol, largest=False)
361::COMM;;embedding = diffusion_map.T
362::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
363::COMM;;# recover u = D^-1/2 x from the eigenvector output x
364::COMM;;embedding = embedding / dd
365::COMM;;if embedding.shape[0] == 1:
366::COMM;;raise ValueError
367::COMM;;if eigen_solver == "lobpcg":
368::COMM;;laplacian = check_array(
369::COMM;;laplacian, dtype=[np.float64, np.float32], accept_sparse=True
370::COMM;;)
371::COMM;;if n_nodes < 5 * n_components + 1:
372::COMM;;# see note above under arpack why lobpcg has problems with small
373::COMM;;# number of nodes
374::COMM;;# lobpcg will fallback to eigh, so we short circuit it
375::COMM;;if sparse.issparse(laplacian):
376::COMM;;laplacian = laplacian.toarray()
377::COMM;;_, diffusion_map = eigh(laplacian, check_finite=False)
378::COMM;;embedding = diffusion_map.T[:n_components]
379::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
380::COMM;;# recover u = D^-1/2 x from the eigenvector output x
381::COMM;;embedding = embedding / dd
382::COMM;;else:
383::COMM;;laplacian = _set_diag(laplacian, 1, norm_laplacian)
384::COMM;;# We increase the number of eigenvectors requested, as lobpcg
385::COMM;;# doesn't behave well in low dimension and create initial
386::COMM;;# approximation X to eigenvectors
387::COMM;;X = random_state.standard_normal(
388::COMM;;size=(laplacian.shape[0], n_components + 1)
389::COMM;;)
390::COMM;;X[:, 0] = dd.ravel()
391::COMM;;X = X.astype(laplacian.dtype)
392::COMM;;tol = None if eigen_tol == "auto" else eigen_tol
393::COMM;;_, diffusion_map = lobpcg(
394::COMM;;laplacian, X, tol=tol, largest=False, maxiter=2000
395::COMM;;)
396::COMM;;embedding = diffusion_map.T[:n_components]
397::COMM;;if norm_laplacian:
398::COMM;;# recover u = D^-1/2 x from the eigenvector output x
399::COMM;;embedding = embedding / dd
400::COMM;;if embedding.shape[0] == 1:
401::COMM;;raise ValueError
402::COMM;;embedding = _deterministic_vector_sign_flip(embedding)
403::COMM;;if drop_first:
404::COMM;;return embedding[1:n_components].T
405::COMM;;else:
406::COMM;;return embedding[:n_components].T

32::COMM;;Parameters

34::COMM;;distances : ndarray of shape (n_samples * (n_samples-1) / 2,)
35::COMM;;Distances of samples are stored as condensed matrices, i.e.
36::COMM;;we omit the diagonal and duplicate entries and store everything
37::COMM;;in a one-dimensional array.
