2141::COMM;;The precision is the ratio ``tp / (tp + fp)`` where ``tp`` is the number of
2142::COMM;;true positives and ``fp`` the number of false positives. The precision is
2143::COMM;;intuitively the ability of the classifier not to label as positive a sample
2144::COMM;;that is negative.
2145::COMM;;The best value is 1 and the worst value is 0.
2146::COMM;;Support beyond :term:`binary` targets is achieved by treating :term:`multiclass`
2147::COMM;;and :term:`multilabel` data as a collection of binary problems, one for each
2148::COMM;;label. For the :term:`binary` case, setting `average='binary'` will return
2149::COMM;;precision for `pos_label`. If `average` is not `'binary'`, `pos_label` is ignored
2150::COMM;;and precision for both classes are computed, then averaged or both returned (when
2151::COMM;;`average=None`). Similarly, for :term:`multiclass` and :term:`multilabel` targets,
2152::COMM;;precision for all `labels` are either returned or averaged depending on the
2153::COMM;;`average` parameter. Use `labels` specify the set of labels to calculate precision
2154::COMM;;for.
2155::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <precision_recall_f_measure_metrics>`.
2156::COMM;;Parameters
2157::COMM;;----------
2158::COMM;;y_true : 1d array-like, or label indicator array / sparse matrix
2159::COMM;;Ground truth (correct) target values. Sparse matrix is only supported when
2160::COMM;;targets are of :term:`multilabel` type.
2161::COMM;;y_pred : 1d array-like, or label indicator array / sparse matrix
2162::COMM;;Estimated targets as returned by a classifier. Sparse matrix is only
2163::COMM;;supported when targets are of :term:`multilabel` type.
2164::COMM;;labels : array-like, default=None
2165::COMM;;The set of labels to include when `average != 'binary'`, and their
2166::COMM;;order if `average is None`. Labels present in the data can be
2167::COMM;;excluded, for example in multiclass classification to exclude a "negative
2168::COMM;;class". Labels not present in the data can be included and will be
2169::COMM;;"assigned" 0 samples. For multilabel targets, labels are column indices.
2170::COMM;;By default, all labels in `y_true` and `y_pred` are used in sorted order.
2171::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.17
2172::COMM;;Parameter `labels` improved for multiclass problem.
2173::COMM;;pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=1
2174::COMM;;The class to report if `average='binary'` and the data is binary,
2175::COMM;;otherwise this parameter is ignored.
2176::COMM;;For multiclass or multilabel targets, set `labels=[pos_label]` and
2177::COMM;;`average != 'binary'` to report metrics for one label only.
2178::COMM;;average : {'micro', 'macro', 'samples', 'weighted', 'binary'} or None, \
2179::COMM;;default='binary'
2180::COMM;;This parameter is required for multiclass/multilabel targets.
2181::COMM;;If ``None``, the metrics for each class are returned. Otherwise, this
2182::COMM;;determines the type of averaging performed on the data:
2183::COMM;;``'binary'``:
2184::COMM;;Only report results for the class specified by ``pos_label``.
2185::COMM;;This is applicable only if targets (``y_{true,pred}``) are binary.
2186::COMM;;``'micro'``:
2187::COMM;;Calculate metrics globally by counting the total true positives,
2188::COMM;;false negatives and false positives.
2189::COMM;;``'macro'``:
2190::COMM;;Calculate metrics for each label, and find their unweighted
2191::COMM;;mean. This does not take label imbalance into account.
2192::COMM;;``'weighted'``:
2193::COMM;;Calculate metrics for each label, and find their average weighted
2194::COMM;;by support (the number of true instances for each label). This
2195::COMM;;alters 'macro' to account for label imbalance; it can result in an
2196::COMM;;F-score that is not between precision and recall.
2197::COMM;;``'samples'``:

2199::COMM;;meaningful for multilabel classification where this differs from

2301::COMM;;The recall is the ratio ``tp / (tp + fn)`` where ``tp`` is the number of
2302::COMM;;true positives and ``fn`` the number of false negatives. The recall is
2303::COMM;;intuitively the ability of the classifier to find all the positive samples.

2443::COMM;;The balanced accuracy in binary and multiclass classification problems to
2444::COMM;;deal with imbalanced datasets. It is defined as the average of recall
2445::COMM;;obtained on each class.

2745::COMM;;The Hamming loss is the fraction of labels that are incorrectly predicted.
2746::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <hamming_loss>`.
2747::COMM;;Parameters
2748::COMM;;----------
2749::COMM;;y_true : 1d array-like, or label indicator array / sparse matrix
2750::COMM;;Ground truth (correct) labels. Sparse matrix is only supported when
2751::COMM;;targets are of :term:`multilabel` type.
2752::COMM;;y_pred : 1d array-like, or label indicator array / sparse matrix
2753::COMM;;Predicted labels, as returned by a classifier. Sparse matrix is only
2754::COMM;;supported when targets are of :term:`multilabel` type.
2755::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
2756::COMM;;Sample weights.
2757::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
2758::COMM;;Returns
2759::COMM;;-------
2760::COMM;;loss : float or int
2761::COMM;;Return the average Hamming loss between element of ``y_true`` and
2762::COMM;;``y_pred``.
2763::COMM;;See Also
2764::COMM;;--------
2765::COMM;;accuracy_score : Compute the accuracy score. By default, the function will
2766::COMM;;return the fraction of correct predictions divided by the total number
2767::COMM;;of predictions.
2768::COMM;;jaccard_score : Compute the Jaccard similarity coefficient score.
2769::COMM;;zero_one_loss : Compute the Zero-one classification loss. By default, the
2770::COMM;;function will return the percentage of imperfectly predicted subsets.
2771::COMM;;Notes
2772::COMM;;-----
2773::COMM;;In multiclass classification, the Hamming loss corresponds to the Hamming
2774::COMM;;distance between ``y_true`` and ``y_pred`` which is equivalent to the
2775::COMM;;subset ``zero_one_loss`` function, when `normalize` parameter is set to
2776::COMM;;True.
2777::COMM;;In multilabel classification, the Hamming loss is different from the
2778::COMM;;subset zero-one loss. The zero-one loss considers the entire set of labels
2779::COMM;;for a given sample incorrect if it does not entirely match the true set of
2780::COMM;;labels. Hamming loss is more forgiving in that it penalizes only the
2781::COMM;;individual labels.
2782::COMM;;The Hamming loss is upperbounded by the subset zero-one loss, when
2783::COMM;;`normalize` parameter is set to True. It is always between 0 and 1,
2784::COMM;;lower being better.
2785::COMM;;References
2786::COMM;;----------
2787::COMM;;.. [1] Grigorios Tsoumakas, Ioannis Katakis. Multi-Label Classification:
2788::COMM;;An Overview. International Journal of Data Warehousing & Mining,
2789::COMM;;3(3), 1-13, July-September 2007.
2790::COMM;;.. [2] `Wikipedia entry on the Hamming distance
2791::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance>`_.
2792::COMM;;Examples
2793::COMM;;--------
2794::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics import hamming_loss
2795::COMM;;>>> y_pred = [1, 2, 3, 4]
2796::COMM;;>>> y_true = [2, 2, 3, 4]
2797::COMM;;>>> hamming_loss(y_true, y_pred)
2798::COMM;;0.25
2799::COMM;;In the multilabel case with binary label indicators:
2800::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
2801::COMM;;>>> hamming_loss(np.array([[0, 1], [1, 1]]), np.zeros((2, 2)))
2802::COMM;;0.75
2838::COMM;;This is the loss function used in (multinomial) logistic regression
2839::COMM;;and extensions of it such as neural networks, defined as the negative
2840::COMM;;log-likelihood of a logistic model that returns ``y_pred`` probabilities
2841::COMM;;for its training data ``y_true``.
2842::COMM;;The log loss is only defined for two or more labels.
2843::COMM;;For a single sample with true label :math:`y \in \{0,1\}` and
2844::COMM;;a probability estimate :math:`p = \operatorname{Pr}(y = 1)`, the log
2845::COMM;;loss is:
2846::COMM;;.. math::
2847::COMM;;L_{\log}(y, p) = -(y \log (p) + (1 - y) \log (1 - p))
2848::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <log_loss>`.
2849::COMM;;Parameters
2850::COMM;;----------
2851::COMM;;y_true : array-like or label indicator matrix
2852::COMM;;Ground truth (correct) labels for n_samples samples.
2853::COMM;;y_pred : array-like of float, shape = (n_samples, n_classes) or (n_samples,)
2854::COMM;;Predicted probabilities, as returned by a classifier's
2855::COMM;;predict_proba method. If ``y_pred.shape = (n_samples,)``
2856::COMM;;the probabilities provided are assumed to be that of the
2857::COMM;;positive class. The labels in ``y_pred`` are assumed to be
2858::COMM;;ordered alphabetically, as done by
2859::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.LabelBinarizer`.
2860::COMM;;`y_pred` values are clipped to `[eps, 1-eps]` where `eps` is the machine
2861::COMM;;precision for `y_pred`'s dtype.
2862::COMM;;normalize : bool, default=True
2863::COMM;;If true, return the mean loss per sample.
2864::COMM;;Otherwise, return the sum of the per-sample losses.
2865::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
2866::COMM;;Sample weights.
2867::COMM;;labels : array-like, default=None
2868::COMM;;If not provided, labels will be inferred from y_true. If ``labels``
2869::COMM;;is ``None`` and ``y_pred`` has shape (n_samples,) the labels are
2870::COMM;;assumed to be binary and are inferred from ``y_true``.
2871::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
2872::COMM;;Returns
2873::COMM;;-------
2874::COMM;;loss : float
2875::COMM;;Log loss, aka logistic loss or cross-entropy loss.
2876::COMM;;Notes
2877::COMM;;-----
2878::COMM;;The logarithm used is the natural logarithm (base-e).
2879::COMM;;References
2880::COMM;;----------
2881::COMM;;C.M. Bishop (2006). Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer,
2882::COMM;;p. 209.

1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
3::COMO;;#
4::COMO;;# Pairwise Distances Reductions
5::COMO;;# =============================
6::COMO;;#
7::COMO;;# Overview
8::COMO;;# --------
9::COMO;;#
10::COMO;;# This module provides routines to compute pairwise distances between a set
11::COMO;;# of row vectors of X and another set of row vectors of Y and apply a
12::COMO;;# reduction on top. The canonical example is the brute-force computation
13::COMO;;# of the top k nearest neighbors by leveraging the arg-k-min reduction.
14::COMO;;#
15::COMO;;# The reduction takes a matrix of pairwise distances between rows of X and Y
16::COMO;;# as input and outputs an aggregate data-structure for each row of X. The
17::COMO;;# aggregate values are typically smaller than the number of rows in Y, hence
18::COMO;;# the term reduction.
19::COMO;;#
20::COMO;;# For computational reasons, the reduction are performed on the fly on chunks
21::COMO;;# of rows of X and Y so as to keep intermediate data-structures in CPU cache
22::COMO;;# and avoid unnecessary round trips of large distance arrays with the RAM
23::COMO;;# that would otherwise severely degrade the speed by making the overall
24::COMO;;# processing memory-bound.
25::COMO;;#
26::COMO;;# Finally, the routines follow a generic parallelization template to process
27::COMO;;# chunks of data with OpenMP loops (via Cython prange), either on rows of X
28::COMO;;# or rows of Y depending on their respective sizes.
29::COMO;;#
30::COMO;;#
31::COMO;;# Dispatching to specialized implementations
32::COMO;;# ------------------------------------------
33::COMO;;#
34::COMO;;# Dispatchers are meant to be used in the Python code. Under the hood, a
35::COMO;;# dispatcher must only define the logic to choose at runtime to the correct
36::COMO;;# dtype-specialized :class:`BaseDistancesReductionDispatcher` implementation based
37::COMO;;# on the dtype of X and of Y.
38::COMO;;#
39::COMO;;#
40::COMO;;# High-level diagram
41::COMO;;# ------------------
42::COMO;;#
43::COMO;;# Legend:
44::COMO;;#
45::COMO;;# A ---⊳ B: A inherits from B
46::COMO;;# A ---x B: A dispatches to B
47::COMO;;#
48::COMO;;#
49::COMO;;# (base dispatcher)
50::COMO;;# BaseDistancesReductionDispatcher
51::COMO;;# ∆
52::COMO;;# |
53::COMO;;# |
54::COMO;;# +------------------+---------------+---------------+------------------+
55::COMO;;# | | | |
56::COMO;;# | (dispatcher) (dispatcher) |
57::COMO;;# | ArgKmin RadiusNeighbors |
58::COMO;;# | | | |
59::COMO;;# | | | |
60::COMO;;# | | (float{32,64} implem.) | |
61::COMO;;# | | BaseDistancesReduction{32,64} | |
62::COMO;;# | | ∆ | |
63::COMO;;# (dispatcher) | | | (dispatcher)
64::COMO;;# ArgKminClassMode | | | RadiusNeighborsClassMode
65::COMO;;# | | +----------+----------+ | |
66::COMO;;# | | | | | |
67::COMO;;# | | | | | |
68::COMO;;# | x | | x |
69::COMO;;# | +-------⊳ ArgKmin{32,64} RadiusNeighbors{32,64} ⊲---+ |
70::COMO;;# x | | ∆ ∆ | | x
71::COMO;;# ArgKminClassMode{32,64} | | | | RadiusNeighborsClassMode{32,64}
72::COMO;;# ===================================== Specializations ============================================
73::COMO;;# | | | |
74::COMO;;# | | | |
75::COMO;;# x | | x
76::COMO;;# EuclideanArgKmin{32,64} EuclideanRadiusNeighbors{32,64}
77::COMO;;#
78::COMO;;#
79::COMO;;# For instance :class:`ArgKmin` dispatches to:
80::COMO;;# - :class:`ArgKmin64` if X and Y are two `float64` array-likes
81::COMO;;# - :class:`ArgKmin32` if X and Y are two `float32` array-likes
82::COMO;;#
83::COMO;;# In addition, if the metric parameter is set to "euclidean" or "sqeuclidean",
84::COMO;;# then some direct subclass of `BaseDistancesReduction{32,64}` further dispatches
85::COMO;;# to one of their subclass for euclidean-specialized implementation. For instance,
86::COMO;;# :class:`ArgKmin64` dispatches to :class:`EuclideanArgKmin64`.
87::COMO;;#
88::COMO;;# Those Euclidean-specialized implementations relies on optimal implementations of
89::COMO;;# a decomposition of the squared euclidean distance matrix into a sum of three terms
90::COMO;;# (see :class:`MiddleTermComputer{32,64}`).
91::COMO;;#

2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

177::COMM;;scikit-learn configuration for `pairwise_dist_chunk_size`,
178::COMM;;and use 256 if it is not set.
179::COMM;;metric_kwargs : dict, default=None
180::COMM;;Keyword arguments to pass to specified metric function.
181::COMM;;strategy : str, {'auto', 'parallel_on_X', 'parallel_on_Y'}, default=None
182::COMM;;The chunking strategy defining which dataset parallelization are made on.
183::COMM;;For both strategies the computations happens with two nested loops,
184::COMM;;respectively on chunks of X and chunks of Y.
185::COMM;;Strategies differs on which loop (outer or inner) is made to run
186::COMM;;in parallel with the Cython `prange` construct:
187::COMM;;- 'parallel_on_X' dispatches chunks of X uniformly on threads.
188::COMM;;Each thread then iterates on all the chunks of Y. This strategy is
189::COMM;;embarrassingly parallel and comes with no datastructures
190::COMM;;synchronisation.
191::COMM;;- 'parallel_on_Y' dispatches chunks of Y uniformly on threads.
192::COMM;;Each thread processes all the chunks of X in turn. This strategy is
193::COMM;;a sequence of embarrassingly parallel subtasks (the inner loop on Y
194::COMM;;chunks) with intermediate datastructures synchronisation at each
195::COMM;;iteration of the sequential outer loop on X chunks.
196::COMM;;- 'auto' relies on a simple heuristic to choose between
197::COMM;;'parallel_on_X' and 'parallel_on_Y': when `X.shape[0]` is large enough,
198::COMM;;'parallel_on_X' is usually the most efficient strategy.
199::COMM;;When `X.shape[0]` is small but `Y.shape[0]` is large, 'parallel_on_Y'
200::COMM;;brings more opportunity for parallelism and is therefore more efficient
201::COMM;;- None (default) looks-up in scikit-learn configuration for
202::COMM;;`pairwise_dist_parallel_strategy`, and use 'auto' if it is not set.
203::COMM;;return_distance : boolean, default=False
204::COMM;;Return distances between each X vector and its
205::COMM;;argkmin if set to True.

548::COMM;;----------
549::COMM;;X : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
550::COMM;;The input array to be labelled.
551::COMM;;Y : ndarray of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features)
552::COMM;;The input array whose class membership is provided through
553::COMM;;the `Y_labels` parameter.
554::COMM;;radius : float
555::COMM;;The radius defining the neighborhood.
556::COMM;;weights : ndarray
557::COMM;;The weights applied to the `Y_labels` when computing the
558::COMM;;weighted mode of the labels.
559::COMM;;Y_labels : ndarray
560::COMM;;An array containing the index of the class membership of the
561::COMM;;associated samples in `Y`. This is used in labeling `X`.
562::COMM;;unique_Y_labels : ndarray
563::COMM;;An array containing all unique class labels.
564::COMM;;outlier_label : int, default=None
565::COMM;;Label for outlier samples (samples with no neighbors in given
566::COMM;;radius). In the default case when the value is None if any
567::COMM;;outlier is detected, a ValueError will be raised. The outlier
568::COMM;;label should be selected from among the unique 'Y' labels. If
569::COMM;;it is specified with a different value a warning will be raised
570::COMM;;and all class probabilities of outliers will be assigned to be 0.
571::COMM;;metric : str, default='euclidean'
572::COMM;;The distance metric to use. For a list of available metrics, see
573::COMM;;the documentation of :class:`~sklearn.metrics.DistanceMetric`.
574::COMM;;Currently does not support `'precomputed'`.
575::COMM;;chunk_size : int, default=None,
576::COMM;;The number of vectors per chunk. If None (default) looks-up in
577::COMM;;scikit-learn configuration for `pairwise_dist_chunk_size`,
578::COMM;;and use 256 if it is not set.
579::COMM;;metric_kwargs : dict, default=None
580::COMM;;Keyword arguments to pass to specified metric function.
581::COMM;;strategy : str, {'auto', 'parallel_on_X', 'parallel_on_Y'}, default=None
582::COMM;;The chunking strategy defining which dataset parallelization are made on.
583::COMM;;For both strategies the computations happens with two nested loops,
584::COMM;;respectively on chunks of X and chunks of Y.
585::COMM;;Strategies differs on which loop (outer or inner) is made to run
586::COMM;;in parallel with the Cython `prange` construct:
587::COMM;;- 'parallel_on_X' dispatches chunks of X uniformly on threads.
588::COMM;;Each thread then iterates on all the chunks of Y. This strategy is
589::COMM;;embarrassingly parallel and comes with no datastructures
590::COMM;;synchronisation.
591::COMM;;- 'parallel_on_Y' dispatches chunks of Y uniformly on threads.
592::COMM;;Each thread processes all the chunks of X in turn. This strategy is
593::COMM;;a sequence of embarrassingly parallel subtasks (the inner loop on Y
594::COMM;;chunks) with intermediate datastructures synchronisation at each
595::COMM;;iteration of the sequential outer loop on X chunks.
596::COMM;;- 'auto' relies on a simple heuristic to choose between
597::COMM;;'parallel_on_X' and 'parallel_on_Y': when `X.shape[0]` is large enough,
598::COMM;;'parallel_on_X' is usually the most efficient strategy.
599::COMM;;When `X.shape[0]` is small but `Y.shape[0]` is large, 'parallel_on_Y'
600::COMM;;brings more opportunity for parallelism and is therefore more efficient
601::COMM;;despite the synchronization step at each iteration of the outer loop
602::COMM;;on chunks of `X`.
603::COMM;;- None (default) looks-up in scikit-learn configuration for
604::COMM;;`pairwise_dist_parallel_strategy`, and use 'auto' if it is not set.
605::COMM;;Returns
606::COMM;;-------
607::COMM;;probabilities : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_classes)
608::COMM;;An array containing the class probabilities for each sample.
1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause

65::COMM;;a binary classifier.

67::COMM;;using predictions from a binary classifier.
68::COMM;;Notes
69::COMM;;-----
70::COMM;;The average precision (cf. :func:`~sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score`) in
71::COMM;;scikit-learn is computed without any interpolation. To be consistent with
72::COMM;;this metric, the precision-recall curve is plotted without any
73::COMM;;interpolation as well (step-wise style).
74::COMM;;You can change this style by passing the keyword argument
75::COMM;;`drawstyle="default"` in :meth:`plot`, :meth:`from_estimator`, or

77::COMM;;consistent with the reported average precision.

92::COMM;;>>> predictions = clf.predict(X_test)
93::COMM;;>>> precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, predictions)
94::COMM;;>>> disp = PrecisionRecallDisplay(precision=precision, recall=recall)
95::COMM;;>>> disp.plot()

10::COMM;;This tool can display "residuals vs predicted" or "actual vs predicted"
11::COMM;;using scatter plots to qualitatively assess the behavior of a regressor,
12::COMM;;preferably on held-out data points.
13::COMM;;See the details in the docstrings of
14::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.metrics.PredictionErrorDisplay.from_estimator` or
15::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.metrics.PredictionErrorDisplay.from_predictions` to
16::COMM;;create a visualizer. All parameters are stored as attributes.
17::COMM;;For general information regarding `scikit-learn` visualization tools, read
18::COMM;;more in the :ref:`Visualization Guide <visualizations>`.
19::COMM;;For details regarding interpreting these plots, refer to the
20::COMM;;:ref:`Model Evaluation Guide <visualization_regression_evaluation>`.
21::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
22::COMM;;Parameters
23::COMM;;----------
24::COMM;;y_true : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
25::COMM;;True values.
26::COMM;;y_pred : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
27::COMM;;Prediction values.
28::COMM;;Attributes
29::COMM;;----------
30::COMM;;line_ : matplotlib Artist
31::COMM;;Optimal line representing `y_true == y_pred`. Therefore, it is a
32::COMM;;diagonal line for `kind="predictions"` and a horizontal line for
33::COMM;;`kind="residuals"`.
34::COMM;;errors_lines_ : matplotlib Artist or None
35::COMM;;Residual lines. If `with_errors=False`, then it is set to `None`.
36::COMM;;scatter_ : matplotlib Artist
37::COMM;;Scatter data points.
38::COMM;;ax_ : matplotlib Axes
39::COMM;;Axes with the different matplotlib axis.
40::COMM;;figure_ : matplotlib Figure
41::COMM;;Figure containing the scatter and lines.
42::COMM;;See Also
43::COMM;;--------
44::COMM;;PredictionErrorDisplay.from_estimator : Prediction error visualization
45::COMM;;given an estimator and some data.
46::COMM;;PredictionErrorDisplay.from_predictions : Prediction error visualization
47::COMM;;given the true and predicted targets.
48::COMM;;Examples
49::COMM;;--------
50::COMM;;>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
51::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
52::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
53::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics import PredictionErrorDisplay
54::COMM;;>>> X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)
55::COMM;;>>> ridge = Ridge().fit(X, y)
56::COMM;;>>> y_pred = ridge.predict(X)
57::COMM;;>>> display = PredictionErrorDisplay(y_true=y, y_pred=y_pred)
58::COMM;;>>> display.plot()
59::COMM;;<...>
60::COMM;;>>> plt.show()

81::COMM;;default="residual_vs_predicted"

21::COMM;;:func:`~sklearn.metrics.RocCurveDisplay.from_cv_results` to create
22::COMM;;a :class:`~sklearn.metrics.RocCurveDisplay`. All parameters are
23::COMM;;stored as attributes.
24::COMM;;For general information regarding `scikit-learn` visualization tools, see
25::COMM;;the :ref:`Visualization Guide <visualizations>`.
26::COMM;;For guidance on interpreting these plots, refer to the :ref:`Model
27::COMM;;Evaluation Guide <roc_metrics>`.
28::COMM;;Parameters
29::COMM;;----------
30::COMM;;fpr : ndarray or list of ndarrays
31::COMM;;False positive rates. Each ndarray should contain values for a single curve.
32::COMM;;If plotting multiple curves, list should be of same length as `tpr`.
33::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
34::COMM;;Now accepts a list for plotting multiple curves.
35::COMM;;tpr : ndarray or list of ndarrays
36::COMM;;True positive rates. Each ndarray should contain values for a single curve.
37::COMM;;If plotting multiple curves, list should be of same length as `fpr`.
38::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
39::COMM;;Now accepts a list for plotting multiple curves.
40::COMM;;roc_auc : float or list of floats, default=None
41::COMM;;Area under ROC curve, used for labeling each curve in the legend.
42::COMM;;If plotting multiple curves, should be a list of the same length as `fpr`
43::COMM;;and `tpr`. If `None`, ROC AUC scores are not shown in the legend.
44::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
45::COMM;;Now accepts a list for plotting multiple curves.
46::COMM;;name : str or list of str, default=None
47::COMM;;Name for labeling legend entries. The number of legend entries is determined
48::COMM;;by the `curve_kwargs` passed to `plot`, and is not affected by `name`.
49::COMM;;To label each curve, provide a list of strings. To avoid labeling
50::COMM;;individual curves that have the same appearance, a list cannot be used in
51::COMM;;conjunction with `curve_kwargs` being a dictionary or None. If a
52::COMM;;string is provided, it will be used to either label the single legend entry
53::COMM;;or if there are multiple legend entries, label each individual curve with
54::COMM;;the same name. If `None`, no name is shown in the legend.
55::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
56::COMM;;`estimator_name` was deprecated in favor of `name`.
57::COMM;;pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None
58::COMM;;The class considered the positive class when ROC AUC metrics computed.
59::COMM;;If not `None`, this value is displayed in the x- and y-axes labels.
60::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
61::COMM;;estimator_name : str, default=None
62::COMM;;Name of estimator. If None, the estimator name is not shown.
63::COMM;;.. deprecated:: 1.7
64::COMM;;`estimator_name` is deprecated and will be removed in 1.9. Use `name`
65::COMM;;instead.
66::COMM;;Attributes
67::COMM;;----------
68::COMM;;line_ : matplotlib Artist or list of matplotlib Artists
69::COMM;;ROC Curves.
70::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
71::COMM;;This attribute can now be a list of Artists, for when multiple curves
72::COMM;;are plotted.
73::COMM;;chance_level_ : matplotlib Artist or None
74::COMM;;The chance level line. It is `None` if the chance level is not plotted.
75::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
76::COMM;;ax_ : matplotlib Axes
77::COMM;;Axes with ROC Curve.
78::COMM;;figure_ : matplotlib Figure
79::COMM;;Figure containing the curve.
80::COMM;;See Also
81::COMM;;--------
82::COMM;;roc_curve : Compute Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
83::COMM;;RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator : Plot Receiver Operating Characteristic
84::COMM;;(ROC) curve given an estimator and some data.
85::COMM;;RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions : Plot Receiver Operating Characteristic
86::COMM;;(ROC) curve given the true and predicted values.
87::COMM;;RocCurveDisplay.from_cv_results : Plot multi-fold ROC curves given
88::COMM;;cross-validation results.
89::COMM;;roc_auc_score : Compute the area under the ROC curve.
90::COMM;;Examples
91::COMM;;--------
92::COMM;;>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
93::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
94::COMM;;>>> from sklearn import metrics
95::COMM;;>>> y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
96::COMM;;>>> y_score = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8])
97::COMM;;>>> fpr, tpr, thresholds = metrics.roc_curve(y_true, y_score)
98::COMM;;>>> roc_auc = metrics.auc(fpr, tpr)
99::COMM;;>>> display = metrics.RocCurveDisplay(fpr=fpr, tpr=tpr, roc_auc=roc_auc,
100::COMM;;... name='example estimator')
101::COMM;;>>> display.plot()
102::COMM;;<...>
103::COMM;;>>> plt.show()
147::COMM;;Parameters
148::COMM;;----------
149::COMM;;ax : matplotlib axes, default=None
150::COMM;;Axes object to plot on. If `None`, a new figure and axes is
151::COMM;;created.
152::COMM;;name : str or list of str, default=None
153::COMM;;Name for labeling legend entries. The number of legend entries
154::COMM;;is determined by `curve_kwargs`, and is not affected by `name`.
155::COMM;;To label each curve, provide a list of strings. To avoid labeling
156::COMM;;individual curves that have the same appearance, a list cannot be used in
157::COMM;;conjunction with `curve_kwargs` being a dictionary or None. If a
158::COMM;;string is provided, it will be used to either label the single legend entry
159::COMM;;or if there are multiple legend entries, label each individual curve with
160::COMM;;the same name. If `None`, set to `name` provided at `RocCurveDisplay`
161::COMM;;initialization. If still `None`, no name is shown in the legend.
162::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
163::COMM;;curve_kwargs : dict or list of dict, default=None
164::COMM;;Keywords arguments to be passed to matplotlib's `plot` function
165::COMM;;to draw individual ROC curves. For single curve plotting, should be
166::COMM;;a dictionary. For multi-curve plotting, if a list is provided the
167::COMM;;parameters are applied to the ROC curves of each CV fold
168::COMM;;sequentially and a legend entry is added for each curve.
169::COMM;;If a single dictionary is provided, the same parameters are applied
170::COMM;;to all ROC curves and a single legend entry for all curves is added,
171::COMM;;labeled with the mean ROC AUC score.
172::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
173::COMM;;plot_chance_level : bool, default=False
174::COMM;;Whether to plot the chance level.
175::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
176::COMM;;chance_level_kw : dict, default=None
177::COMM;;Keyword arguments to be passed to matplotlib's `plot` for rendering
178::COMM;;the chance level line.
179::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.3
180::COMM;;despine : bool, default=False
181::COMM;;Whether to remove the top and right spines from the plot.
182::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
183::COMM;;**kwargs : dict
184::COMM;;Keyword arguments to be passed to matplotlib's `plot`.
185::COMM;;.. deprecated:: 1.7
186::COMM;;kwargs is deprecated and will be removed in 1.9. Pass matplotlib
187::COMM;;arguments to `curve_kwargs` as a dictionary instead.

863::COMM;;assert display.ax_.spines[s].get_visible() is not despine
864::COMM;;if despine:

866::COMM;;assert display.ax_.spines[s].get_bounds() == (0, 1)
2::COMM;;Functions named as ``*_score`` return a scalar value to maximize: the higher
3::COMM;;the better.
4::COMM;;Function named as ``*_error`` or ``*_loss`` return a scalar value to minimize:
5::COMM;;the lower the better.
7::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
8::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
41::COMM;;This is a general function, given points on a curve. For computing the
42::COMM;;area under the ROC-curve, see :func:`roc_auc_score`. For an alternative
43::COMM;;way to summarize a precision-recall curve, see
44::COMM;;:func:`average_precision_score`.
45::COMM;;Parameters
46::COMM;;----------
47::COMM;;x : array-like of shape (n,)
48::COMM;;X coordinates. These must be either monotonic increasing or monotonic
49::COMM;;decreasing.
50::COMM;;y : array-like of shape (n,)
51::COMM;;Y coordinates.
52::COMM;;Returns
53::COMM;;-------
54::COMM;;auc : float
55::COMM;;Area Under the Curve.
56::COMM;;See Also
57::COMM;;--------
58::COMM;;roc_auc_score : Compute the area under the ROC curve.
59::COMM;;average_precision_score : Compute average precision from prediction scores.
60::COMM;;precision_recall_curve : Compute precision-recall pairs for different
61::COMM;;probability thresholds.
62::COMM;;Examples
63::COMM;;--------
64::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
65::COMM;;>>> from sklearn import metrics
66::COMM;;>>> y_true = np.array([1, 1, 2, 2])
67::COMM;;>>> y_score = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8])
68::COMM;;>>> fpr, tpr, thresholds = metrics.roc_curve(y_true, y_score, pos_label=2)
69::COMM;;>>> metrics.auc(fpr, tpr)
70::COMM;;0.75
89::COMO;;# Reductions such as .sum used internally in trapezoid do not return a
90::COMO;;# scalar by default for numpy.memmap instances contrary to
91::COMO;;# regular numpy.ndarray instances.
108::COMM;;AP summarizes a precision-recall curve as the weighted mean of precisions
109::COMM;;achieved at each threshold, with the increase in recall from the previous
110::COMM;;threshold used as the weight:
111::COMM;;.. math::
112::COMM;;\\text{AP} = \\sum_n (R_n - R_{n-1}) P_n
113::COMM;;where :math:`P_n` and :math:`R_n` are the precision and recall at the nth
114::COMM;;threshold [1]_. This implementation is not interpolated and is different
115::COMM;;from computing the area under the precision-recall curve with the
116::COMM;;trapezoidal rule, which uses linear interpolation and can be too
117::COMM;;optimistic.
118::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <precision_recall_f_measure_metrics>`.
119::COMM;;Parameters
120::COMM;;----------
121::COMM;;y_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_classes)
122::COMM;;True binary labels or binary label indicators.
123::COMM;;y_score : array-like of shape (n_samples,) or (n_samples, n_classes)
124::COMM;;Target scores, can either be probability estimates of the positive
125::COMM;;class, confidence values, or non-thresholded measure of decisions
126::COMM;;(as returned by :term:`decision_function` on some classifiers).
127::COMM;;For :term:`decision_function` scores, values greater than or equal to
128::COMM;;zero should indicate the positive class.
129::COMM;;average : {'micro', 'samples', 'weighted', 'macro'} or None, \
130::COMM;;default='macro'
131::COMM;;If ``None``, the scores for each class are returned. Otherwise,
132::COMM;;this determines the type of averaging performed on the data:
133::COMM;;``'micro'``:
134::COMM;;Calculate metrics globally by considering each element of the label
135::COMM;;indicator matrix as a label.
136::COMM;;``'macro'``:
137::COMM;;Calculate metrics for each label, and find their unweighted
138::COMM;;mean. This does not take label imbalance into account.
139::COMM;;``'weighted'``:
140::COMM;;Calculate metrics for each label, and find their average, weighted
141::COMM;;by support (the number of true instances for each label).
142::COMM;;``'samples'``:
143::COMM;;Calculate metrics for each instance, and find their average.
144::COMM;;Will be ignored when ``y_true`` is binary.
145::COMM;;pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=1
146::COMM;;The label of the positive class. Only applied to binary ``y_true``.
147::COMM;;For multilabel-indicator ``y_true``, ``pos_label`` is fixed to 1.
148::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
149::COMM;;Sample weights.
150::COMM;;Returns
151::COMM;;-------
152::COMM;;average_precision : float
153::COMM;;Average precision score.
154::COMM;;See Also
155::COMM;;--------
156::COMM;;roc_auc_score : Compute the area under the ROC curve.
157::COMM;;precision_recall_curve : Compute precision-recall pairs for different
158::COMM;;probability thresholds.
159::COMM;;PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator : Plot the precision recall curve
160::COMM;;using an estimator and data.
161::COMM;;PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions : Plot the precision recall curve
162::COMM;;using true and predicted labels.
163::COMM;;Notes
164::COMM;;-----
165::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.19
166::COMM;;Instead of linearly interpolating between operating points, precisions
167::COMM;;are weighted by the change in recall since the last operating point.
168::COMM;;References
169::COMM;;----------
170::COMM;;.. [1] `Wikipedia entry for the Average precision
171::COMM;;<https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Information_retrieval&
172::COMM;;oldid=793358396#Average_precision>`_
173::COMM;;Examples
174::COMM;;--------
175::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
176::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score
177::COMM;;>>> y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
178::COMM;;>>> y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8])
179::COMM;;>>> average_precision_score(y_true, y_scores)
180::COMM;;0.83
181::COMM;;>>> y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2])
182::COMM;;>>> y_scores = np.array([
183::COMM;;... [0.7, 0.2, 0.1],
184::COMM;;... [0.4, 0.3, 0.3],
185::COMM;;... [0.1, 0.8, 0.1],
186::COMM;;... [0.2, 0.3, 0.5],
187::COMM;;... [0.4, 0.4, 0.2],
188::COMM;;... [0.1, 0.2, 0.7],
189::COMM;;... ])
190::COMM;;>>> average_precision_score(y_true, y_scores)
191::COMM;;0.77
199::COMO;;# Return the step function integral
200::COMO;;# The following works because the last entry of precision is
201::COMO;;# guaranteed to be 1, as returned by precision_recall_curve.
202::COMO;;# Due to numerical error, we can get `-0.0` and we therefore clip it.
205::COMO;;# Convert to Python primitive type to avoid NumPy type / Python str
206::COMO;;# comparison. See https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/6784
246::COMM;;Note: Support beyond :term:`binary` classification tasks, via one-vs-rest or
247::COMM;;one-vs-one, is not implemented.
248::COMM;;The DET curve is used for evaluation of ranking and error tradeoffs in binary
249::COMM;;classification tasks.
250::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <det_curve>`.
251::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
252::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
253::COMM;;An arbitrary threshold at infinity is added to represent a classifier
254::COMM;;that always predicts the negative class, i.e. `fpr=0` and `fnr=1`, unless
255::COMM;;`fpr=0` is already reached at a finite threshold.
256::COMM;;Parameters
257::COMM;;----------
258::COMM;;y_true : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
259::COMM;;True binary labels. If labels are not either {-1, 1} or {0, 1}, then
260::COMM;;pos_label should be explicitly given.
261::COMM;;y_score : ndarray of shape of (n_samples,)
262::COMM;;Target scores, can either be probability estimates of the positive
263::COMM;;class, confidence values, or non-thresholded measure of decisions
264::COMM;;(as returned by "decision_function" on some classifiers).
265::COMM;;For :term:`decision_function` scores, values greater than or equal to
266::COMM;;zero should indicate the positive class.
267::COMM;;pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None
268::COMM;;The label of the positive class.
269::COMM;;When ``pos_label=None``, if `y_true` is in {-1, 1} or {0, 1},
270::COMM;;``pos_label`` is set to 1, otherwise an error will be raised.
271::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
272::COMM;;Sample weights.
273::COMM;;drop_intermediate : bool, default=False
274::COMM;;Whether to drop thresholds where true positives (tp) do not change from
275::COMM;;the previous or subsequent threshold. All points with the same tp value
276::COMM;;have the same `fnr` and thus same y coordinate.
277::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.7
278::COMM;;Returns
279::COMM;;-------
280::COMM;;fpr : ndarray of shape (n_thresholds,)
281::COMM;;False positive rate (FPR) such that element i is the false positive
282::COMM;;rate of predictions with score >= thresholds[i]. This is occasionally
283::COMM;;referred to as false acceptance probability or fall-out.
284::COMM;;fnr : ndarray of shape (n_thresholds,)
285::COMM;;False negative rate (FNR) such that element i is the false negative
286::COMM;;rate of predictions with score >= thresholds[i]. This is occasionally
287::COMM;;referred to as false rejection or miss rate.
288::COMM;;thresholds : ndarray of shape (n_thresholds,)
289::COMM;;Decreasing thresholds on the decision function (either `predict_proba`
290::COMM;;or `decision_function`) used to compute FPR and FNR.
291::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.7
292::COMM;;An arbitrary threshold at infinity is added for the case `fpr=0`
293::COMM;;and `fnr=1`.
294::COMM;;See Also

299::COMM;;predicted labels.
300::COMM;;DetCurveDisplay : DET curve visualization.

323::COMO;;# add a threshold at inf where the clf always predicts the negative class
324::COMO;;# i.e. tps = fps = 0
330::COMO;;# Drop thresholds where true positives (tp) do not change from the
331::COMO;;# previous or subsequent threshold. As tp + fn, is fixed for a dataset,
332::COMO;;# this means the false negative rate (fnr) remains constant while the
333::COMO;;# false positive rate (fpr) changes, producing horizontal line segments
334::COMO;;# in the transformed (normal deviate) scale. These intermediate points
335::COMO;;# can be dropped to create lighter DET curve plots.
356::COMO;;# start with false positives zero, which may be at a finite threshold
362::COMO;;# stop with false negatives zero
365::COMO;;# reverse the output such that list of false positives is decreasing
373::COMM;;if len(np.unique(y_true)) != 2:
374::COMM;;warnings.warn(
375::COMM;;(
376::COMM;;"Only one class is present in y_true. ROC AUC score "
377::COMM;;"is not defined in that case."
378::COMM;;),
379::COMM;;UndefinedMetricWarning,
380::COMM;;)
381::COMM;;return np.nan
382::COMM;;fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, y_score, sample_weight=sample_weight)
383::COMM;;if max_fpr is None or max_fpr == 1:
384::COMM;;return auc(fpr, tpr)
385::COMM;;if max_fpr <= 0 or max_fpr > 1:
386::COMM;;raise ValueError("Expected max_fpr in range (0, 1], got: %r" % max_fpr)
387::COMM;;# Add a single point at max_fpr by linear interpolation
388::COMM;;stop = np.searchsorted(fpr, max_fpr, "right")
389::COMM;;x_interp = [fpr[stop - 1], fpr[stop]]
390::COMM;;y_interp = [tpr[stop - 1], tpr[stop]]
391::COMM;;tpr = np.append(tpr[:stop], np.interp(max_fpr, x_interp, y_interp))
392::COMM;;fpr = np.append(fpr[:stop], max_fpr)
393::COMM;;partial_auc = auc(fpr, tpr)
394::COMM;;# McClish correction: standardize result to be 0.5 if non-discriminant
395::COMM;;# and 1 if maximal
396::COMM;;min_area = 0.5 * max_fpr**2
397::COMM;;max_area = max_fpr
398::COMM;;return 0.5 * (1 + (partial_auc - min_area) / (max_area - min_area))

731::COMM;;def confusion_matrix_at_thresholds(y_true, y_score, pos_label=None, sample_weight=None):
788::COMM;;# Check to make sure y_true is valid
789::COMM;;y_type = type_of_target(y_true, input_name="y_true")
790::COMM;;if not (y_type == "binary" or (y_type == "multiclass" and pos_label is not None)):
791::COMM;;raise ValueError("{0} format is not supported".format(y_type))
792::COMM;;xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(y_true, y_score, sample_weight)
793::COMM;;check_consistent_length(y_true, y_score, sample_weight)
794::COMM;;y_true = column_or_1d(y_true)
795::COMM;;y_score = column_or_1d(y_score)
796::COMM;;assert_all_finite(y_true)
797::COMM;;assert_all_finite(y_score)
798::COMM;;# Filter out zero-weighted samples, as they should not impact the result
799::COMM;;if sample_weight is not None:
800::COMM;;sample_weight = column_or_1d(sample_weight)
801::COMM;;sample_weight = _check_sample_weight(sample_weight, y_true)
802::COMM;;nonzero_weight_mask = sample_weight != 0
803::COMM;;y_true = y_true[nonzero_weight_mask]
804::COMM;;y_score = y_score[nonzero_weight_mask]
805::COMM;;sample_weight = sample_weight[nonzero_weight_mask]
806::COMM;;pos_label = _check_pos_label_consistency(pos_label, y_true)
807::COMM;;# make y_true a boolean vector
808::COMM;;y_true = y_true == pos_label
809::COMM;;# sort scores and corresponding truth values
810::COMM;;desc_score_indices = xp.argsort(y_score, stable=True, descending=True)
811::COMM;;y_score = y_score[desc_score_indices]
812::COMM;;y_true = y_true[desc_score_indices]
813::COMM;;if sample_weight is not None:
814::COMM;;weight = sample_weight[desc_score_indices]
815::COMM;;else:
816::COMM;;weight = 1.0
817::COMM;;# y_score typically has many tied values. Here we extract
818::COMM;;# the indices associated with the distinct values. We also
819::COMM;;# concatenate a value for the end of the curve.
820::COMM;;distinct_value_indices = xp.nonzero(xp.diff(y_score))[0]
821::COMM;;threshold_idxs = xp.concat(
822::COMM;;[distinct_value_indices, xp.asarray([size(y_true) - 1], device=device)]
823::COMM;;)
824::COMM;;# accumulate the true positives with decreasing threshold
825::COMM;;max_float_dtype = _max_precision_float_dtype(xp, device)
826::COMM;;# Perform the weighted cumulative sum using float64 precision when possible
827::COMM;;# to avoid numerical stability problem with tens of millions of very noisy
828::COMM;;# predictions:
829::COMM;;# https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31533#issuecomment-2967062437
830::COMM;;y_true = xp.astype(y_true, max_float_dtype)
831::COMM;;tps = xp.cumulative_sum(y_true * weight, dtype=max_float_dtype)[threshold_idxs]
832::COMM;;if sample_weight is not None:
833::COMM;;# express fps as a cumsum to ensure fps is increasing even in
834::COMM;;# the presence of floating point errors
835::COMM;;fps = xp.cumulative_sum((1 - y_true) * weight, dtype=max_float_dtype)[
836::COMM;;threshold_idxs
837::COMM;;]
838::COMM;;else:
839::COMM;;fps = 1 + xp.astype(threshold_idxs, max_float_dtype) - tps
840::COMM;;tns = fps[-1] - fps
841::COMM;;fns = tps[-1] - tps
842::COMM;;return tns, fps, fns, tps, y_score[threshold_idxs]
843::COMM;;@validate_params(
844::COMM;;{
845::COMM;;"y_true": ["array-like"],
846::COMM;;"y_score": ["array-like"],
847::COMM;;"pos_label": [Real, str, "boolean", None],
848::COMM;;"sample_weight": ["array-like", None],
849::COMM;;"drop_intermediate": ["boolean"],
850::COMM;;},
851::COMM;;prefer_skip_nested_validation=True,
852::COMM;;)
853::COMM;;def precision_recall_curve(
854::COMM;;y_true,
855::COMM;;y_score,
856::COMM;;*,
857::COMM;;pos_label=None,
858::COMM;;sample_weight=None,
859::COMM;;drop_intermediate=False,
860::COMM;;):
936::COMM;;xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(y_true, y_score)
937::COMM;;_, fps, _, tps, thresholds = confusion_matrix_at_thresholds(
938::COMM;;y_true, y_score, pos_label=pos_label, sample_weight=sample_weight
939::COMM;;)
940::COMM;;if drop_intermediate and fps.shape[0] > 2:
941::COMM;;# Drop thresholds corresponding to points where true positives (tps)
942::COMM;;# do not change from the previous or subsequent point. This will keep
943::COMM;;# only the first and last point for each tps value. All points
944::COMM;;# with the same tps value have the same recall and thus x coordinate.
945::COMM;;# They appear as a vertical line on the plot.
946::COMM;;optimal_idxs = xp.where(
947::COMM;;xp.concat(
948::COMM;;[
949::COMM;;xp.asarray([True], device=device),
950::COMM;;xp.logical_or(xp.diff(tps[:-1]), xp.diff(tps[1:])),
951::COMM;;xp.asarray([True], device=device),
952::COMM;;]

1074::COMM;;# Attempt to drop thresholds corresponding to points in between and

1076::COMM;;# appear on a plotted ROC curve (and thus do not affect the AUC).
1077::COMM;;# Here np.diff(_, 2) is used as a "second derivative" to tell if there

1079::COMM;;# thresholds with multiple data points (which are combined in
1080::COMM;;# confusion_matrix_at_thresholds). This keeps all cases where the point should be
1081::COMM;;# kept, but does not drop more complicated cases like fps = [1, 3, 7],
1082::COMM;;# tps = [1, 2, 4]; there is no harm in keeping too many thresholds.

1085::COMM;;xp.concat(

1268::COMM;;def label_ranking_loss(y_true, y_score, *, sample_weight=None):
1310::COMM;;y_true = check_array(y_true, ensure_2d=False, accept_sparse="csr")
1311::COMM;;y_score = check_array(y_score, ensure_2d=False)
1312::COMM;;check_consistent_length(y_true, y_score, sample_weight)
1313::COMM;;y_type = type_of_target(y_true, input_name="y_true")
1314::COMM;;if y_type not in ("multilabel-indicator",):
1315::COMM;;raise ValueError("{0} format is not supported".format(y_type))
1316::COMM;;if y_true.shape != y_score.shape:
1317::COMM;;raise ValueError("y_true and y_score have different shape")
1318::COMM;;n_samples, n_labels = y_true.shape
1319::COMM;;y_true = csr_matrix(y_true)
1320::COMM;;loss = np.zeros(n_samples)
1321::COMM;;for i, (start, stop) in enumerate(zip(y_true.indptr, y_true.indptr[1:])):
1322::COMM;;# Sort and bin the label scores
1323::COMM;;unique_scores, unique_inverse = np.unique(y_score[i], return_inverse=True)
1324::COMM;;true_at_reversed_rank = np.bincount(
1325::COMM;;unique_inverse[y_true.indices[start:stop]], minlength=len(unique_scores)
1326::COMM;;)
1327::COMM;;all_at_reversed_rank = np.bincount(unique_inverse, minlength=len(unique_scores))
1328::COMM;;false_at_reversed_rank = all_at_reversed_rank - true_at_reversed_rank
1329::COMM;;# if the scores are ordered, it's possible to count the number of
1330::COMM;;# incorrectly ordered paires in linear time by cumulatively counting
1331::COMM;;# how many false labels of a given score have a score higher than the
1332::COMM;;# accumulated true labels with lower score.
1333::COMM;;loss[i] = np.dot(true_at_reversed_rank.cumsum(), false_at_reversed_rank)
1334::COMM;;n_positives = count_nonzero(y_true, axis=1)
1335::COMM;;with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
1336::COMM;;loss /= (n_labels - n_positives) * n_positives
1337::COMM;;# When there is no positive or no negative labels, those values should
1338::COMM;;# be consider as correct, i.e. the ranking doesn't matter.
1339::COMM;;loss[np.logical_or(n_positives == 0, n_positives == n_labels)] = 0.0
1340::COMM;;return float(np.average(loss, weights=sample_weight))
1341::COMM;;def _dcg_sample_scores(y_true, y_score, k=None, log_base=2, ignore_ties=False):
1375::COMM;;discount = 1 / (np.log(np.arange(y_true.shape[1]) + 2) / np.log(log_base))
1376::COMM;;if k is not None:
1377::COMM;;discount[k:] = 0
1378::COMM;;if ignore_ties:
1379::COMM;;ranking = np.argsort(y_score)[:, ::-1]
1380::COMM;;ranked = y_true[np.arange(ranking.shape[0])[:, np.newaxis], ranking]
1381::COMM;;cumulative_gains = discount.dot(ranked.T)
1382::COMM;;else:
1383::COMM;;discount_cumsum = np.cumsum(discount)
1384::COMM;;cumulative_gains = [
1385::COMM;;_tie_averaged_dcg(y_t, y_s, discount_cumsum)
1386::COMM;;for y_t, y_s in zip(y_true, y_score)
1387::COMM;;]
1388::COMM;;cumulative_gains = np.asarray(cumulative_gains)
1389::COMM;;return cumulative_gains
1390::COMM;;def _tie_averaged_dcg(y_true, y_score, discount_cumsum):
1419::COMM;;_, inv, counts = np.unique(-y_score, return_inverse=True, return_counts=True)
1420::COMM;;ranked = np.zeros(len(counts))
1421::COMM;;np.add.at(ranked, inv, y_true)
1422::COMM;;ranked /= counts
1423::COMM;;groups = np.cumsum(counts) - 1
1424::COMM;;discount_sums = np.empty(len(counts))
1425::COMM;;discount_sums[0] = discount_cumsum[groups[0]]
1426::COMM;;discount_sums[1:] = np.diff(discount_cumsum[groups])
1427::COMM;;return (ranked * discount_sums).sum()

1526::COMC;;>>> # wrong results:

1543::COMM;;def _ndcg_sample_scores(y_true, y_score, k=None, ignore_ties=False):
1574::COMM;;gain = _dcg_sample_scores(y_true, y_score, k, ignore_ties=ignore_ties)
1575::COMM;;# Here we use the order induced by y_true so we can ignore ties since
1576::COMM;;# the gain associated to tied indices is the same (permuting ties doesn't
1577::COMM;;# change the value of the re-ordered y_true)

1579::COMM;;all_irrelevant = normalizing_gain == 0
1580::COMM;;gain[all_irrelevant] = 0
1581::COMM;;gain[~all_irrelevant] /= normalizing_gain[~all_irrelevant]
1582::COMM;;return gain

750::COMM;;0.85
766::COMO;;# pass None as weights to np.average: uniform mean
773::COMM;;dtype = numerator.dtype
774::COMM;;nonzero_denominator = denominator != 0
775::COMM;;if not force_finite:
776::COMM;;# Standard formula, that may lead to NaN or -Inf
777::COMM;;output_scores = 1 - (numerator / denominator)
778::COMM;;else:
779::COMM;;nonzero_numerator = numerator != 0
780::COMM;;# Default = Zero Numerator = perfect predictions. Set to 1.0
781::COMM;;# (note: even if denominator is zero, thus avoiding NaN scores)
782::COMM;;output_scores = xp.ones([n_outputs], device=device, dtype=dtype)
783::COMM;;# Non-zero Numerator and Non-zero Denominator: use the formula
784::COMM;;valid_score = nonzero_denominator & nonzero_numerator
785::COMM;;output_scores[valid_score] = 1 - (
786::COMM;;numerator[valid_score] / denominator[valid_score]
787::COMM;;)
788::COMM;;# Non-zero Numerator and Zero Denominator:
789::COMM;;# arbitrary set to 0.0 to avoid -inf scores
790::COMM;;output_scores[nonzero_numerator & ~nonzero_denominator] = 0.0
791::COMM;;if isinstance(multioutput, str):
792::COMM;;if multioutput == "raw_values":
793::COMM;;# return scores individually
794::COMM;;return output_scores
795::COMM;;elif multioutput == "uniform_average":
796::COMM;;# pass None as weights to _average: uniform mean
797::COMM;;avg_weights = None
798::COMM;;elif multioutput == "variance_weighted":
799::COMM;;avg_weights = denominator
800::COMM;;if not xp.any(nonzero_denominator):
801::COMM;;# All weights are zero, _average would raise a ZeroDiv error.
802::COMM;;# This only happens when all y are constant (or 1-element long)
803::COMM;;# Since weights are all equal, fall back to uniform weights.
804::COMM;;avg_weights = None
805::COMM;;else:
806::COMM;;avg_weights = multioutput
807::COMM;;result = _average(output_scores, weights=avg_weights, xp=xp)
808::COMM;;if size(result) == 1:
809::COMM;;return float(result)
810::COMM;;return result

2::COMM;;The :mod:`sklearn.metrics.scorer` submodule implements a flexible
3::COMM;;interface for model selection and evaluation using
4::COMM;;arbitrary score functions.
5::COMM;;A scorer object is a callable that can be passed to
6::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` or
7::COMM;;:func:`sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score` as the ``scoring``
8::COMM;;parameter, to specify how a model should be evaluated.
9::COMM;;The signature of the call is ``(estimator, X, y)`` where ``estimator``
10::COMM;;is the model to be evaluated, ``X`` is the test data and ``y`` is the
11::COMM;;ground truth labeling (or ``None`` in the case of unsupervised models).

101::COMM;;`_MultimetricScorer` will return a dictionary of scores corresponding to
102::COMM;;the scorers in the dictionary. Note that `_MultimetricScorer` can be
103::COMM;;created with a dictionary with one key (i.e. only one actual scorer).
104::COMM;;Parameters
105::COMM;;----------
106::COMM;;scorers : dict
107::COMM;;Dictionary mapping names to callable scorers.
108::COMM;;raise_exc : bool, default=True
109::COMM;;Whether to raise the exception in `__call__` or not. If set to `False`
110::COMM;;a formatted string of the exception details is passed as result of
111::COMM;;the failing scorer.
118::COMM;;scores = {}
119::COMM;;cache = {} if self._use_cache(estimator) else None
120::COMM;;cached_call = partial(_cached_call, cache)
121::COMM;;if _routing_enabled():
122::COMM;;routed_params = process_routing(self, "score", **kwargs)
123::COMM;;else:
124::COMM;;# Scorers all get the same args, and get all of them except sample_weight.
125::COMM;;# Only the ones having `sample_weight` in their signature will receive it.
126::COMM;;# This does not work for metadata other than sample_weight, and for those
127::COMM;;# users have to enable metadata routing.
128::COMM;;common_kwargs = {
129::COMM;;arg: value for arg, value in kwargs.items() if arg != "sample_weight"
130::COMM;;}
131::COMM;;routed_params = Bunch(
132::COMM;;**{name: Bunch(score=common_kwargs.copy()) for name in self._scorers}
133::COMM;;)
134::COMM;;if "sample_weight" in kwargs:
135::COMM;;for name, scorer in self._scorers.items():
136::COMM;;if scorer._accept_sample_weight():
137::COMM;;routed_params[name].score["sample_weight"] = kwargs[
138::COMM;;"sample_weight"
139::COMM;;]
140::COMM;;for name, scorer in self._scorers.items():
141::COMM;;try:
142::COMM;;if isinstance(scorer, _BaseScorer):
143::COMM;;score = scorer._score(
144::COMM;;cached_call, estimator, *args, **routed_params.get(name).score
145::COMM;;)
146::COMM;;else:
147::COMM;;score = scorer(estimator, *args, **routed_params.get(name).score)
148::COMM;;scores[name] = score
149::COMM;;except Exception as e:
150::COMM;;if self._raise_exc:
151::COMM;;raise e
152::COMM;;else:
153::COMM;;scores[name] = format_exc()
154::COMM;;return scores

157::COMM;;return f"MultiMetricScorer({scorers})"

448::COMC;;"https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-scoring"
519::COMM;;A scorer is a wrapper around an arbitrary metric or loss function that is called
520::COMM;;with the signature `scorer(estimator, X, y_true, **kwargs)`.
521::COMM;;It is accepted in all scikit-learn estimators or functions allowing a `scoring`
522::COMM;;parameter.
523::COMM;;The parameter `response_method` allows to specify which method of the estimator
524::COMM;;should be used to feed the scoring/loss function.
525::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <scoring_callable>`.
526::COMM;;Parameters
527::COMM;;----------
528::COMM;;score_func : callable
529::COMM;;Score function (or loss function) with signature
530::COMM;;``score_func(y, y_pred, **kwargs)``.
531::COMM;;response_method : {"predict_proba", "decision_function", "predict"} or \
532::COMM;;list/tuple of such str, default="predict"
533::COMM;;Specifies the response method to use get prediction from an estimator
534::COMM;;(i.e. :term:`predict_proba`, :term:`decision_function` or
535::COMM;;:term:`predict`). Possible choices are:
536::COMM;;- if `str`, it corresponds to the name to the method to return;
537::COMM;;- if a list or tuple of `str`, it provides the method names in order of
538::COMM;;preference. The method returned corresponds to the first method in
539::COMM;;the list and which is implemented by `estimator`.
540::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.4
541::COMM;;greater_is_better : bool, default=True
542::COMM;;Whether `score_func` is a score function (default), meaning high is
543::COMM;;good, or a loss function, meaning low is good. In the latter case, the
544::COMM;;scorer object will sign-flip the outcome of the `score_func`.
545::COMM;;**kwargs : additional arguments
546::COMM;;Additional parameters to be passed to `score_func`.
547::COMM;;Returns
548::COMM;;-------
549::COMM;;scorer : callable
550::COMM;;Callable object that returns a scalar score; greater is better.
551::COMM;;Examples

16::COMM;;def _jaccard(a_rows, a_cols, b_rows, b_cols):
24::COMM;;result[i, j] is the Jaccard coefficient of a's bicluster i and b's
25::COMM;;bicluster j.
47::COMM;;Similarity between individual biclusters is computed. Then the best
48::COMM;;matching between sets is found by solving a linear sum assignment problem,
49::COMM;;using a modified Jonker-Volgenant algorithm.
50::COMM;;The final score is the sum of similarities divided by the size of
51::COMM;;the larger set.
52::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <biclustering>`.
53::COMM;;Parameters
54::COMM;;----------
55::COMM;;a : tuple (rows, columns)
56::COMM;;Tuple of row and column indicators for a set of biclusters.
57::COMM;;b : tuple (rows, columns)
58::COMM;;Another set of biclusters like ``a``.
59::COMM;;similarity : 'jaccard' or callable, default='jaccard'
60::COMM;;May be the string "jaccard" to use the Jaccard coefficient, or
61::COMM;;any function that takes four arguments, each of which is a 1d
62::COMM;;indicator vector: (a_rows, a_columns, b_rows, b_columns).
63::COMM;;Returns
64::COMM;;-------
65::COMM;;consensus_score : float
66::COMM;;Consensus score, a non-negative value, sum of similarities
67::COMM;;divided by size of larger set.
68::COMM;;See Also
69::COMM;;--------
70::COMM;;scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment : Solve the linear sum assignment problem.
71::COMM;;References
72::COMM;;----------
73::COMM;;* Hochreiter, Bodenhofer, et. al., 2010. `FABIA: factor analysis
74::COMM;;for bicluster acquisition
75::COMM;;<https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2881408/>`__.
76::COMM;;Examples

132::COMM;;classes, class_idx = np.unique(labels_true, return_inverse=True)
133::COMM;;clusters, cluster_idx = np.unique(labels_pred, return_inverse=True)
134::COMM;;n_classes = classes.shape[0]
135::COMM;;n_clusters = clusters.shape[0]
136::COMM;;# Using coo_matrix to accelerate simple histogram calculation,
137::COMM;;# i.e. bins are consecutive integers
138::COMM;;# Currently, coo_matrix is faster than histogram2d for simple cases
139::COMM;;contingency = sp.coo_matrix(
140::COMM;;(np.ones(class_idx.shape[0]), (class_idx, cluster_idx)),
141::COMM;;shape=(n_classes, n_clusters),
142::COMM;;dtype=dtype,
143::COMM;;)

145::COMM;;contingency = contingency.tocsr()
146::COMM;;contingency.sum_duplicates()
147::COMM;;else:
148::COMM;;contingency = contingency.toarray()
149::COMM;;if eps is not None:
150::COMM;;# don't use += as contingency is integer
151::COMM;;contingency = contingency + eps
152::COMM;;return contingency
153::COMM;;# clustering measures
154::COMM;;@validate_params(
155::COMM;;{

161::COMM;;def pair_confusion_matrix(labels_true, labels_pred):
208::COMM;;labels_true, labels_pred = check_clusterings(labels_true, labels_pred)
209::COMM;;n_samples = np.int64(labels_true.shape[0])
210::COMM;;# Computation using the contingency data
211::COMM;;contingency = contingency_matrix(
212::COMM;;labels_true, labels_pred, sparse=True, dtype=np.int64
213::COMM;;)
214::COMM;;n_c = np.ravel(contingency.sum(axis=1))
215::COMM;;n_k = np.ravel(contingency.sum(axis=0))
216::COMM;;sum_squares = (contingency.data**2).sum()
217::COMM;;C = np.empty((2, 2), dtype=np.int64)
218::COMM;;C[1, 1] = sum_squares - n_samples
219::COMM;;C[0, 1] = contingency.dot(n_k).sum() - sum_squares
220::COMM;;C[1, 0] = contingency.transpose().dot(n_c).sum() - sum_squares
221::COMM;;C[0, 0] = n_samples**2 - C[0, 1] - C[1, 0] - sum_squares
222::COMM;;return C

276::COMM;;denominator = contingency.sum()

278::COMM;;# Special limit cases: no clustering since the data is not split;
279::COMM;;# or trivial clustering where each document is assigned a unique
280::COMM;;# cluster. These are perfect matches hence return 1.0.
281::COMM;;return 1.0

290::COMM;;def adjusted_rand_score(labels_true, labels_pred):
328::COMC;;.. [wk] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rand_index#Adjusted_Rand_index
358::COMM;;(tn, fp), (fn, tp) = pair_confusion_matrix(labels_true, labels_pred)
359::COMM;;# convert to Python integer types, to avoid overflow or underflow
360::COMM;;tn, fp, fn, tp = int(tn), int(fp), int(fn), int(tp)
361::COMM;;# Special cases: empty data or full agreement
362::COMM;;if fn == 0 and fp == 0:
363::COMM;;return 1.0
364::COMM;;return 2.0 * (tp * tn - fn * fp) / ((tp + fn) * (fn + tn) + (tp + fp) * (fp + tn))

644::COMM;;def mutual_info_score(labels_true, labels_pred, *, contingency=None):
697::COMM;;if contingency is None:
698::COMM;;labels_true, labels_pred = check_clusterings(labels_true, labels_pred)
699::COMM;;contingency = contingency_matrix(labels_true, labels_pred, sparse=True)
700::COMM;;else:
701::COMM;;contingency = check_array(
702::COMM;;contingency,
703::COMM;;accept_sparse=["csr", "csc", "coo"],
704::COMM;;dtype=[int, np.int32, np.int64],
705::COMM;;)
706::COMM;;if isinstance(contingency, np.ndarray):
707::COMM;;# For an array
708::COMM;;nzx, nzy = np.nonzero(contingency)
709::COMM;;nz_val = contingency[nzx, nzy]
710::COMM;;else:
711::COMM;;# For a sparse matrix
712::COMM;;nzx, nzy, nz_val = sp.find(contingency)
713::COMM;;contingency_sum = contingency.sum()
714::COMM;;pi = np.ravel(contingency.sum(axis=1))
715::COMM;;pj = np.ravel(contingency.sum(axis=0))
716::COMM;;# Since MI <= min(H(X), H(Y)), any labelling with zero entropy, i.e. containing a
717::COMM;;# single cluster, implies MI = 0
718::COMM;;if pi.size == 1 or pj.size == 1:
719::COMM;;return 0.0
720::COMM;;log_contingency_nm = np.log(nz_val)
721::COMM;;contingency_nm = nz_val / contingency_sum
722::COMM;;# Don't need to calculate the full outer product, just for non-zeroes
723::COMM;;outer = pi.take(nzx).astype(np.int64, copy=False) * pj.take(nzy).astype(
724::COMM;;np.int64, copy=False
725::COMM;;)
726::COMM;;log_outer = -np.log(outer) + log(pi.sum()) + log(pj.sum())
727::COMM;;mi = (
728::COMM;;contingency_nm * (log_contingency_nm - log(contingency_sum))
729::COMM;;+ contingency_nm * log_outer
730::COMM;;)
731::COMM;;mi = np.where(np.abs(mi) < np.finfo(mi.dtype).eps, 0.0, mi)
732::COMM;;return float(np.clip(mi.sum(), 0.0, None))

811::COMM;;clusters = np.unique(labels_pred)
812::COMM;;# Special limit cases: no clustering since the data is not split.
813::COMM;;# It corresponds to both labellings having zero entropy.
814::COMM;;# This is a perfect match hence return 1.0.

816::COMM;;classes.shape[0] == clusters.shape[0] == 1
817::COMM;;or classes.shape[0] == clusters.shape[0] == 0
818::COMM;;):

827::COMM;;emi = expected_mutual_information(contingency, n_samples)
828::COMM;;# Calculate entropy for each labeling
829::COMM;;h_true, h_pred = _entropy(labels_true), _entropy(labels_pred)
830::COMM;;normalizer = _generalized_average(h_true, h_pred, average_method)
831::COMM;;denominator = normalizer - emi
832::COMM;;# Avoid 0.0 / 0.0 when expectation equals maximum, i.e. a perfect match.
833::COMM;;# normalizer should always be >= emi, but because of floating-point
834::COMM;;# representation, sometimes emi is slightly larger. Correct this
835::COMM;;# by preserving the sign.

837::COMM;;denominator = min(denominator, -np.finfo("float64").eps)
838::COMM;;else:
839::COMM;;denominator = max(denominator, np.finfo("float64").eps)
840::COMM;;# The same applies analogously to mi and emi.
841::COMM;;numerator = mi - emi
842::COMM;;if numerator < 0:
843::COMM;;numerator = min(numerator, -np.finfo("float64").eps)
844::COMM;;else:
845::COMM;;numerator = max(numerator, np.finfo("float64").eps)
846::COMM;;return float(numerator / denominator)

26::COMM;;def test_consensus_score_issue2445():
44::COMO;;# B contains 2 of the 3 biclusters in A, so score should be 2/3
25::COMO;;# Dictionaries of metrics
26::COMO;;# ------------------------
27::COMO;;# The goal of having those dictionaries is to have an easy way to call a
28::COMO;;# particular metric and associate a name to each function:
29::COMO;;# - SUPERVISED_METRICS: all supervised cluster metrics - (when given a
30::COMO;;# ground truth value)
31::COMO;;# - UNSUPERVISED_METRICS: all unsupervised cluster metrics
32::COMO;;#
33::COMO;;# Those dictionaries will be used to test systematically some invariance
34::COMO;;# properties, e.g. invariance toward several input layout.
35::COMO;;#
53::COMO;;# Lists of metrics with common properties
54::COMO;;# ---------------------------------------
55::COMO;;# Lists of metrics with common properties are used to test systematically some
56::COMO;;# functionalities and invariance, e.g. SYMMETRIC_METRICS lists all metrics
57::COMO;;# that are symmetric with respect to their input argument y_true and y_pred.
58::COMO;;#

82::COMM;;If Y is None, it is set as a pointer to X (i.e. not a copy).
83::COMM;;If Y is given, this does not happen.
84::COMM;;All distance metrics should use this function first to assert that the
85::COMM;;given parameters are correct and safe to use.

88::COMM;;their elements are floats (or dtype if provided). Finally, the function

106::COMM;;it will be converted to the first listed format. True allows the input
107::COMM;;to be any format. False means that a sparse matrix input will
108::COMM;;raise an error.
109::COMM;;ensure_all_finite : bool or 'allow-nan', default=True
110::COMM;;Whether to raise an error on np.inf, np.nan, pd.NA in array. The
111::COMM;;possibilities are:
112::COMM;;- True: Force all values of array to be finite.
113::COMM;;- False: accepts np.inf, np.nan, pd.NA in array.

177::COMO;;# Only check the number of features if 2d arrays are enforced. Otherwise,

186::COMM;;All paired distance metrics should use this function first to assert that

189::COMM;;then checks that they are at least two dimensional while ensuring that

193::COMM;;----------
194::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
195::COMM;;Y : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features)
196::COMM;;Returns
197::COMM;;-------
198::COMM;;safe_X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
199::COMM;;An array equal to X, guaranteed to be a numpy array.
200::COMM;;safe_Y : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features)
201::COMM;;An array equal to Y if Y was not None, guaranteed to be a numpy array.
202::COMM;;If Y was None, safe_Y will be a pointer to X.
211::COMO;;# Pairwise distances
226::COMM;;Compute the distance matrix between each pair from a feature array X and Y.
227::COMM;;For efficiency reasons, the euclidean distance between a pair of row
228::COMM;;vector x and y is computed as::
229::COMM;;dist(x, y) = sqrt(dot(x, x) - 2 * dot(x, y) + dot(y, y))
230::COMM;;This formulation has two advantages over other ways of computing distances.
231::COMM;;First, it is computationally efficient when dealing with sparse data.
232::COMM;;Second, if one argument varies but the other remains unchanged, then
233::COMM;;`dot(x, x)` and/or `dot(y, y)` can be pre-computed.
234::COMM;;However, this is not the most precise way of doing this computation,
235::COMM;;because this equation potentially suffers from "catastrophic cancellation".
236::COMM;;Also, the distance matrix returned by this function may not be exactly
237::COMM;;symmetric as required by, e.g., :mod:`scipy.spatial.distance` functions.
238::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <metrics>`.
239::COMM;;Parameters
240::COMM;;----------
241::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
242::COMM;;An array where each row is a sample and each column is a feature.
243::COMM;;Y : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features), \
244::COMM;;default=None
245::COMM;;An array where each row is a sample and each column is a feature.
246::COMM;;If `None`, method uses `Y=X`.
247::COMM;;Y_norm_squared : array-like of shape (n_samples_Y,) or (n_samples_Y, 1) \
248::COMM;;or (1, n_samples_Y), default=None
249::COMM;;Pre-computed dot-products of vectors in Y (e.g.,
250::COMM;;``(Y**2).sum(axis=1)``)
251::COMM;;May be ignored in some cases, see the note below.
252::COMM;;squared : bool, default=False
253::COMM;;Return squared Euclidean distances.
254::COMM;;X_norm_squared : array-like of shape (n_samples_X,) or (n_samples_X, 1) \
255::COMM;;or (1, n_samples_X), default=None
256::COMM;;Pre-computed dot-products of vectors in X (e.g.,
257::COMM;;``(X**2).sum(axis=1)``)
258::COMM;;May be ignored in some cases, see the note below.
259::COMM;;Returns
260::COMM;;-------
261::COMM;;distances : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_Y)
262::COMM;;Returns the distances between the row vectors of `X`
263::COMM;;and the row vectors of `Y`.
264::COMM;;See Also
265::COMM;;--------
266::COMM;;paired_distances : Distances between pairs of elements of X and Y.
267::COMM;;Notes
268::COMM;;-----
269::COMM;;To achieve a better accuracy, `X_norm_squared` and `Y_norm_squared` may be
270::COMM;;unused if they are passed as `np.float32`.
271::COMM;;Examples
272::COMM;;--------
273::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import euclidean_distances
274::COMM;;>>> X = [[0, 1], [1, 1]]
275::COMM;;>>> # distance between rows of X
276::COMM;;>>> euclidean_distances(X, X)
277::COMM;;array([[0., 1.],
278::COMM;;[1., 0.]])
279::COMM;;>>> # get distance to origin
280::COMM;;>>> euclidean_distances(X, [[0, 0]])
281::COMM;;array([[1. ],
282::COMM;;[1.41421356]])
313::COMM;;Assumes inputs are already checked.
314::COMM;;If norms are passed as float32, they are unused. If arrays are passed as
315::COMM;;float32, norms needs to be recomputed on upcast chunks.
316::COMM;;TODO: use a float64 accumulator in row_norms to avoid the latter.
335::COMO;;# To minimize precision issues with float32, we compute the distance
336::COMO;;# matrix on chunks of X and Y upcast to float64
339::COMO;;# if dtype is already float64, no need to chunk and upcast
347::COMO;;# Ensure that distances between vectors and themselves are set to 0.0.
348::COMO;;# This may not be the case due to floating point rounding errors.
369::COMM;;Compute the euclidean distance between each pair of samples in X and Y,
370::COMM;;where Y=X is assumed if Y=None. When calculating the distance between a
371::COMM;;pair of samples, this formulation ignores feature coordinates with a
372::COMM;;missing value in either sample and scales up the weight of the remaining
373::COMM;;coordinates:
374::COMM;;.. code-block:: text
375::COMM;;dist(x,y) = sqrt(weight * sq. distance from present coordinates)
376::COMM;;where:
377::COMM;;.. code-block:: text
378::COMM;;weight = Total # of coordinates / # of present coordinates
379::COMM;;For example, the distance between ``[3, na, na, 6]`` and ``[1, na, 4, 5]`` is:
380::COMM;;.. math::
381::COMM;;\\sqrt{\\frac{4}{2}((3-1)^2 + (6-5)^2)}
382::COMM;;If all the coordinates are missing or if there are no common present
383::COMM;;coordinates then NaN is returned for that pair.
384::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <metrics>`.
385::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
386::COMM;;Parameters
387::COMM;;----------
388::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples_X, n_features)
389::COMM;;An array where each row is a sample and each column is a feature.
390::COMM;;Y : array-like of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features), default=None
391::COMM;;An array where each row is a sample and each column is a feature.
392::COMM;;If `None`, method uses `Y=X`.
393::COMM;;squared : bool, default=False
394::COMM;;Return squared Euclidean distances.
395::COMM;;missing_values : np.nan, float or int, default=np.nan
396::COMM;;Representation of missing value.
397::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
398::COMM;;Make and use a deep copy of X and Y (if Y exists).
399::COMM;;Returns
400::COMM;;-------
401::COMM;;distances : ndarray of shape (n_samples_X, n_samples_Y)
402::COMM;;Returns the distances between the row vectors of `X`
403::COMM;;and the row vectors of `Y`.
404::COMM;;See Also
405::COMM;;--------
406::COMM;;paired_distances : Distances between pairs of elements of X and Y.
407::COMM;;References
408::COMM;;----------
409::COMM;;* John K. Dixon, "Pattern Recognition with Partly Missing Data",
410::COMM;;IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Volume: 9, Issue:
411::COMM;;10, pp. 617 - 621, Oct. 1979.
412::COMM;;http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/4310090/
413::COMM;;Examples
414::COMM;;--------
415::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import nan_euclidean_distances
416::COMM;;>>> nan = float("NaN")
417::COMM;;>>> X = [[0, 1], [1, nan]]
418::COMM;;>>> nan_euclidean_distances(X, X) # distance between rows of X
419::COMM;;array([[0. , 1.41421356],
420::COMM;;[1.41421356, 0. ]])
421::COMM;;>>> # get distance to origin
422::COMM;;>>> nan_euclidean_distances(X, [[0, 0]])
423::COMM;;array([[1. ],
424::COMM;;[1.41421356]])
430::COMO;;# Get missing mask for X
432::COMO;;# Get missing mask for Y
434::COMO;;# set missing values to zero
438::COMO;;# Adjust distances for missing values
445::COMO;;# Ensure that distances between vectors and themselves are set to 0.0.
446::COMO;;# This may not be the case due to floating point rounding errors.
452::COMO;;# avoid divide by zero
461::COMM;;Assumes X and Y have float32 dtype.
462::COMM;;Assumes XX and YY have float64 dtype or are None.
463::COMM;;X and Y are upcast to float64 by chunks, which size is chosen to limit
464::COMM;;memory increase by approximately 10% (at least 10MiB).
474::COMO;;# Allow 10% more memory than X, Y and the distance matrix take (at
475::COMO;;# least 10MiB)
484::COMO;;# The increase amount of memory in 8-byte blocks is:
485::COMO;;# - x_density * batch_size * n_features (copy of chunk of X)
486::COMO;;# - y_density * batch_size * n_features (copy of chunk of Y)
487::COMO;;# - batch_size * batch_size (chunk of distance matrix)

584::COMM;;This function computes for each row in X, the index of the row of Y which
585::COMM;;is closest (according to the specified distance). The minimal distances are
586::COMM;;also returned.
587::COMM;;This is mostly equivalent to calling::
588::COMM;;(pairwise_distances(X, Y=Y, metric=metric).argmin(axis=axis),
589::COMM;;pairwise_distances(X, Y=Y, metric=metric).min(axis=axis))
590::COMM;;but uses much less memory, and is faster for large arrays.
591::COMM;;Parameters
592::COMM;;----------

594::COMM;;Array containing points.
595::COMM;;Y : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples_Y, n_features)
596::COMM;;Array containing points.
597::COMM;;axis : int, default=1
598::COMM;;Axis along which the argmin and distances are to be computed.
599::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default='euclidean'
600::COMM;;Metric to use for distance computation. Any metric from scikit-learn
601::COMM;;or :mod:`scipy.spatial.distance` can be used.
602::COMM;;If metric is a callable function, it is called on each
603::COMM;;pair of instances (rows) and the resulting value recorded. The callable
604::COMM;;should take two arrays as input and return one value indicating the
605::COMM;;distance between them. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
606::COMM;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
607::COMM;;Distance matrices are not supported.

612::COMM;;'correlation', 'dice', 'hamming', 'jaccard', 'kulsinski',

614::COMM;;'seuclidean', 'sokalmichener', 'sokalsneath', 'sqeuclidean',
615::COMM;;'yule']
