850::COMM;;routing : MetadataRouter
851::COMM;;A :class:`~sklearn.utils.metadata_routing.MetadataRouter` encapsulating
852::COMM;;routing information.
867::COMM;;Output-code based strategies consist in representing each class with a
868::COMM;;binary code (an array of 0s and 1s). At fitting time, one binary
869::COMM;;classifier per bit in the code book is fitted. At prediction time, the
870::COMM;;classifiers are used to project new points in the class space and the class
871::COMM;;closest to the points is chosen. The main advantage of these strategies is
872::COMM;;that the number of classifiers used can be controlled by the user, either
873::COMM;;for compressing the model (0 < `code_size` < 1) or for making the model more
874::COMM;;robust to errors (`code_size` > 1). See the documentation for more details.
875::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <ecoc>`.
876::COMM;;Parameters
877::COMM;;----------
878::COMM;;estimator : estimator object
879::COMM;;An estimator object implementing :term:`fit` and one of
880::COMM;;:term:`decision_function` or :term:`predict_proba`.
881::COMM;;code_size : float, default=1.5
882::COMM;;Percentage of the number of classes to be used to create the code book.
883::COMM;;A number between 0 and 1 will require fewer classifiers than
884::COMM;;one-vs-the-rest. A number greater than 1 will require more classifiers
885::COMM;;than one-vs-the-rest.
886::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
887::COMM;;The generator used to initialize the codebook.
888::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
889::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
890::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
891::COMM;;The number of jobs to use for the computation: the multiclass problems
892::COMM;;are computed in parallel.
893::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
894::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
895::COMM;;for more details.
896::COMM;;Attributes
897::COMM;;----------
898::COMM;;estimators_ : list of `int(n_classes * code_size)` estimators
899::COMM;;Estimators used for predictions.
900::COMM;;classes_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
901::COMM;;Array containing labels.
902::COMM;;code_book_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes, `len(estimators_)`)
903::COMM;;Binary array containing the code of each class.
904::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
905::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
906::COMM;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
907::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
908::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
909::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Only defined if the
910::COMM;;underlying estimator exposes such an attribute when fit.
911::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0

703::COMM;;-------
704::COMM;;Y_pred : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_classes)
705::COMM;;The predicted values.
714::COMM;;Each model makes a prediction in the order specified by the chain using
715::COMM;;all of the available features provided to the model plus the predictions
716::COMM;;of models that are earlier in the chain.
717::COMM;;For an example of how to use ``ClassifierChain`` and benefit from its
718::COMM;;ensemble, see
719::COMM;;:ref:`ClassifierChain on a yeast dataset
720::COMM;;<sphx_glr_auto_examples_multioutput_plot_classifier_chain_yeast.py>` example.
721::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <classifierchain>`.
722::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
723::COMM;;Parameters
724::COMM;;----------
725::COMM;;estimator : estimator
726::COMM;;The base estimator from which the classifier chain is built.
727::COMM;;order : array-like of shape (n_outputs,) or 'random', default=None
728::COMM;;If `None`, the order will be determined by the order of columns in
729::COMM;;the label matrix Y.::
730::COMM;;order = [0, 1, 2, ..., Y.shape[1] - 1]
731::COMM;;The order of the chain can be explicitly set by providing a list of
732::COMM;;integers. For example, for a chain of length 5.::
733::COMM;;order = [1, 3, 2, 4, 0]
734::COMM;;means that the first model in the chain will make predictions for
735::COMM;;column 1 in the Y matrix, the second model will make predictions
736::COMM;;for column 3, etc.
737::COMM;;If order is `random` a random ordering will be used.
738::COMM;;cv : int, cross-validation generator or an iterable, default=None
739::COMM;;Determines whether to use cross validated predictions or true
740::COMM;;labels for the results of previous estimators in the chain.
741::COMM;;Possible inputs for cv are:
742::COMM;;- None, to use true labels when fitting,
743::COMM;;- integer, to specify the number of folds in a (Stratified)KFold,
744::COMM;;- :term:`CV splitter`,
745::COMM;;- An iterable yielding (train, test) splits as arrays of indices.
746::COMM;;chain_method : {'predict', 'predict_proba', 'predict_log_proba', \
747::COMM;;'decision_function'} or list of such str's, default='predict'
748::COMM;;Prediction method to be used by estimators in the chain for
749::COMM;;the 'prediction' features of previous estimators in the chain.
750::COMM;;- if `str`, name of the method;
751::COMM;;- if a list of `str`, provides the method names in order of
752::COMM;;preference. The method used corresponds to the first method in
753::COMM;;the list that is implemented by `base_estimator`.
754::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.5
755::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, optional (default=None)
756::COMM;;If ``order='random'``, determines random number generation for the
757::COMM;;chain order.
758::COMM;;In addition, it controls the random seed given at each `base_estimator`
759::COMM;;at each chaining iteration. Thus, it is only used when `base_estimator`
760::COMM;;exposes a `random_state`.
761::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls.
762::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
763::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
764::COMM;;If True, chain progress is output as each model is completed.
765::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.2
766::COMM;;base_estimator : estimator, default="deprecated"
767::COMM;;Use `estimator` instead.
768::COMM;;.. deprecated:: 1.7
769::COMM;;`base_estimator` is deprecated and will be removed in 1.9.
770::COMM;;Use `estimator` instead.

1042::COMM;;- array-like: shape (n_features,) where `n_categories[i]` holds the
1043::COMM;;minimum number of categories for the ith column of the input.
1044::COMM;;- None (default): Determines the number of categories automatically
1045::COMM;;from the training data.
1046::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1047::COMM;;Attributes
1048::COMM;;----------
1049::COMM;;category_count_ : list of arrays of shape (n_features,)
1050::COMM;;Holds arrays of shape (n_classes, n_categories of respective feature)
1051::COMM;;for each feature. Each array provides the number of samples
1052::COMM;;encountered for each class and category of the specific feature.
1053::COMM;;class_count_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
1054::COMM;;Number of samples encountered for each class during fitting. This
1055::COMM;;value is weighted by the sample weight when provided.
1056::COMM;;class_log_prior_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
1057::COMM;;Smoothed empirical log probability for each class.
1058::COMM;;classes_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
1059::COMM;;Class labels known to the classifier
1060::COMM;;feature_log_prob_ : list of arrays of shape (n_features,)
1061::COMM;;Holds arrays of shape (n_classes, n_categories of respective feature)
1062::COMM;;for each feature. Each array provides the empirical log probability
1063::COMM;;of categories given the respective feature and class, ``P(x_i|y)``.
1064::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
1065::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
1066::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
1067::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
1068::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
1069::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
1070::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
1071::COMM;;n_categories_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,), dtype=np.int64
1072::COMM;;Number of categories for each feature. This value is
1073::COMM;;inferred from the data or set by the minimum number of categories.
1074::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24

1077::COMM;;BernoulliNB : Naive Bayes classifier for multivariate Bernoulli models.

65::COMM;;def _get_weights(dist, weights):
79::COMM;;if weights in (None, "uniform"):
80::COMM;;return None
81::COMM;;if weights == "distance":
82::COMM;;# if user attempts to classify a point that was zero distance from one
83::COMM;;# or more training points, those training points are weighted as 1.0
84::COMM;;# and the other points as 0.0
85::COMM;;if dist.dtype is np.dtype(object):
86::COMM;;for point_dist_i, point_dist in enumerate(dist):
87::COMM;;# check if point_dist is iterable
88::COMM;;# (ex: RadiusNeighborClassifier.predict may set an element of
89::COMM;;# dist to 1e-6 to represent an 'outlier')
90::COMM;;if hasattr(point_dist, "__contains__") and 0.0 in point_dist:
91::COMM;;dist[point_dist_i] = point_dist == 0.0
92::COMM;;else:
93::COMM;;dist[point_dist_i] = 1.0 / point_dist
94::COMM;;else:
95::COMM;;with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
96::COMM;;dist = 1.0 / dist
97::COMM;;inf_mask = np.isinf(dist)
98::COMM;;inf_row = np.any(inf_mask, axis=1)
99::COMM;;dist[inf_row] = inf_mask[inf_row]
100::COMM;;return dist
101::COMM;;if callable(weights):
102::COMM;;return weights(dist)

459::COMO;;# For minkowski distance, use more efficient methods where available
470::COMO;;# Use the generic minkowski metric, possibly weighted.
493::COMO;;# Precomputed matrix X must be squared
527::COMO;;# A tree approach is better for small number of neighbors or small
528::COMO;;# number of features, with KDTree generally faster when available
548::COMO;;# 'minkowski' with weights is not supported by KDTree but is
549::COMO;;# supported byBallTree.

565::COMO;;# metric as they do not satisfy triangular inequality:
566::COMO;;# they are semi-metrics.
567::COMO;;# algorithm="kd_tree" and algorithm="ball_tree" can't be used because
568::COMO;;# KDTree and BallTree require a proper distance metric to work properly.
569::COMO;;# However, the brute-force algorithm supports semi-metrics.

899::COMM;;class RadiusNeighborsMixin:
903::COMM;;Callback to :func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise.pairwise_distances_chunked`
904::COMM;;Parameters
905::COMM;;----------
906::COMM;;dist : ndarray of shape (n_samples_chunk, n_samples)
907::COMM;;The distance matrix.
908::COMM;;start : int
909::COMM;;The index in X which the first row of dist corresponds to.
910::COMM;;radius : float
911::COMM;;The radius considered when making the nearest neighbors search.
912::COMM;;return_distance : bool
913::COMM;;Whether or not to return the distances.
914::COMM;;Returns
915::COMM;;-------
916::COMM;;dist : list of ndarray of shape (n_samples_chunk,)
917::COMM;;Returned only if `return_distance=True`.
918::COMM;;neigh : list of ndarray of shape (n_samples_chunk,)
919::COMM;;The neighbors indices.
935::COMM;;Return the indices and distances of each point from the dataset
936::COMM;;lying in a ball with size ``radius`` around the points of the query
937::COMM;;array. Points lying on the boundary are included in the results.
938::COMM;;The result points are *not* necessarily sorted by distance to their
939::COMM;;query point.
940::COMM;;Parameters
941::COMM;;----------
942::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of (n_samples, n_features), default=None
943::COMM;;The query point or points.
944::COMM;;If not provided, neighbors of each indexed point are returned.
945::COMM;;In this case, the query point is not considered its own neighbor.
946::COMM;;radius : float, default=None
947::COMM;;Limiting distance of neighbors to return. The default is the value
948::COMM;;passed to the constructor.
949::COMM;;return_distance : bool, default=True
950::COMM;;Whether or not to return the distances.
951::COMM;;sort_results : bool, default=False
952::COMM;;If True, the distances and indices will be sorted by increasing
953::COMM;;distances before being returned. If False, the results may not
954::COMM;;be sorted. If `return_distance=False`, setting `sort_results=True`
955::COMM;;will result in an error.
956::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
957::COMM;;Returns
958::COMM;;-------
959::COMM;;neigh_dist : ndarray of shape (n_samples,) of arrays
960::COMM;;Array representing the distances to each point, only present if
961::COMM;;`return_distance=True`. The distance values are computed according
962::COMM;;to the ``metric`` constructor parameter.
963::COMM;;neigh_ind : ndarray of shape (n_samples,) of arrays
964::COMM;;An array of arrays of indices of the approximate nearest points
965::COMM;;from the population matrix that lie within a ball of size
966::COMM;;``radius`` around the query points.
967::COMM;;Notes
968::COMM;;-----
969::COMM;;Because the number of neighbors of each point is not necessarily
970::COMM;;equal, the results for multiple query points cannot be fit in a
971::COMM;;standard data array.
972::COMM;;For efficiency, `radius_neighbors` returns arrays of objects, where
973::COMM;;each object is a 1D array of indices or distances.
974::COMM;;Examples
975::COMM;;--------
976::COMM;;In the following example, we construct a NeighborsClassifier
977::COMM;;class from an array representing our data set and ask who's
978::COMM;;the closest point to [1, 1, 1]:
979::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
980::COMM;;>>> samples = [[0., 0., 0.], [0., .5, 0.], [1., 1., .5]]
981::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
982::COMM;;>>> neigh = NearestNeighbors(radius=1.6)
983::COMM;;>>> neigh.fit(samples)
984::COMM;;NearestNeighbors(radius=1.6)
985::COMM;;>>> rng = neigh.radius_neighbors([[1., 1., 1.]])
986::COMM;;>>> print(np.asarray(rng[0][0]))
987::COMM;;[1.5 0.5]
988::COMM;;>>> print(np.asarray(rng[1][0]))
989::COMM;;[1 2]
990::COMM;;The first array returned contains the distances to all points which
991::COMM;;are closer than 1.6, while the second array returned contains their
992::COMM;;indices. In general, multiple points can be queried at the same time.

632::COMM;;if not self.outputs_2d_:

655::COMM;;)

675::COMM;;# on many combination of datasets.

679::COMM;;)
680::COMM;;return probabilities
681::COMM;;neigh_dist, neigh_ind = self.radius_neighbors(X)
682::COMM;;outlier_mask = np.zeros(n_queries, dtype=bool)
683::COMM;;outlier_mask[:] = [len(nind) == 0 for nind in neigh_ind]
684::COMM;;outliers = np.flatnonzero(outlier_mask)
685::COMM;;inliers = np.flatnonzero(~outlier_mask)
686::COMM;;classes_ = self.classes_
687::COMM;;_y = self._y
688::COMM;;if not self.outputs_2d_:
689::COMM;;_y = self._y.reshape((-1, 1))
690::COMM;;classes_ = [self.classes_]
691::COMM;;if self.outlier_label_ is None and outliers.size > 0:
692::COMM;;raise ValueError(
693::COMM;;"No neighbors found for test samples %r, "
694::COMM;;"you can try using larger radius, "
695::COMM;;"giving a label for outliers, "
696::COMM;;"or considering removing them from your dataset." % outliers
697::COMM;;)
698::COMM;;weights = _get_weights(neigh_dist, self.weights)
699::COMM;;if weights is not None:
700::COMM;;weights = weights[inliers]
701::COMM;;probabilities = []
702::COMM;;# iterate over multi-output, measure probabilities of the k-th output.
703::COMM;;for k, classes_k in enumerate(classes_):
704::COMM;;pred_labels = np.zeros(len(neigh_ind), dtype=object)
705::COMM;;pred_labels[:] = [_y[ind, k] for ind in neigh_ind]
706::COMM;;proba_k = np.zeros((n_queries, classes_k.size))
707::COMM;;proba_inl = np.zeros((len(inliers), classes_k.size))
708::COMM;;# samples have different size of neighbors within the same radius
709::COMM;;if weights is None:
710::COMM;;for i, idx in enumerate(pred_labels[inliers]):
711::COMM;;proba_inl[i, :] = np.bincount(idx, minlength=classes_k.size)
712::COMM;;else:
713::COMM;;for i, idx in enumerate(pred_labels[inliers]):
714::COMM;;proba_inl[i, :] = np.bincount(
715::COMM;;idx, weights[i], minlength=classes_k.size
716::COMM;;)
717::COMM;;proba_k[inliers, :] = proba_inl
718::COMM;;if outliers.size > 0:
719::COMM;;_outlier_label = self.outlier_label_[k]
720::COMM;;label_index = np.flatnonzero(classes_k == _outlier_label)
721::COMM;;if label_index.size == 1:
722::COMM;;proba_k[outliers, label_index[0]] = 1.0
723::COMM;;else:

725::COMM;;"Outlier label {} is not in training "
726::COMM;;"classes. All class probabilities of "
727::COMM;;"outliers will be assigned with 0."
728::COMM;;"".format(self.outlier_label_[k])
729::COMM;;)
730::COMM;;# normalize 'votes' into real [0,1] probabilities
731::COMM;;normalizer = proba_k.sum(axis=1)[:, np.newaxis]
732::COMM;;normalizer[normalizer == 0.0] = 1.0
733::COMM;;proba_k /= normalizer
734::COMM;;probabilities.append(proba_k)
735::COMM;;if not self.outputs_2d_:
736::COMM;;probabilities = probabilities[0]
737::COMM;;return probabilities

2::COMM;;Kernel Density Estimation
3::COMM;;-------------------------
5::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
6::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMO;;# TODO: implement a brute force version for testing purposes
33::COMO;;# TODO: create a density estimation base class?
36::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <kernel_density>`.
37::COMM;;Parameters
38::COMM;;----------
39::COMM;;bandwidth : float or {"scott", "silverman"}, default=1.0
40::COMM;;The bandwidth of the kernel. If bandwidth is a float, it defines the
41::COMM;;bandwidth of the kernel. If bandwidth is a string, one of the estimation
42::COMM;;methods is implemented.
43::COMM;;algorithm : {'kd_tree', 'ball_tree', 'auto'}, default='auto'
44::COMM;;The tree algorithm to use.
45::COMM;;kernel : {'gaussian', 'tophat', 'epanechnikov', 'exponential', 'linear', \
46::COMM;;'cosine'}, default='gaussian'
47::COMM;;The kernel to use.
48::COMM;;metric : str, default='euclidean'
49::COMM;;Metric to use for distance computation. See the
50::COMM;;documentation of `scipy.spatial.distance
51::COMM;;<https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/spatial.distance.html>`_ and
52::COMM;;the metrics listed in
53::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics` for valid metric
54::COMM;;values.
55::COMM;;Not all metrics are valid with all algorithms: refer to the
56::COMM;;documentation of :class:`BallTree` and :class:`KDTree`. Note that the
57::COMM;;normalization of the density output is correct only for the Euclidean
58::COMM;;distance metric.
59::COMM;;atol : float, default=0
60::COMM;;The desired absolute tolerance of the result. A larger tolerance will
61::COMM;;generally lead to faster execution.
62::COMM;;rtol : float, default=0
63::COMM;;The desired relative tolerance of the result. A larger tolerance will
64::COMM;;generally lead to faster execution.
65::COMM;;breadth_first : bool, default=True
66::COMM;;If true (default), use a breadth-first approach to the problem.
67::COMM;;Otherwise use a depth-first approach.
68::COMM;;leaf_size : int, default=40
69::COMM;;Specify the leaf size of the underlying tree. See :class:`BallTree`
70::COMM;;or :class:`KDTree` for details.
71::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
72::COMM;;Additional parameters to be passed to the tree for use with the
73::COMM;;metric. For more information, see the documentation of
74::COMM;;:class:`BallTree` or :class:`KDTree`.
75::COMM;;Attributes
76::COMM;;----------
77::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
78::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
79::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
80::COMM;;tree_ : ``BinaryTree`` instance
81::COMM;;The tree algorithm for fast generalized N-point problems.
82::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
83::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
84::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
85::COMM;;bandwidth_ : float
86::COMM;;Value of the bandwidth, given directly by the bandwidth parameter or
87::COMM;;estimated using the 'scott' or 'silverman' method.
88::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
89::COMM;;See Also
90::COMM;;--------
91::COMM;;sklearn.neighbors.KDTree : K-dimensional tree for fast generalized N-point
92::COMM;;problems.
93::COMM;;sklearn.neighbors.BallTree : Ball tree for fast generalized N-point
94::COMM;;problems.
95::COMM;;Examples
96::COMM;;--------
97::COMM;;Compute a gaussian kernel density estimate with a fixed bandwidth.
98::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import KernelDensity
99::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
100::COMM;;>>> rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
101::COMM;;>>> X = rng.random_sample((100, 3))
102::COMM;;>>> kde = KernelDensity(kernel='gaussian', bandwidth=0.5).fit(X)
103::COMM;;>>> log_density = kde.score_samples(X[:3])
104::COMM;;>>> log_density
105::COMM;;array([-1.52955942, -1.51462041, -1.60244657])
148::COMO;;# given the algorithm string + metric string, choose the optimal
149::COMO;;# algorithm to compute the result.
151::COMO;;# use KD Tree if possible
156::COMC;;else: # kd_tree or ball_tree
163::COMO;;# KernelDensity.metric is not validated yet
168::COMM;;Parameters
169::COMM;;----------
170::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
171::COMM;;List of n_features-dimensional data points. Each row
172::COMM;;corresponds to a single data point.
173::COMM;;y : None
174::COMM;;Ignored. This parameter exists only for compatibility with
175::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`.
176::COMM;;sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
177::COMM;;List of sample weights attached to the data X.
178::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
179::COMM;;Returns
180::COMM;;-------
181::COMM;;self : object
182::COMM;;Returns the instance itself.
212::COMM;;Parameters
213::COMM;;----------
214::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
215::COMM;;An array of points to query. Last dimension should match dimension
216::COMM;;of training data (n_features).
217::COMM;;Returns
218::COMM;;-------
219::COMM;;density : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
220::COMM;;Log-likelihood of each sample in `X`. These are normalized to be
221::COMM;;probability densities, so values will be low for high-dimensional
222::COMM;;data.
225::COMO;;# The returned density is normalized to the number of points.
226::COMO;;# For it to be a probability, we must scale it. For this reason
227::COMO;;# we'll also scale atol.
247::COMM;;Parameters
248::COMM;;----------
249::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
250::COMM;;List of n_features-dimensional data points. Each row
251::COMM;;corresponds to a single data point.
252::COMM;;y : None
253::COMM;;Ignored. This parameter exists only for compatibility with
254::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`.
255::COMM;;Returns
256::COMM;;-------
257::COMM;;logprob : float
258::COMM;;Total log-likelihood of the data in X. This is normalized to be a
259::COMM;;probability density, so the value will be low for high-dimensional
260::COMM;;data.
265::COMM;;Currently, this is implemented only for gaussian and tophat kernels.
266::COMM;;Parameters
267::COMM;;----------
268::COMM;;n_samples : int, default=1
269::COMM;;Number of samples to generate.
270::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance or None, default=None
271::COMM;;Determines random number generation used to generate
272::COMM;;random samples. Pass an int for reproducible results
273::COMM;;across multiple function calls.
274::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
275::COMM;;Returns
276::COMM;;-------
277::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
278::COMM;;List of samples.
281::COMO;;# TODO: implement sampling for other valid kernel shapes
296::COMO;;# we first draw points from a d-dimensional normal distribution,
297::COMO;;# then use an incomplete gamma function to map them to a uniform
298::COMO;;# d-dimensional tophat distribution.

15::COMM;;The anomaly score of each sample is called the Local Outlier Factor.
16::COMM;;It measures the local deviation of the density of a given sample with respect
17::COMM;;to its neighbors.
18::COMM;;It is local in that the anomaly score depends on how isolated the object
19::COMM;;is with respect to the surrounding neighborhood.
20::COMM;;More precisely, locality is given by k-nearest neighbors, whose distance
21::COMM;;is used to estimate the local density.
22::COMM;;By comparing the local density of a sample to the local densities of its
23::COMM;;neighbors, one can identify samples that have a substantially lower density
24::COMM;;than their neighbors. These are considered outliers.
25::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.19
26::COMM;;Parameters
27::COMM;;----------
28::COMM;;n_neighbors : int, default=20
29::COMM;;Number of neighbors to use by default for :meth:`kneighbors` queries.
30::COMM;;If n_neighbors is larger than the number of samples provided,
31::COMM;;all samples will be used.
32::COMM;;algorithm : {'auto', 'ball_tree', 'kd_tree', 'brute'}, default='auto'
33::COMM;;Algorithm used to compute the nearest neighbors:
34::COMM;;- 'ball_tree' will use :class:`BallTree`
35::COMM;;- 'kd_tree' will use :class:`KDTree`
36::COMM;;- 'brute' will use a brute-force search.
37::COMM;;- 'auto' will attempt to decide the most appropriate algorithm
38::COMM;;based on the values passed to :meth:`fit` method.
39::COMM;;Note: fitting on sparse input will override the setting of
40::COMM;;this parameter, using brute force.
41::COMM;;leaf_size : int, default=30
42::COMM;;Leaf is size passed to :class:`BallTree` or :class:`KDTree`. This can
43::COMM;;affect the speed of the construction and query, as well as the memory
44::COMM;;required to store the tree. The optimal value depends on the
45::COMM;;nature of the problem.
46::COMM;;metric : str or callable, default='minkowski'
47::COMM;;Metric to use for distance computation. Default is "minkowski", which
48::COMM;;results in the standard Euclidean distance when p = 2. See the
49::COMM;;documentation of `scipy.spatial.distance
50::COMM;;<https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/spatial.distance.html>`_ and
51::COMM;;the metrics listed in
52::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.metrics.pairwise.distance_metrics` for valid metric
53::COMM;;values.
54::COMM;;If metric is "precomputed", X is assumed to be a distance matrix and
55::COMM;;must be square during fit. X may be a :term:`sparse graph`, in which
56::COMM;;case only "nonzero" elements may be considered neighbors.
57::COMM;;If metric is a callable function, it takes two arrays representing 1D
58::COMM;;vectors as inputs and must return one value indicating the distance
59::COMM;;between those vectors. This works for Scipy's metrics, but is less
60::COMM;;efficient than passing the metric name as a string.
61::COMM;;p : float, default=2
62::COMM;;Parameter for the Minkowski metric from
63::COMM;;:func:`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances`. When p = 1, this
64::COMM;;is equivalent to using manhattan_distance (l1), and euclidean_distance
65::COMM;;(l2) for p = 2. For arbitrary p, minkowski_distance (l_p) is used.
66::COMM;;metric_params : dict, default=None
67::COMM;;Additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
68::COMM;;contamination : 'auto' or float, default='auto'
69::COMM;;The amount of contamination of the data set, i.e. the proportion
70::COMM;;of outliers in the data set. When fitting this is used to define the
71::COMM;;threshold on the scores of the samples.
72::COMM;;- if 'auto', the threshold is determined as in the
73::COMM;;original paper,
74::COMM;;- if a float, the contamination should be in the range (0, 0.5].
75::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.22
76::COMM;;The default value of ``contamination`` changed from 0.1
77::COMM;;to ``'auto'``.
78::COMM;;novelty : bool, default=False
79::COMM;;By default, LocalOutlierFactor is only meant to be used for outlier
80::COMM;;detection (novelty=False). Set novelty to True if you want to use
81::COMM;;LocalOutlierFactor for novelty detection. In this case be aware that
82::COMM;;you should only use predict, decision_function and score_samples
83::COMM;;on new unseen data and not on the training set; and note that the
84::COMM;;results obtained this way may differ from the standard LOF results.
85::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
86::COMM;;n_jobs : int, default=None
87::COMM;;The number of parallel jobs to run for neighbors search.
88::COMM;;``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
89::COMM;;``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`
90::COMM;;for more details.
91::COMM;;Attributes
92::COMM;;----------
93::COMM;;negative_outlier_factor_ : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
94::COMM;;The opposite LOF of the training samples. The higher, the more normal.
95::COMM;;Inliers tend to have a LOF score close to 1
96::COMM;;(``negative_outlier_factor_`` close to -1), while outliers tend to have
97::COMM;;a larger LOF score.
98::COMM;;The local outlier factor (LOF) of a sample captures its
99::COMM;;supposed 'degree of abnormality'.
100::COMM;;It is the average of the ratio of the local reachability density of
101::COMM;;a sample and those of its k-nearest neighbors.
102::COMM;;n_neighbors_ : int
103::COMM;;The actual number of neighbors used for :meth:`kneighbors` queries.
104::COMM;;offset_ : float
105::COMM;;Offset used to obtain binary labels from the raw scores.
106::COMM;;Observations having a negative_outlier_factor smaller than `offset_`
107::COMM;;are detected as abnormal.
108::COMM;;The offset is set to -1.5 (inliers score around -1), except when a
109::COMM;;contamination parameter different than "auto" is provided. In that
110::COMM;;case, the offset is defined in such a way we obtain the expected
111::COMM;;number of outliers in training.
112::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
113::COMM;;effective_metric_ : str
114::COMM;;The effective metric used for the distance computation.
115::COMM;;effective_metric_params_ : dict
116::COMM;;The effective additional keyword arguments for the metric function.
117::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
118::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
119::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
120::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
121::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
122::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
123::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
124::COMM;;n_samples_fit_ : int
125::COMM;;It is the number of samples in the fitted data.
126::COMM;;See Also
127::COMM;;--------
128::COMM;;sklearn.svm.OneClassSVM: Unsupervised Outlier Detection using
129::COMM;;Support Vector Machine.
130::COMM;;References
131::COMM;;----------
132::COMM;;.. [1] Breunig, M. M., Kriegel, H. P., Ng, R. T., & Sander, J. (2000, May).
133::COMM;;`LOF: identifying density-based local outliers.
134::COMM;;<https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/342009.335388>`_
135::COMM;;In Proceedings of the 2000 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on
136::COMM;;Management of Data, pp. 93-104.
137::COMM;;Examples
138::COMM;;--------
139::COMM;;>>> import numpy as np
140::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
141::COMM;;>>> X = [[-1.1], [0.2], [101.1], [0.3]]
142::COMM;;>>> clf = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=2)
143::COMM;;>>> clf.fit_predict(X)
144::COMM;;array([ 1, 1, -1, 1])
145::COMM;;>>> clf.negative_outlier_factor_
146::COMM;;array([ -0.9821, -1.0370, -73.3697, -0.9821])

193::COMM;;Label is 1 for an inlier and -1 for an outlier according to the LOF
194::COMM;;score and the contamination parameter.

200::COMM;;y : Ignored

2::COMM;;Neighborhood Component Analysis
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
32::COMM;;Neighborhood Component Analysis (NCA) is a machine learning algorithm for
33::COMM;;metric learning. It learns a linear transformation in a supervised fashion
34::COMM;;to improve the classification accuracy of a stochastic nearest neighbors
35::COMM;;rule in the transformed space.
36::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <nca>`.
37::COMM;;Parameters
38::COMM;;----------
39::COMM;;n_components : int, default=None
40::COMM;;Preferred dimensionality of the projected space.
41::COMM;;If None it will be set to `n_features`.
42::COMM;;init : {'auto', 'pca', 'lda', 'identity', 'random'} or ndarray of shape \
43::COMM;;(n_features_a, n_features_b), default='auto'
44::COMM;;Initialization of the linear transformation. Possible options are
45::COMM;;`'auto'`, `'pca'`, `'lda'`, `'identity'`, `'random'`, and a numpy
46::COMM;;array of shape `(n_features_a, n_features_b)`.
47::COMM;;- `'auto'`
48::COMM;;Depending on `n_components`, the most reasonable initialization
49::COMM;;is chosen. If `n_components <= min(n_features, n_classes - 1)`
50::COMM;;we use `'lda'`, as it uses labels information. If not, but
51::COMM;;`n_components < min(n_features, n_samples)`, we use `'pca'`, as
52::COMM;;it projects data in meaningful directions (those of higher
53::COMM;;variance). Otherwise, we just use `'identity'`.
54::COMM;;- `'pca'`
55::COMM;;`n_components` principal components of the inputs passed
56::COMM;;to :meth:`fit` will be used to initialize the transformation.
57::COMM;;(See :class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA`)
58::COMM;;- `'lda'`
59::COMM;;`min(n_components, n_classes)` most discriminative
60::COMM;;components of the inputs passed to :meth:`fit` will be used to
61::COMM;;initialize the transformation. (If `n_components > n_classes`,
62::COMM;;the rest of the components will be zero.) (See
63::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.discriminant_analysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis`)
64::COMM;;- `'identity'`
65::COMM;;If `n_components` is strictly smaller than the
66::COMM;;dimensionality of the inputs passed to :meth:`fit`, the identity
67::COMM;;matrix will be truncated to the first `n_components` rows.
68::COMM;;- `'random'`
69::COMM;;The initial transformation will be a random array of shape
70::COMM;;`(n_components, n_features)`. Each value is sampled from the
71::COMM;;standard normal distribution.
72::COMM;;- numpy array
73::COMM;;`n_features_b` must match the dimensionality of the inputs passed
74::COMM;;to :meth:`fit` and n_features_a must be less than or equal to that.
75::COMM;;If `n_components` is not `None`, `n_features_a` must match it.
76::COMM;;warm_start : bool, default=False
77::COMM;;If `True` and :meth:`fit` has been called before, the solution of the
78::COMM;;previous call to :meth:`fit` is used as the initial linear
79::COMM;;transformation (`n_components` and `init` will be ignored).
80::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=50
81::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations in the optimization.
82::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-5
83::COMM;;Convergence tolerance for the optimization.
84::COMM;;callback : callable, default=None
85::COMM;;If not `None`, this function is called after every iteration of the
86::COMM;;optimizer, taking as arguments the current solution (flattened
87::COMM;;transformation matrix) and the number of iterations. This might be
88::COMM;;useful in case one wants to examine or store the transformation
89::COMM;;found after each iteration.
90::COMM;;verbose : int, default=0
91::COMM;;If 0, no progress messages will be printed.
92::COMM;;If 1, progress messages will be printed to stdout.
93::COMM;;If > 1, progress messages will be printed and the `disp`
94::COMM;;parameter of :func:`scipy.optimize.minimize` will be set to
95::COMM;;`verbose - 2`.
96::COMM;;random_state : int or numpy.RandomState, default=None
97::COMM;;A pseudo random number generator object or a seed for it if int. If
98::COMM;;`init='random'`, `random_state` is used to initialize the random
99::COMM;;transformation. If `init='pca'`, `random_state` is passed as an
100::COMM;;argument to PCA when initializing the transformation. Pass an int
101::COMM;;for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
102::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
103::COMM;;Attributes
104::COMM;;----------
105::COMM;;components_ : ndarray of shape (n_components, n_features)
106::COMM;;The linear transformation learned during fitting.
107::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
108::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
109::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
110::COMM;;n_iter_ : int
111::COMM;;Counts the number of iterations performed by the optimizer.
112::COMM;;random_state_ : numpy.RandomState
113::COMM;;Pseudo random number generator object used during initialization.
114::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
115::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
116::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
117::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
118::COMM;;See Also
119::COMM;;--------
120::COMM;;sklearn.discriminant_analysis.LinearDiscriminantAnalysis : Linear
121::COMM;;Discriminant Analysis.
122::COMM;;sklearn.decomposition.PCA : Principal component analysis (PCA).
123::COMM;;References
124::COMM;;----------
125::COMM;;.. [1] J. Goldberger, G. Hinton, S. Roweis, R. Salakhutdinov.
126::COMM;;"Neighbourhood Components Analysis". Advances in Neural Information
127::COMM;;Processing Systems. 17, 513-520, 2005.
128::COMM;;https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~rsalakhu/papers/ncanips.pdf
129::COMM;;.. [2] Wikipedia entry on Neighborhood Components Analysis
130::COMM;;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighbourhood_components_analysis
131::COMM;;Examples
132::COMM;;--------
133::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis
134::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
135::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
136::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
137::COMM;;>>> X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
138::COMM;;>>> X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y,
139::COMM;;... stratify=y, test_size=0.7, random_state=42)
140::COMM;;>>> nca = NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis(random_state=42)
141::COMM;;>>> nca.fit(X_train, y_train)
142::COMM;;NeighborhoodComponentsAnalysis(...)
143::COMM;;>>> knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)
144::COMM;;>>> knn.fit(X_train, y_train)
145::COMM;;KNeighborsClassifier(...)
146::COMM;;>>> print(knn.score(X_test, y_test))
147::COMM;;0.933333...
148::COMM;;>>> knn.fit(nca.transform(X_train), y_train)
149::COMM;;KNeighborsClassifier(...)
150::COMM;;>>> print(knn.score(nca.transform(X_test), y_test))
151::COMM;;0.961904...

2::COMM;;Nearest Centroid Classification
4::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
5::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
24::COMM;;Each class is represented by its centroid, with test samples classified to
25::COMM;;the class with the nearest centroid.
26::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <nearest_centroid_classifier>`.
27::COMM;;Parameters
28::COMM;;----------
29::COMM;;metric : {"euclidean", "manhattan"}, default="euclidean"
30::COMM;;Metric to use for distance computation.
31::COMM;;If `metric="euclidean"`, the centroid for the samples corresponding to each
32::COMM;;class is the arithmetic mean, which minimizes the sum of squared L1 distances.
33::COMM;;If `metric="manhattan"`, the centroid is the feature-wise median, which
34::COMM;;minimizes the sum of L1 distances.
35::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 1.5
36::COMM;;All metrics but `"euclidean"` and `"manhattan"` were deprecated and
37::COMM;;now raise an error.
38::COMM;;.. versionchanged:: 0.19
39::COMM;;`metric='precomputed'` was deprecated and now raises an error
40::COMM;;shrink_threshold : float, default=None
41::COMM;;Threshold for shrinking centroids to remove features.
42::COMM;;priors : {"uniform", "empirical"} or array-like of shape (n_classes,), \
43::COMM;;default="uniform"
44::COMM;;The class prior probabilities. By default, the class proportions are
45::COMM;;inferred from the training data.
46::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
47::COMM;;Attributes
48::COMM;;----------
49::COMM;;centroids_ : array-like of shape (n_classes, n_features)
50::COMM;;Centroid of each class.
51::COMM;;classes_ : array of shape (n_classes,)
52::COMM;;The unique classes labels.
53::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
54::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
55::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
56::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
57::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
58::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
59::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
60::COMM;;deviations_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes, n_features)
61::COMM;;Deviations (or shrinkages) of the centroids of each class from the
62::COMM;;overall centroid. Equal to eq. (18.4) if `shrink_threshold=None`,
63::COMM;;else (18.5) p. 653 of [2]. Can be used to identify features used
64::COMM;;for classification.
65::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
66::COMM;;within_class_std_dev_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
67::COMM;;Pooled or within-class standard deviation of input data.
68::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
69::COMM;;class_prior_ : ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
70::COMM;;The class prior probabilities.
71::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.6
72::COMM;;See Also
73::COMM;;--------
74::COMM;;KNeighborsClassifier : Nearest neighbors classifier.
75::COMM;;Notes
76::COMM;;-----
77::COMM;;When used for text classification with tf-idf vectors, this classifier is
78::COMM;;also known as the Rocchio classifier.
79::COMM;;References
80::COMM;;----------
81::COMM;;[1] Tibshirani, R., Hastie, T., Narasimhan, B., & Chu, G. (2002). Diagnosis of

83::COMM;;of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America,
84::COMM;;99(10), 6567-6572. The National Academy of Sciences.
85::COMM;;[2] Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., Friedman, J. (2009). The Elements of Statistical
86::COMM;;Learning Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction. 2nd Edition. New York, Springer.

197::COMM;;if self.weights == "uniform":
198::COMM;;# In that case, we do not need the distances to perform
199::COMM;;# the weighting so we do not compute them.
200::COMM;;neigh_ind = self.kneighbors(X, return_distance=False)

210::COMM;;else:
211::COMM;;y_pred = np.empty((neigh_dist.shape[0], _y.shape[1]), dtype=np.float64)
212::COMM;;denom = np.sum(weights, axis=1)
213::COMM;;for j in range(_y.shape[1]):
214::COMM;;num = np.sum(_y[neigh_ind, j] * weights, axis=1)
215::COMM;;y_pred[:, j] = num / denom
216::COMM;;if self._y.ndim == 1:
217::COMM;;y_pred = y_pred.ravel()

258::COMM;;def _backprop(
259::COMM;;self, X, y, sample_weight, activations, deltas, coef_grads, intercept_grads
260::COMM;;):
291::COMM;;n_samples = X.shape[0]
292::COMM;;# Forward propagate
293::COMM;;activations = self._forward_pass(activations)
294::COMM;;# Get loss
295::COMM;;loss_func_name = self.loss
296::COMM;;if loss_func_name == "log_loss" and self.out_activation_ == "logistic":
297::COMM;;loss_func_name = "binary_log_loss"
298::COMM;;loss = LOSS_FUNCTIONS[loss_func_name](y, activations[-1], sample_weight)
299::COMM;;# Add L2 regularization term to loss
300::COMM;;values = 0
301::COMM;;for s in self.coefs_:
302::COMM;;s = s.ravel()
303::COMM;;values += np.dot(s, s)
304::COMM;;if sample_weight is None:
305::COMM;;sw_sum = n_samples
306::COMM;;else:
307::COMM;;sw_sum = sample_weight.sum()
308::COMM;;loss += (0.5 * self.alpha) * values / sw_sum
309::COMM;;# Backward propagate
310::COMM;;last = self.n_layers_ - 2
311::COMM;;# The calculation of delta[last] is as follows:
312::COMM;;# delta[last] = d/dz loss(y, act(z)) = act(z) - y
313::COMM;;# with z=x@w + b being the output of the last layer before passing through the
314::COMM;;# output activation, act(z) = activations[-1].
315::COMM;;# The simple formula for delta[last] here works with following (canonical
316::COMM;;# loss-link) combinations of output activation and loss function:
317::COMM;;# sigmoid and binary cross entropy, softmax and categorical cross
318::COMM;;# entropy, and identity with squared loss
319::COMM;;deltas[last] = activations[-1] - y
320::COMM;;if sample_weight is not None:
321::COMM;;deltas[last] *= sample_weight.reshape(-1, 1)
322::COMM;;# Compute gradient for the last layer
323::COMM;;self._compute_loss_grad(
324::COMM;;last, sw_sum, activations, deltas, coef_grads, intercept_grads
325::COMM;;)
326::COMM;;inplace_derivative = DERIVATIVES[self.activation]
327::COMM;;# Iterate over the hidden layers
328::COMM;;for i in range(last, 0, -1):
329::COMM;;deltas[i - 1] = safe_sparse_dot(deltas[i], self.coefs_[i].T)
330::COMM;;inplace_derivative(activations[i], deltas[i - 1])
331::COMM;;self._compute_loss_grad(
332::COMM;;i - 1, sw_sum, activations, deltas, coef_grads, intercept_grads
333::COMM;;)
334::COMM;;return loss, coef_grads, intercept_grads
335::COMM;;def _initialize(self, y, layer_units, dtype):

378::COMM;;def _init_coef(self, fan_in, fan_out, dtype):
379::COMM;;# Use the initialization method recommended by
380::COMM;;# Glorot et al.
381::COMM;;factor = 6.0
382::COMM;;if self.activation == "logistic":
383::COMM;;factor = 2.0
384::COMM;;init_bound = np.sqrt(factor / (fan_in + fan_out))
385::COMM;;# Generate weights and bias:

387::COMM;;-init_bound, init_bound, (fan_in, fan_out)
388::COMM;;)

390::COMM;;coef_init = coef_init.astype(dtype, copy=False)
391::COMM;;intercept_init = intercept_init.astype(dtype, copy=False)
392::COMM;;return coef_init, intercept_init

463::COMM;;def _fit_lbfgs(
464::COMM;;self,
465::COMM;;X,
466::COMM;;y,
467::COMM;;sample_weight,
468::COMM;;activations,
469::COMM;;deltas,
470::COMM;;coef_grads,
471::COMM;;intercept_grads,
472::COMM;;layer_units,

479::COMM;;for i in range(self.n_layers_ - 1):

481::COMM;;end = start + (n_fan_in * n_fan_out)

494::COMM;;iprint = -1

496::COMM;;self._loss_grad_lbfgs,

498::COMM;;method="L-BFGS-B",

505::COMM;;},

508::COMM;;y,
509::COMM;;sample_weight,

512::COMM;;coef_grads,
513::COMM;;intercept_grads,

518::COMM;;self._unpack(opt_res.x)

648::COMM;;# update no_improvement_count based on training loss or

671::COMM;;if is_stopping:

673::COMM;;else:

675::COMM;;if incremental:

690::COMM;;def _update_no_improvement_count(self, early_stopping, X, y, sample_weight):

694::COMM;;self.validation_scores_.append(val_score)

702::COMM;;self._no_improvement_count += 1

711::COMM;;self._no_improvement_count += 1

742::COMM;;def _score_with_function(self, X, y, sample_weight, score_function):
744::COMO;;# Input validation would remove feature names, so we disable it
755::COMM;;This model optimizes the log-loss function using LBFGS or stochastic
756::COMM;;gradient descent.
757::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.18
758::COMM;;Parameters
759::COMM;;----------
760::COMM;;hidden_layer_sizes : array-like of shape(n_layers - 2,), default=(100,)
761::COMM;;The ith element represents the number of neurons in the ith
762::COMM;;hidden layer.
763::COMM;;activation : {'identity', 'logistic', 'tanh', 'relu'}, default='relu'
764::COMM;;Activation function for the hidden layer.
765::COMM;;- 'identity', no-op activation, useful to implement linear bottleneck,
766::COMM;;returns f(x) = x
767::COMM;;- 'logistic', the logistic sigmoid function,
768::COMM;;returns f(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x)).
769::COMM;;- 'tanh', the hyperbolic tan function,
770::COMM;;returns f(x) = tanh(x).
771::COMM;;- 'relu', the rectified linear unit function,
772::COMM;;returns f(x) = max(0, x)
773::COMM;;solver : {'lbfgs', 'sgd', 'adam'}, default='adam'
774::COMM;;The solver for weight optimization.
775::COMM;;- 'lbfgs' is an optimizer in the family of quasi-Newton methods.
776::COMM;;- 'sgd' refers to stochastic gradient descent.
777::COMM;;- 'adam' refers to a stochastic gradient-based optimizer proposed
778::COMM;;by Kingma, Diederik, and Jimmy Ba
779::COMM;;For a comparison between Adam optimizer and SGD, see
780::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neural_networks_plot_mlp_training_curves.py`.
781::COMM;;Note: The default solver 'adam' works pretty well on relatively
782::COMM;;large datasets (with thousands of training samples or more) in terms of
783::COMM;;both training time and validation score.
784::COMM;;For small datasets, however, 'lbfgs' can converge faster and perform
785::COMM;;better.
786::COMM;;alpha : float, default=0.0001
787::COMM;;Strength of the L2 regularization term. The L2 regularization term
788::COMM;;is divided by the sample size when added to the loss.
789::COMM;;For an example usage and visualization of varying regularization, see
790::COMM;;:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_neural_networks_plot_mlp_alpha.py`.
791::COMM;;batch_size : int, default='auto'
792::COMM;;Size of minibatches for stochastic optimizers.
793::COMM;;If the solver is 'lbfgs', the classifier will not use minibatch.
794::COMM;;When set to "auto", `batch_size=min(200, n_samples)`.
795::COMM;;learning_rate : {'constant', 'invscaling', 'adaptive'}, default='constant'
796::COMM;;Learning rate schedule for weight updates.
797::COMM;;- 'constant' is a constant learning rate given by
798::COMM;;'learning_rate_init'.
799::COMM;;- 'invscaling' gradually decreases the learning rate at each
800::COMM;;time step 't' using an inverse scaling exponent of 'power_t'.
801::COMM;;effective_learning_rate = learning_rate_init / pow(t, power_t)
802::COMM;;- 'adaptive' keeps the learning rate constant to
803::COMM;;'learning_rate_init' as long as training loss keeps decreasing.
804::COMM;;Each time two consecutive epochs fail to decrease training loss by at
805::COMM;;least tol, or fail to increase validation score by at least tol if
806::COMM;;'early_stopping' is on, the current learning rate is divided by 5.
807::COMM;;Only used when ``solver='sgd'``.
808::COMM;;learning_rate_init : float, default=0.001
809::COMM;;The initial learning rate used. It controls the step-size
810::COMM;;in updating the weights. Only used when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
811::COMM;;power_t : float, default=0.5
812::COMM;;The exponent for inverse scaling learning rate.
813::COMM;;It is used in updating effective learning rate when the learning_rate
814::COMM;;is set to 'invscaling'. Only used when solver='sgd'.
815::COMM;;max_iter : int, default=200
816::COMM;;Maximum number of iterations. The solver iterates until convergence
817::COMM;;(determined by 'tol') or this number of iterations. For stochastic
818::COMM;;solvers ('sgd', 'adam'), note that this determines the number of epochs
819::COMM;;(how many times each data point will be used), not the number of
820::COMM;;gradient steps.
821::COMM;;shuffle : bool, default=True
822::COMM;;Whether to shuffle samples in each iteration. Only used when
823::COMM;;solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
824::COMM;;random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None
825::COMM;;Determines random number generation for weights and bias
826::COMM;;initialization, train-test split if early stopping is used, and batch
827::COMM;;sampling when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
828::COMM;;Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
829::COMM;;See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.
830::COMM;;tol : float, default=1e-4
831::COMM;;Tolerance for the optimization. When the loss or score is not improving
832::COMM;;by at least ``tol`` for ``n_iter_no_change`` consecutive iterations,
833::COMM;;unless ``learning_rate`` is set to 'adaptive', convergence is
834::COMM;;considered to be reached and training stops.
835::COMM;;verbose : bool, default=False
836::COMM;;Whether to print progress messages to stdout.
837::COMM;;warm_start : bool, default=False
838::COMM;;When set to True, reuse the solution of the previous
839::COMM;;call to fit as initialization, otherwise, just erase the
840::COMM;;previous solution. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.
841::COMM;;momentum : float, default=0.9
842::COMM;;Momentum for gradient descent update. Should be between 0 and 1. Only
843::COMM;;used when solver='sgd'.
844::COMM;;nesterovs_momentum : bool, default=True
845::COMM;;Whether to use Nesterov's momentum. Only used when solver='sgd' and
846::COMM;;momentum > 0.
847::COMM;;early_stopping : bool, default=False
848::COMM;;Whether to use early stopping to terminate training when validation
849::COMM;;score is not improving. If set to True, it will automatically set
850::COMM;;aside ``validation_fraction`` of training data as validation and
851::COMM;;terminate training when validation score is not improving by at least
852::COMM;;``tol`` for ``n_iter_no_change`` consecutive epochs. The split is
853::COMM;;stratified, except in a multilabel setting.
854::COMM;;If early stopping is False, then the training stops when the training
855::COMM;;loss does not improve by more than ``tol`` for ``n_iter_no_change``
856::COMM;;consecutive passes over the training set.
857::COMM;;Only effective when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
858::COMM;;validation_fraction : float, default=0.1
859::COMM;;The proportion of training data to set aside as validation set for
860::COMM;;early stopping. Must be between 0 and 1.
861::COMM;;Only used if early_stopping is True.
862::COMM;;beta_1 : float, default=0.9
863::COMM;;Exponential decay rate for estimates of first moment vector in adam,
864::COMM;;should be in [0, 1). Only used when solver='adam'.
865::COMM;;beta_2 : float, default=0.999
866::COMM;;Exponential decay rate for estimates of second moment vector in adam,
867::COMM;;should be in [0, 1). Only used when solver='adam'.
868::COMM;;epsilon : float, default=1e-8
869::COMM;;Value for numerical stability in adam. Only used when solver='adam'.
870::COMM;;n_iter_no_change : int, default=10
871::COMM;;Maximum number of epochs to not meet ``tol`` improvement.
872::COMM;;Only effective when solver='sgd' or 'adam'.
873::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.20
874::COMM;;max_fun : int, default=15000
875::COMM;;Only used when solver='lbfgs'. Maximum number of loss function calls.
876::COMM;;The solver iterates until convergence (determined by 'tol'), number
877::COMM;;of iterations reaches max_iter, or this number of loss function calls.
878::COMM;;Note that number of loss function calls will be greater than or equal
879::COMM;;to the number of iterations for the `MLPClassifier`.
880::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.22
881::COMM;;Attributes
882::COMM;;----------
883::COMM;;classes_ : ndarray or list of ndarray of shape (n_classes,)
884::COMM;;Class labels for each output.
885::COMM;;loss_ : float
886::COMM;;The current loss computed with the loss function.
887::COMM;;best_loss_ : float or None
888::COMM;;The minimum loss reached by the solver throughout fitting.
889::COMM;;If `early_stopping=True`, this attribute is set to `None`. Refer to
890::COMM;;the `best_validation_score_` fitted attribute instead.
891::COMM;;loss_curve_ : list of shape (`n_iter_`,)
892::COMM;;The ith element in the list represents the loss at the ith iteration.
893::COMM;;validation_scores_ : list of shape (`n_iter_`,) or None
894::COMM;;The score at each iteration on a held-out validation set. The score
895::COMM;;reported is the accuracy score. Only available if `early_stopping=True`,
896::COMM;;otherwise the attribute is set to `None`.
897::COMM;;best_validation_score_ : float or None
898::COMM;;The best validation score (i.e. accuracy score) that triggered the
899::COMM;;early stopping. Only available if `early_stopping=True`, otherwise the
900::COMM;;attribute is set to `None`.
901::COMM;;t_ : int
902::COMM;;The number of training samples seen by the solver during fitting.
903::COMM;;coefs_ : list of shape (n_layers - 1,)
904::COMM;;The ith element in the list represents the weight matrix corresponding
905::COMM;;to layer i.
906::COMM;;intercepts_ : list of shape (n_layers - 1,)
907::COMM;;The ith element in the list represents the bias vector corresponding to
908::COMM;;layer i + 1.
909::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
910::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
911::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
912::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
913::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
914::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
915::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
916::COMM;;n_iter_ : int
917::COMM;;The number of iterations the solver has run.
918::COMM;;n_layers_ : int
919::COMM;;Number of layers.
920::COMM;;n_outputs_ : int
921::COMM;;Number of outputs.
922::COMM;;out_activation_ : str
923::COMM;;Name of the output activation function.
924::COMM;;See Also
925::COMM;;--------
926::COMM;;MLPRegressor : Multi-layer Perceptron regressor.
927::COMM;;BernoulliRBM : Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM).
928::COMM;;Notes
929::COMM;;-----
930::COMM;;MLPClassifier trains iteratively since at each time step
931::COMM;;the partial derivatives of the loss function with respect to the model
932::COMM;;parameters are computed to update the parameters.
933::COMM;;It can also have a regularization term added to the loss function
934::COMM;;that shrinks model parameters to prevent overfitting.
935::COMM;;This implementation works with data represented as dense numpy arrays or
936::COMM;;sparse scipy arrays of floating point values.

261::COMM;;h_pos = self._mean_hiddens(v_pos)
262::COMM;;v_neg = self._sample_visibles(self.h_samples_, rng)
263::COMM;;h_neg = self._mean_hiddens(v_neg)

265::COMM;;update = safe_sparse_dot(v_pos.T, h_pos, dense_output=True).T
266::COMM;;update -= np.dot(h_neg.T, v_neg)

269::COMM;;self.intercept_visible_ += lr * (

271::COMM;;)

273::COMM;;self.h_samples_ = np.floor(h_neg, h_neg)
274::COMM;;def score_samples(self, X):
290::COMM;;check_is_fitted(self)
291::COMM;;v = validate_data(self, X, accept_sparse="csr", reset=False)
292::COMM;;rng = check_random_state(self.random_state)
293::COMM;;# Randomly corrupt one feature in each sample in v.
294::COMM;;ind = (np.arange(v.shape[0]), rng.randint(0, v.shape[1], v.shape[0]))
295::COMM;;if sp.issparse(v):
296::COMM;;data = -2 * v[ind] + 1
297::COMM;;if isinstance(data, np.matrix): # v is a sparse matrix
298::COMM;;v_ = v + sp.csr_matrix((data.A.ravel(), ind), shape=v.shape)
299::COMM;;else: # v is a sparse array
300::COMM;;v_ = v + sp.csr_array((data.ravel(), ind), shape=v.shape)
301::COMM;;else:
302::COMM;;v_ = v.copy()
303::COMM;;v_[ind] = 1 - v_[ind]
304::COMM;;fe = self._free_energy(v)
305::COMM;;fe_ = self._free_energy(v_)
306::COMM;;# log(expit(x)) = log(1 / (1 + exp(-x)) = -np.logaddexp(0, -x)
307::COMM;;return -v.shape[1] * np.logaddexp(0, -(fe_ - fe))

155::COMM;;class AdamOptimizer(BaseOptimizer):
189::COMM;;def __init__(
190::COMM;;self, params, learning_rate_init=0.001, beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8
191::COMM;;):
192::COMM;;super().__init__(learning_rate_init)
193::COMM;;self.beta_1 = beta_1
194::COMM;;self.beta_2 = beta_2
195::COMM;;self.epsilon = epsilon
196::COMM;;self.t = 0
197::COMM;;self.ms = [np.zeros_like(param) for param in params]
198::COMM;;self.vs = [np.zeros_like(param) for param in params]
199::COMM;;def _get_updates(self, grads):
211::COMM;;self.t += 1
212::COMM;;self.ms = [
213::COMM;;self.beta_1 * m + (1 - self.beta_1) * grad
214::COMM;;for m, grad in zip(self.ms, grads)
215::COMM;;]
216::COMM;;self.vs = [
217::COMM;;self.beta_2 * v + (1 - self.beta_2) * (grad**2)
218::COMM;;for v, grad in zip(self.vs, grads)
219::COMM;;]
220::COMM;;self.learning_rate = (
221::COMM;;self.learning_rate_init
222::COMM;;* np.sqrt(1 - self.beta_2**self.t)

235::COMM;;def _validate_steps(self):
236::COMM;;if not self.steps:
237::COMM;;raise ValueError("The pipeline is empty. Please add steps.")
238::COMM;;names, estimators = zip(*self.steps)
239::COMM;;# validate names

242::COMM;;transformers = estimators[:-1]
243::COMM;;estimator = estimators[-1]
244::COMM;;for t in transformers:

246::COMM;;continue

248::COMM;;t, "transform"

256::COMM;;# We allow last estimator to be None as an identity transformation
257::COMM;;if (
258::COMM;;estimator is not None

260::COMM;;and not hasattr(estimator, "fit")
261::COMM;;):

267::COMM;;def _iter(self, with_final=True, filter_passthrough=True):
273::COMM;;stop = len(self.steps)
274::COMM;;if not with_final:
275::COMM;;stop -= 1

277::COMM;;if not filter_passthrough:

280::COMM;;yield idx, name, trans

1::COMO;;# Authors: The scikit-learn developers
2::COMO;;# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
75::COMM;;The detection is based on its computed variance and on the theoretical
76::COMM;;error bounds of the '2 pass algorithm' for variance computation.
77::COMM;;See "Algorithms for computing the sample variance: analysis and
78::COMM;;recommendations", by Chan, Golub, and LeVeque.
80::COMO;;# In scikit-learn, variance is always computed using float64 accumulators.
88::COMM;;The goal is to avoid division by very small or zero values.
89::COMM;;Near constant features are detected automatically by identifying
90::COMM;;scales close to machine precision unless they are precomputed by
91::COMM;;the caller and passed with the `constant_mask` kwarg.
92::COMM;;Typically for standard scaling, the scales are the standard
93::COMM;;deviation while near constant features are better detected on the
94::COMM;;computed variances which are closer to machine precision by
95::COMM;;construction.
97::COMO;;# if we are fitting on 1D arrays, scale might be a scalar
102::COMO;;# scale is an array
106::COMO;;# Detect near constant values to avoid dividing by a very small
107::COMO;;# value that could lead to surprising results and numerical
108::COMO;;# stability issues.
111::COMO;;# New array to avoid side-effects
127::COMM;;Center to the mean and component wise scale to unit variance.
128::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_scaler>`.
129::COMM;;Parameters
130::COMM;;----------
131::COMM;;X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
132::COMM;;The data to center and scale.
133::COMM;;axis : {0, 1}, default=0
134::COMM;;Axis used to compute the means and standard deviations along. If 0,
135::COMM;;independently standardize each feature, otherwise (if 1) standardize
136::COMM;;each sample.
137::COMM;;with_mean : bool, default=True
138::COMM;;If True, center the data before scaling.
139::COMM;;with_std : bool, default=True
140::COMM;;If True, scale the data to unit variance (or equivalently,
141::COMM;;unit standard deviation).
142::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
143::COMM;;If False, try to avoid a copy and scale in place.
144::COMM;;This is not guaranteed to always work in place; e.g. if the data is
145::COMM;;a numpy array with an int dtype, a copy will be returned even with
146::COMM;;copy=False.
147::COMM;;Returns
148::COMM;;-------
149::COMM;;X_tr : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
150::COMM;;The transformed data.
151::COMM;;See Also
152::COMM;;--------
153::COMM;;StandardScaler : Performs scaling to unit variance using the Transformer
154::COMM;;API (e.g. as part of a preprocessing
155::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`).
156::COMM;;Notes
157::COMM;;-----
158::COMM;;This implementation will refuse to center scipy.sparse matrices
159::COMM;;since it would make them non-sparse and would potentially crash the
160::COMM;;program with memory exhaustion problems.
161::COMM;;Instead the caller is expected to either set explicitly
162::COMM;;`with_mean=False` (in that case, only variance scaling will be
163::COMM;;performed on the features of the CSC matrix) or to call `X.toarray()`
164::COMM;;if he/she expects the materialized dense array to fit in memory.
165::COMM;;To avoid memory copy the caller should pass a CSC matrix.
166::COMM;;NaNs are treated as missing values: disregarded to compute the statistics,
167::COMM;;and maintained during the data transformation.
168::COMM;;We use a biased estimator for the standard deviation, equivalent to
169::COMM;;`numpy.std(x, ddof=0)`. Note that the choice of `ddof` is unlikely to
170::COMM;;affect model performance.
171::COMM;;For a comparison of the different scalers, transformers, and normalizers,
172::COMM;;see: :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_preprocessing_plot_all_scaling.py`.
173::COMM;;.. warning:: Risk of data leak
174::COMM;;Do not use :func:`~sklearn.preprocessing.scale` unless you know
175::COMM;;what you are doing. A common mistake is to apply it to the entire data
176::COMM;;*before* splitting into training and test sets. This will bias the
177::COMM;;model evaluation because information would have leaked from the test
178::COMM;;set to the training set.
179::COMM;;In general, we recommend using
180::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler` within a
181::COMM;;:ref:`Pipeline <pipeline>` in order to prevent most risks of data
182::COMM;;leaking: `pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())`.
183::COMM;;Examples
184::COMM;;--------
185::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import scale
186::COMM;;>>> X = [[-2, 1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
187::COMM;;>>> scale(X, axis=0) # scaling each column independently
188::COMM;;array([[-1., 1., 1.],
189::COMM;;[ 1., -1., -1.]])
190::COMM;;>>> scale(X, axis=1) # scaling each row independently
191::COMM;;array([[-1.37, 0.39, 0.98],
192::COMM;;[-1.22, 0. , 1.22]])
224::COMO;;# Xr is a view on the original array that enables easy use of
225::COMO;;# broadcasting on the axis in which we are interested in
230::COMO;;# Verify that mean_1 is 'close to zero'. If X contains very
231::COMO;;# large values, mean_1 can also be very large, due to a lack of
232::COMO;;# precision of mean_. In this case, a pre-scaling of the
233::COMO;;# concerned feature is efficient, for instance by its mean or
234::COMO;;# maximum.
249::COMO;;# If mean_2 is not 'close to zero', it comes from the fact that
250::COMO;;# scale_ is very small so that mean_2 = mean_1/scale_ > 0, even
251::COMO;;# if mean_1 was close to zero. The problem is thus essentially
252::COMO;;# due to the lack of precision of mean_. A solution is then to
253::COMO;;# subtract the mean again:
266::COMM;;This estimator scales and translates each feature individually such
267::COMM;;that it is in the given range on the training set, e.g. between
268::COMM;;zero and one.
269::COMM;;The transformation is given by::
270::COMM;;X_std = (X - X.min(axis=0)) / (X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0))
271::COMM;;X_scaled = X_std * (max - min) + min
272::COMM;;where min, max = feature_range.
273::COMM;;This transformation is often used as an alternative to zero mean,
274::COMM;;unit variance scaling.
275::COMM;;`MinMaxScaler` doesn't reduce the effect of outliers, but it linearly
276::COMM;;scales them down into a fixed range, where the largest occurring data point
277::COMM;;corresponds to the maximum value and the smallest one corresponds to the
278::COMM;;minimum value. For an example visualization, refer to :ref:`Compare
279::COMM;;MinMaxScaler with other scalers <plot_all_scaling_minmax_scaler_section>`.
280::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_scaler>`.
281::COMM;;Parameters
282::COMM;;----------
283::COMM;;feature_range : tuple (min, max), default=(0, 1)
284::COMM;;Desired range of transformed data.
285::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
286::COMM;;Set to False to perform inplace row normalization and avoid a
287::COMM;;copy (if the input is already a numpy array).
288::COMM;;clip : bool, default=False
289::COMM;;Set to True to clip transformed values of held-out data to
290::COMM;;provided `feature_range`.
291::COMM;;Since this parameter will clip values, `inverse_transform` may not
292::COMM;;be able to restore the original data.
293::COMM;;.. note::
294::COMM;;Setting `clip=True` does not prevent feature drift (a distribution
295::COMM;;shift between training and test data). The transformed values are clipped
296::COMM;;to the `feature_range`, which helps avoid unintended behavior in models
297::COMM;;sensitive to out-of-range inputs (e.g. linear models). Use with care,
298::COMM;;as clipping can distort the distribution of test data.
299::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
300::COMM;;Attributes
301::COMM;;----------

303::COMM;;Per feature adjustment for minimum. Equivalent to
304::COMM;;``min - X.min(axis=0) * self.scale_``
305::COMM;;scale_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
306::COMM;;Per feature relative scaling of the data. Equivalent to
307::COMM;;``(max - min) / (X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0))``
308::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17

320::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17

465::COMM;;Transformed data.
493::COMM;;Parameters

496::COMM;;Input data that will be transformed. It cannot be sparse.
497::COMM;;Returns
498::COMM;;-------
499::COMM;;X_original : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
500::COMM;;Transformed data.
528::COMM;;This estimator scales and translates each feature individually such
529::COMM;;that it is in the given range on the training set, i.e. between
530::COMM;;zero and one.
531::COMM;;The transformation is given by (when ``axis=0``)::
532::COMM;;X_std = (X - X.min(axis=0)) / (X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0))
533::COMM;;X_scaled = X_std * (max - min) + min
534::COMM;;where min, max = feature_range.
535::COMM;;The transformation is calculated as (when ``axis=0``)::
536::COMM;;X_scaled = scale * X + min - X.min(axis=0) * scale
537::COMM;;where scale = (max - min) / (X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0))
538::COMM;;This transformation is often used as an alternative to zero mean,
539::COMM;;unit variance scaling.
540::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_scaler>`.
541::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
542::COMM;;*minmax_scale* function interface
543::COMM;;to :class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler`.
544::COMM;;Parameters
545::COMM;;----------
546::COMM;;X : array-like of shape (n_samples, n_features)
547::COMM;;The data.
548::COMM;;feature_range : tuple (min, max), default=(0, 1)
549::COMM;;Desired range of transformed data.
550::COMM;;axis : {0, 1}, default=0
551::COMM;;Axis used to scale along. If 0, independently scale each feature,
552::COMM;;otherwise (if 1) scale each sample.
553::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
554::COMM;;If False, try to avoid a copy and scale in place.
555::COMM;;This is not guaranteed to always work in place; e.g. if the data is
556::COMM;;a numpy array with an int dtype, a copy will be returned even with
557::COMM;;copy=False.
558::COMM;;Returns
559::COMM;;-------
560::COMM;;X_tr : ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
561::COMM;;The transformed data.
562::COMM;;.. warning:: Risk of data leak
563::COMM;;Do not use :func:`~sklearn.preprocessing.minmax_scale` unless you know
564::COMM;;what you are doing. A common mistake is to apply it to the entire data
565::COMM;;*before* splitting into training and test sets. This will bias the
566::COMM;;model evaluation because information would have leaked from the test
567::COMM;;set to the training set.
568::COMM;;In general, we recommend using
569::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.preprocessing.MinMaxScaler` within a
570::COMM;;:ref:`Pipeline <pipeline>` in order to prevent most risks of data
571::COMM;;leaking: `pipe = make_pipeline(MinMaxScaler(), LogisticRegression())`.
572::COMM;;See Also
573::COMM;;--------
574::COMM;;MinMaxScaler : Performs scaling to a given range using the Transformer
575::COMM;;API (e.g. as part of a preprocessing
576::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline`).
577::COMM;;Notes
578::COMM;;-----
579::COMM;;For a comparison of the different scalers, transformers, and normalizers,
580::COMM;;see: :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_preprocessing_plot_all_scaling.py`.
581::COMM;;Examples
582::COMM;;--------
583::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import minmax_scale
584::COMM;;>>> X = [[-2, 1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
585::COMM;;>>> minmax_scale(X, axis=0) # scale each column independently
586::COMM;;array([[0., 1., 1.],
587::COMM;;[1., 0., 0.]])
588::COMM;;>>> minmax_scale(X, axis=1) # scale each row independently
589::COMM;;array([[0. , 0.75, 1. ],
590::COMM;;[0. , 0.5 , 1. ]])
592::COMO;;# Unlike the scaler object, this function allows 1d input.
593::COMO;;# If copy is required, it will be done inside the scaler object.
614::COMM;;The standard score of a sample `x` is calculated as:
615::COMM;;.. code-block:: text
616::COMM;;z = (x - u) / s
617::COMM;;where `u` is the mean of the training samples or zero if `with_mean=False`,
618::COMM;;and `s` is the standard deviation of the training samples or one if
619::COMM;;`with_std=False`.
620::COMM;;Centering and scaling happen independently on each feature by computing
621::COMM;;the relevant statistics on the samples in the training set. Mean and
622::COMM;;standard deviation are then stored to be used on later data using
623::COMM;;:meth:`transform`.
624::COMM;;Standardization of a dataset is a common requirement for many
625::COMM;;machine learning estimators: they might behave badly if the
626::COMM;;individual features do not more or less look like standard normally
627::COMM;;distributed data (e.g. Gaussian with 0 mean and unit variance).
628::COMM;;For instance many elements used in the objective function of
629::COMM;;a learning algorithm (such as the RBF kernel of Support Vector
630::COMM;;Machines or the L1 and L2 regularizers of linear models) assume that
631::COMM;;all features are centered around 0 and have variance in the same
632::COMM;;order. If a feature has a variance that is orders of magnitude larger
633::COMM;;than others, it might dominate the objective function and make the
634::COMM;;estimator unable to learn from other features correctly as expected.
635::COMM;;`StandardScaler` is sensitive to outliers, and the features may scale
636::COMM;;differently from each other in the presence of outliers. For an example
637::COMM;;visualization, refer to :ref:`Compare StandardScaler with other scalers
638::COMM;;<plot_all_scaling_standard_scaler_section>`.
639::COMM;;This scaler can also be applied to sparse CSR or CSC matrices by passing
640::COMM;;`with_mean=False` to avoid breaking the sparsity structure of the data.
641::COMM;;Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <preprocessing_scaler>`.
642::COMM;;Parameters
643::COMM;;----------
644::COMM;;copy : bool, default=True
645::COMM;;If False, try to avoid a copy and do inplace scaling instead.
646::COMM;;This is not guaranteed to always work inplace; e.g. if the data is
647::COMM;;not a NumPy array or scipy.sparse CSR matrix, a copy may still be
648::COMM;;returned.
649::COMM;;with_mean : bool, default=True
650::COMM;;If True, center the data before scaling.
651::COMM;;This does not work (and will raise an exception) when attempted on
652::COMM;;sparse matrices, because centering them entails building a dense
653::COMM;;matrix which in common use cases is likely to be too large to fit in
654::COMM;;memory.
655::COMM;;with_std : bool, default=True
656::COMM;;If True, scale the data to unit variance (or equivalently,
657::COMM;;unit standard deviation).
658::COMM;;Attributes
659::COMM;;----------
660::COMM;;scale_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or None
661::COMM;;Per feature relative scaling of the data to achieve zero mean and unit
662::COMM;;variance. Generally this is calculated using `np.sqrt(var_)`. If a
663::COMM;;variance is zero, we can't achieve unit variance, and the data is left
664::COMM;;as-is, giving a scaling factor of 1. `scale_` is equal to `None`
665::COMM;;when `with_std=False`.
666::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.17
667::COMM;;*scale_*
668::COMM;;mean_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or None
669::COMM;;The mean value for each feature in the training set.
670::COMM;;Equal to ``None`` when ``with_mean=False`` and ``with_std=False``.
671::COMM;;var_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) or None
672::COMM;;The variance for each feature in the training set. Used to compute
673::COMM;;`scale_`. Equal to ``None`` when ``with_mean=False`` and
674::COMM;;``with_std=False``.
675::COMM;;n_features_in_ : int
676::COMM;;Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
677::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 0.24
678::COMM;;feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
679::COMM;;Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
680::COMM;;has feature names that are all strings.
681::COMM;;.. versionadded:: 1.0
682::COMM;;n_samples_seen_ : int or ndarray of shape (n_features,)
683::COMM;;The number of samples processed by the estimator for each feature.
684::COMM;;If there are no missing samples, the ``n_samples_seen`` will be an
685::COMM;;integer, otherwise it will be an array of dtype int. If
686::COMM;;`sample_weights` are used it will be a float (if no missing data)
687::COMM;;or an array of dtype float that sums the weights seen so far.
688::COMM;;Will be reset on new calls to fit, but increments across
689::COMM;;``partial_fit`` calls.
690::COMM;;See Also
691::COMM;;--------
692::COMM;;scale : Equivalent function without the estimator API.
693::COMM;;:class:`~sklearn.decomposition.PCA` : Further removes the linear
694::COMM;;correlation across features with 'whiten=True'.
695::COMM;;Notes
696::COMM;;-----
697::COMM;;NaNs are treated as missing values: disregarded in fit, and maintained in
698::COMM;;transform.
699::COMM;;We use a biased estimator for the standard deviation, equivalent to
700::COMM;;`numpy.std(x, ddof=0)`. Note that the choice of `ddof` is unlikely to
701::COMM;;affect model performance.
702::COMM;;Examples
703::COMM;;--------
704::COMM;;>>> from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
705::COMM;;>>> data = [[0, 0], [0, 0], [1, 1], [1, 1]]
706::COMM;;>>> scaler = StandardScaler()
707::COMM;;>>> print(scaler.fit(data))
708::COMM;;StandardScaler()
709::COMM;;>>> print(scaler.mean_)
710::COMM;;[0.5 0.5]
711::COMM;;>>> print(scaler.transform(data))
712::COMM;;[[-1. -1.]
713::COMM;;[-1. -1.]
714::COMM;;[ 1. 1.]
715::COMM;;[ 1. 1.]]
716::COMM;;>>> print(scaler.transform([[2, 2]]))
717::COMM;;[[3. 3.]]

978::COMM;;This estimator scales and translates each feature individually such
979::COMM;;that the maximal absolute value of each feature in the
980::COMM;;training set will be 1.0. It does not shift/center the data, and
981::COMM;;thus does not destroy any sparsity.

983::COMM;;`MaxAbsScaler` doesn't reduce the effect of outliers; it only linearly

988::COMM;;----------

990::COMM;;Set to False to perform inplace scaling and avoid a copy (if the input
991::COMM;;is already a numpy array).
992::COMM;;clip : bool, default=False
993::COMM;;Set to True to clip transformed values of held-out data to [-1, 1].
994::COMM;;Since this parameter will clip values, `inverse_transform` may not
995::COMM;;be able to restore the original data.
996::COMM;;.. note::
997::COMM;;Setting `clip=True` does not prevent feature drift (a distribution
998::COMM;;shift between training and test data). The transformed values are clipped
999::COMM;;to the [-1, 1] range, which helps avoid unintended behavior in models
1000::COMM;;sensitive to out-of-range inputs (e.g. linear models). Use with care,
1001::COMM;;as clipping can distort the distribution of test data.
